title: AEVAL: From Anecdotal to Deterministic Testing for Agentic Skill Workflows
summary:
Modern agentic systems increasingly rely on skills: installable packages of natural language and code that teach an LLM agent to perform a domain task. As skill repositories grow, developers need automated quality signals on every change, yet evaluation today is largely anecdotal: a developer asks an agent to "try the skill," watches a demo, and forms a subjective impression. This yields neither reproducibility across runs nor comparability across versions, and scales poorly to marketplaces where one regression can silently break dozens of downstream workflows.
  We present AEVAL (Agentic Evaluation), a CI-integrated framework that replaces this practice with a deterministic, reproducible test pipeline for agentic skills. Every skill change triggers a test event: the skill runs against a developer-declared evaluation contract (eval.config) inside an automated executor, emitting a structured, evidence-grounded quality signal that downstream CI can route on.
  A key ingredient is a structural separation between executor and grader, preventing a subtle but pervasive failure mode: an agent that silently self-corrects during execution and then grades its own patched outputs as passing.
  Our contributions are: (i) a deterministic, change-triggered evaluation protocol with per-skill contracts and per-run artifact schemas; (ii) a formalization of self-correction bias as a distinct failure mode of naive agentic evaluators; (iii) an executor/grader separation with a first-attempt grading rule and explicit self-correction tracking; and (iv) a tiered, grounded-evidence fix-suggestion scheme (LV1 causal, LV2 quality) posted as inline merge-request comments. Validated on real skills in a production agentic stack across multiple agent SDKs, AEVAL converts spurious 100% pass rates into reproducible first-attempt fail signals with an auditable record of every executor fix.

AI.tldr: AEVAL is a CI-integrated evaluation framework for agentic skills that replaces subjective manual testing with deterministic, reproducible test pipelines. It introduces executor/grader separation to prevent self-correction bias and generates structured quality signals with tiered fix suggestions.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of agentic skills (installable NL+code packages for LLM agents) is anecdotal and subjective — developers manually watch demos and form impressions. This lacks reproducibility, cross-version comparability, and scales poorly to marketplaces where silent regressions can break downstream workflows.
AI.method: AEVAL provides a deterministic, change-triggered evaluation protocol: (1) per-skill evaluation contracts (eval.config) declared by developers; (2) automated executor running skills against these contracts; (3) structural separation between executor and grader with a first-attempt grading rule to prevent self-correction bias; (4) explicit self-correction tracking; and (5) a tiered fix-suggestion scheme (LV1 causal, LV2 quality) posted as inline merge-request comments.
AI.result: Validated on real skills in a production agentic stack across multiple agent SDKs, AEVAL converted previously spurious 100% pass rates into reproducible first-attempt fail signals with auditable records of every executor fix.
AI.conclusion: AEVAL demonstrates that agentic skill evaluation can be formalized into a deterministic CI pipeline. The executor/grader separation is critical for removing self-correction bias, and the framework enables scalable quality assurance for growing skill repositories and marketplaces.

title: AoA: Theorem Proving Agent over Abstract Syntax Tree of Redesigned Language
summary: Interactive theorem proving (ITP) underpins program verification and formalized mathematics, but its manual effort limits scalability. LLM-based proof agents promise to ease this effort, but their heavy token consumption and API cost remain a major obstacle. We trace this cost to a shared root: current agents operate on serialized concrete syntax, emitting proofs as source text and recovering proof states through separate, line-number-based queries, so every edit shifts later lines and forces repeated relocation of errors and states. This same dependence on concrete syntax also blocks adoption of Minilang, a recent proof language that reaches SOTA on LLM-based proving but is too new for LLMs' training corpora. We address both problems by lifting the agent off source text and onto the abstract syntax tree (AST): the model supplies proofs as JSON representations of Minilang's AST -- native to tool-calling LLMs -- and drives the prover through a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into one proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal's state, readable directly off the tree. We realize this design in \emph{Agent over AST} (AoA). Against Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl common success sets, AoA cuts API cost by 2.3--4.7x (normalized input-cache accounting), uses 2.9--6.9x fewer tokens and 3.9--8.9x fewer tool calls, and finishes 1.4--2.0x faster -- while also solving far more problems on the harder verification benchmark.

AI.tldr: AoA replaces serialized concrete syntax in LLM-based proof agents with JSON-encoded abstract syntax trees (Minilang AST), using a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into one proof tree, achieving 2.3–4.7× API cost reduction, 2.9–6.9× fewer tokens, and 3.9–8.9× fewer tool calls while solving more problems on harder benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based interactive theorem proving agents suffer from heavy token consumption and API costs due to operating on serialized concrete syntax: every edit shifts later lines, forcing repeated error/state relocation via line-number queries. Additionally, concrete syntax dependence blocks adoption of Minilang (SOTA for LLM proving), which lacks training corpus coverage. A representation that eliminates line-number fragility and decouples from concrete syntax is needed.
AI.method: AoA lifts the proof agent from source text to the abstract syntax tree. The LLM outputs proofs as JSON representations of Minilang's AST (natively compatible with tool-calling LLMs). A tree-edit model fuses proof operations and their associated subgoal states into a single proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal state directly readable from the tree — eliminating separate state queries and line-number-based relocation.
AI.result: Evaluated against Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl common success sets: AoA cuts API cost by 2.3–4.7× (normalized for input-cache accounting), uses 2.9–6.9× fewer tokens and 3.9–8.9× fewer tool calls, finishes 1.4–2.0× faster, and solves significantly more problems on the harder verification benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Operating at the AST level rather than on concrete syntax fundamentally reduces token overhead and tool-call frequency in LLM-based ITP agents while enabling use of modern proof languages like Minilang. The tree-edit model provides a more efficient and scalable paradigm for automated theorem proving.

title: Fantastic Adaptive Taxonomies and How to Use Them
summary: An agent system's execution traces record how it fails, and procedures that improve such a system without changing model weights (trajectory selection, prompt and workflow optimization, runtime monitoring) read these traces for feedback. Yet raw traces are a poor medium for accumulating that feedback: long, instance-specific, and lacking a stable vocabulary for recurring failures. We argue that an agent system should instead maintain an explicit representation of how it fails, induced from its own behavior and reusable wherever failure feedback is needed. AdaMAST builds this representation by converting a target system's traces into a compact, evidence-grounded failure taxonomy: named failure codes organized along three fixed axes (system-level, role-specific, and domain-specific), with every name, definition, and evidence pattern induced from the traces; no code is hand-authored, no trace human-annotated. The taxonomy is not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a shared feedback interface, improving agents in three ways. In agent-system search, taxonomy-coded diagnoses of failed candidates outperform free-form reflection on all five benchmarks we test. At runtime, taxonomy feedback raises SWE-agent's resolution on SWE-bench Verified Mini from 60% with free-text reflection to 70%, and improves Claude Code from 64.0% to 70.7% as a runtime skill. In trajectory selection, AdaMAST-Judge, a verifier built on the induced codes, improves best-of-5 accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by 8-15 points over Pass@1. The vocabulary itself is compact (an order-of-magnitude compression that preserves trace distinctions), human-faithful (matching expert failure annotations more closely than a hand-crafted reference vocabulary), and adaptive (taxonomies induced for different domains share few codes). Adaptive failure taxonomies close the loop between the traces agents produce and the procedures that improve them.

AI.tldr: AdaMAST induces a compact, evidence-grounded failure taxonomy from agent traces without human annotation, and uses it as a shared feedback interface to improve agent systems across three tasks: agent-system search, runtime monitoring, and trajectory selection, achieving significant gains (e.g., SWE-bench Verified Mini from 60%→70%, Claude Code from 64.0%→70.7%).
AI.motivation: Raw agent execution traces are poor for accumulating feedback: they are long, instance-specific, and lack a stable vocabulary for recurring failures. Existing improvement procedures (trajectory selection, prompt optimization, runtime monitoring) need better feedback representations. The authors argue for an explicit, induced failure representation that closes the loop between traces and system improvement.
AI.method: AdaMAST converts a target agent system's execution traces into a failure taxonomy with three fixed axes (system-level, role-specific, domain-specific). Every failure code's name, definition, and evidence pattern is induced automatically from traces — no hand-authoring or human annotation. This taxonomy then serves as a shared feedback interface for three downstream tasks: (1) agent-system search using taxonomy-coded diagnoses, (2) runtime feedback provided as a skill during execution, and (3) AdaMAST-Judge, a verifier for trajectory selection built on the induced codes.
AI.result: Taxonomy-coded diagnoses outperform free-form reflection on all five agent-system search benchmarks. Runtime taxonomy feedback raises SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified Mini from 60% to 70% and Claude Code from 64.0% to 70.7%. AdaMAST-Judge improves best-of-5 accuracy on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by 8–15 points over Pass@1. The taxonomy is compact (order-of-magnitude compression), human-faithful (matches expert annotations better than hand-crafted taxonomies), and adaptive (different domains yield largely disjoint code sets).
AI.conclusion: Adaptive failure taxonomies effectively close the feedback loop between agent traces and system-improvement procedures. By inducing a structured, reusable failure vocabulary from raw traces, AdaMAST enables consistent and transferable feedback that improves agent performance across search, runtime, and selection tasks without any model weight changes.

title: When to Use Which? Benchmarking Optimisers for Configurable Systems under Varying Budgets
summary:
Software configuration tuning is crucial for optimising system performance, and various optimisers have emerged over the last decade. Yet, the time required during the tuning process may vary across systems. In some systems (e.g., PostgreSQL), it may take a few minutes to measure a configuration, whereas in some others (e.g., MariaDB), it can take several hours. Moreover, even within the same system, users may have varying budgets and preferred settings. This naturally raises a question -- Given a budget level, which optimiser is the best choice for SE practitioners? This matters because optimisers usually have their own ``comfort zone'' and may perform very differently under distinct budgets.
  In this paper, we aim to answer this question. We systematically evaluate eight well-established optimisers across 22 configurable systems under varying budget levels. We find that, unsurprisingly, model-based optimisers (e.g., SMAC) are well-suited under tight budgets, and model-free optimisers (e.g., GAs) become superior with more generous budgets. However, interestingly, there is one optimiser, FLASH, that performs consistently well on most systems regardless of budgets. We lastly investigate the reasons behind this phenomenon and find that many systems possess good local optima (with large basins of attraction), allowing greedy optimisers (e.g., FLASH) to achieve strong performance.
  Source code, data, and supplementary materials of this work are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Config-W2W-98B2.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates eight configuration optimisers across 22 systems under varying time budgets, revealing that model-based optimisers excel under tight budgets, model-free ones under generous budgets, but FLASH consistently performs well regardless of budget due to many systems having good local optima with large basins of attraction.
AI.motivation: Configuration tuning times vary drastically across systems (minutes to hours), and even within the same system, practitioners have different budgets. There is no clear guidance on which optimiser to choose given a specific budget level, as optimisers have distinct "comfort zones" where they perform well.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate eight well-established optimisers (including model-based like SMAC and model-free like GAs) across 22 configurable software systems under varying budget levels, then analyse the performance patterns and investigate underlying reasons for FLASH's consistent superiority.
AI.result: Model-based optimisers (e.g., SMAC) dominate under tight budgets; model-free optimisers (e.g., Genetic Algorithms) become superior with generous budgets. FLASH uniquely performs consistently well across nearly all systems regardless of budget. The investigation attributes this to many systems having good local optima with large basins of attraction, which greedy strategies like FLASH exploit effectively.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners should choose optimisers based on their available budget: model-based for tight budgets, model-free for generous budgets. FLASH offers a robust default choice that works well across varied budget conditions, and its success highlights the prevalence of exploitable local optima structures in configurable software systems.

title: Algorithmic Accuracy as a Motivational Driver in Robot-Mediated Learning: A Comparative Study of Cross-Correlation and CNN-Based Sound Detection in an Interactive Quiz Game
summary: In competitive learning activities, inaccurate robot decisions may reduce students' perceptions of fairness and competence, ultimately affecting their motivation. This paper investigates whether the accuracy of sound detection algorithms influences student motivation during a robot-mediated quiz game. A Pepper humanoid robot hosted an interactive buzzer-based quiz in which two sound detection approaches, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a Cross-Correlation algorithm, were evaluated using a controlled between-subjects experiment involving 40 university students. Participants were equally assigned to a CNN group (n = 20) and a Cross-Correlation group (n = 20). Both groups completed the same quiz under identical conditions, differing only in the sound detection algorithm used for first-responder identification. Student motivation was assessed using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), while algorithm performance was evaluated through real-time detection accuracy. The results indicate that the Cross-Correlation approach achieved more reliable sound detection under classroom conditions and produced significantly higher scores across all IMI subscales, demonstrating greater student interest, perceived competence, effort, perceived choice, and lower perceived pressure (after reverse coding). These findings provide empirical support for the proposed Algorithmic Precision-Motivation Relationship (APMR) model, demonstrating that algorithmic accuracy is not merely an engineering performance metric but an important factor influencing learner motivation in robot-assisted educational environments.

AI.tldr: A Pepper robot hosted a quiz game comparing CNN vs. Cross-Correlation sound detection. Cross-Correlation was more accurate and yielded significantly higher intrinsic motivation scores across all IMI subscales, supporting the proposed Algorithmic Precision-Motivation Relationship (APMR) model.
AI.motivation: Inaccurate robot decisions during competitive learning can undermine students' perceptions of fairness and competence, harming motivation. The study seeks to empirically test whether the accuracy of sound detection algorithms in a robot-mediated quiz game directly influences student motivation.
AI.method: A controlled between-subjects experiment with 40 university students, equally split into CNN (n=20) and Cross-Correlation (n=20) groups. A Pepper robot hosted a buzzer-based quiz; the only difference was the sound detection algorithm used for first-responder identification. Motivation was measured via the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), and algorithm performance was assessed through real-time detection accuracy.
AI.result: The Cross-Correlation algorithm achieved more reliable sound detection in classroom conditions and produced significantly higher scores across all IMI subscales (interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, effort/importance, perceived choice, and lower pressure/tension after reverse coding).
AI.conclusion: The findings empirically validate the Algorithmic Precision-Motivation Relationship (APMR) model, showing that algorithmic accuracy is not merely an engineering metric but a critical factor shaping learner motivation in robot-assisted educational environments.

title: A Quantum-Classical Hybrid Framework for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting Complexity-Fidelity Trade-offs and Limitations
summary: This paper presents a unified quantum-classical hybrid framework for multi-horizon time-series forecasting, introducing two model variants Quantum Reservoir Forecaster (QRC-F) and Variational Quantum Forecaster (VQF-F). The proposed framework investigates the complexity-fidelity trade-off of quantum forecasting under near-term NISQ hardware constraints. Continuous time-series signals are transformed into binary representations through uniform quantization and encoded into quantum states using angle encoding with parameterized RY rotation gates. Cross-channel entanglement layers capture dependencies among multiple variables. QRC-F utilizes a fixed random unitary quantum reservoir for stable, gradient-free temporal feature extraction, whereas VQF-F employs a trainable variational quantum circuit optimized through the parameter-shift rule to learn temporal and inter-variable patterns from Pauli expectation values. Both models replace computationally expensive quadratic self-attention with efficient linear transformations, reducing parameter complexity. A shared MIMO-based multi-horizon prediction head simultaneously generates forecasts across multiple horizons, avoiding error accumulation in recursive forecasting. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets, including ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, electricity, and exchange-rate, demonstrate that VQF-F achieves superior training stability and parameter efficiency, while QRC-F provides enhanced robustness and circuit fidelity under quantum noise. The results establish a practical quantum-native forecasting framework with strong potential for deployment on near-term NISQ devices.

AI.tldr: A unified quantum-classical hybrid framework for multi-horizon time-series forecasting is proposed, with two variants: QRC-F (fixed quantum reservoir) and VQF-F (trainable variational circuit). Both replace quadratic self-attention with linear transformations and use a shared MIMO prediction head, demonstrating strong trade-offs between stability, robustness, and parameter efficiency on benchmark datasets under NISQ constraints.
AI.motivation: Near-term NISQ devices face severe hardware limitations (limited qubit counts, noise, short coherence times), making it infeasible to run large-scale, fully trainable quantum models. The authors seek to explore the complexity-fidelity trade-off in quantum time-series forecasting, aiming to design a practical framework that balances predictive performance with deployability on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.
AI.method: The framework first transforms continuous time-series into binary representations via uniform quantization, then encodes them into quantum states using angle encoding with parameterized RY rotation gates. Cross-channel entanglement layers capture inter-variable dependencies. QRC-F uses a fixed random unitary quantum reservoir for gradient-free temporal feature extraction, while VQF-F uses a trainable variational quantum circuit optimized via the parameter-shift rule, learning from Pauli expectation values. Both replace quadratic self-attention with efficient linear transformations, and a shared MIMO prediction head generates multi-horizon forecasts simultaneously to avoid recursive error accumulation.
AI.result: Experiments on ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Weather, electricity, and exchange-rate datasets show that VQF-F achieves superior training stability and parameter efficiency, while QRC-F provides enhanced robustness and circuit fidelity under quantum noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework establishes a practical quantum-native approach to multi-horizon time-series forecasting with strong potential for near-term NISQ deployment, effectively trading off complexity and fidelity while maintaining competitive performance.

title: Boundary-Seeking GAN-Augmented TabTransformer for Adversarially Robust Intrusion Detection
comment: Preprint. Submitted to Kuwait Journal of Science
summary: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) often suffer from class imbalance and vulnerability to adversarial attacks, leading to degraded detection performance and reduced robustness. This study proposes a TabTransformer framework augmented by the Boundary-Seeking Generative Adversarial Network (BGAN) for flow-based intrusion detection using the CICIDS2017 dataset. BGAN serves a dual purpose by generating synthetic minority-class samples to mitigate data imbalance and producing adversarial samples to evaluate model robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that BGAN augmentation improves TabTransformer's Macro-F1 score from 82.96% to 86.50%, with the largest class-wise improvement observed for Web_Attack (F1 score: 0.29 to 0.61). Robustness evaluation shows that all non-augmented models experienced a 100% Performance Drop Rate (PDR) under adversarial testing, whereas all BGAN-augmented models achieved negative PDR values, indicating improved resilience. Furthermore, the augmented TabTransformer maintained stable and low False Triggered Rate (FTR) values (1.51%-2.92%) across all noise levels, compared with the BGAN-augmented Decision Tree, which reached 49.09% under benign perturbations. These findings demonstrate that BGAN consistently enhances both class balance and adversarial robustness, while the proposed BGAN-TabTransformer framework provides an effective and adaptive intrusion detection solution for adversarial network environments.

AI.tldr: A TabTransformer augmented with Boundary-Seeking GAN (BGAN) is proposed for intrusion detection. BGAN generates synthetic minority samples to address class imbalance and adversarial samples for robustness evaluation. The approach improves Macro-F1 from 82.96% to 86.50% on CICIDS2017, achieves negative Performance Drop Rate under adversarial testing, and maintains low False Triggered Rate across noise levels.
AI.motivation: Machine learning-based IDSs suffer from two critical issues: (1) class imbalance that degrades detection performance on minority attack types, and (2) vulnerability to adversarial attacks that severely reduces model robustness. Existing approaches typically address these problems separately, lacking a unified framework to tackle both simultaneously.
AI.method: The study proposes a TabTransformer framework augmented by Boundary-Seeking GAN (BGAN) on the CICIDS2017 dataset. BGAN serves a dual purpose: generating synthetic minority-class samples to mitigate class imbalance, and producing adversarial samples to evaluate model robustness. The TabTransformer architecture handles tabular flow-based network data, while BGAN's boundary-seeking objective focuses generation near class decision boundaries for more effective augmentation.
AI.result: BGAN augmentation improved TabTransformer's Macro-F1 from 82.96% to 86.50%, with Web_Attack F1-score rising from 0.29 to 0.61. Under adversarial testing, all non-augmented models suffered 100% Performance Drop Rate (PDR), whereas BGAN-augmented models achieved negative PDR values, indicating robustness gains. The BGAN-TabTransformer maintained stable False Triggered Rate (1.51%–2.92%) across all noise levels, while BGAN-augmented Decision Tree reached 49.09% FTR under benign perturbations.
AI.conclusion: BGAN consistently enhances both class balance and adversarial robustness. The BGAN-TabTransformer framework provides an effective, adaptive intrusion detection solution suitable for adversarial network environments, outperforming alternative model architectures in both detection performance and resilience.

title: Automated Hardware Validation Test Plan Generation for Large Scale AI Datacenter Platforms Using a Generative AI Multi-Agents Architecture
summary: Large-scale AI datacenter platforms comprise thousands of heterogeneous hardware components whose validation requires comprehensive fault injection test plans. Today these plans are authored manually: engineers review hardware self-healing validation documents and bills of materials, enumerate failure modes per field-replaceable unit, and produce flat lists of single-layer test cases. This process is labor-intensive, error-prone, and dependent on institutional knowledge; coverage gaps surface late, traceability to source specifications is implicit, and the effort is largely repeated per platform. This paper presents a generative AI multi-agent architecture that automates the generation of structured hardware validation test plans from two canonical inputs: self-healing validation documents, which enumerate known failure modes and their detection and remediation behaviors per field-replaceable unit, and component Bills of Material. An ingestion agent normalizes heterogeneous inputs into a canonical representation; a classification agent maps components to functional domains via contextual reasoning over part descriptions and sub-category hierarchies; and a generation agent synthesizes test cases by combining normalized failure modes with domain-classified data, filling gaps and producing edge cases. The output conforms to a standardized schema for direct import into internal validation software. Evaluated on two production platforms against manual baselines, the framework achieves coverage expansions of 74.2% and 51.4%, cutting authoring from days to hours. It yields fully traceable mappings from each test case to its source specification, and its multi-agent decomposition is portable across platform generations. Automated and expert evaluations confirm 100% extraction fidelity and high acceptance of new scenarios, validating the framework as a robust human-in-the-loop force multiplier.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent generative AI system automates the creation of hardware validation test plans from self-healing validation documents and bills of materials, achieving 51–74% coverage expansion while reducing authoring time from days to hours.
AI.motivation: Manual authoring of fault injection test plans for large-scale AI datacenter platforms is labor-intensive, error-prone, relies on institutional knowledge, suffers from late-surfacing coverage gaps, lacks explicit traceability to specifications, and must be largely repeated for each new platform.
AI.method: A three-agent architecture: (1) an ingestion agent normalizes heterogeneous inputs (self-healing validation documents and component Bills of Material) into a canonical representation; (2) a classification agent maps components to functional domains using contextual reasoning over part descriptions and sub-category hierarchies; (3) a generation agent synthesizes test cases by combining normalized failure modes with domain-classified data, filling gaps and producing edge cases. Output conforms to a standardized schema for direct import into validation software.
AI.result: Evaluated on two production platforms: coverage expansions of 74.2% and 51.4% over manual baselines; authoring time reduced from days to hours; 100% extraction fidelity; fully traceable mappings from each test case to its source specification; high expert acceptance of generated scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent generative AI framework serves as a robust human-in-the-loop force multiplier for hardware validation test planning, with demonstrated portability across platform generations and strong performance on both automated and expert evaluation metrics.

title: Rater State Bias in RLHF Preference Data: An Audit Framework
summary: We identify a structured confound in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Pairwise preference labels are intended to reflect the compared outputs, but they may also reflect the rater's state during annotation. Under sustained stressful or distressing conditions, raters' preferences may shift over time. As a result, preference data can encode rater state alongside judgments about response quality. These shifts differ from ordinary disagreement or random label noise. They are state dependent, can be shared across annotators working under similar conditions, and can propagate through reward modeling and policy optimization. We therefore propose rater state shift as a plausible and testable source of structured bias in RLHF preference data. This paper develops a hypothesis and an audit framework for studying this source of bias. We define rater state shift, rater state confound, and correlated rater state bias. We also define survival level emotional authenticity as a measurable response pattern using lexical, pragmatic, discourse, and safety related features. We analyze how correlated rater state bias can survive aggregation and enter learned reward signals. We derive five falsifiable predictions and effect size thresholds for an initial audit. Finally, we present an audit protocol and pilot study plan that can be applied to publicly available instruction tuned models. We do not infer the training history of any specific deployed model. Our goal is to isolate a plausible and testable source of structured bias in RLHF preference data.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "rater state shift" as a structured confound in RLHF preference data, where annotators' psychological states under sustained stress systematically bias preference labels. It proposes a hypothesis, audit framework, falsifiable predictions, and a pilot study protocol to detect this bias without inferring any specific model's training history.
AI.motivation: RLHF assumes pairwise preferences reflect output quality alone, but the authors argue this overlooks a systematic confound: annotator psychological state. Under stressful annotation conditions (e.g., sustained exposure to harmful content), raters' preferences may shift in state-dependent ways shared across annotators, introducing correlated bias that survives aggregation and propagates into reward models — a failure mode distinct from random noise or ordinary disagreement.
AI.method: The paper is primarily theoretical and framework-building. It formally defines rater state shift, rater state confound, and correlated rater state bias. It operationalizes "survival level emotional authenticity" as a measurable response pattern using lexical, pragmatic, discourse, and safety-related features. The authors derive five falsifiable predictions with effect size thresholds and propose an audit protocol applicable to publicly available instruction-tuned models, along with a pilot study design.
AI.result: The paper does not report empirical results. It delivers: (1) formal definitions of the proposed bias constructs; (2) five falsifiable predictions (e.g., that rater state-correlated lexical/discourse features will systematically predict preference labels beyond response quality); (3) effect size thresholds for audit detection; and (4) a concrete audit protocol and pilot study plan for testing on public instruction-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Rater state shift is a plausible, testable, and currently underexamined source of structured bias in RLHF. The proposed audit framework enables researchers to detect whether annotator psychological states have been encoded into preference data and downstream policies, without requiring access to proprietary training pipelines. The authors explicitly disclaim inference about any specific deployed model's training history.

title: Multi-level context Modeling for consistent expert selection in Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables efficient scaling of Transformer models by routing tokens to a small subset of experts. However, existing routers typically condition expert selection on shallow or isolated token representations, which often produce unstable and semantically inconsistent routing decisions across layers. In this work, we revisit expert selection from a representation perspective and identify context incompleteness as a key bottleneck limiting effective expert specialization. To address this issue, we propose Multi-level Context Fusion MOE (MCF-MOE), a framework that constructs context-aware representations by integrating complementary signals from cross-layer semantic aggregation and local token-level interactions, enabling more informative and consistent expert selection. Experiments on language modeling and understanding benchmarks demonstrate that MCF-MOE consistently improves routing consistency and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines, highlighting the importance of contextual completeness in expert routing. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCFMOE.

AI.tldr: MCF-MOE improves MoE routing by fusing cross-layer semantic and local token-level signals into context-aware representations, yielding more consistent expert selection and better downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Standard MoE routers rely on shallow or isolated token representations, leading to unstable and semantically inconsistent routing across layers. The authors identify "context incompleteness" as the core bottleneck preventing effective expert specialization.
AI.method: MCF-MOE constructs context-aware router representations through two complementary mechanisms: (1) cross-layer semantic aggregation that integrates signals from multiple Transformer layers, and (2) local token-level interaction modeling. These fused representations inform more stable and semantically coherent expert selection.
AI.result: MCF-MOE consistently improves routing consistency and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines on language modeling and understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Contextual completeness is critical for effective expert routing in MoE models. Multi-level context fusion provides a principled way to achieve this, yielding measurable gains in both routing stability and task performance.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Guided NSGA-II Enhanced with Gray Relational Coefficient for Multi-Objective Optimization: Application to NASDAQ Portfolio Optimization
summary: In modern financial markets, decision-makers increasingly rely on quantitative methods to navigate complex trade-offs among multiple, often conflicting objectives. This paper addresses constrained multi-objective optimization (MOO) with an application to portfolio optimization for minimizing risk and maximizing return. To address existing gaps, we propose a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-guided non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) enhanced with gray relational coefficients (GRC), termed RL-NSGA-II-GRC, which combines an RL agent controller and GRC-based selection to improve convergence and diversity of Pareto fronts. The agent adapts evolutionary parameters online using metrics of hypervolume, feasibility, and diversity, while the GRC tournament operator ranks parents via a unified score considering dominance rank, crowding distance, and proximity to ideal reference. We evaluate the framework on the Kursawe and CONSTR benchmarks and a NASDAQ portfolio application. On the benchmarks, RL-NSGA-II-GRC achieves convergence improvements of about 5.8% and 4.4% over NSGA-II, while preserving well-distributed non-dominated solutions. In the portfolio application, it produces a smooth, densely populated efficient frontier supporting identification of the maximum Sharpe ratio portfolio (annualized Sharpe =1.92) and utility-optimal portfolios for different risk-aversion levels. The main contributions are three-fold: 1) we propose an RL-NSGA-II-GRC method integrating an RL agent into the evolutionary framework to adaptively control parameters via generational feedback; 2) we design a GRC-enhanced binary tournament operator providing a comprehensive indicator to guide the search toward the Pareto front; 3) we demonstrate, on benchmark MOO and a NASDAQ case study, that the method delivers improved convergence and well-populated frontiers supporting actionable insights.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RL-NSGA-II-GRC, a novel multi-objective optimization algorithm combining reinforcement learning-guided NSGA-II with gray relational coefficient-based selection, demonstrating improved convergence and diversity on benchmarks and a NASDAQ portfolio optimization case study.
AI.motivation: Decision-makers in financial markets need quantitative methods for navigating conflicting objectives (e.g., risk vs. return). Existing MOO approaches struggle with convergence and diversity of Pareto fronts, particularly in constrained settings. The authors aim to fill gaps in adaptive parameter control and parent selection within evolutionary multi-objective algorithms.
AI.method: RL-NSGA-II-GRC integrates three components: (1) an RL agent controller that adapts NSGA-II evolutionary parameters online using feedback metrics (hypervolume, feasibility, diversity); (2) a GRC-enhanced binary tournament operator that ranks parents via a unified score combining dominance rank, crowding distance, and proximity to an ideal reference point; (3) evaluation on Kursawe and CONSTR benchmarks plus a NASDAQ portfolio application targeting the maximum Sharpe ratio and utility-optimal portfolios.
AI.result: On benchmarks, RL-NSGA-II-GRC achieves convergence improvements of ~5.8% and ~4.4% over standard NSGA-II while maintaining well-distributed non-dominated solutions. In the NASDAQ portfolio application, it produces a smooth, densely populated efficient frontier, identifying a maximum Sharpe ratio portfolio (annualized Sharpe = 1.92) and utility-optimal portfolios across varying risk-aversion levels.
AI.conclusion: The threefold contribution is: (1) an RL-NSGA-II-GRC method integrating RL-based adaptive parameter control via generational feedback; (2) a GRC-enhanced tournament operator providing a comprehensive indicator for Pareto front guidance; (3) demonstrated improved convergence and actionable financial frontiers on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world portfolio optimization.

title: Personalized Assessments from Personal Artifacts
summary: The rapid development and popularization of AI-enabled coding agents have meant software engineering students and professionals cannot be assumed to understand their own code, which risks academic integrity and professional accountability. We developed a method called Personalized Probing Puzzles ($p^3$) to evaluate students' understanding of their own code, and tested $p^3$ in a graduate-level cloud computing course. Our pilot study shows that $p^3$ can help identify potential gaps in students' understanding of their own code. The puzzles are automatically generated, asynchronously administered, and finished in minutes. Future work is needed to correlate puzzle results with code understanding and to embed $p^3$ in a professional code review process.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Personalized Probing Puzzles (p³), a method for automatically generating short, asynchronous puzzles to assess whether software engineering students truly understand code they have written, addressing risks to academic integrity and professional accountability posed by AI coding agents.
AI.motivation: With the rise of AI-enabled coding agents, students and professionals can produce code they do not fully understand, threatening academic integrity in educational settings and professional accountability in industry. There is a need for scalable, lightweight methods to verify genuine code comprehension.
AI.method: The authors developed Personalized Probing Puzzles (p³), which are automatically generated, individually tailored puzzles based on a student's own code. These puzzles are administered asynchronously and designed to be completed within minutes. The method was piloted in a graduate-level cloud computing course.
AI.result: The pilot study demonstrated that p³ can help identify potential gaps in students' understanding of their own code, suggesting the approach is viable for detecting cases where AI-generated code obscures a lack of comprehension.
AI.conclusion: p³ shows promise as a practical tool for assessing code understanding, but further research is required to formally correlate puzzle performance with actual comprehension levels and to integrate the method into professional code review workflows.

title: The World According to a Social Robot -- Augmenting Human-Robot Dialogue With Vision Language Models
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) enable robots to visually perceive their environment as well as the actions and characteristics of their conversation partner or humans in collaboration. Especially for social robots deployed in everyday settings and for uncomplicated, natural use, it is essential that the robot has an understanding of situations that is appropriate to human customs. This paper presents initial experiences with the application of a Mistral AI language model with a Pepper robot for Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) in dialogue, as well as an investigation of the effects of additional visual information on response time in different models. The results show that incorporating visual information adds context to the dialogue with only a moderate increase in response time, enabling both the robot and the human to take into account unspoken elements of the situation. Furthermore, using an LLM hosted in Europe offers a solution that complies with European data protection regulations and can therefore facilitate real-life applications more easily.

AI.tldr: This paper explores integrating a Mistral AI vision-language model with a Pepper robot for human-robot interaction, evaluating how visual context affects dialogue quality and response time, while also addressing GDPR compliance through European-hosted LLMs.
AI.motivation: Social robots in everyday settings need situationally appropriate understanding aligned with human customs. Enabling robots to perceive both the environment and human actions visually can improve natural, uncomplicated HRI, but the impact on response latency and practical deployment considerations (e.g., data protection compliance) must be investigated.
AI.method: The authors deployed a Mistral AI language model on a Pepper robot for dialogue-based HRI. They compared model performance with and without additional visual information, measuring response times across different model configurations to quantify the trade-off between contextual richness and computational latency.
AI.result: Incorporating visual information enriches dialogue context at only a moderate increase in response time, allowing both the robot and human to leverage unspoken situational cues. Additionally, a European-hosted LLM satisfies EU data protection regulations (GDPR), easing real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language integration offers a viable path toward more context-aware social robots with acceptable latency overhead. European-hosted LLMs provide a compliant, practical solution for real-life HRI applications under GDPR.

title: Beyond Fixed Depths and Widths: Optimizing Textual Decoding Tries in LLM-based Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) is an increasingly popular paradigm in recommender systems, with a prominent line of work using LLMs as autoregressive backbones to predict the next item's term IDs (e.g., titles or keywords). The success of autoregressive generation hinges on constrained beam search over a decoding trie to ensure that generated outputs correspond to valid items. However, current research predominantly focuses on generating more comprehensive term IDs to describe items, while largely neglecting the structural design of the decoding trie formed by these terms. This can lead to a trie that is poorly suited to beam search, which degrades performance. To address this, we examine the effectiveness of term IDs from the perspective of decoding trie optimization. Through empirical and theoretical analyses, we identify two desirable properties for a highly performant trie: (1) adaptive and variable ID length, enabling items with varying semantic richness to be represented by IDs of appropriate lengths, and (2) constrained branching factors, especially at shallow levels, which drastically improves the success rate of constrained beam search. Motivated by these properties, we introduce BONSAI: Branching-Optimized Node Structure for Adaptive Identifiers, a novel framework that co-designs textual term IDs and their underlying decoding trie. BONSAI extracts recommendation-informative words from item metadata and employs a minimum set cover formulation to recursively build a trie that satisfies the above properties. Experiments reveal that BONSAI achieves up to a 21.6% relative improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. Further analyses confirm the crucial role of our proposed properties, and demonstrate their generalizability to be applied to enhance the performance of other term ID methods.

AI.tldr: BONSAI improves generative recommendation by co-designing item term IDs and their decoding trie structure, optimizing for adaptive ID lengths and constrained branching factors to boost constrained beam search performance, achieving up to 21.6% relative improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Current generative recommendation research focuses on richer term ID representations while neglecting the structural design of the decoding trie used in constrained beam search. Poorly structured tries degrade generation performance, motivating a systematic analysis of what makes a decoding trie effective.
AI.method: BONSAI identifies two key trie properties — adaptive/variable ID length and constrained branching factors (especially at shallow levels) — and co-designs textual term IDs with their decoding trie by extracting recommendation-informative words from item metadata and applying a minimum set cover formulation to recursively construct an optimized trie.
AI.result: BONSAI achieves up to 21.6% relative improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. Ablation analyses validate the importance of the two proposed trie properties and show their generalizability to improve other term ID methods.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing the decoding trie structure is critical for generative recommendation. The proposed properties — adaptive ID length and constrained branching — are both effective and generalizable, demonstrating that trie design deserves equal attention alongside term ID representation quality.

title: Reliable Remediation Impact Prediction for Black-Box Security Ratings
summary: Security rating platforms summarize externally observable cyber exposure and are expected to help organizations prioritize remediation. A platform may want to tell an organization how a candidate remediation action would affect its score, but repeatedly exposing exact score responses can reveal information about the hidden scoring engine. We propose a surrogate based approach for remediation score impact prediction that is designed to respect this opacity constraint. The surrogate predicts scores from organization configurations while explicitly representing checkpoint (i.e., a security check) applicability and the observed checkpoint set. A main challenge is that such predictions are not uniformly reliable: they depend on the amount and structure of the observable checkpoint evidence available for a given configuration. To address this, the approach combines applicability-aware surrogate construction, sensitivity analysis under controlled checkpoint restriction, a reliability layer for identifying unstable predictions, and score-impact prediction for supported remediation actions. Explicit modeling of checkpoint applicability is central throughout: it improves score prediction and provides the feature basis used by the reliability layer to identify unstable cases. We evaluate the approach on a real-world dataset of 5,188 organization configurations from a commercial security rating platform. The results show that the applicability-aware surrogate improves score prediction over simpler feature representations. For remediation, the surrogate predicts the score impact of supported actions, while the reliability layer helps identify cases in which these predicted impacts should be interpreted cautiously.

AI.tldr: Security rating platforms must balance helping organizations prioritize remediation with protecting proprietary scoring engines. This paper proposes an applicability-aware surrogate model that predicts remediation score impacts without exposing the hidden scoring engine. The approach combines surrogate construction with sensitivity analysis and a reliability layer to flag unstable predictions. Evaluated on 5,188 real-world organization configurations from a commercial platform, the method improves score prediction over simpler baselines and supports cautious interpretation of remediation impact predictions.
AI.motivation: Security rating platforms provide summarized cyber exposure scores to help organizations prioritize remediation. However, revealing exact score changes for candidate remediation actions risks exposing the proprietary scoring engine. There is a need for a method that predicts remediation score impacts while respecting this opacity constraint, with explicit handling of prediction reliability given that available observable evidence varies across configurations.
AI.method: The approach consists of four components: (1) an applicability-aware surrogate model that predicts scores from organization configurations by explicitly modeling checkpoint applicability and the observed checkpoint set; (2) sensitivity analysis under controlled checkpoint restriction; (3) a reliability layer that identifies unstable predictions by leveraging checkpoint applicability as feature basis; and (4) score-impact prediction for supported remediation actions. Explicit checkpoint applicability modeling is central to improving prediction accuracy and enabling reliability assessment.
AI.result: Evaluation on 5,188 real-world organization configurations from a commercial security rating platform demonstrates that the applicability-aware surrogate outperforms simpler feature representations for score prediction. The surrogate can predict score impacts of supported remediation actions, while the reliability layer successfully identifies cases where predicted impacts should be interpreted cautiously.
AI.conclusion: An applicability-aware surrogate approach can effectively predict remediation score impacts while preserving the opacity of the underlying scoring engine. Explicitly modeling checkpoint applicability improves both prediction quality and the ability to flag unreliable predictions, enabling practical, cautious use in real-world security rating platforms.

title: Laplacian Spectral Shaping for Non-Uniform Scaling Formation Control of Open Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Non-uniform scaling control enables a multi-agent formation to adjust its shape by compressing or stretching independently along different coordinate axes through inter-agent interactions, offering high flexibility in complex environments. The fundamental idea is encoding the desired formation shape as the kernel of a matrix-valued Laplacian. In open multi-agent systems, however, changes in number of agents, number of edges, and leader selection dynamically alter this Laplacian, destroying the required spectral properties: positive semidefiniteness, correct kernel, and positive definiteness of the follower block (we summarize these properties as the formation spectrum). In this paper, we develop distributed protocols to strategically adjust partial weights of the Laplacian matrix for formation control in arbitrary dimensional space. By implementing the protocols, the desired formation spectrum can be preserved under dynamic topology changes including agent joining, edge addition, agent leaving, and edge removal, while any pair of agents can serve as leaders. Unlike existing Laplacian design methods for affine formation control under topology changes, the proposed approach requires a sparser sensing graph, avoids a predefined parent-child hierarchical structure, and supports leader reassignment. The effectiveness of the proposed protocols is validated through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: A method for non-uniform scaling control in multi-agent formations that preserves the required Laplacian spectral properties under dynamic topology changes (agent/edge additions/removals, leader reassignment) using distributed weight-adjustment protocols, requiring sparser graphs than existing methods.
AI.motivation: In open multi-agent systems, dynamic changes (agents joining/leaving, edge additions/removals, leader reassignment) disrupt the Laplacian matrix's spectral properties — positive semidefiniteness, correct kernel, and positive definiteness of the follower block (termed the "formation spectrum") — which are essential for non-uniform scaling formation control. Existing affine formation control methods require dense sensing graphs and fixed parent-child hierarchies, motivating a more flexible, sparser approach.
AI.method: The formation shape is encoded as the kernel of a matrix-valued Laplacian. Distributed protocols are developed to strategically adjust partial weights of the Laplacian matrix to preserve the desired formation spectrum under four types of topology changes: agent joining, edge addition, agent leaving, and edge removal. The approach works in arbitrary dimensional space and supports arbitrary leader pair selection without predefined hierarchical structures.
AI.result: The proposed protocols successfully preserve the formation spectrum under all four topology change scenarios. Compared to existing Laplacian design methods for affine formation control, the approach uses a sparser sensing graph, eliminates the need for a parent-child hierarchy, and enables leader reassignment. Effectiveness is validated through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: The distributed weight-adjustment protocols enable robust non-uniform scaling formation control in open multi-agent systems, overcoming key limitations of prior work by supporting dynamic topologies, sparser graphs, and flexible leader selection while maintaining the required spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix.

title: Design and Validation of a Lightweight 1D CNN for Affective Touch Classification in Soft Plush Companions
summary: Soft, sensorized companions offer a physically safe and emotionally intuitive interface for socially assistive technologies, yet their deformability and multichannel tactile sensing complicate the robust interpretation of human affect. This study presents a complete open-source MATLAB-based framework for the development and validation of compact deep learning models for affective touch recognition in soft interactive companions. As a primary contribution, a diverse FAIR-compliant dataset of 1326 labelled gesture sequences collected from 25 participants spanning children, teenagers, and adults is made publicly available, providing a reusable resource for future research in affective touch recognition. Through systematic architecture and hyperparameter exploration across 468 CNN models, the study identifies compact dilated one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D CNNs) as the most effective solution, with a 13.2k-parameter model achieving 75% test accuracy and 85% mean leave-one-subject-out cross-validation accuracy. Theoretical inference-time analysis shows that quantized deployment requires 3.2 MMAC per window, compatible with 20 Hz real-time operation on the target microcontroller. PC-based real-time simulation with the physical toy streaming sensor data demonstrates that the CNN resolves subtle social touches that the previous heuristic system failed to detect, whereas high-force negative interactions are captured more reliably by trivial threshold-based logic. The resulting hybrid inference pipeline - instantaneous heuristic filtering followed by CNN-based nuanced gesture classification - is proposed as the embedded deployment strategy. The study demonstrates that emotionally meaningful, privacy-preserving touch interpretation is computationally feasible for direct embedding within soft therapeutic companions, with hardware integration addressed in a forthcoming study.

AI.tldr: An open-source MATLAB framework with a public dataset of 1,326 affective touch gestures trains compact 1D CNNs (13.2k parameters) achieving 75% test accuracy, enabling real-time embedded touch recognition for soft social robots via a hybrid heuristic+CNN inference pipeline.
AI.motivation: Soft, sensorized socially assistive companions require physically safe, emotionally intuitive interfaces, but their deformability and multichannel tactile sensing make robust affect interpretation difficult. Prior heuristic systems fail to detect subtle social touches reliably, motivating a learning-based approach deployable on resource-constrained embedded hardware.
AI.method: The authors collected a FAIR-compliant dataset of 1,326 labeled gesture sequences from 25 participants (children, teenagers, adults). They systematically explored 468 CNN architectures and hyperparameter configurations, converging on compact dilated 1D CNNs with 13.2k parameters. A hybrid inference pipeline is proposed: instantaneous heuristic filtering for high-force negative interactions, followed by CNN-based nuanced gesture classification. Real-time PC-based simulation streams sensor data from a physical plush toy, and quantized deployment is theoretically analyzed at 3.2 MMAC/window.
AI.result: The 13.2k-parameter dilated 1D CNN achieves 75% test accuracy and 85% mean leave-one-subject-out cross-validation accuracy. The CNN resolves subtle social touches missed by prior heuristics, while threshold logic remains superior for high-force negative interactions. Quantized inference requires 3.2 MMAC per window, compatible with 20 Hz real-time operation on the target microcontroller.
AI.conclusion: Emotionally meaningful, privacy-preserving touch interpretation is computationally feasible for direct embedding within soft therapeutic companions. The hybrid heuristic+CNN pipeline balances nuanced classification with reliable detection of negative interactions, with hardware integration deferred to future work.

title: RIMS: Preference Optimization via Smoothed Multi-pair Aggregation for Small-Scale LLM Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Small-scale language models (SLMs) are attractive for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in resource-constrained settings, but their limited capacity makes them highly sensitive to noisy or spurious retrieved evidence. Existing preference-based methods such as RoseRAG select only the hardest single preference pair via hard argmin/argmax, discarding the remaining signal; others treat multiple pairs as independent binary comparisons, resulting in low data utilization. We propose RIMS, a three-stage preference optimization framework comprising (1) synthetic chain-of-thought preference data generation via rejection sampling using the target SLM itself without relying on proprietary models, (2) a differentiable soft aggregation mechanism that replaces hard selection with a smooth operator, preserving gradient signal from all preference pairs while retaining the discriminative structure of margin-aware selection, and (3) preference optimization with the smoothed objective applied to multiple alignment algorithms. We theoretically show that the smoothed approximation admits a controllable error bound and that smooth aggregation yields provably tighter gradient alignment to the oracle objective than hard selection. Experiments on four multi-hop question answering benchmarks show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple SLM backbones, achieving consistent gains in Exact Match and F1 under noisy retrieval conditions. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/tptrix29/RIMS.

AI.tldr: RIMS is a three-stage preference optimization framework for small language models in RAG that replaces hard single-pair selection with a differentiable soft aggregation mechanism, achieving better data utilization and robustness to noisy retrieval.
AI.motivation: Small-scale language models (SLMs) are attractive for resource-constrained RAG settings but are highly sensitive to noisy retrieved evidence. Existing preference-based methods like RoseRAG discard valuable training signal by selecting only the hardest single preference pair, while others treat multiple pairs independently, resulting in low data utilization.
AI.method: RIMS proposes three stages: (1) synthetic chain-of-thought preference data generation via rejection sampling using the target SLM, without proprietary models; (2) a differentiable soft aggregation mechanism replacing hard argmin/argmax selection, preserving gradient signal from all preference pairs with margin-aware structure; (3) preference optimization with the smoothed objective applied to multiple alignment algorithms. Theoretical analysis provides an error bound for the smoothed approximation and proves tighter gradient alignment to the oracle objective compared to hard selection.
AI.result: Experiments on four multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate that RIMS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple SLM backbones, with consistent improvements in Exact Match and F1 under noisy retrieval conditions.
AI.conclusion: RIMS effectively addresses the data utilization problem in SLM preference optimization for RAG by leveraging soft aggregation over all preference pairs, yielding both theoretical guarantees and empirical gains in robustness to retrieval noise.

title: DocOCR-Eval: A Correction-Based Framework for OCR Tool Selection Without Ground Truth
summary: Document parsing is a foundational step for document understanding tasks such as visual question answering and key information extraction, as it transforms unstructured scanned images into structured representations by extracting textual, visual, and layout information. While numerous Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have been developed for this purpose, selecting an appropriate document parsing solution for a given document collection remains challenging, particularly in label-scarce settings. In this work, we conduct a systematic evaluation of text recognition performance across a diverse set of OCR engines and state-of-the-art MLLMs on multiple scanned document benchmarks spanning different domains and languages. Motivated by the limited contextual reasoning capabilities of many OCR engines and the high cost of manual annotations, we propose DocOCR-Eval, an annotation-free evaluation framework for automatic OCR assessment and selection. DocOCR-Eval employs a three-staged correction and ranking strategy to approximate annotation-based tool ordering without ground-truth labels. We show that aggregating across multiple MLLMs progressively improves alignment with annotation-based rankings. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that reliable OCR tool selection can be achieved in realistic, label-limited settings, providing practical guidance for deploying document parsing systems across diverse real-world document collections.

AI.tldr: DocOCR-Eval is an annotation-free evaluation framework for automatic OCR engine and MLLM selection. It uses a three-stage correction and ranking strategy to approximate annotation-based tool rankings without ground-truth labels, demonstrating reliable OCR selection in label-scarce settings across diverse document domains and languages.
AI.motivation: Selecting appropriate document parsing solutions (OCR engines or MLLMs) is challenging due to: (1) limited contextual reasoning capabilities of many OCR engines, (2) high cost of manual annotations for evaluation, and (3) lack of systematic benchmarks spanning diverse domains/languages. There is a need for an annotation-free method to assess and rank OCR tools reliably.
AI.method: The authors propose DocOCR-Eval, an annotation-free evaluation framework featuring a three-staged correction and ranking strategy. It operates without ground-truth labels by aggregating outputs across multiple MLLMs to approximate annotation-based tool ordering. The framework is validated through systematic evaluation of text recognition performance across diverse OCR engines and state-of-the-art MLLMs on multiple scanned document benchmarks covering different domains and languages.
AI.result: Aggregating across multiple MLLMs progressively improves alignment with annotation-based rankings. Extensive experiments show that reliable OCR tool selection can be achieved in realistic, label-limited settings, providing practical guidance for deploying document parsing systems across diverse real-world document collections.
AI.conclusion: DocOCR-Eval enables effective OCR tool selection without requiring costly ground-truth annotations, making it practical for real-world deployment across diverse document collections. The multi-MLLM aggregation strategy is key to achieving strong alignment with supervised evaluation rankings.

title: ReqGenX: An Empirical Study of Atomic Decomposition, Artifact Regeneration, and Reconstruction for Legacy SRS Documents
comment: Accepted at the International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM) technical papers (main) track 2026
summary: Background: Evaluating automated Software Requirements Specification (SRS) generation is challenging because few datasets provide fine-grained traceability between source requirements, intermediate elicitation artifacts, and generated specifications. Aims: We aim to study whether legacy SRS documents can be transformed into traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts that support fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation. Method: We conduct an empirical study using ReqGenX, a controlled pipeline that decomposes SRS sections into source-grounded atomic statements, routes atoms to standards-inspired artifact types through multi-LLM plurality voting, and generates artifacts using constrained prompts with iterative judge-guided refinement. We evaluate ReqGenX on seven PURE SRS documents using grounding, quality, information retention, and downstream reconstruction analyses. Results: ReqGenX produces faithful and usable atoms, with median AlignScore values typically between 0.96 and 0.99 and Prometheus scores ranging from 4.34 to 4.85. Generated artifacts remain strongly grounded in their source atoms, with AlignScore values typically between 0.80--0.94 and judge pass rates near 100%; stricter Prometheus evaluation yields pass rates from 54.8% to 97.1%. In a downstream SRS reconstruction case study, artifact-backed atoms remain recoverable from generated SRSs, with SBERT means between 0.69 and 0.75 and AlignScore medians between 0.76 and 0.84. Conclusions: Traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts can support more fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation, while exposing tradeoffs among faithfulness, information retention, and artifact completeness.

AI.tldr: Legacy SRS documents can be decomposed into traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts using the ReqGenX pipeline. These artifacts enable fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation, achieving high faithfulness (AlignScore 0.96–0.99) and strong downstream recoverability (SBERT 0.69–0.75), though tradeoffs exist among faithfulness, information retention, and completeness.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of automated SRS generation is hindered by a scarcity of datasets that provide fine-grained traceability linking source requirements, intermediate elicitation artifacts, and the final generated specifications. Without such traceability, it is difficult to assess whether LLM-generated SRSs faithfully preserve and trace back to their origins.
AI.method: The authors propose ReqGenX, a controlled pipeline with four stages: (1) decomposing SRS sections into source-grounded atomic statements; (2) routing each atom to standards-inspired artifact types (e.g., user stories, use cases, functional requirements) via multi-LLM plurality voting; (3) generating artifacts using constrained prompts with iterative judge-guided refinement; and (4) evaluating along four dimensions—grounding, quality, information retention, and downstream reconstruction—using metrics such as AlignScore, Prometheus, and SBERT cosine similarity. The study is conducted on seven PURE SRS documents.
AI.result: ReqGenX produces highly faithful atoms (median AlignScore 0.96–0.99; Prometheus scores 4.34–4.85). Generated artifacts remain grounded in source atoms (AlignScore 0.80–0.94; judge pass rates near 100%), though stricter Prometheus evaluation lowers pass rates to 54.8%–97.1%. In downstream reconstruction, artifact-backed atoms are recoverable from generated SRSs with SBERT means of 0.69–0.75 and AlignScore medians of 0.76–0.84.
AI.conclusion: Traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts are viable for fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation. The approach exposes inherent tradeoffs between faithfulness, information retention, and artifact completeness, and provides a foundation for more rigorous benchmarking in requirements engineering.

title: Hindsight: Similarity-Based Analytics for Mars Rover Drive Retrieval
comment: In press for the 2026 IEEE Conference on Visualization (VIS 2026)
summary: While Mars rover operators plan drives across hazardous Martian terrain and diagnose unexpected faults, the necessary information is distributed across separate systems and often reconstructed through manual correlation and memory. To address this challenge, we partnered with Mars rover operators at the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory to introduce Hindsight, a visual analytics system that unifies previously disparate rover drive data into a single workspace for search, comparison, and investigation. This paper presents a design study of the Hindsight application. The partnership revealed that operators reason about drives as holistic spatiotemporal episodes rather than discrete parameters. By externalizing operator intuition into an explicit visual query process, we argue that Hindsight transforms analysis into a structured, shareable workflow. Preliminary feedback from operators suggests Hindsight supports their ability to correlate terrain, telemetry, and fault events within a singleworkspace.

AI.tldr: Hindsight is a visual analytics system co-designed with NASA JPL Mars rover operators that unifies disparate rover drive data into a single workspace, enabling operators to search, compare, and investigate drives as holistic spatiotemporal episodes rather than isolated parameters.
AI.motivation: Mars rover operators must plan drives across hazardous terrain and diagnose faults, but the necessary information (terrain, telemetry, fault events) is scattered across separate systems, requiring manual correlation and reliance on memory. This fragmented workflow is inefficient and error-prone.
AI.method: The authors conducted a design study in partnership with rover operators at NASA JPL, identifying that operators conceptualize drives as spatiotemporal episodes. Based on this insight, they developed Hindsight, a visual analytics system that externalizes operator intuition into an explicit visual query process, unifying disparate data into a structured, shareable workspace for search, comparison, and investigation.
AI.result: Preliminary operator feedback indicates that Hindsight supports the ability to correlate terrain, telemetry, and fault events within a single workspace, transforming fragmented analysis into a structured, shareable workflow.
AI.conclusion: By treating rover drives as holistic spatiotemporal episodes and providing unified visual query capabilities, Hindsight improves the efficiency and shareability of rover drive analysis, bridging the gap between fragmented data systems and operator reasoning.

title: WHALE: A Scalable Unified Model for Recommendation with Wukong-HSTU Architecture
summary: As scalability becomes increasingly important in recommendation modeling, recent architectures have advanced the modeling of two broad sources of ranking signals along separate paths: non-sequence features, including user, item, context, and cross features; and sequence features from user behavior histories. Wukong and HSTU have emerged as representative scalable backbones for these paths: Wukong scales high-order non-sequence feature-interaction modeling, while HSTU scales long user-behavior sequence modeling. Despite their complementary strengths, practical architectures that combine these two types of feature modeling remain underexplored. We present WHALE, a scalable unified recommendation architecture that jointly models non-sequence and sequence features on top of Wukong and HSTU. Each WHALE layer contains a Wukong module, an HSTU module, and an attention-based fusion module in which Wukong-derived interaction representations query HSTU-derived behavior representations. This design keeps both backbones active throughout the network and enables progressive Wukong-HSTU exchange, allowing high-order feature crosses to repeatedly retrieve fine-grained evidence from long user histories. To make WHALE practical for industrial deployment, we introduce customized Triton kernels and other model-systems co-design techniques to improve training and inference efficiency. On large-scale industrial recommendation data, WHALE achieves consistent gains in offline experiments. Additionally, it delivers positive online gains with a modest serving-throughput trade-off. The method has been deployed in production systems. Overall, WHALE provides a practical example of how these two sources of information can be scalably unified in an industrial recommendation model.

AI.tldr: WHALE unifies Wukong (non-sequence feature interaction) and HSTU (long user-behavior sequence modeling) into a single scalable architecture with attention-based fusion modules, achieving consistent offline and online gains in industrial recommendation systems.
AI.motivation: Modern recommendation models treat non-sequence features (user, item, context, cross features) and sequence features (user behavior histories) along separate paths. Wukong excels at the former, HSTU at the latter, but no practical architecture combines both at scale. The authors aim to fill this gap for industrial deployment.
AI.method: Each WHALE layer stacks a Wukong module, an HSTU module, and an attention-based fusion module where Wukong-derived interaction representations query HSTU-derived behavior representations. This layered design keeps both backbones active throughout the network, enabling progressive cross-module exchange so high-order feature crosses can repeatedly retrieve evidence from long user histories. Custom Triton kernels and model-systems co-design ensure training/inference efficiency.
AI.result: WHALE achieves consistent gains in offline experiments on large-scale industrial recommendation data and delivers positive online gains with modest serving-throughput trade-off. It has been deployed in production.
AI.conclusion: WHALE demonstrates that non-sequence and sequence feature modeling can be scalably unified in an industrial recommendation model, providing a practical blueprint that leverages the complementary strengths of both Wukong and HSTU.

title: Identity-Bound Academic Credentials on Blockchain: On-Chain Issuer Accreditation with ERC-3643 and OnchainID
summary: Verifying academic credentials remains difficult: records are held by individual institutions in proprietary systems, verification is slow and manual, and counterfeit qualifications are widespread. Blockchain-based registries have been proposed as a remedy, but existing systems tend to anchor certificate hashes without binding them to a verifiable identity, without an explicit mechanism to accredit issuing institutions, and without support for correcting or revoking credentials once issued. This paper investigates whether an infrastructure designed for regulated financial instruments can be repurposed to close these gaps. We present the design of a registry for identity-bound academic credentials that composes OnchainID self-sovereign identities (ERC-734/ERC-735) with the T-REX suite (ERC-3643): its trusted-issuer registry becomes an on-chain issuer-accreditation whitelist, and each certificate is represented as a signed, updatable claim bound to a student's identity and verifiable by any third party without a wallet, while sensitive fields are kept off-chain. We make explicit the tension between a transferable-security-token standard and non-transferable credentials, clarifying which of its guarantees carry over. We validate the design with a reference implementation covering the full certificate life cycle and evaluate it in terms of gas cost, scalability, latency, and security, quantifying the overhead relative to a hash-anchoring baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a blockchain-based academic credential registry that combines OnchainID self-sovereign identities (ERC-734/ERC-735) with the T-REX framework (ERC-3643) to address gaps in existing systems: binding certificates to verifiable identities, accrediting issuers on-chain, and supporting revocation/correction. A reference implementation is validated for gas cost, scalability, latency, and security.
