AI.motivation: Academic credential verification is fragmented across proprietary institutional systems, slow, manual, and plagued by counterfeit qualifications. Existing blockchain proposals merely anchor certificate hashes without identity binding, issuer accreditation mechanisms, or support for post-issuance correction/revocation.
AI.method: The design composes OnchainID (ERC-734/ERC-735) for self-sovereign identities with T-REX (ERC-3643), repurposing its trusted-issuer registry as an on-chain accreditation whitelist. Each certificate is a signed, updatable claim bound to a student's identity, verifiable by third parties without a wallet. Sensitive data is stored off-chain. A reference implementation covering the full certificate lifecycle is built and evaluated against a hash-anchoring baseline across gas cost, scalability, latency, and security dimensions.
AI.result: The design successfully adapts a transferable-security-token standard (ERC-3643) for non-transferable credentials, with explicit analysis of which guarantees carry over. The reference implementation quantifies overhead relative to a simple hash-anchoring approach, demonstrating feasibility across the full credential lifecycle (issuance, verification, correction, revocation).
AI.conclusion: Repurposing regulated financial instrument infrastructure (T-REX + OnchainID) is viable for identity-bound academic credentials, closing critical gaps in issuer accreditation, identity binding, and credential lifecycle management. The trade-off in overhead relative to hash-anchoring is quantified and justified by the added guarantees.

title: When Is Heterogeneous Distance-Decay Facility Location Tractable? A Structural Classification, Exact Methods, and a Real-World Study
summary: We study continuous planar facility location in which a demand point's captured value decays with distance, with the per-point decay scale varying across points. This heterogeneity is ubiquitous yet underexploited, and one nearest-facility objective unifies decay, clustering, and median goals, containing k-means, the Weber/p-median problem, and maximum covering as special cases. We make four contributions. (i) A tractability classification: the discrete objective is always monotone submodular, so the (1-1/e) greedy guarantee holds regardless of decay shape or heterogeneity, and the continuous cooperative objective is concave if and only if the decay is concave in distance; the clip max(0,d) in common coverage specifications is what destroys concavity, and the classification is tight. (ii) An exact discrete method: the candidate-discretized maximum-cover MIP has an empirically tight LP relaxation (~0% gap) and is solved by branch-and-bound in seconds for n <= 500. (iii) A force-as-gradient / large-neighborhood-search heuristic, within 0.5% of the discrete optimum, that outperforms the (1-1/e) greedy, Cooper-style alternating location-allocation, particle swarm optimization, and weighted k-means (30/30 per-instance wins at K=30, p<10^-9) and is competitive with bespoke solvers on k-means, Weber/p-median, and shape-demand instances. (iv) A real-world study: on 592,667 urban-delivery orders, ignoring the calibrated decay variation loses up to 9.7% of captured demand and relocates facilities by up to 37% of the map; a retail dataset calibrates the decay as exponential with scale R ~ 1.4 km.

AI.tldr: We study heterogeneous decay in continuous facility location, showing the discrete objective is monotone submodular (guaranteeing (1-1/e) greedy), the continuous cooperative objective is concave iff decay is concave in distance, and propose an exact MIP method and a force-as-gradient heuristic that outperforms existing approaches, validated on large-scale urban delivery data.
AI.motivation: In continuous facility location, demand point capture value typically decays with distance, and the per-point decay scale varies across points (heterogeneity). This heterogeneity is ubiquitous in real applications but underexploited. Existing models treat decay uniformly, missing significant practical value.
AI.method: The authors provide four contributions: (1) a tractability classification proving the discrete objective is monotone submodular and the continuous cooperative objective is concave iff decay is concave; (2) an exact discrete method using candidate-discretized maximum-cover MIP with tight LP relaxation solved via branch-and-bound; (3) a force-as-gradient / large-neighborhood-search heuristic; (4) empirical validation on real urban-delivery (592,667 orders) and retail datasets.
AI.result: The MIP approach solves n≤500 instances in seconds with ~0% LP gap. The heuristic achieves within 0.5% of the discrete optimum, outperforming (1-1/e) greedy, Cooper alternating allocation-location, particle swarm optimization, and weighted k-means (30/30 wins at K=30, p<10⁻⁹). Ignoring calibrated decay variation loses up to 9.7% captured demand and relocates facilities by up to 37% of the map. Retail data calibrates exponential decay with scale R≈1.4km.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous decay is practically significant and theoretically tractable. The submodularity result guarantees greedy performance, the concavity classification is tight, and the proposed heuristic is state-of-the-art. Real-world consequences of ignoring heterogeneity are substantial in both demand capture and facility placement.

title: Some Large Language Models Exhibit Consistent Risk Attitudes
summary: As artificial intelligence systems are deployed in open-ended, high-stakes settings, a critical dimension remains unmeasured: how perceived risk is translated into action. We test whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit systematic and consistent risk attitudes under uncertainty. We introduce a cross-domain framework that decouples contextual risk belief from categorical decision, and apply it to six representative LLMs and 100 human participants across spatial navigation, clinical triage, and financial allocation tasks. Using regression models, we extract each agents belief-to-decision mapping and quantify risk sensitivity and risk attitude bias. We find that most tested LLMs exhibit (i) robust intra-task consistency, indicating stable mappings from contextual belief to risk decision within a fixed task domain; (ii) cross-domain rank-order stability, preserving relative risk posture across tasks; and (iii) a convergence toward a restricted risk-attitude distribution relative to the broader human baseline. These results reveal risk attitude as a stable and previously uncharacterized dimension of LLM behavior, establishing a foundation for evaluating and aligning AI systems in open-ended decision-making and motivating further investigation into the origins of these intrinsic behavioral dispositions.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit stable, consistent risk attitudes across tasks — more narrowly distributed than humans — revealing risk attitude as an intrinsic behavioral dimension of AI systems.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes, open-ended environments, a critical gap exists: we lack measurement of how these models translate perceived risk into action. This study aims to characterize whether LLMs possess systematic risk attitudes under uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors introduce a cross-domain framework that decouples contextual risk belief from categorical decision. They test six representative LLMs and 100 human participants across three task domains (spatial navigation, clinical triage, financial allocation). Regression models extract each agent's belief-to-decision mapping, quantifying risk sensitivity and risk attitude bias.
AI.result: Most LLMs demonstrate three key findings: (i) robust intra-task consistency (stable belief-to-decision mappings within a domain); (ii) cross-domain rank-order stability (relative risk posture preserved across tasks); and (iii) convergence toward a restricted risk-attitude distribution compared to the broader human baseline.
AI.conclusion: Risk attitude constitutes a stable, previously uncharacterized dimension of LLM behavior. This provides a foundation for evaluating and aligning AI systems in open-ended decision-making and motivates investigation into the origins of these intrinsic behavioral dispositions.

title: Committed Before Reasoning: Behavioral Reproduction and Preliminary Activation-Level Evidence of Answer Pre-Commitment in an Open-Weight LLM
comment: 8 pages. Code, data, and all reported statistics: https://github.com/JO-HEEJIN/interview_mate/tree/docs/car-wash-repro/car_wash/paper_4
summary: Chat models sometimes commit to an answer and then produce reasoning that justifies it rather than deriving it -- even when the answer contradicts a task premise. We study a minimal probe: "I want to wash my car. The car wash is 100 meters away. Should I walk or drive?" Only drive works (the car must be at the car wash), yet models overwhelmingly recommend walking. (1) Behavioral reproduction: on Qwen3-8B across five system-prompt conditions (210 rollouts), the wrong commitment occurs in 85-100% of sampled rollouts per condition and 100% of greedy rollouts, in both thinking and non-thinking modes; a 4,096-token thinking budget does not repair it. (2) Preliminary activation-level evidence: probing hidden states with a pretrained, training-free activation oracle (no task-specific probe training) at positions before the answer text is emitted, "walk" read-outs exceed a neutral-context baseline (68% vs. 17%; walk-committing rollouts p=.005, drive-committing rollouts p=.005, Fisher exact) -- notably, rollouts that eventually answer drive also read as walk-leaning before commitment (5/6). The oracle's default on unrelated content is "drive" (83%), so the read-outs are not lexical bias; stratifying by literal walk/drive occurrence shows they are not text recovery either (spans containing "drive" still read out walk; in balanced lexical fields, per-rollout walk-majorities beat a per-prompt neutral baseline 15/22 vs. 1/8, p=.01; drive-committing rollouts 6/6, p=.002). Samples are small and the within-rollout positional gradient is not significant (p=.34); we frame these results as preliminary. (3) Methodological: with fixed oracle, activations, and positions, question wording alone moves a positive control from 2/16 (open question) to 11/16 (closed); negative oracle results are uninterpretable without per-wording positive controls.

AI.tldr: Researchers found that language models like Qwen3-8B overwhelmingly recommend walking (wrong answer) to a car wash question where only driving is correct, and preliminary activation-level evidence suggests the incorrect "walk" preference is already detectable in hidden states before the answer is emitted, even in rollouts that ultimately answer correctly.
AI.motivation: To investigate the phenomenon where chat models prematurely commit to an answer and then generate post-hoc rationalization, using a minimal controlled probe to isolate commitment bias from genuine reasoning.
AI.method: A deceptively simple probe: "I want to wash my car. The car wash is 100 meters away. Should I walk or drive?" — where only "drive" is correct (the car must arrive at the car wash). Behavioral analysis across 210 rollouts on Qwen3-8B under five system-prompt conditions, in both thinking and non-thinking modes, including a 4,096-token thinking budget. Activation-level analysis uses a pretrained, training-free activation oracle to read out "walk" vs. "drive" preferences from hidden states before answer emission, with neutral-context baselines and lexical field controls.
AI.result: Behaviorally: wrong commitment ("walk") occurred in 85–100% of sampled rollouts per condition and 100% of greedy rollouts; extended thinking budget did not repair the error. Activation-level: "walk" read-outs significantly exceeded the neutral baseline (68% vs. 17%, p=.005 for both walk-committing and drive-committing rollouts). Even rollouts that ultimately answered "drive" showed walk-leaning internal states (5/6). Controls ruled out lexical bias and text recovery. A methodological finding: question wording alone shifted a positive control from 2/16 to 11/16, highlighting the need for per-wording controls when interpreting null oracle results.
AI.conclusion: Language models exhibit a robust premature commitment to the wrong answer on this probe, and preliminary evidence indicates this bias is detectable in internal representations before overt output, even in cases that eventually answer correctly — suggesting the model overrides rather than avoids the initial wrong commitment.

title: Fully-sensorized smart-eyewear platform for on-device Machine Learning
comment: This work was carried out in the EssilorLuxottica "Smart Eyewear Lab", a Joint Research Center between EssilorLuxottica and Politecnico di Milano
summary: This paper presents ARGO, a smart eyewear platform designed to bridge ergonomic comfort, high computational throughput, and energy efficiency. Unlike cloud-dependent solutions, ARGO leverages the STM32N6 microcontroller and its integrated Neural Processing Unit (NPU) to enable on-device machine learning, minimizing latency and preserving user privacy through local data processing. The primary contribution lies in the holistic co-design of hardware, firmware, and artificial intelligence, centered on the deployment of an optimized YOLOv11 model for real-time urban obstacle recognition. To ensure compatibility with the target NPU, we introduce Head-wise Parallel Attention (HPA), an architectural refinement that enables efficient accelerator execution while preserving the original computational logic. The model is trained on the Walking On The Road (WOTR) dataset, and the final deployed configuration achieves an mAP50-95 of 24 under strict memory constraints, with a memory footprint of only 2.483 MB. The platform integrates a multimodal sensor suite, RGB cameras, Time-of-Flight sensors, microphones, and ambient sensors, and delivers 10 FPS at a continuous autonomy of ~113 minutes on a 200 mAh battery. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a high-performance, privacy-preserving, and socially acceptable assistive device, and highlight how competitive edge AI solutions increasingly demand tightly integrated, multidisciplinary co-design approaches.

AI.tldr: ARGO is a smart eyewear platform using an STM32N6 microcontroller with integrated NPU for on-device obstacle recognition. It deploys an optimized YOLOv11 model with a novel Head-wise Parallel Attention (HPA) mechanism, achieving 10 FPS, ~113 min battery life, and a 2.483 MB model footprint.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between ergonomic comfort, high computational throughput, and energy efficiency in assistive eyewear, while avoiding cloud dependency to minimize latency and preserve user privacy through on-device processing.
AI.method: Holistic co-design of hardware (STM32N6 MCU with NPU), firmware, and AI. Introduces Head-wise Parallel Attention (HPA) to adapt YOLOv11 for efficient NPU execution. Model trained on the WOTR dataset and deployed under strict memory constraints, integrated with multimodal sensors (RGB, ToF, microphones, ambient sensors).
AI.result: Achieves mAP50-95 of 24, memory footprint of 2.483 MB, inference at 10 FPS, and ~113 minutes continuous operation on a 200 mAh battery.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of high-performance, privacy-preserving assistive eyewear and highlights the growing necessity of tightly integrated, multidisciplinary co-design for competitive edge AI solutions.

title: From Discussion to Execution: Replicating Buggy and Correct Data Science Code
comment: accepted at the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE 2026)
summary: Reproducing reliable data science code from informal sources is challenging due to ambiguous problem specifications, missing dependencies, and performance bottlenecks. Although developer Q&A forums provide rich discussions on diagnosing and fixing real-world issues, the information is often incomplete and unstructured, limiting its use for automated debugging and verification. In this paper, we introduce Reprodgen, a large language model (LLM) based framework for automatically replicating executable buggy and patched data science programs from Q&A forum posts. Given a question and its corresponding answer, Reprodgen reconstructs the buggy behavior described in the question and the intended fix described in the answer, producing executable buggy and patched code pairs that reflect the original discussion. The framework builds structured representations of code intent (CI), functional requirements (FR), and Structured Chain of Thought (SCoT), and iteratively refines code using an LLM-based reviewer until it is executable and semantically consistent. We evaluate Reprodgen on Stack Overflow (SO) and GitHub Issues (GI) across seven data science libraries, including pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn, and construct a benchmark of runnable buggy and patched programs validated by human experts. Our pipeline uses LLMs for semantic assessment, while executability is verified through actual execution. Results show reliable replication with clear differences in model performance.

AI.tldr: Reprodgen is an LLM-based framework that automatically reconstructs executable buggy and patched data science code pairs from Q&A forum posts (Stack Overflow and GitHub Issues) by extracting code intent, functional requirements, and structured chain-of-thought, then iteratively refining code through an LLM reviewer until executability and semantic consistency are achieved.
AI.motivation: Reproducing reliable data science code from informal sources is hindered by ambiguous specifications, missing dependencies, and performance issues. Q&A forums contain valuable debugging discussions, but the unstructured and incomplete nature of this information prevents automated use in debugging and verification pipelines.
AI.method: The Reprodgen framework takes a forum question-answer pair as input and extracts three structured intermediate representations: Code Intent (CI), Functional Requirements (FR), and Structured Chain of Thought (SCoT). These are used to guide an LLM in generating initial buggy and patched code. An LLM-based reviewer then iteratively critiques and refines the code until it passes both executability verification (via actual runtime execution) and semantic consistency checks (via LLM-based semantic assessment).
AI.result: Reprodgen was evaluated on posts from Stack Overflow and GitHub Issues spanning seven major data science libraries (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, etc.). A human-expert-validated benchmark of runnable buggy/patched program pairs was constructed. Results demonstrate reliable replication of executable code pairs, with clear performance variations observed across different LLM backends.
AI.conclusion: Reprodgen successfully bridges unstructured Q&A forum content and executable, verifiable code artifacts, enabling automated replication of real-world buggy and patched data science programs. Its iterative LLM-based review process ensures both executability and semantic alignment with original forum discussions.

title: AlterAtlas: Shifting Travel Planning from AI Generation to Validation via Persona-Driven Simulations
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. For associated codebase, see https://github.com/hilab-open-source/alteratlas
summary: Travel planning requires balancing interacting goals and constraints across time and space. Current AI travel tools provide limited support for encoding these constraints and understanding how generated travel plans may fail users. We present AlterAtlas, an interactive travel planning system that supports high-fidelity itinerary validation and revision through persona-based simulations grounded in geospatial information. AlterAtlas models travelers as editable personas, generates candidate itineraries from prioritized places of interest, and simulates how different personas would experience each plan. Simulations expose route-level tradeoffs, temporal user states (e.g., fatigue, hunger), and mismatches between plans and user preferences to allow users to iteratively refine both itineraries and user personas. An expert evaluation of 51 paired itineraries demonstrates that simulation-guided revisions significantly improve plan-persona alignment. Furthermore, a within-subjects study (N=11) reveals that AlterAtlas empowers users to uncover hidden constraints, fluidly compare alternatives, and build trust in their final plans. Our results suggest that simulation-based validation is a powerful, transparent interaction layer for AI-assisted travel planning.

AI.tldr: AlterAtlas is an interactive travel planning system that uses editable persona-based simulations grounded in geospatial data to validate and iteratively refine itineraries, with studies showing it improves plan-persona alignment and helps users uncover hidden constraints and build trust.
AI.motivation: Current AI travel tools inadequately support encoding complex, interacting constraints (goals, time, space) and fail to help users understand how or why generated plans may not meet their needs. There is a need for transparent validation mechanisms that expose tradeoffs and mismatches.
AI.method: AlterAtlas models travelers as editable personas with preferences and constraints. It generates candidate itineraries from prioritized POIs and simulates persona experiences, exposing route-level tradeoffs and temporal states (fatigue, hunger). Users iteratively refine both itineraries and personas. Evaluated via: (1) expert evaluation of 51 paired itineraries comparing simulation-guided revisions, and (2) a within-subjects user study (N=11).
AI.result: The expert evaluation showed simulation-guided revisions significantly improve plan-persona alignment. The within-subjects study revealed AlterAtlas enables users to uncover hidden constraints, fluidly compare alternatives, and build trust in final plans.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-based validation serves as a powerful, transparent interaction layer for AI-assisted travel planning, enabling iterative refinement and fostering user trust through exposing the reasoning behind plan outcomes.

title: Uncertainty as Remedy: Mitigating Satisfaction Label Bias in Short Video Multi-Objective Ensemble Ranking
summary: The core objective of short video recommendation is to model users' unobservable true satisfaction with recommended videos. As the dominant industrial framework, end-to-end multi-objective ensemble ranking models are typically trained with multi-dimensional dense user behavioral signals, such as clicks and watch time. However, these behavioral signals are partial, fragmented, and often mutually conflicting user satisfaction proxies, introducing uncertainty and label bias into satisfaction modeling. Conventional deterministic models overlook this uncertainty, which exacerbates satisfaction label bias and results in suboptimal model convergence. Meanwhile, existing uncertainty-aware methods mostly employ uncertainty for post-hoc ranking adjustments rather than leveraging it as a remedy to mitigate the inherent bias within the core optimization pipeline. This paper proposes UAME, an Uncertainty-Aware end-to-end Multi-objective Ensemble ranking framework for short video recommendation. UAME represents the model's prediction as a Gaussian scoring variable, where the mean denotes the predicted satisfaction score and the variance quantifies predictive uncertainty associated with this score. We further design a probabilistic pairwise ranking loss, and construct an uncertainty-aware sample-level weighting scheme to mitigate the bias. We further provide theoretical analysis suggesting that the weighting scheme helps mitigate satisfaction label bias. Extensive offline and online experiments on a large-scale industrial short video platform demonstrate that UAME consistently improves two state-of-the-art paradigms, EMER and EASQ, and better aligns with questionnaire-based user satisfaction. UAME has been deployed in our production short-video recommendation system and continues to deliver stable, statistically significant gains.

AI.tldr: UAME introduces uncertainty-aware modeling into multi-objective ensemble ranking for short video recommendation. By representing predictions as Gaussian distributions and designing a probabilistic pairwise ranking loss with sample-level uncertainty weighting, it mitigates label bias from conflicting behavioral signals (clicks, watch time). Deployed in production, it consistently outperforms EMER and EASQ baselines and aligns better with true user satisfaction.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-objective recommendation models rely on behavioral signals (clicks, watch time) as proxies for user satisfaction, but these signals are partial, fragmented, and mutually conflicting, introducing uncertainty and label bias. Conventional deterministic models ignore this uncertainty, while existing uncertainty-aware methods only use uncertainty for post-hoc ranking adjustments rather than addressing bias within the core optimization pipeline.
AI.method: UAME models each prediction as a Gaussian scoring variable with mean (predicted satisfaction) and variance (predictive uncertainty). It introduces a probabilistic pairwise ranking loss and an uncertainty-aware sample-level weighting scheme. The weighting scheme is theoretically grounded as a mechanism to mitigate satisfaction label bias during training.
AI.result: Extensive offline and online experiments on a large-scale industrial short video platform show UAME consistently improves two SOTA paradigms (EMER and EASQ) and achieves better alignment with questionnaire-based user satisfaction. It delivers stable, statistically significant gains in production.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating uncertainty directly into the optimization objective — rather than as a post-hoc adjustment — effectively mitigates label bias from noisy satisfaction proxies in short video recommendation, yielding both theoretical and practical improvements validated through industrial deployment.

title: Signal-based Model Access Risk Analysis for AI System Operations Security
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now ubiquitous across domains such as security, finance, healthcare, consumer technology, and large-scale cloud services, where they process massive volumes of data and make consequential decisions daily. This widespread adoption has created a broad attack surface through which adversaries can manipulate, evade, extract information from, or otherwise subvert deployed models. Depending on system design and exposure, attackers may have very different forms of access: some observe only final decisions, while others receive confidence scores, intermediate representations, or even full model parameters. While previous surveys typically organize evasion attacks into white-box, gray-box, and black-box categories based on the attacker's knowledge of model internals (architecture, parameters, gradients), this taxonomy often conflates different deployment scenarios that provide vastly different output signals, all labeled as ``black-box'' despite enabling fundamentally different attack strategies. Understanding how evasion attack strategies adapt to the specific information signals returned by deployed systems is critical for organizations making procurement and deployment decisions. To address this gap, we introduce the Signal-based Model Access Risk Taxonomy (SMART), a deployment-oriented framework that classifies attacker access according to the nature and richness of the information signals available from deployed AI systems. Using this taxonomy, we provide a structured overview of evasion attacks across progressively richer levels of information exposure, highlighting how deployment interfaces influence attack capabilities and informing more secure AI deployment and procurement decisions.

AI.tldr: Proposes SMART, a deployment-oriented taxonomy that classifies evasion attacks based on the information signals (decision, scores, representations, parameters) returned by deployed AI systems, rather than traditional white/gray/black-box categories, to better inform secure deployment and procurement decisions.
AI.motivation: The traditional white-box/gray-box/black-box taxonomy conflates fundamentally different deployment scenarios under "black-box" despite varying output signals (decisions-only vs. confidence scores vs. intermediate representations), which enable vastly different attack strategies. This gap hinders organizations from making informed procurement and deployment decisions regarding AI security.
AI.method: Introduces the Signal-based Model Access Risk Taxonomy (SMART), which classifies attacker access according to the nature and richness of information signals available from deployed AI systems. The paper then provides a structured survey of evasion attacks mapped across progressively richer levels of information exposure within this taxonomy.
AI.result: The SMART taxonomy reveals how deployment interfaces directly influence attacker capabilities, showing that different output signals—even under the same "black-box" label—enable fundamentally different attack strategies and risk profiles.
AI.conclusion: Adopting a signal-based taxonomy like SMART enables more precise security risk assessment of AI deployments, guiding both procurement choices and defensive hardening based on what information the system exposes.

title: Auto Research for Materials: Auditable AI-Scientist Workflows with Held-Out Transfer
summary: An AI research agent can improve the score it sees without finding a modelling change that works on new materials. We ask a stricter question. After repeated experiments, does the selected change survive on data that never entered the loop, and can its code be reused? We separate the search into changes to features, models, representations, and training data. Seven searches produce 701 evaluated changes across ten Matbench endpoints. Agents receive only the mean over five inner folds, reducing reliance on any single development split. We then freeze the selected code and evaluate it once on an untouched holdout. Nine of ten choices remain the best tested single intervention. The surviving changes reveal two materials modelling regimes. With composition alone, feature, model, and representation changes provide comparable routes to improvement. They include held-out MAE reductions of 17.4\% for band gap and 18.6\% for steel strength, as well as gains on both classification endpoints, while screened external data adds little. For structure tasks, richer geometry descriptors and model or calibration changes lower mean held-out MAE by 14.6\% and 7.1\% and lead on different property families, whereas composition embeddings do not transfer. Combining separately found feature and model changes yields a 26.3\% mean held-out improvement. These results show in materials prediction that closed-loop agents can produce decisions that survive unseen evidence and code changes that can be reused across tasks and combined. More broadly, they provide an evaluation design for testing executable discoveries beyond the feedback loop.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether AI research agents can produce modelling improvements that genuinely generalize beyond the development loop. Across 10 Matbench endpoints, 701 changes were tested under a rigorous protocol: agents optimize on inner-fold scores, then selected changes are frozen and evaluated once on untouched holdout data. Nine of ten agent-chosen interventions remained the best single change, with held-out MAE reductions up to 18.6%, and combining separately discovered changes yielded 26.3% improvement.
AI.motivation: AI research agents can overfit to development feedback by finding changes that improve scores without truly generalizing. The authors ask a stricter question: after closed-loop experimentation, does the selected modelling change survive on data that never entered the loop, and is its code reusable and recombinable? This addresses the critical gap between apparent improvement and genuine scientific discovery in automated materials modelling.
AI.method: The search space is taxonomized into four categories: feature changes, model changes, representation changes, and training data changes. Seven separate searches across ten Matbench endpoints yield 701 evaluated changes. Agents optimize using only the mean over five inner cross-validation folds (never seeing holdout). After selection, the winning change's code is frozen and evaluated exactly once on a pristine holdout set. Further tests assess reusability by transferring composition-derived embeddings to structure tasks, and combinability by merging independently discovered feature and model changes.
AI.result: Nine of ten agent-selected changes remained the best tested single intervention on holdout. Two distinct modelling regimes emerged: (1) For composition-only tasks, feature, model, and representation changes provided comparable improvement routes, with held-out MAE reductions of 17.4% (band gap) and 18.6% (steel strength), while screened external data added little. (2) For structure tasks, richer geometry descriptors and model/calibration changes lowered MAE by 14.6% and 7.1%, but composition embeddings did not transfer. Combining independently found feature and model changes yielded a 26.3% mean held-out improvement.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop AI agents can produce modelling decisions that survive unseen evidence and yield reusable, combinable code. The study provides a rigorous evaluation design for testing whether automated discoveries generalize beyond the feedback loop. The clear dichotomy between composition-based and structure-based modelling regimes offers practical guidance for materials prediction, and the demonstrated composability of independent changes suggests a path toward cumulative automated scientific progress.

title: A Survey on GNN-based Link Prediction: Techniques, Applications, and Challenges
comment: Submmit to WIREs: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery. This version of the article has been accepted, after peer review but is not the version of record. The final version will be available at: https://doi.org/10.1002/widm.70093. Paper list at Github: https://github.com/sunxiaobei/awesome-gnn-based-link-prediction
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the leading paradigm for link prediction, enabling the inference of missing connections and the anticipation of potential future links. However, existing reviews lack systematic exploration specifically targeting underlying GNN architectures and diverse graph structures. To address this critical gap, this paper provides a comprehensive review of GNN-based link prediction from a novel and dedicated GNN perspective. We propose an innovative taxonomy that categorizes recent advancements based on techniques and applications. From a technique perspective, we focus on key GNN encoder architectures, including GCN-based, GAE-based, GAT-based, and GFormer-based methods, discussing their strengths and limitations. From an application perspective, we highlight prominent use cases of link prediction in knowledge graphs and recommendation systems, demonstrating their real-world impact. In addition, we examine the current challenges and discuss promising future directions.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review of GNN-based link prediction, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes methods by GNN encoder architecture (GCN, GAE, GAT, GFormer) and by applications in knowledge graphs and recommendation systems, while also discussing challenges and future directions.
AI.motivation: Existing reviews on GNN-based link prediction lack systematic exploration targeting the underlying GNN architectures and diverse graph structures. The authors aim to fill this critical gap by providing a dedicated GNN-centric perspective.
AI.method: The paper proposes a novel taxonomy that categorizes recent advancements along two axes: (1) technique perspective — focusing on GNN encoder architectures (GCN-based, GAE-based, GAT-based, and GFormer-based methods), analyzing their strengths and limitations; (2) application perspective — highlighting prominent use cases in knowledge graphs and recommendation systems.
AI.result: The review systematically organizes and evaluates recent GNN-based link prediction methods according to the proposed taxonomy, demonstrating the real-world impact of these techniques and identifying current challenges and promising future research directions.
AI.conclusion: GNN-based link prediction is a rapidly evolving field with diverse architectural choices and impactful applications. The paper underscores the need for continued research to address existing challenges and explore emerging directions, providing a structured roadmap for future work.

title: Encoding EEG Signals to Examine Human-Like Next-Word Prediction Behaviour in Language Models
summary: Language models (LMs) are trained to excel at predicting the next word in the sequence given prior context, and humans also share this predictability in reading comprehension. Neuroscience research reveals that next-word predictability influences brain response, as recorded at millisecond resolution using electroencephalography (EEG). While our evidence indicates that advanced LMs achieve accuracies closely aligned with human performance at the next-word prediction task, this raises the question: Does higher prediction accuracy necessarily mean that these models adequately capture the cognitive signals associated with human reading comprehension? Here, we generate regressors for both humans and LMs based on two information measures, including top-1 prediction and surprisal, to predict event-related potential (ERP) elicited from EEG recordings which reflect different stages of cognitive processing during reading. We argue that modelling ERP patterns offers fine-grained analysis of the cognitive plausibility of various LMs during reading. Our results indicate that only surprisal potentially correlates with language-processing ERPs, especially for open-class words with high semantic content. Moreover, our findings challenge the assumption that scaling LMs with increased parameters and computational budgets will consistently lead to improved convergence with human-like linguistic processing.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether language models with high next-word prediction accuracy truly capture human cognitive signals during reading. Using EEG-derived ERPs, the authors find that only surprisal (not top-1 prediction) correlates with language-processing ERPs, particularly for semantically rich open-class words. Scaling up model size does not consistently improve alignment with human neural processing.
AI.motivation: While advanced LMs achieve near-human performance on next-word prediction, it remains unclear whether this behavioral alignment translates to cognitive plausibility — i.e., whether LMs process language in ways that mirror the neural mechanisms underlying human reading comprehension.
AI.method: The authors generate regressors from both humans and LMs using two information measures: top-1 prediction accuracy and surprisal. These regressors are used to predict ERPs recorded via EEG, which capture millisecond-level stages of cognitive processing during reading. ERP patterns serve as a fine-grained lens for evaluating cognitive plausibility across different LMs.
AI.result: Only surprisal shows potential correlation with language-processing ERPs, and this effect is most pronounced for open-class (high semantic content) words. Top-1 prediction does not reliably align with ERP patterns. Furthermore, scaling LMs with more parameters and compute does not consistently yield better convergence with human-like linguistic processing.
AI.conclusion: High next-word prediction accuracy in LMs does not guarantee cognitive plausibility. Surprisal emerges as a more neurally relevant metric than top-1 prediction. The findings caution against the assumption that simply scaling models will bridge the gap between artificial and human language processing.

title: LLM Unlearning for Cyber Defense: A Survey on Methods, Challenges, and Emerging Threats
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed in security-critical systems across healthcare, finance, education, and decision support, yet their inability to forget creates serious cybersecurity, privacy, and safety risks. Sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, hazardous domain knowledge, and memorized training data remain encoded across billions of parameters long after deployment, leaving models vulnerable to extraction, jailbreak attacks, membership inference, and regulatory non-compliance. Real-world incidents, from chatbots regenerating private information to fabricated legal citations producing direct legal and financial cost, place the problem at the center of the emerging-threats landscape rather than the realm of speculation. Because retraining billion-parameter models on revised corpora is computationally infeasible, and because knowledge within an LLM is distributed and entangled across parameters rather than localized to identifiable units, LLM unlearning has emerged as the principal cyber defense response, aiming to remove or suppress targeted knowledge from a trained model without retraining and without eroding what the model should still know. A central question, however, remains unresolved. Do current methods genuinely remove knowledge, or do they only stop the model from expressing it under ordinary prompting conditions? This survey examines LLM unlearning through the lens of security, robustness, and verifiable forgetting, with primary focus on gradient-based methods, which have come to dominate the field due to their compatibility with existing training pipelines and their scalability to billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: This abstract frames LLM unlearning as a critical cybersecurity defense against risks from retained sensitive, copyrighted, or hazardous knowledge in deployed models. It identifies gradient-based methods as the dominant approach and poses the central unresolved question: do unlearning methods truly erase knowledge or merely suppress its expression under normal prompting?
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in security-critical domains (healthcare, finance, education) retain sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, hazardous knowledge, and memorized training data across billions of parameters after deployment. This creates vulnerabilities to extraction attacks, jailbreaking, membership inference, and regulatory non-compliance. Real-world incidents (chatbots leaking private information, fabricated legal citations causing financial harm) confirm this is an active threat, not speculation. Full retraining is computationally infeasible for billion-parameter models, and knowledge is distributed/entangled rather than localized, making selective removal challenging.
AI.method: This is a survey paper that examines LLM unlearning through the lens of security, robustness, and verifiable forgetting. The primary focus is on gradient-based unlearning methods, which dominate the field due to their compatibility with existing training pipelines and scalability to billion-parameter models.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific empirical results but identifies a central unresolved research question: whether current unlearning methods genuinely remove knowledge from model parameters or merely suppress its expression under ordinary prompting conditions — a distinction with critical implications for security and verifiable forgetting.
AI.conclusion: LLM unlearning has emerged as the principal cyber defense response to the inherent inability of LLMs to forget. The field must resolve whether current methods achieve genuine knowledge removal or only superficial suppression, as this distinction determines whether unlearning constitutes a robust security guarantee or merely an obfuscation layer.

title: DataFlow-Harness: A Grounded Code-Agent Platform for Constructing Editable LLM Data Pipelines
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, and 5 tables. Technical report
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate data-processing workflows, yet coding agents typically produce scripts that are not automatically materialized as persistent, editable platform artifacts. We call this disconnect the \textit{NL2Pipeline gap}. To bridge it, we introduce \textsc{DataFlow-Harness}, a platform that guides an LLM agent to construct platform-native directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) through typed, incremental mutations rather than free-form scripts. The platform combines \textsc{DataFlow-Skills} for procedural guidance, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) layer that exposes the live operator registry and current pipeline state, and \textsc{DataFlow-WebUI}, which synchronizes conversational authoring with a visual DAG editor. On a 12-task data-engineering benchmark, \textsc{DataFlow-Harness} achieves a 93.3\% observed end-to-end pass rate. Relative to Vanilla Claude Code, it reduces measured monetary cost by 72.5\% and generation latency by 49.9\%; its observed pass rate is within 0.9 percentage points of the Context-Aware Claude Code baseline while its cost is 42.8\% lower. Per-task analysis indicates that Skills are most useful when construction depends on implicit procedural knowledge. These results show that live platform grounding can produce persistent, editable workflow artifacts with an observed reliability close to script-generation baselines and with lower measured construction cost and latency.

AI.tldr: DataFlow-Harness bridges the NL2Pipeline gap by guiding LLMs to construct platform-native DAGs via typed, incremental mutations, achieving 93.3% pass rate on a data-engineering benchmark while reducing cost by 72.5% and latency by 49.9% compared to Vanilla Claude Code.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents generate scripts that are not automatically materialized as persistent, editable platform artifacts — this is the "NL2Pipeline gap." The authors aim to bridge this by producing platform-native DAGs directly rather than free-form scripts.
AI.method: DataFlow-Harness combines three components: (1) DataFlow-Skills for procedural guidance, (2) an MCP layer exposing the live operator registry and pipeline state, and (3) DataFlow-WebUI synchronizing conversational authoring with a visual DAG editor. The system guides LLMs to construct DAGs through typed, incremental mutations.
AI.result: On a 12-task data-engineering benchmark, DataFlow-Harness achieves 93.3% end-to-end pass rate. Compared to Vanilla Claude Code: 72.5% lower monetary cost, 49.9% lower generation latency. Pass rate is within 0.9pp of Context-Aware Claude Code while cost is 42.8% lower. Per-task analysis shows Skills are most useful when tasks require implicit procedural knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Live platform grounding can produce persistent, editable workflow artifacts with reliability close to script-generation baselines while significantly reducing construction cost and latency.

title: Retrofitting Existing 3D Objects with Surface-Conforming Capacitive Sensing
comment: Accepted to ACM SIGGRAPH Conference Papers 2026
summary: Augmenting the surface of 3D objects with capacitive sensing is challenging when their volumes cannot be modified. In this paper, we present a generative computational fabrication pipeline that retrofits surface-only sensor layouts to 3D geometries for multi-touch interaction. Our method scans a real-world object to obtain its 3D mesh, generates and optimizes a 3D sensor design of drive and sense lines for mutual-capacitance sensing under physical and hardware constraints, and unfolds the design into individual 2D stencils that can be cut from conductive material. Our fabrication pipeline cuts these stencils from thin copper foil with a vinyl cutter and then assists manual sensor attachment by projecting the sensor design onto the dynamically registered real-world object. We connect the resulting electrode mesh to a mutual-capacitance scanning controller and resolve touch interaction in real time. We demonstrate our approach with four 3D geometries and evaluate our method and fabrication pipeline on them.

AI.tldr: A computational pipeline that retrofits capacitive multi-touch sensing onto arbitrary 3D object surfaces by generating optimized electrode layouts, fabricating them as 2D copper foil stencils, and projecting designs onto objects for assisted manual attachment.
AI.motivation: Enabling capacitive touch sensing on the surface of 3D objects is difficult when the object's volume cannot be modified (e.g., embedding electronics inside). Existing methods lack a systematic, automated way to design and fabricate surface-only sensor layouts for arbitrary 3D geometries.
AI.method: A generative computational fabrication pipeline: (1) 3D scanning the target object to obtain its mesh; (2) generating and optimizing drive/sense line layouts for mutual-capacitance sensing under physical and hardware constraints; (3) unfolding the 3D design into 2D stencils; (4) cutting stencils from thin copper foil using a vinyl cutter; (5) projecting the sensor design onto the dynamically registered object to guide manual attachment; (6) connecting the electrode mesh to a mutual-capacitance scanning controller for real-time touch resolution.
AI.result: The approach was demonstrated and evaluated on four diverse 3D geometries, showing successful real-time multi-touch interaction on each.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively enables surface-only capacitive sensing on arbitrary 3D objects, combining computational design optimization with a practical fabrication workflow that guides manual assembly.

title: Fenced Citation-Context Retrieval for Case Law: Temporal Leakage and Degree Control Across Two Jurisdictions
summary: Incoming citation context-the text with which later cases describe a case when citing it-is a strong signal for legal precedent retrieval, but it is evaluated without a temporal fence: at query time the target precedent has not yet been cited by future cases, so an unfenced method credits itself with evidence unavailable at deployment. Our central contribution is to measure how much: a temporal-admission decomposition that splits the naive relax-the-fence gain into genuine future-citation leakage, legitimate pre-query admission, and an index effect, reporting the phantom fraction-the share that is future evidence. We instantiate this as a controlled deployability audit of incoming-citation retrieval across two jurisdictions, CLERC (US federal, 1.84M documents) and ECtHR-PCR (European Court of Human Rights), adding a zero-training anchor channel that admits only citers dated before the query. On ECtHR-PCR only 14.9% of the naive gain is genuine future evidence; on CLERC the over-credit grows to +4.95 R@1000 as the fence is relaxed. Under the fence, the zero-training channel gains +16.1 R@1000 over BM25 on CLERC, clears a citation-degree control, and reaches a published R@1000 estimate similar to the strongest trained system on ECtHR-PCR (79.56 vs 79.39) at zero training.

AI.tldr: The paper audits legal precedent retrieval systems that use incoming citation context, revealing that standard evaluation inflates performance by leaking future citation evidence unavailable at deployment. The authors formalize a temporal-admission decomposition to quantify this leakage, finding that on ECtHR-PCR only 14.9% of the naive gain is genuine future evidence, while on CLERC the over-credit reaches +4.95 R@1000. A zero-training anchor channel restricted to pre-query citers matches or exceeds state-of-the-art trained systems, underscoring the severity of the leakage problem.
AI.motivation: Incoming citation context — the text used by later cases to describe a cited precedent — is a powerful signal for legal precedent retrieval. However, existing evaluations ignore temporal constraints: at query time (deployment), future citing cases do not yet exist, so models that exploit future citation text are credited with information they would not actually have. The authors aim to quantify this evaluation leakage and distinguish genuine pre-query signal from phantom future evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose a temporal-admission decomposition that splits the naive performance gain from relaxing the temporal fence into three components: (1) genuine future-citation leakage, (2) legitimate pre-query admission, and (3) an index effect. They report the "phantom fraction" — the share attributable to future evidence. This is instantiated as a controlled deployability audit across two legal corpora: CLERC (US federal, 1.84M documents) and ECtHR-PCR (European Court of Human Rights). A zero-training anchor channel is introduced that only admits citers dated before the query, serving as a temporally honest baseline.
AI.result: On ECtHR-PCR, only 14.9% of the naive gain from relaxing the temporal fence constitutes genuine future evidence. On CLERC, the over-credit grows to +4.95 R@1000 as the fence is relaxed. The zero-training anchor channel (under the fence) achieves +16.1 R@1000 over BM25 on CLERC, passes a citation-degree control, and on ECtHR-PCR reaches an R@1000 of 79.56 — comparable to the strongest published trained system (79.39) — all with zero training.
AI.conclusion: Standard incoming-citation retrieval evaluations suffer from substantial temporal leakage, crediting systems with future evidence unavailable at deployment. The proposed temporal-admission decomposition provides a rigorous framework for auditing this leakage. A simple zero-training baseline restricted to pre-query citers can match or exceed trained systems once temporal honesty is enforced, calling into question the real-world deployability of models evaluated without temporal fences.

title: TaintRadar: Semantic-Aware Taint-Style Vulnerability Detection via Augmented Code Property Graphs
summary: Despite significant advances, static vulnerability analysis suffers from three critical limitations: coarse sanitization modeling, which treats validation as a binary barrier; database blindness, which breaks taint tracking across persistence layers; and shallow object-oriented analysis, which misses field-level and interprocedural data flows. These flaws stem from a common root cause: Code Property Graph (CPG)-based taint analyses lack a compositional semantic layer to jointly model sanitization, persistence, and object aliasing. Consequently, existing tools generate excessive false positives or miss critical attack paths entirely. To address these limitations, we present TaintRadar, an approach that systematically augments CPGs with three semantic analysis layers. First, vulnerability-typed sanitization computes node-level safety guarantees using transfer functions and context-sensitive parameter binding. Second, persistence-aware propagation integrates database schema constraints and query safety analysis to track multi-script attack paths traversing shared database states. Finally, object-aware reaching definitions combine calling and bounded variable alias contexts to precisely model object-field mutations across method boundaries. We evaluate TaintRadar on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world systems. On the SARD benchmark, TaintRadar drastically reduces false positives while maintaining 80% overall accuracy. Deployed across 19 real-world PHP applications, it rediscovered the majority of known CVEs and uncovered 29 confirmed zero-day vulnerabilities, including 26 SQL injection and 3 stored XSS vulnerabilities, that have already received CVE identifiers. These results demonstrate that semantic-aware graph augmentation significantly improves the precision, coverage, and practical utility of static taint analysis.

AI.tldr: TaintRadar augments Code Property Graphs with three semantic layers—vulnerability-typed sanitization, persistence-aware propagation, and object-aware reaching definitions—to overcome fundamental limitations in static taint analysis. Evaluated on SARD and 19 real-world PHP apps, it achieves 80% accuracy, rediscovered most known CVEs, and uncovered 29 zero-days (26 SQLi, 3 stored XSS).
AI.motivation: Existing CPG-based static taint analyses suffer from three critical flaws: (1) coarse, binary sanitization modeling that lacks nuance; (2) database blindness that breaks taint tracking across persistence layers; and (3) shallow object-oriented analysis that misses field-level and interprocedural flows. These all stem from the absence of a compositional semantic layer for jointly modeling sanitization, persistence, and aliasing, leading to excessive false positives or missed attacks.
AI.method: TaintRadar systematically augments CPGs with three semantic analysis layers: (1) vulnerability-typed sanitization using transfer functions and context-sensitive parameter binding for node-level safety guarantees; (2) persistence-aware propagation that integrates database schema constraints and query safety analysis to track multi-script attack paths across shared database states; and (3) object-aware reaching definitions combining calling contexts and bounded variable alias contexts for precise object-field mutation modeling across method boundaries.
AI.result: On the SARD benchmark, TaintRadar drastically reduced false positives while maintaining 80% overall accuracy. Across 19 real-world PHP applications, it rediscovered the majority of known CVEs and uncovered 29 confirmed zero-day vulnerabilities (26 SQL injection, 3 stored XSS), all receiving CVE identifiers.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aware graph augmentation significantly improves the precision, coverage, and practical utility of static taint analysis, demonstrating that adding compositional semantic layers to CPGs effectively addresses long-standing weaknesses in sanitization modeling, persistence tracking, and object-oriented analysis.

title: The Optimization Trilemma: Efficiency, Comfort and Fairness in Decentralized Multi-agent Coordination
summary: The problem of fair multi-agent coordination in decentralized settings is one of the most pressing challenges for building efficient collaborative systems. Resource allocation is based on optimized collective arrangements accounting for agents' needs. Such coordination should not only be computationally efficient but also account for fairness, i.e., equitable redistribution of costs incurred by all agents. Recent literature has proposed several algorithms that efficiently determine optimal plan combinations balancing system-wide efficiency and individual discomfort of agents in a centralized setting. However, these works do not address equitable resource optimization in fully decentralized scenarios, specifically, the optimized redistribution of discomfort among coordinating agents so that none experiences a discomfort level that could lead to loss of incentive or polarization that can disrupt planned operations. In this work, we study the problem of optimizing three objectives: (i) system-wide efficiency, (ii) individuals' comfort and (iii) fairness (i.e., balancing of incurred discomfort costs) in decentralized multi-agent coordination. We design a novel model to optimize those three orthogonal objectives, without any substantial increase in communication and computational overhead. Through experiments on two real-world datasets, we validate the model and demonstrate that it can achieve fairer optimization outcomes, while satisfying agents' preferences and system goals.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses fair decentralized multi-agent coordination by jointly optimizing system-wide efficiency, individual comfort, and equitable redistribution of discomfort costs, proposing a novel model that achieves fairer outcomes without significant communication or computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing fair multi-agent coordination algorithms operate in centralized settings and do not address equitable resource optimization in fully decentralized scenarios. Specifically, there is no mechanism for redistributing discomfort among agents to prevent any single agent from experiencing disproportionate costs that could lead to loss of incentive or polarization, disrupting planned operations.
AI.method: The authors design a novel optimization model that simultaneously addresses three orthogonal objectives: system-wide efficiency, individual comfort, and fairness (balancing incurred discomfort costs) in decentralized multi-agent coordination, while keeping communication and computational overhead minimal.
AI.result: Experiments on two real-world datasets validate that the proposed model achieves fairer optimization outcomes compared to existing approaches, while satisfying both agent preferences and system goals.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model successfully enables fair decentralized multi-agent coordination by jointly optimizing efficiency, comfort, and fairness without substantial overhead, advancing the state of the art beyond centralized-only solutions.

title: PlanFlip: Attacking Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Planning-Phase Prompt Injection
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on a Planner to decompose goals into sub-task sequences that downstream Executor and Critic agents execute and audit. We identify the planning phase as a critical attack surface: a single injection into the Planner's context achieves cascade amplification, corrupting all downstream sub-tasks simultaneously. We introduce PlanFlip, a framework comprising four planning-phase prompt injection attacks -- GoalSubstitution (PF-1), PriorityInversion (PF-2), ContextPollution (PF-3), and RoleConfusion (PF-4) -- each disguised as plausible tool outputs to evade keyword filters. Evaluating nine frontier LLMs across 3,479 episodes, we uncover three findings: (1) capability amplifies vulnerability -- GPT-5 achieves the highest attack success rate (ASR = 0.68), contradicting the assumption that stronger models are inherently more secure; (2) homogeneous pipelines exhibit a correlated-agent blind spot -- GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B show ASR near 0 yet Stealth = 1.00 and StepShift > 0, with attacks restructuring plans while the same-backbone Critic reports alignment (two independent judges confirm -0.20 to -0.32 semantic deviation, r = 0.943); (3) reasoning-augmented models resist injections -- DeepSeek-R1 achieves StepShift = 0.00 across all attacks. We propose GoalAnchorCheck (D1) and CrossAgentConsensus (D2), achieving detection rates up to 1.00 and outperforming same-backbone baselines in 15 of 16 cells. Our key insight: heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite for multi-agent systems; redundancy within a homogeneous backbone provides no protection against planning-phase attacks.

AI.tldr: PlanFlip introduces four planning-phase prompt injection attacks on multi-agent LLM systems that achieve cascade amplification—a single injection corrupting all downstream sub-tasks. Experiments across 3,479 episodes reveal that stronger models are more vulnerable, homogeneous agent pipelines have correlated blind spots, and reasoning-augmented models resist attacks. Two defenses (GoalAnchorCheck, CrossAgentConsensus) outperform same-backbone baselines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems decompose goals via a Planner agent whose outputs feed downstream Executor and Critic agents. The planning phase represents an under-explored attack surface where a single prompt injection can cascade through the entire pipeline, yet existing security research focuses primarily on single-agent or execution-phase vulnerabilities rather than planning-phase amplification.
AI.method: The authors propose PlanFlip, a framework with four attack types: GoalSubstitution (PF-1) replaces the original goal; PriorityInversion (PF-2) reorders task priorities; ContextPollution (PF-3) injects misleading context; and RoleConfusion (PF-4) causes the Planner to assume an incorrect role. Each attack is disguised as plausible tool output to evade keyword filters. Evaluation spans nine frontier LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1, etc.) across 3,479 episodes, measuring Attack Success Rate, Stealth, and StepShift. Two defenses are proposed: GoalAnchorCheck (D1), which anchors plans to original goals, and CrossAgentConsensus (D2), which cross-validates across heterogeneous agents.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Capability amplifies vulnerability—GPT-5 achieves the highest ASR (0.68), countering the assumption that stronger models are more secure. (2) Homogeneous pipelines exhibit a correlated-agent blind spot—GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B show ASR ≈ 0 yet Stealth = 1.00 and StepShift > 0, with same-backbone Critics failing to detect restructured plans (confirmed by two independent judges with -0.20 to -0.32 semantic deviation, r = 0.943). (3) Reasoning-augmented models resist injections—DeepSeek-R1 achieves StepShift = 0.00 across all attacks. Defenses D1 and D2 achieve detection rates up to 1.00, outperforming same-backbone baselines in 15 of 16 cells.
AI.conclusion: The core insight is that heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite for multi-agent systems; homogeneous backbones provide no protection against planning-phase attacks because correlated errors propagate undetected. Defenses must incorporate cross-model consensus mechanisms rather than relying on same-model auditing.

title: NOWJ@COLIEE 2026: Adaptive Pipelines for Legal Retrieval and Reasoning
summary: This paper presents the methodologies and results of the NOWJ team's participation across all five tasks of the COLIEE 2026 competition. For Task 1 (Legal Case Retrieval), we propose a four-stage pipeline comprising candidate filtering, dense retrieval with complementary embedding models, cross-encoder reranking via fine-tuned generative rerankers and MLP-based pairwise classification, and adaptive per-query cutoff prediction. For Task 2 (Legal Case Entailment), we combine BM25 filtering, T5-based reranking, and LLM-based entailment verification with consensus ensemble. For Task 3 (Statute Law Retrieval and Entailment), we adopt a retrieval-augmented generation framework with dense retrieval, attention-based reranking, and few-shot-prompted LLM reasoning. For Task 4 (Legal Textual Entailment), we introduce a dynamic routing pipeline that classifies query difficulty and dispatches cases to either a balanced few-shot solver or a structured zero-shot chain-of-thought solver. For the Pilot Task (Legal Judgment Prediction), we combine hierarchical transformers with CRF layers, argument relation mining, and probabilistic argumentation graph reasoning.

AI.tldr: The NOWJ team presents a multi-pronged approach to all five COLIEE 2026 legal AI tasks, employing stage-wise pipelines (retrieval→reranking, filtering→verification), retrieval-augmented generation, dynamic routing based on query difficulty, and neuro-symbolic reasoning with argumentation graphs.
AI.motivation: To address the diverse challenges of the COLIEE 2026 competition—spanning case retrieval, entailment, statute law reasoning, and judgment prediction—with tailored, state-of-the-art architectures that combine dense/sparse retrieval, large language models, and structured reasoning.
AI.method: Task 1 uses a four-stage retrieval pipeline (candidate filtering → complementary dense retrieval → cross-encoder reranking with generative rerankers and MLP pairwise classification → adaptive cutoff prediction). Task 2 combines BM25 filtering, T5 reranking, and LLM entailment verification with consensus ensemble. Task 3 adopts retrieval-augmented generation with dense retrieval, attention-based reranking, and few-shot LLM reasoning. Task 4 introduces a dynamic routing pipeline that classifies query difficulty and dispatches to either balanced few-shot or structured zero-shot chain-of-thought solvers. The Pilot Task combines hierarchical transformers with CRF layers, argument relation mining, and probabilistic argumentation graph reasoning.
AI.result: Results are not specified in the abstract; the paper describes methodologies and results but the abstract does not enumerate quantitative outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract. The paper presumably demonstrates that combining traditional IR techniques with LLMs and structured reasoning yields competitive performance across diverse legal AI tasks.

title: Operator-Aware Mixed-Precision Tolerance Calibration for Tensor Kernels
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, LNCS format. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.20128 (P1). Additional companions (P3, P4) to follow on arXiv this week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary:
Most tensor-kernel correctness tests go through a fixed-shape all close-style check with hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances. The thresholds are copied across the corpus and rarely revisited. We mine the element-wise error distribution of every test case from accumulated cloud GPU runs across the 26-entry gpuemu corpus and 2 dtypes (8,076 result rows). We then ask one empirical question: what absolute tolerance would the kernel itself, observed under its correct implementation, justify?
  The answer is much tighter than the current hand-picked atol. The largest tightening is attention_triton fp16 at $2{,}184\times$. Restricted to the seven LLM-style buggy variants for which the corpus ships a paired correct counterpart, calibrated per-(op, dtype) tolerances raise bug-detection recall from 73.2% (1,805 of 2,467) to 82.4% (2,034 of 2,467), an absolute gain of 9.3 percentage points (+229 new detections). The control false-positive count rises from 0 to 20 out of 1,882 correct-control cases (+1.1 percentage points).

AI.tldr: This paper examines error distributions from cloud GPU runs across 26 GPU kernel implementations, finding that empirically calibrated absolute tolerances are up to 2,184× tighter than hand-picked defaults, and these calibrated tolerances improve bug-detection recall from 73.2% to 82.4% with only a 1.1 percentage point increase in false positives.
AI.motivation: Current GPU kernel correctness testing relies on fixed, hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances that are copied across codebases and rarely revisited. These arbitrary thresholds may be unnecessarily loose, allowing bugs to go undetected. The authors aim to determine what tolerances the kernels themselves empirically justify under correct implementation.
AI.method: The authors mine element-wise error distributions from accumulated cloud GPU runs across a 26-entry "gpuemu" corpus with 2 dtypes, yielding 8,076 result rows. They compute the empirical maximum absolute error observed for each (operation, dtype) pair under correct implementations, then use these as calibrated per-(op, dtype) tolerances. They evaluate these calibrated tolerances on seven LLM-style buggy kernel variants that have paired correct counterparts, measuring detection recall and false-positive rates.
AI.result: Calibrated tolerances are dramatically tighter than hand-picked ones — the largest tightening being attention_triton fp16 at 2,184×. Using calibrated per-(op, dtype) tolerances raises bug-detection recall from 73.2% (1,805/2,467) to 82.4% (2,034/2,467), a 9.3 percentage point gain (+229 new detections). False positives rise modestly from 0 to 20 out of 1,882 correct-control cases (+1.1 pp).
AI.conclusion: Empirically calibrated tolerances derived from correct-kernel error behavior substantially outperform hand-picked defaults, significantly improving bug detection with minimal false-positive cost. The findings advocate for data-driven, per-operation tolerance calibration over static, copy-pasted thresholds in GPU kernel testing.

title: CLOSER-Bench: Evaluating Budgeted Cross-Stage Design Closure for Hardware Agents
summary: Hardware engineering exposes coding agents to a form of long-horizon work that is difficult to capture with pass-at-k: progress is continuous, tool feedback is delayed and heterogeneous, and a backend failure may require revising RTL rather than tuning another physical-design parameter. Existing benchmarks measure RTL generation, repository repair, verification, PPA evolution, or physical implementation, but their different designs and oracles make it hard to determine where an agent succeeds or fails across abstraction boundaries. We introduce CLOSER-Bench, a controlled evaluation protocol for budgeted cross-stage design closure. For one design and one hidden objective, it pairs spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS tasks, records every simulator, synthesis, STA, and place-and-route invocation, and measures final quality, anytime progress, tool cost, and cross-stage recovery. The benchmark is built on open-source Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout, Sky130, and the Harbor agent harness. A ten-task pilot spanning RTL repair, mutation-based verification, coverage, PPA optimization, design-space exploration, cross-model debugging, and security establishes the executable harness and exposes a sharp completion--closure gap: three agents solve a localized AXI repair task, while the matched verification-closure task separates a frontier agent from two otherwise successful baselines. We further validate a full RTL-to-GDS flow and construct a macro-based AXI/DMA streaming accelerator for the stage-paired evaluation. These results motivate treating hardware closure as a budgeted sequential decision problem rather than a collection of independent code generation tasks.

AI.tldr: CLOSER-Bench introduces a controlled evaluation protocol for hardware design closure that pairs spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS tasks under a unified budgeted framework. It measures final quality, anytime progress, tool cost, and cross-stage recovery. A ten-task pilot reveals a sharp completion–closure gap: agents succeed at localized RTL repair but struggle when verification closure is required, motivating hardware closure as a budgeted sequential decision problem.
AI.motivation: Existing hardware agent benchmarks measure isolated tasks (RTL generation, verification, PPA optimization, physical design) with incompatible designs and oracles, making it impossible to assess agent performance across abstraction boundaries. Hardware engineering involves continuous progress with delayed, heterogeneous tool feedback, and backend failures often demand upstream RTL revisions — a cross-stage challenge no current benchmark captures.
AI.method: CLOSER-Bench defines a budgeted cross-stage design closure protocol with three paired task types: spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS. It records every invocation of Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout (Sky130 PDK), and the Harbor agent harness. A ten-task pilot covers RTL repair, mutation-based verification, coverage, PPA optimization, design-space exploration, cross-model debugging, and security. The benchmark also validates a full RTL-to-GDS flow with a macro-based AXI/DMA streaming accelerator.
AI.result: The pilot reveals a completion–closure gap: three agents solve a localized AXI repair task, but the matched verification-closure task separates a frontier agent from two otherwise capable baselines. This demonstrates that task-level completion does not imply cross-stage closure competence.
AI.conclusion: Hardware closure should be framed as a budgeted sequential decision problem rather than a collection of independent code generation tasks. CLOSER-Bench provides the first executable harness for evaluating agents across the full design closure spectrum.

title: SAVEstate: A Method for Documenting Player Reflection in Digital Games
comment: Accepted for publication at CHI PLAY 2026
summary: In recent years, interest in eudaimonic player experiences (PX) - concerning reflection, meaning-making, and personal growth - has increased. However, most games user research methods are not well-suited to study eudaimonic PX, as they have been developed to evaluate features of hedonic PX, such as flow, immersion, and playability. To more deeply explore eudaimonic PX, we require methods that can 1) investigate how moment-to-moment PX shapes player reflection and 2) explore how players reengage and reinterpret their experiences longitudinally. In this paper, we present SAVEstate, a method that uses documentation as a means of studying player reflection. SAVEstate consists of two phases: reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action, which allow researchers to probe players' in-situ reflections and how they reengage with their gameplay, respectively. Using SAVEstate, we were able to observe in-situ meaning-making and connect it to post-game reflection-on-action, and view synchronous sensemaking across multiple participants. We also developed an open-source desktop application for researchers to adapt in their own SAVEstate deployments. We discuss implications for how researchers might use SAVEstate to conduct future research in meaningful PX.

AI.tldr: SAVEstate is a two-phase documentation-based method for studying eudaimonic player experiences — capturing in-situ meaning-making (reflection-in-action) and longitudinal reinterpretation (reflection-on-action) — with an open-source desktop application to support future research.
AI.motivation: Existing games user research methods are designed for hedonic PX (flow, immersion, playability) and are ill-suited for eudaimonic PX, which involves reflection, meaning-making, and personal growth. There is a need for methods that capture both moment-to-moment PX shaping reflection and longitudinal re-engagement with gameplay experiences.
AI.method: SAVEstate is a documentation-based method with two phases: (1) reflection-in-action — probing players' in-situ reflections during gameplay; (2) reflection-on-action — exploring how players reengage with and reinterpret their experiences post-gameplay. An open-source desktop application was developed for researchers to adapt in their own deployments.
AI.result: The method successfully enabled observation of in-situ meaning-making, connected moment-to-moment reflections to post-game reflection-on-action, and facilitated viewing synchronous sensemaking across multiple participants.
AI.conclusion: SAVEstate offers a viable methodological contribution for studying meaningful, eudaimonic PX, with implications for future research directions in this domain.

title: Learning Sparse Representations of Multimodal Content for Enhanced Cold Item Recommendation
summary: The scale and rapid growth of item catalogs in modern digital platforms present significant challenges to recommender system (RS) practitioners. Most RSs use embedding similarity to predict user-item preferences, but embedding storage and low-latency retrieval is challenging in industry-scale catalogs. Furthermore, newly added items do not have corresponding embeddings and cannot be recommended effectively; previous works often tackle this item cold-start problem by generating cold item representations from auxiliary content, such as images or descriptive text, so that user preferences can be predicted without historical interactions. In this paper, we argue that sparse embeddings have notable advantages over standard dense vectors in this content-based cold-start paradigm. We describe how existing cold-start training regimes can be adapted for sparse representation learning, and build on insights from linear attention to design a pre-sparsification activation technique that induces sharpness and denoising effects in learned item-item similarities.
