We show that the resulting sparse embeddings achieve significant improvements in cold-start recommendation accuracy over dense embeddings at considerably lower storage costs, especially for users with multiple interests. Through comprehensive experiments on four multimodal RS datasets, we also demonstrate the interpretability of sparse content embeddings and their robustness in the trade-off between size and accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using sparse embeddings instead of dense vectors for content-based cold-start recommendation. The authors adapt cold-start training for sparse representation learning and introduce a pre-sparsification activation technique inspired by linear attention to improve similarity sharpness and denoising. Sparse embeddings achieve better cold-start accuracy with significantly lower storage costs, especially for multi-interest users, and offer interpretability benefits.
AI.motivation: Modern RS platforms face two key challenges: (1) embedding storage and low-latency retrieval at industry scale, and (2) the item cold-start problem where new items lack embeddings from historical interactions. While prior work uses auxiliary content (images, text) to generate dense embeddings for cold items, the authors argue that sparse embeddings offer compelling advantages in this content-based cold-start paradigm that have been underexplored.
AI.method: The authors adapt existing cold-start training regimes for sparse representation learning. They leverage insights from linear attention mechanisms to design a pre-sparsification activation function that induces sharpness and denoising in learned item-item similarities. The resulting sparse content embeddings are trained and evaluated on multimodal RS datasets.
AI.result: Sparse embeddings achieve significant improvements in cold-start recommendation accuracy over dense embeddings at substantially lower storage costs. Benefits are especially pronounced for users with multiple interests. The approach also demonstrates interpretability and robustness in the size-accuracy trade-off across four multimodal RS datasets.
AI.conclusion: Sparse embeddings are a superior alternative to dense vectors for content-based cold-start recommendation, offering better accuracy, lower storage, interpretability, and robustness. The pre-sparsification activation technique derived from linear attention is key to achieving these gains.

title: Fuzz'EMup: Leveraging EM Side-Channel Emanation to Guide Black-Box Embedded Firmware Fuzzing
summary: As IoT and embedded devices proliferate across various domains, securing their firmware has become critical. Fuzzing offers a systematic approach to uncovering vulnerabilities in firmware, and coverage feedback can improve its effectiveness by guiding exploration. However, many devices make coverage information impossible to obtain by preventing firmware extraction, instrumentation, or accurate emulation; in such cases, testers are left with only inefficient black-box fuzzing. In this paper, we present an approach that leverages electromagnetic (EM) side-channel emanations to guide firmware fuzzing in purely black-box settings. However, turning raw EM measurements into reliable guidance is challenging: EM traces are noisy, and timing jitter causes corresponding features in different traces to shift in time. We address these challenges by combining frequency band selection based on the activity-to-idle signal contrast with dynamic time warping to align per-input traces and detect sustained divergence, while maintaining scalability by organizing executions in a tree structure based on their divergence times. We evaluate our approach on four real firmware targets and demonstrate that EM-derived feedback enhances path exploration, yielding higher code coverage than unguided fuzzing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a black-box firmware fuzzing approach guided by electromagnetic (EM) side-channel emanations, overcoming the lack of coverage information when firmware extraction, instrumentation, or emulation is infeasible. It combines frequency band selection, dynamic time warping (DTW), and a tree-structured execution organization to handle noisy EM traces with timing jitter, demonstrating improved code coverage over unguided fuzzing on four real firmware targets.
AI.motivation: Many IoT and embedded devices prevent firmware extraction, instrumentation, or accurate emulation, making traditional coverage-guided fuzzing impossible and leaving testers with only inefficient black-box fuzzing. The authors aim to recover a guidance signal from the physical side-channel (EM emanations) to improve fuzzing effectiveness in these purely black-box settings.
AI.method: The approach uses EM side-channel emanations as a coverage proxy. Raw EM traces are processed through: (1) frequency band selection based on activity-to-idle signal contrast to isolate informative frequency components; (2) dynamic time warping (DTW) to align per-input traces and detect sustained divergence despite timing jitter; and (3) a tree-structured organization of executions based on their divergence times to maintain scalability. This divergence-based feedback then guides the fuzzer's exploration.
AI.result: Evaluation on four real firmware targets shows that EM-derived feedback enhances path exploration, yielding higher code coverage compared to unguided (black-box) fuzzing.
AI.conclusion: EM side-channel emanations can serve as a viable and effective coverage proxy for guiding firmware fuzzing in black-box scenarios where traditional instrumentation is unavailable, and the proposed signal processing techniques (frequency band selection + DTW + tree-based divergence tracking) are key to making this reliable and scalable.

title: A Digital Twin-Based Method for Evaluating Local Collective Tariffs in Distribution-Level Energy Systems
summary: This work addresses the need for engineering-grounded evaluation of implement-ed tariff mechanisms in distribution-level energy systems. A digital twin-based method is proposed for assessing local collective tariffs under realistic behavioral and infrastructural conditions. The approach integrates agent-based modeling of household consumption and generation, virtual aggregation through a shared metering abstraction, and explicit representation of tariff logic within a unified simulation environment. The method is demonstrated through its application to the Danish Local Collective Tariff across representative residential energy community configurations, including scenarios with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, and electric vehicle charging. Results indicate that aggregation of heterogeneous demand profiles reduces peak coincidence and enables more efficient allocation of tariff components, leading to measurable cost reductions at the community level. At the same time, the outcomes reveal sensitivity to the temporal alignment of consumption and generation, influencing the degree of cost neutrality across participants. The findings illustrate how digital twin-based evaluation can support systematic assessment of tariff mechanisms by capturing the interaction between infrastructure, user behavior, and regulatory design. The proposed approach provides a basis for analyzing and comparing tariff structures in distribution-level energy systems beyond the specific case considered.

AI.tldr: A digital twin-based method integrating agent-based modeling and virtual metering is proposed to evaluate local collective tariffs in distribution-level energy systems. Demonstrated on the Danish Local Collective Tariff, results show that demand aggregation reduces peak coincidence and costs, though outcomes are sensitive to temporal alignment of consumption and generation.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of engineering-grounded evaluation methods for implemented tariff mechanisms in distribution-level energy systems, particularly under realistic behavioral and infrastructural conditions.
AI.method: A digital twin-based methodology integrating: (1) agent-based modeling of household consumption and generation, (2) virtual aggregation via a shared metering abstraction, and (3) explicit representation of tariff logic within a unified simulation environment. The method is applied to the Danish Local Collective Tariff across residential energy community configurations with PV, battery storage, and EV charging.
AI.result: Aggregation of heterogeneous demand profiles reduces peak coincidence and enables more efficient tariff allocation, yielding measurable community-level cost reductions. However, cost neutrality across participants is sensitive to temporal alignment of consumption and generation.
AI.conclusion: Digital twin-based evaluation effectively captures the interaction between infrastructure, user behavior, and regulatory design, providing a systematic basis for analyzing and comparing tariff structures in distribution-level energy systems beyond the specific Danish case.

title: Deterministic Replay for AI Agent Systems
summary:
AI agent systems that couple large language models (LLMs) with external tools and APIs are inherently non-deterministic: LLM sampling variance, external API state, CDN infrastructure headers, and execution-environment noise collectively prevent any prior agent run from being faithfully re-executed. Existing observability platforms capture execution logs but cannot reproduce a run in isolation. We present agrepl, a developer-first CLI framework for deterministic replay of agent executions. agrepl intercepts all external interactions at the transport layer via a man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy, serialises them as structured execution traces, and replays them in a strictly isolated environment with zero outbound network access. We formalise the agent execution model, define the request-key matching function K(s), and prove the determinism invariant. We introduce a noise-aware diff algorithm classifying HTTP header divergence into signal and noise tiers. Empirical evaluation across five workloads (n = 250 replay instances) demonstrates replay fidelity F = 1.0 and a median per-step latency reduction of 98.3%. agrepl is implemented in Go, ships as a single static binary, and is released under the MIT licence.
  Keywords: AI agents, deterministic replay, LLM debugging, reproducibility, MITM proxy, execution tracing, record/replay systems.

AI.tldr: agrepl is a CLI framework that enables deterministic replay of AI agent executions by intercepting all external interactions via a MITM proxy, serializing them as structured traces, and replaying them in a fully isolated, network-disabled environment. It achieves perfect replay fidelity (F=1.0) and 98.3% latency reduction.
AI.motivation: AI agent systems combining LLMs with external tools/APIs are inherently non-deterministic due to LLM sampling variance, external API state changes, CDN headers, and execution-environment noise. Existing observability tools can log executions but cannot faithfully reproduce a prior run, making debugging and reproducibility impossible.
AI.method: agrepl uses a man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy at the transport layer to intercept all external interactions, serializes them as structured execution traces, and replays them in a strictly isolated environment with zero outbound network access. It formalizes an agent execution model, defines a request-key matching function K(s), proves a determinism invariant, and introduces a noise-aware diff algorithm that classifies HTTP header divergence into signal and noise tiers.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across five workloads with 250 replay instances shows replay fidelity F = 1.0 (perfect reproduction) and a median per-step latency reduction of 98.3% compared to live execution.
AI.conclusion: agrepl provides a practical, formally-grounded solution for deterministic replay of non-deterministic LLM-agent executions, significantly improving debugging workflows for AI agent developers. Implemented as a single Go binary under the MIT license.

title: From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Existing memory systems for long-horizon LLM agents often retrieve prior traces as passive context rather than converting them into executable capabilities. In this paper, we propose MSCE, a training-free Memory--Skill Co-Evolution framework that organizes agent experience into grounded step traces, reusable procedural policies, and declarative environmental cognition. MSCE crystallizes evidence-backed L2 policies with positive estimated gain into callable skills that retain evidence links, applicability boundaries, decision guidance, verification rules, and reliability estimates. It further introduces reflection-weighted value backfilling, which propagates sparse terminal feedback through dense local self-reflections to produce evidence-calibrated trace values for governing memory and skill evolution. Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo demonstrate that MSCE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art skill-augmented and memory-driven agent baselines, exhibiting strong cross-domain transferability and lifelong-evolution capabilities.

AI.tldr: MSCE is a training-free framework that co-evolves agent memory and skills by converting interaction traces into callable, evidence-backed procedural policies with reliability estimates, and introduces reflection-weighted value backfilling to propagate sparse terminal feedback into dense trace values for governing lifelong agent evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for long-horizon LLM agents passively store and retrieve prior traces as context, failing to convert accumulated experience into structured, executable capabilities. There is a need for a framework that actively organizes experience into reusable skills with grounded evidence and reliability estimates.
AI.method: MSCE organizes agent experience into three layers: (1) grounded step traces, (2) reusable procedural policies (L2 policies), and (3) declarative environmental cognition. Key mechanisms include: crystallizing evidence-backed L2 policies with positive estimated gain into callable skills (retaining evidence links, applicability boundaries, decision guidance, verification rules, and reliability estimates), and reflection-weighted value backfilling, which propagates sparse terminal feedback through dense local self-reflections to produce evidence-calibrated trace values for governing memory and skill evolution.
AI.result: Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo demonstrate that MSCE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art skill-augmented and memory-driven agent baselines, exhibiting strong cross-domain transferability and lifelong-evolution capabilities.
AI.conclusion: MSCE provides an effective training-free approach for enabling LLM agents to continuously convert passive experience into executable skills, supporting robust lifelong learning and cross-domain transfer through evidence-calibrated memory-skill co-evolution.

title: RouteCost: A Production-Inspired Multi-Stage Framework for Pre-Order Shipping Cost Estimation in E-Commerce
summary: Accurate pre-order shipping cost estimation is important in e-commerce because it affects price presentation, margin planning, and conversion. In practice, shipping cost is shaped not only by distance but also by destination demand mix, billable weight, dimensional pricing, surcharge triggers, and latent operational effects such as shipment consolidation. Static lookup methods therefore miss important sources of variation, while monolithic regressors may exploit strong but non-causal correlations. We propose RouteCost, a production-inspired multi-stage framework that decomposes the problem into time-aware demand forecasting, fee-card-informed baseline pricing, Stage 2 residual correction, and proxy-based box-consolidation inference. Route-level cost estimates are aggregated through a route-weighted expectation formulation to produce product-level shipping cost predictions. Across over 250,000 orders, 260 products, and 18 months of order history, the framework improves predictive quality and aggregate calibration while preserving route-level interpretability.

AI.tldr: RouteCost is a multi-stage framework for pre-order shipping cost estimation that decomposes the problem into demand forecasting, fee-card-based pricing, residual correction, and box-consolidation inference, improving accuracy and calibration over static methods and monolithic regressors while preserving interpretability.
AI.motivation: Accurate pre-order shipping cost estimation is critical for e-commerce pricing and margin planning. Static lookup methods ignore key cost drivers (demand mix, billable weight, dimensional pricing, surcharges, consolidation effects), while monolithic regressors risk exploiting non-causal correlations. A principled, interpretable decomposition is needed.
AI.method: RouteCost decomposes shipping cost estimation into four stages: (1) time-aware demand forecasting to capture destination mix dynamics, (2) fee-card-informed baseline pricing using carrier rate structures, (3) Stage 2 residual correction to capture unmodeled operational effects, and (4) proxy-based box-consolidation inference to account for shipment consolidation. Route-level estimates are aggregated via a route-weighted expectation formulation for product-level predictions.
AI.result: Evaluated on over 250,000 orders, 260 products, and 18 months of order history, RouteCost demonstrates improved predictive quality and aggregate calibration compared to baselines while maintaining route-level interpretability.
AI.conclusion: A multi-stage, production-inspired decomposition of shipping cost estimation outperforms both static lookup methods and black-box regression approaches, offering a practical solution that balances accuracy, calibration, and interpretability for e-commerce applications.

title: Falsification-Based Verification of LLM-Generated Optimization Models: Sound Test Batteries and Their Detection Limits
summary: Large language models now translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into solver-ready optimization models, but they fail silently. A generated model often runs and still formulates the wrong problem. This paper develops a theory of falsification-based verification for this setting. Every numeric quantity in the description is a typed slot, and a candidate model is tested only through solver calls on slot-transformed instances; no reference model or label is consulted. From duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limit arguments we derive a battery of test classes covering directions, curvature, crush probes, prohibitive limits, annihilation, and exchange. Every test is sound, so a violation certifies unfaithfulness and the false-positive rate is zero by design. We characterize what such verification can never see, give conditions under which the canonical error classes are detected with certainty, and prove that no fixed-threshold perturbation tester is simultaneously sound and nontrivial. Experiments on 326 ground-truth models from NL4OPT and four benchmark families confirm the theory. The battery attains a 0.0% false-positive rate against 54.9% for a threshold tester, detects 70.0% of certified conditional-class mutants, convicts 40.4% of the mutants invisible to execution-accuracy scoring, and reproduces the predicted detectability pattern including its zeros.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a falsification-based verification framework for optimization models generated by LLMs from natural language. Using typed slots, duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limits, it derives sound test classes (zero false-positive rate by design) that detect when a generated model formulates the wrong problem. Experiments confirm the theory, achieving 0% false positives and detecting many mutants invisible to execution-accuracy scoring.
AI.motivation: LLMs can translate natural-language decision problem descriptions into optimization models, but they fail silently — a generated model may run successfully yet encode the wrong problem. There is no existing verification approach that tests faithfulness without requiring a reference model or ground-truth labels.
AI.method: The authors treat every numeric quantity in the description as a typed slot and test candidate models solely through solver calls on slot-transformed instances. They derive a battery of test classes (directions, curvature, crush probes, prohibitive limits, annihilation, exchange) grounded in duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limit arguments. Each test is sound by construction (zero false-positive rate). They characterize inherent limitations of such verification, prove conditions for guaranteed detection of canonical error classes, and prove that no fixed-threshold perturbation tester can be both sound and nontrivial.
AI.result: On 326 ground-truth models from NL4OPT and four benchmark families: the battery achieves a 0.0% false-positive rate (vs. 54.9% for a threshold tester), detects 70.0% of certified conditional-class mutants, convicts 40.4% of mutants invisible to execution-accuracy scoring, and reproduces predicted detectability patterns including zeros.
AI.conclusion: Falsification-based verification provides a principled, sound approach to detecting unfaithful LLM-generated optimization models without reference models. The theoretical framework explains both the power and inherent limits of such testing, and experiments validate its practical effectiveness.

title: Strategic Gaze: Attention Allocation and Transition Patterns Across Functional Areas of Interest by Gameplay Outcome
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (PACM HCI), to be presented at CHI PLAY 2026
summary: Video games present players with complex, spatially distributed information across interface elements, with attention shaped by visual features and task goals. Eye tracking provides a useful method for examining player attention through gaze behaviour during gameplay. Yet empirical game research has relied on accumulated fixation measures that capture where attention is directed and how long it is maintained within regions, leaving less known about how gaze moves between regions to coordinate distributed information. We address this gap by integrating distribution-, duration-, and transition-based gaze measures across functionally organised interface regions in relation to gameplay outcomes. We conducted a within-subject study with 32 participants using a deck-building game, defining six functional Areas of Interest (AOIs) within the turn-based combat interface, spanning enemy, player, action, and auxiliary elements. We computed AOI hit, dwell time, transition probabilities, and entropy to compare gaze behaviour across outcome groups. Players in the win group showed more selective attention allocation extending to peripheral auxiliary resources, with more frequent action-oriented gaze transitions, a wider range of AOI pairs, and a more even distribution across AOIs. Within a strategic game setting, our findings show that gameplay outcomes are reflected in how players distribute, sustain, and shift visual attention across functional interface elements, offering a more comprehensive account of attention organisation in gameplay.

AI.tldr: This study integrates distribution-, duration-, and transition-based gaze measures across functionally organized interface regions to examine how attention coordination relates to gameplay outcomes in a strategic deck-building game, finding that winning players exhibit more selective attention to peripheral resources, more frequent action-oriented transitions, and more even distribution of gaze across interface areas.
AI.motivation: Existing eye-tracking research in games has relied predominantly on accumulated fixation measures (where/how long attention is directed within regions), leaving a gap in understanding how gaze transitions between interface regions to coordinate distributed information during gameplay.
AI.method: A within-subject study with 32 participants playing a deck-building game. Six functional Areas of Interest (AOIs) were defined across the turn-based combat interface (enemy, player, action, auxiliary elements). AOI hit counts, dwell time, transition probabilities, and entropy measures were computed and compared across win vs. loss outcome groups.
AI.result: Players in the win group demonstrated more selective attention allocation extending to peripheral auxiliary resources, more frequent action-oriented gaze transitions, a wider range of AOI pairs visited, and a more even distribution of gaze across AOIs compared to the loss group.
AI.conclusion: Gameplay outcomes are reflected in how players distribute, sustain, and shift visual attention across functional interface elements. Transition-based measures complement traditional fixation metrics to provide a more comprehensive account of attention organization during strategic gameplay.

title: Adapting Embedding Models for Agent Capability Retrieval
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at the AgentSearch Workshop, SIGIR 2026
summary: Open agent marketplaces list native agents, tool bundles, and reusable skill packages in the same search interface, yet practitioners still have little guidance on how to retrieve across this mixed catalog. We study whether off-the-shelf retrieval models, trained for general text retrieval, can be adapted to match user queries to executable agent capabilities, and whether the learned signal transfers beyond the benchmark used for tuning. We fine-tune three open retrieval backbones, BGE-base, KaLM-v1.5, and EasyRec, on AgentSelect, which represents marketplace-visible units as capability profiles derived from public metadata, and test transfer on two catalogs not seen during training: MuleRun native agents and a ClawHub benchmark of 50 skills with 1,000 queries. Adaptation helps on both catalogs. Code and data will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether general-purpose text retrieval models can be fine-tuned to retrieve executable agent capabilities from marketplace catalogs, and whether this learned retrieval signal transfers to unseen catalogs. Experiments with BGE-base, KaLM-v1.5, and EasyRec fine-tuned on AgentSelect show positive transfer to MuleRun and ClawHub benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Open agent marketplaces mix native agents, tool bundles, and skill packages in unified search interfaces, but practitioners lack guidance on effective retrieval across these heterogeneous catalogs. Existing retrieval models are trained for general text, not for matching user queries to executable agent capabilities.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune three open retrieval backbones (BGE-base, KaLM-v1.5, EasyRec) on the AgentSelect dataset, which represents marketplace-visible units as capability profiles derived from public metadata. Transfer performance is evaluated on two held-out catalogs: MuleRun native agents and a ClawHub benchmark comprising 50 skills with 1,000 queries.
AI.result: Fine-tuning for agent capability retrieval yields consistent improvements on both unseen catalogs, demonstrating that the learned retrieval signal transfers beyond the training benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Domain-adapted retrieval models can effectively bridge user queries to executable agent capabilities across heterogeneous marketplaces, with transferable improvements to unseen catalogs.

title: Enhanced Multi-Class DDoS Attack Identification using a Meta-Learning Ensemble
summary: Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks continue to pose significant threats to network availability and security. While many detection systems focus on binary classification (attack vs. benign), effective mitigation often requires identifying the specific type of DDoS attack. This paper introduces a robust intrusion detection framework centered around a high-accuracy, multi-class classification model designed to precisely identify various DDoS attack types. We propose an ensemble architecture integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Random Forest (RF) models, whose outputs are synthesized by a Logistic Regression meta-learner. This approach explicitly addresses the ambiguity often encountered when combining predictions from multiple independent classifiers. Evaluated on the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset, our proposed ensemble meta-learning model achieves 96% accuracy in the multi-class identification task, significantly outperforming a baseline chain model (combining individual binary classifiers), which reached 92% accuracy and suffered from high ambiguity. Furthermore, integration and testing within a Software-Defined Networking (SDN) environment using Mininet and the Ryu controller demonstrated the practical applicability of our model, achieving 93% accuracy in identifying DDoS types in the emulated network traffic. Our work highlights the value of meta-learning ensembles for nuanced DDoS threat identification, paving the way for more adaptive and effective defense mechanisms.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning ensemble (LSTM + KNN + Random Forest with Logistic Regression meta-learner) achieves 96% multi-class DDoS attack type identification on CIC-DDoS2019, outperforming a baseline chain model (92%) and demonstrating practical deployability in SDN environments with 93% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Binary DDoS detection is insufficient for effective mitigation; identifying specific attack types is critical. Existing approaches using multiple independent classifiers suffer from ambiguity when combining predictions, motivating a meta-learning solution that synthesizes outputs coherently.
AI.method: An ensemble architecture combining LSTM, KNN, and Random Forest base classifiers, with a Logistic Regression meta-learner that synthesizes their predictions to resolve ambiguity. Evaluated on the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset. Validated in an SDN environment using Mininet and the Ryu controller.
AI.result: The proposed meta-learning ensemble achieved 96% accuracy on multi-class DDoS identification, outperforming a baseline chain model (92%) which also exhibited high ambiguity. In the emulated SDN environment, the model achieved 93% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Meta-learning ensembles offer significant value for nuanced, multi-class DDoS threat identification, enabling more adaptive and effective defense mechanisms suitable for real-world SDN deployments.

title: Value-Aware Prediction for Robust Multi-Agent Coordination Under Communication Loss
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Robust multi-agent coordination relies heavily on inter-agent communication, which is frequently disrupted by physical and environmental constraints in real-world deployments. To maintain operation during these intermittent communication failures, agents can employ internal prediction models to estimate missing shared state information. However, predictors trained with standard reconstruction objectives treat all transitions equally. In a Reinforcement Learning context, this forces the model to waste capacity learning stochastic exploration noise and the outdated dynamics of suboptimal policies. In this paper, we propose a value-aware extension of Multi-Agent Observation Sharing under Communication Dropout (MARO) to patch communication gaps; we refer to this method as Value-Aware MARO. By dynamically weighting the predictor's loss function using advantage estimates derived from the underlying actor-critic architecture, our objective explicitly couples the predictor's learning process to the policy's evolution. This formulation focuses the model's capacity on the intentional, high-return dynamics actively reinforced by the agents. We evaluate our framework on several tasks within the Multi-Agent Particle Environment under varying communication reliability levels. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach maintains performance under declining communication reliability, particularly below 40%. While our method performs comparably in tasks where the baseline already maintains high coordination, our value-aware weighting effectively prevents the performance collapse observed in the standard predictor during high-attrition scenarios. In these environments, our method achieves an average improvement in mean returns of more than 20% and reduces performance variance by a mean of 64.7% compared to the standard unweighted baseline.

AI.tldr: Proposes Value-Aware MARO, which uses advantage estimates from actor-critic to weight a predictor's reconstruction loss, focusing model capacity on high-return transitions and preventing performance collapse under severe communication dropout (<40% reliability).
AI.motivation: Standard observation predictors in multi-agent RL treat all transitions equally, wasting capacity on stochastic exploration noise and outdated suboptimal dynamics. Under severe communication dropout, this causes performance collapse.
AI.method: Value-Aware MARO extends Multi-Agent Observation Sharing under Communication Dropout by dynamically weighting the predictor's reconstruction loss using advantage estimates from the underlying actor-critic architecture, coupling the predictor's learning to the policy's evolution.
AI.result: In high-attrition scenarios (<40% reliability), the method prevents performance collapse seen in the unweighted baseline, achieving >20% average improvement in mean returns and 64.7% reduction in performance variance. Performance is comparable to the baseline when communication is already reliable.
AI.conclusion: Value-aware loss weighting effectively focuses predictor capacity on intentional, high-return dynamics, enabling robust multi-agent coordination under severe communication constraints without sacrificing performance under normal conditions.

title: Generative Ontology Induction: Domain-Agnostic Schema Discovery from Document Corpora Using Large Language Models
summary:
Ontology engineering remains a critical bottleneck in knowledge-intensive AI systems. Existing automated approaches either depend on predefined schemas, operate within narrow domains, or produce unstructured outputs unsuitable for downstream pipelines.
  We introduce Generative Ontology Induction (GOI), a domain-agnostic framework that induces a generative blueprint - entities, dimensions, properties, relationships, and constraints - from a corpus of examples and exports it as a typed graph (six node types, seven edge types) in YAML/JSON. We introduce the Node Coverage Score, a novel evaluation metric that measures the fraction of structural ontology nodes (classes, properties, and dimensions) appearing in generated outputs.
  A controlled generative validation on four contrasting ontologies - a familiar Software Services Invoice schema, a custom Job Description Ontology, a confidential Pain-Management Clinical Visit Record Ontology, and a Professional Services Contract & Statement of Work Ontology - shows that GOI-prompted generation covers 95-100% of the structural backbone in every case; a generic three-field template holds at 97.8% on the invoice schema but drops to 52.2% on the Job Description Ontology, 62.2% on the Pain-Management ontology, and 78.3% on the Professional Services Contract ontology. The structural coverage holds regardless of how familiar the document type is to the model.

AI.tldr: GOI is a domain-agnostic framework that induces structured ontologies (typed graphs with six node types, seven edge types) from example corpora and exports them as YAML/JSON. It introduces the Node Coverage Score metric and achieves 95–100% structural coverage across four diverse ontologies, dramatically outperforming a generic template baseline.
AI.motivation: Ontology engineering is a critical bottleneck in knowledge-intensive AI systems. Existing automated approaches are limited by reliance on predefined schemas, narrow domain scoping, or unstructured outputs that cannot feed downstream pipelines.
AI.method: The authors propose Generative Ontology Induction (GOI), a domain-agnostic framework that induces a generative blueprint — entities, dimensions, properties, relationships, and constraints — from a corpus of examples. The output is a typed graph with six node types and seven edge types, serialized in YAML/JSON. They also introduce the Node Coverage Score, a novel evaluation metric measuring the fraction of structural ontology nodes (classes, properties, dimensions) present in generated outputs. Validation is performed via controlled generative prompting across four contrasting ontologies.
AI.result: GOI-prompted generation achieves 95–100% structural backbone coverage across all four ontologies tested: Software Services Invoice, Job Description Ontology, Pain-Management Clinical Visit Record Ontology, and Professional Services Contract & Statement of Work Ontology. In contrast, a generic three-field template achieves 97.8% on the invoice schema but drops sharply to 52.2% (Job Description), 62.2% (Pain-Management), and 78.3% (Professional Services Contract). Structural coverage is robust regardless of the model's familiarity with the document type.
AI.conclusion: GOI demonstrates that high-fidelity, domain-agnostic ontology induction from example corpora is feasible. The framework's consistent 95–100% coverage across diverse and unfamiliar domains suggests it can substantially reduce the ontology engineering bottleneck, and the Node Coverage Score provides a principled metric for future comparative evaluation.

title: OpenLanguageModel: Readable and Composable Small-Language-Model Pretraining for Education and Research
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table. Website: https://openlanguagemodel.github.io/openlanguagemodel/. Code: https://github.com/openlanguagemodel/openlanguagemodel
summary: OpenLanguageModel (OLM) is an open-source PyTorch library for building and pretraining small language models while keeping their machinery visible. In OLM, model code reads like the architecture: components are ordinary modules, while Block, Residual, Repeat, and Parallel describe how they are wired. The resulting model can move unchanged from a teaching notebook to a complete pretraining run or a research ablation. OLM connects this readable model layer to tokenizers, local and streaming datasets, optimization, mixed precision, callbacks, checkpoints, and hardware-aware CPU, single-GPU, and single-node multi-GPU execution. We demonstrate the full path by tracing GPT-2 from diagram to code, launching a FineWeb-Edu training script, replacing one attention component, and letting AutoTrainer configure the available machine. The package includes 27 presets across nine familiar model families and documentation that progresses from LM fundamentals to architecture research. Validation shows close agreement with independent reference implementations, 90.6% four-GPU weak-scaling efficiency for a 348M-parameter workload, compact architecture edits, and positive early usability results. OLM is MIT-licensed and available through PyPI, GitHub, and its documentation site.

AI.tldr: OpenLanguageModel (OLM) is an open-source PyTorch library for transparently building and pretraining small language models, featuring readable architecture-as-code design, modular components, and built-in support for tokenization, datasets, optimization, and multi-GPU execution, with 27 presets across nine model families.
AI.motivation: Existing LM training frameworks often obscure internal model machinery behind complex abstractions, making it difficult for researchers and students to understand, teach, and modify model architectures. OLM aims to make every component visible and modifiable, bridging the gap from educational notebooks to full-scale pretraining runs.
AI.method: OLM implements models using ordinary PyTorch modules with explicit structural components (Block, Residual, Repeat, Parallel) so that code reads like the architecture diagram. It connects the model layer to tokenizers, local/streaming datasets, optimization, mixed precision, callbacks, checkpoints, and hardware-aware execution (CPU, single-GPU, single-node multi-GPU). An AutoTrainer automates hardware configuration.
AI.result: Validation shows close agreement with independent reference implementations, 90.6% four-GPU weak-scaling efficiency for a 348M-parameter workload, compact architecture edit capabilities, and positive early usability feedback. The library ships with 27 presets across nine model families.
AI.conclusion: OLM successfully provides a transparent, hackable, and scalable framework for small LM pretraining and research, validated through strong scaling efficiency and implementation fidelity. It is MIT-licensed and available via PyPI, GitHub, and documentation.

title: Orthogonal Gradient Constraints Shape Noisy-Label Memorization Dynamics
comment: 7 pages, accepted into the ICML HiLD workshop 2026 @Seoul
summary: Modern neural networks can fit corrupted training labels, making noisy-label learning a useful setting for studying memorization-driven overfitting. Most regularization methods modify the objective, architecture, or data distribution; here we instead study a geometric intervention on the optimizer update itself. We evaluate OrthoGrad, which removes the component of each weight gradient parallel to the current weight vector, in noisy-label image classification. On MNIST with small-data regimes, OrthoGrad improves test accuracy most clearly for CNNs while reducing corrupted-label fitting. Mechanism diagnostics based on weight norms and gradient-weight cosine similarity suggest that the projection has the strongest effect when the raw gradient contains a nontrivial radial component, and becomes weaker in larger-data regimes where gradients are already nearly orthogonal to weights. Additional CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 experiments show that the method can alter memorization trajectories but does not prevent eventual noisy-label memorization. These results support orthogonal update constraints as a useful diagnostic for studying learning dynamics, while showing that OrthoGrad is regime-dependent rather than universally regularizing.

AI.tldr: OrthoGrad removes the radial (weight-parallel) component from weight gradients. In small-data MNIST, it improves CNN test accuracy and reduces corrupted-label fitting. The effect is strongest when gradients have a nontrivial radial component and weakens in larger-data regimes. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, it alters memorization trajectories but does not prevent eventual noisy-label memorization. The method is regime-dependent, not universally regularizing.
AI.motivation: Modern neural networks can memorize corrupted training labels, making noisy-label learning a valuable setting to study memorization-driven overfitting. While most regularization approaches modify the objective, architecture, or data distribution, this work explores a geometric intervention applied directly to the optimizer update: removing the component of each weight gradient that is parallel to the current weight vector (the radial component).
AI.method: The authors evaluate OrthoGrad, which projects out the weight-parallel (radial) component from each weight gradient during optimization. They conduct experiments on MNIST under small-data regimes with CNNs, and on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, using noisy-label image classification. Diagnostics include measuring weight norms and gradient-weight cosine similarity to understand when the projection matters. They analyze memorization trajectories and the regime-dependence of the orthogonal update constraint.
AI.result: On small-data MNIST, OrthoGrad improves CNN test accuracy and reduces fitting of corrupted labels. The projection is most effective when raw gradients have a nontrivial radial component; in larger-data regimes, gradients are already nearly orthogonal to weights, making the intervention weaker. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, OrthoGrad alters memorization trajectories but does not prevent eventual memorization of noisy labels.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal update constraints serve as a useful diagnostic tool for studying learning dynamics, but OrthoGrad is regime-dependent rather than universally regularizing. Its effectiveness hinges on the presence of a meaningful radial gradient component, which diminishes as dataset size grows.

title: How Do You Choose Your AI Component? An Interview Study of Secure AI Integration in Practice
summary:
The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) as AI components in modern software systems introduces distinct security risks to the software supply chain. While many considerations and safety mechanisms are in place for components of the traditional software supply chain, the recent rapid adoption of AI components and platforms has overlooked these hard learned lessons. Selecting and integrating AI models without clear guidance on how these choices affect system security may leave applications vulnerable to threats, such as malicious components, data leakage, and unintended behavior. The goal of this study is to understand practitioners' decision making process and security considerations in selecting and integrating AI components through an exploratory semi-structured interview study. Toward this goal, we conducted semistructured interviews with 22 software developers, architects, and AI practitioners across diverse organizations about how they integrate AI components into their software.
  Our analysis finds that practitioners' model selection is predominantly driven by functional criteria, including performance, accuracy, cost, and specific features, e.g., tool calling or multimodal support, while security is rarely considered as an evaluation criterion. We observe a consistent lack of security concern throughout the AI component integration process, with established software supply chain lessons overlooked or ignored. The industry is repeating the historically costly mistakes of early software dependency management, prioritizing rapid reuse and availability over security and provenance. We distill our findings into actionable recommendations for AI adopters, model providers, and researchers, advocating for a proactive, security-by-design approach that integrates security evaluation into component selection and sustains it throughout the software development lifecycle.

AI.tldr: Practitioners overwhelmingly prioritize functional criteria (performance, accuracy, cost) over security when selecting and integrating LLM components, mirroring the historically costly mistakes of early software dependency management. Based on interviews with 22 practitioners, the paper calls for a security-by-design approach to AI component integration.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs as AI components in software systems introduces distinct supply chain security risks (malicious components, data leakage, unintended behavior), yet there is little understanding of how practitioners make decisions about selecting and integrating these components, and whether security factors into those decisions at all.
AI.method: An exploratory semi-structured interview study with 22 software developers, architects, and AI practitioners from diverse organizations, analyzed to understand their decision-making processes and security considerations when integrating AI components.
AI.result: Model selection is dominated by functional criteria — performance, accuracy, cost, and features like tool calling or multimodal support — with security rarely considered. A consistent lack of security concern pervades the entire AI component integration process, with established software supply chain security lessons being overlooked or ignored.
AI.conclusion: Industry is repeating the costly mistakes of early software dependency management, favoring rapid reuse and availability over security and provenance. The authors distill actionable recommendations for AI adopters, model providers, and researchers, advocating for proactive, security-by-design integration sustained throughout the software development lifecycle.

title: PocketPPD: Screening for Postpartum Depression Risk Using Passive Smartphone Sensing
summary: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a serious perinatal mental health condition affecting approximately 20% of new mothers worldwide. Common screening approaches for PPD, such as self-report questionnaires and active digital logs, rely heavily on user input and thus impose a substantial burden on participants, limiting their feasibility for long-term use. Recent passive mobile sensing (PMS) approaches have enabled low-burden detection of depressive symptoms using machine learning methods with multi-modal sensor data from off-the-shelf mobile devices including smartphones. However, the postpartum period entails distinct behavioral patterns, raising uncertainty about whether sensing-based indicators for general depression and mental disorders generalize to PPD. To address this gap, we propose PocketPPD, a PMS-based PPD screening method that detects PPD risk using maternal contextual features, such as disruptions in behavioral rhythms and shifts in stability, collected through a smartphone. In our exploratory four-week feasibility study with 61 postpartum women, the PMS-only model achieved an AUC of 0.75, while the best-performing model, integrating PMS-oriented data and self-report features, achieved an AUC of 0.83. Moreover, we find that morning and late-night routine volatility ranks among the top digital biomarkers, dynamically moderated by maternal contexts such as infant developmental stage and employment status. This work provides empirical evidence for low-burden PPD risk screening and our findings lay the groundwork for continuous perinatal mental health monitoring.

AI.tldr: PocketPPD uses passive mobile sensing to detect postpartum depression risk, achieving AUC 0.75 with sensor-only data and 0.83 when combined with self-reports. Morning and late-night routine volatility emerged as key digital biomarkers, moderated by maternal context.
AI.motivation: Existing PPD screening methods (self-report questionnaires, active digital logs) impose heavy user burden and are infeasible for long-term use. While passive mobile sensing has shown promise for general depression detection, it is uncertain whether these indicators generalize to PPD given the distinct behavioral patterns of the postpartum period.
AI.method: The authors developed PocketPPD, a PMS-based screening method leveraging maternal contextual features (behavioral rhythm disruptions, stability shifts) collected via smartphone. An exploratory four-week feasibility study was conducted with 61 postpartum women, evaluating both PMS-only models and hybrid models integrating self-report features.
AI.result: The PMS-only model achieved an AUC of 0.75; the best-performing model integrating PMS and self-report features reached AUC 0.83. Morning and late-night routine volatility were identified as top digital biomarkers, dynamically moderated by infant developmental stage and maternal employment status.
AI.conclusion: Passive mobile sensing provides a low-burden, feasible approach for PPD risk screening and lays the foundation for continuous perinatal mental health monitoring, with contextual factors playing a key moderating role.

title: The Matryoshka Hypencoder
summary: The Hypencoder is a recently-proposed retrieval approach that encodes queries as shallow neural networks ("Q-Nets") that estimate relevance over pre-computed document embeddings. Inspired by Matryoshka Representation Learning, we show that the Hypencoder can be extended to support multiple sizes of Q-Nets, allowing trade-offs between effectiveness and efficiency when deployed. We find that this "Matryoshka Hypencoder" achieves comparable in-domain effectiveness with approximately 7x fewer active parameters in-domain and half as many active parameters out-of-domain, which corresponds to a 1.6-3.4x increase in scoring throughput. This work paves the way for practical deployment of Hypencoders.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Hypencoder retrieval model using Matryoshka Representation Learning to create Q-Nets of multiple sizes, enabling flexible efficiency-effectiveness trade-offs. The Matryoshka Hypencoder achieves comparable in-domain performance with ~7x fewer parameters and 1.6–3.4x faster scoring throughput.
AI.motivation: Hypencoders, while effective for retrieval, are computationally expensive to deploy due to the size of their query-encoding neural networks (Q-Nets). The authors seek a practical way to dynamically trade off retrieval effectiveness for scoring efficiency, making Hypencoders viable for real-world deployment under varying latency and throughput constraints.
AI.method: The authors apply Matryoshka Representation Learning to the Hypencoder framework, nesting multiple Q-Net capacities within a single model (a "Matryoshka Hypencoder"). Smaller Q-Nets are trained as nested subsets of larger ones, allowing truncated inference with fewer active parameters while reusing the same pre-computed document embeddings.
AI.result: The Matryoshka Hypencoder achieves in-domain effectiveness comparable to the full model while using approximately 7x fewer active parameters. Out-of-domain, it uses roughly half the active parameters with minimal degradation. This yields a 1.6–3.4x increase in scoring throughput.
AI.conclusion: The Matryoshka Hypencoder offers a practical path toward deploying Hypencoder-based retrieval systems by enabling flexible, size-adjustable Q-Nets that preserve effectiveness while significantly improving inference efficiency.

title: A Control-Driven Framework for Secure SaaS Onboarding in Regulated Enterprises
summary: As enterprises increasingly adopt Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms for mission-critical functions, onboarding these services has emerged as a complex challenge extending well beyond procurement and basic security review. In regulated environments, SaaS onboarding must address multiple interdependent control domains, including Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM), cybersecurity assessment, Identity and Access Management (IAM), and disaster recovery (DR), which are often executed in isolation, resulting in delayed go-lives, duplicated assessments, unclear ownership, and residual operational risk. This paper proposes a control-driven, end-to-end SaaS onboarding framework that integrates TPRM, cybersecurity, IAM, and DR into a unified lifecycle model. The framework introduces a stage-based approach spanning intake and risk scoping, architecture validation, identity design, resilience assessment, and post-production governance. Key contributions include: (1) a structured SaaS onboarding lifecycle emphasizing sequencing and dependency management across control domains; (2) a cross-domain control mapping highlighting failure modes caused by siloed reviews; and (3) practical design patterns for secure connectivity, federated identity, least-privilege access, and shared-responsibility disaster recovery. Supported by operational lessons from enterprise-scale implementations and a reference governance checklist, the framework helps organizations reduce onboarding friction, improve auditability, and strengthen the security and resilience posture of SaaS-enabled platforms.

AI.tldr: A control-driven, end-to-end SaaS onboarding framework that unifies TPRM, cybersecurity, IAM, and disaster recovery into a stage-based lifecycle model, reducing friction, improving auditability, and strengthening security posture in regulated enterprises.
AI.motivation: Enterprise SaaS onboarding in regulated environments is fragmented across siloed control domains (TPRM, cybersecurity, IAM, DR), leading to delayed deployments, duplicated assessments, unclear ownership, and residual operational risk.
AI.method: Proposes a stage-based SaaS onboarding lifecycle framework with five phases: intake/risk scoping, architecture validation, identity design, resilience assessment, and post-production governance. Introduces cross-domain control mapping and practical design patterns for secure connectivity, federated identity, least-privilege access, and shared-responsibility DR.
AI.result: The framework yields reduced onboarding friction, improved auditability, and a strengthened security/resilience posture, supported by operational lessons from enterprise-scale implementations and a reference governance checklist.
AI.conclusion: Integrating previously siloed control domains into a unified, sequenced SaaS onboarding lifecycle enables organizations to accelerate go-live timelines, eliminate redundant assessments, clarify ownership, and mitigate residual operational risk.

title: PRIME: Plasticity Recovery in Multi-Agent Environments for UAV-Assisted Emergency Communication Networks
summary: Most reinforcement learning controllers for these networks assume stationary conditions, and the few that handle change react to the external environment while leaving the network's internal state unexamined. We show that sustained non-stationarity damages this internal state directly: as objectives shift, neurons progressively fall dormant and the shared policy loses the capacity to learn. The obvious remedy, resetting dormant neurons, is unsafe under shared-parameter multi-agent training: many neurons that appear inactive are still receiving strong training gradients, and whether a neuron appears dormant depends on which agent's observations it processes. PRIME (Plasticity Recovery In Multi-agent Environments) therefore verifies both directions before intervening. Extending the bidirectional Silent Neuron framework to cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, it aggregates activation and gradient statistics over the full team batch, reads the backward signal from the gradient the training loss has already deposited , not from a hand-crafted proxy, and reinitializes only neurons that are simultaneously activation-dormant and gradient-silent. Useful representations are preserved while learning capacity is restored. On a phase-switching UAV emergency communication simulator, PRIME improves interquartile mean return by 24.9\% over MAPPO and holds dormant neuron fractions at 10--20\% versus 40--45\%; ablations attribute the gains to the gradient signal and team-level aggregation rather than to the specific reset operator. A dynamic regret bound shows that the perturbation cost scales with the small silent-subspace dimension rather than the full parameter count.

AI.tldr: PRIME introduces a bidirectional verification method for resetting dormant neurons in cooperative multi-agent RL, using both activation and gradient signals aggregated across the full team to safely restore plasticity without damaging useful representations, achieving 24.9% improvement over MAPPO in non-stationary environments.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent RL controllers assume stationary conditions or react only to external environmental changes. The paper identifies that sustained non-stationarity directly damages internal network state: neurons progressively fall dormant as objectives shift, degrading the shared policy's learning capacity. Simply resetting dormant neurons is unsafe because many inactive-appearing neurons still receive strong training gradients, and dormancy depends on which agent's observations are being processed.
AI.method: PRIME (Plasticity Recovery In Multi-agent Environments) extends the bidirectional Silent Neuron framework to cooperative MARL. It aggregates activation and gradient statistics over the full team batch, reads the backward signal from the actual training loss gradient (not a hand-crafted proxy), and reinitializes only neurons that are simultaneously activation-dormant AND gradient-silent. This dual-condition verification preserves useful representations while restoring learning capacity.
AI.result: On a phase-switching UAV emergency communication simulator, PRIME improves interquartile mean return by 24.9% over MAPPO and maintains dormant neuron fractions at 10-20% versus 40-45% for baselines. Ablations show gains are attributable to the gradient signal and team-level aggregation rather than the specific reset operator. A dynamic regret bound demonstrates perturbation cost scales with the small silent-subspace dimension rather than full parameter count.
AI.conclusion: Sustained non-stationarity in multi-agent RL causes internal neural network degradation via progressive neuron dormancy. PRIME's bidirectional, team-aggregated criterion for safe neuron reinitialization effectively restores plasticity while preserving learned representations, offering both empirical gains and theoretical guarantees.

title: Democratizing AI with Small Language Models: Structured Benchmarking and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Local Deployment
summary: AI democratization is not primarily a question of matching frontier-scale generality; it is a question of whether capable models can be selected, audited, and specialized under hardware and governance constraints that ordinary institutions can actually satisfy. This paper studies that problem through a controlled evaluation of nine open-weight language models between 135M and 3B parameters on a 1,085-example, 16-topic multiple-choice benchmark designed for structured local deployment. The benchmark emphasizes symbolic precision, constrained formatting, extraction, and short-horizon semantic decision making under a strict one-letter output protocol. A shared parameter-efficient fine-tuning pipeline then adapts a subset of models using 4-bit NF4 quantization with DoRA/LoRA-style adapters on an NVIDIA L4-class budget. In base evaluation, Qwen Coder 3B leads at 75.67% strict accuracy, followed by Qwen2.5 1.5B at 67.10%, Qwen3.5 2B at 64.98%, and Granite 3.3 2B at 64.61%. On the shared 108-example held-out fine-tuning split, adaptation improves Qwen Coder 3B by +26.85 points, SmolLM2 1.7B by +25.92, Qwen2.5 1.5B by +19.44, SmolLM2 360M by +10.18, and SmolLM2 135M by +5.55. Across ranking, topic-level heterogeneity, difficulty strata, failure composition, efficiency frontiers, and topic-conditioned transfer, the same conclusion recurs: a disciplined workflow of benchmark construction, cross-model evaluation, and low-cost specialization already makes a subset of sub-3B models viable as local experts for structured niche workloads.

AI.tldr: A controlled evaluation of nine sub-3B open-weight language models on a structured 1,085-example benchmark demonstrates that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (QDoRA/LoRA, 4-bit NF4) on consumer-grade hardware (NVIDIA L4) can transform small models into viable local domain experts, with Qwen Coder 3B reaching 75.67% base accuracy and gaining +26.85 points after adaptation.
AI.motivation: AI democratization hinges not on frontier-scale capability but on whether models can be selected, audited, and specialized under hardware and governance constraints that ordinary institutions can satisfy. The paper aims to demonstrate that a disciplined workflow of benchmark-driven selection and low-cost fine-tuning can produce competent niche experts from sub-3B models.
AI.method: Nine open-weight language models (135M–3B parameters) were evaluated on a custom 1,085-example, 16-topic multiple-choice benchmark emphasizing symbolic precision, constrained formatting, extraction, and short-horizon semantic decisions under a strict one-letter output protocol. A subset of models underwent parameter-efficient fine-tuning using 4-bit NF4 quantization with DoRA/LoRA-style adapters on an NVIDIA L4-class GPU budget, tested on a 108-example held-out split.
AI.result: Base evaluation: Qwen Coder 3B led at 75.67% strict accuracy, followed by Qwen2.5 1.5B (67.10%), Qwen3.5 2B (64.98%), and Granite 3.3 2B (64.61%). After fine-tuning, Qwen Coder 3B improved by +26.85 points, SmolLM2 1.7B by +25.92, Qwen2.5 1.5B by +19.44, SmolLM2 360M by +10.18, and SmolLM2 135M by +5.55. Consistent findings emerged across ranking, topic heterogeneity, difficulty strata, failure analysis, efficiency frontiers, and topic-conditioned transfer.
AI.conclusion: A disciplined workflow of benchmark construction, cross-model evaluation, and low-cost parameter-efficient specialization renders a subset of sub-3B models viable as local experts for structured niche workloads, reinforcing that AI democratization is achievable without frontier-scale models.

title: SpecLA: Efficient Speculative Decoding for Linear-Attention Models
summary: Linear-attention models replace the growing KV cache with recurrent states, but autoregressive decoding still reads, updates, and writes these states one token at a time. Speculative decoding can reduce this cost by verifying several draft tokens in one target pass, yet existing speculative systems are designed for Transformer KV caches. For stateful linear-attention targets, verification must follow recurrent dependencies across chains and branches, acceptance must update only the accepted state trajectory, and the drafter must avoid submitting candidates that waste stateful verification work. This paper presents SpecLA, a speculative decoding runtime for stateful linear-attention models. SpecLA verifies chains and trees with topology-aware kernels, stores compact factors produced during verification to recover accepted states, and uses confidence pruning plus a target-aligned EAGLE-style drafter to feed useful candidates to the verifier. On an NVIDIA H100 with a public GDN-1.3B target, SpecLA achieves up to 1.70x end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: SpecLA is a speculative decoding system tailored for stateful linear-attention models, achieving up to 1.70× speedup over autoregressive decoding by using topology-aware verification, state recovery from compact factors, and a target-aligned drafter with confidence pruning.
AI.motivation: Linear-attention models replace KV caches with recurrent states, but existing speculative decoding systems are designed for Transformer KV caches and cannot handle the recurrent state dependencies, chain-branch verification, and selective state acceptance required by stateful linear-attention targets.
AI.method: SpecLA introduces three techniques: (1) topology-aware kernels that verify token chains and trees while respecting recurrent dependencies; (2) compact factor storage during verification to recover accepted state trajectories without recomputation; and (3) confidence pruning combined with a target-aligned EAGLE-style drafter that avoids submitting candidates likely to be rejected, minimizing wasted verification work.
AI.result: On an NVIDIA H100 GPU with a GDN-1.3B target model, SpecLA achieves up to 1.70× end-to-end speedup over standard autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding can be effectively adapted to stateful linear-attention models by addressing their unique recurrent state dynamics, enabling meaningful speedups while preserving output equivalence to autoregressive decoding.

title: From Weights to Words: Expressing and Editing Preference Model Inferences in Natural Language
comment: 42 pages, 22 figures, 14 tables; main text 11 pages, remainder appendices
summary: The growing use of statistical learning algorithms to infer human preferences from high-dimensional choice data runs up against a fundamental challenge: choice alternatives typically differ in many ways simultaneously, so it is generally unclear which factors actually drove an observed decision and should be credited as preferences. Compounding this problem, the opacity of these methods leaves human operators unable to inspect, contest, or correct models when they err. We introduce \emph{weights to words}, a method that takes a dataset of choice problems as input and automatically discovers a collection of domain-relevant preference dimensions, each described in natural language and paired with a vector in the model's representational space. These dimensions address both under-determination and opacity: they can be applied to concentrate attribution on a small set of meaningful factors, and they can externalize the model's inferences in natural language so that users can inspect and edit them in real time. We first qualitatively illustrate the method's versatility on four diverse domains: moral dilemmas, movies, wines, and free-form LLM responses. We then report two pre-registered human-subjects experiments, on moral dilemmas ($N=450$) and movie selection ($N=449$), that demonstrate its benefits for learning preference models: (1) regularizing a preference model toward the learned basis increases prediction accuracy on held-out choices, and (2) incorporating participants' structured edits further improves accuracy. In head-to-head comparisons, participants prefer the method's inferred preference profiles and endorse its predictions as more accurate.

AI.tldr: Weights to Words is a method that automatically discovers interpretable preference dimensions from choice data, describing each in natural language with a corresponding vector. It addresses the under-determination and opacity problems in preference learning by enabling attribution concentration and real-time user inspection/editing, with experiments showing improved prediction accuracy and user preference.
AI.motivation: Statistical learning algorithms for inferring preferences from high-dimensional choice data face two key challenges: (1) under-determination — it's unclear which of many simultaneously varying factors actually drove a decision, and (2) opacity — human operators cannot inspect, contest, or correct these black-box models when they make errors.
AI.method: The authors introduce "weights to words," which takes a dataset of choice problems as input and automatically discovers domain-relevant preference dimensions. Each dimension is described in natural language and paired with a vector in the model's representational space. These dimensions can concentrate attribution on meaningful factors and externalize model inferences for real-time user inspection and editing.
AI.result: The method was qualitatively demonstrated across four domains (moral dilemmas, movies, wines, LLM responses). Two pre-registered experiments (moral dilemmas N=450, movie selection N=449) showed that: (1) regularizing toward the learned basis increased held-out prediction accuracy, (2) incorporating participants' structured edits further improved accuracy, and (3) in head-to-head comparisons, participants preferred the method's inferred profiles and endorsed its predictions as more accurate.
AI.conclusion: Weights to words effectively addresses both under-determination and opacity in preference learning by providing interpretable, editable preference dimensions. The approach not only improves predictive accuracy but also aligns better with human judgment, offering a promising direction for human-in-the-loop preference modeling.

title: Specification-Driven Development as the Foundation of AI-Native Enterprise Software Engineering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI are shifting software engineering from manual coding toward intent specification, architecture, and governance. Two paradigms have emerged: vibe coding, an intuition-driven approach accepting AI artifacts via observed behavior, and Specification-Driven Development (SDD), which uses structured specifications as the authoritative source of truth. This article makes three contributions. First, based on a verified literature corpus, it identifies failure modes of ungoverned conversational generation: the productivity-reliability paradox, architectural erosion from limited context, security exposure, and technical debt. Second, it introduces the Specification Governance Reference Model (SGRM). This tool-independent framework defines four-component specification contracts, constrains stochastic generation via deterministic validation, formalizes three rigor levels, and integrates generation, verification, and governance into a closed-loop architecture. Third, it evaluates SGRM against ISO/IEC 25010, mapping quality characteristics to governance mechanisms. Empirical evidence supports this, reporting a 73% reduction in security defects under constitutional constraints and a 50% reduction in time-to-market through specification-governed agentic delivery. The analysis concludes that while vibe coding is valuable for ideation and rapid prototyping, enterprise software requires specification governance to transform probabilistic AI generation into deterministic, auditable engineering. Boundary conditions, threats to validity, and future research directions are discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper contrasts "vibe coding" (intuition-driven AI code generation) with Specification-Driven Development (SDD), introduces the Specification Governance Reference Model (SGRM) for constraining stochastic AI generation via structured contracts, and validates it quantitatively—showing a 73% reduction in security defects and 50% faster time-to-market.
AI.motivation: The shift from manual coding to intent-driven, agentic AI introduces governance gaps: conversational generation leads to productivity-reliability paradoxes, architectural erosion, security vulnerabilities, and technical debt accumulation. A structured, verifiable governance framework is needed to transform probabilistic AI output into deterministic, auditable software engineering.
AI.method: The paper first conducts a literature review to catalog failure modes of ungoverned LLM code generation. It then proposes the SGRM—a tool-independent framework defining four-component specification contracts, deterministic validation gateways, three rigor levels, and a closed-loop architecture integrating generation, verification, and governance. Finally, it evaluates SGRM by mapping quality characteristics against ISO/IEC 25010 and presents empirical evidence from two metrics: security defect reduction and time-to-market improvement.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation under SGRM governance shows a 73% reduction in security defects (via constitutional constraints) and a 50% reduction in time-to-market (via specification-governed agentic delivery). The ISO/IEC 25010 mapping demonstrates SGRM's coverage of key quality characteristics through specific governance mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Vibe coding suits ideation and prototyping, but enterprise-grade software demands specification governance to ensure deterministic, auditable engineering from probabilistic AI generation. The paper acknowledges boundary conditions, threats to validity, and outlines future research directions.

title: TaskArtisan: Designing Composable Generative Widgets for LLM-Assisted Analysis
summary: People increasingly use chatbots such as ChatGPT for everyday analysis tasks. While chatbots unify many analysis functions (e.g., scripts, visualizations, summaries), long conversations become hard to navigate, making it difficult to revisit prior steps or reuse successful workflows. LLMs now generate high-fidelity GUI code that enables people to create customized analysis tools beyond text. Yet, what new opportunities generative UIs bring to analysis work remain unclear. We interviewed six professionals about analysis with chatbots, analyzed publicly shared LLM-generated GUI tools, and conducted a comparison study (N=12) between a chatbot and TaskArtisan, a technology probe that enables people to create and assemble generative analysis UI widgets for sequential and fan-out composition. We find that GUI improved clarity and visual presentation but also introduced rigidity and additional prompting challenges. We summarize the trade-offs into a provisional design framework (malleability, specification, interoperability) to inform future generative UI in LLM-assisted analysis workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how generative UI widgets created by LLMs can augment chatbot-based analysis workflows. Through interviews, artifact analysis, and a comparative study using a prototype called TaskArtisan, the authors find that generative UIs improve clarity and visual presentation but introduce rigidity and prompting overhead. They propose a design framework centered on malleability, specification, and interoperability.
AI.motivation: Long chatbot conversations for analysis tasks become difficult to navigate, revisit, and reuse. While LLMs can now generate high-fidelity GUI code, the opportunities and trade-offs that generative UIs introduce to analysis work remain unexplored.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) semi-structured interviews with six professionals who use chatbots for analysis, (2) analysis of publicly shared LLM-generated GUI tools, and (3) a controlled comparison study (N=12) between a standard chatbot and TaskArtisan, a technology probe supporting creation and composition of generative analysis UI widgets (sequential and fan-out).
AI.result: Generative UIs improved clarity and visual presentation of analysis outputs. However, they also introduced rigidity in workflows and additional prompting challenges compared to purely conversational interfaces.
AI.conclusion: The authors distill observed trade-offs into a provisional design framework with three dimensions — malleability, specification, and interoperability — to guide future design of generative UI in LLM-assisted analysis workflows.

title: HyCoRec: Hypergraph-Enhanced Multi-Preference Learning for Alleviating Matthew Effect in Conversational Recommendation
summary: The Matthew effect is a notorious issue in Recommender Systems (RSs), \emph{i.e.}, the rich get richer and the poor get poorer, wherein popular items are overexposed while less popular ones are regularly ignored. Most methods examine Matthew effect in static or nearly-static recommendation scenarios. However, the Matthew effect will be increasingly amplified when the user interacts with the system over time. To address these issues, we propose a novel paradigm, Hypergraph-Enhanced Multi-Preference Learning for Alleviating Matthew Effect in Conversational Recommendation (HyCoRec), which aims to alleviate the Matthew effect in conversational recommendation. Concretely, HyCoRec devotes to alleviate the Matthew effect by learning multi-aspect preferences, \emph{i.e.}, item-, entity-, word-, review-, and knowledge-aspect preferences, to effectively generate responses in the conversational task and accurately predict items in the recommendation task when the user chats with the system over time. Extensive experiments conducted on two benchmarks validate that HyCoRec achieves new state-of-the-art performance and the superior of alleviating Matthew effect. Our code is available at https://github.com/zysensmile/HyCoRec.

AI.tldr: HyCoRec is a conversational recommendation framework that mitigates the Matthew effect (popularity bias) by learning multi-aspect user preferences (item, entity, word, review, knowledge) from a hypergraph-enhanced architecture, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The Matthew effect ("rich get richer") in recommender systems causes popular items to be overexposed while less popular items are ignored. Existing methods primarily address this in static or near-static settings, but the problem is progressively amplified in dynamic, interactive scenarios where users engage with the system over time. This gap motivates a conversational recommendation approach that explicitly tackles the compounding Matthew effect.
AI.method: HyCoRec employs a hypergraph-enhanced multi-preference learning paradigm.
