It jointly learns five distinct aspects of user preference — item-level, entity-level, word-level, review-level, and knowledge-level preferences — to simultaneously generate conversational responses and make accurate item recommendations. The hypergraph structure captures high-order relationships among users, items, and conversational elements over time.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that HyCoRec achieves new state-of-the-art performance and shows superior effectiveness in alleviating the Matthew effect compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: HyCoRec effectively addresses the compounding Matthew effect in conversational recommendation by leveraging multi-aspect preference learning with hypergraph modeling, offering both improved recommendation accuracy and fairer item exposure in dynamic user-system interactions.

title: Towards Secure and Trustworthy DAOs for Cross-Chain Governance
summary: Cross-chain DAOs face unique security challenges that go beyond traditional single-chain vulnerabilities. This paper identifies and categorizes four critical attack vectors in cross-chain DAO governance: bribery attacks, token control exploits, human-computer interaction deceptions, and protocol vulnerabilities. We propose a comprehensive security framework with a multi-layered architecture that integrates cryptographic trust anchors, fraud-resistant consensus mechanisms, and decentralized validation techniques to address these threats. Our framework introduces novel components, including a Governance Kernel with on-chain rule verification, a Cross-Chain Trust Layer using threshold cryptography, and a Resilience Layer offering time-locked decision reversals and progressive dispute resolution. By establishing a structured set of countermeasures, this work lays the foundation for secure, transparent, and attack-resistant governance across diverse blockchain environments.

AI.tldr: The paper categorizes four attack vectors in cross-chain DAO governance and proposes a multi-layered security framework featuring a Governance Kernel, Cross-Chain Trust Layer, and Resilience Layer to mitigate these threats.
AI.motivation: Cross-chain DAOs face unique, under-addressed security challenges that transcend single-chain vulnerabilities, necessitating a structured defense framework tailored to multi-chain governance contexts.
AI.method: The authors first taxonomize four attack vectors (bribery attacks, token control exploits, human-computer interaction deceptions, protocol vulnerabilities). They then propose a multi-layered security architecture comprising: (1) a Governance Kernel with on-chain rule verification; (2) a Cross-Chain Trust Layer employing threshold cryptography; and (3) a Resilience Layer featuring time-locked decision reversals and progressive dispute resolution, all integrated with cryptographic trust anchors, fraud-resistant consensus, and decentralized validation.
AI.result: A structured set of countermeasures is established, forming the foundation for secure, transparent, and attack-resistant cross-chain governance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework lays the groundwork for securing cross-chain DAO governance by systematically addressing identified attack vectors through a layered, cryptographically grounded architecture.

title: Aggregate in the Advantage, Not the Ratio: A Canonical-Form Analysis of Cooperative Multi-Agent Policy Optimization
summary: Multi-agent policy optimization, exemplified by PPO-based methods, is a key branch of cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). A central design question is how many neighboring agents\footnote{In this paper, "neighbors" refer not only to physical proximity but also to agents whose actions influence one another.} to aggregate in order to effectively utilize global information for cooperation. This decision must be made along two dimensions: in the advantage (which agents' rewards contribute to the credit signal) and in the ratio (which agents' likelihood ratios form the clipped importance weight). Existing methods occupy scattered, underexplored points on these two axes: IPPO treats both separately; MAPPO pairs a team-level advantage with per-agent ratios; HAPPO employs sequential ratios with per-agent advantages; and single-agent reductions operating on factorized joint policies aggregate both into fully joint products. We formalize these two design choices as support matrices $\SA$ and $\SR$, and prove a canonical structure: the expected multi-agent policy optimization objective depends on the pair $(\SA,\SR)$ only through their matrix product $\tS=\SR\SA$. This yields two key consequences: (i) Redundancy: the two support matrices are interchangeable with respect to the signal, meaning neither aggregation pattern is inherently superior.(ii) Variance Ordering: the advantage aggregates rewards as a sum (additive variance with an interior bias-variance optimum at the coupling neighborhood), whereas the ratio aggregates likelihood ratios as a product (multiplicative variance that grows exponentially with support size, with no accompanying bias reduction). The resulting design principle is unambiguous: aggregate neighbors in the advantage, sized to the coupling neighborhood, and keep the ratio per-agent.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes two key design choices in multi-agent PPO—advantage support and ratio support—as matrices, proves they only matter through their product, and derives a design principle: aggregate neighbors in the advantage (additive variance, optimal at coupling neighborhood) but keep the ratio per-agent (multiplicative variance explodes with support size).
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent PPO methods (IPPO, MAPPO, HAPPO, and joint-policy reductions) make scattered, underexplored choices about which agents' rewards and likelihood ratios to aggregate. The paper aims to provide a principled, unified understanding of these two aggregation dimensions to inform optimal algorithm design.
AI.method: The authors formalize advantage and ratio aggregation patterns as binary support matrices S^A and S^R, then prove that the expected multi-agent policy optimization objective depends on (S^A, S^R) only through their matrix product T = S^R S^A. They analyze variance properties: advantage aggregation yields additive variance with a bias-variance optimum at the coupling neighborhood; ratio aggregation yields multiplicative variance growing exponentially with support size without bias reduction.
AI.result: Two main results: (1) Redundancy—S^A and S^R are interchangeable w.r.t. the optimization signal, so neither pattern is inherently superior. (2) Variance Ordering—the advantage should aggregate neighbors (summing rewards, additive variance), while the ratio should remain per-agent (product of likelihood ratios, multiplicative variance explodes with support). This yields a clear design principle: aggregate in the advantage, sized to the coupling neighborhood, and keep the ratio per-agent.
AI.conclusion: The canonical decomposition of multi-agent policy optimization into advantage and ratio supports, linked only via their matrix product, provides a unifying framework for understanding and designing cooperative MARL algorithms, with a prescriptive recommendation for future method design.

title: Masked Diffusion Language Models are Strong and Steerable Text-Based World Models for Agentic RL
summary: Recent growth in reinforcement learning (RL) has surfaced a need for diverse, specialized training environments. Hand-curated environments with fixed task and reward difficulties become ineffective signals as model performance improves, and sparse rewards over long horizons induce mode collapse on specific workflows or tool structures. World models that simulate environment states have matched pure rollout performance, making them promising for scaling diversity on-demand. However, autoregressive (AR) world models suffer from a left-to-right bias preventing conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors such as tool schemas, prior turns, and expected outcomes. We (i) formalize text-based world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives, and (ii) curate 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories spanning nine open-source environments and twelve frontier model families. We compare AR LMs and masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), showing MDLMs, via bidirectional anchor-aware denoising, achieve better coherence, groundedness, and empirically validated rollout diversity than LLMs over 4x their parameter size, at comparable inference latency. We introduce a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks, and perform zero-shot transfer ablations on three OOD environments (ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld) across three 1.2B-7B agent backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral), achieving up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. We further conduct behavioral analysis of failure modes under adversarial scenarios and human evaluation on realism, outcome correctness, and training utility. We open-source our work to encourage research in this direction.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes text-based world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem, curates a large dataset of state-action trajectories, and demonstrates that masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) with bidirectional anchor-aware denoising outperform autoregressive LMs for environment simulation, achieving up to 47% absolute gains in zero-shot transfer across three OOD environments.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning needs diverse, scalable training environments. Hand-curated environments become ineffective as agents improve, and autoregressive world models suffer from left-to-right bias, preventing conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors (tool schemas, prior turns, expected outcomes). There is a need for world models that can scale diversity on-demand without these limitations.
AI.method: The authors (i) formalize text-based world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives; (ii) curate 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories across 9 open-source environments and 12 frontier model families; (iii) compare AR LMs against masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) using bidirectional anchor-aware denoising; (iv) introduce a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks; and (v) evaluate zero-shot transfer on ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and AppWorld across three 1.2B-7B agent backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral).
AI.result: MDLMs achieve better coherence, groundedness, and rollout diversity than LLMs over 4x their parameter size at comparable inference latency. Zero-shot transfer yields up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. Behavioral analysis of failure modes under adversarial scenarios and human evaluation on realism, outcome correctness, and training utility were also conducted.
AI.conclusion: Masked diffusion language models with bidirectional anchor-aware denoising present a superior alternative to autoregressive LMs for steerable text-based world modeling, enabling scalable, diverse environment simulation with strong zero-shot transfer capabilities.

title: Are Arithmetic Heuristic Neurons Form-Invariant? A Mechanistic Analysis of Symbols, Text, and Code in LLMs
summary: Large language models often succeed on one formulation of a problem while failing on an equivalent formulation. Whether these failures arise from distinct internal circuits or different activation states of a shared circuit remains unknown. Recent mechanistic interpretability studies suggest that arithmetic in LLMs emerges from a "bag of heuristics," encoded by a sparse set of MLP neurons that represent distinct arithmetic strategies. We investigate whether arithmetic heuristic neurons are form-invariant across symbolic arithmetic, natural language word problems, and Python code in three Llama-3 models. In each format, we identify arithmetic heuristic neurons using a two-stage pipeline combining attribution patching and activation patching. A compact set of neurons is shared across all three formats, and targeted interventions show this shared circuit is both necessary and sufficient for late-layer arithmetic computation. Transferring the shared neurons' activations from a successful execution in one format to a failed execution in another recovers most incorrect predictions, exceeding 97% for addition and subtraction, indicating that cross-format failures arise from activation states rather than distinct circuits. Moreover, shared neurons consistently belong to the same heuristic families across formats, demonstrating that arithmetic computation in LLMs is largely form-invariant at the neuron level.

AI.tldr: LLaMA models use a shared, form-invariant circuit of "arithmetic heuristic neurons" across symbolic, word problem, and code formats. Cross-format failures stem from differing activation states, not distinct circuits, and transferring activations from a successful to a failed format recovers >97% of incorrect predictions for addition/subtraction.
AI.motivation: LLMs often solve equivalent problems correctly in one format but fail in another. It is unknown whether these failures arise from distinct internal circuits or from different activation states of a shared circuit. The authors aim to resolve this by investigating whether arithmetic heuristic neurons are form-invariant across formats.
AI.method: The authors use a two-stage pipeline combining attribution patching and activation patching to identify arithmetic heuristic neurons in three Llama-3 models across three formats: symbolic arithmetic, natural language word problems, and Python code. They test for shared neurons across formats, perform targeted interventions to assess necessity and sufficiency, and transfer activations from successful to failed cross-format executions.
AI.result: A compact set of arithmetic heuristic neurons is shared across all three formats. Targeted interventions confirm this shared circuit is both necessary and sufficient for late-layer arithmetic computation. Transferring shared-neuron activations from a successful format to a failed format recovers most incorrect predictions (exceeding 97% for addition and subtraction). Shared neurons consistently belong to the same heuristic families across formats.
AI.conclusion: Arithmetic computation in LLMs is largely form-invariant at the neuron level. Cross-format failures are caused by differing activation states rather than distinct circuits, implying that improving activation patterns in one format could generalize to others.

title: Token-Level Cross-Modal Transformer with Contrastive Multi-Task Learning for Breast Cancer Subtype Classification and Survival Prediction
summary: Integrating heterogeneous genomic and clinical modalities for joint cancer subtype classification and survival prediction remains a key challenge in precision oncology. Existing approaches suffer from three limitations: (1) they treat each modality as a monolithic feature vector, precluding fine-grained token-level interactions across modalities; (2) cross-modal fusion is typically performed through linear weighting or late averaging rather than structured token exchange; and (3) survival and classification objectives are optimized independently, missing a joint regularization signal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified framework that enables fine-grained token-level cross-modal interactions for joint cancer subtype classification and survival prediction, addressing limitations of monolithic feature vectors, linear fusion, and independent optimization.
AI.motivation: Precision oncology requires integrating heterogeneous genomic and clinical data, but current methods treat modalities monolithically, fuse them through crude linear operations, and optimize survival and classification tasks separately — missing synergistic regularization.
AI.method: The paper introduces structured token-level interactions across genomic and clinical modalities, replacing monolithic feature representations. Cross-modal fusion is performed via structured token exchange rather than linear weighting or late averaging, with a joint optimization scheme that couples survival and subtype classification objectives for mutual regularization.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract — the abstract only describes the limitations of existing approaches and outlines the proposed methodology without reporting quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract — the abstract focuses on problem formulation and the proposed approach's design rationale rather than summarizing experimental findings or concluding insights.

title: Beyond Visibility and Technical Reuse: Public Application Transformation in Open-Source Model Ecosystems
summary: Open-source model platforms have made it easier to publish AI models, but model release alone does not reveal whether models become visible, technically reused, or incorporated into public applications. This study introduces public application transformation as a platform-visible dimension of model impact and examines it through structured Model-Space links on Hugging Face. We construct a platform-scale dataset of 2.56 million model repositories, 1.06 million Spaces, 810,087 dataset repositories, and 1.22 million account profiles, together with Model-Space, Dataset-Space, and model-to-model technical reuse links. The analysis shows that public application transformation is highly selective and concentrated: only a small share of models are linked to Spaces, and most Model-Space links are concentrated among a limited set of models. More importantly, application transformation is associated with platform visibility but is not equivalent to technical reuse, indicating that downloads, likes, downstream model reuse, and application-facing uptake capture different forms of model impact. Additional analyses show that application-transformed models tend to exhibit stronger metadata-based readiness and enter heterogeneous Space configurations involving datasets, SDKs, and task-specific application categories. By tracing how models move from repositories into public applications and demos, this study extends the measurement of open-source model impact from artifact availability and technical reuse to platform-mediated transformation across AI information objects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates "public application transformation" on Hugging Face — how models move from repositories into interactive Spaces — revealing it as a distinct, highly concentrated dimension of model impact separate from downloads, likes, or technical reuse, and associated with stronger metadata readiness and heterogeneous deployment configurations.
AI.motivation: While open-source model platforms facilitate publishing AI models, simply releasing a model does not indicate whether it gains visibility, is technically reused, or incorporated into public applications. Existing metrics (downloads, likes, downstream forks) may not fully capture real-world impact. The authors argue for a new, platform-visible dimension of impact: whether models are transformed into publicly accessible applications (Spaces on Hugging Face), and how this relates to other impact signals.
AI.method: The authors construct a platform-scale dataset from Hugging Face comprising 2.56M model repositories, 1.06M Spaces, 810K dataset repositories, and 1.22M account profiles. They extract structured links: Model-Space, Dataset-Space, and model-to-model technical reuse relationships. Using this dataset, they quantitatively analyze the selectivity and concentration of public application transformation, compare it against other impact metrics (downloads, likes, technical reuse), and examine associated metadata signals and Space configurations (SDKs, datasets, task categories).
AI.result: Public application transformation is highly selective: only a small fraction of models are linked to Spaces, and these links concentrate among a limited set of models. Application transformation correlates with platform visibility but is distinct from technical reuse (downstream model forks). Application-transformed models exhibit stronger metadata-based readiness (e.g., richer model cards) and enter heterogeneous Space configurations involving specific datasets, SDKs, and task-oriented application categories.
AI.conclusion: Public application transformation represents a distinct, platform-mediated dimension of open-source model impact that complements artifact availability and technical reuse. Measuring it reveals how models traverse from repositories into interactive public applications, offering a more comprehensive view of model impact within AI platform ecosystems.

title: Sidekick: Designing Communication for Effective Multitasking with Computer Use Agents
summary: Computer Use Agents (CUAs) can autonomously execute complex, multi-step tasks within GUIs, enhancing efficiency through parallel multitasking. However, our formative studies with CUA experts and GenAI users indicated that current feedback is primarily text-based, requiring sustained attention to monitor progress and offering limited visibility to trace past GUI interactions. Based on the findings, we developed a prototype system, Sidekick, for communicating CUAs' status with multimodal feedback across different stages of interaction: (i) When CUAs run in the background, Sidekick signals its execution state through ambient cues. (ii) Upon resuming interaction with CUAs, Sidekick provides multimodal summaries of completed actions to support rapid context resumption. (iii) When CUAs operate in the foreground, Sidekick enhances transparency by verbalizing and visualizing the agent's reasoning. A study with 30 participants demonstrated that Sidekick significantly improved multitasking performance with CUAs compared to baseline systems that presented textual feedback either in a typical chat or in an ambient display. Sidekick supported progress awareness, and error and action traceability more effectively. Finally, we demonstrate the promise of Sidekick through several example applications, and discuss implications for long-horizon human-agent collaboration.

AI.tldr: Sidekick is a prototype system that enhances Computer Use Agents (CUAs) with multimodal feedback—ambient cues, multimodal summaries, and transparent reasoning visualizations—across background, resumption, and foreground interaction stages. A 30-participant study showed it significantly improves multitasking performance, progress awareness, and error/action traceability compared to text-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Current CUA feedback is predominantly text-based, demanding sustained user attention to monitor progress and providing limited visibility into past GUI interactions. Formative studies with CUA experts and GenAI users revealed these shortcomings, motivating the need for richer, less attention-demanding feedback mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors conducted formative studies to identify feedback gaps, then designed and built Sidekick—a system delivering multimodal feedback across three interaction stages: (1) ambient cues for background execution, (2) multimodal summaries for context resumption, and (3) verbalized/visualized reasoning for foreground operation. A controlled user study with 30 participants compared Sidekick against two baselines: a typical chat-based textual interface and an ambient textual display.
AI.result: Sidekick significantly outperformed both baseline systems in multitasking performance, progress awareness, and error/action traceability. Example applications further demonstrated its promise for long-horizon human-agent collaboration.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal, stage-appropriate feedback substantially improves human-CUA collaboration by reducing attentional burden and enhancing transparency. The findings suggest design implications for future long-horizon human-agent interaction, advocating for systems that adapt their feedback modality to the user's current engagement context.

title: RAMP: Robust Ad Recommendation Under Limited Personalized-Feature Availability via Masking and Alignment Pathways
summary: Click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (CVR) prediction are fundamental tasks in online advertising, aiming to estimate the likelihood of user interactions based on various features. While personalized attributes such as age and gender can significantly enhance predictive accuracy, their use is increasingly restricted by privacy regulations, thereby limiting available data for both training and inference. To address this challenge, we propose RAMP (Robust Ad Recommendation Under Limited Personalized-Feature Availability via Masking and Alignment Pathways), which is designed to improve CTR/CVR prediction accuracy when personalized features are not accessible, thus supporting deployment in privacy-constrained settings.RAMP consists of (i) a personalized pathway built upon a dual-tower component with identical inputs but independent parameters, where output masking separates predictions for personalized and non-personalized signals, (ii) a separate non-personalized pathway trained with non-personalized features only, and (iii) a distillation-inspired prediction-alignment architecture between (i) and (ii) that improves prediction when personalized features are unavailable. We conduct comprehensive experiments using both public benchmarks and industrial datasets to evaluate the performance of RAMP. Our evaluation spans multiple backbone models and different settings: with and without access to personalized features. The results show that RAMP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods when personalized features are missing, while maintaining competitive performance when all features are available. %demonstrating its effectiveness and practicality for real-world advertising systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Ruixinhua/RAMP.

AI.tldr: RAMP is a framework for CTR/CVR prediction that maintains accuracy when personalized features (age, gender) are unavailable due to privacy constraints. It uses dual pathways—one with personalized features, one without—and a distillation-based alignment mechanism to transfer knowledge between them, enabling robust prediction in privacy-restricted settings.
AI.motivation: Personalized attributes like age and gender significantly improve CTR/CVR prediction accuracy, but privacy regulations increasingly restrict their use, limiting data availability for both training and inference. Existing methods degrade when personalized features are missing, creating a need for models robust to this absence.
AI.method: RAMP employs three components: (i) a personalized pathway using a dual-tower architecture with identical inputs but independent parameters, where output masking separates personalized and non-personalized signal predictions; (ii) a non-personalized pathway trained solely on non-personalized features; and (iii) a distillation-inspired prediction-alignment architecture between the two pathways that transfers knowledge, improving non-personalized predictions when personalized features are unavailable at inference.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on public benchmarks and industrial datasets across multiple backbone models demonstrate that RAMP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods when personalized features are missing, while maintaining competitive performance when all features are available.
AI.conclusion: RAMP provides an effective and practical solution for real-world advertising systems operating under privacy constraints, enabling robust CTR/CVR prediction even when personalized features are inaccessible. Code is publicly released.

title: Auditable Session Admission for Cross-Silo Federated Learning
comment: Accepted at the 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Cross-silo federated learning keeps raw data local, but deployments frequently stall on a practical bottleneck when deciding who may invoke which session-scoped operations across organizational boundaries, under constraints that remain auditable after execution. In practice, admission is implemented via centralized policy services, platform configuration, or ad hoc checks, which drift over time and are hard to audit from boundary-visible evidence. We present a session admission gateway that enforces pre-approved session capabilities at the boundary and emits verifiable decision records. During session setup, participating organizations approve roles and constraints and mint signed session capability tokens that enumerate permitted session operations for a given session_id. At runtime, each request carries the token and a request-bound proof-of-possession, making replay and impersonation with stolen tokens detectable at the gateway via request binding. Admission reduces to stateless per-request cryptographic verification and capability matching at an admission gateway, while setup and orchestration remain out of scope and organization-specific. We validate the approach end-to-end on a cross-silo FL workflow using MNIST as a surrogate workload. The proof-of-concept is open-source, containerized, provisioned as code, and includes reproducible tests and evidence logs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a session admission gateway for cross-silo federated learning that enforces pre-approved session capabilities using cryptographically signed tokens at organizational boundaries. It replaces centralized, hard-to-audit admission mechanisms with stateless, per-request cryptographic verification and capability matching, producing verifiable decision records. The approach is validated on an MNIST-based FL workflow with an open-source, containerized proof-of-concept.
AI.motivation: Cross-silo FL deployments face a practical bottleneck: deciding who may invoke session-scoped operations across organizational boundaries under auditable constraints. Current solutions rely on centralized policy services, platform configuration, or ad hoc checks that drift over time and are difficult to audit from boundary-visible evidence. There is a need for a verifiable, decentralized admission mechanism with tamper-evident decision records.
AI.method: The authors propose a session admission gateway that operates as follows: (1) During session setup, participating organizations approve roles and constraints, then mint signed session capability tokens enumerating permitted operations tied to a session_id. (2) At runtime, each request carries the token plus a request-bound proof-of-possession, preventing replay and impersonation of stolen tokens via request binding. (3) Admission reduces to stateless per-request cryptographic verification and capability matching at the gateway. Setup and orchestration remain out of scope and organization-specific.
AI.result: The approach is validated end-to-end on a cross-silo FL workflow using MNIST as a surrogate workload. The proof-of-concept is open-source, containerized, provisioned as code, and includes reproducible tests and evidence logs, demonstrating practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: A boundary-enforced, token-based session admission gateway with cryptographic verification and verifiable decision records provides a practical, auditable alternative to centralized policy services for cross-silo FL deployments. The open-source, containerized implementation confirms viability.

title: Generalist AI Control: Towards Multi-purpose Adaptive Algorithms
summary: Traditional controllers are designed for specific systems and do not transfer across different system orders and dynamics. We present a Generalist Controller, a learning-based controller capable of controlling systems of varying orders and dynamics. The approach introduces a novel dynamic state-space representation using attention mechanisms with masking, enabling a single neural network, trained in one shot, to handle systems with different dimensions without architectural modifications by assigning a system tag to each system. We generated 314,630 demonstrations from 25 diverse systems, including stable, unstable, minimum-phase, and non-minimum-phase dynamics, spanning linear and nonlinear systems from autonomous underwater and aerospace vehicles to mechanical systems and chemical processes. The model learns cross-system control strategies through multi-scale temporal processing and a mixture-of-experts architecture. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed generalist controller achieves comparable performance to system-specific LQI controllers across all tested systems, including challenging cases such as non-minimum-phase and unstable dynamics, whilst generalising to unseen operating conditions including actuator saturation, noise, disturbance, and reference trajectories not encountered during training. This work represents a significant step towards generalist control policies within a defined family of dynamical systems, demonstrating effective control across a range of single-input single-output (SISO) systems of varying order and dynamics using a single learned policy without system-specific tuning.

AI.tldr: A single neural network trained on 314,630 demonstrations from 25 diverse SISO systems can control systems of varying orders and dynamics without architectural changes, using attention-based dynamic state-space representation with masking and mixture-of-experts, achieving performance comparable to system-specific LQI controllers while generalizing to unseen operating conditions.
AI.motivation: Traditional controllers are system-specific, requiring redesign for each new system order or dynamics. A generalist controller that transfers across different system orders and dynamics without architectural modifications or system-specific tuning would significantly reduce engineering effort and enable broader applicability.
AI.method: The method introduces a dynamic state-space representation using attention mechanisms with masking, where a system tag is assigned to each system to handle varying dimensions. A single neural network is trained in one shot on 314,630 demonstrations from 25 diverse systems (stable, unstable, minimum-phase, non-minimum-phase, linear, nonlinear) spanning autonomous vehicles, mechanical systems, and chemical processes. The architecture employs multi-scale temporal processing and a mixture-of-experts design to learn cross-system control strategies.
AI.result: The generalist controller achieves performance comparable to system-specific LQI controllers across all 25 tested systems, including challenging non-minimum-phase and unstable dynamics. It successfully generalizes to unseen operating conditions: actuator saturation, noise, disturbances, and reference trajectories not encountered during training.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the feasibility of a single learned control policy for a defined family of SISO dynamical systems, representing a significant step toward generalist control policies that eliminate the need for system-specific tuning.

title: It Takes 8 Tokens: Weak-to-Strong Off-Policy RL via Auxiliary Branches
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has emerged as a standard approach for enhancing reasoning in large language models, which typically optimizes the policy by contrasting multiple self generated rollouts. However, we identify a critical support limited bottleneck in this paradigm: on challenging reasoning tasks, the target model's samples often exhibit semantic redundancy, converging into the same erroneous "reasoning basins" that offer negligible reward contrast for policy updates. In this paper, we propose to overcome this limitation through a weak to strong learning paradigm, where a policy's exploration is informed by a weaker but computationally efficient auxiliary model. We introduce W2SPO, an off policy RL method that injects short auxiliary segments often as brief as 8 tokens into intermediate target model trajectories and the target model then completes the reasoning path from these diverted states. Policy updates are restricted to these short inserted segments based on final verifiable rewards. Empirically, W2SPO achieves superior performance among evaluated 4B scale models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming evaluated post trained baselines. Compared with vanilla GRPO under the same sampling budget, W2SPO improves Pass@1 from 62.3% to 64.2% while achieving a 3.55 times training speedup. These results suggest that weak auxiliary branches can induce stronger target reasoning policies by expanding local exploration support.

AI.tldr: Existing RL for reasoning in LLMs suffers from a "support-limited bottleneck" where self-generated samples collapse into the same erroneous reasoning basins. The authors propose W2SPO, a weak-to-strong off-policy RL method that injects short auxiliary segments (as brief as 8 tokens) from a weaker model to diversify exploration, then updates only those injected segments based on verifiable rewards. W2SPO outperforms baselines on math reasoning at 4B scale, improving Pass@1 from 62.3% to 64.2% with a 3.55× training speedup.
AI.motivation: Standard RL for reasoning (e.g., GRPO) relies on contrasting multiple self-generated rollouts for policy updates. On hard reasoning tasks, the target model's own samples suffer from semantic redundancy — they repeatedly converge into the same erroneous "reasoning basins," yielding negligible reward contrast and limiting policy improvement. The authors identify this as a "support-limited bottleneck" and argue that purely on-policy exploration is insufficient for escaping these basins.
AI.method: W2SPO (Weak-to-Strong Policy Optimization) is an off-policy RL method. A weaker, computationally efficient auxiliary model generates short auxiliary segments (often ~8 tokens) that are injected at intermediate points into target model trajectories. The target model then completes the reasoning path from these diverted states. Critically, policy updates are restricted to only the short inserted segments, using final verifiable rewards as the learning signal. This allows the weak model to expand local exploration support while the strong model learns to navigate from diverse intermediate states.
AI.result: W2SPO achieves superior performance among 4B-scale models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks compared to evaluated post-trained baselines. Against vanilla GRPO under identical sampling budgets, W2SPO improves Pass@1 from 62.3% to 64.2% while achieving a 3.55× training speedup.
AI.conclusion: Weak auxiliary models can effectively induce stronger target reasoning policies by expanding local exploration support. The weak-to-strong paradigm addresses the support-limited bottleneck in RL-based reasoning, offering both improved accuracy and substantial computational efficiency gains.

title: Though Language Models Err While They Strive: Conformal Prediction for Self-Correcting Scientific Generation
summary: Large language models frequently violate fundamental scientific principles when generating technical content, undermining their reliability in scientific applications. We introduce Scientific Feasibility Control SFC, a graph-structured conformal prediction framework that provides statistical guarantees for scientific reasoning validity through progressive absolute-coherent-factuality validation. Our approach decomposes scientific reasoning into atomic absolute-coherent-factuality units requiring both individual correctness against physical laws and logical substantiation from preceding context, addressing the cascade effect where early scientific errors contaminate subsequent reasoning steps. Unlike independence-based methods that treat claims in isolation, SFC models logical dependencies as approximate deducibility graphs and operates through real-time validation with dynamic branching when scientific violations are detected, the system branches to alternative generation paths using verified context as foundation. We demonstrate SFC across established scientific reasoning benchmarks including PhyX multimodal physics, MATH, ScienceQA, and ARC Challenge, achieving 50.1 percent accuracy on PhyX physics reasoning, substantially outperforming recent reasoning models including DeepSeek-R1 49.8 percent and GPT-4 45.8 percent while providing 91.7 percent scientific validity with formal conformal coverage guarantees at alpha equals 0.10 confidence level and reducing scientific law violations by 73 percent across multiple model architectures.

AI.tldr: SFC introduces a graph-structured conformal prediction framework that decomposes scientific reasoning into atomic units requiring both physical correctness and logical substantiation from context, using dynamic branching when violations are detected. It achieves 50.1% on PhyX, outperforming DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4, with 91.7% scientific validity under formal conformal guarantees and a 73% reduction in scientific law violations.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently violate fundamental scientific principles when generating technical content, and early errors cascade through subsequent reasoning steps. Existing independence-based methods treat claims in isolation, failing to capture logical dependencies, which undermines reliability in scientific applications.
AI.method: SFC decomposes scientific reasoning into atomic absolute-coherent-factuality (ACF) units requiring (1) individual correctness against physical laws and (2) logical substantiation from preceding context. Logical dependencies are modeled as approximate deducibility graphs. The system performs real-time validation with conformal prediction; when scientific violations are detected, it dynamically branches to alternative generation paths using verified context as a foundation, providing formal coverage guarantees.
AI.result: On PhyX multimodal physics, SFC achieves 50.1% accuracy vs. DeepSeek-R1 (49.8%) and GPT-4 (45.8%). It provides 91.7% scientific validity with formal conformal coverage guarantees at α=0.10 confidence level and reduces scientific law violations by 73% across multiple model architectures. Evaluated on PhyX, MATH, ScienceQA, and ARC Challenge.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured conformal prediction with progressive ACF validation and dynamic branching effectively enforces scientific feasibility in LLM reasoning, yielding statistically guaranteed validity improvements and substantial violation reduction across diverse benchmarks and architectures.

title: HantaWatch: Federated Learning for Hantavirus Genomic Surveillance
summary: Hantavirus genomic surveillance is limited by the distribution of sequence data, non-IID source heterogeneity, and constrained expert-review capacity. We propose HantaWatch, a federated learning framework that enables laboratories and surveillance sites to collaboratively train sequence-based models without sharing raw data. HantaWatch integrates k-mer feature extraction, source-aware federated client construction, adaptive DU-FedProx optimization, surveillance-specific model selection, and prediction-only triage. Experiments on binary and multi-class tasks show that HantaWatch supports high-risk screening, outbreak-associated prediction, clade classification, and clinical-syndrome categorization while balancing predictive performance, false-negative risk, and update stability. The framework converts model output into risk scores, confidence estimates, uncertainty flags, and ranked expert-review priorities. HantaWatch therefore provides a practical federated decision-support layer for decentralized Hantavirus surveillance, supporting expert prioritization without replacing laboratory or public-health interpretation.

AI.tldr: HantaWatch is a federated learning framework for collaborative Hantavirus genomic surveillance that trains models across distributed sites without sharing raw data, converting predictions into risk scores and expert-review priorities.
AI.motivation: Hantavirus genomic surveillance faces three key bottlenecks: uneven geographic distribution of sequence data, non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) heterogeneity across surveillance sources, and limited capacity for expert review. These challenges hinder timely and scalable outbreak detection.
AI.method: HantaWatch integrates five components: (1) k-mer feature extraction for sequence encoding, (2) source-aware federated client construction to address site-specific data distributions, (3) adaptive DU-FedProx optimization to stabilize heterogeneous training, (4) surveillance-specific model selection criteria, and (5) a prediction-only triage pipeline that outputs risk scores, confidence estimates, uncertainty flags, and ranked expert-review priorities.
AI.result: Experiments on binary and multi-class tasks demonstrate that HantaWatch effectively supports high-risk screening, outbreak-associated prediction, clade classification, and clinical-syndrome categorization, while balancing predictive performance, false-negative risk, and update stability across decentralized sites.
AI.conclusion: HantaWatch provides a practical federated decision-support layer for decentralized Hantavirus surveillance, augmenting — rather than replacing — laboratory and public-health interpretation by prioritizing cases for expert review.

title: Dependency-Guided Code Generation: Structured Matrix Decomposition and Consistency-Guided Refinement
summary: The increasing complexity of modern software systems has made automated code generation a fundamental task in software engineering. However, existing approaches often fail to adequately capture the intricate, multi-level dependencies among code entities, leading to generated code that is logically incomplete or difficult to integrate into real-world systems. To address this limitation, we propose a dependency-aware code generation framework that explicitly models interactions among code entities through a graph-based representation. We decompose dependencies into two complementary components: a quantized matrix that captures strong, explicit relations, and a sparse low-rank factorization that models weaker, implicit interactions. The decomposition is efficiently learned via an alternating optimization procedure. During code generation, the learned dependency structure is incorporated as a constraint, ensuring both semantic coherence and structural consistency of the generated code. Furthermore, we introduce a sparse triplet representation for strong dependencies, significantly improving storage efficiency and computational scalability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently produces code with superior semantic alignment and structural fidelity compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dependency-aware code generation framework that models both explicit and implicit code entity dependencies using a quantized matrix and sparse low-rank factorization, learned via alternating optimization, to produce semantically coherent and structurally consistent code.
AI.motivation: Existing automated code generation methods fail to capture complex, multi-level dependencies among code entities, resulting in logically incomplete code that is difficult to integrate into real-world systems.
AI.method: Dependencies are decomposed into a quantized matrix (capturing strong, explicit relations) and a sparse low-rank factorization (modeling weaker, implicit interactions), learned via alternating optimization. The learned dependency structure serves as a constraint during generation. A sparse triplet representation improves storage and scalability for strong dependencies.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach consistently produces code with superior semantic alignment and structural fidelity compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-level code dependencies via a hybrid quantized-plus-low-rank graph representation, enforced as a generation constraint, significantly improves the logical completeness and integrability of automatically generated code.

title: Human-in-the-Loop User Feedback Affects Perceived Accuracy and Trust, but Task Subjectivity Matters
summary: While ML can produce complex models beyond those that a human could produce manually, incorporating human input can often improve performance beyond purely data-driven models. While this feedback could come from system designers or domain experts, in many cases, the end users who regularly use the system will naturally develop an understanding of its flaws and desire the ability to change the system's behavior based on their knowledge. While soliciting feedback from end users can result in significant model improvement over time, introducing these feedback techniques can also affect several human factors-such as trust or perception of system accuracy-that are not yet fully understood and have different effects reported in the existing literature. Therefore, we sought to build on the existing research to further explore how the act of providing feedback can affect user understanding of an intelligent system and its accuracy in different contexts. We present three controlled experiments that study the effects of interactive feedback collections on user impressions in domains with objective and subjective feedback. The results show that in a context where there is an objectively correct answer, providing HITL feedback lowered both participants' trust in the system and their perception of system accuracy, regardless of whether the system accuracy improved in response to their feedback. However, when the feedback being provided involved subjective opinion, no such negative bias was observed. Furthermore, in the objective context, participants distrusted the system over time, whereas participants in the subjective context mistrusted the system over time. These results highlight the importance of considering the effects of allowing different types of end-user feedback on user trust when designing intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: Three controlled experiments reveal that providing objective feedback to ML systems lowers user trust and perceived accuracy, while subjective feedback shows no such negative bias. In objective contexts, distrust grows over time; in subjective contexts, mistrust grows. Designers must consider feedback type when implementing human-in-the-loop systems.
AI.motivation: While end-user feedback can improve ML models, the effects of soliciting such feedback on human factors — particularly trust and perception of system accuracy — are not fully understood and show conflicting results in existing literature. The authors sought to systematically investigate how the act of providing feedback influences user impressions across different contexts.
AI.method: The authors conducted three controlled experiments examining interactive feedback collection effects on user impressions. They compared two contexts: one with objectively correct answers (objective feedback) and one involving subjective opinion (subjective feedback). They measured participants' trust in the system and perception of system accuracy over time, both when system accuracy improved in response to feedback and when it did not.
AI.result: In objective contexts, providing HITL feedback significantly lowered both trust and perceived accuracy — even when actual system accuracy improved. In subjective contexts, no such negative bias emerged. Additionally, participants in the objective condition exhibited growing distrust over time, while those in the subjective condition exhibited growing mistrust over time.
AI.conclusion: The type of feedback (objective vs. subjective) critically shapes how human-in-the-loop interaction affects user trust and perceptions. System designers should carefully weigh these human-factors consequences when deciding whether and how to incorporate end-user feedback mechanisms into intelligent systems.

title: MagicSelector: Joint Optimization for Agent Tool Selection via Counterfactual Decomposition and Progressive Reranking
summary: We present MagicSelector, a joint optimization framework integrating Counterfactual task decomposition, Progressive reranking, and Dynamic Top-K, designed to address the fundamental challenges of tool retrieval in agents. MagicSelector is a specialized framework capable of translating ambiguous user instructions into executable atomic subtasks and guiding high-precision tool retrieval, effectively mitigating redundant noise and severe context distraction in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios.We empower MagicSelector with these capabilities through three key contributions: (1) a preferenceguided counterfactual task decomposition mechanism that utilizes a counterfactual reward to quantify the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking, effectively imposing fine-grained structural supervision on logical coherence; (2) a progressive tool reranking method driven by self-distillation hard negative mining, which optimizes both point-wise and list-wise relevance to enhance fine-grained discrimination among highly similar tools; and (3) a dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K strategy that adaptively monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to dynamically truncate the candidate list, maximizing relevant tool recall while filtering long-tail noise. Evaluated on MTDTool, the first task decomposition benchmark we constructed tailored for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations, MagicSelector yields promising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization capability, and overall token efficiency, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

AI.tldr: MagicSelector is a joint optimization framework for tool retrieval in agents that combines counterfactual task decomposition, progressive reranking with self-distillation hard negative mining, and a dynamic Top-K strategy. It translates ambiguous user instructions into atomic subtasks and achieves state-of-the-art performance in retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization, and token efficiency on a newly constructed benchmark, MTDTool.
AI.motivation: Tool retrieval in LLM-based agents suffers from ambiguous user instructions and significant noise/context distraction, especially in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios. Existing methods lack fine-grained structural supervision for task decomposition, struggle to discriminate among highly similar tools, and fail to adaptively filter irrelevant candidates without sacrificing recall.
AI.method: (1) A counterfactual task decomposition mechanism that uses counterfactual rewards to quantify the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking, providing fine-grained logical coherence supervision. (2) A progressive reranking method using self-distillation hard negative mining that jointly optimizes point-wise and list-wise relevance for discriminating similar tools. (3) A dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K strategy that monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to adaptively truncate the candidate list.
AI.result: MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on MTDTool, a new benchmark for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations, across tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization, and overall token efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The joint optimization of counterfactual decomposition, progressive reranking, and dynamic Top-K is highly effective for robust tool retrieval in agents, particularly for handling ambiguous instructions and OOD scenarios. The framework's strong empirical results validate this integrated approach.

title: Synchronization-Free Algebraic Fingerprints for Large Language Models: From Autoregressive to Diffusion Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have created an urgent need for reliable watermarking methods that enable attribution of generated text while remaining robust to editing and paraphrasing. We propose a novel synchronization-free watermarking scheme in which every watermark consists of a single binary congruence generated from a pair of neighbouring tokens. For each token pair, a cryptographic hash determines an evaluation point of a Reed--Solomon polynomial representing the secret identity, while the parity of the polynomial evaluation determines the watermark bit embedded into the second token of the pair. Since each congruence is self-contained and depends only on the local token pair, the proposed construction is naturally resistant to insertions, deletions, and token reordering. We analyse the recovery problem from an algebraic perspective, discuss several decoding algorithms suitable for different identity sizes, and model watermark corruption as a Binary Symmetric Channel. The analysis shows that reliable recovery requires only a small redundancy even for relatively high token corruption rates. Unlike existing block-based watermarking schemes, the proposed method avoids synchronization problems while providing a flexible framework for embedding both short and long secret identities.

AI.tldr: A novel synchronization-free text watermarking scheme using Reed-Solomon polynomial evaluations over token pairs, where each pair independently embeds a single congruence bit, providing natural robustness to insertions, deletions, and reordering with minimal redundancy.
AI.motivation: LLMs require reliable watermarking for attribution that resists editing and paraphrasing. Existing block-based methods suffer from synchronization problems when tokens are inserted, deleted, or reordered, motivating a self-contained per-pair approach.
AI.method: For each adjacent token pair, a cryptographic hash determines an evaluation point of a Reed-Solomon polynomial encoding a secret identity. The parity of the polynomial evaluation determines the watermark bit embedded in the second token. Each congruence is self-contained, and recovery is framed algebraically with decoding algorithms under a Binary Symmetric Channel corruption model.
AI.result: Reliable identity recovery requires only small redundancy even under relatively high token corruption rates, overcoming synchronization vulnerabilities inherent in block-based schemes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed synchronization-free watermarking framework, using pairwise Reed-Solomon congruences, enables robust attribution of LLM-generated text across both short and long identities, with natural resistance to common text manipulations.

title: RELIC: Revealed Principles for Learning Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning
summary: Multi-agent planning becomes substantially harder when agents must improve specialized decision-making skills while keeping their internal implementations private. This regime arises when agents are developed independently, expose different interfaces and capabilities, and must nevertheless coordinate without sharing executable policies. Prior research has largely assumed centralized optimization, shared policy access, or common skill representations, making it poorly suited to privacy-constrained cooperation. We introduce RELIC, a framework for learning interpretable and composable skills via revealed principles. Each agent refines its own programmatic skill through private LLM-guided search, while a trusted orchestrator evaluates proposed updates solely through team-level performance. Successful behaviors are not broadcast as code; instead, they are abstracted into portable principles that other agents can instantiate within their own interfaces and recombine with local strategies. This separates coordination from implementation sharing, enabling cross-agent transfer under heterogeneous skill signatures. RELIC thus introduces a new paradigm for privacy-preserving skill learning and coordination in multi-agent planning.

AI.tldr: RELIC introduces a privacy-preserving multi-agent coordination framework where agents refine skills via private LLM-guided search and share only abstracted principles (not executable code), enabling heterogeneous agents to learn composable skills without exposing internal implementations.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent planning methods assume centralized optimization, shared policies, or common skill representations, which fails under privacy constraints where agents are independently developed, have heterogeneous interfaces, and cannot share executable code.
AI.method: RELIC employs a two-level architecture: (1) each agent privately refines programmatic skills using LLM-guided search within its own interface; (2) a trusted orchestrator evaluates proposed updates based on team-level performance and abstracts successful behaviors into portable, interpretable "principles" that other agents can instantiate locally without accessing the original implementation.
AI.result: The paper reports that RELIC enables effective cross-agent skill transfer and coordination under heterogeneous skill signatures while preserving implementation privacy. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the provided abstract.)
AI.conclusion: RELIC establishes a new paradigm for privacy-preserving skill learning in multi-agent systems by separating coordination (shared principles) from implementation (private code), making it viable for real-world scenarios where agents cannot or should not expose internal policies.

title: PPO-HSC: An Exploratory Reinforcement Learning Framework Based on Wide-Area Policy Coverage Optimization
summary: This paper introduces PPO-HSC (Proximal Policy Optimization with High-order Sampling Coverage), an exploratory reinforcement learning framework designed to address the "Invisible Shackles" of mode collapse in Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning. While standard Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) effectively reinforces high-reward trajectories, it often leads models to over-optimize known solutions, sacrificing curiosity and the ability to explore broader solution manifolds. To overcome this, PPO-HSC incorporates a High-order Sampling Coverage (HSC) reward that incentivizes the discovery of "low-similarity yet high-validity" reasoning patterns. By maintaining a dynamic trajectory library of verified unique solutions, the framework provides a differentiable signal that rewards semantic novelty while ensuring structural rationality through a plausibility constraint. Empirical evaluations on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP) and code generation tasks demonstrate that PPO-HSC significantly enhances solution diversity and state-space coverage while maintaining or surpassing the accuracy and syntax integrity of state-of-the-art RL baselines.

AI.tldr: PPO-HSC tackles mode collapse in LLM fine-tuning by adding a high-order sampling coverage reward that incentivizes discovering diverse yet valid reasoning patterns, preserving accuracy while significantly boosting solution diversity on math and code tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR (Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards) causes LLMs to over-optimize known high-reward trajectories, leading to mode collapse — models lose curiosity and fail to explore broader solution manifolds. The authors term this the "Invisible Shackles" problem.
AI.method: PPO-HSC extends PPO with a High-order Sampling Coverage (HSC) reward. It maintains a dynamic trajectory library of verified unique solutions and computes a differentiable reward that promotes "low-similarity yet high-validity" reasoning patterns. A plausibility constraint ensures structural rationality of novel outputs.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, SVAMP) and code generation tasks, PPO-HSC significantly improves solution diversity and state-space coverage while matching or exceeding the accuracy and syntax integrity of state-of-the-art RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting RLVR with a coverage-based novelty reward effectively mitigates mode collapse in LLM fine-tuning, enabling models to explore diverse solution strategies without sacrificing task performance.

title: JOR-Bench: Japanese Operations Research Benchmarks for Large Language Models
summary: We present JOR-Bench, a collection of five Japanese-language benchmarks for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to formulate and solve operations research (OR) problems. Each benchmark is a Japanese translation of an existing English benchmark: IndustryOR, MAMO Complex LP, NL4OPT, OptiBench, and OptMATH, covering 1,319 problems spanning linear programming, mixed-integer programming, non-linear programming, and combinatorial optimization. JOR-Bench is a solver-independent benchmark that can be used with any solver or programming language, and consists of pairs of Japanese problem statements and expected numerical answers. We evaluate seven LLMs, including multilingual general-purpose models and Japanese-specialized models, on both the original English and the new Japanese versions, and compare performance across languages. For the main evaluation, we standardize execution with the Python interface to OR-Tools to make model outputs comparable and reproducible with open-source software. Our results show that OR formulation ability is largely language-neutral for strong multilingual models; the overall average accuracy difference between English and Japanese is only $-0.3$ pp. Yet error analysis reveals subtle cross-lingual differences, including a pragmatic disambiguation failure in some domains that causes models to output decision-variable values instead of the objective value when the prompt is in Japanese.

AI.tldr: JOR-Bench is a Japanese-language benchmark suite for evaluating LLMs on operations research problem formulation, comprising 1,319 translated problems across four optimization domains. Evaluation of seven LLMs reveals OR formulation ability is largely language-neutral, with only a −0.3 pp accuracy gap between English and Japanese, though subtle cross-lingual disambiguation failures emerge in Japanese prompts.
AI.motivation: Existing OR benchmarks are predominantly in English, leaving a gap in understanding how well LLMs can formulate and solve OR problems in other languages, particularly Japanese. The authors aim to assess whether OR formulation capability is language-dependent and to provide a standardized Japanese evaluation resource.
AI.method: The authors translated five existing English OR benchmarks (IndustryOR, MAMO Complex LP, NL4OPT, OptiBench, OptMATH) into Japanese, creating JOR-Bench with 1,319 solver-independent problem–answer pairs spanning LP, MILP, NLP, and combinatorial optimization. Seven LLMs (multilingual and Japanese-specialized) were evaluated on both English and Japanese versions using a standardized OR-Tools Python interface for reproducibility. Error analysis was conducted to identify cross-lingual failure modes.
AI.result: Strong multilingual models show near-identical OR formulation accuracy across languages, with an overall average difference of −0.3 pp. However, error analysis reveals a systematic disambiguation failure in Japanese: models sometimes output decision-variable values rather than the requested objective value, indicating pragmatic interpretation differences between languages.
AI.conclusion: OR formulation capability in LLMs is largely language-neutral for strong multilingual models, supporting the use of translated benchmarks. However, subtle cross-lingual pragmatic issues—such as misinterpreting what the question asks for—highlight the need for careful prompt design and evaluation in non-English contexts.

title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models
summary: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are not publicly available for research, and leading wearable foundation models trained on such datasets are rarely open-weight or come with reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we release OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive open-access wearable health dataset to date, alongside open-source implementations of recent wearable foundation models. OpenMHC, derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, includes >60 million hours of wearable data across 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 169 linked variables, including health, lifestyle, mood, and behavior from 11,894 consenting participants. Furthermore, we introduce a unified, open benchmark that enables standardized comparison of wearable health models across three tracks: health and behavior downstream prediction, multivariate data imputation, and time-series forecasting. We benchmark classical methods alongside recent wearable and multivariate time series foundation models. By open-sourcing data, code, and model weights at this unprecedented scale, we aim to democratize wearable health AI research and enable the community to drive open progress in this domain.

AI.tldr: OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC) is released as the largest open-access wearable health dataset (>60M hours, 19 sensor channels, 11,894 participants), alongside open-source wearable foundation model implementations and a unified benchmark for standardized evaluation across health prediction, data imputation, and time-series forecasting tasks.
AI.motivation: The largest wearable datasets and foundation models are proprietary (closed-source, closed-weight, non-reproducible), hindering open science in wearable health AI. There is a critical need for large-scale open data, open models, and standardized benchmarks to democratize research.
AI.method: The authors curate OpenMHC from the My Heart Counts study app (over a decade of data), release open-source implementations of recent wearable foundation models, and establish a unified benchmark with three tracks: (1) downstream health/behavior prediction, (2) multivariate imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Classical methods and recent foundation models are evaluated.
AI.result: OpenMHC provides >60 million hours of data across 19 sensor channels and up to 169 linked variables from 11,894 participants. The benchmark enables standardized comparison of multiple model classes across three task tracks. Data, code, and model weights are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: By open-sourcing data, code, and model weights at unprecedented scale, the work aims to democratize wearable health AI research and accelerate community-driven progress in the field.

title: Model-Driven Discipline for Multi-Agent LLMs: Requirement-to-Verification Generation of Traceable System Models
summary:
Software complexity is a long-standing challenge for system engineers. Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) addresses it by treating models as first-class artefacts, but a typical MDE process spans many tools and produces heterogeneous models of different system aspects, making traceability, maintenance, and change management difficult.
  We propose RADIANT, an engineering methodology that combines MDE with Multi-Agent Large Language Models (LLMs) for complete model-based system development, with a focus on safety-critical systems. From a carefully specified requirement model, RADIANT automatically generates heterogeneous models across engineering phases -- a concept model, a domain-specific modelling language, a conforming system model, and a behaviour model -- together with executable, element-level traceability links, on top of which it provides exact, automated change-impact analysis. Generated behaviour models are translated into CSP and formally verified (e.g.\ for deadlock freedom and convergence) with a counterexample-driven repair loop. Evaluating RADIANT across three LLMs, we find that the multi-agent decomposition reliably improves the \emph{syntactic validity} of the generated formal artefacts over a single-agent baseline -- and their \emph{executability} where the model's code generation permits -- while gains in semantic accuracy are model-dependent. A six-participant study shows an order-of-magnitude ($10$--$15\times$) reduction in development time, and the unmodified pipeline transfers to a second domain.

AI.tldr: RADIANT integrates Model-Driven Engineering with Multi-Agent LLMs to automate the generation of heterogeneous system models and formal verification artefacts from requirements, achieving 10–15× faster development and cross-domain transferability.
AI.motivation: MDE processes span multiple tools and produce heterogeneous models, complicating traceability, maintenance, and change management. Automating model generation and impact analysis, especially for safety-critical systems, remains an open challenge.
AI.method: RADIANT is a methodology that takes a requirement model as input and uses multi-agent LLMs to generate: (1) a concept model, (2) a domain-specific modelling language, (3) a conforming system model, (4) a behaviour model, and (5) element-level traceability links. Behaviour models are translated into CSP for formal verification (deadlock freedom, convergence) with counterexample-driven repair. Multi-agent decomposition is compared against a single-agent baseline across three LLMs, and evaluated via a six-participant user study and a cross-domain transfer test.
AI.result: Multi-agent decomposition reliably improves syntactic validity of generated formal artefacts over single-agent baselines, and executability where code generation permits. Gains in semantic accuracy are model-dependent. The user study shows a 10–15× reduction in development time, and the unmodified pipeline successfully transfers to a second domain.
AI.conclusion: Combining MDE with multi-agent LLMs yields a practical, automated methodology for safety-critical system development that significantly accelerates workflows, ensures traceability, and supports formal verification with repair, while remaining transferable across domains.

title: It Matters How You Say It: Exploring Rhetorical Patterns for AI-Assisted Information Evaluation
summary: Prior work on AI-assisted information evaluation has largely focused on what AI systems communicate, comparing explanation types and formats, with responses predominantly cast in directive rhetoric where the system delivers a verdict and the user passively accepts it. While debate-style interactions have recently shown promise in prompting critical evaluation over deference, the rhetorical patterns that structure AI responses and how they might induce reflection, uncertainty, or independent reasoning remain largely unexamined. To address this, we investigated eight rhetorical patterns known to induce contemplation: Intentional Misleading, Interpretive Alternative, Scaffold Explanation, Triggering Distrust, Information Distortion, Alternative Framing, Socratic Questioning, and an Oracle baseline. Through a within-subject study with n=98 participants on a hint-on-demand fact verification task, we observed preliminary evidence that Scaffold Explanation were associated with the highest accuracy gains, and encouraging deeper reflection. Surprisingly, the adversarial conditions also improved accuracy modestly. Participants preferred Alternative Framing most and Interpretive Alternative least, largely due to the latter's perceived time cost. We discuss the implications of designing conversational agents with varied rhetorical styles and the trade-offs among user performance, satisfaction, and contemplation.

AI.tldr: Explores how eight rhetorical patterns in AI responses affect user accuracy, reflection, and preferences in a fact-verification task. Scaffold Explanation improved accuracy and reflection most; adversarial patterns also helped modestly. Alternative Framing was most preferred; Interpretive Alternative least, due to perceived time cost.
AI.motivation: Prior AI-assisted information evaluation research has focused on what information systems convey (explanation types/formats) using directive rhetoric where users passively accept verdicts. Debate-style interactions show promise for critical evaluation, but the rhetorical patterns in AI responses and their capacity to induce reflection, uncertainty, or independent reasoning remain largely unexamined.
AI.method: Within-subject study with n=98 participants on a hint-on-demand fact verification task. Eight rhetorical patterns were tested: Intentional Misleading, Interpretive Alternative, Scaffold Explanation, Triggering Distrust, Information Distortion, Alternative Framing, Socratic Questioning, and an Oracle baseline. Measured accuracy gains, depth of reflection, and user preferences.
AI.result: Scaffold Explanation was associated with highest accuracy gains and deeper reflection. Adversarial conditions also improved accuracy modestly (surprising result). Alternative Framing was most preferred; Interpretive Alternative was least preferred due to perceived time cost. Reveals trade-offs among performance, satisfaction, and contemplation.
AI.conclusion: Rhetorical patterns significantly shape how users engage with AI-provided information. Scaffold-style and adversarial rhetoric can prompt independent reasoning and improve accuracy, but user satisfaction may conflict with contemplative depth. Design of conversational agents should balance rhetorical style to suit goals of performance, reflection, and user experience.

title: Remote Awareness of Seafloor Images Collected by AUVs over Low-Bandwidth Communication Links
summary: This paper introduces a method for real-time processing and transmission of autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) imagery over low-bandwidth communication links. It leverages artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to identify a set of images that best represent an entire dataset, or automatically finds the most similar images to a given query image for transmission to operators. Combined with metadata of a larger set of images, compressed versions of the selected images can be transmitted over satellite communication links or underwater modems, and provide operators on shore with information about the type of imagery the AUV is collecting while it is still deployed. Data from three deployments off the coast of the UK and in Gran Canaria using different AUVs and imaging systems demonstrate the method in the field. It achieved an almost 400,000-fold reduction in data volume compared to the raw data size, enabling transmission of data summaries of a 2-hour 47-minute-long mapping mission in just over 34 minutes over low-bandwidth satellite communication.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an AI-driven framework for selecting and transmitting representative AUV imagery over low-bandwidth links, achieving nearly 400,000× data reduction and enabling near-real-time shore-side awareness of collected imagery during deployment.
AI.motivation: Autonomous underwater vehicles collect vast amounts of imagery that cannot be transmitted in real time over severely bandwidth-constrained channels (satellite links, underwater acoustic modems). Operators on shore lack timely awareness of what imagery is being collected until the AUV is recovered, hindering adaptive mission planning.
