AI.method: AI-based image selection: the system either (1) identifies a representative subset of images that best summarizes the entire dataset, or (2) retrieves images most similar to a user-supplied query image. Selected images are compressed and transmitted alongside metadata from the broader image set over satellite or underwater communication links.
AI.result: Field validation from three deployments (off the UK coast and Gran Canaria) using different AUVs and imaging systems demonstrated a ~400,000-fold reduction in data volume. A 2-hour 47-minute mapping mission's data summary was transmitted in just over 34 minutes over low-bandwidth satellite communication.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AI-assisted selective transmission framework is practical and effective for providing operators with timely situational awareness of AUV-collected imagery during missions, despite severe bandwidth constraints.

title: VIGIL: Verifying Identity via Gated Intermittent Likelihoods for Continuous Biometric Authentication
summary: Continuous multi-modal authentication has emerged as a necessity for securing modern environments against persistent threats. Existing temporal fusion techniques fail to identify a persistent attacker from a genuine user with poor signal strength. In this study, we propose VIGIL (Verifying Identity via Gated Intermittent Likelihoods for Continuous Biometric Authentication), a highly adaptive continuous authentication framework. We introduce configurable cross-modal fusion with per-modality weighting, enabling operators to select their choice of integration strategy. We improve temporal fusion using dual-state State Transition Machines (STM) with unidirectional transition matrices. A three-zone verification decision model that enables multi-round verification when evidence is inconclusive is used in combination with an adaptive shrinking verification window. Monotonic decay, backflow elimination and analytical evaluation demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively addresses the limitations of existing approaches and reduces the time to detect intrusions while maintaining high usability for legitimate users.

AI.tldr: VIGIL is a continuous multi-modal authentication framework that improves persistent attacker detection through configurable cross-modal fusion, dual-state State Transition Machines with unidirectional transitions, and a three-zone adaptive verification window — reducing intrusion detection time while preserving usability.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal fusion techniques fail to distinguish persistent attackers from legitimate users experiencing poor signal strength, creating a critical security gap in continuous authentication systems.
AI.method: VIGIL introduces three key innovations: (1) configurable cross-modal fusion with per-modality weighting for flexible integration strategies; (2) dual-state State Transition Machines (STM) with unidirectional transition matrices for improved temporal fusion; and (3) a three-zone verification decision model (accept/reject/inconclusive) combined with an adaptive shrinking verification window that enables multi-round verification when evidence is inconclusive. Monotonic decay and backflow elimination are analytically validated.
AI.result: The framework reduces time-to-detect intrusions while maintaining high usability for legitimate users. Analytical evaluation confirms that monotonic decay and backflow elimination effectively address limitations of prior temporal fusion approaches.
AI.conclusion: VIGIL effectively addresses the core limitation of prior work — the inability to disambiguate persistent attackers from genuine users with weak signals — through its STM-based temporal fusion and adaptive verification mechanisms, offering a more robust and operator-configurable continuous authentication solution.

title: Agentic ERP: Multi-Agent Large Language Model Architecture for Autonomous Enterprise Resource Planning
summary: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems record transactions reliably but still delegate almost all operational decision-making to human specialists, because classical rule-based automation cannot reason about exceptions and monolithic AI assistants degrade when asked to coordinate across functional boundaries. This paper presents Agentic ERP, an expert-system architecture that combines role-aligned large-language-model (LLM) agents with a risk-tiered human-in-the-loop harness and a graph-based orchestrator to execute end-to-end business workflows on a production ERP backend. First, autonomous ERP operation is formulated as a constrained sequential-decision problem over a structured enterprise state, with a decomposition argument linking role-aligned agents to a measurable reduction in per-step tool-selection complexity. Second, a graph-based Planner--Executor--Reflector--Responder orchestration decouples generation from evaluation through externalised grading criteria and sprint contracts, packaging recent harness-engineering principles as inspectable expert-system artefacts. Third, the system is evaluated at three levels: a scenario-based task suite, a comprehensive comparison of six orchestration paradigms on cross-functional crisis tasks, and a 365-day agent-in-the-loop simulation against rule-based RPA and no-intervention baselines. Across these levels the proposed multi-agent method is significantly better than the baseline, and the system sustains a simulated year of operation with zero stockouts while the rule-based baseline accumulates hundreds under the same demand stream. The work shows that role-aligned LLM agents under human oversight can move an ERP system from passively recording transactions to actively executing operational decisions, and it provides a reference architecture and an evaluation protocol for autonomous enterprise resource planning.

AI.tldr: Proposes Agentic ERP, a multi-agent LLM architecture with risk-tiered human oversight and graph-based orchestration that transforms ERP systems from passive transaction recorders into active decision-executors, achieving zero stockouts over a simulated year vs. hundreds for rule-based RPA.
AI.motivation: ERP systems capture transactions reliably but leave operational decisions to humans because rule-based automation fails on exceptions and monolithic AI assistants break down when coordinating across functional boundaries (e.g., finance, inventory, procurement). There is no existing architecture that safely enables autonomous cross-functional ERP decision-making at production scale.
AI.method: (1) Formalizes autonomous ERP operation as a constrained sequential-decision problem over structured enterprise state, with a decomposition proof that role-aligned agents reduce per-step tool-selection complexity. (2) Introduces a graph-based Planner–Executor–Reflector–Responder orchestration pipeline using externalized grading criteria and sprint contracts for decoupled generation and evaluation. (3) Evaluates via a scenario-based task suite, a six-paradigm comparison on cross-functional crisis tasks, and a 365-day agent-in-the-loop simulation against rule-based RPA and no-intervention baselines.
AI.result: The proposed multi-agent method significantly outperforms all baselines across all three evaluation levels. In the 365-day simulation, the Agentic ERP system sustains a full year with zero stockouts, while the rule-based RPA baseline accumulates hundreds of stockouts under identical demand conditions.
AI.conclusion: Role-aligned LLM agents under structured human oversight can shift ERP systems from passive recording to active operational decision-making. The paper contributes both a reference architecture and a reproducible evaluation protocol for autonomous enterprise resource planning.

title: JUMP: Single-Pass Membership Inference on Fine-Tuned Diffusion Language Models
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) test whether a candidate example appeared in a model's training data. We study MIAs for fine-tuned discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs), where membership means inclusion in the target model's fine-tuning set. Unlike autoregressive language models, dLLMs allow an attacker to choose arbitrary mask sets and obtain token distributions for all masked positions in parallel. The prior dLLM attack, SAMA, follows a natural loss-mimicking strategy by averaging reconstruction signals over many randomly sampled masks, but it uses the any-order interface only as randomization and requires many target/reference queries. We propose JUMP (Joint Uncertainty-Guided Mask Probing), a single-pass scoring attack that exploits both distinctive properties of dLLMs: any-order decodability is used to select low-reference-confidence positions, and parallel decodability is used to score all selected positions through one joint masked query per model. JUMP masks the selected positions jointly and computes a clipped target/reference reconstruction-gap statistic. On fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Base across six MIMIR domains, JUMP improves mean ROC-AUC from 0.82 to 0.90 over SAMA and substantially improves low-FPR detection, while requiring only one selector pass and one scoring pass through each of the target and reference models.

AI.tldr: JUMP is a single-pass membership inference attack for discrete diffusion language models that exploits any-order and parallel decodability to jointly mask low-reference-confidence positions and score them via a clipped reconstruction-gap statistic, achieving 0.90 mean ROC-AUC vs. SAMA's 0.82 on fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Base.
AI.motivation: Prior MIAs for dLLMs (e.g., SAMA) treat any-order decoding merely as randomization, require many target/reference queries, and fail to fully exploit the parallel decodability and any-order properties unique to discrete diffusion models. This motivates a more efficient, higher-performing attack.
AI.method: JUMP uses (1) any-order decodability to select positions where the reference model has low confidence, (2) parallel decodability to jointly mask and query all selected positions in a single pass per model, and (3) a clipped target/reference reconstruction-gap statistic for scoring. Only one selector pass and one scoring pass through each of the target and reference models are needed.
AI.result: On fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Base across six MIMIR domains, JUMP improves mean ROC-AUC from 0.82 (SAMA) to 0.90, with substantial gains in low-FPR detection, while requiring dramatically fewer queries.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the structural properties of dLLMs—any-order and parallel decodability—enables a highly query-efficient and accurate membership inference attack (JUMP), significantly outperforming prior loss-mimicking baselines.

title: Cascading versus Joint Modeling for Hierarchical Offensive Language Detection
summary: Fine-grained offensive language detection organizes labels into a hierarchical structure, for which two modeling paradigms exist: cascaded decomposition and joint multi-task modeling. Prior work rarely provides a direct, controlled comparison of the two paradigms in terms of accuracy, parameter count, and inference latency, and rarely verifies whether a chosen class-imbalance handling strategy is actually optimal. This paper proposes a three-level cascaded detection system whose training strategy is customized per subtask, together with two verification mechanisms. First, a controlled ablation study determines the best class-imbalance handling strategy for each subtask. Second, a joint multi-task model with a shared encoder is trained as an architectural control, yielding real measurements along the dimensions of accuracy, parameter count, and inference latency. Experiments show that the cascaded system attains macro-F1 scores of 0.795, 0.716, and 0.557 on the three subtasks of the official test set. The ablation study reveals that configuring the loss function purely by imbalance-severity intuition is suboptimal; reconfiguring based on the ablation results improves both performance and stability. End-to-end cascade evaluation shows that roughly one-fifth of the errors in the cascade pipeline originate from the first-stage filter and cannot be corrected by subsequent stages. Relative to the joint multi-task model, the cascaded architecture achieves higher accuracy on all three subtasks, with a 7.1-point macro-F1 gain on the most severely imbalanced subtask, at the cost of three times the parameters and 1.67 times the inference latency. Together, these results establish an explicit, quantifiable trade-off between the accuracy advantage of cascaded architectures and their deployment cost.

AI.tldr: This paper compares cascaded decomposition vs. joint multi-task modeling for fine-grained offensive language detection, showing cascaded models achieve higher accuracy (+7.1 macro-F1 on the hardest subtask) but at roughly 3× parameters and 1.67× inference latency. An ablation study further reveals that naive class-imbalance handling is suboptimal; data-driven loss reconfiguration improves both performance and stability.
AI.motivation: Prior work on hierarchical offensive language detection lacks a direct, controlled comparison between cascaded and joint multi-task paradigms across accuracy, parameter count, and inference latency. Additionally, class-imbalance handling strategies are often chosen by intuition without empirical verification of optimality.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-level cascaded detection system with per-subtask customized training. Two verification mechanisms are employed: (1) a controlled ablation study to identify the best class-imbalance handling strategy per subtask, and (2) a joint multi-task model with a shared encoder serving as an architectural control for measuring accuracy, parameter count, and inference latency trade-offs.
AI.result: The cascaded system achieves macro-F1 scores of 0.795, 0.716, and 0.557 on the three subtasks. Ablation shows intuition-driven loss configuration is suboptimal; reconfiguration based on ablation improves performance and stability. About 20% of cascade errors originate from the first-stage filter and are irrecoverable downstream. Compared to the joint model, the cascaded architecture yields higher accuracy on all subtasks, with a 7.1-point macro-F1 gain on the most imbalanced subtask, at the cost of 3× parameters and 1.67× inference latency.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes an explicit, quantifiable accuracy–deployment cost trade-off between cascaded and joint multi-task architectures for hierarchical offensive language detection, and demonstrates the importance of empirically validating class-imbalance handling strategies rather than relying on intuition.

title: The Failures of Marginal Influence-Based Attribution Methods for Global Time Series Explanations
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026)
summary: Explainability methods for time series models predominantly produce flat attribution scores: they quantify the direct influence of a feature at a timestamp by a scalar. We prove that the dominant failure mode of such methods is not the scalar format itself but a fundamental computational mismatch: existing methods compute scores via marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients, both of which conflate direct temporal dependencies with mediated ones under autocorrelation. We also define DAG-faithfulness: an explanation is DAG-faithful if the temporal dependency graph it encodes is Markov-equivalent to the temporal directed acyclic graph (DAG) implicitly learned by the model. Particularly, we observe that standard attribution methods, specifically SHAP, are not DAG-faithful in general, and that recent time-series-aware extensions inherit the same computational limitation.

AI.tldr: Standard time series explainability methods produce flat scalar attributions that conflate direct and mediated temporal dependencies due to computational mismatches (marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients). The authors introduce DAG-faithfulness as a criterion requiring explanation-encoded dependency graphs to be Markov-equivalent to the model's learned temporal DAG, and show that SHAP and its time-series variants fail this criterion.
AI.motivation: Existing explainability methods for time series models produce flat attribution scores that fail to distinguish between direct temporal dependencies and those mediated through autocorrelated intermediates. This fundamental computational mismatch — rooted in marginal conditioning and off-manifold gradient computation — represents the dominant failure mode of current approaches, yet has not been formally characterized or addressed.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally prove that marginal conditioning and off-manifold gradients conflate direct and mediated temporal dependencies under autocorrelation; (2) define the concept of DAG-faithfulness, requiring that the temporal dependency graph encoded by an explanation be Markov-equivalent to the temporal DAG implicitly learned by the model; and (3) analyze SHAP and its time-series-specific extensions through this lens, demonstrating their lack of DAG-faithfulness in general.
AI.result: Standard SHAP is provably not DAG-faithful in general settings. Recent time-series-aware SHAP extensions inherit the same fundamental computational limitation — namely, reliance on marginal conditioning or off-manifold interventions — and thus also fail to achieve DAG-faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: The core problem with current time series explainability is not the scalar format of attributions but the computational mechanisms that conflate direct and mediated effects. DAG-faithfulness provides a principled criterion for evaluating and designing explanation methods that respect the temporal dependency structure actually learned by the model.

title: Agentic Code Review in the Terminal: A Trajectory-Level Analysis of Behavior, Cost, and Human-Alignment
summary: Agentic code review in terminal-based environments enables early feedback during local development before pull request creation. However, existing evaluations remain performance-centric and fail to capture the dynamic behaviors of repository-grounded agentic reviewers. Understanding these behaviors is critical for identifying how agentic reviewers succeed, fail, and incur hidden operational costs in practice. Then, we analyze the reviewers' behavior based on their trajectories. Our results show that agentic reviewers achieve higher review precision but incur substantial exploration and validation overhead, while successful reviews are associated with stronger planning and less downstream validation. These findings highlight the potential benefits of trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive evaluation of future agentic code review systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the behavioral trajectories of agentic code reviewers in terminal-based environments, finding they achieve higher precision but incur significant exploration/validation overhead. Successful reviews correlate with stronger planning and reduced downstream validation, advocating for trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive evaluation frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of agentic code review systems are performance-centric (e.g., precision/recall) and fail to capture the dynamic, repository-grounded behaviors of these agents. Understanding how they succeed, fail, and what hidden operational costs they incur is essential for practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors conduct a behavioral analysis of agentic reviewers by examining their execution trajectories — sequences of actions, decisions, and interactions with the repository during local, terminal-based code review prior to pull request creation.
AI.result: Agentic reviewers achieve higher review precision but at the cost of substantial exploration and validation overhead. Successful reviews are characterized by stronger planning behaviors and less downstream validation, suggesting that efficient planning reduces the need for costly re-verification.
AI.conclusion: Future agentic code review systems should incorporate trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive evaluation metrics that account not only for review accuracy but also for the operational overhead of agent behaviors, promoting more practical and efficient designs.

title: Informal Learning Emerges in Everyday Human-LLM Interaction
summary: As LLMs become increasingly capable of completing tasks for users, a central concern is that everyday AI use may become primarily cognitive offloading, eroding the opportunities through which people develop their own capabilities. We analyse large-scale human--LLM conversations to ask whether informal learning behaviors also emerge in this setting: whether users engage in exchanges in ways that preserve opportunities to learn. Across 128,569 naturalistic conversations, we translated learning-science constructs into turn-level behavioural signatures. Cognitive engagement, users' cognitive effort as reflected in the exchange, appeared in 31.9% of 491,685 user turns, whereas constructive engagement, the deepest observable form of learning-oriented engagement, appeared in 4.9%, showing that deeper sense-making was recurrent but selective. Our study further identifies factors associated with these forms of engagement. Scaffolded assistant support consistently marked richer constructive participation, with associations varying by user framing, task ecology, support form, timing and prior user state. Together, these findings show that everyday human--LLM interaction is not only answer delivery or cognitive offloading; it also contains measurable, selective and conditionally organized behavioural signatures of informal learning. They shift AI evaluation from answer-delivery efficiency toward the preservation of cognitive opportunities for users to reason, test ideas and construct understanding in the course of everyday problem-solving.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 128,569 human–LLM conversations reveals that informal learning behaviors do emerge in everyday AI use: 31.9% of user turns show cognitive engagement and 4.9% show deeper constructive engagement. Scaffolded assistant support is consistently associated with richer learning-oriented participation, challenging the view that LLM use is merely cognitive offloading.
AI.motivation: Concern that widespread LLM adoption may reduce opportunities for users to develop their own cognitive capabilities through passive answer consumption (cognitive offloading). The authors investigate whether informal learning behaviors can and do emerge in naturalistic human–LLM interactions.
AI.method: Large-scale behavioral analysis of 128,569 naturalistic human–LLM conversations (491,685 user turns). The authors translated learning-science constructs (cognitive engagement, constructive engagement) into turn-level behavioral signatures and identified factors associated with these engagement forms: assistant support scaffolding, user framing, task ecology, support form, timing, and prior user state.
AI.result: Cognitive engagement appeared in 31.9% of user turns; constructive engagement (deeper sense-making) appeared in 4.9% — recurrent but selective. Scaffolded assistant support consistently marked richer constructive participation, with associations varying by contextual factors. The findings demonstrate measurable, selective, and conditionally organized behavioral signatures of informal learning in everyday LLM use.
AI.conclusion: Everyday human–LLM interaction is not solely answer delivery or cognitive offloading but contains genuine informal learning behaviors. This shifts AI evaluation frameworks from optimizing answer-delivery efficiency toward preserving cognitive opportunities for users to reason, test ideas, and construct understanding during problem-solving.

title: Evidence-in-the-Loop: Trace-Driven Optimization for Customer-Service LLM Agents
summary: Production customer-service bots must improve answer quality across iterative releases, yet large language models must not bypass evidence boundaries, policy rules, or human-handoff safeguards. We present an \textbf{Evidence-Grounded Customer-Service Agent Workflow} deployed in a real-world customer-service setting. BM25 recall, issue-title-vector recall, issue-description-vector recall, weighted RRF fusion, and cross-encoder reranking construct grounded FAQ evidence for controlled LLM decisions. Policy-guided orchestration then combines this RAG evidence with scenario-specific rule evidence, conversation memory, and clarification state inside a fixed LangGraph DAG~\cite{langgraph2024}. The paper contributes three reusable deployment patterns: \textbf{hybrid RAG evidence construction}, where multi-channel retrieval and reranking produce auditable FAQ candidates; \textbf{evidence-grounded issue/action decision}, where an Evidence-Grounded Decision Module selects an issue/action from typed FAQ evidence and scenario-specific rule evidence; and \textbf{trace-driven RAG and reranker improvement}, where traces diagnose whether failures come from recall, ranking, final candidate selection, clarification, rule-derived evidence, or action policy, and where reranker fine-tuning is evaluated not only for in-domain gain but also for forgetting risk.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a production customer-service agent workflow that combines hybrid RAG evidence construction, evidence-grounded decision-making, and trace-driven improvement to ensure LLM answers remain grounded in FAQ evidence and policy rules without bypassing safeguards.
AI.motivation: Customer-service bots must improve answer quality across releases while ensuring LLMs do not hallucinate beyond evidence boundaries, violate policy rules, or bypass human-handoff safeguards. Existing RAG approaches lack structured orchestration that integrates multi-source evidence with policy constraints in production settings.
AI.method: A three-component architecture: (1) Hybrid RAG evidence construction using BM25, dual vector recall (issue-title and issue-description), weighted RRF fusion, and cross-encoder reranking to produce grounded FAQ candidates; (2) An Evidence-Grounded Decision Module that selects issues/actions from typed FAQ evidence and scenario-specific rule evidence within a LangGraph DAG orchestrating conversation memory and clarification state; (3) Trace-driven diagnostics that categorize failures across recall, ranking, selection, clarification, rules, and action policy, with reranker fine-tuning evaluated for both in-domain gain and forgetting risk.
AI.result: The deployed system demonstrates improved answer quality in a real-world customer-service setting. Trace-driven analysis enables systematic diagnosis of failure sources, and reranker fine-tuning shows in-domain gains while monitoring forgetting risk.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes three reusable deployment patterns — hybrid RAG evidence construction, evidence-grounded decision-making, and trace-driven RAG/reranker improvement — that together form a blueprint for building auditable, policy-compliant customer-service agents in production.

title: SABLE: Minimalist Instruction-Level Authenticated Encryption for Constrained Confidential Computing
summary: Conventional processor designs expose code and data as plaintext throughout execution, rendering them inherently vulnerable to attacks that recover intellectual property or modify security/safety checks. Instruction-level encryption (ILE) enables CPU-level decryption, execution, and optionally authentication of individual encrypted program instructions at runtime. However, existing proposals depend on specific micro-architectures, detect corrupted instructions after they have executed, rely on non-standard ciphers, or require complex analyses of program state. In this work, we introduce and present a design exploration of a RISC-V processor architecture (SABLE) that enables minimally invasive instruction-level authenticated encryption of programs. SABLE is agnostic to the underlying micro-architecture, remaining compatible with the standard RISC-V toolchain with minor changes to post-process compiled ELF binaries. We integrate a decrypt-and-verify stage at two points (the instruction-memory wrapper and the CPU frontend) and explore seven ILE micro-architectures from a single-cycle (combinational) design to six multi-cycle (sequential) variants. We implement and evaluate the designs using ASCON-128a on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA with the open-source NEORV32 system on chip. Relative to baseline performance, the configurations span LUT, performance, power, and energy-per-instruction overheads of 1.6-9.3$\times$, 4.1-10.0$\times$, 1.5-8.0$\times$, and 10.4-80.0$\times$, respectively, using the Dhrystone benchmarking suite. Finally, we discuss design trade-offs, highlighting area-, performance-, and energy-aware design points.

AI.tldr: SABLE proposes a RISC-V processor architecture enabling instruction-level authenticated encryption (ILE) that is micro-architecture-agnostic. Using ASCON-128a on FPGA, it explores seven ILE designs spanning area, performance, power, and energy trade-offs, with overheads of 1.6–9.3× (LUT), 4.1–10.0× (performance), 1.5–8.0× (power), and 10.4–80.0× (energy/instruction) over baseline.
AI.motivation: Conventional processors expose code and data as plaintext, making them vulnerable to IP theft and security/safety check tampering. Existing ILE solutions are limited by micro-architecture specificity, post-execution corruption detection, non-standard ciphers, or complex program-state analysis. A minimally invasive, standards-compatible ILE architecture is needed.
AI.method: The authors design SABLE, a RISC-V architecture that integrates a decrypt-and-verify stage at either the instruction-memory wrapper or CPU frontend. They explore seven ILE micro-architectures (one single-cycle combinational, six multi-cycle sequential), use ASCON-128a for authenticated encryption, implement on a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA with the NEORV32 SoC, and evaluate with minor post-processing of ELF binaries (standard toolchain compatible).
AI.result: Relative to baseline (Dhrystone benchmark): LUT overhead ranges from 1.6× to 9.3×; performance overhead from 4.1× to 10.0×; power overhead from 1.5× to 8.0×; and energy-per-instruction overhead from 10.4× to 80.0× across the seven micro-architecture configurations.
AI.conclusion: SABLE demonstrates a practical, minimally invasive ILE solution for RISC-V processors. The design exploration reveals distinct area-, performance-, and energy-aware design points, offering system designers flexibility in security-overhead trade-offs without requiring micro-architecture-specific customization.

title: Quantifying Diversity of Thought: A Predictive Law of Weighted LLM Ensemble Lift
summary: This paper provides an experimentally verified formal law for calculating the uplift that diversity of thought provides in Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles. From first principles, we derive an exact decomposition of LLM ensemble lift into rescue and damage masses, which yields a compact heuristic for calculating uplift. From this we extract the metrics which predict ensemble performance: an accuracy adjusted correctness correlation, $φ_{\mathrm{adj}}$, together with the accuracy gap and collective accuracy of the pair. We test the law on 767,520 inferences from ten open-weight models over two graduate-level science benchmarks, together with a novel agentic cybersecurity benchmark in which each model conducts digital-forensics investigations by multi-turn tool use in a network-isolated sandbox (23,520 graded trials including abstentions); all votes are released openly. Calibrated once on SuperGPQA at a 40:60 vote split, the heuristic predicts lift on the calibration set with Spearman's $ρ=0.84$ and, with its coefficients frozen, transfers to two datasets never used in calibration ($ρ=0.51$ on GPQA Diamond and $0.84$ on the forensic tasks), whilst the measured swap mass tracks realised lift with $R^2\ge 0.96$ throughout. Raw $φ$ has almost no predictive power ($R^2\le 0.09$ throughout); the accuracy-adjusted $φ_{\mathrm{adj}}$ is markedly superior ($R^2=0.67$ on SuperGPQA), and the heuristic combining these metrics is the most stable pre pooling predictor across the three datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper derives and experimentally validates a formal law for quantifying diversity-of-thought uplift in LLM ensembles. It decomposes ensemble lift into rescue and damage masses, yielding a heuristic based on accuracy-adjusted correctness correlation (φ_adj), accuracy gap, and collective accuracy. Tested on 767,520 inferences across three benchmarks, the heuristic transfers robustly without recalibration, while raw φ proves nearly useless.
AI.motivation: Ensemble methods benefit from diversity, but no formal, experimentally verified law exists to quantify how diversity of thought translates into uplift in LLM ensembles. Existing metrics like raw correctness correlation (φ) fail to predict ensemble gains, motivating a principled decomposition and a predictive heuristic.
AI.method: From first principles, the authors derive an exact decomposition of ensemble lift into rescue mass (cases where the ensemble corrects individual errors) and damage mass (cases where it introduces errors). This yields a compact heuristic combining: (1) accuracy-adjusted correctness correlation φ_adj, (2) the accuracy gap between models, and (3) their collective accuracy. The law is calibrated once on SuperGPQA at a 40:60 vote split and tested on 767,520 inferences from ten open-weight LLMs across three benchmarks: SuperGPQA, GPQA Diamond (graduate-level science), and a novel agentic cybersecurity forensics benchmark (23,520 graded trials with multi-turn tool use).
AI.result: The heuristic predicts lift on the calibration set with Spearman's ρ=0.84. With frozen coefficients, it transfers to GPQA Diamond (ρ=0.51) and the forensic benchmark (ρ=0.84). Measured swap mass tracks realized lift with R² ≥ 0.96 throughout. Raw φ has negligible predictive power (R² ≤ 0.09), while φ_adj is markedly superior (R²=0.67 on SuperGPQA). The combined heuristic is the most stable pre-pooling predictor across all three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble uplift is predictable using a parsimonious set of metrics, provided correctness correlation is adjusted for accuracy. Raw φ is insufficient; φ_adj, accuracy gap, and collective accuracy together form a robust, transferable heuristic. The framework offers a principled foundation for LLM ensemble design and selection.

title: ColGraphRAG: Late-Interaction Evidence Retrieval for Multimodal GraphRAG
summary: Graph-grounded multimodal question answering organizes text, tables, and images in a structured evidence graph, yet end-to-end accuracy depends on which multimodal assets are ranked highly enough to enter downstream reasoning; for graph-linked images, single-vector bi-encoder similarity can discard patch- and token-level structure needed for fine-grained alignment. We evaluate replacing the visual candidate-ranking operator over graph-linked image nodes with late-interaction MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring in the ColBERT/ColPali lineage, while keeping offline graph construction, text- and table-side retrieval, structured extraction, and downstream reasoning unchanged. On MultimodalQA, this change is associated with improved retrieval-stage point estimates for graph-linked image candidates and downstream QA gains, with larger movement where visual evidence matters most and mixed trends on text-dominant questions; we interpret the pattern as mechanism-level evidence for graph-linked visual evidence inclusion, while broader validation and finer graph-level diagnostics remain important future work.

AI.tldr: Replacing single-vector bi-encoder similarity with late-interaction multi-vector scoring (ColBERT/ColPali lineage) for ranking graph-linked image nodes improves retrieval and downstream QA accuracy on MultimodalQA, particularly for questions requiring visual evidence, while text-dominant questions show mixed results.
AI.motivation: Standard single-vector bi-encoder similarity for ranking graph-linked images in multimodal QA discards fine-grained patch- and token-level alignment structure. The authors hypothesize that late-interaction multi-vector scoring can better capture this granular alignment, improving which visual assets enter downstream reasoning.
AI.method: The authors substitute the visual candidate-ranking operator over graph-linked image nodes with MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring (from the ColBERT/ColPali family), while holding all other pipeline components constant: offline graph construction, text/table retrieval, structured extraction, and downstream reasoning.
AI.result: The switch yields improved retrieval-stage point estimates for graph-linked image candidates and downstream QA gains on MultimodalQA. Improvements are largest where visual evidence is critical; text-dominant questions show mixed trends.
AI.conclusion: The pattern constitutes mechanism-level evidence that late-interaction scoring facilitates graph-linked visual evidence inclusion. Broader validation and finer-grained graph-level diagnostics remain as future work.

title: Diagnosing Correctness Probes under Self-Judgement Confounding
summary: Hidden-state readouts can predict whether language-model outputs are correct, but objective correctness (OC) usually agrees with the model's own self-judgement (SJ), leaving the decoded signal semantically ambiguous. We construct conflict cases in which OC and SJ predict opposite readout orderings. On high-confidence disagreements, conventional correctness-labelled contrasts often rank incorrect/self-endorsed responses above correct/self-rejected responses, following SJ rather than OC. We estimate factorial SJ- and OC-associated directions and evaluate their polarity across mathematical reasoning and factual recall. Across four instruction-tuned models up to 14B parameters, the SJ-associated direction transfers above chance in both cross-domain directions for every model, whereas the OC-associated direction has a below-chance point estimate for the expected OC ordering in every corresponding condition. This transfer asymmetry develops across middle-to-late layers, persists under answer-likelihood, sequence-length, and null-direction controls, and extends to MMLU and binary TruthfulQA without target-domain direction fitting. Across the studied models and diagnostic subsets, the most reliably transferable component preserves SJ-associated polarity. Transferability alone therefore does not establish objective-correctness semantics.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that linear readouts from language-model hidden states track the model's self-judgment (SJ) rather than objective correctness (OC). By constructing conflict cases where SJ and OC diverge, the authors demonstrate that the SJ-associated direction transfers across domains while the OC-associated direction does not, cautioning that transferability alone cannot establish objective-correctness semantics.
AI.motivation: Prior work claims that linear probes trained on correctness labels reveal "truth" directions in language model representations. However, objective correctness (OC) and the model's self-judgment (SJ) are usually confounded. The authors aim to disentangle these signals to determine whether decoded readouts genuinely track OC or merely reflect the model's own assessment of its outputs.
AI.method: The authors construct conflict cases where OC and SJ predict opposite orderings (e.g., incorrect/self-endorsed vs. correct/self-rejected responses). Using linear readouts trained on high-confidence disagreements, they estimate factorial SJ- and OC-associated directions in hidden-state space. Transfer experiments are conducted across mathematical reasoning and factual recall domains using four instruction-tuned models (up to 14B). Controls include answer likelihood, sequence length, and null-direction baselines, with extension to MMLU and binary TruthfulQA.
AI.result: The SJ-associated direction transfers above chance across both cross-domain directions for every model tested. In contrast, the OC-associated direction yields below-chance point estimates for the expected OC ordering in every corresponding condition. This asymmetry emerges in middle-to-late layers, persists under all controls, and extends to MMLU and TruthfulQA without target-domain direction fitting. The most reliably transferable component consistently preserves SJ-associated polarity.
AI.conclusion: Transferability of a decoded direction does not establish that it encodes objective correctness. The dominant transferable signal reflects the model's self-judgment. This calls for re-evaluation of interpretability claims based solely on cross-domain or cross-model transfer of linear probes, and highlights the need for explicit conflict-case evaluation when attributing semantic content to representation-space directions.

title: Quantizing Recursive Reasoning Models
summary: Recursive reasoning models solve hard puzzles by applying compact, weight-tied blocks over many refinement steps. Because these blocks are reused many times, quantizing them creates a unique dynamical problem: the quantization error is incurred at every step. While 8-bit quantization (integer or float) preserves accuracy, moving to a per-tensor 4-bit format causes a systematic bias to accumulate. The ensuing drift catastrophically degrades exact-solution accuracy on Sudoku from 84.1% to 0.0% (only ~25% of cells correct). In this work, we show that this collapse is caused by activation-scaling granularity rather than bit-width or number format. Crucially, moving to per-block scaling completely restores the transition. To implement this, we apply MXInt4, a blockwise integer activation format, to recursive reasoning models. It is competitive with blockwise float formats on our tasks, while keeping integer elements and power-of-two block scales. Finally, recursion depth and reuse modulate quantization sensitivity, with the deepest architecture we test (the EqR equilibrium model) the most sensitive. Yet blockwise scaling overcomes this vulnerability, staying robust across these architectures and transferring to the open-ended ARC-AGI benchmark.

AI.tldr: Recursive reasoning models collapse under 4-bit per-tensor quantization due to systematic bias accumulation over repeated block reuse. The failure stems from activation-scaling granularity, not bit-width or number format. Switching to per-block (blockwise) scaling with MXInt4 completely restores accuracy, and robustness holds across varying recursion depths and the ARC-AGI benchmark.
AI.motivation: Recursive reasoning models reuse weight-tied blocks over many refinement steps, making them uniquely vulnerable to quantization error accumulation. While 8-bit quantization works, aggressive 4-bit compression causes catastrophic drift that destroys exact-solution accuracy (e.g., Sudoku drops from 84.1% to 0.0%). The authors aim to diagnose the root cause and find a fix.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare per-tensor vs. per-block activation quantization for recursive reasoning models under 4-bit formats. They introduce MXInt4 — a blockwise integer activation format with power-of-two block scales — and evaluate it against blockwise float formats on Sudoku solving and ARC-AGI. They also test how recursion depth and block reuse modulate quantization sensitivity across architectures including the EqR equilibrium model.
AI.result: Per-tensor 4-bit quantization causes Sudoku accuracy to collapse from 84.1% to 0.0% (~25% cells correct). Switching to per-block scaling fully restores the transition. MXInt4 is competitive with blockwise float formats. Deeper recursive architectures (e.g., EqR) are most sensitive, but blockwise scaling overcomes this vulnerability and transfers robustly to ARC-AGI.
AI.conclusion: The quantization collapse in recursive reasoning models is a scaling-granularity problem, not a bit-width or format problem. Blockwise activation quantization (MXInt4) solves it, enabling aggressive 4-bit compression without accuracy loss, even for deep equilibrium models and open-ended reasoning benchmarks.

title: A Preliminary Study on the Impact of AI in the Creativity and Collaboration in Software Teams
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping software engineering work, increasingly acting as cognitive partners rather than purely instrumental aids. Most AI tooling remains optimized for individual use, yet software development is inherently collaborative and creative, raising open questions about how AI affects team-based work. This paper examines how software engineering professionals perceive and integrate AI tools focusing on creativity and collaboration within teams. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 13 software professionals from four companies, each representing a distinct team. Our analysis identifies three central themes - AI Use, Consequences of AI, and Collaboration and Team Dynamics, alongside Emotions as a cross-cutting dimension. Key findings include: AI broadens developers' creative repertoires but may narrow independent ideation; developers increasingly consult AI instead of colleagues, weakening peer learning and mentoring; and teams are developing emerging triadic collaboration patterns in which developers, colleagues, and AI reason together.

AI.tldr: A qualitative interview study with 13 software professionals across 4 teams reveals that GenAI tools serve as cognitive partners in software engineering, broadening creative repertoires while potentially narrowing independent ideation, shifting peer consultation toward AI, and giving rise to triadic collaboration patterns among developers, colleagues, and AI.
AI.motivation: Most AI tooling is optimized for individual use, yet software development is inherently collaborative and creative. This gap raises open questions about how GenAI tools affect team-based work, creativity, and collaborative dynamics in professional software engineering contexts.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 13 software professionals from four distinct companies, each representing a different team. Thematic analysis identified three central themes — AI Use, Consequences of AI, and Collaboration and Team Dynamics — with Emotions as a cross-cutting dimension.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) AI broadens developers' creative repertoires but may narrow independent ideation; (2) developers increasingly consult AI instead of colleagues, weakening peer learning and mentoring; (3) teams are developing emerging triadic collaboration patterns where developers, colleagues, and AI reason together.
AI.conclusion: GenAI tools are transforming software engineering from purely instrumental aids into cognitive partners, reshaping team collaboration structures, creativity practices, and peer learning dynamics in ways that warrant further attention to both the benefits and unintended consequences.

title: I wanted it to feel more personal: Customization of social AI as AI individualism in practice
summary: Despite the growing availability of customizable social artificial intelligence (AI), such as ChatGPT, Grok, and Character.ai, we know little about how users actively shape social AI to reflect their personal preferences. This study examines why and how users (N = 169) customize social AI through the lens of the newly developed concept of AI individualism. Through reflexive thematic analysis of open-ended responses, we identified several motivations for customization, including (1) enhanced pragmatic support, (2) emotional support or companionship, (3) trust and reliability, (4) pushback, (5) a tailored degree of human likeness, (6) creativity or playfulness, and (7) having the AI function as an extension of the self. In line with the concept of AI individualism, our findings show that, for many users, customization is a co-creative process between the human and the AI that is perceived as strengthening support, autonomy, ownership, and engagement, potentially contributing to a closer and more personal relationship. Through customization users may come to view social AI as a personalized social resource that increases their sense of individualism, freedom, and control. We discuss how these perceptions may foster pseudo-autonomy, whereby customization creates an illusion of individual control over powerful social AI systems.

AI.tldr: Users customize social AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Character.ai) for pragmatic support, emotional companionship, trust, pushback, tailored human-likeness, creativity, and self-extension. Customization emerges as a co-creative human-AI process that enhances autonomy, ownership, and engagement, but may also foster "pseudo-autonomy"—an illusion of user control over powerful AI systems.
AI.motivation: Despite the proliferation of customizable social AI platforms, little is known about why and how users actively personalize these systems. The study introduces the novel concept of "AI individualism" to frame this underexplored phenomenon and investigate the user motivations behind customization.
AI.method: A qualitative study with N = 169 participants. Data were collected through open-ended survey responses and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.
AI.result: Seven motivations for customization were identified: (1) enhanced pragmatic support, (2) emotional support or companionship, (3) trust and reliability, (4) pushback, (5) a tailored degree of human likeness, (6) creativity or playfulness, and (7) having the AI function as an extension of the self. Customization was found to be a co-creative human-AI process that strengthens support, autonomy, ownership, and engagement, fostering closer personal relationships with the AI.
AI.conclusion: Customization enables users to view social AI as a personalized resource enhancing individualism, freedom, and control. However, this perception may constitute "pseudo-autonomy," an illusion of individual agency that obscures the actual power wielded by the AI systems and their developers.

title: FinSAgent: Corpus-Aligned Multi-Agent RAG Framework for Evidence-Grounded SEC Filing Question Answering
summary: Financial question answering over U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings requires retrieving and synthesizing heterogeneous evidence dispersed across long, standardized, and highly redundant disclosures. Existing retrieval-augmented and multi-agent systems typically derive retrieval queries directly from the user's question and rank candidates by semantic similarity. Together, these choices create prior-corpus misalignment: a mismatch between model priors and the target filings' structure, terminology, and evidence standards. As a result, query generation misses corpus-specific evidence, while semantic reranking favors topically similar but evidentially invalid false-positive chunks. We propose FinSAgent, an evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that reframes SEC filing QA as corpus-aligned retrieval planning and corrects both ends with a single principle: inject corpus-side conditioning wherever model priors would otherwise dominate. FinSAgent combines (1) role-specialized agents anchored to the mandated 10-K item structure, (2) database-aware query decomposition that conditions each agent's sub-queries on a lightweight, summary-level view of the local corpus, and (3) multi-path retrieval with a learned feature-gated reranker that separates evidential validity from semantic similarity. Across five offline financial QA benchmarks, FinSAgent improves retrieval coverage and answer correctness over strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines; in a three-arm randomized online experiment with 1,000 anonymous user ratings, it also receives higher scores than baselines.

AI.tldr: FinSAgent is a multi-agent framework for SEC filing QA that addresses prior-corpus misalignment by conditioning retrieval queries on corpus structure and using a feature-gated reranker to separate evidential validity from semantic similarity, achieving improved retrieval coverage and answer correctness over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG and multi-agent systems for SEC filing QA derive queries directly from user questions and rank by semantic similarity, causing prior-corpus misalignment: queries miss corpus-specific evidence, and semantic reranking favors topically similar but evidentially invalid false positives. The SEC filings' long, standardized, and highly redundant nature exacerbates this mismatch.
AI.method: FinSAgent introduces three corpus-aligned components: (1) role-specialized agents anchored to the mandated 10-K item structure; (2) database-aware query decomposition that conditions each agent's sub-queries on a lightweight, summary-level view of the local corpus; and (3) multi-path retrieval with a learned feature-gated reranker that decouples evidential validity from semantic similarity.
AI.result: Across five offline financial QA benchmarks, FinSAgent improves retrieval coverage and answer correctness over strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines. In a three-arm randomized online experiment with 1,000 anonymous user ratings, it also receives higher scores than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Injecting corpus-side conditioning at both the query-generation and reranking stages—rather than relying on model priors—effectively resolves prior-corpus misalignment in SEC filing QA, yielding both measurable offline improvements and higher user satisfaction.

title: Rollback-Free Cross-Chain Atomicity Through Forward-Only Correction
summary: Blockchain platforms have grown into an ecosystem of independent networks, and a growing class of applications now requires smart contracts on separate chains to act as one. Such operations must be atomic, yet immutability makes this fundamentally harder: a confirmed transaction cannot be reversed, so the rollback on which classical atomic commitment protocols depend is unavailable. Two challenges follow. Contract state must be held across an operation whose outcome is not yet known, and each chain's execution outcome must be established even though no chain can observe another. In response, we introduce a framework that achieves atomicity through forward-only correction, resolving incomplete operations with new on-chain transactions rather than reversal. The framework bounds how long contract state is held and confines contention to the state an operation touches, and it establishes outcomes from an on-chain record of what each chain executed, without relying on any single coordinating party. This work lays the foundation for atomic coordination of general smart contract operations across heterogeneous blockchains.

AI.tldr: A framework for cross-chain atomic smart contract operations that uses forward-only correction via new on-chain transactions instead of classical rollback, since blockchain immutability precludes reversal — bounding state holding time, confining contention, and establishing outcomes without a central coordinator.
AI.motivation: Blockchain ecosystems now comprise many independent networks, yet emerging applications require atomic operations spanning multiple chains. Classical atomic commitment protocols (e.g., two-phase commit) depend on rollback for abort handling, but blockchain immutability makes confirmed transactions irreversible. This creates two core challenges: (1) contract state must be held pending an operation whose final outcome is unknown, and (2) each chain must determine execution outcomes despite being unable to observe other chains.
AI.method: A framework based on forward-only correction: instead of rolling back incomplete multi-chain operations, it resolves them by issuing new on-chain transactions that bring contracts to a consistent final state. The framework bounds the duration for which contract state is locked, limits contention to only the state touched by the operation, and uses on-chain execution records so each chain can independently determine outcomes without reliance on a single coordinating party.
AI.result: The framework successfully achieves atomicity across heterogeneous blockchains without rollback. It provides formal bounds on state-holding time, confines contention scope, and enables decentralized outcome establishment via on-chain records, eliminating the need for a trusted coordinator.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for atomic coordination of general smart contract operations across heterogeneous blockchains, solving the fundamental tension between atomicity requirements and blockchain immutability without introducing a central point of trust.

title: The Curvature Shadow: An Apparent Failure of Maximum-Entropy Equilibrium Selection is a Removable Artifact
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Diagnostic companion to arXiv:2606.28308. Fully reproducible: a single self-contained notebook regenerates every number, table, and figure
summary: In two-player zero-sum games whose Nash equilibria form a convex set, regularized solvers such as Regularized Nash Dynamics (R-NaD) empirically select the maximum-entropy member: the information projection (I-projection) of a uniform reference onto the Nash set. On a panel of small games this match is exact, with one apparent exception: in Kuhn poker R-NaD lands at bluff coordinate 0.180 while the maximum-entropy member sits at 0.201, a coordinate gap of about 0.021, even though R-NaD attains 99.7 percent of the maximum entropy. We ask whether this gap is a genuine selection bias or an artifact, and answer it quantitatively. We show that for selection on a one-dimensional Nash manifold the coordinate gap factorizes as $\mathrm{gap} \approx \sqrt{2δ/κ}$, where $δ$ is the entropy shortfall of the solver and $κ$ is the curvature of the entropy landscape at its peak. Across five games this relation holds to within $2 \times 10^{-4}$ (under 1 percent relative error). The four matrix games have $δ\approx 0$ (R-NaD reaches the maximum-entropy member exactly) and therefore no gap regardless of curvature; only the sequential game (Kuhn) has $δ> 0$. A causal sweep of the magnet strength drives $δ\to 0$ and the gap toward zero along the predicted curve (fitted scaling exponent 0.50, $R^2 > 0.999999$, against the exact prediction of 1/2), until the dynamics destabilize at a stability floor: behavior consistent with a removable shortfall and inconsistent with a fixed bias. We quantify the curvature half of the law from measured curvatures and flag a moving-target pitfall in the natural Tsallis-entropy experiment. The Kuhn gap is thus the curvature shadow of a small, removable entropy shortfall on an unusually flat peak; the I-projection account is upheld up to a flatness-limited residual.

AI.tldr: In two-player zero-sum games with convex Nash sets, regularized solvers like R-NaD empirically select the maximum-entropy equilibrium, but Kuhn poker shows a small coordinate gap (~0.021). The authors prove this gap factorizes as gap ≈ √(2δ/κ), where δ is entropy shortfall and κ is entropy landscape curvature, confirming the I-projection account up to a flatness-limited residual.
AI.motivation: Regularized Nash Dynamics (R-NaD) empirically selects the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium (the I-projection of a uniform prior), but Kuhn poker exhibits a persistent coordinate gap of ~0.021 from the max-entropy member. The authors investigate whether this gap represents a genuine selection bias in the solver or is merely an artifact explainable by residual entropy shortfall, aiming to provide a quantitative answer.
AI.method: The authors derive a factorization relation for selection on a one-dimensional Nash manifold: gap ≈ √(2δ/κ), where δ measures the solver's entropy shortfall from the maximum and κ is the curvature of the entropy landscape at its peak. They validate this across five games (four matrix games, one sequential: Kuhn poker), perform a causal sweep of magnet strength to drive δ → 0, fit the scaling exponent (predicted 1/2, observed 0.50 with R² > 0.999999), and quantify curvature from measured values while flagging a moving-target pitfall in Tsallis-entropy experiments.
AI.result: The gap relation holds across all five games within 2×10⁻⁴ (under 1% relative error). Matrix games show δ ≈ 0 and thus no gap regardless of curvature; only Kuhn poker has δ > 0. The magnet-strength sweep drives δ → 0 and the gap toward zero along the predicted curve with fitted exponent 0.50 and R² > 0.999999, until destabilization at a stability floor — behavior consistent with a removable shortfall, not a fixed bias.
AI.conclusion: The Kuhn gap is fully explained as the curvature shadow of a small, removable entropy shortfall on an unusually flat entropy peak. The I-projection account is upheld, with any residual limited by flatness. The finding reconciles the apparent exception and provides a quantitative law for solver selection bias on one-dimensional Nash manifolds.

title: Shapley Context Pruning: A Cooperative Game Perspective for Context Reranking and Pruning
summary: Context reranking and pruning have become essential for improving the efficiency of modern Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, yet an interpretable and unified framework remains underexplored. Previous work has primarily emphasized lexical retrieval, cross-encoder architectures, model distillation, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), mostly relying on heuristic loss functions and empirical attribution. This paper presents Shapley Context Pruning (SCP), a novel framework for context reranking that establishes a cooperative-game-theory perspective for importance attribution by modeling the context as a cooperative game. Balancing the trade-off between fine-grained and coarse-grained representations, we employ a Deep Sets architecture to approximate a permutation-invariant value function at the sentence level, utilizing pre-trained language models as sentence embedders and optimizing via a pairwise margin ranking loss. To ensure practical scalability without sacrificing mathematical rigor, we leverage Monte-Carlo sampling for efficient training and inference, providing formal theoretical error bounds and sample complexity guarantees for preserving Top-K subset rankings. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive experiments-spanning supporting-sentence recall, Needle-in-the-Haystack (NIAH) evaluations, long-context QA, and multi-hop reasoning-alongside rigorous ablation studies on embedding quality and attribution strategies. The model achieves competitive downstream QA performance against robust baselines.

AI.tldr: SCP frames context pruning as a cooperative game, using Shapley values for importance attribution, a Deep Sets architecture for permutation-invariant scoring, Monte-Carlo sampling with theoretical guarantees, and achieves competitive QA performance.
AI.motivation: Existing context reranking and pruning methods for RAG rely on heuristic losses and empirical attribution, lacking an interpretable, unified, and theoretically grounded framework for determining which context elements truly matter.
AI.method: SCP models context as a cooperative game where sentences are players. A Deep Sets architecture with pretrained sentence embedders approximates a permutation-invariant value function, optimized via pairwise margin ranking loss. Shapley values are computed using Monte-Carlo sampling for importance attribution, with formal error bounds and sample complexity guarantees for preserving Top-K subset rankings.
AI.result: SCP achieves competitive downstream QA performance against robust baselines across supporting-sentence recall, Needle-in-the-Haystack, long-context QA, and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, supported by ablation studies on embedding quality and attribution strategies.
AI.conclusion: Shapley value-based cooperative game theory provides a principled and interpretable alternative to heuristic pruning methods, enabling effective context reranking with theoretical guarantees and practical scalability.

title: Schema-Constrained Document-Level Event Argument Extraction with Lightweight LLM Fine-Tuning
summary:
Event Argument Extraction (EAE) converts documents into structured event records by identifying argument spans and assigning them schema-defined roles. Document-level EAE is challenging due to long-range dependencies between triggers and arguments, cross-sentence context, and strict role constraints, which often lead to boundary errors, uncertainty in roles, and inconsistencies with restricted schemas.
  In this paper, we study whether mid-sized open LLMs can perform schema-constrained EAE reliably at the document level on MAVEN-ARG. Our approach combines (i) role-set injection in prompts for schema compliance, (ii) parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning (LoRA) using the same JSON-only interface used at inference, and (iii) deterministic decoding with post-processing that validates JSON, filters invalid roles, de-duplicates arguments, and aligns spans to the document window. Under the official MAVEN-ARG evaluator, fine-tuned mid-sized open models outperform previously reported GPT baselines across mention, entity-coreference, and event-coreference evaluations; our best model (Phi-4, 14B) reaches 42.39\% F1 at the event-coreference level. Code to reproduce experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/dessertlab/EAE/.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether mid-sized open LLMs can reliably perform document-level Event Argument Extraction (EAE) under schema constraints. Using role-set injection, LoRA fine-tuning, and deterministic decoding with validation, the authors show that fine-tuned models (best: Phi-4 14B at 42.39% F1) outperform GPT baselines on MAVEN-ARG across all evaluation levels.
AI.motivation: Document-level EAE is difficult due to long-range trigger-argument dependencies, cross-sentence context, and strict schema role constraints, causing boundary errors, role uncertainty, and schema inconsistencies. Prior work relied heavily on prompting large proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT), but the authors aim to explore whether smaller, open-source LLMs can be effectively adapted for this task with proper schema grounding.
AI.method: The approach integrates three components: (1) Role-set injection in prompts to enforce schema compliance by explicitly providing the allowed roles; (2) Parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning via LoRA using a consistent JSON-only interface for both training and inference; (3) Deterministic decoding with post-processing that validates JSON output, filters invalid roles, de-duplicates arguments, and aligns predicted spans to the document window. Evaluation uses the official MAVEN-ARG evaluator.
AI.result: Fine-tuned mid-sized open models surpass previously reported GPT baselines across mention-level, entity-coreference, and event-coreference evaluations on MAVEN-ARG. The best-performing model, Phi-4 (14B), achieves 42.39% F1 at the event-coreference level.
AI.conclusion: Mid-sized open LLMs, when fine-tuned with schema-aware prompting and structured decoding, can outperform large proprietary models on document-level EAE, demonstrating a viable and reproducible path for schema-constrained information extraction without reliance on closed-source APIs.

title: Diffusion-corrected Autoregressive Fourier Neural Operator for Droplet Evolution Prediction
summary: Predicting droplet evolution in material jetting, or Inkjet Printing (IJP), is essential for maintaining printing quality. However, long-horizon forecasts remain challenging due to error accumulation and the complex coupling of process variables. In this work, we introduce the Diffusion-corrected Auto-Regressive Fourier Neural Operator (DiffARFNO), a two-stage framework that combines an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet with a conditional Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) corrector. Fourier-MIONet is trained as a coarse predictor and deployed autoregressively for long-horizon forecasting. In the second stage, a DDIM-based conditional corrector refines the coarse prediction within each sliding window through efficient iterative denoising. By combining coarse predictions from Fourier-MIONet with a DDIM corrector that restores fine details, DiffARFNO aims to provide high-fidelity predictions for long-horizon forecasts. Extensive experiments on droplet datasets from ANSYS Fluent demonstrate that DiffARFNO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: DiffARFNO combines an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet for coarse long-horizon droplet prediction with a DDIM-based conditional corrector that iteratively denoises and restores fine details, significantly outperforming existing models on CFD droplet datasets.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon droplet evolution forecasting in material jetting/inkjet printing is challenging due to error accumulation in autoregressive prediction and the complex coupling among process variables. Existing methods struggle to maintain fidelity over extended time horizons.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Fourier-MIONet is trained as a coarse predictor and deployed autoregressively for long-horizon forecasting; (2) a conditional Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) corrector refines the coarse prediction within each sliding window via efficient iterative denoising, restoring fine-grained details lost in the coarse prediction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on droplet datasets generated from ANSYS Fluent show that DiffARFNO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models for long-horizon droplet evolution forecasting.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach of coupling a Fourier neural operator for coarse temporal forecasting with a diffusion-based corrector for detail restoration effectively mitigates error accumulation, enabling high-fidelity long-horizon predictions in inkjet printing applications.

title: A Non-Intrusive Traffic Analysis Framework for Authorization Risk Detection and Coordinated Response in Web Applications
comment: 25 pages; bilingual English-Chinese version. The complete English version is followed by the complete Chinese version; each version contains 3 figures and 5 tables
summary: Authorization violations under valid Web sessions are difficult to identify and handle in real time from traffic because they depend strongly on business semantics and exhibit few distinctive protocol-level features. This paper proposes a non-intrusive traffic analysis framework for authorization risk detection and coordinated response. Request-response transactions are correlated to extract the access subject, business endpoint, object identifier, authentication state, and behavioral sequence. Object-access evidence, identity consistency, behavioral anomalies, authentication context, network environment, and endpoint-operation risk are mapped to interpretable risk components. Weighted fusion and high-risk priority constraints produce graded decisions that drive allow, alert, block, and external policy actions. The risk components are instantiated using deterministic and interpretable rules to evaluate multi-source evidence organization, risk fusion, and the coordinated-response loop at the framework level. In a controlled local testbed containing 2,000 balanced labeled samples, the framework classified 998 of 1,000 authorization-risk events as risky and produced no false positives among 1,000 normal accesses, achieving 99.90% accuracy, 100.00% precision, 99.80% recall, and a 99.90% F1 score. Removing runtime object evidence reduced the F1 score to 81.31%, while removing the high-risk priority constraint reduced it to 73.90%. In a prototype feasibility test with 100 concurrent requests and 1,000 total requests, mean risk-decision computation latency was 0.077 ms and P99 latency was 0.137 ms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of organizing heterogeneous runtime evidence and establishing an executable authorization-risk decision and coordinated-response loop without modifying application code, but do not establish general applicability in production environments.

AI.tldr: A non-intrusive traffic analysis framework detects authorization violations by correlating HTTP transactions to extract semantic risk components (identity, behavior, context, endpoint-operation), fusing them with weighted rules, and triggering graded responses. In a 2,000-sample testbed, it achieved 99.90% accuracy, 100% precision, and 99.80% recall, with mean decision latency of 0.077 ms.
AI.motivation: Authorization violations during valid web sessions are hard to detect in real time from network traffic alone because they are deeply tied to business semantics and lack distinctive protocol-level signatures. Existing approaches cannot identify these semantically-driven violations without invasive application-level instrumentation.
AI.method: A non-intrusive traffic analysis framework that: (1) correlates request-response transactions to extract access subject, business endpoint, object identifier, authentication state, and behavioral sequence; (2) maps six interpretable risk components — object-access evidence, identity consistency, behavioral anomalies, authentication context, network environment, and endpoint-operation risk; (3) applies weighted fusion with high-risk priority constraints to produce graded decisions (allow, alert, block, external policy); and (4) instantiates all components using deterministic, interpretable rules.
AI.result: On a balanced 2,000-sample controlled local testbed (1,000 authorization-risk events, 1,000 normal accesses), the framework flagged 998/1,000 risky events with zero false positives — yielding 99.90% accuracy, 100.00% precision, 99.80% recall, and 99.90% F1 score. Ablation: removing runtime object evidence dropped F1 to 81.31%; removing the high-risk priority constraint dropped F1 to 73.90%. In a 100-concurrent/1,000-total-request prototype test, mean risk-decision latency was 0.077 ms, P99 was 0.137 ms.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates feasibility of organizing heterogeneous runtime evidence into executable authorization-risk decisions and a coordinated-response loop without application code modifications. However, general applicability in production environments remains unestablished.

title: AlphaOracle: Oracle bone script decipherment via human-workflow-inspired deep learning
summary: Approximately 3,000 of the 4,500 oracle bone script (OBS) characters remain undeciphered due to fragmentary inscriptions and sparse evidence. Current AI approaches fail to replicate expert workflows that integrate form analysis, contextual semantics, and philological reasoning. We introduce AlphaOracle, a human-workflow-inspired framework that systematizes OBS decipherment using the largest digitized corpus to date. Its multi-stage pipeline comprises: (i) rubbing parsing; (ii) radical-based morphological analysis with diachronic modeling; (iii) contextual retrieval with semantic alignment; and (iv) philological validation against classical sources. Each stage generates explicit, confidence-weighted evidence chains, culminating in interpretable reports for scholarly verification. Across multiple test characters, AlphaOracle's readings strongly agreed with expert interpretations. In a study of 86 domain specialists, it reduced analysis time by 64% and 79% of participants rated it highly useful. Notably, AlphaOracle resolves the character "Lao" as a toponymic or clan designation, offering concrete revisions to Shang administrative and social interpretations. These results suggest that computational methods aligned with philological practice can facilitate OBS research and provide a conceptual reference for studies of other undeciphered scripts.

AI.tldr: AlphaOracle is a human-workflow-inspired AI framework for deciphering oracle bone script, employing a multi-stage pipeline of rubbing parsing, radical-based morphological analysis, contextual semantic retrieval, and philological validation. It generates confidence-weighted evidence chains, significantly reduced expert analysis time by 64%, and resolved the character "Lao" as a toponymic/clan designation, revising Shang administrative interpretations.
AI.motivation: Approximately 3,000 of 4,500 oracle bone script characters remain undeciphered due to fragmentary inscriptions and sparse evidence. Existing AI approaches fail to replicate the integrated expert workflow combining form analysis, contextual semantics, and philological reasoning. There is a clear need for a computational framework that systematizes and accelerates the decipherment process while aligning with established philological practice.
AI.method: AlphaOracle employs a multi-stage pipeline built on the largest digitized OBS corpus to date: (i) rubbing parsing to extract character images from fragmented inscriptions; (ii) radical-based morphological analysis with diachronic modeling to trace character evolution over time; (iii) contextual retrieval with semantic alignment to leverage surrounding text for meaning inference; and (iv) philological validation against classical textual sources. Each stage produces explicit, confidence-weighted evidence chains, culminating in interpretable reports suitable for scholarly verification.
AI.result: AlphaOracle's readings showed strong agreement with expert interpretations across multiple test characters. In a study with 86 domain specialists, the framework reduced analysis time by 64%, and 79% of participants rated it highly useful. Critically, AlphaOracle resolved the character "Lao" as a toponymic or clan designation, providing concrete revisions to interpretations of Shang dynasty administrative and social structures.
AI.conclusion: Computational methods that are carefully aligned with philological practice can significantly facilitate oracle bone script research. AlphaOracle not only demonstrates practical utility in accelerating decipherment but also offers a conceptual reference framework applicable to the study of other undeciphered scripts.

title: jina-reranker-v3.5: An Efficient Listwise Reranker with Hybrid Attention and Self-Distillation
summary: Listwise rerankers are the discriminative core of agentic retrieval pipelines, yet production deployment demands efficiency, domain robustness, and fluency on semi-structured data at the same time. We present jina-reranker-v3.5, a 0.6B-parameter listwise reranker that meets these demands together without sacrificing the cross-document comparison that makes its predecessor jina-reranker-v3 effective. jina-reranker-v3.5 keeps the last-but-not-late (LBNL) interaction of jina-reranker-v3 and reworks it along three axes. It replaces uniform global attention with a hybrid schedule of three sliding-window layers followed by two global layers, pinning the terminal layer to global as LBNL readout requires. It trains on a curated multi-domain mixture that spans legal, medical, financial, multilingual, and structured retrieval. It transfers quality through a three-stage self-distillation recipe in which a full-attention teacher sets an upper bound that a sparse-attention student then recovers under a staged adaptation protocol. jina-reranker-v3.5 reaches 63.20 nDCG@10 on BEIR, matching a 4B model at roughly 7x fewer parameters, and improves over jina-reranker-v3 on MIRACL and RTEB as well. Its largest gains come on semi-structured retrieval, where it lifts nDCG@10 by 9.6 points over jina-reranker-v3 and leads all rerankers of comparable size.
