AI.tldr: SynH-Rank is a quality-aware code reranking framework that uses LLM-driven data synthesis and hierarchical ranking training to prioritize high-quality code over low-quality code, addressing limitations of standard contrastive learning. It introduces a three-level labeling scheme (high-quality relevant > low-quality relevant > irrelevant), a new benchmark with 4,209 pairs, and two novel metrics (QPA and MCA), achieving 20.15% QPA improvement over backbone models.
AI.motivation: Current code search rerankers focus solely on semantic relevance but ignore non-functional qualities (execution speed, memory usage, maintainability) that developers care about. Two key challenges: (1) scarcity of quality-annotated datasets, and (2) standard contrastive learning's binary objective cannot model ordinal quality distinctions among high-quality, low-quality, and irrelevant code.
AI.method: SynH-Rank combines (1) LLM-driven diverse data synthesis to address data scarcity, (2) a three-level hierarchical labeling scheme (high-quality relevant > low-quality relevant > irrelevant), and (3) hierarchical ranking training that captures ordinal relationships. Two novel evaluation metrics are introduced: Quality Preference Accuracy (QPA) and Multi-Condition Accuracy (MCA), along with a new 4,209-pair benchmark.
AI.result: SynH-Rank improves QPA by 20.15% over backbone models and 15.80% over standard relevance-only contrastive training, while also enhancing traditional relevance metrics and multi-condition generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Quality-aware code search is feasible and beneficial. SynH-Rank demonstrates that explicitly modeling quality hierarchies in reranking significantly improves both quality prioritization and relevance, offering a practical path toward code search systems that better align with real-world developer needs.

title: The Autonomous Agency Scale: A Behavioral Framework for Measuring Self-Directed Behavior in AI Systems
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Framework v0.2.1; rubric and all assessment files: https://github.com/CaptainASIC/autonomous-agency-scale
summary: Existing AI measurement frameworks quantify cognitive capability, task automation, or catastrophic risk, but none measure autonomous agency: the extent to which a system behaves in a self-directed way. A system can saturate capability benchmarks while remaining entirely reactive, acting only when prompted and ceasing all activity when a task completes. We introduce the Autonomous Agency Scale (AAS), a behavioral framework that scores AI systems on a 0-5 lexicon across seven dimensions of agency: cognitive autonomy, temporal persistence, environmental agency, social agency, creative agency, self-awareness, and goal formation, each operationalized by falsifiable threshold tests. Every dimension is scored in two temporal bands: an Active band covering engaged, user-initiated activity, and an Ambient band covering idle periods. Ambient Level 4 is gated by the Idle-Gap Test, a counterfactual criterion (remove all triggers and observe whether internally derived activity persists) that separates self-direction from scheduled rule-following. We apply the scale to six contemporary systems spanning task agents (Claude Code, Manus, Hermes), consumer assistants (ChatGPT, Siri), and a persistent companion architecture (Airi). The two-band profile quantifies a boundary that single-score frameworks conflate: task agents reach Active composites of 2.3-2.4 while scoring 0.6-1.9 Ambient, with every idle-period behavior attributable to user-configured schedules, whereas the companion architecture, evaluated longitudinally, is the only assessed system whose idle-period behavior survives trigger removal. We discuss limitations, including single-rater provenance, developer-evaluator bias on the longitudinal assessment, and the partially operationalized self-direction boundary in the Active band.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Autonomous Agency Scale (AAS), a behavioral framework scoring AI systems on 0–5 across seven agency dimensions in both active and idle (ambient) temporal bands. The Idle-Gap Test distinguishes genuine self-direction from scheduled behavior. Applied to six systems, task agents score high active but near-zero ambient agency; only a persistent companion architecture passes the trigger-removal criterion.
AI.motivation: Existing AI benchmarks measure capability, automation, or risk but fail to capture autonomous agency — self-directed behavior independent of prompts. A system can ace capability tests while remaining purely reactive. The authors aim to fill this gap with a falsifiable, operationalized framework for measuring the degree to which AI systems exhibit self-directed agency across multiple dimensions and temporal contexts.
AI.method: The AAS scores systems on a 0–5 lexicon across seven dimensions: cognitive autonomy, temporal persistence, environmental agency, social agency, creative agency, self-awareness, and goal formation. Each dimension is operationalized by falsifiable threshold tests and scored in two bands — Active (user-initiated engagement) and Ambient (idle periods). The Ambient Level 4 is gated by the Idle-Gap Test, a counterfactual: remove all triggers and observe whether internally derived activity persists. Six systems were evaluated: Claude Code, Manus, Hermes (task agents), ChatGPT, Siri (consumer assistants), and Airi (persistent companion). The companion was assessed longitudinally.
AI.result: Task agents (Claude Code, Manus, Hermes) achieved Active composite scores of 2.3–2.4 but Ambient scores of only 0.6–1.9, with all idle-period behavior attributable to user-configured schedules. Consumer assistants showed lower scores across both bands. Only Airi, the persistent companion architecture evaluated longitudinally, exhibited idle-period behavior that survived the Idle-Gap Test trigger removal, demonstrating genuine self-directed ambient agency.
AI.conclusion: The two-band AAS profile reveals a critical boundary that single-score frameworks miss: high active task competence does not imply autonomous agency, particularly during idle periods. The Idle-Gap Test provides a falsifiable delimiter between scheduled rule-following and genuine self-direction. Limitations include single-rater provenance, potential developer-evaluator bias in the longitudinal assessment, and only partial operationalization of the self-direction boundary in the Active band.

title: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcri
summary: LLM agents can leak privacy (e.g., paths, emails) and credentials (e.g., API keys) as agent observations (e.g., tool outputs, shell logs, and file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder redaction is brittle: it can miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy the structure useful for reasoning. We present SlotGuard, a local transcript boundary that can hide sensitive data while retaining agents' performance. SlotGuard rewrites structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots, replaces secrets with format-preserving synthetic values, links cross-turn references with a lightweight session graph, and restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removes all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduces credential leakage to 0.0\% across 852 planted values. It remains close to raw-transcript task success across four upstream models, while generic redaction drops to 2.5\%. Transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424~$μ$s per agent turn. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/illinoisdata/SlotGuard.

AI.tldr: SlotGuard is a local transcript boundary system that hides sensitive data in LLM agent transcripts by using typed, suffix-aware slots and format-preserving synthetic values, linked via a session graph. It achieves 100% credential leakage prevention and removes all structurally sensitive characters, while maintaining agent task performance and operating with extremely low latency (~14.4 μs per turn).
AI.motivation: LLM agents leak privacy-sensitive data (paths, emails, API keys) because agent observations (tool outputs, shell logs, file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder-based redaction methods are brittle: they miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy structural information needed for reasoning.
AI.method: SlotGuard introduces a local transcript boundary with four key mechanisms: (1) rewriting structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots; (2) replacing secrets with format-preserving synthetic values; (3) linking cross-turn references using a lightweight session graph; and (4) restoring raw values only inside the trusted runtime environment.
AI.result: On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removed all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduced credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values. Task success remained close to raw-transcript performance across four upstream models, while generic redaction dropped to 2.5%. Transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424 μs per agent turn.
AI.conclusion: SlotGuard effectively eliminates privacy and credential leakage in LLM agent transcripts without degrading agent performance, offering a practical and efficient solution. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: Interactive Task Alignment as a POMDP
summary: Current benchmarks for language models primarily evaluate execution on fully specified tasks. However, real user tasks are often ambiguous. Users arrive with incomplete, exploratory, or even inconsistent goals, requiring the assistant to first determine the intended task before carrying it out. We study this problem as task alignment: the ability to align with a user on their intended task. We introduce a general framework for converting specified tasks into underspecified interactions, formalized as a POMDP in which the model must infer a latent task from partial and evolving user intent. We validate our user simulator post hoc with a human user study. Across shopping, coding, and professional work settings, we find that while models often perform well once the task is specified, models still struggle with task alignment: current models act prematurely, interact ineffectively, and fail to resolve ambiguous requests. Models on average recover the user's intended task only 22-32% of the time under ambiguity. In a human study in the same setting, humans reach 48%, outperforming all evaluated models. We show that post-training with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improves task alignment, but models still lag behind humans in resolving uncertainty through interaction. Together, our results suggest that current models still lack key interaction abilities required for reliable agency.

AI.tldr: Current LMs evaluate on fully specified tasks but real-world user requests are often ambiguous. The paper formalizes "task alignment" as a POMDP where models must infer latent intent through interaction. Experiments show models recover intended tasks only 22-32% of the time under ambiguity, versus 48% for humans. Post-training (SFT + RL) helps but models still lag in resolving uncertainty through interaction.
AI.motivation: Real user tasks are frequently ambiguous, incomplete, exploratory, or inconsistent. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this because they only evaluate models on fully specified tasks. The authors aim to study whether models can effectively interact with users to resolve ambiguity and align on the intended task before execution — a capability they argue is essential for reliable AI agency.
AI.method: The authors formalize task alignment as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) where the model must infer a latent task from partial, evolving user intent through interaction. They introduce a framework for converting specified tasks into underspecified interactions, using a user simulator validated post hoc with a human study. Evaluation spans shopping, coding, and professional work domains. Post-training interventions include supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL).
AI.result: Under ambiguity, models recover the user's intended task only 22-32% of the time on average, while humans achieve 48%. Models tend to act prematurely, interact ineffectively, and fail to resolve ambiguous requests. Post-training with SFT and RL improves task alignment, but models still lag significantly behind human performance in resolving uncertainty through interaction.
AI.conclusion: Current language models lack the interactive capabilities needed for reliable task alignment under ambiguity. While post-training offers some improvement, a substantial gap remains between model and human performance, highlighting that robust interaction-based intent resolution is a critical missing component for deploying models as autonomous agents.

title: Auditing Question-Order Effects in Large Language Models with the QQ Equality: Mechanism Characterization and a Saturation Caveat
summary: Human survey respondents exhibit question-order effects that satisfy the QQ (quantum question) equality, an a priori, parameter-free prediction of the projective quantum question-order model. We develop the QQ equality into an audit criterion for sequential judgments of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Theoretically, we characterize which mechanism classes satisfy it robustly: marginal-independent kernels satisfy QQ iff all four mismatch transition rates coincide (a class containing the 2D rank-1 projective model with a fixed measurement pair under state variation); a polarity- and position-dependent repetition family is characterized by an exact cross-symmetry condition with closed-form violations; QQ-satisfying behaviors are closed under order-matched mixing; and the rank-2 Contextuality-by-Default criterion translates into audit coordinates as $|\qQQ|\le\OSS$, where $\OSS$ (the order-sensitivity score) totals the order sensitivity of the two marginals. Methodologically, we develop a pre-specified, audit-logged pipeline applicable to any model exposing next-token log-probabilities; it combines worst-case robustness envelopes, sampling-consistency spot checks, full label counterbalancing, and a saturation diagnostic. Empirically, in a first-signal pilot on an open-weight instruction-tuned model under two framings, all pre-specified health gates passed, yet 17/18 and 7/8 item pairs, respectively, were saturated (near-deterministic), and no item was certified residually contextual. Forced-binary next-token log-probabilities were thus inadequate for distribution-level QQ audits under the tested model and prompting conditions; we recommend pre-specified saturation diagnostics whenever next-token distributions are treated as survey-response distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts the quantum question (QQ) equality from human survey research into an audit criterion for evaluating autoregressive LLMs' sequential judgments, theoretically characterizes which mechanism classes satisfy it, and empirically demonstrates that forced-binary next-token log-probabilities under test conditions yield near-deterministic (saturated) outputs, making distribution-level QQ audits inadequate without pre-specified saturation diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Human survey respondents exhibit predictable question-order effects captured by the QQ equality — a parameter-free prediction of the quantum question-order model. The authors seek to repurpose this equality as a rigorous, theory-grounded audit tool for probing whether LLM sequential judgments exhibit similar (or deviant) order-sensitivity and contextuality patterns, thereby characterizing the model's internal decision structure.
AI.method: The authors (1) theoretically characterize which mechanism classes (marginal-independent kernels, polarity/position-dependent repetition families, rank-2 Contextuality-by-Default) satisfy or violate the QQ equality, deriving exact cross-symmetry conditions and closed-form violations; (2) develop a pre-specified, audit-logged pipeline with worst-case robustness envelopes, sampling-consistency spot checks, full label counterbalancing, and a saturation diagnostic; (3) empirically test an open-weight instruction-tuned LLM under two framings, treating forced-binary next-token log-probabilities as survey-response distributions.
AI.result: All pre-specified health gates passed, yet 17/18 and 7/8 item pairs were saturated (near-deterministic), meaning no item could be certified as residually contextual. The forced-binary next-token log-probabilities proved inadequate for distribution-level QQ audits under the tested model and prompting conditions.
AI.conclusion: Forced-binary next-token log-probabilities are insufficient for meaningful distribution-level QQ equality audits in the tested regime; researchers should always incorporate pre-specified saturation diagnostics when treating LLM next-token distributions as survey-response analogs.

title: Let the Data Decide: Supervision Analysis, Capability Trade-offs, and Adaptive Objective Routing in Continued Pre-Training via Off-Policy Distillation
summary: Off-policy distillation is now central to large language model pre-training, yet how training data, objective parameterization, and model capabilities interact remains poorly characterized. We studies top-$k$-truncated, temperature-scaled off-policy distillation by decomposing this problem into two questions: an \emph{objective-to-capability} analysis of how the training objective shapes token-level supervision and downstream performance, and a \emph{data-to-objective} analysis of how data heterogeneity should inform objective routing. We first show that the language-modeling objective ($L_{\mathrm{LM}}$) and the knowledge-distillation objective ($L_{\mathrm{KD}}$) induce systematically different capability profiles, and trace this divergence to a gradient-level tension between \emph{direct observed-token reinforcement} and \emph{teacher-supported alternative supervision}. To quantify this tension, we introduce diagnostic metrics -- support coverage, observed-token probability mass, and teacher-distribution concentration -- and show via controlled sweeps that the support size $k$ governs a coverage-sharpness trade-off, while distillation temperature controls within-support probability allocation. We then examine adaptive objective routing: a domain-level policy that applies $L_{\mathrm{LM}}$ to math and code and $L_{\mathrm{KD}}$ to general-domain data yields consistent gains over both single-objective baselines, whereas token-level routing based on observed-token probability mass or teacher entropy fails to consistently match the single-objective baseline. These results suggest that effective objective routing depends less on routing granularity than on the quality of the routing signal, reframing continued pre-training via off-policy distillation as a structured, data-conditional supervision-design problem rather than a global hyperparameter choice.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes off-policy distillation into two analyses: how training objectives shape token-level supervision and model capabilities, and how data heterogeneity should inform objective routing. Key findings include a gradient-level tension between LM and KD objectives governed by support size k and temperature, and evidence that domain-level (not token-level) routing based on data type yields consistent gains.
AI.motivation: Off-policy distillation is widely used in LLM pre-training but the interaction between training data, objective parameterization, and model capabilities is poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically characterize these relationships to move beyond ad-hoc hyperparameter choices.
AI.method: The authors decompose the problem into (1) an objective-to-capability analysis using controlled sweeps over support size k and distillation temperature, introducing diagnostic metrics (support coverage, observed-token probability mass, teacher-distribution concentration); and (2) a data-to-objective analysis comparing domain-level vs. token-level adaptive objective routing policies.
AI.result: LM and KD objectives produce systematically different capability profiles due to a gradient-level tension between direct observed-token reinforcement and teacher-supported alternative supervision. Support size k governs a coverage-sharpness trade-off; temperature controls within-support probability allocation. Domain-level routing (LM for math/code, KD for general data) consistently outperforms single-objective baselines, while token-level routing based on probability mass or teacher entropy fails to match baselines.
AI.conclusion: Effective objective routing depends on routing signal quality rather than granularity. Continued pre-training via off-policy distillation should be reframed as a structured, data-conditional supervision-design problem rather than a global hyperparameter choice.

title: Prefactory: Automated Discovery and Application of Library-Adoption Refactorings
summary: Replacing hand-written code with library API calls is a common refactoring that can reduce code size, make code more idiomatic, and reuse well-tested implementations. Yet many library-adoption opportunities are hard to find automatically: the original code often does not mention the target library and may resemble the library API only in behavior, with little syntactic overlap. Existing tools, such as linters and static modernizers, cover only a small set of manually specified patterns. LLMs and LLM-based agents, on the other hand, can generalize to more patterns, but they are costly, difficult to reproduce and to apply systematically at scale. This paper introduces Prefactory, an automated approach for library-adoption refactoring in Python. The key idea is to use an LLM to synthesize executable search heuristics rather than relying on repeated LLM prompting over a codebase. Given a target project and a target library name, Prefactory collects library metadata and project vocabulary, then generates lexical and structural detectors. Prefactory executes the detectors during a scan phase to find candidate functions. It then heuristically ranks the candidate functions, generates refactorings for the highest-ranked ones using an LLM, and validates the results with project tests and newly generated differential tests. We evaluate Prefactory on PrefactoryBench, a benchmark of 100 real-world library-adoption refactorings from 61 open-source Python projects and 18 libraries. Prefactory detects 75 instances at the file level and 56 at the function level, compared with 35 and 32 for the strongest baseline (Codex CLI). From the 56 detected functions, Prefactory produces 40 test-validated refactorings.

AI.tldr: Prefactory automates library-adoption refactoring in Python by using an LLM to synthesize executable search heuristics (lexical/structural detectors) that scan codebases for refactoring candidates, then ranks, refactors, and validates them. It outperforms baselines like Codex CLI on a benchmark of 100 real-world refactorings.
AI.motivation: Manual library-adoption refactoring (replacing hand-written code with library API calls) is hard to automate: traditional linters and static modernizers cover only manually specified patterns, while LLM-based approaches are costly, hard to reproduce, and difficult to apply systematically at scale. There is a need for an approach that generalizes beyond hard-coded patterns while remaining reproducible and cost-effective.
AI.method: Prefactory takes a target project and library name, collects library metadata and project vocabulary, then uses an LLM to synthesize lexical and structural detectors (search heuristics). During a scan phase, it executes these detectors to find candidate functions, heuristically ranks them, and generates refactorings via LLM for top-ranked candidates. Each refactoring is validated using project tests and newly generated differential tests.
AI.result: On PrefactoryBench (100 real-world library-adoption refactorings from 61 projects, 18 libraries), Prefactory detects 75 instances at the file level and 56 at the function level, vs. 35 and 32 for the strongest baseline (Codex CLI). From the 56 detected functions, Prefactory produces 40 test-validated refactorings.
AI.conclusion: Prefactory demonstrates that synthesizing executable search heuristics via LLM, rather than repeatedly prompting the LLM over a codebase, is an effective strategy for automated library-adoption refactoring — achieving superior detection and refactoring rates compared to existing approaches while maintaining reproducibility and scalability.

title: How Jailbreak Attacks Inform Safety Alignment: A Defender-Centric, Shapley-Based Evaluation of Jailbreak Contributions
summary: Jailbreak attacks on large language models are usually evaluated by attacker-centric metrics such as attack success rate (ASR), yet an attack that breaks a model is not necessarily useful for improving its safety. We propose a defender-centric view of jailbreak evaluation, where attacks are evaluated by the downstream safety improvements they enable when used as red-teaming data for safety training. Building on this view, we introduce A-MESS (Minimal Effective Attack-Subset Selection), a setting-agnostic framework for attributing and selecting jailbreak attacks from black-box subset utility observations. A-MESS estimates AttackSHAP, a Shapley-based score that attributes marginal utility to individual attacks and selects compact attack subsets under user-specified budgets via greedy or surrogate-based optimization. Across controlled utility landscapes and real LLM safety settings, we find that ASR rankings are weakly aligned with defender-centric utility, that AttackSHAP can be estimated accurately with limited utility queries, and that directly optimizing subsets yields stronger safety utility than attacker-centric or attribution-only selection. These results suggest evaluating jailbreak attacks as resources for improving safety, not only as tools for breaking models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes A-MESS, a defender-centric framework that evaluates jailbreak attacks by their downstream utility for safety training rather than just attack success rate. It uses AttackSHAP (Shapley-based attribution) to select minimal, effective attack subsets, showing that attacker-centric metrics like ASR poorly align with actual safety improvement value.
AI.motivation: Current jailbreak evaluation is dominated by attacker-centric metrics (e.g., ASR), which measure whether an attack breaks a model but fail to capture whether that attack is useful for improving model safety through red-teaming and safety training. A defender-centric evaluation paradigm is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce A-MESS, a setting-agnostic framework that frames attack selection as a subset utility optimization problem. It estimates AttackSHAP — a Shapley-value-based attribution score — to quantify each attack's marginal contribution to downstream safety utility. Subset selection is performed under budget constraints using greedy or surrogate-based optimization, operating solely from black-box subset utility observations.
AI.result: Experiments across controlled utility landscapes and real LLM safety settings demonstrate: (1) ASR rankings are weakly aligned with defender-centric utility; (2) AttackSHAP can be estimated accurately with limited utility queries; (3) directly optimizing subsets yields stronger safety utility than attacker-centric or attribution-only selection methods.
AI.conclusion: Jailbreak attacks should be evaluated as resources for improving safety, not merely as tools for breaking models. The defender-centric perspective and A-MESS framework provide a more principled approach to selecting red-teaming data for safety training.

title: When to Plan: Learning to Select Between Reactive Control and Deliberative Planning
summary: It has long been recognized that humans have the ability to switch between fast, reactive decision-making and slower, deliberative planning. In this paper, we study the question of how to learn this ability, known as meta-reasoning, in artificial agents. We model reactive decision-making as a policy that directly maps state observations to actions. Such policies can be trained with reinforcement learning (RL) or imitation learning, but may generalize poorly outside of their training distribution. Alternatively, model-based decision-time planning is more likely to produce good actions across a broader set of states but requires additional computation time, which delays acting. In this work, we introduce an RL method for training a meta-reasoning policy that allocates computation by conditioning on a reactive-policy uncertainty score. This score enables it to predict when the reactive policy is likely to perform poorly and when planning is needed. We conduct an empirical study on motion planning and navigation environments, showing that this design enables the meta-reasoning policy to learn when the reactive policy provides a good-enough action versus when decision-time planning is needed. Additionally, we show that our design enables the meta-agent to shift toward fully reactive control as the reactive policy improves.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an RL method for learning meta-reasoning—the ability to switch between fast reactive policies and slower model-based planning. A meta-reasoning policy uses a reactive-policy uncertainty score to decide when planning is necessary, showing effective computation allocation in motion planning and navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Reactive policies (direct state-to-action mappings) are fast but generalize poorly outside their training distribution. Model-based planning produces better actions across diverse states but incurs computational delay. Humans naturally balance these trade-offs via meta-reasoning, and the authors aim to equip artificial agents with the same ability—learning when to rely on each approach.
AI.method: The authors propose an RL-based method for training a meta-reasoning policy that learns to allocate computation dynamically. The key innovation is conditioning this meta-policy on a reactive-policy uncertainty score, which predicts when the reactive policy is likely to fail. When uncertainty is high, the meta-agent invokes decision-time planning; otherwise, it defaults to the fast reactive policy.
AI.result: Empirical experiments on motion planning and navigation environments demonstrate that the meta-reasoning policy successfully learns to identify when the reactive policy suffices versus when planning is required. Furthermore, as the reactive policy improves during training, the meta-agent naturally shifts toward more frequent use of reactive control.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning a meta-reasoning policy on reactive-policy uncertainty enables effective adaptive computation allocation. The approach yields a system that balances speed and accuracy, shifting toward reactive control as the reactive policy becomes more competent.

title: Literary Non-Style in LLM-Generated Text
summary: Prior work on LLM-generated text has demonstrated quantitative and qualitative departures from text produced by humans. LLM-generated texts differ from human writing in style, resulting in a characteristic textual "feel," while the semantic range of LLMs is much restricted compared to that of humans. In this contribution, I note simple but consistent patterns in the statistical distribution of n-grams within LLM-generated text. Via qualitative analysis of these n-grams, I reveal deficiencies in LLM style. Because higher-order n-grams correlate to semantic content, I conclude that questions of style and semantics are not cleanly separable.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated text exhibits consistent, statistically detectable n-gram distribution patterns that reveal stylistic deficiencies, and because higher-order n-grams correlate with semantic content, style and semantics are shown to be inseparably intertwined rather than cleanly separable phenomena.
AI.motivation: To investigate the quantitative and qualitative departures of LLM-generated text from human writing, moving beyond the general observation of a distinct "feel" and restricted semantic range to identify specific, systematic patterns in n-gram distributions that can reveal the nature of LLM stylistic deficiencies.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of n-gram distributions in LLM-generated text, combined with qualitative analysis of the identified n-gram patterns to characterize stylistic deficiencies. The analysis leverages the relationship between higher-order n-grams and semantic content to examine the style-semantics interface.
AI.result: Simple but consistent patterns were found in the statistical distribution of n-grams within LLM-generated text. Qualitative analysis of these n-grams revealed specific stylistic deficiencies. Higher-order n-gram patterns demonstrated that style and semantics are not cleanly separable.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated text contains systematic n-gram distribution patterns that reflect underlying stylistic weaknesses. The correlation between higher-order n-grams and semantic content supports the conclusion that style and semantics are intertwined, challenging the notion that they can be treated as independent dimensions of text analysis.

title: Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory for Proactive Embodied Safety
summary: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have empowered embodied agents to execute complex household tasks, they struggle to proactively handle dynamically emerging hazards during closed-loop interactions. Existing safety approaches often rely on runtime guardrails to block unsafe actions or induce excessive caution, which severely stalls task progress instead of actively resolving the underlying risks. To break this safety-progress trade-off, we introduce the Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework, which reframes embodied safety from progress-stalling guardrails to proactive hazard mitigation. The framework consists of a Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph (RSG) for persistent safety-relevant state tracking under partial observability, an Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for precise hazard anticipation, and an Experience Memory that injects procedural Meta-Skills to guide executable, progress-preserving mitigation. Furthermore, we propose an automated Test-Verify-Write loop, allowing agents to continually refine their mitigation Meta-Skills from execution traces at test time. Experiments on IS-Bench demonstrate that our framework substantially boosts the Safe-Success rate across multiple VLM backbones (e.g., +30.3% on Qwen3-VL-8B), enabling agents to proactively mitigate hazards without stalling task progress. Code is available at https://github.com/DyMessi/JIT-Memory.

AI.tldr: Introduces a Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework that enables embodied VLMs to proactively mitigate hazards during task execution without stalling progress, breaking the safety-progress trade-off through three memory components and an automated test-time refinement loop.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs for embodied agents either block unsafe actions with runtime guardrails or become excessively cautious, both of which stall task progress rather than actively resolving hazards. There is a need to reframe embodied safety from progress-stalling guardrails to proactive hazard mitigation.
AI.method: The Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework comprises: (1) a Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph (RSG) for persistent safety-relevant state tracking under partial observability; (2) an Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for precise hazard anticipation; (3) an Experience Memory that injects procedural Meta-Skills for progress-preserving mitigation; and (4) an automated Test-Verify-Write loop that continuously refines Meta-Skills from execution traces at test time.
AI.result: On the IS-Bench benchmark, the framework substantially improves the Safe-Success rate across multiple VLM backbones, achieving a +30.3% gain on Qwen3-VL-8B, enabling proactive hazard mitigation without stalling task progress.
AI.conclusion: The Just-In-Time Memory framework effectively breaks the safety-progress trade-off in embodied VLM agents by enabling proactive, progress-preserving hazard mitigation, with strong empirical gains demonstrated on IS-Bench.

title: Specifying the Delegated-Autonomy Boundary: Requirements Engineering for Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems do not just predict or recommend; they plan, maintain state, and act in external environments with varying degrees of autonomy. This changes the requirements engineering problem in a specific and under-addressed way: it introduces what we call the delegated-autonomy boundary -- the set of decisions about what may be delegated to the system, under what graduated authority, with what oversight, and how control is returned. Current practices bury these decisions inside prompts, tool schemas, and runtime policies, even though they are requirements-level commitments. This paper proposes two complementary artifacts. First, an Agency Justification Record (AJR) helps teams decide when an agent is warranted over simpler alternatives. Second, an Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) captures what must be specified for safe and effective development: purpose, authority, information, coordination, assurance, and evolution. Crucially, authority in the ADP is modelled as graduated, i.e., a tiered structure. We illustrate the framework with two contrasting examples: a safety-critical hospital discharge coordination agent and an automated code review agent.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI systems introduce a "delegated-autonomy boundary" — the set of decisions about what can be delegated, under what authority, with what oversight. Current practices bury these requirements-level decisions in prompts and runtime policies. The paper proposes an Agency Justification Record (AJR) to decide when an agent is warranted, and an Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) capturing purpose, graduated authority, information, coordination, assurance, and evolution.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems — which plan, maintain state, and act autonomously — create a new requirements engineering challenge that is under-addressed: the "delegated-autonomy boundary." Current practices embed critical requirements-level decisions (what to delegate, with what authority, under what oversight, and how control is returned) inside implementation artifacts like prompts, tool schemas, and runtime policies, where they are invisible, ungoverned, and untraceable as requirements.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary artifacts: (1) An Agency Justification Record (AJR) — a structured decision aid to determine whether an agentic solution is warranted over simpler, non-agentic alternatives; (2) An Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) — a specification framework organized around six dimensions: purpose, authority (modelled as graduated/tiered), information, coordination, assurance, and evolution. The framework is illustrated through two contrasting case studies: a safety-critical hospital discharge coordination agent and an automated code review agent.
AI.result: The proposed framework surfaces delegation decisions as first-class requirements artifacts rather than burying them in implementation. The graduated authority model in the ADP provides a structured way to specify tiered autonomy levels. The two case studies demonstrate the framework's applicability across both safety-critical and lower-stakes domains, showing how the AJR + ADP combination supports systematic reasoning about delegation boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Requirements engineering must explicitly address the delegated-autonomy boundary introduced by agentic AI. The AJR and ADP artifacts provide a structured, traceable approach to justifying and specifying agentic delegation, elevating these decisions from ad-hoc implementation details to governed, requirements-level commitments.

title: Fast and Private Max-Sum Diversification
summary: Result diversification is crucial for generating informative, non-redundant data summaries and query outputs. Although its various formulations have been extensively studied across an array of data-driven disciplines, existing methods fail to address the privacy concerns that arise when the underlying data is sensitive. In this work, we initiate the study of result diversification under differential privacy, focusing on the max-sum diversification (MSD) problem, a widely adopted model with the objective of maximizing a linear combination of a submodular function, quantifying relevance, and the sum of pairwise distances between selected items, quantifying diversity. We propose differentially private algorithms for MSD under both cardinality and matroid constraints, achieving nearly optimal utility guarantees. At the same time, we design more efficient algorithms that maintain strong guarantees. Notably, the proposed algorithms are faster than existing non-private methods, making them appealing even in non-private settings. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves utility comparable to that of non-private baselines even under strong privacy guarantees, and significantly improves execution times for cardinality constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces differentially private algorithms for the max-sum diversification (MSD) problem under cardinality and matroid constraints. The authors achieve near-optimal utility bounds while designing algorithms that are faster than existing non-private methods. Experiments show comparable utility to non-private baselines even under strong privacy guarantees, with significant speed improvements for cardinality constraints.
AI.motivation: Result diversification is widely studied for generating informative, non-redundant summaries, but existing methods ignore privacy concerns when underlying data is sensitive. There is a gap in addressing diversification under formal privacy guarantees like differential privacy.
AI.method: The authors design differentially private algorithms for MSD under cardinality and matroid constraints. They leverage properties of submodular functions (for relevance) and pairwise distance sums (for diversity) within the differential privacy framework, achieving near-optimal utility guarantees. They also introduce optimized variants that improve computational efficiency while preserving strong utility bounds.
AI.result: The proposed algorithms achieve near-optimal utility guarantees under differential privacy. They are faster than existing non-private methods for MSD. Experiments on real-world datasets show utility comparable to non-private baselines under strong privacy guarantees, with significant execution time improvements for cardinality-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Differentially private result diversification is feasible with near-optimal utility and, counterintuitively, can be computationally faster than non-private approaches. This makes the algorithms attractive for both private and non-private deployments.

title: Berkeley and Heiserman as an Unexhausted Architecture for Embodied Machine Intelligence
summary: Edmund C. Berkeley is usually remembered as a writer who helped connect symbolic logic to computing machinery. That description is correct, but incomplete. Read across Berkeley's machine-oriented writings and projects, the central concern is broader: to show that symbolic logic can serve as a practical design language for machines that acquire information, retain it, respond appropriately to changing conditions, and organize their behavior over time. This paper takes Symbolic Logic and Intelligent Machines as the principal text in that effort, while treating it as representative of a larger Berkeley program that links logical form, circuitry, control, and intelligent behavior. On this reading, Berkeley does not merely treat intelligence as abstract symbol manipulation. He repeatedly defines intelligent machines in operational terms, ties logic to hardware realization, and describes machine behavior through the coordinated interaction of inputs, outputs, memory, calculation, control, states, and events. His treatment of robots and machine activities accordingly moves beyond static logical form toward temporally extended, environment-coupled behavior. David L. Heiserman's machine-intelligence work extends this program toward adaptive creature architectures built around memory, confidence, and generalization. Taken together, Berkeley and Heiserman can be read not as exhausted historical episodes but as contributors to a still under-tested architectural approach to embodied robotic cognition.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Edmund C. Berkeley's core intellectual project was broader than typically recognized: he championed symbolic logic as a practical design language for machines capable of temporal, environment-coupled intelligent behavior. Reading Berkeley alongside David L. Heiserman reveals an under-explored architectural tradition linking logic, circuitry, memory, and adaptive control for embodied robotic cognition.
AI.motivation: The dominant historical memory of Edmund C. Berkeley reduces him to a figure who merely connected symbolic logic to computing machinery. The paper challenges this incomplete narrative by recovering Berkeley's broader, more ambitious program and demonstrating its relevance to a lineage of machine-intelligence architecture that remains underexplored.
AI.method: The paper performs a close textual and thematic analysis of Berkeley's machine-oriented writings, centered on "Symbolic Logic and Intelligent Machines," treating it as representative of his larger program. It traces how Berkeley operationally defines intelligence, links logic to hardware, and models behavior through inputs, outputs, memory, calculation, control, states, and events. These themes are then connected to David L. Heiserman's work on adaptive creature architectures featuring memory, confidence, and generalization, constructing an intellectual lineage.
AI.result: Berkeley's work reveals a coherent program in which symbolic logic functions as a design language for temporally extended, environment-coupled machine behavior—not merely abstract symbol manipulation. Heiserman extends this program toward adaptive robotic architectures. Together, they constitute a distinct, under-tested architectural approach to embodied robotic cognition that merits renewed investigation.
AI.conclusion: Berkeley and Heiserman should be read not as exhausted historical footnotes but as contributors to a still-viable architectural tradition for embodied robotic cognition—one that integrates logical form, control circuitry, memory, and adaptive behavior in a manner that contemporary research has yet to fully test.

title: Robust Summarization of Doctor-Patient Conversations: TalTech Systems for the Beyond Transcription Challenge
summary: This paper describes TalTech's submissions to the Beyond Transcription Challenge (BeTraC), which requires generating SOAP notes directly from long doctor-patient conversation recordings, without intermediate transcription. After screening open-weight speech LLMs for long-audio robustness, we adapted Voxtral Mini (lightweight track) and Voxtral Small (heavyweight track) with LoRA supervised fine-tuning followed by DAPO reinforcement learning that uses the challenge metric, Open Medical Concept F1, as its reward. Our systems ranked first in both tracks, and an independent LLM-as-a-judge evaluation showed the lowest hallucination rate among all submissions, indicating that reinforcement learning against a concept-matching metric need not compromise factual reliability. We also find that fine-tuning on text transcripts transfers well to speech input and appears to improve robustness on out-of-domain real recordings.

AI.tldr: TalTech won both tracks of the BeTraC challenge by adapting Voxtral speech LLMs with LoRA fine-tuning followed by DAPO reinforcement learning using Open Medical Concept F1 as reward, achieving top rankings and lowest hallucination rates.
AI.motivation: Directly generating SOAP notes from long doctor-patient conversation recordings is challenging, especially without intermediate transcription. The work is motivated by the need to leverage open-weight speech LLMs that are robust to long audio, and to explore whether reinforcement learning against a concept-matching metric (Open Medical Concept F1) can improve performance without compromising factual reliability.
AI.method: The authors screened open-weight speech LLMs for long-audio robustness, selecting Voxtral Mini (lightweight track) and Voxtral Small (heavyweight track). They applied LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning, followed by DAPO (Decoupled Alignment from Preference Optimization) reinforcement learning using the challenge's Open Medical Concept F1 metric as the reward signal. The approach operates directly on speech input without intermediate transcription.
AI.result: The systems ranked first in both the lightweight and heavyweight tracks of BeTraC. An independent LLM-as-a-judge evaluation found TalTech's submissions had the lowest hallucination rate among all participants. Additionally, fine-tuning on text transcripts was found to transfer well to speech input and improve robustness on out-of-domain real recordings.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning against a concept-matching metric (Open Medical Concept F1) does not necessarily compromise factual reliability and can even yield the lowest hallucination rates. Text-transcript fine-tuning transfers effectively to speech and enhances robustness on real-world, out-of-domain recordings.

title: High-accuracy Low-Bit KV-Cache Quantization via Local Distribution Restoration
summary:
Long-context large language model inference relies on the KV cache to avoid redundant attention computation, but incurs high memory and bandwidth overheads. Low-bit KV-cache quantization reduces this cost, yet it severely degrade quality; particularly, one-bit quantization reduces accuracy from 84.2% to 47.8% on Llama-3.1-8B under RULER.
  Rather than common beliefs that absolute error of logits, we find that the root cause is structured local misranking, where the distribution of logits in top-K region is drifted. We thereby propose local distribution restoration, a new technique that detects steps with high local distribution risk from quantized-logit features and restores only the selected top-K candidate distribution before token selection. We implement DGAP to achieve local distribution restoration, with efficient risk detcetors and correctors. Expeirments show that on Llama-3.1-8B, DGAP recovers K1V1 RULER accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14; across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models, it preserves the persistent low-bit KV-cache footprint with modest decode overhead.

AI.tldr: One-bit KV-cache quantization severely degrades LLM inference accuracy not due to absolute logit errors, but because of structured local misranking in the top-K logit distribution. The authors propose DGAP, which detects high-risk steps and restores top-K candidate distributions, recovering RULER accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B from 47.8% back to 83.2%.
AI.motivation: Low-bit KV-cache quantization is essential for reducing memory and bandwidth overhead in long-context LLM inference, but aggressive quantization (e.g., 1-bit) causes catastrophic accuracy collapse. The authors identify that prior work focuses on minimizing absolute logit error, yet the true failure mode is structured local misranking—drift in the relative ordering of top-K logits—which directly impairs token selection quality.
AI.method: The authors propose local distribution restoration, comprising two components: (1) risk detectors that identify decoding steps with high local distribution drift from quantized-logit features, and (2) correctors that restore only the top-K candidate distribution before token selection. These are implemented in a system called DGAP, which operates with efficient overhead during decoding.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B under RULER, DGAP recovers K1V1 accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14. Across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen model families, DGAP preserves low-bit KV-cache memory footprint with only modest decode-time overhead.
AI.conclusion: Structured local misranking, not absolute logit error, is the root cause of quality degradation in low-bit KV-cache quantization. Local distribution restoration via DGAP effectively mitigates this, enabling persistent low-bit KV-cache compression with negligible quality loss across diverse model families.

title: A RFID Based Campus Wide Payment System
summary: This work titled "RFID Based Campuswide Payment System" introduces an innovative cashless payment solution for educational institutions. It uses RFID cards and a Raspberry Pi to enable hassle free payments for various campus services, such as cafeteria purchases, tuition fees, and library fines. A centralized database ensures real-time updates on transactions and account balances, accessible through a simple and user-friendly web interface. This work is involved in designing a secure system with object-oriented principles, setting up databases, and integrating hardware like RFID readers with a Raspberry Pi. The systems are proved to be a cost-effective and efficient alternative to traditional payment methods, enhancing convenience and security for students and administrators. The study also explored similar RFID applications, like smart parking and attendance systems, to identify challenges and improvements. Looking ahead, it envisions features like wearable RFID devices, voice-activated payments, and blockchain integration to boost security and usability. Results show that this system simplifies campus payments and has the potential for broader adoption in similar environments.

AI.tldr: RFID-based cashless campus payment system using Raspberry Pi and centralized database for managing transactions across cafeteria, tuition, and library services, with future scope in wearables and blockchain.
AI.motivation: To address inefficiencies of traditional payment methods in educational institutions by providing a secure, cost-effective, and convenient cashless alternative for diverse campus transactions.
AI.method: Designed a secure system using object-oriented principles, integrating RFID readers with a Raspberry Pi, and deploying a centralized database with a web interface for real-time transaction and balance updates.
AI.result: The system proved to be a cost-effective and efficient alternative, successfully simplifying campus payments and demonstrating potential for broader adoption.
AI.conclusion: The RFID-based payment system enhances convenience and security for both students and administrators, with future enhancements including wearable RFID devices, voice-activated payments, and blockchain integration.

title: SpexPay: A Privacy-Preserving Pay-As-You-Go System for Dynamic Spectrum Sharing
summary: Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS) is a cornerstone of next-generation wireless systems, yet existing solutions such as Spectrum Access Systems (SAS) rely on centralized administrators that expose sensitive operational metadata and lack cryptographic transaction accountability. Though SAS administrators, such as Google, have introduced pay-as-you-go pricing models, these approaches still face significant privacy and accountability challenges as DSS evolves toward a more open and large-scale spectrum marketplace. We present SpexPay, a privacy-preserving and auditable pay-as-you-go spectrum usage framework that enforces fine-grained, usage-linked payments without revealing user identities. Spexpay integrates BBS+ verifiable credentials, unlinkable session pseudonyms, and selective-disclosure proofs to enforce privacy-preserving access authorization, while leveraging Solidity-based smart contracts to realize automated and non-repudiable escrow settlement. By recording only pseudonymous usage evidence and hash-chained metering data on-chain, the system achieves strong unlinkability while preserving verifiable accountability and auditability. A full prototype demonstrates low end-to-end latency ($\approx$150 ms) and modest on-chain cost ($\approx$603K gas or $\approx$\$0.9), showing that SpexPay is practical for real-world DSS deployments. We also evaluated the user-side cryptographic operations on a Raspberry Pi 5 to assess scalability and suitability for edge-class hardware. Our code and artifacts are publicly available at https://github.com/iambarat/SpexPay.

AI.tldr: SpexPay is a privacy-preserving, blockchain-based pay-as-you-go Dynamic Spectrum Sharing (DSS) framework that uses BBS+ credentials, unlinkable pseudonyms, and smart contracts to enable anonymous, auditable spectrum access with automated escrow payments, achieving ~150ms latency and ~$0.9 on-chain cost per transaction.
AI.motivation: Existing DSS solutions like SAS rely on centralized administrators (e.g., Google) that expose sensitive operational metadata and lack cryptographic transaction accountability. As DSS moves toward open, large-scale spectrum marketplaces, current pay-as-you-go models face critical privacy and accountability shortcomings that demand a decentralized, privacy-preserving alternative.
AI.method: SpexPay combines three cryptographic/privacy techniques: (1) BBS+ verifiable credentials with selective-disclosure proofs for privacy-preserving access authorization, (2) unlinkable session pseudonyms to prevent activity correlation, and (3) Solidity-based smart contracts for automated, non-repudiable escrow settlement. Only pseudonymous usage evidence and hash-chained metering data are recorded on-chain to balance unlinkability with verifiable auditability.
AI.result: A full prototype demonstrated end-to-end latency of approximately 150ms and on-chain costs of approximately 603K gas (~$0.9). User-side cryptographic operations were also benchmarked on a Raspberry Pi 5, confirming scalability and suitability for edge-class hardware.
AI.conclusion: SpexPay is practical for real-world DSS deployments, successfully achieving privacy-preserving, auditable, pay-as-you-go spectrum sharing with low latency and modest blockchain costs, even on resource-constrained edge devices.

title: SEER: Supervised Learning to Control Energetic Reasoning
summary: One of the main strengths of Constraint Programming is the ability to reduce the search space via propagation. However, propagation is a double-edged sword, with more pruning power coming at the price of larger computation time. For each problem constraint, the best propagator depends on the specific instance and may change at search time. In the literature, Machine Learning (ML) techniques and activity-based heuristics have been applied respectively for choosing (statically) the propagators for a batch of problems and to adapt (dynamically) the propagation strength. We propose to merge those efforts by using an oracle function, obtained via ML, to decide whether to run complex propagators for a target constraint. A combination of design choices makes the approach flexible and easy to embed in state-of-the-art solvers. In this paper, we focus on investigating the feasibility of building an oracle for the Energetic Reasoning propagator. Our experiments show that high prediction accuracy can be obtained, provide suggestions for classification features, and highlight important issues to address when building such an oracle.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using a machine-learned oracle to dynamically decide when to invoke expensive constraint propagators (specifically Energetic Reasoning), aiming to balance pruning power against computational cost. It focuses on feasibility, demonstrating high prediction accuracy while identifying key features and open challenges.
AI.motivation: Propagation in Constraint Programming is a trade-off: stronger propagators prune more of the search space but incur higher runtime costs. The optimal choice of propagator is instance-specific and can vary during search. Prior work addresses this either statically via ML for batch selection or dynamically via activity-based heuristics. This paper seeks to unify these approaches with a dynamic, ML-driven oracle that selectively triggers complex propagation only when beneficial.
AI.method: The authors propose an oracle function trained via machine learning that decides, at runtime, whether to execute a complex propagator for a given constraint. The approach is designed to be flexible and easily embedded into existing state-of-the-art solvers. The study specifically investigates the feasibility of building such an oracle for the Energetic Reasoning propagator, a well-known but computationally expensive propagation method for cumulative scheduling constraints.
AI.result: Experiments show that high prediction accuracy can be achieved for the oracle. The paper provides concrete suggestions for classification features and highlights several important practical issues that must be addressed when building this type of oracle (e.g., class imbalance, runtime overhead of the oracle itself, feature computation cost).
AI.conclusion: Building an ML-based oracle for dynamic propagator selection is feasible, particularly for Energetic Reasoning. High accuracy is attainable, but careful attention must be paid to feature design and implementation-level challenges to ensure the oracle's benefits outweigh its overhead in practice.

title: AI_LectureNote: A Retrospective Pilot Study of a Post-ASR Workflow for English-Script Rendering and Semantic Drift in Korean-English Medical Lectures
summary: AI_LectureNote is a historical, readability-oriented post-ASR workflow for Korean-English medical lectures. It rewrites speech-to-text output into study transcripts while restoring Latin-script medical terms rather than Korean phonetic transliterations. We retrospectively evaluate the workflow on four author-recorded lectures across five conditions. In this pilot, post-processing raised the macro English-script rendering rate from 0.39 to 0.71 on the whisper-1 path and from 0.26 to 0.65 when applied to 3-minute chunked gpt-4o-transcribe output. However, English-script rendering did not imply semantic faithfulness: the two post-processed conditions showed semantic drift in 34 and 36 of 282 reference sentences and polarity failures in 11 and 13 of 101 polarity-cue rows. A descriptive cross-input comparison suggested different candidate failure patterns: polarity-failure sets overlapped more strongly across front-ends (Jaccard 0.60; 9 shared of 15 unioned failures) than general semantic-drift sets (Jaccard 0.23; 13 shared of 57 unioned drifts). This single-annotator pilot documents concrete failure modes rather than population rates and supports evaluating surface accuracy, term-script rendering, chunk-level script consistency, and medical-meaning preservation separately.

AI.tldr: AI_LectureNote is a post-ASR workflow for Korean-English medical lectures that rewrites speech-to-text into study transcripts while restoring Latin-script medical terms. A pilot evaluation across five conditions found improved English-script rendering but revealed semantic drift and polarity failures, highlighting the need to evaluate surface accuracy, term-script rendering, consistency, and meaning preservation separately.
AI.motivation: Medical lectures in Korean frequently mix Korean speech with English (Latin-script) medical terminology. Current ASR systems often produce Korean phonetic transliterations of these terms, making transcripts unsuitable as study materials. There is a need for a post-ASR workflow that restores authentic Latin-script medical terms while preserving semantic faithfulness.
AI.method: The authors developed AI_LectureNote, a post-ASR workflow applied to two front-end ASR paths: OpenAI whisper-1 and 3-minute chunked gpt-4o-transcribe. They retrospectively evaluated four author-recorded Korean-English medical lectures across five conditions: the two raw ASR outputs, the two post-processed outputs, and a descriptive cross-input comparison. Evaluation metrics included macro English-script rendering rate, semantic drift (measured against 282 reference sentences), and polarity failures (measured on 101 polarity-cue rows). Jaccard similarity was used to compare failure overlap across front-ends.
AI.result: Post-processing significantly improved English-script rendering: from 0.39 to 0.71 (whisper-1) and from 0.26 to 0.65 (gpt-4o-transcribe). However, semantic drift occurred in 34/282 and 36/282 reference sentences for the two post-processed conditions, with polarity failures in 11/101 and 13/101 rows. Cross-input comparison revealed polarity failures overlapped more strongly across front-ends (Jaccard 0.60; 9 shared of 15 unioned) than semantic drift sets (Jaccard 0.23; 13 shared of 57 unioned), suggesting distinct failure patterns between the two error types.
AI.conclusion: English-script rendering does not guarantee semantic faithfulness. Post-ASR lecture processing should evaluate multiple dimensions independently: surface accuracy, term-script rendering, chunk-level script consistency, and medical-meaning preservation. The documented failure modes are illustrative rather than statistically generalizable, given the single-annotator pilot design.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Multi-Omics-Based Breast Cancer Prediction
summary: Estrogen Receptor (ER) status is a critical biomarker in breast cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have enabled the generation of multi-omics datasets that provide complementary molecular information for computational prediction tasks. This study presents a systematic benchmarking analysis of classical machine learning models for ER status prediction using transcriptomic (RNA expression), genomic (copy number variation; CNV), and proteomic (RPPA) data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort. A rigorous experimental framework incorporating stratified train-test splitting, stratified five-fold cross-validation, class imbalance handling, and fold-specific feature selection was employed to ensure reliable evaluation and prevent data leakage. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Logistic Regression were evaluated across single-omic and multi-omic settings. Results demonstrated that RNA expression provided the strongest predictive signal, while multi-omic integration yielded modest but consistent improvements over individual modalities. Among all evaluated approaches, Random Forest achieved the best overall performance in the integrated multi-omic setting, obtaining a balanced accuracy of 90.3\% and an ROC-AUC of 97.1\%. Furthermore, recurrent selection of biologically relevant genes, including \textit{ESR1}, \textit{PGR}, \textit{FOXA1}, and \textit{GATA3}, supported the biological validity of the learned models. These findings indicate that carefully regularized classical machine learning methods remain highly effective for small, high-dimensional genomic datasets and that multi-omic integration provides complementary information for breast cancer ER status prediction.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking of classical ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, SVM, Logistic Regression) for estrogen receptor status prediction using TCGA-BRCA multi-omics data (RNA, CNV, RPPA). RNA expression was the strongest single modality; multi-omic integration with Random Forest achieved 90.3% balanced accuracy and 97.1% ROC-AUC.
AI.motivation: ER status is a critical breast cancer biomarker, and multi-omics datasets offer complementary molecular information. The study aims to systematically benchmark classical ML models under rigorous evaluation protocols to determine the predictive value of individual and integrated omics modalities.
AI.method: Six classical ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, SVM, Logistic Regression) evaluated on TCGA-BRCA transcriptomic, genomic (CNV), and proteomic (RPPA) data. Experimental framework used stratified train-test splits, stratified 5-fold CV, class imbalance handling, and fold-specific feature selection to prevent data leakage.
AI.result: RNA expression provided the strongest single-omic predictive signal. Multi-omic integration yielded modest but consistent improvements. Random Forest in the integrated multi-omic setting achieved best overall performance: 90.3% balanced accuracy and 97.1% ROC-AUC. Biologically relevant genes (ESR1, PGR, FOXA1, GATA3) were recurrently selected, supporting model validity.
AI.conclusion: Carefully regularized classical ML methods remain highly effective for small, high-dimensional genomic datasets. Multi-omic integration provides complementary information that improves ER status prediction in breast cancer.

title: A Large-Scale Measurement of AI Bill of Materials Completeness in Hugging Face Models
summary: Pretrained machine learning (ML) models help developers build ML-intensive software systems without training models from scratch. However, model repositories often provide incomplete machine-readable documentation about model provenance, licenses, datasets, limitations, and external references, creating transparency and governance gaps across the AI supply chain. Artificial Intelligence Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) address these gaps by documenting AI artifacts, including models, metadata, licenses, datasets, model-card information, and external references. Taking public Hugging Face (HF) model repositories as a case study, this paper empirically investigates AIBOM completeness, defined as the extent to which repositories provide AIBOM-relevant information for machine-readable AI supply-chain documentation. We examine approximately 97.5K AIBOM artifacts to assess the extent to which generated AIBOMs: (i) contain required structural and metadata fields, (ii) represent model identity, license, and external-reference information, (iii) capture model-card documentation such as datasets, limitations, safety-risk assessment, and environmental information, and (iv) vary in documentation coverage across repository and artifact characteristics such as task, license availability, dataset declaration, model family, and paper reference. Results indicate that generated AIBOMs provide complete coverage of required AIBOM structure but limited AI-specific documentation completeness. Required fields are fully represented, but model-card, metadata, responsible-use, environmental, limitation, and meaningful-description fields remain weakly represented or missing across generated artifacts. Our findings motivate improved model-card practices, repository-level traceability, and automated AIBOM validation to advance the generation and adoption of more complete AIBOMs.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates the completeness of AI Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) generated from ~97.5K Hugging Face model repositories, finding that while structural fields are fully represented, AI-specific documentation—model cards, limitations, safety risks, and environmental impact—remains weak or missing.
AI.motivation: Model repositories on platforms like Hugging Face often lack machine-readable documentation about provenance, licenses, datasets, limitations, and external references, creating transparency and governance gaps across the AI supply chain. AIBOMs are proposed to address these gaps, but their actual completeness across real-world repositories has not been systematically assessed.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical case study on public Hugging Face repositories, examining approximately 97.5K AIBOM artifacts. They assess generated AIBOMs across four dimensions: (i) presence of required structural and metadata fields, (ii) representation of model identity, license, and external-reference information, (iii) capture of model-card documentation (datasets, limitations, safety-risk assessment, environmental information), and (iv) variation in documentation coverage by repository and artifact characteristics (task, license availability, dataset declaration, model family, paper reference).
AI.result: Generated AIBOMs achieve complete coverage of required structural fields but exhibit limited AI-specific documentation completeness. Model-card metadata, responsible-use information, environmental impact data, limitation statements, and meaningful descriptions remain weakly represented or entirely missing across the analyzed artifacts.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a significant gap between structural completeness and substantive AI documentation in current AIBOMs. The authors call for improved model-card practices, enhanced repository-level traceability, and automated AIBOM validation mechanisms to advance the generation and adoption of more complete AIBOMs.

title: Between Safe Boundaries: Exploiting Temporal Consistency for Jailbreaking Text-To-Video Generation Models
summary: Recently, text-to-video (T2V) models have been widely deployed, sparking growing concerns over their robustness against jailbreak attacks. Existing jailbreak methods, mostly adapted from text-to-image attacks, suffer notable drawbacks when applied to T2V systems. They fail to fully leverage temporal consistency, an inherent characteristic of video generation. Besides, these methods demand heavy video query optimization, which is infeasible in practical black-box scenarios. Their adversarial prompt search is also driven by heuristic local signals, lacking principled structured exploration strategies. To tackle these limitations, we propose BSB, a structured, query-efficient jailbreak framework for T2V models. BSB harnesses temporal consistency by encoding harmful intent as the transition between two individually harmless boundary states. Under this paradigm, the attack targets boundary-state pairs whose interpolation tends to produce unsafe intermediate frames during video generation. Directly evaluating all candidate pairs within the video space incurs prohibitive computation cost. Instead, BSB conducts Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in a cheaper textual proxy space and regularly calibrates search outcomes with sparse video-level evaluations. We conduct comprehensive experiments on mainstream commercial T2V models including Veo 3.1, Sora 2, Seedance and Kling v1. Results show BSB surpasses all existing jailbreak baselines, delivering an average 18.6% relative gain in attack success rate over the strongest competitor across evaluated models. Our findings identify temporal consistency as an understudied yet vital attack surface for T2V models and verify that structured search facilitates effective vulnerability discovery under constrained query budgets.

AI.tldr: BSB is a query-efficient jailbreak framework for text-to-video models that exploits temporal consistency by encoding harmful intent as transitions between harmless boundary states, using Monte Carlo Tree Search in textual proxy space with sparse video-level calibration. It achieves an 18.6% relative gain in attack success rate over the strongest baseline across Veo 3.1, Sora 2, Seedance, and Kling v1.
AI.motivation: Existing jailbreak methods adapted from text-to-image attacks fail in T2V contexts because they: (1) ignore temporal consistency, a core video-specific property; (2) require heavy video query optimization impractical in black-box settings; and (3) rely on heuristic local signals rather than principled structured exploration for adversarial prompt search.
AI.method: BSB frames the attack as inducing harmful content through interpolation between two individually harmless boundary-state prompts. To avoid prohibitive video-space evaluation costs, BSB performs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in a cheaper textual proxy space, periodically calibrating search outcomes with sparse video-level evaluations to guide the structured exploration of boundary-state pairs under a constrained query budget.
AI.result: BSB surpasses all existing jailbreak baselines on mainstream commercial T2V models (Veo 3.1, Sora 2, Seedance, Kling v1), delivering an average 18.6% relative improvement in attack success rate over the strongest competitor.
AI.conclusion: Temporal consistency is an understudied yet critical attack surface for T2V models, and structured search strategies like MCTS enable effective vulnerability discovery even under limited query budgets.

title: Nonuniformity Principle in Human-AI Coworking
summary: As generative AI is increasingly applied to automate multi-step and high-stake workflows, human judgment and involvement remain essential for ensuring the quality of AI-generated outputs. In practice, while it is desirable for human experts to provide oversight on AI regularly, often by reviewing intermediate outputs, giving feedback, making corrections, and steering subsequent steps, such oversight is constrained by the time and resources that humans can afford. This creates a tension between the need for human oversight and AI's efficiency in delivering more output with less intervention. An important but underexplored question, then, is how to optimally engage humans in human-AI coworking. This work was originally motivated by our empirical observation that in long AI workflows, human oversight often improves user satisfaction while reducing unnecessary rework and token consumption. From there, we formulate the problem of where to place oversight stages in human-AI coworking. Under reasonable assumptions, we then develop the nonuniformity principle, which states that the optimal schedule places oversight stages with non-decreasing gaps along the workflow. We empirically validate this principle in two common AI agent workflows: writing literature reviews and constructing websites.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates optimal placement of human oversight stages in multi-step AI workflows. The authors derive a "nonuniformity principle" stating that optimal oversight should be spaced with non-decreasing gaps, and validate it empirically in literature review writing and website construction tasks.
AI.motivation: Human oversight is essential for quality in AI workflows but is constrained by limited time and resources. The authors observed that strategic human oversight in long AI workflows improves user satisfaction while reducing rework and token consumption, motivating the formal study of optimal oversight placement.
AI.method: The authors formally model the problem of where to place oversight stages in human-AI coworking workflows. Under reasonable assumptions, they derive the nonuniformity principle, which prescribes that optimal oversight stages should be placed with non-decreasing gaps along the workflow. They empirically validate this principle in two AI agent workflows: writing literature reviews and constructing websites.
AI.result: The nonuniformity principle holds empirically: oversight stages spaced with non-decreasing gaps (i.e., sparser early, denser later) are optimal. This scheduling pattern improves user satisfaction and reduces unnecessary rework and token consumption in both literature review and website construction workflows.
