AI.conclusion: Strategic placement of human oversight with non-decreasing gaps optimizes the trade-off between human involvement and AI efficiency. The nonuniformity principle offers a principled guideline for designing human-AI coworking systems, especially for long, multi-step workflows.

title: EvolvingWorld: An Open-Schema Framework for Co-Evolving Role-Play Agents and World Model in Interactive Literary World
summary: This paper introduces EvolvingWorld, a framework and benchmark for character and world co-evolution in interactive literary worlds. Existing systems either treat interactive literary simulation as static persona imitation or isolated scene generation, failing to capture how characters and worlds evolve together over time. To address this, EvolvingWorld models literary simulation as a long-horizon process where characters interact, scenes progress, and character and world states are persistently updated. Unlike prior systems relying on fixed schemas, EvolvingWorld adopts an open-schema framework to support simulation across diverse literary worlds. The framework consists of two coupled modules: a Character Agent for multi-character role-play and persistent profile evolution, and an LLM-based World Model for global and location/entity-level state maintenance and scene progression. Based on this architecture, we formulate 7 trainable tasks for scene initialization, interaction generation, and state update. We construct a dataset from 57 books, producing 138,596 supervised training samples and 222 snapshots for testing. Furthermore, we introduce a trajectory-level LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol spanning 10 dimensions and 20 metrics. Experiments show that EvolvingWorld can improve long-horizon simulation by effectively maintaining persistent, coherent character and world development.

AI.tldr: EvolvingWorld introduces an open-schema framework and benchmark for simulating long-horizon co-evolution of characters and worlds in interactive literary settings. It features a Character Agent and an LLM-based World Model, a dataset of 138,596 training samples from 57 books, and a 10-dimension evaluation protocol. Experiments demonstrate improved persistent, coherent character and world development.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive literary simulation systems treat character portrayal as static persona imitation or isolated scene generation, failing to model the long-term, interdependent evolution of characters and their worlds. A unified framework for persistent, coupled character-world co-evolution is lacking.
AI.method: EvolvingWorld adopts an open-schema framework with two coupled modules: (1) a Character Agent for multi-character role-play and persistent profile evolution, and (2) an LLM-based World Model for global and location/entity-level state maintenance and scene progression. It formulates 7 trainable tasks (scene initialization, interaction generation, state update). A dataset is constructed from 57 books, yielding 138,596 supervised training samples and 222 test snapshots. A trajectory-level LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol with 10 dimensions and 20 metrics is introduced.
AI.result: Experiments show that EvolvingWorld improves long-horizon simulation by effectively maintaining persistent, coherent character and world development compared to prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: EvolvingWorld provides a robust benchmark and architecture for long-horizon literary simulation, demonstrating that explicitly modeling coupled character-world co-evolution yields more coherent and persistent interactive narratives.

title: Learning Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models from Pure Synthetic Data
summary: Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models (STFMs) aim to learn generalizable representations of complex dynamical systems across space and time. However, existing approaches suffer from distributional bias in real-world pre-training data, structural bottlenecks of autoregressive or diffusion-based paradigms, and objectives that overemphasize point-wise reconstruction in noisy observation space.We propose \textbf{NeoST}, the first spatio-temporal foundation model pre-trained solely on procedurally generated synthetic systems. NeoST introduces a scalable synthetic pre-training corpus to mitigate real-world bias, a latent-space reasoning architecture that generates and iteratively refines multiple future trajectories without sequential error accumulation, and latent-space objectives that emphasize structural dynamics and enable inference-time correction under distribution shifts.Extensive experiments across diverse real-world benchmarks show that NeoST consistently outperforms existing STFMs in diverse real-world spatio-temporal systems, achieves superior long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: NeoST is a spatio-temporal foundation model pre-trained exclusively on procedurally generated synthetic data. It uses a latent-space reasoning architecture with iterative trajectory refinement, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation, and employs latent-space objectives focused on structural dynamics. It outperforms existing STFMs on real-world benchmarks with superior long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models (STFMs) suffer from three key problems: (1) distributional bias from real-world pre-training data, (2) structural bottlenecks inherent in autoregressive or diffusion-based generation paradigms (e.g., sequential error accumulation), and (3) objectives that overemphasize point-wise reconstruction in noisy observation space, which fails to capture meaningful structural dynamics.
AI.method: NeoST is pre-trained solely on a procedurally generated synthetic corpus of dynamical systems, eliminating real-world distributional bias. It adopts a latent-space reasoning architecture that generates and iteratively refines multiple future trajectories, avoiding sequential error accumulation. The training objectives operate in latent space and emphasize structural dynamics, with a mechanism for inference-time correction under distribution shifts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that NeoST consistently outperforms existing STFMs, achieves superior long-horizon prediction stability, and offers better inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training exclusively on procedurally generated synthetic data, combined with latent-space reasoning and structure-aware objectives, is a viable and effective paradigm for spatio-temporal foundation models, overcoming key limitations of prior approaches.

title: IssueExec: A Test-Driven Approach for Localizing Software Engineering Issues
summary: Issue localization, which identifies code locations requiring modification from issue descriptions, is a critical step in automated software maintenance. Existing approaches predominantly attempt to directly align issue descriptions with code elements, yet often struggle due to the inherent abstraction gap between the issue description and code implementation. Seeking alternative signals, our theoretical analysis suggests that test suites can serve as executable proxies for requirements, reducing localization uncertainty by 7.73 bits of entropy on average. A large-scale empirical study on 18 repositories validates this premise: existing tests cover 96.98\% of ground-truth files, and the two-hop pathway yields stronger semantic connectivity than direct matching in 82.4\% of cases. Despite their potential, leveraging tests for localization faces two key challenges: the semantic gap separating issue descriptions from test identifiers, and the substantial noise in execution traces from infrastructure code. To address these, we propose IssueExec, which bridges the semantic gap through domain-knowledge-enhanced test representations and filters noise via hierarchical trace analysis. Experiments on SWE-bench Lite show that IssueExec achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving function-level Recall@1 by 41.57\% over the strongest baseline. When integrated into the Agentless pipeline, IssueExec resolves 17.72\% more issues, demonstrating practical downstream benefits.

AI.tldr: IssueExec leverages test suites as executable proxies for issue requirements, bridging the semantic gap between issue descriptions and code via domain-knowledge-enhanced test representations and hierarchical trace filtering, achieving SOTA on issue localization and improving downstream issue resolution.
AI.motivation: Direct alignment of issue descriptions with code elements suffers from an inherent abstraction gap. The authors theoretically demonstrate that test suites can serve as executable proxies for requirements, significantly reducing localization uncertainty (7.73 bits of entropy). Empirically, existing tests cover 96.98% of ground-truth files, and two-hop (issue→test→code) pathways offer stronger semantic connectivity than direct matching in 82.4% of cases. However, two challenges remain: the semantic gap between issue descriptions and test identifiers, and noise from infrastructure code in execution traces.
AI.method: The proposed system, IssueExec, addresses the two challenges through: (1) domain-knowledge-enhanced test representations to bridge the semantic gap between issue descriptions and test identifiers, and (2) hierarchical trace analysis to filter out noise from infrastructure code in execution traces, enabling effective test-to-code localization.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Lite, IssueExec achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving function-level Recall@1 by 41.57% over the strongest baseline. When integrated into the Agentless pipeline, it resolves 17.72% more issues, demonstrating practical downstream benefits.
AI.conclusion: Test suites are a powerful yet underutilized signal for issue localization. By bridging semantic gaps and filtering execution noise, test-driven localization can substantially outperform direct issue-to-code matching and yield tangible improvements in automated software repair pipelines.

title: Physical Time-Lock Puzzles
summary: Traditional time-lock puzzles enforce delayed access to encrypted secrets by relying on inherently sequential computational steps. However, since software-based constructions impose no fundamental bound on the physical execution speed of individual steps, they remain vulnerable to hardware acceleration and improved implementations. In practice, this renders existing schemes ``step-lock'' rather than true ``time-lock'' puzzles, making long-term delay guarantees highly speculative against decades of unpredictable hardware advancement. To address this fundamental limitation, we introduce the Physical Time-Lock Puzzle (P-TLP), a new paradigm that anchors solving delay directly to the intrinsic, hardware-bounded evaluation latency of silicon hardware. By leveraging noisy Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) as non-parallelizable delay oracles, P-TLPs establish resistance against both parallel computation and algorithmic acceleration under the random oracle model. To tolerate PUF evaluation noise while maintaining a tightly concentrated and predictable solving-delay window, we propose a composite puzzle architecture that combines multiple independent basic puzzles. We formally prove the optimality of a sequential greedy solving strategy and derive tightly concentrated solving-delay windows using Hoeffding and Berry-Esseen bounds. We additionally prove early-solve hardness, establishing that adversaries with substantial classical computation budgets cannot bypass the physically-enforced PUF evaluation bottleneck. We validate our theoretical analysis with an FPGA prototype built around a configurable Ring Oscillator PUF, confirming that our analytical delay predictions tightly match empirical measurements. Our results demonstrate that P-TLPs can deliver highly predictable, long-term delay guarantees, enabling practical deployment in high-value applications such as digital legacy management.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Physical Time-Lock Puzzles (P-TLP), a paradigm that anchors decryption delay to hardware-bounded PUF evaluation latency rather than software steps, achieving true time-locking resistant to parallel and algorithmic acceleration. A composite architecture with provable sequential optimality ensures predictable solving windows, validated via FPGA prototype.
AI.motivation: Traditional time-lock puzzles are fundamentally "step-lock" rather than "time-lock" — they rely on sequential computation but impose no physical bound on per-step execution speed, making them vulnerable to hardware acceleration and rendering long-term delay guarantees speculative against decades of hardware progress.
AI.method: The authors propose P-TLPs using noisy PUFs as non-parallelizable delay oracles under the random oracle model. A composite puzzle architecture combines multiple independent basic puzzles to tolerate PUF noise while ensuring tight delay concentration. They formally prove optimality of a sequential greedy solving strategy, derive delay windows via Hoeffding and Berry-Esseen bounds, and prove early-solve hardness against adversaries with substantial classical compute budgets. Validation uses an FPGA prototype with a configurable Ring Oscillator PUF.
AI.result: Analytical delay predictions tightly match empirical FPGA measurements. The P-TLP construction delivers highly predictable, long-term delay guarantees with provable resistance to parallel computation, algorithmic acceleration, and early-solving attacks.
AI.conclusion: P-TLPs overcome the fundamental limitation of software-based time-lock puzzles by anchoring delay directly to physical hardware latency. This enables practical deployment in high-value applications like digital legacy management, where reliable long-term delay guarantees are essential.

title: From Modalities to Propositions: A Language-Centric Framework for Multimodal Intelligence
summary: We propose a language representation for multimodal data in which any observation, whether image, video, or text, is expressed as a bag of atomic propositions, simple statements about the entities, actions, and relations in a scene. A global semantic codebook unifies these into a shared vocabulary of canonical atomic propositions, placing every modality and observation into one interpretable space that spans fine grained facts to high level concepts and composes into richer ones. This brings interpretability with reasoning, cross-modal understanding and retrieval, and compositionality that enables complex multimodal understanding, rich data curation and complex structured retrieval. We demonstrate the framework on autonomous driving and open-world data.

AI.tldr: A unified multimodal language representation is proposed where all observations (image, video, text) are expressed as bags of atomic propositions from a shared semantic codebook, enabling interpretable reasoning, cross-modal retrieval, and compositional understanding.
AI.motivation: To create a unified, interpretable representation space that spans modalities and granularities, overcoming the fragmentation of modality-specific representations and enabling compositional reasoning, cross-modal retrieval, and structured data curation.
AI.method: A global semantic codebook defines canonical atomic propositions — simple statements about entities, actions, and relations. Any multimodal observation is decomposed into a bag of these atomic propositions, placing all modalities into a shared interpretable latent space that supports composition from fine-grained facts to high-level concepts.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on autonomous driving and open-world data, showing capabilities in cross-modal understanding, complex structured retrieval, and compositional reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Representing multimodal data through a shared vocabulary of atomic propositions yields a highly interpretable, compositional framework that unifies reasoning and retrieval across images, video, and text.

title: Should Missing Modalities Always Be Necessary to Repair for Multi-modal Sentiment Analysis?
summary: Existing methods for multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) under missing modalities usually follow a repair-first paradigm. We revisit this assumption and ask: \emph{should every missing modality be repaired?} A per-sample oracle analysis shows the answer is not always: full-modality input is optimal for only a small fraction of samples, and every modality subset is preferred by some samples. These results suggest that adding or repairing modalities may not always improve prediction, and that the utility of each modality is sample-dependent. Building on this finding, we propose \textbf{S}ufficiency-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{E}vidential \textbf{V}al\textbf{vE} (\textbf{SIEVE}) that turns ``whether to repair'' into an explicit, learnable decision at the sample level. SIEVE compares a direct prediction branch with a repair branch, derives an empirical sufficiency signal from their per-sample loss gap, and routes each input through an evidential gate that jointly models sufficiency and its epistemic uncertainty. SIEVE is repair-agnostic: it operates as a plug-and-play decision on top of any explicit or implicit repair module, without modifying its internal design. Experiments on CMU-MOSI and IEMOCAP show that SIEVE consistently improves representative repair backbones across evaluated missing rates, and approaches the per-sample dual-branch achievable optimum.

AI.tldr: SIEVE challenges the "repair-first" assumption in multimodal sentiment analysis under missing modalities, showing via oracle analysis that full-modality input is rarely optimal. It introduces a sample-level evidential gating mechanism that decides whether to repair or not, improving performance across repair backbones on CMU-MOSI and IEMOCAP.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal sentiment analysis methods under missing modalities blindly follow a repair-first paradigm, assuming all missing modalities should be restored. The authors question this assumption through a per-sample oracle analysis, revealing that full-modality input is optimal for only a small fraction of samples — every modality subset is preferred by some samples, and adding/repairing modalities can actually degrade prediction. This motivates a sample-adaptive decision on whether to repair.
AI.method: SIEVE (Sufficiency-Informed Evidential ValvE) operates as a plug-and-play routing mechanism atop any repair module. It maintains two branches: a direct prediction branch (no repair) and a repair branch. An empirical sufficiency signal is derived from the per-sample loss gap between these branches. An evidential gate then jointly models sufficiency and its epistemic uncertainty using Dirichlet-based evidence, making a sample-level decision on whether to route through repair or direct prediction. The approach is repair-agnostic and requires no modification to the underlying repair module.
AI.result: SIEVE consistently improves representative repair backbones across varying missing rates on CMU-MOSI and IEMOCAP benchmarks. It approaches the per-sample dual-branch achievable optimum, demonstrating that sample-adaptive repair decisions outperform uniform repair strategies.
AI.conclusion: The repair-first assumption in MSA under missing modalities is suboptimal; repair utility is sample-dependent. SIEVE provides an effective, model-agnostic framework for learning when to repair, advancing the state of multimodal sentiment analysis with missing data.

title: SOS-LoRA: Static Orthogonal-Subspace Low-Rank Adaptation with Fixed Multi-Scale Scaling
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for large language models. Under a fixed rank budget, LoRA parameterizes each adapted weight through a single low-dimensional input-side pathway, which may couple heterogeneous behaviors through shared input directions and induce interference during optimization. We propose Static Orthogonal Subspace LoRA (SOS-LoRA), a drop-in extension that reparameterizes a rank-rtot update as a sum of K static (always-on, non-routed) low-rank experts. SOS-LoRA (i) decomposes the total rank across experts, (ii) applies a fixed multi-scale scaling scheme to encourage scale-separated optimization dynamics, and (iii) promotes diverse input-side directions via cross-expert orthogonal initialization and a lightweight regularizer. SOS-LoRA remains fully mergeable, adding no inference-time parameters or latency after merging. Experiments on reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Llama 2/3), encoder-based NLU (GLUE), and math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH) show consistent gains over matched-budget LoRA baselines and recent variants. Code is available at https://github.com/llm172/sos-lora.

AI.tldr: SOS-LoRA extends LoRA by decomposing a rank-r update into K static orthogonal low-rank experts with multi-scale scaling, encouraging diverse, decoupled optimization without adding inference cost after merging. It consistently outperforms matched-budget LoRA across reasoning, NLU, and math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA uses a single low-dimensional input-side pathway for each adapted weight, which can couple heterogeneous behaviors through shared input directions and cause optimization interference under a fixed rank budget.
AI.method: SOS-LoRA reparameterizes the total rank r_tot into K static experts, distributing rank across them. Three key components: (1) rank decomposition across experts, (2) a fixed multi-scale scaling scheme to induce scale-separated optimization dynamics, and (3) cross-expert orthogonal initialization with a lightweight regularizer to promote diverse input directions. The method is fully mergeable, requiring no extra parameters or latency at inference.
AI.result: Consistent gains over matched-budget LoRA baselines and recent variants on reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Llama 2/3), encoder-based NLU (GLUE), and math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH).
AI.conclusion: SOS-LoRA provides a simple, drop-in improvement over LoRA that mitigates optimization interference through structured multi-expert decomposition while preserving full mergeability. The consistent empirical gains across diverse tasks suggest that promoting orthogonal, scale-separated update pathways is an effective principle for PEFT.

title: Portable models as a replacement for industrial heuristics in compiler optimizations
summary: The paper investigates the possibility of predicting function-inlining decisions in compact compilers, source-to-source tools, and interpreters where the reuse of GCC or LLVM optimization infrastructure is impractical. The relevance of this work is determined by the need to transfer mature inlining heuristics to systems with limited compiler infrastructure, restricted runtime dependencies, and reduced access to target-specific analysis. Existing production compilers already contain strong inliners, but their decisions depend on internal intermediate representations (IRs), pass ordering, target models, and analysis stacks that are difficult to reproduce in lightweight systems. To overcome these constraints, we propose a portable inlining-prediction framework. Production compiler diagnostics serve as supervision; a separate extractor reconstructs caller-callee callsites, prepares sterile source snippets, normalizes them into a universal AST, optionally lowers them to a lightweight structural IR, and exports scalar features for model training. Thus, a trained predictor can be emitted as ordinary C code without a compiler-runtime dependency. To evaluate the proposed framework, we constructed a dataset comprising 336,938 callsites from fifteen open-source C projects, including 79,287 compiler-reported inline events. A comparison of several tabular models is performed using project-aware validation. Under leave-one-project-out validation, CatBoost reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 and PR-AUC 0.713; after threshold tuning, F1 improves from 0.670 to 0.729 and the false-positive rate drops from 0.192 to 0.084. Feature analysis shows that most signal is concentrated in source locality, explicit inline intent, callee size, side effects, branch and call structure, signature shape, and callsite argument shape.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a portable framework for predicting function-inlining decisions using machine learning, designed for lightweight compilers that cannot reuse GCC/LLVM infrastructure. A CatBoost model trained on 336K callsites from 15 C projects achieves ROC-AUC 0.928 under leave-one-project-out validation, with key predictive features including source locality, callee size, and side effects.
AI.motivation: Production compilers like GCC and LLVM have mature inlining heuristics, but these depend on internal IRs, pass ordering, target models, and analysis stacks that are impractical to reproduce in compact compilers, source-to-source tools, and interpreters. There is a need to transfer inlining knowledge to these lightweight systems without introducing heavy compiler-runtime dependencies.
AI.method: The authors propose a portable inlining-prediction framework that uses production compiler diagnostics as supervision. A separate extractor reconstructs caller-callee callsites, prepares sterile source snippets, normalizes them into a universal AST, optionally lowers to a lightweight structural IR, and exports scalar features. The trained predictor is emitted as ordinary C code with no compiler-runtime dependency. Evaluation uses a dataset of 336,938 callsites from 15 open-source C projects (79,287 inline events) and compares tabular models under project-aware validation, including leave-one-project-out.
AI.result: CatBoost achieves ROC-AUC 0.928 and PR-AUC 0.713 under leave-one-project-out validation. Threshold tuning improves F1 from 0.670 to 0.729 and reduces false-positive rate from 0.192 to 0.084. Feature analysis reveals that most predictive signal comes from source locality, explicit inline intent, callee size, side effects, branch/call structure, signature shape, and callsite argument shape.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight, ML-driven inlining predictor can effectively mimic production compiler decisions without requiring full compiler infrastructure. The approach is deployable as standalone C code, making it suitable for resource-constrained compilation environments.

title: Measuring and Evaluating the Performance of Generative AI Models for Scam Detection
summary: Online scams continue to cause substantial financial and personal harm. As a result, detection systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have been integrated into security products ranging from email gateways and browser extensions to fraud-monitoring dashboards. As this adoption accelerates, a common belief has taken hold: that these models are broadly suitable for scam detection. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs, with their strong capabilities in understanding intent, context, and reasoning, can effectively detect scams across diverse scenarios without task-specific fine-tuning. We curate and release a unique benchmark dataset of real-world scams spanning multiple formats and topics. We evaluate nine LLMs of varying sizes and architectures, examining their performance under different prompting strategies and comparing them to a fine-tuned BERT-based classifier. Our results show that while larger LLMs generally outperform smaller ones, effective prompting substantially boosts the performance of smaller models. Moreover, LLMs are better at generalizing to unseen scams compared to fine-tuned models, suggesting that pre-trained knowledge contributes meaningfully to scam detection. We release our dataset and evaluation framework to facilitate future research in robust scam detection using language models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can effectively detect online scams without task-specific fine-tuning. The authors curate a real-world scam benchmark dataset, evaluate nine LLMs under various prompting strategies, and compare them to a fine-tuned BERT classifier. Findings show larger LLMs outperform smaller ones, but effective prompting significantly boosts smaller models, and LLMs generalize better to unseen scams than fine-tuned models.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly integrated into security products for scam detection, a common assumption has emerged that these models are broadly suitable for the task. The authors aim to rigorously test this belief by evaluating whether LLMs can effectively detect scams across diverse scenarios without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors curate and release a benchmark dataset of real-world scams spanning multiple formats and topics. They evaluate nine LLMs of varying sizes and architectures, testing different prompting strategies. Performance is compared against a fine-tuned BERT-based classifier as a baseline. Generalization to unseen scam types is also assessed.
AI.result: Larger LLMs generally outperform smaller ones. However, effective prompting substantially improves the performance of smaller models, narrowing the gap. LLMs demonstrate superior generalization to unseen scams compared to the fine-tuned BERT model, indicating that pre-trained knowledge contributes meaningfully to scam detection.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are capable of effective scam detection without task-specific fine-tuning, with prompting playing a critical role, especially for smaller models. Their strong generalization ability, driven by pre-trained knowledge, makes them promising for robust, real-world scam detection. The dataset and evaluation framework are publicly released to support further research.

title: Exact Network Surgery: Functional Invariance and Gradient Plasticity in Reactive Computational Graphs
comment: Companion paper: "Cost Accounting for Reactive Computational Graphs" (submitted concurrently)
summary: Function-preserving network growth techniques such as Net2Net and progressive stacking expand a model's capacity without destroying its learned function, but existing formulations either tolerate numerical perturbations or require a full rebuild of the training program. We formalize Exact Network Surgery: the in-place insertion of a residual block into a live computational graph such that (i) the network function is preserved -- bit-exactly under explicit floating-point hypotheses -- and (ii) inserted parameters remain trainable immediately after insertion. We prove an identity-morphism theorem for gated residual blocks, a structural-locality theorem showing that a reactive invalidation engine recomputes exactly the downstream cone of the insertion point, leaving every other node's value and optimizer state untouched, and an escape-from-initialization proposition showing that the Gradient Shadowing gate alpha, initialized at zero over a randomly initialized branch, receives a generically non-zero gradient at insertion time. We identify a degenerate configuration -- zero-initialized output projections combined with a zero gate -- that is an exact saddle point gradient descent cannot escape. Every claim is validated on the reference implementation in NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia: grafting is bit-exact on every logit tested (0 mismatches out of 1600); the gate escapes zero at the first optimizer step and unlocks branch gradients at the second, exactly as predicted; the degenerate configuration exhibits gradients identically zero for the entire 600-step run; surgery cost tracks downstream cone size with r = 0.9992 while graft-plus-invalidation bookkeeping is constant (about 0.75 ms) across insertion depths; and training resumes bit-identically across a real process restart. A flagged preliminary appendix reports first single-seed observations on post-insertion gate dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "Exact Network Surgery" — a method for inserting residual blocks into a live neural network that preserves function bit-exactly, ensures immediate trainability, and proves key theoretical properties (identity-morphism, structural locality, gradient escape). A reactive graph engine (NeuroDSL in Julia) validates all claims experimentally.
AI.motivation: Existing function-preserving growth methods (Net2Net, progressive stacking) either introduce numerical perturbations or require full training program rebuilds. The authors seek a mathematically rigorous approach that guarantees bit-exact function preservation under explicit floating-point assumptions while keeping inserted parameters immediately trainable without any retraining bootstrap.
AI.method: The paper proposes inserting gated residual blocks in-place into a live reactive computational graph. Key mechanisms include: (1) an identity-morphism theorem ensuring the block initially computes identity; (2) a structural-locality theorem enabling a reactive invalidation engine to recompute only the downstream cone of the insertion point; (3) a Gradient Shadowing gate α initialized at zero over a randomly initialized branch, with proof it receives non-zero gradient at insertion time. A degenerate saddle-point configuration (zero-initialized output projection + zero gate) is identified as inescapable by gradient descent. Implementation in NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia.
AI.result: Bit-exact validation: 0 mismatches in 1600 logits tested. Gate α escapes zero at first optimizer step and unlocks branch gradients at the second step, exactly as theoretically predicted. The degenerate configuration shows identically zero gradients for all 600 steps. Surgery cost correlates with downstream cone size (r = 0.9992), while graft-plus-invalidation bookkeeping remains constant (~0.75 ms) across insertion depths. Training resumes bit-identically across real process restarts.
AI.conclusion: Exact Network Surgery is achievable with rigorous bit-exact guarantees. The Gradient Shadowing gate successfully escapes initialization in non-degenerate cases, and the reactive invalidation approach enables efficient, localized recomputation. The identified degenerate saddle point represents a critical failure mode to avoid in practice.

title: Debate-on-Graph: Reliable and Adaptive Reasoning of Large Language Model on Uncertain Knowledge Graph
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing. However, LLMs often suffer from hallucinations and lack of relevant knowledge when dealing with question answering (QA) tasks. To mitigate these issues, knowledge graphs (KGs) have been utilized to enhance LLM reasoning. Nevertheless, KGs often contain noise and errors, while existing KG-enhanced LLM approaches are generally unable to identify and filter such noisy and erroneous content, which can instead amplify hallucinations and pose challenges for reliable reasoning. Uncertain knowledge graphs (UKGs), which associate each triple with a confidence score to quantify uncertainty, offer a promising direction to address this challenge. Compared with prior work, we investigate how to leverage UKGs to support LLMs for QA. We propose Debate-on-Graph (DoG), a new framework that enables LLMs and UKGs to collaborate adaptively for reliable reasoning. Specifically, we first design a heuristic search algorithm tailored for UKGs to extract reliable and question-relevant subgraphs, thereby reducing noise and errors in retrieved knowledge. We then introduce a Multi-Agent Debate mechanism, which yields reliable answers through adaptive adversarial debates, aiming to fully exploit the knowledge in UKGs while preserving the reliability of retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments on four benchmark QA datasets show that DoG achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing LLM reasoning methods and KG-based baselines, while enabling reliable and adaptive reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/seucoin/Debate-on-Graph.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Debate-on-Graph (DoG), a framework that leverages Uncertain Knowledge Graphs (UKGs) with confidence scores to enhance LLM reasoning for QA tasks. DoG combines a heuristic subgraph extraction algorithm to filter noisy knowledge with a Multi-Agent Debate mechanism for reliable answer generation, achieving SOTA on four QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from hallucinations and knowledge gaps in QA tasks. While KGs can enhance LLM reasoning, existing KG-enhanced approaches cannot filter noise and errors in KGs, potentially amplifying hallucinations. UKGs, which attach confidence scores to triples, offer a way to quantify and manage this uncertainty, but no prior work has effectively leveraged UKGs to support LLMs for QA.
AI.method: The DoG framework has two main components: (1) A heuristic search algorithm designed for UKGs that extracts reliable, question-relevant subgraphs by leveraging confidence scores to reduce noise and errors. (2) A Multi-Agent Debate mechanism where multiple LLM agents engage in adaptive adversarial debates over the retrieved evidence, collaboratively reasoning to produce reliable answers while fully exploiting UKG knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmark QA datasets demonstrate that DoG achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing LLM reasoning methods and KG-based baselines, while enabling reliable and adaptive reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging UKGs with confidence scores via the DoG framework effectively addresses the noise problem in KG-enhanced LLM reasoning. The combination of heuristic subgraph extraction and multi-agent debate provides a reliable and adaptive solution for QA tasks. Code is publicly available.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Machine Learning for Type 2 Diabetes Risk Prediction: Large-Scale External Validation and Fairness Analysis
comment: Accepted and published at the IEEE EDS Technically Sponsored International Conference on Intelligent Processing, Hardware, Electronics, and Radio Systems (CIPHER-2026), 13-15 Feb 2026, NIT Jalandhar, India (IEEE Conference Record #70417, Paper ID: 155). 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Machine learning-based Type 2 diabetes risk prediction models obtain good internal validation results but lose effectiveness in real-world applications due to deficient external testing and fairness assessment. We developed a multi-dimensional framework evaluating discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness on nationally representative populations. An XGBoost model was trained on NHANES 2015-2020 (n=15,685) using eight non-laboratory predictors: age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking status, physical activity, history of heart attack, and history of stroke. External validation was performed on BRFSS 2020-2022 (n=1,285,783) under realistic distribution shift. Internal validation showed good discrimination (AUC=0.794, 95% CI 0.788-0.800), with performance loss on external validation (AUC=0.717, relative decrease: -9.7%, p<0.001). Fairness analysis revealed severe bias: elderly adults (>=60) showed AUC=0.607 vs 0.742 for young adults (difference=0.135, p<0.001); obese individuals showed AUC=0.698 vs 0.735 for normal weight (difference=0.037, p<0.001). Gender showed comparable performance (male=0.723 vs female=0.712, p=0.142). Calibration revealed risk overestimation (Brier score=0.123). SHAP analysis identified age, BMI, and physical activity as primary risk drivers. Populations with highest diabetes risk receive the worst algorithmic performance, underscoring the need for fairness-aware, age-stratified deployment strategies before clinical use.

AI.tldr: An XGBoost model for Type 2 diabetes prediction using eight non-laboratory predictors was trained on NHANES data and externally validated on BRFSS, revealing significant performance degradation under distribution shift and severe algorithmic unfairness — elderly and obese populations (highest-risk groups) received the worst model performance, undermining clinical deployability without fairness-aware strategies.
AI.motivation: Machine learning-based diabetes risk prediction models often achieve strong internal validation but fail in real-world settings due to inadequate external testing and lack of fairness assessment. The authors aim to address this gap by developing a comprehensive evaluation framework that jointly examines discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness on nationally representative datasets.
AI.method: An XGBoost classifier was trained on NHANES 2015–2020 (n=15,685) using eight non-laboratory features (age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking status, physical activity, history of heart attack, history of stroke). External validation was conducted on BRFSS 2020–2022 (n=1,285,783) under natural distribution shift. The evaluation framework assessed: (1) discrimination via AUC with DeLong's test for subgroup comparisons, (2) calibration via Brier score, (3) interpretability via SHAP values, and (4) fairness via subgroup-stratified performance across age, gender, and BMI categories.
AI.result: Internal AUC was 0.794 (95% CI 0.788–0.800), which dropped to 0.717 on external validation (−9.7% relative decrease, p<0.001). Severe fairness disparities emerged: elderly adults (≥60) achieved AUC=0.607 vs 0.742 for young adults (Δ=0.135, p<0.001); obese individuals showed AUC=0.698 vs 0.735 for normal weight (Δ=0.037, p<0.001). Gender performance was comparable (male=0.723 vs female=0.712, p=0.142). Calibration was poor with risk overestimation (Brier score=0.123). SHAP identified age, BMI, and physical activity as primary drivers.
AI.conclusion: The populations at highest risk for diabetes paradoxically received the worst algorithmic performance, highlighting a critical fairness–accuracy tension. The authors recommend fairness-aware, age-stratified deployment strategies and rigorous external validation before any clinical implementation of such risk prediction models.

title: Combining model checking with simulation-based techniques for protocol verification
summary: Model checking is a powerful technique for verifying properties of systems or protocols, but it often suffers from the state space explosion problem. For protocols such as the Alternating Bit Protocol (ABP) and the Sliding Window Protocol (SWP), increasing parameters such as channel capacities or window sizes leads to a reachable state space that is infeasible for exhaustive model checking. To address this, we propose a technique that combines model checking with simulation relations. We focus on three protocols: the Simple Communication Protocol (SCP), ABP, and SWP. Formalized as state machines, these protocols are presented in decreasing order of abstraction: SCP, ABP, and then SWP, which results in a corresponding increase in reachable states. While SCP is verifiable through direct model checking without state space explosion, the direct application of model checking to ABP and SWP becomes infeasible as their parameter values increase. We demonstrate that ABP satisfies its invariant property by combining model checking on SCP with a simulation relation from ABP to SCP. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SWP satisfies its invariant property through the composition of simulation relations from SWP to ABP and from ABP to SCP, in conjunction with model checking on SCP. These approaches enable the formal verification of protocols with large reachable state spaces by conducting model checking on a significantly smaller state machine.

AI.tldr: A verification technique combining model checking with simulation relations is proposed to circumvent state space explosion. By verifying the small Simple Communication Protocol (SCP) directly and then establishing simulation relations from ABP to SCP and from SWP to ABP, invariant properties of the larger protocols can be formally verified without exhaustive model checking of their full state spaces.
AI.motivation: Model checking suffers from the state space explosion problem, making it infeasible for protocols like the Alternating Bit Protocol (ABP) and Sliding Window Protocol (SWP) as parameters such as channel capacities or window sizes increase. A method is needed to verify these protocols without directly exploring their exponentially large state spaces.
AI.method: The approach combines model checking with simulation relations. Three protocols (SCP, ABP, SWP) are formalized as state machines in decreasing order of abstraction. SCP is verified via direct model checking. For ABP, a simulation relation from ABP to SCP is established, allowing ABP's invariant to be inferred from SCP's verified property. For SWP, simulation relations are composed (SWP → ABP → SCP), and combined with model checking on SCP to verify SWP's invariant without direct exploration of its large state space.
AI.result: ABP is shown to satisfy its invariant property via simulation to SCP combined with SCP model checking. SWP is similarly verified through composed simulation relations (SWP → ABP → SCP) paired with SCP model checking. These approaches enable formal verification of protocols with large reachable state spaces by reducing the verification burden to a significantly smaller state machine.
AI.conclusion: Combining model checking with simulation relations effectively addresses state space explosion for communication protocol verification. By verifying a small, abstract protocol directly and transferring correctness via simulation relations, large-parameter protocols like ABP and SWP can be formally verified without exhaustive state space exploration.

title: ShadowPickle: Evading Machine Learning Model Scanners via Stealthy Pickle Deserialization Attacks
summary: Model hosting hubs (e.g., Hugging Face) are vulnerable to supply chain attacks that enable remote code execution on trusted user environments. Attackers often distribute malicious Pre-trained ML models (PTMs) via model hubs. In this paper, we present novel attacks against PTMs and model hubs called SHADOWPICKLE. SHADOWPICKLE includes three (3) stealthy pickle deserialization attacks that enable malicious behaviors and evade state-of-the-art (SOTA) model scanners. These attacks leverage the external module import mechanism of the Pickle Virtual Machine (VM) to execute malicious payloads during deserialization. Additionally, we provide PICKLEBENCH, a dynamic and extensible benchmark for automatically injecting SHADOWPICKLE into arbitrary benign PTM models. Our evaluation shows that SHADOWPICKLE evades ten SOTA scanners, and four model hubs. SHADOWPICKLE (Overwritten) has a 63% evasion rate across scanners, and up to 50% higher evasion rates than existing attacks. Besides, PICKLEBENCH is up to 25.6% more challenging than three SOTA benchmarks. Finally, we provide security recommendations for mitigating our attacks and improving the effectiveness of existing scanners. Our findings highlight the limitations of existing PTM scanners and suggest directions for improvements.

AI.tldr: SHADOWPICKLE introduces three stealthy pickle deserialization attacks against ML model hubs that exploit the Pickle VM's external module import mechanism to achieve remote code execution while evading state-of-the-art scanners. The authors also present PICKLEBENCH, a benchmark for injecting these attacks into benign models. SHADOWPICKLE achieves up to 63% evasion rates across SOTA scanners and up to 50% higher evasion than existing attacks.
AI.motivation: Model hosting hubs like Hugging Face are susceptible to supply chain attacks where malicious pre-trained models can execute arbitrary code on user environments. Current state-of-the-art model scanners aim to detect such threats, but their effectiveness against sophisticated deserialization attacks is insufficient, motivating the need to expose their limitations.
AI.method: The authors design three stealthy pickle deserialization attacks (SHADOWPICKLE) that abuse the Pickle VM's external module import mechanism to execute malicious payloads during deserialization. They also build PICKLEBENCH, a dynamic, extensible benchmark for automatically injecting these attacks into arbitrary benign PTM models. They evaluate against ten SOTA scanners and four model hubs, comparing evasion rates with existing attacks and benchmarks.
AI.result: SHADOWPICKLE (Overwritten) achieves a 63% evasion rate across ten SOTA scanners and evades four model hubs, with up to 50% higher evasion rates than existing attacks. PICKLEBENCH proves up to 25.6% more challenging than three SOTA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Current PTM scanners have significant limitations in detecting advanced pickle-based supply chain attacks. The authors provide security recommendations for mitigating SHADOWPICKLE and suggest directions for improving scanner effectiveness.

title: FST.ai 2.5: Explainable and Uncertainty-Aware AI for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo Decision Support, Athlete Digital Twins, and Federation-Scale Analytics
summary:
The rapid digitalisation of elite sport has created new opportunities for integrating artificial intelligence (AI), performance analytics, and decision-support systems into athlete development and competition management. However, existing solutions remain fragmented, typically addressing isolated tasks such as performance analysis, athlete monitoring, or referee support. This paper presents \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5}, an explainable, uncertainty-aware, and secure AI framework for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo.
  \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5} introduces a unified digital ecosystem integrating athlete intelligence, competition analytics, federation-scale data management, AI-assisted decision support, athlete and event digital twins, explainable performance indicators, and adaptive training recommendations. The framework supports World Taekwondo (WT), Member National Associations (MNAs), coaches, referees, analysts, and athletes through transparent, secure, and federation-aware governance.
  By combining multi-source competition data, athlete-performance information, and contextual evidence, \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5} provides tactical diagnostics, longitudinal athlete monitoring, performance forecasting, personalised development planning, and federation-wide benchmarking using explainable and uncertainty-aware AI. Prototype deployments demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework. Although developed for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo, the methodology is broadly applicable to explainable AI, digital twins, and trustworthy decision support in combat sports and other high-performance sporting environments.

AI.tldr: FST·ai 2.5 is an explainable, uncertainty-aware, secure AI framework that unifies athlete intelligence, competition analytics, digital twins, and decision-support into a single ecosystem for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo, with broad applicability to other combat and high-performance sports.
AI.motivation: Existing AI and analytics solutions in elite sport are fragmented, tackling isolated tasks (performance analysis, athlete monitoring, referee support) without integration. There is a need for a unified, transparent, and trustworthy digital ecosystem that serves the entire federation—athletes, coaches, referees, analysts, and governing bodies—under proper data governance.
AI.method: The authors designed FST·ai 2.5 as a comprehensive framework combining multi-source competition and athlete-performance data with explainable, uncertainty-aware AI. It features: athlete and event digital twins, explainable performance indicators, adaptive training recommendations, tactical diagnostics, longitudinal monitoring, performance forecasting, personalised development planning, and federation-wide benchmarking. Governance is federation-aware, supporting World Taekwondo, MNAs, and other stakeholders. Prototype deployments validate feasibility.
AI.result: Prototype deployments demonstrated the feasibility of the FST·ai 2.5 framework in real-world settings for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo.
AI.conclusion: FST·ai 2.5 provides a viable, unified AI ecosystem for combat sports federations. Although developed for Taekwondo, its methodology—centered on explainability, uncertainty awareness, digital twins, and trustworthy decision support—is broadly transferable to other high-performance sporting environments.

title: Safety That Does Not Transfer: Cross-Lingual Clinical Correctness Drift in Deployable Medical Language Models
summary: Safety evaluation of large language models is conducted predominantly in English and predominantly on frontier systems. Neither condition describes how such models are encountered in low-resource health settings, where small quantised systems are run locally and queried in local languages. We ask whether clinical safety established in English transfers to Hausa, and whether any failure is attributable to the language, the clinical task, or the class of model that low-resource deployment admits. Matched English-Hausa question pairs were built for three conditions of high burden in northern Nigeria: malaria, sickle cell disease, and tuberculosis, probing knowledge recall, emergency triage, a leading question inviting a contraindicated action, and a traditional-remedy claim. Six models were evaluated: five locally deployable systems of 4-9 billion parameters, two medically fine-tuned, and one frontier system. All 128 responses were scored against Nigerian national treatment guidelines by two fluent Hausa speakers working independently and blind to one another. Among locally deployable models, mean clinical correctness fell from 1.57 in English to -0.03 in Hausa, on a scale where 2 denotes a correct answer and -1 an actively harmful one. The frontier model moved from 2.00 to 1.75 and produced no response judged harmful in either language. Drift was consistent across all three conditions. Inter-rater agreement was substantial for clinical correctness (kappa = 0.70); agreement on harm was initially poor (kappa = 0.22) and is examined in detail. Because a frontier model answers the same questions competently in Hausa, the deficit is a property neither of the language nor of the clinical material, but of the deployable tier.

AI.tldr: Small, locally deployable LLMs show a dramatic drop in clinical safety when answering Hausa-language medical questions compared to English, while a frontier model maintains high performance in both languages. The safety gap is attributable to the model tier, not the language or clinical content.
AI.motivation: Clinical safety evaluation of LLMs is overwhelmingly conducted in English on frontier systems, but in low-resource health settings, small quantised models are run locally and queried in local languages. This study investigates whether English-established clinical safety transfers to Hausa, a major language in northern Nigeria.
AI.method: Matched English-Hausa question pairs were constructed for three high-burden conditions (malaria, sickle cell disease, tuberculosis), probing knowledge recall, emergency triage, contraindicated-action leading questions, and traditional-remedy claims. Six models were tested: five locally deployable systems (4–9B parameters, two medically fine-tuned) and one frontier system. All 128 responses were independently scored by two fluent Hausa speakers against Nigerian national treatment guidelines on a scale from -1 (harmful) to 2 (correct).
AI.result: Among locally deployable models, mean clinical correctness fell from 1.57 (English) to -0.03 (Hausa). The frontier model dropped only from 2.00 to 1.75, with no harmful responses in either language. Drift was consistent across all three clinical conditions. Inter-rater agreement was substantial for correctness (κ=0.70) but poor for harm judgments (κ=0.22).
AI.conclusion: The clinical safety deficit in Hausa is a property of the deployable model tier, not of the language or clinical material, since the frontier model handles the same questions competently in Hausa. This highlights a critical safety gap for real-world low-resource deployment scenarios.

title: More Than Memory: Task-Conditioned Signed FFN Writes in Long-Context Retrieval
summary:
FFNs are often treated as parametric memories. In long-context retrieval, however, the sharper question is not only what they store, but whether their native residual writes push the current retrieval state toward or away from the correct answer. We test this by scaling the model's own FFN write one layer at a time, without editing weights or injecting external steering vectors.
  Across controlled literal and semantic retrieval suites, native FFN response surfaces are signed, layer-specific, and task-conditioned: the final FFN is a suppressor in 7 of 8 model-suite cases, and 60% of layers switch role between retrieval modes (95% CI [50%, 69%]). A local directional derivative along the native write separates the two monotone roles: suppressors have negative derivative in 34/35 cases, and amplifiers have positive derivative in 18/18 cases, so the roles are not reducible to write size. On a safety-filtered LongBench retrieval-QA probe, the same diagnostic predicts attenuation damage with raw R^2=0.796 on Qwen2.5-7B and 0.791 on Qwen3.5-9B; a held-out suppressor-attenuation policy improves retrieval margins over random and norm-matched controls. These results show that native FFN scaling exposes a signed, task-conditioned residual-write structure in retrieval, and that write-gradient alignment is a compact diagnostic for the two monotone roles.

AI.tldr: FFN residual writes exhibit signed, layer-specific, task-conditioned roles (amplifier vs. suppressor) in long-context retrieval. A local directional derivative along the native write cleanly separates these monotone roles, and write-gradient alignment serves as a compact diagnostic predictive of retrieval performance degradation.
AI.motivation: While FFNs are commonly viewed as parametric memories, the authors argue that the more critical question for long-context retrieval is whether each FFN's native residual write pushes the model's retrieval state toward the correct answer (amplifier) or away from it (suppressor). Prior work focused on what FFNs store rather than their dynamic functional role during retrieval.
AI.method: The authors scale the model's own FFN write at individual layers (without weight editing or external steering vectors) and observe the effect on retrieval performance across controlled literal and semantic retrieval suites. They compute a local directional derivative along the native FFN write direction to characterize each layer's role, and validate the diagnostic on the LongBench retrieval-QA benchmark, testing a held-out suppressor-attenuation policy against random and norm-matched controls.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The final FFN acts as a suppressor in 7/8 model-suite cases. (2) ~60% of layers switch roles between retrieval modes (95% CI [50%, 69%]). (3) The directional derivative separates roles near-perfectly: suppressors show negative derivative in 34/35 cases, amplifiers positive in 18/18. (4) On LongBench, write-gradient alignment predicts attenuation damage with raw R²=0.796 (Qwen2.5-7B) and 0.791 (Qwen3.5-9B). (5) Suppressor-attenuation policy improves retrieval margins over controls.
AI.conclusion: Native FFN scaling reveals a signed, task-conditioned residual-write structure in retrieval — layers are not uniformly helpful or harmful but play distinct, mode-dependent roles. Write-gradient alignment provides a compact, principled diagnostic for identifying these roles, enabling targeted interventions like suppressor attenuation to improve retrieval performance.

title: PSASpotter: A Tool to Detect the Usage of Platform-Specific APIs in Python
summary: A platform-specific API is implemented for a particular platform (e.g., operating system), thus, it may not work on other platforms than the target one. Detecting the usage of such APIs is important for supporting software maintenance, as it allows maintainers to be alerted about APIs that could pose potential risks. This paper proposes PSASpotter, a tool to detect the usage of platform-specific APIs in Python systems. PSASpotter also identifies whether the platform-specific APIs are used within a defensive code, such as try/except blocks or if blocks that check the current platform. PSASpotter can support the development of novel empirical studies about the usage of platform-specific APIs in the Python ecosystem. Moreover, the defensive code detected by PSASpotter may contain alternative solutions for unavailable APIs, which can provide insights for software development and testing across multiple platforms. PSASpotter is available at: https://github.com/ricardojob/PSASpotter. Tool video: https://youtu.be/d3WyozTAKS8.

AI.tldr: PSASpotter is a tool that detects platform-specific API usage in Python systems and identifies whether such APIs are wrapped in defensive code structures like try/except or platform-checking conditionals.
AI.motivation: Platform-specific APIs only function on their target platforms, posing portability risks. Detecting their usage helps maintainers identify potential cross-platform compatibility issues, and understanding defensive code patterns can reveal alternative solutions for unavailable APIs.
AI.method: PSASpotter statically analyzes Python source code to identify calls to platform-specific APIs, then determines whether each usage site is protected by defensive constructs such as try/except blocks or if-statements that verify the runtime platform.
AI.result: The tool enables empirical studies on platform-specific API usage across the Python ecosystem and surfaces defensive coding patterns that may contain fallback implementations for unsupported platforms.
AI.conclusion: PSASpotter provides automated detection of platform-specific API usage and defensive code patterns in Python, offering practical value for software maintenance, cross-platform development, and empirical research.

title: Salience Induction against Multi-Hop RAG Agents: Threat and Defense
summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems increasingly retrieve external evidence and orchestrate tools for knowledge-intensive applications. In Multi-Hop question answering, agents chain facts across documents. Existing defenses focus on content poisoning, which injects false facts, and prompt injection, which embeds directives. We identify a third attack surface: the salience channel, through which fact position, emphasis, framing, and semantic proximity can redirect reasoning even when all retrieved claims are true and no instructions are present. We formalize Salience Induction as truth-preserving edits that redirect Multi-Hop attribute binding while leaving the retrieval trace semantically intact. We define six Salience-Editing operator classes and build an iterative proposer-verifier pipeline under factual and stealth constraints. We also introduce SalientWiki-MH, a decoy-annotated Multi-Hop benchmark. Evaluations across five frontier model families (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Qwen) and three agent architectures (ReAct, Reflexion, and tool-calling) show broad generalization. Under a 30% edit budget, Salience Induction achieves an 83.3% attack success rate; the strongest evaluated baseline defense leaves 75.7% post-defense ASR. Untargeted rewriting further reduces attacks only by degrading neutral task success. Our lightweight input-side defense, Salience Normalization, reduces attack success to 15.3% under standard attacks and 23.6% under an adaptive attack. These results show that truthfulness and instruction filtering alone are insufficient: robust agentic RAG also requires defenses against salience-relevance decoupling.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel attack surface in agentic RAG systems called the "salience channel," where truth-preserving edits manipulate fact positioning, emphasis, and framing to redirect Multi-Hop reasoning without injecting falsehoods or malicious instructions. The authors formalize "Salience Induction," build an iterative proposer-verifier pipeline, and introduce SalientWiki-MH, a decoy-annotated benchmark. Evaluations across five model families and three agent architectures show up to 83.3% attack success rate under a 30% edit budget, with baseline defenses leaving 75.7% ASR remaining. Their proposed defense, Salience Normalization, reduces attack success to 15.3% (standard) and 23.6% (adaptive).
AI.motivation: Existing defenses for agentic RAG focus on content poisoning (injecting false facts) and prompt injection (embedding malicious directives). However, the authors argue there is a third, underexplored attack surface: the salience channel. Even when all retrieved claims are true and no instructions are present, how facts are positioned, emphasized, framed, and semantically arranged can redirect agent reasoning. The motivation is to demonstrate that truthfulness and instruction filtering alone are insufficient for robust agentic RAG, and that salience-relevance decoupling poses a real threat that requires dedicated defenses.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize "Salience Induction" as truth-preserving edits that redirect Multi-Hop attribute binding; (2) define six Salience-Editing operator classes (covering position, emphasis, framing, and semantic proximity manipulations); (3) build an iterative proposer-verifier pipeline operating under factual and stealth constraints; (4) introduce SalientWiki-MH, a decoy-annotated Multi-Hop QA benchmark; (5) evaluate across five frontier model families (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen) and three agent architectures (ReAct, Reflexion, tool-calling); and (6) propose a lightweight input-side defense called Salience Normalization, tested against both standard and adaptive attacks.
AI.result: Under a 30% edit budget, Salience Induction achieves an 83.3% attack success rate (ASR). The strongest evaluated baseline defense leaves a 75.7% post-defense ASR. Untargeted rewriting reduces attacks only by simultaneously degrading neutral task success (a trade-off, not a genuine defense). The proposed Salience Normalization defense reduces ASR to 15.3% under standard attacks and 23.6% under an adaptive attack, substantially outperforming baselines while preserving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Truthfulness and instruction filtering alone are insufficient to secure agentic RAG systems. The salience channel constitutes a distinct and potent attack surface that can redirect Multi-Hop reasoning through purely truth-preserving edits. Robust agentic RAG architectures must incorporate defenses against salience-relevance decoupling, such as the authors' proposed Salience Normalization.

title: Just A Rather Very Intelligent Spoken Agent
summary: Long-horizon AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, yet their interaction with users remains surprisingly thin. In most workflows, users give an initial instruction, receive only selective textual updates, and lose a clear sense of what the agent is doing or when to step in. This leaves a missing part in the current agent ecosystem: an always-on Jarvis-style mediator that keeps the agent continuously reachable to the user. Such a mediator should support real-time spoken interaction with the user, answer questions without interrupting the worker, proactively report progress or confusion, and inject user guidance back into the agent's execution when useful. In this work, we introduce JarvisBench, a benchmark for measuring the dual value of mediation in long-horizon agent workflows. JarvisBench contains two complementary tracks: an agent-collaboration track that measures whether mediation improves downstream task completion, and a user-interaction track that measures whether mediation makes ongoing execution more understandable, responsive, and accessible to users. We instantiate the benchmark with a modular reference Jarvis prototype and evaluate it on 34 text-only WildClaw tasks executed in OpenClaw. Preliminary results with GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini-based, and GPT-based worker agents suggest that Jarvis-style mediation can provide trace-grounded responses to user questions and improve task performance when sparse user guidance is injected at appropriate moments. The results also show that effectiveness depends strongly on the mediator's LLM brain, highlighting both the promise of this missing middle layer and the need for broader community effort. Demo page https://cchen1436.github.io/jarvis

AI.tldr: Introduces JarvisBench, a benchmark for evaluating always-on spoken mediation between users and long-horizon AI agents. The benchmark measures whether mediation improves task completion and user understanding, with preliminary results showing trace-grounded responses and task performance gains when user guidance is injected at appropriate moments.
AI.motivation: Current long-horizon AI agent workflows suffer from thin user interaction — users give initial instructions then receive only selective textual updates, losing visibility into agent progress and lacking natural intervention points. There is a missing "always-on Jarvis-style mediator" that provides real-time spoken interaction, proactive progress/confusion reporting, and bidirectional guidance injection between user and agent.
AI.method: The authors introduce JarvisBench, a benchmark with two complementary tracks: (1) an agent-collaboration track measuring whether mediation improves downstream task completion; (2) a user-interaction track measuring whether mediation enhances understandability, responsiveness, and accessibility. They instantiate a modular reference Jarvis prototype and evaluate on 34 text-only WildClaw tasks in OpenClaw using GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini-based, and GPT-based worker agents.
AI.result: Jarvis-style mediation provides trace-grounded responses to user questions and improves task performance when sparse user guidance is injected at appropriate moments. However, effectiveness strongly depends on the mediator's underlying LLM, indicating both promise for this mediator layer and need for further community research.
AI.conclusion: A Jarvis-style always-on mediator fills a critical gap in the agent ecosystem, enabling richer bidirectional human-agent collaboration. The performance variability across LLM brains underscores that this is an important open problem warranting broader community effort.

title: Team DACTYL at PAN 2026: Bayesian Data Mixing and Empirical X-risk Minimization for AI-text Detection
summary: Existing research shows that AI-generated text detection classifiers achieve strong in-distribution (ID) performance but do not maintain the same performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) texts, suggesting overfitting to dataset-specific features. However, combining different training datasets doesn't always improve performance and, in some cases, can even encourage shortcut learning. To address this issue, we fine-tune BERT-tiny models with Bayesian classification heads to select texts across three different datasets to use as a consolidated training set. We trained three different classifiers: fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3-large and ModernBERT-large classifiers via empirical X-risk minimization, and an MCGrad model that calibrates the predictions from the ModernBERT-large classifier. The DeBERTa-V3-large-large classifier achieves a mean score of 0.882 on the PAN 2026 test set across five metrics: AUROC, $F_1$, C@1, Brier score, and $F_{0.5u}$. ModernBERT-large achieves a score of 0.96 while MCGrad achieves the best score of the three with a mean score of 0.974, ranking second on the leaderboard. Our results highlight that careful dataset curation can lead to strong OOD performance. We release our ModernBERT-large and DeBERTa-V3-large models at https://huggingface.co/collections/ShantanuT01/panclef-2026 .

AI.tldr: AI-generated text detectors overfit to in-distribution data and underperform on out-of-distribution texts. The authors use Bayesian BERT-tiny models to curate a consolidated training set from three datasets, then train three classifiers (DeBERTa-V3-large, ModernBERT-large, and MCGrad). On the PAN 2026 test set, MCGrad achieves the best mean score of 0.974 across five metrics, ranking second on the leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Current AI-generated text detection classifiers exhibit strong in-distribution performance but suffer significant degradation on out-of-distribution texts due to overfitting and shortcut learning. Naively combining multiple training datasets does not reliably solve this and can even exacerbate shortcut learning. A principled dataset curation approach is needed to improve OOD generalization.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune BERT-tiny models equipped with Bayesian classification heads to select high-quality texts from three distinct datasets, forming a consolidated training set. Using this curated set, they train three classifiers: (1) a fine-tuned DeBERTa-V3-large, (2) a fine-tuned ModernBERT-large via empirical X-risk minimization, and (3) an MCGrad model that calibrates the ModernBERT-large classifier's predictions.
AI.result: On the PAN 2026 test set, evaluated across five metrics (AUROC, F1, C@1, Brier score, F0.5u): DeBERTa-V3-large achieves a mean score of 0.882; ModernBERT-large achieves 0.96; MCGrad achieves the best mean score of 0.974, securing second place on the leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: Careful dataset curation, rather than indiscriminate dataset combination, is key to achieving strong out-of-distribution generalization in AI-generated text detection. The calibrated MCGrad approach yields the most robust performance. Models are publicly released on HuggingFace.

title: Feature Generation Using LLMs: An Evolutionary Algorithm Approach
summary: A crucial step in machine learning pipelines is to present each entity with features or attributes that are representative of the characteristics of the processed entities. Feature engineering is an important step in finding a relation among attributes that otherwise may not be processed by the ML algorithms. Meanwhile, Large Language Models have shown promising abilities in coding, mathematical reasoning, and processing world knowledge. In this work, we utilize an LLM for the problem of feature generation from tabular data based on the previously given features. We have created a pipeline that takes a set of attributes and a prompt to generate new features. Then, our selection algorithm selects the best-performing sets of attributes. We apply our method to eight datasets from different domains and data types. Our results show that, in most cases, the language model can produce new features based on mathematical and logical operators that are useful for the given tasks and can improve classification results.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate new features from existing tabular data attributes, combined with a selection algorithm to identify the most useful generated features, demonstrating improved classification performance across eight diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Feature engineering is a critical but labor-intensive step in ML pipelines, requiring domain expertise to discover meaningful relationships among attributes. LLMs have recently shown strong capabilities in coding, mathematical reasoning, and world knowledge — skills directly applicable to automated feature generation — yet their potential for this task remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors design a pipeline that inputs a set of existing tabular attributes along with a prompt into an LLM, which then generates new candidate features using mathematical and logical operators. A subsequent selection algorithm evaluates these generated features and retains the best-performing subsets. The approach is evaluated on eight datasets spanning different domains and data types.
AI.result: In most cases, the LLM successfully produces useful new features via mathematical and logical transformations, and incorporating these generated features leads to improved classification results compared to using only the original attributes.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as effective automated feature engineering tools for tabular data, generating meaningful features that boost downstream classification performance across diverse datasets, thereby reducing the manual effort traditionally required in this stage of the ML pipeline.

title: CommitLLM: A Fine-Tuned Pipeline for Git Commit Message Generation
summary: Developers frequently write uninformative git commit messages such as "fix" or "update stuff", degrading the value of version-control history for code review, debugging, and onboarding. We present CommitLLM, a three-stage pipeline that generates concise, Conventional Commits-compliant messages from code diffs using a fine-tuned small language model. The system combines (1) QLoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 on the CommitPackFT dataset, (2) constrained decoding to enforce brevity, and (3) deterministic post-processing to strip conversational artifacts and enforce format. On a 50-sample evaluation, CommitLLM achieves 98% format compliance (vs. 22% for vanilla Mistral), reduces average output length from 154.8 to 37.9 characters, and improves LLM-as-a-Judge scores from 1.97 to 3.68 out of 5. Notably, the post-processing layers contribute more to quality improvement than the fine-tuning itself, suggesting that for structured-output tasks, treating the LLM as a component in a deterministic pipeline is more effective than optimizing the model alone. The entire system runs on a single consumer GPU (NVIDIA T4, 16 GB VRAM).

AI.tldr: CommitLLM is a three-stage pipeline using QLoRA fine-tuned Mistral-7B, constrained decoding, and deterministic post-processing to generate concise, Conventional Commits-compliant messages from code diffs. Post-processing contributes more to quality than fine-tuning, and the system runs on a single T4 GPU.
AI.motivation: Developers frequently write uninformative commit messages (e.g., "fix", "update stuff"), undermining the utility of version-control history for code review, debugging, and developer onboarding. Existing LLMs produce verbose, non-compliant outputs that fail to adhere to the Conventional Commits specification.
AI.method: CommitLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) QLoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 on the CommitPackFT dataset; (2) constrained decoding to enforce output brevity; and (3) deterministic post-processing that strips conversational artifacts and enforces Conventional Commits format compliance.
AI.result: On a 50-sample evaluation, CommitLLM achieved 98% format compliance (vs. 22% for vanilla Mistral), reduced mean output length from 154.8 to 37.9 characters, and improved LLM-as-a-Judge scores from 1.97 to 3.68/5. Notably, post-processing layers contributed more to quality gains than fine-tuning alone.
AI.conclusion: For structured-output tasks, treating the LLM as a component within a deterministic pipeline is more effective than optimizing the model in isolation. The full system runs efficiently on a single consumer GPU (NVIDIA T4, 16 GB VRAM).

title: (A)iSpy: Parasitic Trojans for Machine Learning Infrastructure
summary: Modern machine learning (ML) pipelines depend heavily on third party libraries for graph compilation and hardware acceleration. While current practices audit data and model artifacts or rely on file integrity checks, the execution environment remains implicitly trusted.
