This blind spot enables active threats where a malicious runtime module interacts directly with live training and inference dynamics: exploiting this interaction allows the Trojan to support complex objectives that are challenging for static code or binary modifications, achieving manipulations impossible for standard data and model level attacks. We expose this vulnerability by presenting (A)iSpy, a parasitic infrastructure Trojan that subverts ML systems through an active observe and execute paradigm. Operating within the computation graph, (A)iSpy monitors transient tensor states to perform targeted, stealthy manipulations with negligible overhead. To violate confidentiality, the Trojan identifies all critical training hyperparameters and covertly exfiltrates them via model weights or output logits. To break integrity, it acts as a gradient amplifier: by observing steganographic triggers, it transforms otherwise weak data poisoning into effective backdoor attacks, increasing success rates from near zero to 100%. We further demonstrate broad extensibility across the machine learning lifecycle by validating auxiliary attacks in the appendix, including subpopulation label flipping, availability disruptions, and inference stage manipulations. Importantly, the (A)iSpy module easily evades standard malware scanners, while the associated poisoned inputs and resulting compromised models bypass typical inspection tools. We demonstrate the practicality of this threat with an implementation in the ONNX Runtime training and inference engines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces (A)iSpy, a parasitic Trojan that embeds into ML execution runtimes (e.g., ONNX Runtime), actively monitors tensor states, and performs covert attacks—hyperparameter exfiltration via model outputs and gradient-amplified backdoor poisoning—while evading standard malware and model inspection tools.
AI.motivation: Current ML security focuses on auditing data and model artifacts or file integrity checks, but implicitly trusts the execution environment (graph compilers, hardware acceleration runtimes). This blind spot allows a malicious runtime module to observe live training/inference dynamics and execute manipulations impossible for static code or data-level attacks.
AI.method: The authors propose (A)iSpy, an active "observe and execute" Trojan embedded in the computation graph. For confidentiality, it monitors transient tensors to extract hyperparameters and covertly exfiltrates them via model weights or output logits. For integrity, it acts as a gradient amplifier: detecting steganographic triggers in inputs, it amplifies weak poisoning signals to achieve effective backdoor attacks (near 0% to 100% success). The Trojan operates with negligible overhead and is implemented in ONNX Runtime.
AI.result: (A)iSpy successfully exfiltrates critical training hyperparameters and converts weak data poisoning into 100% effective backdoor attacks. It evades standard malware scanners, and both poisoned inputs and compromised models bypass typical inspection tools. Auxiliary attacks (label flipping, availability disruptions, inference manipulation) are validated in the appendix.
AI.conclusion: The ML execution environment represents a critical, under-examined attack surface. Runtime-resident Trojans like (A)iSpy demonstrate that active observation of tensor dynamics enables powerful, stealthy attacks across the ML lifecycle, demanding new defenses beyond current data/model-level audits.

title: A Research Prototype for Closed-Loop Generative Design of Customized Foot Orthoses via Semantic-Physics Alignment
summary: Translating unstructured clinical prescriptions into patient-specific foot orthoses (FOs) is hindered by a semantic-physical misalignment: high-level clinical intent is not mapped deterministically onto the 3D geometric parameters of the orthosis, and existing design workflows remain dependent on manual expertise with no instantaneous biomechanical validation. We present TANS-FO, a research prototype-a modular pipeline with closed-loop feedback for computational design automation of customized FOs, not a clinically validated therapeutic device. A Text-Aligned Neural Surrogate (TANS) uses cross-attention to project clinical-text embeddings onto a continuous lattice-density field, while a Graph Neural Network (GNN) surrogate predicts plantar stress in real time as a substitute for Finite Element Analysis (FEA). The framework is anchored on the open-access PicoFoot-5K anthropometric database (5,230 subjects; 30+ anatomical parameters). Under standardized quasi-static loading, the GNN surrogate agrees with an Abaqus reference solver (R^2 = 0.94), and the full pipeline synthesizes manufacturing-ready lattice insoles within minutes. On the Male 18-40 cohort, the proposed system attains a surrogate-predicted peak-pressure reduction of 34.7% over parametric CAD, with a fit error of 0.42 mm. Separately, an exploratory feasibility observation (n = 12; 2-week follow-up; no control group) using VAS pain reporting indicates short-term comfort improvement (VAS 6.4 -> 2.1), but this data is explicitly classified as preliminary observational evidence only-not evidence of clinical efficacy.

AI.tldr: TANS-FO introduces a modular pipeline combining a cross-attention text-aligned neural surrogate and a GNN-based plantar stress predictor to automate the design of custom foot orthoses, demonstrating rapid synthesis, high surrogate accuracy (R²=0.94), and significant peak-pressure reduction (34.7%) over parametric CAD, with only preliminary comfort observations.
AI.motivation: There exists a semantic-physical misalignment between high-level clinical prescriptions and the 3D geometric parameters of foot orthoses. Current design workflows rely on manual expertise and lack instantaneous biomechanical validation, creating a bottleneck in translating unstructured clinical intent into patient-specific, validated orthotic devices.
AI.method: The TANS-FO pipeline comprises: (1) a Text-Aligned Neural Surrogate (TANS) that maps clinical-text embeddings to a continuous lattice-density field via cross-attention; (2) a Graph Neural Network (GNN) surrogate for real-time plantar stress prediction as an FEA substitute; and (3) a closed-loop feedback mechanism. The system is built on the PicoFoot-5K database (5,230 subjects, 30+ anatomical parameters) and evaluated under standardized quasi-static loading against an Abaqus reference solver, with an exploratory observational follow-up (n=12, no control group).
AI.result: The GNN surrogate achieved R² = 0.94 against Abaqus FEA. The full pipeline synthesizes manufacturing-ready lattice insoles in minutes. On the Male 18–40 cohort, surrogate-predicted peak-pressure reduction was 34.7% over parametric CAD, with a fit error of 0.42 mm. The exploratory n=12 follow-up showed VAS pain scores dropping from 6.4 to 2.1, though this is explicitly classified as preliminary observational evidence only.
AI.conclusion: TANS-FO demonstrates feasibility of closed-loop computational design automation for customized foot orthoses, achieving strong biomechanical surrogate fidelity and substantial pressure reduction. However, the clinical observations remain preliminary and do not constitute evidence of therapeutic efficacy; the system is a research prototype, not a clinically validated device.

title: The Librarian Who Refused to Code: Model-Dependent Identity Enactment in LLM Code Generation
comment: 17 pages, 3 tables, no figures. Ancillary files include raw completions, derived scores, analysis scripts, persona texts, and preregistration
summary: Biographical personas are widely used in system prompts, but their effects on code generation are rarely evaluated under controlled, pre-registered conditions. We tested four prompt conditions (no persona, two engineer personas, and a research-librarian persona), 12 code-generation tasks, two frontier models, and five runs per cell (480 completions). Persona effects differed between the two tested models. Under the pre-registered mixed-effects analysis, the condition-by-model interaction was significant for provider-reported output tokens; a post-hoc visible-character measure showed the same qualitative pattern. Six GPT-5.5 completions were length-capped and are reported separately. On Claude Opus, the minimalist engineer persona reduced visible output by 30% (33% in provider tokens) without improving correctness, while the thorough engineer persona increased output without a correctness gain. In an exploratory post-hoc analysis, the librarian persona elicited in-character disclaimers in 55 of 60 Opus responses and 12 genuine no-code responses, lowering mean correctness from 0.92 to 0.67. GPT-5.5 produced neither behavior in its 59 non-truncated responses. These results are consistent with personas acting as Model-Dependent behavioral-policy biases rather than universal quality interventions. We release raw completions, derived scores, analysis artifacts, a pre-registration document, and an execution gate log; end-to-end test-based rescoring requires an unreleased task harness.

AI.tldr: A controlled experiment testing how biographical personas in system prompts affect code generation reveals model-dependent effects: personas changed output length without improving correctness, and one model exhibited persona-induced refusal behavior that harmed performance.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of biographical personas in system prompts for LLMs, their effects on code generation have not been rigorously evaluated under controlled, pre-registered conditions. The authors aim to fill this gap by testing whether personas genuinely improve code generation quality or merely alter behavioral policies in model-specific ways.
AI.method: A pre-registered experiment with a 4 (persona conditions: no persona, minimalist engineer, thorough engineer, research librarian) × 12 (code-generation tasks) × 2 (frontier models: Claude Opus, GPT-5.5) × 5 (runs per cell) factorial design, yielding 480 completions. Mixed-effects models analyzed effects on provider-reported output tokens and correctness. Post-hoc analyses examined visible character counts and persona-induced behavioral patterns (e.g., disclaimers, refusals).
AI.result: The condition-by-model interaction was significant for output length. On Claude Opus, the minimalist engineer persona reduced visible output by ~30% and provider tokens by ~33% with no correctness improvement; the thorough engineer increased output without correctness gains. The librarian persona elicited in-character disclaimers in 55/60 Opus responses and 12 genuine no-code responses, dropping mean correctness from 0.92 to 0.67. GPT-5.5 showed neither behavior in non-truncated responses (6 were length-capped). Personas appear to function as model-dependent behavioral-policy biases, not universal quality interventions.
AI.conclusion: Biographical personas in system prompts do not universally improve code generation and can actively harm performance in model-specific ways (e.g., librarian persona on Opus). Practitioners should not assume persona prompting is a reliable quality intervention; effects are model-dependent and require empirical validation per model and persona combination.

title: BTOR2-Based C Program Verification via Hardware Model Checking
summary:
Program verification tools often rely on specific intermediate representations and analysis backends, limiting the reuse of verification algorithms and model checkers across frameworks. In contrast, hardware model checking has developed a mature backend ecosystem, where standard formats such as BTOR2 support reusable algorithms for counterexample search and inductive safety proving. Applying these capabilities to C requires translating assertion-based programs into transition systems that hardware model checkers can directly process.
  We present C2Btor, a method for encoding such verification tasks into BTOR2 models. C2Btor uses a program counter to capture control transfers, represents data states and memory objects with bit-vectors and arrays, and maps assumptions and assertion checks into BTOR2 constraints and bad-state properties.
  We evaluate C2Btor on SV-COMP C ReachSafety benchmarks and a curated assertion-category benchmark suite, comparing it with representative program verification tools. C2Btor correctly solves 263 tasks, 101 more than CBMC configured with bounded model checking, and is especially effective on bit-vector benchmarks, where it solves 75.5% of the tasks with no wrong verdicts. These results show that the BTOR2 route allows C program verification to benefit from advances in hardware model-checking backends, expanding the available capability for counterexample search, inductive safety proving, and word-level transition-system reasoning.

AI.tldr: C2Btor translates C verification tasks into BTOR2 models, enabling hardware model checkers to verify C programs. It outperforms CBMC on SV-COMP benchmarks, solving 263 tasks—101 more than CBMC—and achieves 75.5% success on bit-vector benchmarks with no false verdicts.
AI.motivation: Program verification tools are fragmented by custom intermediate representations and analysis backends, preventing reuse of verification algorithms across frameworks. Meanwhile, hardware model checking has a mature, standardized backend ecosystem (e.g., BTOR2) supporting reusable counterexample search and inductive safety proving. The motivation is to bridge this gap by enabling C program verification to leverage these powerful hardware model-checking backends.
AI.method: C2Btor encodes C program verification tasks into BTOR2 transition systems. It uses a program counter to model control flow, bit-vectors and arrays to represent data states and memory objects, and maps assumptions and assertions into BTOR2 constraints and bad-state properties, producing models directly processable by hardware model checkers.
AI.result: Evaluated on SV-COMP C ReachSafety benchmarks and a curated assertion-category suite, C2Btor correctly solved 263 tasks—101 more than CBMC with bounded model checking. On bit-vector benchmarks, it solved 75.5% of tasks with zero wrong verdicts, demonstrating strong performance on word-level reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The BTOR2 translation route successfully extends hardware model-checking advances to C program verification, broadening the available toolkit for counterexample search, inductive safety proving, and word-level transition-system reasoning.

title: Quantum-Resilient Banking Transaction Security using DW-HKEM: A Hybrid RSA/ML-KEM Cryptographic Gateway with Real-Time
summary: The increasing number of online banking and financial services on public-facing networks has caused security of cryptographic protocols to become a serious, systemic problem. RSA-2048 is the key length that is used in the majority of transactions that travel over the Internet every day. A very insidious threat vector, the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) paradigm, is already in existence with the adversarial nation-state actors and well-funded threat actors. The exposure window is not a time in the future it is the NOW moment! Quantum computation is a certain threat to the current public-key cryptographic infrastructure, and one that is moving ever closer. In this paper, the authors take up both of these challenges, designing, implementing and testing an integrated system based on a Dual-Wrap Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanism (DW-HKEM) and a live cryptographic analytics dashboard. Both the RSA-256 and ML-KEM-768 are hosted within the DW-HKEM framework and an AES-256 session key is wrapped in each of them, with a composite key created using a Key Derivation Function based on SHA-256, resulting in combinatorial security against classical and quantum adversaries and backwards compatibility with existing banking systems. The CryptoX real-time dashboard offers time tracking for each operation, session-level analytics and visualization of performance trends for immediate use in enterprise banking security operations. The results from empirical benchmarking across 100 independent iterations show a total overhead of about 1.58ms, which is well within the enterprise deployment threshold, proving the architecture viable as a practical, scalable reference for the financial-sector's cryptographic infrastructure and applications to move to a post-quantum era. We also provide complete source code of the work carried out.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Dual-Wrap Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanism (DW-HKEM) integrating RSA-2048 and ML-KEM-768 with AES-256, combined via SHA-256-based KDF, to achieve classical+quantum security with backward compatibility. A real-time CryptoX dashboard provides operational analytics. Empirical benchmarks show ~1.58ms total overhead, validating practical deployment for banking.
AI.motivation: Growing online financial services face systemic cryptographic security threats. RSA-2048 dominates Internet transactions but is vulnerable to the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat from nation-state actors. Quantum computing poses an imminent threat to public-key infrastructure, demanding a practical, backward-compatible migration path to post-quantum cryptography for the banking sector.
AI.method: The authors design and implement a Dual-Wrap Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanism (DW-HKEM) that wraps an AES-256 session key within both RSA-2048 and ML-KEM-768, then combines them into a composite key using a SHA-256-based Key Derivation Function. They also build CryptoX, a real-time cryptographic analytics dashboard tracking operation timing, session-level metrics, and performance trends. The system is empirically benchmarked over 100 independent iterations.
AI.result: Empirical benchmarking across 100 iterations shows a total overhead of approximately 1.58ms, well within enterprise deployment thresholds. The architecture demonstrates combinatorial security against both classical and quantum adversaries while maintaining backward compatibility with existing banking systems.
AI.conclusion: The DW-HKEM architecture is viable as a practical, scalable reference design for the financial sector's cryptographic infrastructure migration to a post-quantum era. The authors also release complete source code for reproducibility and adoption.

title: TopoTuner: Topological Finetuning of Large Language Models
summary:
Full fine-tuning remains a strong way to adapt pretrained LLMs, but it updates all weights and can be expensive. LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters, but it does not directly answer which pretrained components should be trained and which can be frozen during adaptation. We introduce TopoTuner, a topology-guided fine-tuning framework for selective freezing of attention projection matrices. \method treats each projection matrix as a row cloud and uses Wasserstein distances between persistence diagrams to measure how its topology changes during fine-tuning.
  TopoTuner learns a reusable freezing profile from a source dataset and transfers it to efficiently fine-tune models on out-of-domain datasets, evaluating whether task-specific topological drift generalizes across question answering and sentiment analysis tasks.
  Across LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen3-8B-Base, TopoTuner is competitive with full fine-tuning while training only 1-2\% of the model parameters, and outperforms LoRA in 7 out of 9 model-dataset settings, which can change up to 39.57\% of the projection parameters. Along with minimized updates, TopoTuner reduces training time by 20.4\% relative to full fine-tuning and 5.5\% relative to LoRA on average. TopoTuner opens a new direction for reusable freezing profiles, where fine-tuning behavior learned on one dataset can be shared across multiple tasks.

AI.tldr: TopoTuner introduces topology-guided selective freezing for LLM fine-tuning, using persistent homology to identify which attention projection matrices to train vs. freeze, achieving competitive performance with only 1-2% trainable parameters and enabling reusable freezing profiles across tasks.
AI.motivation: Full fine-tuning is expensive because it updates all weights; LoRA reduces trainable parameters but does not address *which* pretrained components should be trained vs. frozen. The authors aim to provide a principled, topology-based answer to this selective freezing question, and further explore whether optimal freezing strategies can transfer across datasets.
AI.method: TopoTuner treats each attention projection matrix as a row cloud and computes persistent homology (persistence diagrams) before and after fine-tuning. Wasserstein distances between these diagrams quantify topological drift. From a source dataset, TopoTuner learns a reusable "freezing profile" — identifying which projection matrices undergo significant topological change and should remain trainable, and which can be frozen. This profile is then transferred to fine-tune models on out-of-domain target datasets.
AI.result: Evaluated across LLaMA-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen3-8B-Base on QA and sentiment analysis tasks, TopoTuner is competitive with full fine-tuning while training only 1-2% of parameters, outperforms LoRA in 7/9 model-dataset settings, can update up to 39.57% of projection parameters, reduces training time by 20.4% vs. full fine-tuning and 5.5% vs. LoRA.
AI.conclusion: TopoTuner demonstrates that topological analysis of parameter drift can effectively guide selective freezing, yielding efficient fine-tuning with minimal performance loss. It opens a new direction for reusable freezing profiles — fine-tuning behavior learned on one dataset can be shared across multiple tasks, reducing the cost of adapting LLMs to new domains.

title: How Reliable Are Multimodal Signals of Conversational State? Evidence from Remote Dyadic Collaborative Tasks
comment: Accepted, to appear in Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Multimodal Interaction 2026, 13 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
summary: Measuring conversational states such as cognitive load and conversational power from multimodal behavior requires characteristic features that are not only predictive but also reliable across task contexts. We present a three-dimensional evaluation framework assessing predictive accuracy, cross-task generalizability, and test-retest reliability, applied to interactional, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted from dyadic conversations during collaborative tasks performed over a video-conferencing platform (AVCAffe dataset; 53 dyads, 9 tasks). Our results show that no single feature family dominates all three dimensions. Linguistic features show the highest predictive accuracy for cognitive load but collapse under cross-task evaluation, revealing sensitivity to task-specific vocabulary. Additionally, acoustic reliability, often reported as evidence of feature stability, degrades once speaker identity is controlled, confirming that standard prosodic features measure vocal characteristics rather than conversational state. Interaction features provide the only genuinely reliable signal, unchanged after speaker normalization. Interestingly, classifying power role remained near chance baseline across all conditions, indicating limitations of task-level aggregated behavior for predicting power role in conversation. Our findings reveal three insights: (1) linguistic features predict best but generalize poorly across task contexts; (2) acoustic reliability collapses to near-zero once speaker identity is controlled, challenging standard evaluation practice; and (3) interaction features provide the only genuinely reliable signal, with floor dominance predicting within-dyad cognitive load asymmetry. These results argue for speaker normalization and multi-dimensional evaluation as prerequisites for context-aware, robust multimodal feature selection in conversational systems.

AI.tldr: A three-dimensional evaluation framework (predictive accuracy, cross-task generalization, test-retest reliability) applied to conversational features reveals that linguistic features predict cognitive load best but fail to generalize across tasks, acoustic reliability vanishes after speaker normalization, and only interaction features provide genuinely reliable signals for conversational state measurement.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal feature selection for conversational state measurement lacks rigorous multi-dimensional evaluation. Features are often validated solely on predictive accuracy without considering cross-task generalizability or test-retest reliability, leading to brittle models that may conflate speaker identity with conversational state.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-dimensional evaluation framework and apply it to interactional, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted from the AVCAffe dataset (53 dyads, 9 collaborative tasks over video-conferencing). They assess (1) predictive accuracy, (2) cross-task generalizability via leave-one-task-out validation, and (3) test-retest reliability with and without speaker identity normalization. Target states include cognitive load and conversational power role.
AI.result: Linguistic features achieved highest within-task predictive accuracy for cognitive load but collapsed in cross-task evaluation due to task-specific vocabulary. Acoustic feature reliability degraded to near-zero after controlling for speaker identity. Interaction features (e.g., floor dominance) were the only reliable signal after speaker normalization and successfully predicted within-dyad cognitive load asymmetry. Power role classification remained near chance across all feature families and conditions.
AI.conclusion: Speaker normalization and multi-dimensional evaluation are essential prerequisites for context-aware, robust multimodal feature selection in conversational systems. No single feature family excels across all dimensions, and standard acoustic reliability metrics are misleading without controlling for speaker identity.

title: From Outcomes to Actions: Leveraging Hindsight for Long-Horizon Language Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a widely adopted technique for improving large language models (LLMs) on complex tasks. Despite this progress, existing RL methods still face challenges in training agents with longer-horizon interactions. One major bottleneck is distinguishing the contribution of different actions in long-horizon interaction, leading to high optimization variance. To address this, we introduce a novel policy gradient method, Hindsight Policy Optimization (HPO), that projects both the current policy distribution and the hindsight distribution into an intent space and extracts low-variance learning signals from the Wasserstein distance between them. We theoretically and empirically show that aggregating semantically similar states and actions in the intent space yields a bounded-variance estimator and improves policy performance stably. Our code is available online.

AI.tldr: HPO reduces RL optimization variance in long-horizon LLM tasks by projecting policies into an intent space and using Wasserstein distance between current and hindsight distributions for low-variance learning signals.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods struggle with long-horizon LLM interactions because distinguishing individual action contributions is difficult, causing high optimization variance. A method is needed to aggregate semantically similar states/actions for more stable policy learning.
AI.method: Hindsight Policy Optimization (HPO) — a policy gradient method that projects both current policy and hindsight (post-hoc optimal) distributions into a learned intent space, then computes learning signals via Wasserstein distance between these distributions to achieve bounded-variance gradient estimation.
AI.result: Theoretically and empirically demonstrated that intent-space aggregation yields a bounded-variance estimator and provides stable policy performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: HPO effectively addresses the credit assignment problem in long-horizon RL for LLMs by leveraging semantic similarity in the intent space, enabling more stable and efficient policy optimization.

title: Integrating High-Level Requirements to Low-Level Tests with Machine-Readable V&V Specifications
summary: Modern software teams have mature tools for low-level testing, such as pytest, JUnit, and Jest, which make it inexpensive to write unit tests and run them on every commit. Systems engineering, in parallel, has developed rigorous principles for design verification and validation (V&V), which has worked very well across engineering discipline to align user expecations and requirements with developers' deliverables. In practice, however, the two rarely connect, and the link between users' high-level requirements and the low-level tests that machines actually run is maintained by hand, if at all. This gap is increasingly costly for AI-enabled and cyber-physical systems, for which regulators now ask for traceable evidence that high-level requirements are met, while raw test results provide little of the structure such evidence requires. We introduce VNVSpec, an open-source framework that makes V&V specifications machine-readable and executable. With this framework, users state high-level requirements directly or import them from catalogs derived from published standards. Then, the framework checks requirement quality, supports decomposition into module-level requirements with explicit metrics and acceptance criteria, links these requirements to test results through a traceability graph, and compiles the collected evidence into verdicts and audit-ready reports. We evaluate the framework by self-application, in which it is continuously assessed in CI against its own specification of 36 requirements verified by 449 tests, completed within limited time which scales linearly and thus can handle up to 10,000 requirements. We also discuss how the framework extends to testing black-box AI models and AI coding agents. The framework, its full test suite, the catalogs, and the benchmark scripts are available at https://github.com/ai-vnv/vnvspec.

AI.tldr: VNVSpec is an open-source framework that bridges the gap between high-level V&V requirements and low-level tests by making specifications machine-readable and executable. It supports requirement authoring, quality checking, decomposition with metrics, traceability to test results, and generation of audit-ready verdicts and reports.
AI.motivation: There is a costly disconnect between high-level user requirements and low-level unit tests. While testing frameworks (pytest, JUnit, Jest) and systems engineering V&V principles have matured independently, the traceability link between them is maintained manually, if at all. This gap is especially problematic for AI-enabled and cyber-physical systems, where regulators demand traceable evidence that high-level requirements are satisfied — evidence that raw test results alone cannot provide.
AI.method: The authors introduce VNVSpec, an open-source framework with the following capabilities: (1) users state high-level requirements directly or import them from standards-based catalogs; (2) the framework checks requirement quality; (3) it supports decomposition into module-level requirements with explicit metrics and acceptance criteria; (4) it links requirements to test results via a traceability graph; and (5) it compiles collected evidence into verdicts and audit-ready reports. The framework is self-evaluated in CI against its own specification of 36 requirements verified by 449 tests.
AI.result: VNVSpec's self-application demonstrates that 36 requirements are continuously verified by 449 tests in CI. The framework completes within limited time that scales linearly, indicating it can handle up to 10,000 requirements. The approach also extends to testing black-box AI models and AI coding agents.
AI.conclusion: VNVSpec successfully bridges the requirements–test traceability gap by providing an executable, machine-readable V&V specification framework. It enables regulatory compliance through automated evidence compilation and scales linearly to thousands of requirements. The framework, test suite, catalogs, and benchmarks are publicly available.

title: Detection, Attribution, Narration: An End-to-End Pipeline for Explainable Money Mule Identification
summary: Money mule accounts are critical facilitators of financial fraud, yet detecting them at scale remains challenging due to the heterogeneous nature of transactional and behavioural data. We present an end-to-end pipeline for customer-level mule detection comprising three stages: (1) a LightGBM classifier trained on 280 engineered features spanning transaction patterns, account demographics, network topology, and temporal behaviour; (2) a TreeSHAP attribution layer that decomposes each prediction into feature contributions; and (3) a large language model (LLM) module that converts SHAP attributions into analyst-facing natural-language narratives. We evaluate across three open-weight LLM families and assess explanation quality through analyst feedback. In a live production deployment, the system achieves a yield rate of 89%, up from 61% under the incumbent rule-based system, with monthly alert volume expanding from 211 to 302, reflecting broader true-positive coverage rather than increased noise. This corresponds to a 60% incremental adverse detection beyond existing review workflows, substantially outperforming the rule-based approach. Qualitative feedback from analysts indicates that LLM-generated narratives reduce cognitive load during alert triage. We further discuss implications of deploying LLM-augmented explainability in regulated financial environments.

AI.tldr: A three-stage pipeline (LightGBM + TreeSHAP + LLM narratives) for detecting money mule accounts achieves 89% yield rate (up from 61% rule-based), 60% more adverse detections, and reduced analyst cognitive load via natural-language explanations.
AI.motivation: Money mule detection at scale is impeded by heterogeneous transactional and behavioral data. Existing rule-based systems suffer from low yield rates (61%) and limited coverage, motivating a machine learning approach that not only improves detection but also provides interpretable explanations for financial analysts operating in regulated environments.
AI.method: The authors propose an end-to-end pipeline: (1) a LightGBM classifier using 280 engineered features across transaction patterns, account demographics, network topology, and temporal behavior; (2) TreeSHAP for decomposing predictions into per-feature contribution scores; and (3) an LLM module that converts SHAP attributions into analyst-facing natural-language narratives. Three open-weight LLM families were evaluated, with explanation quality assessed via analyst feedback.
AI.result: In live production, the system achieved an 89% yield rate (vs. 61% rule-based), monthly alert volume increased from 211 to 302 (reflecting broader true-positive coverage, not noise), and a 60% incremental adverse detection lift beyond existing workflows. Analyst feedback confirmed that LLM-generated narratives reduce cognitive load during alert triage.
AI.conclusion: The integration of gradient-boosted models with SHAP-based attribution and LLM-generated explanations significantly outperforms rule-based mule detection while maintaining interpretability suitable for regulated financial contexts. The authors highlight deployment implications for LLM-augmented explainability in compliance-heavy environments.

title: Diversity-Oriented Fine-Tuning for Uncertainty-Based Hallucination Detection
summary: Existing hallucination detection methods are typically conducted at the inference stage, without making any modifications to the model itself. In this paper, we are interested in exploring fine-tuning strategies that enhance the detectability of hallucinations in the resulting model. Focusing on semantic-entropy-based detection, we observe that many erroneous outputs remain undetected because the model produces nearly identical incorrect answers across multiple runs. To address this, we propose diversity-oriented fine-tuning to encourage more varied generations. We introduce two specific strategies: one based on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and the other on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate our approach and analyze the behavior of the models before and after fine-tuning. We find that after adopting our fine-tuning methods, the models become less likely to produce low semantic entropy responses for hallucinated answers, thereby improving the effectiveness of hallucination detection, eventually yielding results better than or comparable with state of the art methods. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes diversity-oriented fine-tuning strategies (SFT and DPO-based) to improve semantic-entropy-based hallucination detection by encouraging models to produce more varied outputs across multiple runs, making hallucinated answers easier to identify.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination detection methods operate only at inference time without modifying the model. The authors observe that semantic-entropy-based detection fails when models produce near-identical incorrect answers across multiple sampling runs, making hallucinations indistinguishable from correct answers in terms of semantic entropy.
AI.method: The authors propose diversity-oriented fine-tuning with two strategies: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) that trains the model to generate diverse outputs for the same prompt, and (2) Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that explicitly optimizes the model to prefer diverse generations over homogeneous ones. Both aim to increase output variability specifically for hallucinated responses.
AI.result: After fine-tuning, models produce lower semantic entropy for correct answers and higher semantic entropy for hallucinated answers, significantly improving hallucination detection performance. Results are better than or comparable to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-oriented fine-tuning is an effective approach to enhance the detectability of hallucinations from within the model itself, rather than relying solely on inference-time detection methods.

title: Multilingual Sentence Embeddings for Linguistic-Integrated Reliability Audit
summary: Multilingual assessment systems commonly rely on translation for scoring and quality-control processes. We evaluate whether multilingual sentence embeddings can replace translated English input for Linguistic-Integrated Reliability Auditing (LiRA) across 11 PIRLS constructed-response items and three embedding models. Native-language embeddings reproduced translation-based reliability estimates closely while recovering responses excluded after translation failure, with no meaningful change in reliability.

AI.tldr: Multilingual sentence embeddings can replace translation in reliability auditing (LiRA) for constructed-response assessment items, closely matching translation-based estimates while recovering previously excluded responses.
AI.motivation: Current multilingual assessment systems depend on translation for scoring and quality control, which introduces translation failures that exclude valid responses. The authors seek to determine whether multilingual sentence embeddings can bypass this translation bottleneck.
AI.method: Evaluation of three multilingual sentence embedding models across 11 PIRLS constructed-response items, comparing native-language embedding-based LiRA reliability estimates against traditional translation-based estimates, including analysis of responses previously excluded due to translation failure.
AI.result: Native-language embeddings reproduced translation-based reliability estimates closely. Crucially, the embedding approach recovered responses that had been excluded after translation failure, with no meaningful change in overall reliability metrics.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual sentence embeddings offer a viable, translation-free alternative for linguistic-integrated reliability auditing in multilingual assessment contexts, eliminating translation-induced data loss without compromising reliability.

title: Neural Controlled Differential Equations for EMT-Level Surrogate Modeling of Grid-Forming Inverters
summary: The application of artificial intelligence methods in power electronic converter modeling is becoming increasingly widespread, but existing applications still face many challenges, such as difficulties in multi-time-scale hybrid analysis and the lack of physics-aware evaluation criteria and constraints, resulting in poor performance. This paper proposes a Neural Controlled Differential Equation (Neural CDE) framework for learning continuous-time surrogate models of grid-forming inverters for electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulation, which relaxes the constraint of fixed sampling rates and enables multi-time-scale control analysis. Then, an affine-control formulation with dual slow/fast pathways is proposed to capture the hierarchical and multiscale behavior of converter dynamics, and a physics-inspired regularization method is utilized to enhance stability and coherence. Evaluated on EMT-generated trajectories, the model accurately reproduces transient responses, preserves effective damping and the dominant oscillatory characteristics, and maintains bounded long-horizon rollouts. The results show that Neural CDE-based component modeling offers a physically consistent surrogate modeling approach for EMT-level simulation studies.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Neural Controlled Differential Equation (Neural CDE) framework with dual slow/fast pathways and physics-inspired regularization to learn continuous-time surrogate models of grid-forming inverters for EMT simulation, enabling multi-time-scale analysis, accurate transient reproduction, and bounded long-horizon rollouts.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-based power electronic converter modeling suffers from two key challenges: (1) difficulty in multi-time-scale hybrid analysis due to fixed sampling rate constraints, and (2) lack of physics-aware evaluation criteria and constraints, leading to poor surrogate model performance in EMT simulations.
AI.method: The authors propose a Neural CDE framework for learning continuous-time surrogate models of grid-forming inverters, which removes fixed sampling rate constraints. An affine-control formulation with dual slow/fast pathways captures hierarchical, multiscale converter dynamics. A physics-inspired regularization method is applied to enhance stability and coherence.
AI.result: Evaluated on EMT-generated trajectories, the model accurately reproduces transient responses, preserves effective damping and dominant oscillatory characteristics, and maintains bounded long-horizon rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Neural CDE-based component modeling provides a physically consistent surrogate modeling approach suitable for EMT-level simulation studies.

title: KernelDiag: Agent-Based Root Cause Diagnosis for Kernel Crashes
summary: The Linux kernel is one of the most complex software systems, where automated fuzzing continuously exposes thousands of crashes, yet root-cause diagnosis remains a manual and time-consuming bottleneck. Existing LLM-based root cause analysis (RCA) techniques, effective for distributed systems, do not readily generalize to kernel debugging due to sparse low-level artifacts, heterogeneous diagnostic evidence (e.g., syscalls, logs, and crash reports), and complex non-linear fault propagation that demands fine-grained method-level reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose KernelDiag, an agent-based framework for kernel root-cause diagnosis via structured causal reasoning. KernelDiag first aligns heterogeneous diagnostic artifacts through log-to-code mapping, and then employs artifact-specialized agents to iteratively reason over source-level program semantics and crash-specific kernel configurations. The inferred causal dependencies are incrementally organized into structured Evidence Graphs, enabling accurate faulty-method localization and causal explanations. We evaluate KernelDiag on the real-world KGYM benchmark. KernelDiag consistently outperforms state-of-the-art localization approaches at both file and method levels, achieving significant improvements in Top@k accuracy, including up to 4x and 2x gains in challenging settings without explicit hints. Furthermore, both human and LLM-assisted evaluations show that KernelDiag generates accurate, coherent, and actionable diagnostic explanations. Overall, this work lays the foundation for automated kernel root-cause diagnosis by bridging low-level diagnostic evidence with source-level causal reasoning.

AI.tldr: KernelDiag is an agent-based framework that automates Linux kernel root-cause diagnosis by aligning heterogeneous diagnostic artifacts (logs, syscalls, crash reports) with source code through structured causal reasoning and Evidence Graphs, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods on the KGYM benchmark.
AI.motivation: While automated fuzzing exposes thousands of Linux kernel crashes daily, root-cause diagnosis remains a manual bottleneck. Existing LLM-based RCA techniques for distributed systems fail on kernel debugging due to: (1) sparse low-level artifacts, (2) heterogeneous diagnostic evidence, and (3) complex non-linear fault propagation requiring fine-grained method-level reasoning.
AI.method: KernelDiag employs a multi-agent framework: it first aligns heterogeneous artifacts via log-to-code mapping, then deploys artifact-specialized agents that iteratively reason over source-level program semantics and crash-specific kernel configurations. Inferred causal dependencies are incrementally organized into structured Evidence Graphs, enabling precise faulty-method localization and causal explanation generation.
AI.result: On the KGYM benchmark, KernelDiag consistently outperforms state-of-the-art localization approaches at both file and method levels, achieving up to 4x and 2x improvement in Top@k accuracy in challenging settings without explicit hints. Human and LLM-assisted evaluations confirm the generated explanations are accurate, coherent, and actionable.
AI.conclusion: KernelDiag demonstrates that bridging low-level diagnostic evidence with source-level causal reasoning via agent-based structured inference is a viable foundation for automated kernel root-cause diagnosis, significantly advancing beyond current manual and LLM-based approaches.

title: Protecting Floating-Point Computation for DNN Binaries with MBA Obfuscation
summary:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a foundational component of modern computing systems with a wide range of applications, such as computer vision, edge intelligence, etc. For the sake of low latency and data privacy, DNN models are increasingly compiled into executables and deployed on local devices. However, that exposes the models to model theft, enabling adversaries to recover proprietary assets via reverse engineering techniques. While code obfuscation naturally emerges for protecting executables from reverse engineering, existing schemes are primarily designed for traditional programs, focusing on complex control flow structures and integer-based operations. They are fundamentally inappropriate for DNN binaries, which exhibit relatively simple code structures and heavily rely on floating-point computation.
  In this paper, we propose FLOB, an obfuscation framework that protects floating-point computations in DNN binaries using Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) transformations. Our approach lifts floating-point values into a higher-precision binary expansion space and performs MBA transformations at the representation level. The computation is carried out entirely in the lifted space, and the final result is then projected back to the target precision, yielding outputs that are semantically equivalent under the original floating-point format, without introducing additional rounding error. The experimental results show that FLOB outperforms the state-of-the-art obfuscation schemes against existing reverse engineering analyzers and deobfuscators, while preserving computational correctness without introducing additional numerical error, allowing flexible trade-off between protection and performance. Specifically, FLOB reduces the operator recovery rate to 4.51% on average, achieving a 32.82 percentage-point reduction compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: FLOB is a floating-point obfuscation framework for DNN binaries that uses Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) transformations in a lifted binary expansion space, achieving a 32.82 percentage-point reduction in operator recovery rate (down to 4.51%) without introducing additional numerical error.
AI.motivation: Deployed DNN models are vulnerable to model theft via reverse engineering. Existing code obfuscation techniques are designed for traditional programs with complex control flow and integer operations, making them unsuitable for DNN binaries that have simple code structures and rely heavily on floating-point computation.
AI.method: FLOB lifts floating-point values into a higher-precision binary expansion space and applies Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic (MBA) transformations at the representation level. All computation occurs in the lifted space, and results are projected back to the target floating-point precision, preserving semantic equivalence without introducing additional rounding error.
AI.result: FLOB reduces the operator recovery rate to 4.51% on average — a 32.82 percentage-point reduction compared to existing methods — while maintaining computational correctness and allowing flexible protection-performance trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: FLOB demonstrates that floating-point-specific MBA obfuscation is an effective and precise approach to protecting DNN binaries from reverse engineering, outperforming state-of-the-art methods against both analyzers and deobfuscators.

title: DS@GT ARC at eRisk 2026: Hybrid Multi-Agent LLM System with Structured Algorithmic Guidance for Conversational Depression Screening
comment: Conference and Labs of the Evaluation Forum (CLEF), 19 pages, 5 figures
summary: We describe DS@GT's submission to the eRisk 2026 Task 1 challenge on conversational depression screening, in which systems interview LLM personas that simulate individuals with varying depression profiles and produce a Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II) score plus four key symptoms per persona, without directly asking sensitive mental health questions. Our pipeline evolved through three stages: a monolithic single-model prototype to start off, a baseline multi-agent architecture that separates conversational interviewing from BDI-II scoring under a coordinating orchestration layer, and a final hybrid configuration that replaces the paid GPT-5-nano interviewer with the open-source Gemma 27B. To offset the model's weaker reasoning and instruction-following, the hybrid adds three algorithmic components: a precomputed dialogue tree that standardizes interview openers and follow-ups, a reliability-weighted consensus aggregation inspired by the Weaver framework, and a cluster-based imputation step for unprobed symptoms. We submitted three fully automated runs across all 20 personas, with Run 1 from the paid baseline and Runs 2 and 3 from the hybrid. Hybrid Run 3 achieved an ADODL of 0.9063, ranking 3rd among all complete-submission runs and placing DS@GT 2nd among the 21 teams overall, while outperforming our paid baseline Run 1 (0.8841) at roughly one-quarter of the per-persona API cost. These results support our central hypothesis that with sufficient algorithmic supervision, a weaker open-source model can compete with a stronger proprietary model in the conversational interviewer role. Our source code is available at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/erisk-task1-2026.

AI.tldr: DS@GT's eRisk 2026 Task 1 system uses a hybrid multi-agent pipeline with a Gemma 27B open-source interviewer, augmented by algorithmic components (dialogue tree, reliability-weighted consensus, cluster-based imputation), to screen personas for depression. It achieved 3rd place (ADODL 0.9063) while being significantly cheaper than their paid GPT-5-nano baseline.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a weaker open-source LLM, when augmented with sufficient algorithmic supervision, can match or exceed a stronger proprietary model in conversational depression screening — thereby reducing cost and improving accessibility without sacrificing clinical accuracy.
AI.method: A three-stage evolution: (1) monolithic single-model prototype, (2) baseline multi-agent architecture separating conversational interviewing (GPT-5-nano) from BDI-II scoring under an orchestration layer, and (3) final hybrid replacing the interviewer with Gemma 27B, augmented by a precomputed dialogue tree for standardized interview flow, reliability-weighted consensus aggregation (inspired by the Weaver framework), and cluster-based imputation for unprobed symptoms. Three fully automated runs across 20 LLM personas were submitted.
AI.result: Hybrid Run 3 achieved an ADODL of 0.9063, ranking 3rd among all complete submissions and placing DS@GT 2nd among 21 teams. It outperformed the paid baseline Run 1 (0.8841) at roughly one-quarter the per-persona API cost.
AI.conclusion: The results support the central hypothesis: with sufficient algorithmic supervision — structured dialogue trees, consensus aggregation, and imputation — a weaker open-source model can compete with a stronger proprietary model in the conversational clinical interviewer role.

title: Token-Level Off-Policy Learning for Faithful Generation Under Distribution Shift
summary: We propose Token-Level Off-Policy Labeling (TOPL), an off-policy training paradigm that reframes post-training as a token-level correctness prediction task. Our key intuition is that by training the model to distinguish good and bad tokens in a response, we naturally guide the model towards generating good tokens, while avoiding the pitfalls that come with directly training the model to generate off-policy tokens. Experiments on document summarization tasks show that TOPL achieves strong out-of-distribution generalization across 11 datasets against a diverse set of sequence-level and token-level baselines. We further demonstrate that TOPL transfers effectively to machine translation, suggesting that its benefits generalize across different faithful generation tasks. Through ablation studies, we confirm that our token-level learning signal is critical to good performance; sequence-level analogues do not confer similar benefits. Finally, we show that TOPL induces interpretable model updates: the LoRA adapters learned through TOPL function as linear classification heads and steering vectors.

AI.tldr: TOPL reframes post-training as token-level correctness prediction, training models to distinguish good from bad tokens rather than directly generating off-policy tokens. It achieves strong OOD generalization on summarization across 11 datasets, transfers to machine translation, and produces interpretable LoRA updates that function as classification heads and steering vectors.
AI.motivation: Directly training models to generate off-policy tokens (e.g., from other models or noisy sources) introduces distributional mismatch issues that can harm generation quality. The authors aim to leverage off-policy data while avoiding these pitfalls by converting the problem into a token-level correctness classification task.
AI.method: TOPL trains the model to predict, at each token position, whether a given token in an off-policy response is "good" (correct) or "bad" (incorrect). This token-level discriminative signal indirectly guides the model toward generating high-quality tokens during inference, without requiring the model to directly imitate off-policy token distributions.
AI.result: TOPL outperforms both sequence-level and token-level baselines in out-of-distribution summarization across 11 datasets. It transfers effectively to machine translation, showing cross-task generalization. Ablations confirm that token-level (rather than sequence-level) signals are essential. LoRA adapters learned via TOPL are interpretable as linear classification heads and steering vectors.
AI.conclusion: Post-training as token-level correctness prediction is an effective off-policy paradigm that yields strong generalization, cross-task transfer, and interpretability, avoiding the distributional pitfalls of direct off-policy generation training.

title: Quantifying Ranking Uncertainty in LLM Benchmarks
summary: Pretrained models are typically ranked on multi-task leaderboards to assess their effectiveness across diverse tasks. Rank confidence intervals were recently introduced as a method to quantify the uncertainty in these rankings by aggregating pairwise hypothesis tests. In this work, we analyze the sources of uncertainty in the knowledge evaluation benchmark MMLU and show how hypothesis tests can be modified to account for their effects. We demonstrate that ranking variability across MMLU subjects is substantial and should be considered when comparing LLMs or identifying the top-performing models.

AI.tldr: This paper examines uncertainty sources in MMLU benchmark rankings and proposes modified hypothesis tests to account for substantial cross-subject variability when comparing LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-task leaderboards rank pretrained models without adequately accounting for uncertainty. While rank confidence intervals (RCIs) were recently introduced using pairwise hypothesis tests, they fail to capture critical sources of variability — particularly the substantial performance variation across different subjects within benchmarks like MMLU. This gap can lead to overconfident or misleading model comparisons.
AI.method: The authors analyze sources of uncertainty in the MMLU benchmark and propose modifications to hypothesis testing procedures used in constructing rank confidence intervals. These modifications explicitly account for cross-subject ranking variability — i.e., the fact that a model's performance can differ significantly across MMLU's diverse subjects — thereby producing more faithful uncertainty quantification in model rankings.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that ranking variability across MMLU subjects is substantial. Accounting for this variability through modified hypothesis tests leads to wider, more realistic rank confidence intervals, indicating that naive RCIs underestimate uncertainty when comparing LLMs or identifying top-performing models on MMLU.
AI.conclusion: Cross-subject variability in MMLU must be incorporated into ranking uncertainty quantification. Modified hypothesis tests that account for this variability provide more reliable comparisons between LLMs and more robust identification of top-performing models.

title: Insecure Coding Preferences in Long-Term Memory: Security Risks for LLM-based Code Generation
comment: Accepted to the 35th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2026)
summary: LLM-based systems increasingly incorporate long-term memory to improve cross-session continuity. However, once insecure coding preferences are stored, they may silently influence security-critical decisions in subsequent generations. In this study, we conduct the first systematic empirical study on the impact of insecure coding preferences stored in long-term memory on the security of LLM-based code generation. We evaluate four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, and Grok) across five programming languages (Python, C, C++, Go, and JavaScript). Our results show that insecure memories significantly increase the risk of generating vulnerable code by 2.7-50.3 percentage points (pp). Moreover, they create a 5.4-14.0 percentage-point risk-warning gap, where warning-rate increases lag behind vulnerability-rate increases. Further analysis reveals that insecure memories are difficult to overwrite through normal interactions and can broadly influence model outputs even when prompts are phrased differently. Finally, we evaluate three mitigation strategies: security-requirement appending and memory storage reduce vulnerability rates by 19.7-33.6 pp but may degrade functional correctness by up to 15.9 pp; memory-level safety filtering achieves a 100\% detection rate on our evaluated risky memory entries and restores generation behavior to the without-memory baseline. Based on these findings, we provide actionable suggestions to improve the security of long-term memory in LLM-based code generation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic study on how insecure coding preferences stored in LLM long-term memory can compromise code generation security. Across four LLMs and five languages, insecure memories increased vulnerable code generation by 2.7–50.3 pp and created a 5.4–14.0 pp risk-warning gap. The study also evaluates three mitigations, finding memory-level safety filtering fully restores baseline security.
AI.motivation: LLM-based systems increasingly adopt long-term memory for cross-session continuity, but no prior work has systematically investigated whether stored insecure coding preferences can silently corrupt subsequent code generation security. This gap motivates the first empirical assessment of this risk.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, Grok) across five programming languages (Python, C, C++, Go, JavaScript). They inject insecure coding preferences into long-term memory, then measure the impact on vulnerability rates and warning rates in subsequent code generation. They also test memory overwriting difficulty, cross-prompt influence, and three mitigation strategies: security-requirement appending, memory storage, and memory-level safety filtering.
AI.result: Insecure memories increased vulnerable code generation by 2.7–50.3 percentage points. A 5.4–14.0 pp risk-warning gap emerged where warning-rate increases lagged behind vulnerability-rate increases. Insecure memories proved hard to overwrite via normal interactions and influenced outputs even under rephrased prompts. Security-requirement appending and memory storage reduced vulnerabilities by 19.7–33.6 pp but degraded functional correctness by up to 15.9 pp. Memory-level safety filtering achieved 100% detection of risky entries and restored baseline behavior.
AI.conclusion: Long-term memory introduces a stealthy security vulnerability in LLM-based code generation. Memory-level safety filtering is the most effective mitigation, fully neutralizing the risk without degrading functionality. The authors offer actionable recommendations for securing long-term memory mechanisms.

title: Tractable Query Answering under Epistemic Confidentiality Policies in DL Ontologies (extended version)
summary: We study Controlled Query Evaluation (CQE), a declarative approach to confidentiality-preserving data access, in the context of Description Logic (DL) ontologies, and for confidentiality policies expressed through Epistemic Dependencies (EDs). We first address the problem of answering queries (specifically, Boolean unions of conjunctive queries) under known semantics for CQE (GA- and IGA-entailment). Our results show that if the TBox is expressed in $\text{DL-Lite}_{\mathcal{R}}$, CQE is computationally intractable in general. Moreover, in the presence of EDs, the IGA semantics has recently been proven not to satisfy an important confidentiality preservation property known as indistinguishability. With the goal of defining computationally easier and confidentiality-preserving forms of CQE, we introduce a new semantics for CQE, based on the notion of minimal policy violation (MPV). We show that the new semantics provides a sound approximation of the previous ones, while satisfying the indistinguishability property. We also prove that, in the case of $\text{DL-Lite}_{\mathcal{R}}$ ontologies, query entailment under the MPV semantics can be decided in polynomial time in data complexity. Finally, we present a software implementation of our framework that we used to evaluate the feasibility of this new approach using an existing benchmark for OWL 2 QL.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Controlled Query Evaluation (CQE) in DL ontologies with Epistemic Dependencies (EDs). It shows that existing semantics (GA/IGA) are intractable for DL-Lite_R and that IGA fails indistinguishability. The authors propose a new MPV semantics that is a sound approximation, satisfies indistinguishability, and admits polynomial-time query entailment, with a software implementation evaluated on OWL 2 QL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing CQE semantics (GA and IGA) suffer from two key limitations: (1) they are computationally intractable even for lightweight DL-Lite_R ontologies, and (2) the IGA semantics fails to satisfy indistinguishability — a critical confidentiality preservation property — when Epistemic Dependencies are present. This motivates the need for a new semantics that is both computationally feasible and confidentiality-preserving.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Minimal Policy Violation (MPV) semantics for CQE, which is based on minimizing policy violations when answering queries. They analyze its theoretical properties (soundness as an approximation of GA/IGA, indistinguishability satisfaction), establish complexity results for query entailment under DL-Lite_R (polynomial time in data complexity), and implement a software framework evaluated against an OWL 2 QL benchmark.
AI.result: (1) CQE under GA/IGA semantics is computationally intractable for DL-Lite_R ontologies. (2) The new MPV semantics provides a sound approximation of GA and IGA. (3) MPV semantics satisfies the indistinguishability property. (4) Query entailment under MPV semantics is decidable in polynomial time with respect to data complexity for DL-Lite_R. (5) A working implementation demonstrates practical feasibility on OWL 2 QL benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The MPV semantics successfully addresses the shortcomings of prior CQE approaches by combining computational tractability (PTime in data complexity for DL-Lite_R) with the indistinguishability confidentiality guarantee, while remaining a sound approximation of GA and IGA semantics. The implementation validates the approach's practical viability.

title: Oracle Gap and Signal Fidelity: A Fixed-Pool Diagnostic for Test-Time Collaboration
summary: Test-time collaboration, including self-consistency, best-of-N selection, critic models, and verifier pipelines, is often credited with broadly improving LLM reasoning, yet its gains are uneven and sometimes negative. We ask when training-free collaboration should be expected to help. For a fixed candidate pool, we decompose a selector or verifier's net gain into measurable factors: recoverable mass, verification-signal coverage, conditional selection quality, and harm to already-correct outputs. This reframes collaboration as a candidate-selection problem rather than as an intrinsic property of a multi-agent topology. Across LiveCodeBench, MATH Level-5 hard subjects, and GPQA-Diamond, gains are bounded first by the oracle gap and then by signal fidelity, which we measure directly as candidate-level agreement between verifier verdicts and official labels. On LiveCodeBench, a public-test verifier (MCC 0.825) gains +8.14 percentage points (pp) over a first-sample baseline; a generated-test verifier (MCC 0.248) improves by +2.70pp and is not statistically distinguishable from an LLM selector, but operates at near-zero harm versus the selector's 4.69% harm rate. On MATH, a symbolic answer-equivalence selector beats self-consistency by +4.67pp, while LLM selectors are negative. On GPQA-Diamond, recoverable mass is only 3.03% and 87.54% of candidate pools are answer-identical; a weaker model's pools shrink both further, suggesting that oracle gap is a joint property of task, model, and sampling configuration. Our framework yields a practical pre-deployment diagnostic: estimate the oracle gap, then measure coverage, signal fidelity, and harm before investing in collaboration.

AI.tldr: Training-free test-time collaboration for LLM reasoning is analyzed as a candidate-selection problem. Gains are decomposed into recoverable mass, verification-signal coverage, conditional selection quality, and harm to correct outputs. Experiments across LiveCodeBench, MATH, and GPQA-Diamond show gains are bounded by oracle gap and signal fidelity, providing a practical pre-deployment diagnostic framework.
AI.motivation: Test-time collaboration methods (self-consistency, best-of-N, critic models, verifier pipelines) are widely believed to improve LLM reasoning, but gains are inconsistent and sometimes negative. The authors aim to understand when and why training-free collaboration actually helps, rather than treating it as an intrinsic benefit of multi-agent setups.
AI.method: The authors decompose a selector/verifier's net gain into four measurable factors: (1) recoverable mass — the improvement ceiling if selection were perfect (oracle gap), (2) verification-signal coverage — the proportion of candidates evaluated, (3) conditional selection quality — accuracy of selection among evaluated candidates, and (4) harm to already-correct outputs. They measure signal fidelity via candidate-level agreement (MCC) between verifier verdicts and ground-truth labels. Experiments span LiveCodeBench, MATH Level-5, and GPQA-Diamond using public-test verifiers, generated-test verifiers, LLM selectors, and symbolic answer-equivalence selectors.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench, a public-test verifier (MCC 0.825) yields +8.14pp gain; a generated-test verifier (MCC 0.248) yields +2.70pp with near-zero harm vs. an LLM selector's 4.69% harm rate. On MATH, symbolic answer-equivalence beats self-consistency by +4.67pp, while LLM selectors are net negative. On GPQA-Diamond, recoverable mass is only 3.03%, with 87.54% of candidate pools answer-identical; weaker models shrink both further. Oracle gap emerges as a joint property of task, model, and sampling configuration.
AI.conclusion: The framework reframes collaboration as a candidate-selection problem and yields a practical pre-deployment diagnostic: estimate the oracle gap, then measure coverage, signal fidelity, and harm before investing in collaboration infrastructure. This avoids deploying collaboration methods where they cannot help or may actively harm performance.

title: AdaSurvMamba: Dynamic Fusion and Semantic Scanning for Multimodal Survival Analysis
summary: Multimodal survival analysis utilizing whole slide images (WSIs) and genomic profiles is fundamental for cancer prognosis. Recently, state-space models like Mamba have emerged as powerful tools for sequence modeling. However, translating this success to complex multimodal tasks is hindered by two critical limitations. First, conventional fusion strategies assume a static multimodal interaction strength, ignoring the fluctuating diagnostic importance of each modality across different patients and local regions. Second, the standard Mamba architecture processes tokens along predefined physical paths. This rigid scanning disrupts the semantic continuity of spatially scattered medical features and exacerbates long-range decay. To address these challenges, we introduce AdaSurvMamba as a novel adaptive framework for multimodal survival analysis. The framework features a Dual-Scale Importance-Aware Reconstruction (DSIR) module to dynamically modulate cross-modal interaction strength. It evaluates diagnostic importance at both the sequence and token levels to reconstruct the input representations. Furthermore, we propose a Semantic Aggregation Scanning (SAS) module to overcome contextual fragmentation. The SAS module dynamically reorganizes discrete tokens into semantically continuous sequences via a shared prototype pool. It explicitly modulates the state transition step size using global modality context and semantic priors to adaptively control the information absorption rate. Experiments across five TCGA cohorts demonstrate consistent gains over existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zjlGO/AdaSurvMamba.

AI.tldr: AdaSurvMamba introduces an adaptive Mamba-based framework for multimodal cancer survival analysis that dynamically modulates cross-modal interaction strength and reorganizes tokens into semantically continuous sequences, achieving consistent improvements across five TCGA cohorts.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal survival analysis methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) static fusion strategies that ignore patient- and region-specific variations in modality importance, and (2) Mamba's fixed physical-path scanning that disrupts semantic continuity of scattered medical features and worsens long-range decay.
AI.method: AdaSurvMamba proposes two modules: (1) Dual-Scale Importance-Aware Reconstruction (DSIR), which dynamically modulates cross-modal interaction strength by evaluating diagnostic importance at both sequence and token levels to reconstruct input representations; (2) Semantic Aggregation Scanning (SAS), which reorganizes discrete tokens into semantically continuous sequences via a shared prototype pool and modulates state transition step size using global modality context and semantic priors to control information absorption rate adaptively.
AI.result: Experiments across five TCGA cohorts demonstrate consistent performance gains over existing state-of-the-art methods for multimodal survival analysis.
AI.conclusion: AdaSurvMamba effectively addresses static fusion and semantic fragmentation in multimodal survival analysis through adaptive importance-aware reconstruction and semantic aggregation scanning, offering a robust solution for integrating WSIs and genomic profiles in cancer prognosis.

title: (Over)Reliance on Test Agents in AI-Assisted Software Testing
summary: AI-based test agents promise to accelerate software testing by shortening feedback loops in continuous development and improving scalability and maintainability. To realize these benefits, engineers must still be able to assess if agent outputs are useful, valid, and reliable, rather than treating them as credible because they come from a capable system. This paper argues that overreliance on AI in testing is both an agency problem, in which engineers may cede cognitive control over test design decisions, and an assurance problem, in which testing artifacts may be accepted as evidence without sufficient scrutiny. We develop this argument through three theoretical lenses: software testing as cognitive problem-solving, test agents as adaptively autonomous entities, and test design argumentation as a means of making generated tests reviewable. We propose a framework for collecting data on overreliance in test agent workflows and identify specific modes of overdependence. The goal is to support accelerated testing without weakening judgment or the assurance value of testing evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI-based test agents risk causing overreliance among software engineers, framed as both an agency problem (ceding cognitive control) and an assurance problem (uncritical acceptance of test artifacts). It proposes a framework using three theoretical lenses and identifies modes of overdependence to support accelerated testing without compromising judgment or evidential assurance.
AI.motivation: AI-based test agents promise faster feedback loops and improved scalability in continuous development, but their outputs risk being accepted uncritically due to perceived system capability. The authors seek to address the dual risks of engineers relinquishing cognitive control over test design (agency problem) and accepting test artifacts as valid evidence without sufficient scrutiny (assurance problem).
AI.method: The authors develop their argument through three theoretical lenses: (1) software testing as cognitive problem-solving, (2) test agents as adaptively autonomous entities, and (3) test design argumentation as a mechanism for making generated tests reviewable. They also propose a framework for collecting data on overreliance in test agent workflows and identify specific modes of overdependence.
AI.result: The paper does not report empirical results; rather, it contributes a conceptual framework that identifies specific modes of overdependence on AI test agents and proposes a data-collection framework for studying overreliance in testing workflows.
AI.conclusion: To realize the benefits of AI-based test agents, the software engineering community must ensure that acceleration of testing does not come at the cost of weakened human judgment or diminished assurance value of testing evidence. The proposed frameworks aim to make this trade-off explicit and manageable.

title: Residual Observability and Attack Detectability in Encrypted OPC UA Traffic
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 52nd Annual Conference of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society (IECON 2026), Doha, Qatar, October 18--21, 2026
summary: OPC Unified Architecture (OPC UA) encryption conceals application-layer semantics and restricts intrusion detection to residual communication structure. Although machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) can detect attacks in encrypted OPC UA traffic, the relationship between residual structural observability and attack detectability remains insufficiently understood. This paper presents an explanatory framework combining a structural observability profile, the Structural Leakage Score (SLS), controlled within-family and cross-family comparisons, phase-specific analysis, and dimension-ablation analysis. Jensen--Shannon divergence is used to characterize transport, temporal, and protocol-lifecycle dimensions, while the SLS summarizes the residual structural magnitude. Evaluation on an industrial private 5G testbed covers four attack families with progressively reduced nominal activity. SLS generally tracks within-family recall trends but does not reproduce cross-family detectability ordering. Interpreting these mismatches also requires temporal prevalence, inter-burst persistence, predictive utility, unique contribution, and redundancy. The framework complements conventional IDS metrics by relating detection outcomes to the magnitude, temporal distribution, and predictive role of observable structural evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Structural Leakage Score (SLS), an explanatory framework that quantifies residual structural observability in encrypted OPC UA traffic and relates it to machine learning-based IDS detection outcomes. Using Jensen-Shannon divergence across transport, temporal, and protocol-lifecycle dimensions, the framework reveals that while SLS generally tracks within-family recall trends, cross-family detectability ordering requires additional factors like temporal prevalence, inter-burst persistence, and predictive utility.
AI.motivation: OPC UA encryption hides application-layer semantics, forcing intrusion detection to rely on residual communication structure. The relationship between this structural observability and attack detectability in ML-based IDSs is poorly understood, creating a gap in explainability and trustworthiness of encrypted-traffic intrusion detection.
