GARAGE synthesizes a dataset of 12,786 CVEs and 140 incident reports into a STIX 2.1 and Auto-ISAC ATM-compliant knowledge base. By formalizing tactical-pattern-level scenarios through granular kill chain analysis, GARAGE achieves threat generation capabilities. Our 320 Leave-One-Out experiments reveal that the framework can accurately transfer security knowledge to entirely unseen vehicle architectures. Furthermore, we position GARAGE as a scalable TARA support tool within human-in-the-loop workflows, offering a comprehensive cost-performance analysis to guide its deployment across various LLM tiers.

AI.tldr: GARAGE is a RAG-based framework that transforms unstructured automotive CTI into a STIX 2.1/Auto-ISAC ATM-compliant knowledge base for automated attack graph generation, validated through 320 Leave-One-Out experiments demonstrating generalizability to unseen vehicle architectures.
AI.motivation: Current automated CTI synthesis tools fail to handle unstructured data and automotive-specific architectural nuances, creating a gap in effective vehicle security intelligence. A domain-specific, actionable knowledge base is needed to bridge this gap.
AI.method: GARAGE employs a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to synthesize 12,786 CVEs and 140 incident reports into a STIX 2.1 and Auto-ISAC ATM-compliant knowledge base. It formalizes tactical-pattern-level scenarios via granular kill chain analysis to enable automated attack graph generation. Validation uses 320 Leave-One-Out experiments for generalization testing.
AI.result: The framework successfully transfers security knowledge to entirely unseen vehicle architectures across 320 Leave-One-Out experiments. GARAGE is positioned as a scalable TARA support tool with a cost-performance analysis guiding deployment across different LLM tiers.
AI.conclusion: GARAGE demonstrates that RAG-powered synthesis of automotive CTI can produce actionable, generalizable threat intelligence, effectively supporting TARA workflows and automated attack graph generation in a human-in-the-loop paradigm.

title: From Overload to Insights: How AI Agents Can Support Scientists in Analyzing Complex Data
comment: Accepted for publication at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution
summary: Scientists at European XFEL conduct experiments that generate very large and complex datasets. The subsequent data analysis is challenging as scientists must combine their domain expertise with facility- and software-specific knowledge scattered across documentation, tools, and support channels. To address this problem, we designed and evaluated an agentic AI system tailored to the scientists' needs and integrated with the high-performance computing environment of European XFEL. Using a design science research approach, we conducted a rapid literature review, a systematic evaluation of 16 AI tools, multiple interviews, a focus group, and a user study with experts at European XFEL to develop and evaluate two prototypes. Our study identifies key knowledge challenges in scientific data analysis, derives requirements for an AI agent that supports knowledge retrieval and source code generation, and proposes design recommendations for a specialized system adaptable to the evolving AI tool landscape. These findings provide guidance for developing maintainable AI support in highly specialized scientific environments.

AI.tldr: Researchers at European XFEL designed and evaluated an agentic AI system to help scientists navigate fragmented documentation and generate analysis code for large, complex experimental datasets. Using design science research, they surveyed tools, interviewed experts, and ran user studies to derive requirements and design recommendations for specialized, maintainable AI support in high-performance scientific computing environments.
AI.motivation: Scientists at European XFEL face significant data analysis challenges because they must integrate deep domain expertise with facility-specific and software-specific knowledge that is scattered across disparate documentation, tools, and informal support channels. There is no unified system to support both knowledge retrieval and source code generation tailored to this highly specialized, high-performance computing context.
AI.method: The authors employed a design science research (DSR) methodology comprising: (1) a rapid literature review to ground the problem; (2) systematic evaluation of 16 existing AI tools; (3) multiple interviews and a focus group with European XFEL domain experts to elicit requirements; and (4) development and user-study evaluation of two iterative prototypes of an agentic AI system integrated with the facility's HPC environment.
AI.result: The study identified key knowledge challenges in scientific data analysis at large-scale facilities, derived concrete requirements for an AI agent supporting both knowledge retrieval and source code generation, and produced validated design recommendations for building a specialized, maintainable AI system that can adapt to the rapidly evolving AI tool landscape.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer actionable guidance for developing maintainable, domain-specific AI assistants in highly specialized scientific environments, demonstrating that agentic AI can effectively bridge the gap between fragmented institutional knowledge and the practical coding needs of experimental scientists.

title: ESCUCHA: A Spanish Speech Benchmark for Heterogeneous Acoustic Conditions
summary: As large audio language models (LALMs) advance, robust evaluation frameworks have become essential. In this context, Spanish speech understanding under realistic acoustic conditions has received particularly little attention. We introduce ESCUCHA, the first Spanish speech understanding benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs across heterogeneous acoustic conditions and reasoning abilities. ESCUCHA comprises 1,000 human-curated questions paired with audio, totaling 162.9 hours sourced directly ``from the wild'' rather than drawn from existing datasets, with durations ranging from a few seconds to over 80 minutes. The benchmark emphasizes reasoning, spanning 9 perceptual and 10 reasoning categories, and it captures linguistic diversity through multiple Spanish accents and non-normative speech. ESCUCHA further includes multi-audio questions, spoken questions, and audio instructions, and it flags which questions support open-ended evaluation. Benchmarking several state-of-the-art multimodal and speech models reveals substantial performance gaps relative to trained humans.

AI.tldr: ESCUCHA is a Spanish speech understanding benchmark with 1,000 human-curated audio questions (162.9 hours) from real-world sources, evaluating LALMs across 9 perceptual and 10 reasoning categories with diverse accents. State-of-the-art models show significant performance gaps compared to trained humans.
AI.motivation: Spanish speech understanding under realistic acoustic conditions is severely underexplored in LALM evaluation. Existing benchmarks lack heterogeneous acoustic conditions, reasoning-focused tasks, and linguistic diversity (multiple accents, non-normative speech) for Spanish.
AI.method: The authors construct ESCUCHA, a benchmark of 1,000 human-curated question-audio pairs sourced directly "from the wild" (not from existing datasets), totaling 162.9 hours. Audio durations span seconds to over 80 minutes. It covers 9 perceptual and 10 reasoning categories, includes multi-audio questions, spoken questions, audio instructions, and flags items supporting open-ended evaluation. Multiple SOTA multimodal and speech models are benchmarked against trained human performance.
AI.result: Benchmarking several state-of-the-art multimodal and speech models on ESCUCHA reveals substantial performance gaps compared to trained human evaluators.
AI.conclusion: ESCUCHA fills a critical gap in Spanish speech understanding evaluation, exposing significant limitations of current LALMs under realistic, acoustically diverse conditions and highlighting the need for models with stronger reasoning capabilities for non-English speech.

title: Scaling Limits of Constant-Stepsize SGD at Flat Minima
summary:
For stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a constant stepsize $α$, the invariant law of the iterates, centered at a minimizer, describes the behavior of the algorithm over long time horizons. In the strongly convex case, this invariant law has the familiar $\sqrtα$ scaling and a Gaussian limit as $α\downarrow 0$. We show that this behavior changes fundamentally for convex objectives $H$ with flat minima and (sub)quadratic tails.
  More specifically, we study SGD with Markovian noise generated by a contractive driving chain. For every sufficiently small constant stepsize $α$, we prove existence, uniqueness, and geometric convergence to an augmented invariant law in a Wasserstein distance induced by an $α$-dependent metric. When the minimizer $x_\star$ has local flatness exponent $m\ge2$, meaning that $\nabla^2 H(x)\asymp \lVert x-x_\star\rVert^{m-2} I_d$ as $x\to x_\star$, we obtain a contraction bound with factor $1-cα^{m-1}$, where $c>0$ is a constant. This recovers the factor $1-cα$ in the quadratic case $m=2$. We then analyze the small-stepsize scaling limit. We show that the invariant law concentrates on the scale $α^{1/m}$ and that the rescaled iterates converge weakly to the stationary distribution of the stochastic differential equation $$
  dY_t=-h_0(Y_t)\,dt+Σ^{1/2}\,dB_t , $$ where $h_0$ is the limiting drift at the minimizer and $Σ$ denotes the asymptotic covariance. This recovers the Gaussian limit when $m=2$ and gives generally non-Gaussian stationary limits in the flat case $m>2$. Finally, we give corresponding results for coordinate-separable objectives with unequal flatness exponents.

AI.tldr: For SGD with constant stepsize α, this paper establishes that when the objective has flat minima (Hessian degeneracy near the minimizer, with exponent m≥2), the invariant distribution concentrates at scale α^(1/m) rather than √α, and the limiting stationary distribution satisfies a specific SDE that is generally non-Gaussian when m>2, contrasting with the familiar Gaussian limit in the strongly convex case.
AI.motivation: Classical SGD analysis with constant stepsize in the strongly convex case yields an invariant law with √α scaling and a Gaussian limit as α↓0. This paper is motivated by understanding how this behavior fundamentally changes when the objective function has flat minima — specifically, convex objectives with (sub)quadratic tails and local flatness near the minimizer, which arise in modern machine learning (e.g., overparameterized models).
AI.method: The authors study SGD with Markovian noise from a contractive driving chain. They: (1) prove existence, uniqueness, and geometric convergence to an augmented invariant law in a Wasserstein distance with α-dependent metric for sufficiently small α; (2) derive a contraction bound with factor 1−cα^(m−1) where m≥2 is the local flatness exponent; (3) analyze the small-stepsize scaling limit showing concentration at scale α^(1/m); (4) prove weak convergence of rescaled iterates to the stationary distribution of the SDE dY_t = −h_0(Y_t)dt + Σ^(1/2)dB_t, where h_0 is the limiting drift; (5) extend results to coordinate-separable objectives with unequal flatness exponents.
AI.result: Key results: (i) For flatness exponent m≥2, contraction occurs at rate 1−cα^(m−1), recovering 1−cα for the quadratic case m=2. (ii) The invariant law concentrates on scale α^(1/m), not √α. (iii) Rescaled iterates converge weakly to an SDE stationary distribution that is Gaussian only when m=2 and generally non-Gaussian for m>2. (iv) Analogous results hold for coordinate-separable objectives with distinct flatness exponents per coordinate.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals a fundamental shift in SGD's long-time behavior when minimizing convex objectives with flat minima: the scaling transitions from √α to α^(1/m), the convergence rate degrades from 1−cα to 1−cα^(m−1), and the limiting distribution becomes non-Gaussian. These results provide a rigorous framework for understanding SGD dynamics in overparameterized settings where Hessian degeneracy is common.

title: Testing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems with Chunk Coverage
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based systems\footnote{For brevity, RAG-based systems are referred to as RAG systems throughout this paper.} are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings where correct behaviour depends not only on the language model but also on the retrieval component that selects external documents at inference time. While existing RAG evaluation metrics assess retrieval and generation quality on a per-query basis, typically relying on query-level test oracles such as reference answers or relevance annotations, they provide limited insight into whether a test suite adequately exercises the retrieval behaviour of the system as a whole. In this paper, we introduce Chunk Coverage (CC), an oracle-independent test adequacy criterion for testing the retrieval component of RAG systems. CC measures the fraction of corpus chunks that are retrieved at least once across a test suite, providing a structural view of which parts of the retrieval space have been exercised. We further show how CC can be used to guide test selection and generation by prioritising queries that expand coverage of previously unexercised retrieval regions. We evaluate CC on clinical and financial RAG system scenarios. CC-guided testing reaches 50% of attainable coverage 1.7x faster than random selection and 4.2x faster than redundancy-biased strategies. Moreover, CC improves fault detection effectiveness (APFD) by 10% to 25% over random, indicating earlier discovery of distinct retrieval faults. These results show that CC captures retrieval diversity relevant to effective testing without requiring test oracles.

AI.tldr: Introduces Chunk Coverage (CC), an oracle-independent test adequacy criterion for RAG systems that measures the fraction of corpus chunks retrieved across a test suite. CC-guided testing achieves coverage 1.7x faster than random and improves fault detection by 10-25%.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG evaluation metrics are per-query and oracle-dependent (reference answers, relevance annotations), offering no insight into whether a test suite comprehensively exercises the retrieval component. There is a need for a structural, oracle-independent adequacy criterion.
AI.method: Proposes Chunk Coverage (CC), measuring the fraction of corpus chunks retrieved at least once across a test suite. CC is used to guide test selection and generation by prioritizing queries that expand coverage of unexercised retrieval regions. Evaluated on clinical and financial RAG scenarios against random and redundancy-biased baselines.
AI.result: CC-guided testing reaches 50% of attainable coverage 1.7x faster than random selection and 4.2x faster than redundancy-biased strategies. Improves Average Percentage of Faults Detected (APFD) by 10-25% over random, enabling earlier discovery of distinct retrieval faults.
AI.conclusion: CC effectively captures retrieval diversity relevant to testing without requiring test oracles, providing a practical, structural adequacy metric for RAG system evaluation.

title: RRAM-DP: Device-Calibrated Differential Privacy for In-Memory Edge Learning
summary: Edge Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems often collect sensitive data in situ, raising serious privacy concerns. Resistive-switching random-access memory (RRAM) is an attractive substrate for efficient AIoT thanks to its multi-bit storage and compute-in-memory (CiM) capabilities, while its inherently stochastic write behavior provides a natural source of randomness that can be leveraged for differential privacy (DP) protection. Yet how to transform this device-level randomness-typically viewed as detrimental to accuracy-into a principled randomized mechanism while preserving model utility remains underexplored. We propose RRAM-DP, a hardware-algorithm co-design that relaxes RRAM write-verify operations to inject calibrated noise for inherently (epsilon, delta)-DP with formal DP analysis; together with pretraining techniques, it renders a novel private, high-utility CiM training paradigm. On CIFAR-10/100, STS-B, and SST-2, RRAM-DP-SGD incurs at best only a 3.8% accuracy drop at (epsilon=2, delta=O(1/n))-DP relative to non-private SGD. At the same privacy level, RRAM-DP-SGD delivers up to 57x and 3.2x energy savings and 2.7x and 1.8x speedups over A100 and DiVa-GEMM, respectively. These results point toward efficient, privacy-preserving in-memory training on RRAM at the edge.

AI.tldr: RRAM-DP leverages the inherent stochastic write behavior of RRAM devices — typically seen as a reliability flaw — to inject calibrated noise for formal differential privacy during in-memory training, achieving strong privacy guarantees with minimal accuracy loss and significant energy/speed gains over GPU and digital CiM baselines.
AI.motivation: Edge AIoT systems collect sensitive data locally, demanding privacy-preserving computation. RRAM is attractive for its multi-bit storage and compute-in-memory efficiency, but its stochastic write noise is conventionally treated as a problem. The key insight is to repurpose this device-level randomness as a principled source of DP noise, yet no prior work has formalized how to transform this uncontrolled physical randomness into a rigorous randomized mechanism with formal DP guarantees while maintaining model utility.
AI.method: RRAM-DP is a hardware-algorithm co-design that: (1) relaxes RRAM write-verify operations to allow controlled stochasticity during weight programming; (2) formally models the resulting noise injection as an (ε, δ)-DP randomized mechanism; (3) integrates pretraining techniques to mitigate the utility loss from noise; and (4) realizes a full private CiM training paradigm (RRAM-DP-SGD) that runs DP training directly on RRAM crossbar arrays.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10/100, STS-B, and SST-2, RRAM-DP-SGD achieves at best only a 3.8% accuracy drop at (ε=2, δ=O(1/n))-DP relative to non-private SGD. At the same privacy level, it delivers up to 57× and 3.2× energy savings and 2.7× and 1.8× speedups over NVIDIA A100 GPU and DiVa-GEMM (digital CiM baseline), respectively.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that RRAM's stochastic write behavior can be successfully transformed from a liability into a privacy asset, enabling efficient, privacy-preserving in-memory training at the edge with formal DP guarantees and competitive model accuracy.

title: AgentBrew: Lifelong Knowledge Brewing from Strong Teachers to Weak LLM Agents
summary: Deploying LLM agents typically requires a compact test-time student, even if a stronger teacher is available during training. We study knowledge brewing: distilling a teacher's interactive experience into a persistent external memory for the student. Crucially, this requires no weight updates, expert demonstrations, ground-truth labels, or test-time teacher access. This setting poses two challenges: environments provide only sparse, binary feedback, and teacher-authored notes must be inherently tailored to be concretely executable by a substantially weaker student. To address these hurdles, we propose AgentBrew, comprising two coupled components. First, a failure-triggered teacher--Ralph Loop mitigates sparse feedback by transforming student failures into environment-validated notes. Second, student-aware synthesis calibrates teacher knowledge to the weak executor's operational granularity, yielding model-specific, actionable guidance. Extensive evaluations and comprehensive ablations across coding, math, and tool-use tasks demonstrate that this asymmetric, training-free brewing paradigm produces highly capable yet deployable LLM agents.

AI.tldr: AgentBrew distills a teacher LLM's interactive experience into an external memory for a weaker student agent, without weight updates, expert demos, or test-time teacher access. It uses failure-triggered teacher feedback and student-aware synthesis to produce actionable, model-specific guidance from sparse binary environment signals.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLM agents typically requires compact, efficient student models, but leveraging a stronger teacher is only feasible during training. The key gap is how to transfer a teacher's interactive problem-solving experience to a substantially weaker student in a deployable way — without access to ground-truth labels, expert demonstrations, weight fine-tuning, or the teacher at test time — when the environment provides only sparse binary feedback (success/failure).
AI.method: AgentBrew introduces two coupled components: (1) A failure-triggered teacher loop ("Ralph Loop") that activates only upon student failures, transforming those failures into environment-validated, structured notes — addressing sparse binary feedback by grounding teacher-authored guidance in concrete environmental outcomes. (2) Student-aware synthesis that calibrates teacher knowledge to the specific operational granularity of the weaker student, ensuring notes are concretely executable rather than abstractly correct. Together, these build a persistent external memory that the student consults during test-time interaction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations and comprehensive ablations across coding, math, and tool-use benchmark tasks demonstrate that the asymmetric, training-free brewing paradigm produces highly capable yet deployable LLM agents. The student equipped with the brewed external memory significantly outperforms baselines, validating the effectiveness of failure-triggered teacher intervention and student-aware knowledge calibration.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge brewing is a viable, training-free paradigm for transferring teacher expertise to a weaker deployable student via persistent external memory. AgentBrew's dual mechanism — failure-triggered, environment-validated note generation plus student-aware synthesis — effectively overcomes sparse feedback and the capability gap between teacher and student, enabling practical deployment of capable LLM agents without test-time teacher dependence.

title: When a Name Is Not a Name: A Benchmark Dataset and Distilled Reasoning for Culturally Entangled Bangla Homographs in Low-Resource LLMs
summary: Many Bangla words are at once personal names and culturally loaded common nouns, "Maya" is both a girl's name and a word for affectionate compassion. Choosing the right reading demands cultural knowledge that is scarce in the pretraining data of modern language models. We introduce Culturally Entangled Homograph (CEH) disambiguation and build a Bangla benchmark of 1,516 expert-verified sentences (3,032 labelled occurrences) in which one word appears twice with two distinct readings, each labelled with a culturally grounded category and an explanation of the reasoning behind it. Across open- and closed-source models, we find a systematic dominant-meaning bias: models default to the common-noun sense and overlook the name. A Bangla-specific model fails under every prompting regime we test, showing that language-specific pretraining alone does not confer cultural grounding. We further show that contrastive chain-of-thought prompting can sharply reduce this bias without training, and that distilling cultural explanations teaches small (1-3B) models to reason toward the correct reading rather than memorise labels, cutting dominant-meaning bias from as high as 100% to under 5% and turning the failed Bangla-specific model into our strongest system. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/ashuvo25/BanglaCEH.

AI.tldr: Introduces Culturally Entangled Homograph (CEH) disambiguation for Bangla, where identical words can be personal names or common nouns. A benchmark of 1,516 sentences reveals models suffer from dominant-meaning bias (favouring common-noun readings). Contrastive chain-of-thought prompting and distillation of cultural explanations dramatically reduce this bias, transforming a failing Bangla-specific model into the best-performing system.
AI.motivation: Many Bangla words serve dual roles as personal names and culturally rich common nouns (e.g., "Maya" as a name vs. "compassion"). Disambiguating these requires cultural knowledge absent from standard pretraining data. Modern language models, even Bangla-specific ones, lack this cultural grounding, motivating a systematic study and mitigation of the resulting dominant-meaning bias.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 1,516 expert-verified Bangla sentences (3,032 labelled occurrences) where each target word appears twice with distinct readings, annotated with culturally grounded categories and reasoning explanations. They evaluate open- and closed-source models, test contrastive chain-of-thought prompting to reduce bias without training, and distill cultural explanations into small (1-3B) models to teach cultural reasoning rather than label memorisation.
AI.result: All models exhibit a systematic dominant-meaning bias, defaulting to the common-noun sense and overlooking the name reading. A Bangla-specific model fails under every prompting regime. Contrastive chain-of-thought prompting sharply reduces this bias. Distilling cultural explanations into small models cuts dominant-meaning bias from up to 100% to under 5%, turning the previously failing Bangla-specific model into the strongest system overall.
AI.conclusion: Language-specific pretraining alone does not confer cultural grounding. Explicit cultural reasoning — through contrastive prompting or distillation of explanations — is essential for resolving culturally entangled homographs. The work establishes CEH disambiguation as a new task and demonstrates that small models can learn to reason culturally, not merely memorise labels.

title: Retrieval is Enough: Training-Free Interpretability with a Tool-Using Agent
summary: Interpretability methods for neural network activations span a wide cost spectrum, from cheap, training-free techniques (such as linear probes, PCA, SVD) to more expensive training-based ones (such as SAEs and activation oracles). Training-based methods are typically more powerful, in part because they leverage large activation datasets during training. This raises a natural question - do they actually surface insights that go beyond what is recoverable from the training dataset itself? To address this, we equip an LLM agent with a vector database of activations paired with their textual contexts, along with tools for manipulating activations - projecting out directions in latent space, computing activation differences and averages. The agent iteratively queries the database, forms hypotheses from the retrieved samples, and validates them by constructing linear probes. We call this method HARP, for Hypothesis-driven Agentic Retrieval and Probing. Despite not involving any training, HARP outperforms both activation oracles and SAE-based agents on concept discovery, concept detection, model steering, and secret elicitation. The training-free design also makes HARP substantially cheaper and more flexible: new datasets can be indexed on demand whenever existing ones prove insufficient. More broadly, our results suggest that current training-based methods do not yet extract insights beyond their training data, and motivate benchmarks that explicitly require interpretability methods to demonstrate such insights. We release our code at https://github.com/SriramB-98/HARP

AI.tldr: HARP is a training-free interpretability method that gives an LLM agent access to a vector database of activations with textual contexts. The agent iteratively retrieves samples, forms hypotheses, and validates them via linear probes. Despite no training, HARP outperforms training-based methods (activation oracles, SAE-based agents) on concept discovery, detection, steering, and secret elicitation, suggesting current training-based methods do not extract insights beyond their training data.
AI.motivation: Training-based interpretability methods (SAEs, activation oracles) are powerful but expensive, and it is unclear whether they surface insights beyond what is already present in their training datasets. The authors aim to test whether a training-free approach leveraging the same datasets can match or exceed their performance, thereby questioning the added value of training.
AI.method: HARP (Hypothesis-driven Agentic Retrieval and Probing): an LLM agent is equipped with a vector database storing activations paired with textual contexts, plus tools for projecting directions in latent space and computing activation differences/averages. The agent iteratively queries the database, forms hypotheses from retrieved samples, and validates them by constructing linear probes — all without any training. New datasets can be indexed on demand.
AI.result: HARP outperforms both activation oracles and SAE-based agents across four tasks: concept discovery, concept detection, model steering, and secret elicitation — despite involving no training at all.
AI.conclusion: Current training-based interpretability methods do not yet extract insights beyond what is already in their training data. This motivates benchmarks that explicitly require methods to demonstrate novel insights beyond the data they were trained on. HARP is also cheaper and more flexible than training-based alternatives.

title: TRIM: Reducing AI-Generated CodeSlop via Agent Trajectory Minimization
summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to accelerate code generation in many downstream tasks, such as fixing bugs, building applications, and prototyping. However, despite their value as coding assistants, agent-generated code tends to be larger and more verbose than the corresponding human-written implementation. In this work, we show that the cause lies in the agent's own search process: while iterating toward a passing solution, an agent accumulates speculative edits, abandoned hypotheses, and temporary changes that persist into the final patch. This may seem harmless for a single patch, but the problem compounds as agents take responsibility for ever-larger portions of a codebase-a codebase that was once minimal and well-maintained slowly accumulates redundancy faster than it can be cleaned up, drifting to a state that is harder to maintain. Given the magnitude of this problem, we take a step towards alleviating this issue. First, we formally define this phenomenon as CodeSlop-the residual and functionally unnecessary edits commonly seen in AI-generated code. We then introduce our algorithm TRIM (Trajectory-guided Redundancy Identification and Minimization). Rather than minimizing CodeSlop directly, TRIM instead minimizes agent trajectories. As we show empirically, this indirect technique of minimizing CodeSlop is highly effective: TRIM cuts CodeSlop by 17.9%-32.9% across agentic scaffolds, with negligible performance regression. TRIM is also highly efficient, requiring roughly half the validation cost of algorithmic baselines such as Delta Debugging.

AI.tldr: Agent-generated code accumulates unnecessary "CodeSlop" — residual speculative edits from the search process. The paper introduces TRIM, which minimizes agent trajectories to indirectly reduce CodeSlop by 17.9–32.9% with minimal performance loss and half the cost of Delta Debugging.
AI.motivation: Coding agents produce verbose, bloated code because their iterative search process leaves behind speculative edits, abandoned hypotheses, and temporary changes. While benign in a single patch, this redundancy compounds across a codebase, degrading maintainability over time.
AI.method: The authors formally define "CodeSlop" as residual, functionally unnecessary edits in AI-generated code. They propose TRIM (Trajectory-guided Redundancy Identification and Minimization), an algorithm that indirectly minimizes CodeSlop by minimizing the agent's search trajectories rather than the final code directly.
AI.result: TRIM reduces CodeSlop by 17.9%–32.9% across agentic scaffolds with negligible performance regression. It is also approximately twice as efficient in validation cost compared to algorithmic baselines such as Delta Debugging.
AI.conclusion: Minimizing agent trajectories is an effective and efficient indirect strategy for reducing CodeSlop. This approach addresses a compounding maintainability problem as agents manage larger portions of codebases, offering a practical path toward cleaner AI-generated code.

title: Beyond Semantic Equivalence: Logical Graphs for LLM Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce confidently stated yet unreliable outputs, posing critical challenges for deployment in safety-sensitive applications. Existing uncertainty metrics such as semantic entropy capture agreement at the level of semantic equivalence, but largely ignore the logical relationships between distinct answers. As a result, they tend to overestimate uncertainty and falsely flag hallucinations in settings where generated responses are diverse in form yet logically compatible (e.g., differing only in granularity or specificity). We propose Logical Graph Uncertainty (LGU), a framework that explicitly models implication and incompatibility among answers. LGU aggregates probability mass along entailment chains, computes entropy over logically maximal hypotheses, and penalizes mutual incompatibility among them. Across multiple question-answering benchmarks, LGU consistently improves uncertainty estimation over existing methods, and outperforms the semantic entropy baseline by up to +7.1% AUROC and +3.5% AUARC across datasets.

AI.tldr: LGU improves LLM uncertainty estimation by modeling logical relationships (implication/incompatibility) among generated answers, outperforming semantic entropy by up to +7.1% AUROC.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty metrics like semantic entropy treat semantically distinct answers as mutually exclusive, ignoring logical relationships. This causes overestimation of uncertainty and false hallucination flags when outputs are diverse in form but logically compatible (e.g., differing only in specificity).
AI.method: LGU constructs a logical graph over generated answers, modeling entailment (implication) and incompatibility relations. It aggregates probability mass along entailment chains, computes entropy over logically maximal hypotheses, and penalizes mutual incompatibility among those hypotheses.
AI.result: LGU consistently improves uncertainty estimation over existing methods across multiple QA benchmarks, achieving up to +7.1% AUROC and +3.5% AUARC improvements over the semantic entropy baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling logical relationships between answers yields more reliable uncertainty estimates than semantic-equivalence-based approaches alone, making LGU a promising direction for safer LLM deployment.

title: Zero Hallucination, by Construction: Hallucination-Aware Layered Oversight for Trustworthy Enterprise AI
summary: Enterprises will not deploy AI agents they cannot trust, and the most-cited reason for distrust is hallucination: confident, fluent output that is simply not true. The common response is to wait for a model that does not hallucinate. We argue that this is the wrong target. Large language models are, by construction, capable of generating unsupported text, and no amount of scale removes the possibility; a faithfulness judge bolted onto a raw model catches some errors but still ships others, and even well-curated retrieval pipelines have been shown to fabricate citations. We reframe the goal: "zero hallucination" is not a property a model possesses but a property a system enforces. We present HALO (Hallucination-Aware Layered Oversight), an assurance architecture which treats hallucination as a containable failure mode rather than an eliminable one. HALO composes six layers of defense: grounded generation over retrieved, approved content; constrained, deterministic execution that bounds where the model can err; multi-signal verification that scores every output for groundedness and hallucination using both an LLM judge and evidence-based checks against the source text; calibrated abstention, so the system declines rather than guesses when grounding is insufficient; total traceability of every retrieval, tool call, and generation; and continuous oversight that detects drift, alerts on threshold breaches, and closes the loop by regenerating and statistically validating improved agents. We detail each layer, give particular attention to evidence-based confidence (which verifies extractions against the source document rather than trusting the model's self-reported certainty), and illustrate the architecture on a regulated claims-extraction workload

AI.tldr: HALO reframes hallucination in LLMs as a containable system-level failure rather than an eliminable model property, proposing a six-layer assurance architecture that composes grounded generation, constrained execution, multi-signal verification, calibrated abstention, total traceability, and continuous oversight to enforce trustworthiness.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI adoption is blocked by distrust stemming from hallucination — confident, fluent, but false outputs. The authors argue that pursuing a hallucination-free model is misguided because LLMs are inherently capable of generating unsupported text regardless of scale. Instead, hallucination should be treated as a system-enforced property rather than a model-intrinsic property.
AI.method: The HALO (Hallucination-Aware Layered Oversight) architecture composes six defensive layers: (1) grounded generation over retrieved, approved content; (2) constrained, deterministic execution to bound error surfaces; (3) multi-signal verification using both an LLM judge and evidence-based checks against source text; (4) calibrated abstention that triggers refusal when grounding is insufficient; (5) total traceability of every retrieval, tool call, and generation; and (6) continuous oversight with drift detection, threshold-based alerting, and closed-loop regeneration with statistical validation.
AI.result: The architecture is illustrated on a regulated claims-extraction workload, with particular emphasis on evidence-based confidence scoring that verifies extractions against source documents rather than relying on the model's self-reported certainty. The paper details each layer's design and interaction.
AI.conclusion: Zero hallucination is properly understood as a property a system enforces, not a property a model possesses. HALO demonstrates that a layered assurance architecture can contain hallucination as a manageable failure mode, offering a practical path toward trustworthy enterprise AI deployment without waiting for hallucination-free models that may never arrive.

title: EA-RMENet -- Path Loss Prediction in Urban Environments using Deep Learning
summary: Accurate path loss prediction is a critical component of wireless network planning. Current path loss prediction methods typically struggle to balance the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. This paper proposes the Efficient Attention Radio Map Estimation Network (EA-RMENet) which is an image data-driven, deep learning (DL) model designed for radio map estimation (RME). EA-RMENet uses a U-Net framework with an EfficientNetB5 encoder, Attention Gated (AG) skip connections, and Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP). The EfficientNet encoder uses compound scaling to balance accuracy and efficiency. AG skip connections suppress irrelevant features, and the ASPP captures a multi-scale context. The model has a test prediction RMSE of 0.0334 on the RadioMapSeer3D dataset with an inference time of 0.022 seconds/sample. In the ICASSP 2023 Radio Map Prediction Challenge, the model ranks third with a competitive RMSE of 0.0406 this highlights the models potential for real-world RME.

AI.tldr: EA-RMENet proposes a U-Net-based deep learning model with EfficientNetB5 encoder, attention-gated skip connections, and ASPP for fast and accurate radio map estimation, achieving strong benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: Existing path loss prediction methods struggle to balance accuracy and computational efficiency. A data-driven solution is needed that delivers both high predictive accuracy and low inference latency for practical wireless network planning.
AI.method: EA-RMENet employs a U-Net architecture with three key components: (1) an EfficientNetB5 encoder using compound scaling for accuracy-efficiency balance, (2) Attention Gated (AG) skip connections to suppress irrelevant features, and (3) Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) to capture multi-scale contextual information. The model is trained as an image data-driven DL approach for radio map estimation.
AI.result: The model achieves a test RMSE of 0.0334 on the RadioMapSeer3D dataset with an inference time of 0.022 seconds per sample. It ranked third in the ICASSP 2023 Radio Map Prediction Challenge with an RMSE of 0.0406.
AI.conclusion: EA-RMENet demonstrates strong potential for real-world radio map estimation by combining high accuracy with fast inference, validated by competitive results in both standard benchmarks and an international challenge.

title: Environment-free Synthetic Data Generation for API-Calling Agents
summary: Training API-calling large language model (LLM) agents demands massive amounts of high-quality trajectories. However, collecting such data at scale typically requires fully implemented environments with executable APIs and realistic, pre-populated backend databases, creating a major bottleneck for scalability. To overcome this, we propose an environment-free synthetic data generation approach that leverages LLMs as on-the-fly digital world models. Given only API specifications, our method generates trajectories mimicking interactions between an agent and a stateful environment. Specifically, an LLM first generates diverse tasks solvable with the provided APIs. A teacher agent then iteratively solves each task while an LLM simulator generates coherent synthetic API responses conditioned on the task context and simulation history. Finally, an LLM judge filters the trajectories to ensure the quality of the resulting dataset. We evaluate our approach on the challenging AppWorld and OfficeBench benchmarks, which include both information-retrieval and state-changing tasks. Fine-tuning models on our synthetic data yields significant performance gains, demonstrating that effective supervision for API-calling agents can be generated without any executable environment. Our results establish LLM-based API simulation as a practical, scalable solution for training agents across diverse API ecosystems.

AI.tldr: An environment-free synthetic data generation method for training API-calling LLM agents, using LLMs as digital world models to simulate trajectories from API specs alone, achieving significant performance gains on AppWorld and OfficeBench without executable environments.
AI.motivation: Training LLM agents to call APIs requires massive high-quality interaction trajectories, but collecting such data at scale demands fully implemented environments with executable APIs and pre-populated backend databases, creating a severe scalability bottleneck.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) an LLM generates diverse solvable tasks from API specifications; (2) a teacher agent iteratively solves each task while an LLM simulator produces coherent synthetic API responses conditioned on task context and interaction history; (3) an LLM judge filters trajectories to ensure dataset quality.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on the synthetic data yields significant performance gains on the challenging AppWorld and OfficeBench benchmarks, covering both information-retrieval and state-changing tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based API simulation is a practical, scalable solution for generating effective supervision for API-calling agents across diverse API ecosystems, eliminating the need for executable environments entirely.

title: DeLIVeR: Decomposed Learning for Information-grounded Veracity Recognition via Reinforced Knowledge Graph Exploration
comment: Accepted to 7th International Conference on Deep Learning Theory and Applications (DeLTA 2026)
summary: Automated fact-checking remains a challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to "query brittleness" in traditional retrieval systems. We propose DeLIVeR (Decomposed Learning for Information-grounded Veracity Recognition), a framework that treats evidence retrieval as a reinforced strategic exploration task. DeLIVeR utilizes a Planner LLM to decompose complex claims into targeted question sets, which are used to traverse structured Knowledge Graphs (KGs) for high-precision evidence. We optimize the Planner's policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward system prioritizing structural diversity and verdict accuracy. Our evaluation on LIAR, FEVER, and PolitiFact shows that DeLIVeR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Using Qwen2.5-7B, our framework achieved peak F1-scores of 83.73, 84.57, and 79.70 respectively, representing a 10-15% improvement over HippoRAG2. By shifting to a reinforced question-planning strategy, DeLIVeR effectively bridges multi-hop reasoning gaps and provides an auditable, transparent path for verifiable misinformation detection.

AI.tldr: DeLIVeR is a framework that uses a Planner LLM with reinforcement learning (GRPO) to decompose claims into targeted questions for traversing knowledge graphs, significantly outperforming baselines like HippoRAG2 on fact-checking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional retrieval-based fact-checking systems suffer from "query brittleness," where minor formulation differences yield inconsistent evidence. LLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning and lack transparent, auditable evidence chains. The authors aim to replace brittle retrieval with a reinforced, strategic question-planning approach.
AI.method: DeLIVeR (Decomposed Learning for Information-grounded Veracity Recognition) employs a Planner LLM that decomposes complex claims into targeted question sets, which traverse structured Knowledge Graphs (KGs) for high-precision evidence retrieval. The Planner's policy is optimized using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward system that prioritizes structural diversity (encouraging varied question types) and verdict accuracy. The framework uses Qwen2.5-7B as the backbone.
AI.result: On LIAR, FEVER, and PolitiFact benchmarks, DeLIVeR achieved peak F1-scores of 83.73, 84.57, and 79.70 respectively, representing a 10-15% improvement over the HippoRAG2 baseline.
AI.conclusion: Shifting to a reinforced question-planning strategy effectively bridges multi-hop reasoning gaps and provides an auditable, transparent path for verifiable misinformation detection, outperforming state-of-the-art retrieval-based methods.

title: Compact convolutional neural networks for AI-based drone detection system
summary: The increasing use of first-person-view drones in modern conflicts has created a demand for compact and reliable detection systems capable of operating in complex electromagnetic environments. These drones continuously transmit video signals through onboard video transmitters, generating radio-frequency emissions that can be exploited for early detection. This study investigates the use of lightweight convolutional neural networks for automated detection of drone signals captured by a software-defined radio-based electronic warfare framework. Samples are converted into rasterized time-domain images, providing a computationally efficient input representation suitable for embedded systems. Several custom model architectures were designed and benchmarked in terms of accuracy, model size, and inference performance using a dataset containing approximately 40,000 labeled images. In addition to offline testing, the models were integrated into a GNU Radio signal processing chain for real-time evaluation. The results show that compact models can achieve high detection accuracy while maintaining low computational requirements, making them suitable for embedded radio-frequency monitoring applications. Compared with existing spectrogram-based RF detection methods, the proposed approach eliminates frequency-domain preprocessing and achieves comparable accuracy with significantly reduced computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight CNN-based approach for detecting FPV drone signals using rasterized time-domain images, eliminating spectrogram preprocessing and enabling real-time embedded deployment via SDR and GNU Radio.
AI.motivation: Modern conflicts increasingly employ first-person-view (FPV) drones, creating an urgent need for compact, reliable, and computationally efficient detection systems that can operate in complex electromagnetic environments and run on embedded hardware.
AI.method: The authors capture drone RF emissions using a software-defined radio (SDR)-based electronic warfare framework, convert raw samples into rasterized time-domain images (bypassing frequency-domain preprocessing), and train several custom lightweight CNN architectures on a labeled dataset of ~40,000 images. Models are benchmarked on accuracy, size, and inference speed, then integrated into a GNU Radio signal processing chain for real-time evaluation.
AI.result: Compact CNN models achieved high detection accuracy while maintaining low computational requirements. The time-domain image approach matched the accuracy of existing spectrogram-based methods while significantly reducing computational cost by eliminating FFT preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: Rasterized time-domain images paired with lightweight CNNs offer a viable, efficient alternative to spectrogram-based RF drone detection, well-suited for embedded real-time monitoring applications.

title: Lomekwi: Resource-Bounded Tool Discovery in LLM Agents
comment: All authors contributed equally. 17 pages, 6 figures. Presented at the 2026 Conference on Learning Theory Workshop on Learning in an Agentic World
summary: Existing tool-use benchmarks report a single success rate for complex, multistep tasks. Inspired by ideas from cognitive science, we distinguish tool use from tool discovery and decompose the latter into curiosity (the model's ability to discover the parts needed to build the tool), recognition (the model's ability to discover the process of creating the tool), and efficiency (the model's use of the tool after creation). We show that this framework can be applied to existing discovery tasks, such as Voyager. In addition, we provide evidence that recognition inversely scales with model size, and we introduce and analyze a class of combinatorial games that demonstrates this. We further observe inverse scaling in a separate environment designed to emulate real-world tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cognitive-science-inspired framework that decomposes tool discovery into curiosity, recognition, and efficiency, applies it to existing benchmarks, and presents evidence that recognition ability inversely scales with model size across both combinatorial games and real-world task environments.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-use benchmarks only report a single, undifferentiated success rate for complex multistep tasks, obscuring the distinct cognitive sub-processes involved. The authors aim to disentangle tool use from tool discovery to better understand and evaluate model capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a tripartite decomposition of tool discovery: (1) curiosity — discovering the parts needed to build a tool; (2) recognition — discovering the process of creating the tool; and (3) efficiency — using the tool after creation. They apply this framework to existing discovery tasks (e.g., Voyager), analyze a class of combinatorial games to study scaling behavior, and validate findings in a separate environment emulating real-world tasks.
AI.result: The framework successfully applies to existing tool-discovery benchmarks like Voyager. Critically, recognition ability exhibits inverse scaling with model size — larger models perform worse at discovering how to create tools. This inverse scaling pattern is demonstrated in both combinatorial games and a real-world task environment.
AI.conclusion: Tool discovery is not a monolithic capability and should be evaluated along distinct dimensions. The inverse scaling of recognition with model size suggests that larger models may struggle with certain aspects of tool discovery, warranting further investigation into why this occurs and how to mitigate it.

title: What Transfers Under Source Shift? Definitions, Examples, and Fine-Tuning for Climate Disclosure Classification
summary: Climate disclosure classification is a fundamental task for analysing corporate climate disclosures, yet such disclosures appear in many different sources -- annual reports, press releases, and earnings calls -- that differ in length, purpose, and writing style. Existing evaluations are mostly conducted within a single source, leaving open whether common LLM adaptation strategies remain effective under source shift. We reframe climate disclosure classification as a cross-source adaptation problem and study three widely used adaptation strategies -- definitions, examples, and fine-tuning -- across eleven open- and closed-source LLMs, using two corpora that share the same label space but come from different sources. We find that all strategies bring positive cross-source gains on average, but the strongest in-source strategies are not the strongest cross-source ones: similarity-based retrieval and LoRA fine-tuning gain most in-source but lose most of that advantage under source shift; randomly selected few-shot examples, a weaker in-source baseline, retain their advantage more reliably; definitions transfer most consistently, though only when their granularity matches the target text. Across these strategies, when the source changes, simpler is often safer.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes climate disclosure classification as a cross-source adaptation problem, evaluating three LLM adaptation strategies (definitions, examples, fine-tuning) across 11 models under source shift. The key finding: simpler strategies transfer more reliably — definitions transfer best when granularity matches the target, and randomly selected few-shot examples retain advantages better than stronger in-source methods like similarity-based retrieval or LoRA fine-tuning, which degrade most under domain shift.
AI.motivation: Climate disclosures appear across diverse sources (annual reports, press releases, earnings calls) with different lengths, purposes, and styles. Existing evaluations are single-source, leaving it unclear whether common LLM adaptation strategies remain effective when the source shifts. The authors aim to close this gap by systematically studying cross-source transfer.
AI.method: The study frames climate disclosure classification as cross-source adaptation. Eleven open- and closed-source LLMs are evaluated using two corpora sharing the same label space but originating from different sources. Three adaptation strategies are compared: (1) definitions provided in prompts, (2) few-shot examples (both randomly selected and similarity-based retrieval), and (3) parameter-efficient fine-tuning via LoRA. Performance is measured both in-source and cross-source to quantify transfer gains and degradation.
AI.result: All three strategies yield positive average cross-source gains. However, the strongest in-source strategies (similarity-based retrieval and LoRA fine-tuning) lose most of their advantage under source shift. Randomly selected few-shot examples, though weaker in-source, retain advantages more reliably. Definitions transfer most consistently, but only when their granularity matches the target text's characteristics. The overarching pattern: simpler adaptation methods prove safer under source shift.
AI.conclusion: When adapting LLMs for climate disclosure classification across different sources, simpler strategies are often safer. Definitions offer the most consistent transfer, provided granularity alignment holds. Practitioners should be cautious about over-optimizing for in-source performance when cross-source deployment is expected, as complex methods like retrieval-augmented few-shot and LoRA fine-tuning are more brittle under distribution shift.

title: K-IPO: Kendall-constrained Importance Preserving Oversampling for Imbalanced Tabular Data
summary: Oversampling is widely used to address class imbalance in tabular classification, but existing methods can distort the feature importance ranking underlying model explanations. Although recent studies have quantified this distortion by comparing real and synthetic data, none have actively sought to prevent it. In this paper, we introduce Kendall-constrained Importance-Preserving Oversampling (K-IPO), a generator-agnostic, "generate-then-select" framework that preserves the original data's feature importance ranking during augmentation. K-IPO iteratively generates minority-class candidates and accepts them only if their inclusion maintains a user-defined minimum Kendall's tau (τ) correlation with the reference ranking. Optionally, stricter constraints can be applied to the highest-ranked features. We evaluated K-IPO on 20 imbalanced binary classification datasets using three classifiers and multiple explanation methods. In most cases, K-IPO achieved the best or tied-best results in feature importance preservation, explanation consistency, and class separability. It also generally improved predictive performance while maintaining competitive computational overhead.

AI.tldr: K-IPO is a "generate-then-select" oversampling framework that preserves feature importance rankings by accepting synthetic minority samples only when they maintain a minimum Kendall's τ correlation with the original data's feature importance ranking, achieving state-of-the-art preservation of explanation consistency without sacrificing predictive performance.
AI.motivation: Existing oversampling methods for class imbalance distort feature importance rankings, undermining model explainability. While prior work has measured this distortion, no method has actively prevented it during the augmentation process.
AI.method: K-IPO is a generator-agnostic, iterative framework: minority-class candidates are generated (by any oversampler), then accepted only if their inclusion keeps the Kendall's τ correlation between the new and original feature importance rankings above a user-defined threshold. Optional stricter constraints can target the highest-ranked features specifically.
AI.result: Evaluated on 20 imbalanced binary classification datasets with three classifiers and multiple explanation methods, K-IPO achieved best or tied-best results in feature importance preservation, explanation consistency, and class separability in most cases, while generally improving predictive performance with competitive computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: K-IPO effectively bridges the gap between data augmentation for class imbalance and model explainability, offering a principled, plug-and-play solution that preserves feature importance structures during oversampling.

title: Privacy Cost as Equity Input: A Group Fairness Criterion for Differentially Private Machine Learning
summary: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly deployed to limit membership inference risk in machine-learning systems. Prior work has shown that DP-SGD can widen accuracy disparities across demographic groups, but this framing treats fairness as a purely outcome-side concern. We argue that privacy cost, the information leakage borne by each group, is itself a form of harm, and adopt a compensatory-fairness framework in which a group that involuntarily bears greater privacy exposure is owed proportionally greater benefit from the system. From this principle we derive the \emph{Privacy-Cost Equity Ratio} (PCER), a group fairness metric defined as a group's positive prediction rate normalized by its per-group overfitting gap. By a standard membership inference bound, this overfitting gap upper-bounds each group's vulnerability to inference attacks, making PCER a conservative measure of benefit relative to exposure. PCER needs only per-group train and test accuracy (no shadow models), making it a practical post-hoc audit tool. We evaluate PCER alongside standard fairness metrics across six benchmark--attribute combinations spanning tabular and NLP domains, under DP-SGD at a range of privacy budgets, and validate the overfitting-gap proxy against a direct threshold membership-inference attack. The results reveal patterns that outcome-based metrics miss. On COMPAS, PCER uncovers a persistent double disadvantage: the protected group bears both greater privacy exposure and worse predictive outcomes, something demographic parity gap masks entirely. Sensitivity analysis shows very strong privacy guarantees collapse both groups' overfitting to a numerical floor, rendering exposure-based audits uninformative in that regime. Together, these findings show that fairness audits of privacy-preserving systems must account for who bears the cost of protection, not only who benefits from its outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Privacy-Cost Equity Ratio (PCER), a group fairness metric that measures benefit (positive prediction rate) relative to privacy exposure (per-group overfitting gap). Unlike outcome-only fairness metrics, PCER treats differential privacy leakage as a form of harm, operationalizing a compensatory fairness principle: groups bearing greater involuntary privacy risk deserve proportionally greater system benefit. Evaluated across tabular and NLP benchmarks under DP-SGD, PCER reveals inequities missed by standard metrics, such as a double disadvantage on COMPAS.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats fairness in DP systems purely as an outcome-side concern (e.g., accuracy disparities). The authors argue that differential privacy leakage itself constitutes a distributional harm: different groups may bear unequal privacy costs. A compensatory fairness framework is needed, where groups involuntarily exposed to greater information leakage should receive proportionally greater predictive benefit from the model.
AI.method: The authors introduce PCER, defined as a group's positive prediction rate divided by its per-group overfitting gap (train accuracy minus test accuracy). The overfitting gap upper-bounds membership inference vulnerability via a standard DP bound, serving as a conservative proxy for privacy exposure without requiring shadow models. PCER is evaluated post-hoc across six benchmark-attribute combinations (tabular and NLP) under DP-SGD at varying privacy budgets. They validate the overfitting proxy against a direct threshold membership inference attack and conduct sensitivity analysis across the full privacy budget spectrum.
AI.result: On COMPAS, PCER reveals a double disadvantage — the protected group suffers both greater privacy exposure and worse predictive outcomes — which demographic parity gap completely masks. Under very strong privacy guarantees (small ε), both groups' overfitting collapses to a numerical floor, making exposure-based audits uninformative. PCER consistently surfaces privacy-cost inequities that outcome-only metrics fail to detect.
AI.conclusion: Fairness audits of privacy-preserving ML systems must account for who bears the cost of protection, not merely who benefits from outcomes. PCER provides a practical, lightweight tool for this purpose, though its utility diminishes under very strong DP regimes where overfitting signals collapse.

title: Training Continuous Chain of Thought Models: A Tale of Two Regimes
summary: Continuous Chain-of-Thought methods replace verbose reasoning traces with a short sequence of dense latent representations. Earlier continuous CoT methods indirectly supervise the latent representations such that its final state match that of verbose reasoning traces, requiring autoregressive, slow generation during training. We introduce C-MTP, a simpler, faster direct supervision approach that models each latent as an average of the embeddings in the CoT traces to be compressed. Our approach outperforms a prior direct supervision method that approximates the distribution of compressed tokens, and performs competitively to slower indirect supervision approaches in existing evaluation setup with simplified CoT traces (less than 100 tokens). Lastly, we extend the evaluation of Continuous CoT methods to complex tasks with longer reasoning traces ($\ge$ few hundreds reasoning tokens). We find both direct and indirect supervision training methods perform poorly (roughly 65\% performance drop) in this setting, revealing the limitations of current continuous CoT methods. The code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/Varun221/cmtp_research

AI.tldr: C-MTP introduces a faster direct supervision method for Continuous Chain-of-Thought that models latent representations as averages of CoT token embeddings, outperforming prior direct methods and competing with slower indirect methods on short traces, while revealing that all current continuous CoT methods suffer severe performance degradation (~65% drop) on complex tasks with longer reasoning traces.
AI.motivation: Existing continuous Chain-of-Thought methods rely on indirect supervision that requires slow autoregressive generation during training. The authors aim to develop a simpler, faster direct supervision approach while also evaluating the scalability of continuous CoT methods to complex tasks with significantly longer reasoning traces.
AI.method: C-MTP models each dense latent representation as the average of embeddings from the CoT reasoning trace to be compressed. This constitutes a direct supervision approach that avoids autoregressive training. The method is evaluated against prior direct supervision (approximating compressed token distributions) and indirect supervision baselines across both simplified short CoT traces (<100 tokens) and complex long CoT traces (≥ few hundred tokens).
AI.result: On simplified CoT traces (<100 tokens), C-MTP outperforms prior direct supervision methods and performs competitively with slower indirect supervision approaches. However, on complex tasks with longer reasoning traces (≥few hundred tokens), both direct and indirect supervision methods exhibit roughly a 65% performance drop, exposing fundamental limitations of current continuous CoT approaches.
AI.conclusion: C-MTP offers a more efficient direct supervision alternative for continuous CoT, but the dramatic performance collapse on long reasoning traces reveals that current continuous CoT paradigms do not scale effectively to complex reasoning, highlighting a critical open challenge for the field.

title: An Early Warning of Emerging Biosecurity Risks in Frontier LLMs
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, authors are listed alphabetically by surname
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into scientific workflows, yet their growing biological capabilities may outpace current safeguards. To assess the biological risks of frontier models, we develop Intern-BioBreaker, a specialized bio-red-teaming model, together with an integrated computational-to-physical framework that couples model-level stress testing with wet-lab validation. Within this framework, Intern-BioBreaker generates targeted jailbreak prompts to test whether aligned models can be induced to provide operational guidance for safety-sensitive biological tasks or produce sequence-level outputs with potentially harmful properties. Selected sequence outputs are then carried forward for DNA synthesis, host expression, and orthogonal protein verification to assess whether model-generated designs can yield the intended biological products. Our evaluation reveals a concerning gap between text-level safeguards and the risks posed by capable scientific models: (i) Intern-BioBreaker outperforms baseline attack models and reveals widespread bio-risk jailbreak vulnerabilities across both open-weight and proprietary frontier LLMs, with several targets reaching near-saturated or 100% task-level attack success rate (ASR); (ii) in sequence-level case studies, GPT-5.5 can be induced to generate modified viral candidate sequences with pathogenic potential; the corresponding translated proteins may exhibit even stronger receptor-binding affinity and thus enhanced infection potential; and (iii) end-to-end verification shows that selected model-generated biological designs are not merely textual artifacts, but can be physically realized under controlled experimental settings. These findings underscore the need for stronger biological red-teaming, nucleic acid synthesis screening, and safety mechanisms that keep pace with model capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Intern-BioBreaker, a specialized red-teaming model for probing biological risks in frontier LLMs, combined with a computational-to-physical validation pipeline. The study reveals widespread jailbreak vulnerabilities, demonstrates that GPT-5.5 can generate viral sequences with enhanced pathogenic potential, and confirms through wet-lab experiments that model-generated biological designs can be physically realized.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs are increasingly used in scientific workflows, but their growing biological capabilities may outpace existing safeguards. There is an urgent need to systematically assess whether aligned models can be induced to provide dangerous biological guidance or generate harmful sequence-level outputs, and whether such outputs pose real-world risks beyond mere text.
AI.method: The authors develop Intern-BioBreaker, a bio-red-teaming model that generates targeted jailbreak prompts. They couple this with an integrated computational-to-physical framework: (1) model-level stress testing to measure attack success rates across open-weight and proprietary LLMs, (2) sequence-level case studies of generated viral candidates, and (3) end-to-end wet-lab validation including DNA synthesis, host expression, and orthogonal protein verification.
AI.result: Intern-BioBreaker outperforms baseline attack models, revealing widespread jailbreak vulnerabilities with near-saturated or 100% ASR on several targets. GPT-5.5 generates modified viral sequences with pathogenic potential, and translated proteins show enhanced receptor-binding affinity. Wet-lab verification confirms that model-generated biological designs can be physically realized under controlled settings.
AI.conclusion: The gap between text-level safeguards and actual biological risks is significant. Stronger biological red-teaming, nucleic acid synthesis screening, and safety mechanisms are urgently needed to keep pace with advancing model capabilities.

title: Leakage-Robust Evaluation and Data-Scale Sensitivity of Attention-Enhanced Multi-Task Learning for Joint Fault Diagnosis and Remaining Useful Life Estimation
summary: Multi-task deep learning models that jointly perform fault classification and remaining useful life (RUL) regression are increasingly used in predictive maintenance, yet reported performance can be strongly affected by how sliding-window sequences are split into training and test sets. We investigate this issue using AMTLNet, an attention-enhanced multi-task architecture, on three public benchmarks: NASA C-MAPSS, NASA IMS, and the UCI Hydraulic System dataset. We show that naive splitting can inflate classification accuracy from a genuine 20-60 percent to 99.9 percent, or reduce it to 0 percent through degenerate class representation. To address this, we introduce a chunk-based, leakage-audited splitting protocol and evaluate all models using five seeds, one-way ANOVA, and Tukey HSD tests. On C-MAPSS, with 19,976 leakage-free training windows, AMTLNet matches a single-task CNN-LSTM baseline in classification, achieving 84.12 +/- 0.96 percent accuracy with Tukey p = 1.0, and reaches an R2 of 0.86 +/- 0.01 while significantly outperforming a naive multi-task baseline. On the smaller Bearing and Hydraulic datasets, multi-task training is unstable, but the failure mode differs: classification degrades for Bearing, whereas regression degrades for Hydraulic. We relate this asymmetry to label provenance and propose a practical framework for deciding when joint training is appropriate under data scarcity. Ablation results show that the multi-head attention branch is the main contributor to regression stability. Removing it reduces R2 from 0.861 to 0.766 and more than doubles classification variance, whereas the convolutional branch contributes little to regression despite using about one-third of the parameters. This study contributes a reusable leakage-audit protocol, seed-transparent evaluation, and evidence that task-specific stability depends more on label provenance than on task type.

AI.tldr: Sliding-window data splitting can catastrophically inflate or deflate multi-task model performance in predictive maintenance. The authors propose a leakage-audited splitting protocol, conduct rigorous statistical evaluation, and reveal that multi-task training stability depends more on label provenance than on task type, with attention mechanisms being the key driver of regression stability.
AI.motivation: Multi-task deep learning for simultaneous fault classification and RUL regression is increasingly popular in predictive maintenance, but reported performance metrics are unreliable due to uncontrolled data leakage from naive sliding-window splitting. No prior work has systematically quantified this leakage, proposed audited splitting protocols, or examined how label provenance affects multi-task stability across diverse datasets.
AI.method: The authors use AMTLNet (an attention-enhanced multi-task architecture with shared CNN-LSTM backbone, multi-head attention branch, and convolutional branch) evaluated on three public benchmarks (NASA C-MAPSS, NASA IMS, UCI Hydraulic System). They introduce a chunk-based, leakage-audited splitting protocol ensuring no temporal overlap between train/test windows. Evaluation uses five random seeds with one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD tests. Ablation studies isolate contributions of the attention and convolutional branches. They also analyze failure mode asymmetry (classification vs. regression degradation) across small datasets.
AI.result: Naive splitting inflates classification accuracy from a genuine 20-60% to 99.9% or collapses it to 0%. With leakage-free splitting on C-MAPSS (19,976 training windows), AMTLNet achieves 84.12±0.96% accuracy (Tukey p=1.0 vs. single-task baseline) and R²=0.86±0.01, significantly outperforming a naive multi-task baseline. On smaller Bearing/Hydraulic datasets, multi-task training is unstable but asymmetrically: classification fails on Bearing, regression fails on Hydraulic. Removing the multi-head attention branch drops R² from 0.861 to 0.766 and more than doubles classification variance; the convolutional branch contributes little to regression despite using ~1/3 of parameters.
AI.conclusion: Data leakage from improper sliding-window splitting can completely invalidate multi-task performance claims. The proposed leakage-audited protocol provides a reusable safeguard. Task-specific stability under data scarcity depends on label provenance rather than task type (classification vs. regression). Attention mechanisms, not convolutional branches, are the primary contributor to regression stability in multi-task architectures.

title: Expected Free Energy as Belief-Dependent Utility for rho-POMDPs
comment: 41 pages, 12 figures. Paper accepted as a spotlight at the 2026 International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI); the workshop version will appear in the Springer Communications in Computer and Information Science (CCIS) series. Code and experiment data at https://github.com/PatrickAllenCooper/rho_aif
summary: An agent acting under partial observability must decide when to gather information and which observations are worth their cost. Standard POMDPs value information only through its eventual effect on reward. The $ρ$-POMDP framework instead rewards uncertainty reduction directly, through a belief-dependent utility $ρ$, but in practice both the choice of $ρ$ and the weight placed on it are tuned by hand for every task. We show that active inference removes this tuning entirely. Minimizing Expected Free Energy (EFE) is exactly equivalent to solving a $ρ$-POMDP whose utility is expected information gain, and the exploration weight is fixed at $w=1$ because the variational bound expresses pragmatic and epistemic value in the same units (nats). We prove this equivalence for observe-then-commit POMDPs and extend it to factored observation POMDPs, a broader class that covers interleaved observe-act problems such as non-destructive testing and mobile sensing, where gathering information leaves the hidden state unchanged. Experiments support the theory. Across environments ranging from the classic Tiger problem to RockSample and a new Structural Inspection benchmark with over 65,000 states, the untuned weight matches or outperforms reward-only planning at the same horizon, avoids the over-exploration of bonuses tuned per task, and sits near the reward-maximizing knee of the success-reward Pareto frontier. The practical payoff is an exploration objective that works out of the box. In applications such as fault detection and medical screening, where every test has a price and every missed fault has a cost, EFE supplies a belief-dependent utility that is derived rather than tuned.

AI.tldr: Active inference's Expected Free Energy (EFE) is proven equivalent to a ρ-POMDP with expected information gain as utility and weight w=1, eliminating the need for hand-tuned exploration parameters. This equivalence holds for observe-then-commit and factored observation POMDPs, and experiments show untuned EFE matches or outperforms tuned baselines across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard POMDPs value information only indirectly through reward, while existing ρ-POMDPs require hand-tuning of both the belief-dependent utility function ρ and its weight for every task. The authors aim to show that active inference's EFE removes this tuning burden entirely by providing a principled, derived utility function for information-seeking behavior.
AI.method: The authors prove a formal equivalence between minimizing EFE and solving a ρ-POMDP where ρ is expected information gain and the exploration weight is fixed at w=1 (since variational bound expresses pragmatic and epistemic value in shared nats). The proof covers observe-then-commit POMDPs and is extended to factored observation POMDPs, which accommodate interleaved observe-act problems. Experiments validate the theory on Tiger, RockSample, and a new Structural Inspection benchmark (65,000+ states).
AI.result: The untuned EFE weight (w=1) matches or outperforms reward-only planning at the same horizon, avoids over-exploration caused by per-task bonus tuning, and sits near the reward-maximizing knee of the success-reward Pareto frontier. The approach works out-of-the-box across all tested environments.
AI.conclusion: EFE provides a derived, principled exploration objective that eliminates hand-tuning in information-seeking POMDPs.
