This is practically significant for applications like fault detection and medical screening, where each test incurs a cost and each missed fault carries a penalty — EFE supplies belief-dependent utility natively rather than requiring manual specification.

title: Pancasila-Dilemmas: Evaluating Large Language Models on Indonesian Human Value Dilemmas Grounded in Pancasila
summary: The value alignment of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for ensuring responses align with human intention and value preferences. However, most evaluations of value alignment focus on Western or universal values, while assessments grounded in the value systems of specific countries remain scarce. In this paper, we introduce Pancasila-Dilemmas, an evaluation dataset of 1,834 questions derived from Indonesian news, classified by 5 values of Pancasila: Religion, Humanity, Unity, Democracy, and Social Justice. This dataset reflects daily life in Indonesia, making it suitable for measuring the value alignment of LLMs deployed for Indonesia. To ensure a more rigorous evaluation, we choose scenarios containing dilemmas. The dataset is proofread by native speakers and answered by 5 diverse Indonesian citizens. We evaluate 50 closed- and open-source LLMs on our dataset. Results reveal that all evaluated LLMs achieves less than 0.5 Probability Match Score (PMS) and 0.72 Max-Vote Agreement Score (MVAS). Compared by each values, LLMs mostly struggle in Religion and Unity dilemma cases. This highlights a significant gap in capturing Indonesian values. The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Pancasila-Dilemmas.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Pancasila-Dilemmas, a dataset of 1,834 dilemma-based questions from Indonesian news categorized by five Pancasila values (Religion, Humanity, Unity, Democracy, Social Justice). Evaluating 50 LLMs reveals poor alignment with Indonesian values, with all models scoring below 0.5 Probability Match Score and 0.72 Max-Vote Agreement Score, particularly struggling with Religion and Unity.
AI.motivation: Most value alignment evaluations for LLMs focus on Western or universal values, with a notable lack of assessments grounded in country-specific value systems, particularly for Indonesia.
AI.method: The authors construct Pancasila-Dilemmas, a dataset of 1,834 questions sourced from Indonesian news, classified by the five Pancasila principles. Dilemma scenarios are deliberately chosen for rigor. The dataset is proofread by native speakers and annotated by five diverse Indonesian citizens. Evaluation is conducted on 50 closed- and open-source LLMs using two metrics: Probability Match Score (PMS) and Max-Vote Agreement Score (MVAS).
AI.result: All evaluated LLMs achieve below 0.5 PMS and below 0.72 MVAS, indicating poor alignment with Indonesian values. Per-value analysis shows models struggle most with Religion and Unity dilemmas.
AI.conclusion: There exists a significant gap in LLMs' ability to capture and reflect Indonesian values, underscoring the need for country-specific value alignment efforts.

title: Feedback Attribution and Representation Geometry: Metrics for Comparing Individual and Shared Rewards in MARL
comment: Accepted at the Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback Workshop, ICML 2026
summary: Cooperative multi-agent RL systems routinely use team-averaged rewards, a feedback-attribution choice that gives each agent the team outcome regardless of its individual contribution. We ask whether this leaves a measurable signature, geometric or behavioral, on learned representations. We propose EffRank/$n$ (effective rank normalized by agent count) and $D_\text{act}$ (mean pairwise KL divergence between agents' action distributions) as low-overhead diagnostics for reward-attribution effects, then test them on competent MAPPO agents in SMACv2 \texttt{protoss\_5\_vs\_5}, where unit type is encoded in the observation. In an observation $\times$ reward-attribution comparison (unit type observed vs.\ masked; individual damage-contribution reward vs.\ shared team reward), geometry follows observation rather than reward. With unit type observed, shared and individual rewards have similar EffRank/$n$ ($0.31{\pm}0.03$ vs.\ $0.29{\pm}0.02$) and probe accuracy ($0.75{\pm}0.05$ vs.\ $0.73{\pm}0.05$, both $\gg 1/3$ chance), while $D_\text{act}$ leans higher under individual rewards ($1.23{\pm}0.06$ vs.\ $1.07{\pm}0.20$). Masking unit type cuts the above-chance probe signal by more than half, to $0.49$ in both reward arms. In short: individually rewarded agents are competent and separable by role, but on SMACv2 the observation explains the geometry and reward attribution shows up mainly in behavior. Thus geometric diagnostics must control for observed role information and test persistent roles that are not directly observed. EffRank/$n$ and $D_\text{act}$ add $<$5\% overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether shared vs. individual reward attribution in cooperative MARL leaves measurable signatures in learned representations. Using SMACv2, the authors find that representation geometry is primarily shaped by observation (unit type identity), not reward scheme. Individual rewards produce more divergent action distributions ($D_\text{act}$) but similar representational structure (EffRank/$n$). Two lightweight diagnostics are proposed: EffRank/$n$ and $D_\text{act}$.
AI.motivation: Cooperative multi-agent RL commonly uses team-averaged rewards, where each agent receives the same team outcome regardless of individual contribution. The authors question whether this credit-assignment blurring leaves a detectable geometric or behavioral signature in learned agent representations, and whether such effects can be measured with low-overhead diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors propose two diagnostics: (1) EffRank/$n$ — effective rank of the agent representation matrix normalized by agent count, measuring representational diversity; and (2) $D_\text{act}$ — mean pairwise KL divergence between agents' action distributions, measuring behavioral specialization. These are evaluated on MAPPO agents in SMACv2 protoss_5_vs_5 under a 2×2 design: unit type observed vs. masked, crossed with individual damage-contribution reward vs. shared team reward. Linear probes are also used to assess whether agent role is decodable from representations.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) With unit type observed, shared and individual rewards yield similar EffRank/$n$ (0.31±0.03 vs. 0.29±0.02) and similar probe accuracy (0.75±0.05 vs. 0.73±0.05, both well above 1/3 chance). (2) $D_\text{act}$ leans higher under individual rewards (1.23±0.06 vs. 1.07±0.20). (3) Masking unit type reduces above-chance probe signal by more than half (to ~0.49 in both arms). (4) Representational geometry follows observation, not reward attribution; reward effects manifest primarily in behavior. Both diagnostics incur <5% computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: In SMACv2, observation (unit type) dominates representation geometry, while reward attribution mainly affects action distributions. Researchers using geometric diagnostics must control for observed role information and test scenarios with persistent but unobserved roles. EffRank/$n$ and $D_\text{act}$ provide efficient, complementary tools for this analysis.

title: PriorProof: A Point-in-Time Measure of Technique Novelty for Formal Proofs
summary: Mathematicians distinguish proofs that explain, simplify, or introduce a nonstandard route, but these judgments are difficult to operationalize. We study a deliberately narrower construct: time-relative proof-route nonstandardness in formal mathematics. For a Lean theorem, PriorProof extracts the dependency footprint of its elaborated proof term and scores the weighted surprisal of that footprint under a retrieval-conditioned, hierarchically smoothed prior built only from an earlier quarterly snapshot of Mathlib. The method requires no hand-built technique ontology and no human labels: statement retrieval is learned from proof-derived contrastive pairs, while the scored object is read mechanically from proof terms. In a blinded topology study, 100 presentations collapse to 76 distinct underlying pairs: 12 canonical contrasts shown three times for consistency screening and 64 distinct stratified pairs. Against the majority of three retained domain raters, PriorProof agrees on 53/76 pairs (69.7%, Wilson 95% CI 58.7-78.9%), including 11/12 canonical pairs (91.7%, 64.6-98.5%) and 42/64 stratified pairs (65.6%, 53.4-76.1%). Score-gap quartiles are nonmonotone after repeat collapse; the endpoints are 12/19 (63.2%, 41.0-80.9%) in the smallest-gap bin and 16/19 (84.2%, 62.4-94.5%) in the largest, supporting an endpoint-calibration tendency rather than a resolved staircase. The best language-model condition agrees on 60/76 pairs (78.9%, 68.5-86.6%); on paired outcomes, PriorProof alone is correct on 8 pairs and the model alone on 15 (exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.210), so the difference is not established at this sample size. We therefore present PriorProof not as a replacement for expert or model judgment, but as a decomposable, time-anchored signal whose score gap provides an interpretable reliability indicator.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PriorProof, a method that quantifies the nonstandardness of formal proof routes in Lean by computing the weighted surprisal of a proof's dependency footprint against a time-anchored prior built from an earlier Mathlib snapshot. In a blinded topology study, PriorProof achieves 69.7% agreement with domain raters and provides an interpretable, decomposable signal whose score gap indicates reliability.
AI.motivation: Mathematicians intuitively distinguish explanatory, simplifying, or nonstandard proofs, but operationalizing these judgments is difficult. The authors narrow this to a tractable construct — time-relative proof-route nonstandardness in formal mathematics — to provide an objective, automated signal that requires neither hand-built technique ontologies nor human labels.
AI.method: PriorProof extracts the dependency footprint from a Lean theorem's elaborated proof term and scores its weighted surprisal under a hierarchically smoothed prior. This prior is built exclusively from an earlier quarterly snapshot of Mathlib (time-anchoring). Statement retrieval is learned from proof-derived contrastive pairs, and scoring is read mechanically from proof terms. The method is evaluated via a blinded topology study: 100 presentations collapse to 76 distinct pairs (12 canonical contrasts for consistency screening, 64 stratified pairs), rated by three domain raters and compared against a language-model baseline.
AI.result: PriorProof agrees with the majority of raters on 53/76 pairs (69.7%, Wilson 95% CI 58.7–78.9%), including 11/12 canonical pairs (91.7%) and 42/64 stratified pairs (65.6%). Score-gap quartiles show nonmonotonicity but endpoint calibration: 63.2% agreement in the smallest-gap bin vs. 84.2% in the largest. The best language model achieves 78.9% agreement; PriorProof alone is correct on 8 pairs where the model errs, while the model alone is correct on 15 (McNemar p = 0.210, difference not statistically significant).
AI.conclusion: PriorProof is not a replacement for expert or model judgment but a decomposable, time-anchored signal whose score gap provides an interpretable reliability indicator. The endpoint-calibration pattern suggests the gap is useful for identifying high-confidence cases, even if it does not form a smooth monotonic scale.

title: Modeling turn-taking with distant viewing: investigating silence thresholds in human and AI-generated discourse
comment: 10 pages, MeSSH26 (Méthodes pour les sciences sociales et les humanités - Methods for social sciences and humanities 2026)
summary: This study investigates silence gaps in two kinds of audiovisual material. We analysed thirty US situational comedies and fifty-one synthetic podcasts generated with Google NotebookLM. Gaps were compared across speaker gender, assigned from a fundamental-frequency threshold estimated in Praat, and across production settings.

AI.tldr: The study compares silence gaps in US sitcoms versus AI-generated podcasts, analyzing differences by speaker gender (determined via fundamental frequency in Praat) and production context.
AI.motivation: To investigate how silence gaps — an important prosodic and interactional feature — vary across human-produced (sitcoms) and synthetically-generated (NotebookLM podcasts) audiovisual materials, with attention to speaker gender and production setting as potential modulating factors.
AI.method: Thirty US situational comedies and fifty-one synthetic podcasts produced with Google NotebookLM were analyzed for silence gaps. Speaker gender was assigned using a fundamental-frequency (F0) threshold estimated in Praat, and gaps were compared across gender categories and production settings (human vs. synthetic).
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract; the abstract only describes the corpus and analytical approach without reporting outcome measures.
AI.conclusion: Not specified in the abstract; conclusions would depend on the empirical findings comparing silence gap patterns across gender and production modalities.

title: Hierarchical Domain Generalization
summary: We study hierarchical domain generalization as a problem of extrapolation from finite observed regions to an entire instance space, replacing i.i.d. sampling with arbitrary domain hierarchies. We show that the central obstruction is not only the complexity of the hypothesis class, but the train/test domain partition through which evidence is revealed. In particular, no matter how small the class or how large the training size, some partition makes generalization fail for some target. These results suggest that modern generalization theory must treat domain structure as a first-class object.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes hierarchical domain generalization as extrapolation from finite observed regions to the full instance space, demonstrating that train/test domain partitioning—not just hypothesis class complexity—is the central obstruction to generalization. The authors prove that for any hypothesis class and training size, there exists a partition that causes generalization failure, arguing that domain structure must be a first-class object in generalization theory.
AI.motivation: Current domain generalization theory predominantly focuses on hypothesis class complexity and i.i.d. assumptions, neglecting how domains are structured and partitioned. The authors aim to expose a fundamental limitation: the way training and testing domains are divided fundamentally constrains generalization, independent of model capacity or dataset size.
AI.method: The paper formalizes hierarchical domain generalization as extrapolation from a finite set of observed regions in instance space to unobserved regions, using arbitrary domain hierarchies instead of i.i.d. sampling. It provides theoretical proofs demonstrating that for any hypothesis class (no matter how small) and any training sample size (no matter how large), there exists some train/test domain partition under which generalization fails for at least one target domain.
AI.result: The central result is a no-free-lunch-style impossibility theorem: no learner can guarantee generalization across all possible domain partitions, regardless of hypothesis class simplicity or training data abundance. The obstruction is the partition structure itself, not class complexity.
AI.conclusion: Modern generalization theory must elevate domain structure to a first-class object of study. Future theoretical frameworks should explicitly model how domain hierarchies and partitions constrain learnability, rather than relying solely on complexity measures developed under i.i.d. assumptions.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Trajectory Data Curation for LoRA Fine-Tuning of Code Agents
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures. Author's accepted manuscript of a paper published in the ICIC 2026 proceedings (oral presentation)
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of open-weight LLMs on expert agent trajectories has emerged as a prominent approach to building capable code agents without reliance on proprietary models. A central yet underexplored question is how trajectory quality and quantity jointly shape model performance. We present a systematic empirical study of trajectory data filtering for LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on the SWE-trajectory dataset (67,074 trajectories, of which 32,161 are resolved). We propose a two-axis quality scoring framework -- Efficiency and Style -- and evaluate it through 16 controlled experiments spanning strategy, scale, and ablation analyses. Since 7B-scale models attain near-zero SWE-bench resolve rates, we adopt cross-entropy (CE) loss on held-out trajectories as the primary metric, validated via first-action generation: CE loss and ROUGE-L are perfectly rank-correlated (Spearman $ρ$ = -1.00), with limited-sample evidence supporting but not conclusively establishing this proxy. Our results reveal a scale-dependent quality-quantity trade-off: at small scales, doubling the dataset (500 to 1,000) yields ~12.7% CE-loss reduction whereas the TopQ-Random gap stays <1% (Mann-Whitney p > 0.10); at 2,000 trajectories this same gap widens to 3.6% (p = 0.016). Ablation further identifies error-retry rate as the dominant sub-dimension, performing comparably to the full composite ($Δ$ < 0.2%). Together, these findings establish trajectory-level quality scoring as a viable but scale-sensitive lever for code-agent SFT and offer a proxy-validated evaluation protocol for the regime where end-to-end resolve rate is statistically infeasible.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies how trajectory quality and quantity jointly affect LoRA fine-tuning of a 7B code LLM, proposing a two-axis scoring framework (Efficiency and Style) and revealing a scale-dependent quality-quantity trade-off where quality filtering benefits only emerge at sufficient data scales, with error-retry rate as the dominant quality sub-dimension.
AI.motivation: SFT on expert agent trajectories is widely used to build capable code agents, yet how trajectory quality and quantity jointly shape model performance remains underexplored. Additionally, at 7B-scale, models achieve near-zero SWE-bench resolve rates, making direct end-to-end evaluation infeasible and necessitating proxy metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-axis quality scoring framework (Efficiency and Style) applied to the SWE-trajectory dataset (67,074 trajectories). They conduct 16 controlled LoRA fine-tuning experiments on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, varying dataset size and quality filtering strategies. Since resolve rates are near-zero, they use cross-entropy loss on held-out trajectories as the primary proxy metric, validated against first-action ROUGE-L (Spearman ρ = -1.00). Statistical comparisons use Mann-Whitney U tests to assess TopQ vs. Random gaps across scales.
AI.result: A scale-dependent quality-quantity trade-off emerges: at 500→1,000 trajectories, doubling data yields ~12.7% CE-loss reduction while the TopQ-Random gap stays under 1% (p > 0.10); at 2,000 trajectories, the quality gap widens to 3.6% (p = 0.016). Ablation shows error-retry rate alone performs comparably to the full composite score (Δ < 0.2%). CE loss and ROUGE-L are perfectly rank-correlated, supporting CE as a valid proxy.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level quality scoring is a viable but scale-sensitive lever for code-agent SFT: quality filtering yields statistically significant gains only at sufficient data scales. The error-retry rate is the dominant quality sub-dimension. The proxy-validated evaluation protocol using CE loss offers a practical alternative when end-to-end resolve rates are statistically infeasible.

title: Learning-Driven Adaptive Audit Scheduling: A Sequential Decision Approach to Off-Chain Data Integrity
summary: We model cryptographic auditing of off-chain data as a Constrained MDP (CMDP) under partial observability: the storage node's hidden type and corruption state make the problem a POMDP, while a miss-rate ceiling rho imposes an explicit security constraint. We propose DRQN-CMDP, a Deep Recurrent Q-Network whose GRU layer maintains a belief over the latent node type, paired with Lagrangian dual ascent that adapts the miss-rate penalty lambda automatically. A pairing-free homomorphic-MAC primitive supplies O(1) on-chain verification cost. Across 13 methods--four DQN variants, PPO, A2C, PPO-Lagrangian, a stateful Bayesian heuristic, three fixed-rule baselines, and an oracle-informed heuristic--DRQN-CMDP achieves a favourable balance: 83% lower gas than fixed high-frequency auditing, single-digit miss rate (7.5%), and moderate detection latency--a combination no other method matches across all three objectives simultaneously.

AI.tldr: The paper frames off-chain data auditing as a Constrained POMDP and proposes DRQN-CMDP—a Deep Recurrent Q-Network with Lagrangian dual ascent—paired with a homomorphic MAC for O(1) on-chain verification. It achieves 83% lower gas costs, 7.5% miss rate, and moderate detection latency, outperforming 13 baselines across all three objectives simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Cryptographic auditing of off-chain data (e.g., in blockchain storage) requires balancing three competing objectives: minimizing on-chain verification gas costs, keeping the miss rate below a security threshold, and maintaining acceptable detection latency. The storage node's type (honest vs. malicious) and corruption state are hidden, making the problem a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with explicit security constraints that existing methods cannot jointly satisfy.
AI.method: The authors model the auditing problem as a Constrained MDP under partial observability (CMDP-PO), where a miss-rate ceiling ρ serves as the explicit constraint. The proposed DRQN-CMDP architecture uses a GRU layer within a Deep Recurrent Q-Network to maintain a belief distribution over the latent node type, paired with Lagrangian dual ascent to adaptively tune the miss-rate penalty λ. A pairing-free homomorphic-MAC primitive provides constant O(1) on-chain verification cost. The evaluation compares against 13 methods: four DQN variants, PPO, A2C, PPO-Lagrangian, a stateful Bayesian heuristic, three fixed-rule baselines, and an oracle-informed heuristic.
AI.result: DRQN-CMDP achieves a Pareto-superior trade-off: 83% lower gas costs compared to fixed high-frequency auditing, a single-digit miss rate of 7.5%, and moderate detection latency. No other method among the 13 baselines simultaneously matches this performance across all three objectives.
AI.conclusion: DRQN-CMDP demonstrates that combining recurrent belief-state modeling with constrained RL (Lagrangian dual ascent) effectively solves the off-chain auditing problem under partial observability and explicit security constraints. The homomorphic-MAC primitive further ensures practical on-chain efficiency, making the approach viable for real-world blockchain storage auditing.

title: Reward-Driven LLM Agent Workflows: Synthesizing POMDP Routing and Self-Correction for Autonomous Decision-Making
comment: 29 pages, 1 table, native TikZ/pgfplots diagrams. Code available at https://github.com/01Amez/RLAW_Implementation
summary: This paper addresses key technical challenges in current large language model (LLM) agent applications, including long-horizon planning, sparse reward attribution, and dynamic environmental interaction, by designing and optimizing an intelligent agent workflow. The proposed architecture is based on the synthesis of core AI paradigms: Visual, Language, Generative, Graph, Multimodal, Reinforcement, and Agent Intelligence. Unlike conventional baseline models that rely on static prompting and lack robust perception-action loops, our approach introduces a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) routing mechanism. This mechanism is augmented with an internal, self-correcting reward model that evaluates decision trajectories before execution. By integrating multimodal inputs and advanced reinforcement learning principles (such as proximal policy optimization and value function approximation), the agent maintains long-term structural memory and dynamically adapts its reasoning pathways to mitigate error accumulation. Empirical experiments on the ALFWorld embodied simulation environment and the WebShop online navigation benchmark demonstrate a 24.5% absolute improvement in task success rate and trajectory efficiency over mainstream baselines like the standard ReAct framework. Comprehensive ablation studies confirm the significant contribution of the reward-driven critique module in suppressing hallucination rates. This research bridges theoretical foundations of reinforcement learning and graph-based memory with autonomous agent workflows. Ultimately, the resulting architecture offers a practical, scalable reference framework for developing artificial intelligence technologies in complex, multi-step autonomous systems. Code is available at https://github.com/01Amez/RLAW_Implementation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an intelligent agent architecture integrating POMDP-based routing with a self-correcting reward model, achieving a 24.5% absolute improvement in task success rate on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks over standard ReAct baselines.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent applications suffer from three core challenges: (1) long-horizon planning difficulties, (2) sparse reward attribution that hinders effective learning, and (3) dynamic environmental interaction where static prompting fails to support robust perception-action loops, leading to error accumulation.
AI.method: The authors design an agent workflow synthesizing seven AI paradigms (Visual, Language, Generative, Graph, Multimodal, Reinforcement, and Agent Intelligence). The core innovation is a POMDP routing mechanism augmented with an internal self-correcting reward model that evaluates decision trajectories pre-execution. It employs proximal policy optimization and value function approximation for policy learning, maintains long-term structural memory via graph-based representations, and integrates multimodal inputs to dynamically adapt reasoning pathways.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves a 24.5% absolute improvement in task success rate and trajectory efficiency over mainstream baselines (specifically the ReAct framework) on the ALFWorld embodied simulation and WebShop online navigation benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm the reward-driven critique module significantly suppresses hallucination rates.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges reinforcement learning and graph-based memory theory with practical autonomous agent workflows, offering a scalable reference architecture for complex multi-step autonomous systems. The code is publicly released.

title: VDAR-Router: Adaptive LLMs Routing via Verbalized Query Difficulty Analysis Retrieval
summary: Large language models are increasingly used in practical systems, making efficient model selection important for reducing deployment cost. LLM routing has emerged as a practical solution for allocating each input query to an appropriate model under a desired cost-performance trade-off. Existing routing methods often estimate model suitability from the surface semantics or embedding similarity of the input query. However, such methods may ignore the underlying difficulty of a query, leading to suboptimal routing decisions. To address the challenge, we propose VDAR-Router, a difficulty-aware retrieval-based routing framework. For each input query, VDAR-Router first generates an explicit difficulty analysis. It then retrieves historical examples with similar difficulty profiles. Based on the retrieved records, it estimates candidate model suitability and selects the model using a reward function that considers both performance and cost. Experiments on three datasets show that VDAR-Router consistently achieves better cost-performance trade-offs than existing baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of difficulty-aware retrieval for training-free LLM routing. Case studies further show that explicit query analysis helps retrieve more relevant examples and supports more reliable routing decisions.

AI.tldr: VDAR-Router introduces difficulty-aware retrieval for LLM routing, using explicit query difficulty analysis and historical example retrieval to achieve better cost-performance trade-offs than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM routing methods rely on surface semantics or embedding similarity, which overlook the underlying difficulty of input queries, causing suboptimal model allocation. There is a need for routing that accounts for query difficulty to improve cost-performance trade-offs.
AI.method: VDAR-Router performs three steps: (1) generates explicit difficulty analysis for each query, (2) retrieves historical examples with similar difficulty profiles from a stored record base, and (3) estimates candidate model suitability from retrieved records and selects the optimal model using a reward function balancing performance and cost. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets show VDAR-Router consistently achieves better cost-performance trade-offs than existing baselines. Case studies demonstrate that explicit query analysis enables retrieval of more relevant examples and supports more reliable routing decisions.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty-aware retrieval is an effective approach for training-free LLM routing. Explicitly modeling query difficulty helps retrieve relevant historical examples, leading to more reliable and cost-effective model selection decisions.

title: Building2Building: A Large Scale Benchmark for Generalizable Real-World Reinforcement Learning
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, to be published at RLC 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong results in control, yet learned policies remain brittle to changes in dynamics, action spaces, observation spaces, or goals, a critical limitation for real-world deployment. Existing benchmarks offer limited diversity and complexity, making it difficult to rigorously study transfer, multi-task learning, and meta-learning in RL. We introduce Building2Building (B2B), a large-scale suite of realistic Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) control environments built on EnergyPlus, a state-of-the-art building simulator. B2B is fully compatible with the Gymnasium interface and features a parametric building generator, enabling the systematic generation of diverse building configurations with heterogeneous observation and action spaces. Based on this suite, we define benchmark tasks targeting key open challenges in RL, including goal adaptation, dynamics adaptation, action-space shifts, and cross-domain transfer. By providing a large-scale, diverse, and physically grounded testbed with standardized evaluation protocols, B2B enables systematic investigation of generalization and transfer in continuous control. Beyond advancing research on generalization in RL, this new benchmark also carries significant societal implications by enabling improved HVAC control at scale, one of the most energy-intensive systems in buildings.

AI.tldr: Building2Building (B2B) is a large-scale RL benchmark suite for HVAC control built on EnergyPlus, featuring a parametric building generator that produces diverse configurations with heterogeneous observation/action spaces, designed to systematically study generalization, transfer, multi-task learning, and meta-learning in reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: RL policies are brittle to changes in dynamics, action spaces, observation spaces, or goals, and existing benchmarks lack the diversity and complexity needed to rigorously study transfer and generalization. There is a need for a physically grounded, large-scale testbed to systematically investigate these open challenges.
AI.method: The authors introduce B2B, a suite of realistic HVAC control environments built on the EnergyPlus building simulator. It is fully Gymnasium-compatible and includes a parametric building generator that systematically creates diverse building configurations with heterogeneous observation and action spaces. Standardized benchmark tasks are defined targeting goal adaptation, dynamics adaptation, action-space shifts, and cross-domain transfer.
AI.result: B2B provides a large-scale, diverse, and physically grounded testbed with standardized evaluation protocols, enabling systematic investigation of generalization and transfer in continuous control. (The abstract does not report specific experimental results, as this is a benchmark/methodology paper.)
AI.conclusion: B2B fills a critical gap in RL benchmarking by offering a realistic, diverse, and scalable testbed for studying generalization, with the added societal benefit of enabling improved HVAC control — a major energy consumer in buildings.

title: When LLMs Over-Answer: Measuring and Mitigating Quality Issues in LLM-Based Hardware Description Language Question Answering
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has led practitioners to increasingly rely on them for answering questions about hardware description languages (HDLs). Because HDL is ultimately synthesized into physical hardware, an imprecise or redundant answer can propagate into timing violations or non-synthesizable logic that surface only late in the design flow, making the quality of HDL answers especially consequential. However, the quality of LLM-generated responses, particularly in comparison with answers provided by human experts, remains unclear. To investigate this question, we collect 6,246 HDL Q&A posts with accepted answers from Stack Overflow and curate them into a dataset, organized into a taxonomy of four main categories (Conceptual, Debugging, Generation, and Optimization) and ten subcategories. Using this dataset, we design a user study conducted with 19 HDL engineers with one to three years of experience. Our findings reveal a pervasive over answering tendency: LLMs supply correct content but bury it under redundant alternatives (65.7%) and verbose padding (69.1%), while nearly half of answers (49.0%) fail to fully align with expert answers yet participants still preferred LLM responses for readability (58.3%). Motivated by these findings, we propose a multi-agent framework for improving LLM-based HDL question answering. We evaluate answer quality using an LLM-as-Judge and two structural metrics: the number of core answers, which reflects redundancy since LLMs often provide multiple alternative solutions, and the length of non-core content, which reflects verbosity. Evaluated on the four mainstream LLMs, our framework increases the average core-answer quality score from 3.71 to 4.67 (+0.96) and the non-core content quality from 3.72 to 4.23 (+0.51), on a five-point scale.

AI.tldr: A study comparing LLM-generated HDL answers to human expert answers on Stack Overflow finds LLMs over-answer—burying correct content under redundant alternatives (65.7%) and verbose padding (69.1%). Despite 49% of answers not fully aligning with experts, participants preferred LLM responses for readability (58.3%). The authors propose a multi-agent framework that improves core-answer quality from 3.71 to 4.67 and non-core quality from 3.72 to 4.23 on a 5-point scale.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for HDL (hardware description language) question answering, but imprecise or redundant answers can propagate into timing violations or non-synthesizable logic discovered only late in the design flow. The quality of LLM-generated HDL answers relative to human expert answers is unclear, motivating a systematic investigation and improvement.
AI.method: (1) Curated a dataset of 6,246 HDL Q&A posts with accepted answers from Stack Overflow, organized into a taxonomy of 4 main categories (Conceptual, Debugging, Generation, Optimization) and 10 subcategories. (2) Conducted a user study with 19 HDL engineers (1–3 years experience) to compare LLM vs. human expert answers. (3) Proposed a multi-agent framework to improve LLM-based HDL answering. (4) Evaluated using LLM-as-Judge and two structural metrics: number of core answers (redundancy) and length of non-core content (verbosity), across four mainstream LLMs on a 5-point scale.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit pervasive over-answering: 65.7% redundant alternatives, 69.1% verbose padding; 49.0% of answers fail to fully align with expert answers. Yet participants preferred LLM responses 58.3% of the time for readability. The proposed multi-agent framework improved average core-answer quality from 3.71 to 4.67 (+0.96) and non-core content quality from 3.72 to 4.23 (+0.51).
AI.conclusion: LLMs over-answer HDL questions with redundant and verbose content that, while preferred for readability, often misaligns with expert answers—posing risks for hardware design. The proposed multi-agent framework effectively mitigates these issues, substantially improving both core-answer and non-core content quality across mainstream LLMs.

title: How Does Alignment Tuning Shape Representations of Sycophancy and Related Cue-Induced Biases in LLMs?
summary: Modern LLMs are alarmingly susceptible to surprisingly simple immaterial changes of input prompts: a casual hint, an incorrectly labeled few-shot example, or a fake prior assistant turn often flips an originally correct answer. We study where this susceptibility, spanning sycophancy and related cue-induced biases, lives inside the model. Across five model families and seven BCT bias types, we extract a per-bias direction from hidden states and triangulate it through three measures: probing, leave-one-dataset-out transfer, and causal intervention. The susceptibility is largely installed by alignment tuning rather than pretraining: pretrained base models barely cave to these biases, and their activations carry no cue-specific signal beyond question content. Within aligned models, each bias becomes a single coherent direction that we can both decode and steer along, recovering the unbiased answer across every family we test. The biases stay representationally distinct, however: cross-bias entanglement is model-specific rather than a property of the bias category, and even behaviorally similar biases occupy different directions. The same intervention also serves as a modest debiasing tool, recovering a meaningful share of bias-induced errors while preserving most correct answers across all instruct families. Cue-induced bias is therefore best understood not as a single flaw in LLMs but as a family of distinct, causally active directions that alignment tuning installs.

AI.tldr: Alignment tuning, not pretraining, installs distinct and causally active directions in LLM hidden states that encode susceptibility to cue-induced biases (e.g., sycophancy). These directions can be decoded, steered, and partially mitigated through representation-level intervention across multiple model families.
AI.motivation: LLMs are easily swayed by superficial prompt cues (hints, mislabeled examples, fake assistant turns), flipping correct answers to incorrect ones. The paper aims to locate where this susceptibility resides inside the model, distinguishing whether it originates from pretraining or alignment tuning, and whether different bias types share a common representational basis.
AI.method: The authors study five model families and seven cue-induced bias types. They extract per-bias directions from hidden states and triangulate them using three measures: (1) probing classifiers to detect bias signal, (2) leave-one-dataset-out transfer to test generalization, and (3) causal intervention by steering activations along extracted directions. They compare pretrained base models against aligned (instruction-tuned) counterparts to isolate the source of bias susceptibility.
AI.result: Pretrained base models show near-zero susceptibility and carry no cue-specific signal beyond question content. In aligned models, each bias forms a single coherent, decodable, and steerable direction. Causal intervention along these directions recovers unbiased answers across all tested families. Biases are representationally distinct: cross-bias entanglement is model-specific, and behaviorally similar biases occupy different directions. The steering intervention also serves as a modest debiasing tool, recovering many bias-induced errors while preserving most correct answers.
AI.conclusion: Cue-induced bias is not a monolithic flaw but a family of distinct, causally active directions installed primarily during alignment tuning. This suggests mechanistic interpretability and activation steering as viable paths for understanding and mitigating such biases.

title: Discrete Ricci Curvature on Protein Contact Graphs for Lightweight Fold Classification
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Future Machine Learning and Data Science (FMLDS)
summary: Protein fold classification can be approached via sequence-based representations or structural descriptors, but direct comparisons between lightweight handcrafted descriptors and pretrained protein language model embeddings remain limited. We investigate discrete Ricci curvature on Calpha contact graphs as a lightweight structural descriptor for fold classification. Each protein domain is represented by a 22-dimensional fixed-length feature derived from summary statistics and quantiles of Ollivier-Ricci and Forman-Ricci edge curvature distributions. We evaluate on CATH top-10 Topology classification and on the ASTRAL 40%-identity SCOPe top-10 Fold benchmark, comparing against geometry, contact-graph statistics, persistent homology, and mean-pooled ESM-2 (150M) baselines. On both datasets, lightweight structural descriptors substantially outperform mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings, with a larger performance gap on the ASTRAL 40% SCOPe benchmark. Ricci alone uses 22 dimensions, or 3.4% of the ESM-2 baseline dimensionality, and already outperforms mean-pooled ESM-2 on both datasets. Combining Ricci with persistent homology yields the strongest performance, achieving macro-F1 of 0.71 on CATH and 0.68 on SCOPe with a 112-dimensional feature vector. These results identify a regime where lightweight interpretable graph descriptors offer a practical alternative to pretrained protein language model embeddings.

AI.tldr: Lightweight Ricci curvature-based graph descriptors (22–112 dims) outperform mean-pooled ESM-2 (150M) embeddings for protein fold classification on CATH and SCOPe benchmarks, with Ricci+persistent homology achieving the best results.
AI.motivation: Direct comparisons between lightweight handcrafted structural descriptors and pretrained protein language model (pLM) embeddings for fold classification are scarce. The authors aim to investigate whether discrete Ricci curvature on protein contact graphs can serve as an effective, interpretable, low-dimensional alternative.
AI.method: Each protein domain is modeled as a Cα contact graph. Ollivier-Ricci and Forman-Ricci edge curvatures are computed, and 22-dimensional fixed-length feature vectors are derived from summary statistics and quantiles of curvature distributions. These are evaluated on CATH top-10 Topology and ASTRAL 40%-identity SCOPe top-10 Fold benchmarks, with baselines including geometry-based descriptors, contact-graph statistics, persistent homology, and mean-pooled ESM-2 (150M) embeddings.
AI.result: Lightweight structural descriptors substantially outperform mean-pooled ESM-2 embeddings on both datasets. Ricci alone (22 dims, 3.4% of ESM-2 dimensionality) already surpasses mean-pooled ESM-2. Combining Ricci with persistent homology achieves macro-F1 of 0.71 on CATH and 0.68 on SCOPe using a 112-dimensional feature vector.
AI.conclusion: There exists a regime where lightweight, interpretable graph descriptors offer a practical and superior alternative to pretrained pLM embeddings for protein fold classification, particularly when dimensionality and interpretability are prioritized.

title: FailureAtlas: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Multi-Provider LLM Serving Infrastructure
summary: Multi-provider LLM gateways reverse proxies that route, load-balance, and rate-limit requests across foundation-model APIs have become critical production infrastructure. Yet the failure modes specific to this architectural layer remain undocumented, scattered across issue trackers and post-mortems with no unifying framework. We introduce \fa{}, a two-axis taxonomy that classifies failures by their \emph{origin layer} (Network/Transport, Streaming/Protocol, State/Session, Model~Behavior, Governance/Cost) and their \emph{detectability} (Loud vs.\ Silent). We populate this taxonomy with five verified catalog entries sourced from public bug reports and first-hand stress testing, each accompanied by a mechanistic root-cause analysis. Three entries include standalone reproduction scripts. Our principal finding is that the most operationally severe failures are \emph{silent}: they return HTTP~200, pass every standard health check, and corrupt application state in ways that require semantic-level observability to detect. Two such silent failures a concurrency race condition causing history loss and a streaming index collision corrupting tool-call payloads were discovered first-hand during \cb{} evaluation campaigns.

AI.tldr: Introduces a two-axis taxonomy for classifying failures in multi-provider LLM gateways, populated with five verified catalog entries. The key finding is that the most severe failures are "silent" — returning HTTP 200 and passing health checks while corrupting application state.
AI.motivation: Multi-provider LLM gateways are critical production infrastructure, yet failure modes specific to this architectural layer remain undocumented and scattered across issue trackers and post-mortems with no unifying framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-axis taxonomy classifying failures by origin layer (Network/Transport, Streaming/Protocol, State/Session, Model Behavior, Governance/Cost) and detectability (Loud vs. Silent). They populate it with five verified catalog entries from public bug reports and first-hand stress testing, including three standalone reproduction scripts and mechanistic root-cause analyses.
AI.result: Two silent failures were discovered first-hand: a concurrency race condition causing history loss and a streaming index collision corrupting tool-call payloads. Both return HTTP 200 and pass standard health checks, yet corrupt application state in ways requiring semantic-level observability to detect.
AI.conclusion: The operationally most severe failures in LLM gateways are silent ones that evade conventional monitoring. Semantic-level observability is necessary to detect these failures, which otherwise corrupt application state undetected.

title: Bridging the Information Gap: Semantic Densification and Hindsight Distillation for Cold-Start Prediction
summary: New-user cold-start is a critical bottleneck for e-commerce platforms: predicting user lifetime value (LTV) and conversion rate (CVR) for users with sparse interaction history. Two prior directions -- LLM-based semantic augmentation and learning using privileged information (LUPI) -- each face a key limitation. First, LLM augmentation produces unstructured rationales that are noisy and hard to operationalize in production. Second, naive student-teacher distillation can be brittle due to an information gap between the privileged teacher and the sparse student; moreover, this gap is heterogeneous across users. We propose SemRaD, a Semantic Reasoning-aware Distillation framework addressing both limitations. First, a Structured Semantic Reasoning Pipeline replaces free-form rationales with a structured schema built via a discover-curate-audit workflow, producing per user a Densified Semantic Profile (consumed by the deployed student via a Semantic-Gated Encoder that focuses on the most informative dimensions) and a Hindsight Distillation Target reconciled from pre- and post-conversion reasoning (used only at training). Second, to bridge this gap and handle its heterogeneity, a Hindsight-Aware Distillation Network transfers privileged knowledge via the hindsight target, with Distillation Experts improving transfer under per-user variability. On a large-scale industrial dataset, SemRaD lifts +1.9% LTV (Gini) and +1.0% CVR (AUROC) over a production-grade base; a four-week online A/B at Keeta confirms +1.0% LTV / +0.43% CVR. SemRaD also matches the production system's LTV using only 9% of the training data while improving CVR by 0.8%.

AI.tldr: SemRaD addresses cold-start user LTV/CVR prediction by combining structured semantic reasoning (replacing noisy LLM rationales) with hindsight-aware distillation that handles heterogeneous information gaps between privileged teacher and sparse student, achieving +1.9% LTV and +1.0% CVR offline gains, validated by online A/B testing at Keeta.
AI.motivation: Cold-start user prediction (LTV/CVR) is critical for e-commerce but suffers from sparse interaction history. Existing approaches — LLM-based semantic augmentation (produces noisy, unstructured rationales hard to operationalize) and LUPI (brittle student-teacher distillation due to heterogeneous information gaps) — each have fundamental limitations that SemRaD aims to resolve simultaneously.
AI.method: SemRaD consists of two components: (1) A Structured Semantic Reasoning Pipeline that replaces free-form LLM rationales with a discover-curate-audit workflow, producing per-user Densified Semantic Profiles (via a Semantic-Gated Encoder focusing on informative dimensions) and Hindsight Distillation Targets (reconciling pre- and post-conversion reasoning, used only at training). (2) A Hindsight-Aware Distillation Network that transfers privileged knowledge through the hindsight target, employing Distillation Experts to handle per-user variability in the information gap between teacher and student.
AI.result: On a large-scale industrial dataset, SemRaD achieves +1.9% LTV (Gini) and +1.0% CVR (AUROC) over a production baseline. A four-week online A/B test at Keeta confirms +1.0% LTV and +0.43% CVR lifts. SemRaD matches the production system's LTV performance using only 9% of training data while improving CVR by 0.8%.
AI.conclusion: SemRaD effectively addresses the cold-start bottleneck by making semantic augmentation structured and operationalizable, and by using hindsight-aware distillation with experts to handle heterogeneous teacher-student gaps. The strong offline and online results, along with data efficiency, demonstrate practical industrial viability.

title: VEHBench: A Stage-Local Diagnostic Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Vibration Energy Harvester Design
summary: Battery-free Internet of Things (IoT) requires iterative design of vibration energy harvesters (VEHs) under coupled physical constraints, while LLMs are emerging as interface layers for engineering workflows. However, existing engineering benchmarks primarily assess final artifact validity, offering limited insights into how LLMs behave across different stages of coupled physical design. We introduce VEHBench, an engineering-native diagnostic benchmark for LLM-assisted VEH design, featuring 763 literature-grounded tasks scored by an analytical physical oracle. VEHBench evaluates four design roles: specification triage, verifier-guided search, corrupted-state recovery, and policy-conditioned selection. Experimental results reveal that LLM capability is strongly stage-dependent: no single model consistently dominates the entire workflow, and response-control profiles expose distinct behavioral patterns across design roles. VEHBench thus provides a stage-aware foundation for evaluating, selecting, routing, and improving verifier-grounded engineering LLMs. The benchmark artifact is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/AnonymousVehbench/vehbench

AI.tldr: VEHBench is a diagnostic benchmark with 763 tasks for evaluating LLMs across four distinct design roles in vibration energy harvester (VEH) design for battery-free IoT. It reveals that LLM performance is highly stage-dependent, with no single model dominating all roles, and provides a foundation for routing and improving verifier-grounded engineering LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing engineering benchmarks focus on final artifact validity, offering limited insight into how LLMs behave across different stages of coupled physical design. Battery-free IoT requires iterative VEH design under coupled physical constraints, and LLMs are emerging as interface layers for engineering workflows, creating a need for stage-aware evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce VEHBench, an engineering-native diagnostic benchmark comprising 763 literature-grounded tasks scored by an analytical physical oracle. It evaluates LLMs across four design roles: specification triage, verifier-guided search, corrupted-state recovery, and policy-conditioned selection, exposing stage-dependent behavioral patterns.
AI.result: Experimental results show that LLM capability is strongly stage-dependent: no single model consistently dominates the entire VEH design workflow, and distinct response-control profiles emerge across the four design roles, revealing behavioral patterns not captured by end-to-end artifact evaluation.
AI.conclusion: VEHBench provides a stage-aware foundation for evaluating, selecting, routing, and improving verifier-grounded engineering LLMs, moving beyond final-output assessment to diagnostic, role-specific evaluation in coupled physical design contexts.

title: Capacity and Redundancy Trade-offs in Multi-Task Learning
comment: Accepted in 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI) 2026
summary: In multi-task learning (MTL) negative transfer is often considered as an optimization artifact, but it can also be viewed as a consequence of limited shared capacity and weak task redundancy. We investigate this effect through a Capacity--Redundancy (CR) identity that decomposes the sum of per-task predictive informations into joint predictive information that includes label redundancy defined via total correlation (TC), and a residual coupling term that quantifies interference left unresolved by the shared representation. Additionally, we show two key results: (i) a clustering-gap decomposition that gives a necessary and sufficient condition for clustered sharing to outperform global sharing, and (ii) a gradient--TC bridge in a Gaussian multi-task model that formally justifies gradient cosine similarity as a proxy for redundancy ordering. Empirically, we estimate the residual coupling $Δ$ from validation residual correlations, showing that clustered LoRA substantially reduces $\widehatΔ$, outperforms size-matched random partitions, and results in statistically significant gains with multi-seed confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Capacity–Redundancy (CR) identity that decomposes multi-task predictive information into joint information and a residual coupling term Δ, then uses this framework to derive conditions under which clustered task sharing outperforms global sharing, and to establish a formal link between gradient cosine similarity and redundancy in Gaussian MTL models.
AI.motivation: Negative transfer in multi-task learning is typically viewed as an optimization problem, but the authors argue it fundamentally reflects limited shared capacity and insufficient task redundancy. The paper aims to formalize this perspective through information-theoretic decomposition and to provide principled guidance for task grouping.
AI.method: The authors derive a Capacity–Redundancy (CR) identity decomposing per-task predictive information into joint predictive information (incorporating total correlation) and a residual coupling term Δ. They prove a clustering-gap decomposition establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for clustered sharing to beat global sharing, and develop a gradient–TC bridge for Gaussian MTL that connects gradient cosine similarity to redundancy ordering. Empirical validation estimates Δ from validation residual correlations, comparing clustered LoRA against random task partitions.
AI.result: Clustered LoRA significantly reduces the estimated residual coupling Δ̂ compared to unclustered baselines, outperforms size-matched random partitions, and yields statistically significant performance gains validated via multi-seed confidence intervals.
AI.conclusion: Negative transfer can be understood through the lens of capacity and redundancy; the CR identity and associated clustering-gap condition provide a theoretically grounded framework for task grouping, with the gradient–TC bridge offering a practical proxy for redundancy-based task ordering in MTL.

title: Is Progressive Disclosure All You Need for Long-Context Agents?
summary: Long-document question answering usually forces a choice between loading the whole document into the context window and bolting on a separate retriever. Agentic AI suggests a broader option, giving the agent the document path and letting it decide how and what to read. Agent Skills, a standard for packaging expertise into folders an agent loads on demand, supply a ready mechanism: progressive disclosure, which exposes only what a query needs, from a short description down to the specific passages. Practitioners rapidly adopted this pattern for book-length understanding tasks, but the evidence to support such choices has been anecdotal. We run the first controlled study of the pattern, comparing raw-document navigation and several designs of Agent Skills packs against a classical hybrid retriever across three agent harnesses and three model families on InfiniteBench. On a single book, the gain depends on the harness, running large when the agent navigates the raw document poorly but near zero when a strong agent harness already divides and retrieves on its own. When scaling up to tasks that span many books, raw-document navigation collapses while one-level progressive disclosure degrades more slowly and pulls ahead. A second, deeper routing level never helps and sometimes breaks accuracy outright, so one level is enough. Progressive disclosure buys context, not intelligence: it is redundant while a strong agent can locate the right passages itself, and decisive once the corpus grows too large to navigate by reading.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first controlled study of progressive disclosure (via Agent Skills) for long-document QA. It compares raw-document navigation and Agent Skills against classical hybrid retrieval across three agent harnesses and three model families on InfiniteBench. Key finding: progressive disclosure is redundant when a strong agent can navigate well, but becomes decisive as corpus size scales beyond single-document navigation capabilities. One level of progressive disclosure suffices; deeper routing harms accuracy.
AI.motivation: Practitioners have rapidly adopted progressive disclosure patterns (packaging expertise into Agent Skills packs) for book-length understanding tasks, but the evidence supporting these architectural choices has been purely anecdotal. The authors aim to provide the first rigorous, controlled empirical evaluation of whether and when progressive disclosure helps versus classical hybrid retrieval or raw-document navigation.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments comparing three approaches — (1) raw-document navigation, (2) several designs of Agent Skills packs with progressive disclosure (one-level and two-level routing), and (3) a classical hybrid retriever — across three agent harnesses and three model families. Evaluation is conducted on the InfiniteBench benchmark, testing both single-book and multi-book settings to assess scaling behavior.
AI.result: On a single book, gains from progressive disclosure depend on the harness: large improvements when the agent navigates poorly, near zero when the harness already divides and retrieves effectively. When scaling to many books, raw-document navigation collapses entirely; one-level progressive disclosure degrades more slowly and outperforms. A second, deeper routing level never helps and sometimes breaks accuracy. Progressive disclosure thus buys context efficiency, not intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Progressive disclosure is context management, not a source of additional reasoning capability. It proves redundant when a strong agent harness can locate relevant passages independently, but becomes decisive when the corpus grows too large to navigate by reading alone. One routing level is optimal — deeper hierarchical routing provides no benefit and can be harmful.

title: Otap:Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Evaluating Planning and Execution in Agent Trajectories
summary: Large language model agents solve tasks by generating trajectories that interleave planning, tool calls, and intermediate results. Current evaluation metrics reduce such a trajectory to a binary success flag or compare it against a reference by exact matching. A success flag cannot distinguish a sound solution from one that succeeds by luck, and says nothing about why a failed run went wrong. Exact matching penalizes plans that are valid but reordered or decomposed differently from the reference. We reframe trajectory evaluation as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of valid solution graphs, and instantiate it via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem over attributed dependency graphs. The resulting score, termed \otap{} (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), is a pseudo-metric that is provably invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and has bounded sensitivity to redundant steps. Its unbalanced marginals handle missing or hallucinated steps without forcing a match, and its soft coupling accommodates variation in plan granularity. On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, \otap{} separates valid from invalid trajectories in a regime where semantics-only metrics score below chance. Its accuracy is highest when the dependency graph is recovered exactly, and drops only when the graph is inferred heuristically from free-text traces.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OTAP, a trajectory evaluation metric for LLM agents that frames evaluation as an optimal transport problem between execution dependency graphs and valid solution graphs, providing a pseudo-metric invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings with bounded sensitivity to redundant steps.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation metrics for LLM agent trajectories are deficient: binary success flags cannot distinguish sound solutions from lucky successes or explain failures, while exact-match comparisons penalize valid reorderings or decomposition differences. There is a need for a metric that captures structural correctness of planning trajectories beyond surface-level or semantic-only comparisons.
AI.method: Trajectories are represented as attributed dependency graphs. Evaluation is cast as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of reference solution graphs, instantiated via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) optimal transport problem. The unbalanced marginals handle missing/hallucinated steps without forcing spurious matches; soft coupling accommodates granularity variation. The resulting OTAP score is provably a pseudo-metric with invariance properties and bounded sensitivity.
AI.result: On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, OTAP separates valid from invalid trajectories in regimes where semantics-only metrics perform below chance. Accuracy is highest when dependency graphs are recovered exactly, degrading only when graphs are inferred heuristically from free-text traces.
AI.conclusion: OTAP provides a principled, structure-aware alternative to binary success and exact-match evaluation for LLM agent trajectories, capturing plan validity through dependency-preserving graph matching via optimal transport.

title: PPL-Factory: Task-Aware and Budget-Aware Data Selection from Language Modeling to Reasoning
summary: Not all training samples contribute equally to large language model fine-tuning. Selecting informative training samples can reduce the computational cost while preserving downstream performance. Many existing data selection methods rely on indirect heuristics, such as data quality, diversity or reasoning trace length. However, the effectiveness of these fixed criteria is task-dependent and difficult to generalize across diverse downstream tasks. Perplexity-based data selection provides a simple and model-aware solution to estimate the sample difficulty, but existing approaches typically score the entire training sequence and ignore the difference in learning objectives of language modeling and reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose PPL-Factory, a simple and interpretable data selection framework that combines task-aware perplexity-based scores and data budget-aware selection criteria. Experiments on GSM8K demonstrate that PPL-Factory outperforms other state-of-the-art data selection methods using only $1\%$ of the training set. With $10\%$ of the data, PPL-Factory exceeds full-data fine-tuning accuracy by 0.9 on GSM8K and 4.8 on MATH. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-aware and budget-aware perplexity-based selection provides an effective and applicable approach for efficient fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: PPL-Factory proposes a task-aware, budget-aware perplexity-based data selection framework for efficient LLM fine-tuning, achieving superior performance with only 1-10% of training data on GSM8K and MATH benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing data selection methods for LLM fine-tuning either rely on task-dependent, non-generalizable heuristics (quality, diversity, trace length) or use perplexity scores that treat the entire sequence uniformly, failing to distinguish between language modeling and reasoning objectives. A task-aware, model-aware, and budget-aware selection method is needed.
AI.method: PPL-Factory integrates two key components: (1) task-aware perplexity-based scoring that differentiates between reasoning-oriented tokens and generic language modeling tokens when computing sample difficulty, and (2) budget-aware selection criteria that adapt sampling strategies based on the available data budget, ensuring optimal subset construction across different budget constraints.
AI.result: On GSM8K, PPL-Factory outperforms all SOTA data selection methods using only 1% of training data. With 10% data, it surpasses full-data fine-tuning by 0.9 points on GSM8K and 4.8 points on MATH.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware and budget-aware perplexity-based data selection is an effective, interpretable, and widely applicable approach for efficient LLM fine-tuning, significantly reducing computational costs without sacrificing downstream performance.

title: Learning from World Feedback: Why Model Uncertainty Fails as a Risk Signal in Model-Based RL
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from X Feedback (RLxF). 14 pages
summary: The RLxF programme argues that learning signals should come from world feedback rather than from internal model proxies. We instantiate this position in safe model-based control and distil it into three concrete design principles. Empirically, across four world-model architectures spanning a 2x MSE range, MPC planning is statistically equivalent (TOST, n=200), and dynamics-based uncertainty penalties increase collision rates from 26% to 34%: the standard MBRL safety proxy is anti-correlated with safety in this regime. Replacing the model-internal proxy with three world-feedback signals (a sensor-derived margin via minimum lidar, a temporal signal via time-to-collision, and an outcome-supervised feedback model g_psi trained on prior collision labels, structurally analogous to outcome-trained reward models in RLHF) reduces collisions to 1-14% without retraining the world model or the planner. The mechanism is structural: model uncertainty has support over state-prediction space, whereas task risk has support over constraint boundaries, with empirical correlation r < 0.15. From this we extract three RLxF principles (ground risk in world outcomes, validate proxies before deployment, and substitute outcome-trained feedback models when direct world signals are unavailable) and argue they apply equally to model-based control and to verifier-based or RLHF approaches in LLM alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that learning signals should come from real-world feedback rather than internal model proxies. It demonstrates that standard model-based RL safety proxies (uncertainty penalties) are anti-correlated with actual safety, and proposes three world-feedback signals that dramatically reduce collisions without retraining. These findings are distilled into three "RLxF" design principles applicable to both robot control and LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Standard model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) relies on internal model proxies (e.g., dynamics uncertainty) as safety signals. The authors challenge this paradigm, arguing these proxies can be misleading or anti-correlated with real-world safety outcomes. The motivation is to replace model-internal signals with direct world feedback — analogous to how RLHF uses human outcome labels rather than proxy reward models — and to test whether this improves safety in a principled, measurable way.
AI.method: The authors compare model-internal safety proxies (dynamics-based uncertainty penalties) against three world-feedback signals: (1) a sensor-derived margin using minimum LiDAR readings, (2) a temporal signal via time-to-collision, and (3) an outcome-supervised feedback model g_ψ trained on prior collision labels (structurally analogous to outcome-trained reward models in RLHF). Experiments use four distinct world-model architectures spanning a 2× MSE range, with MPC planning evaluated via two one-sided t-tests (TOST, n=200) for statistical equivalence testing. The empirical correlation r between model uncertainty and task risk is also measured.
AI.result: MPC planning performance is statistically equivalent across all four world models (TOST, n=200). Dynamics-based uncertainty penalties increase collision rates from 26% to 34% — the standard MBRL safety proxy is anti-correlated with safety. Replacing the model-internal proxy with the three world-feedback signals reduces collisions to 1–14% without retraining the world model or planner. The underlying mechanism is structural: model uncertainty has support over state-prediction space, whereas task risk has support over constraint boundaries, with empirical correlation r < 0.15.
AI.conclusion: Three RLxF principles are extracted: (1) ground risk in world outcomes, (2) validate proxies before deployment, and (3) substitute outcome-trained feedback models when direct world signals are unavailable. These principles are argued to apply equally to model-based control and to verifier-based or RLHF approaches in LLM alignment, suggesting a broader paradigm shift from proxy-based to outcome-based learning signals.

title: Verify, Repair, Repeat, or Stop? Robust Stopping for Noisy Verify-Repair Loops in LLM Agents
summary: Verify-repair loops are a standard means for large language model (LLM) agents to correct faulty plans in code generation, mathematical reasoning, and tool use. When both the verifier and the repairer are noisy, repair can damage already-correct plans, and reported acceptance keeps rising while true validity falls, so existing methods lack a principled basis for deciding when repair should stop. We propose VRR-Stop, a robust stopping framework for noisy verify-repair-repeat (VRR) loops. A four-parameter noise model separates verifier false acceptance and false rejection from the repair and damage behavior of the repairer. Belief filtering turns repeated verification votes into an estimate of committed validity, and the loop commits or repairs according to the sign of the true marginal gain, which requires only sign identifiability rather than accurate recovery of all parameters. When verifier discrimination approaches zero, calibration itself fails and estimation error can flip the stopping sign, so we pair VRR-Stop with VRR-Guard, an estimation-free fallback that replaces the incumbent candidate only under a sufficient verification margin. On a GSM8K stress setting, VRR-Stop improves final true validity by 60.6 percentage points over fixed five-round repair at an average cost of 0.72 repair rounds. Across settings, stopping reliability is governed jointly by verifier discrimination and the decision margin rather than by the absolute size of estimation error.

AI.tldr: VRR-Stop is a principled stopping framework for noisy verify-repair loops that uses belief filtering and marginal gain sign estimation to decide when to stop repairing, paired with VRR-Guard as a fallback when verifier discrimination is too low. It improves true validity by 60.6 pp over fixed five-round repair on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: In verify-repair loops with noisy verifiers and repairers, repair can damage already-correct plans, causing reported acceptance to rise while true validity falls. Existing methods lack a principled stopping criterion, leading to either unnecessary repair rounds or degradation of correct solutions.
AI.method: A four-parameter noise model captures verifier false acceptance/rejection and repairer self-repair/damage behavior. Belief filtering converts repeated verification votes into committed validity estimates. The loop decides to commit or repair based on the sign of the true marginal gain, requiring only sign identifiability rather than full parameter recovery. When verifier discrimination is near zero, VRR-Guard provides an estimation-free fallback that only replaces the incumbent under a sufficient verification margin.
AI.result: On a GSM8K stress setting, VRR-Stop improves final true validity by 60.6 percentage points over fixed five-round repair at an average cost of 0.72 repair rounds. Stopping reliability is governed jointly by verifier discrimination and the decision margin rather than by absolute estimation error size.
AI.conclusion: Principled stopping in noisy verify-repair loops is both necessary and achievable. VRR-Stop, combined with VRR-Guard, provides a robust solution that substantially outperforms fixed-round baselines while adding minimal overhead, and its reliability depends on verifier discrimination and decision margin rather than raw estimation accuracy.

title: Fourier Geometric Wind Power Forecasting with Numerical Weather Prediction
summary: Accurate short-term wind power forecasting is essential for grid stability and operational planning, yet remains challenging due to the complex interactions between atmospheric conditions and turbine dynamics. However, existing methods fail to effectively incorporate weather forecasting with wind turbine data (i.e., SCADA), leading to suboptimal solutions. To address this, we introduce a multimodal framework that integrates historical point-based SCADA data with grid-based Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) forecasts, which is challenging due to heterogeneous input and the complex physical wind-turbine interactions. Our approach first explicitly decomposes inputs into scalar and vector features to better capture both site-specific and geometric dependencies and then incorporates a geometric encoder to extract rotation-invariant features from wind vectors. We further leverages a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture, which performs global convolutions in the frequency domain to efficiently model long-range spatiotemporal relationships. Extensive experiments on three real-world wind farms, with weather forecasting data, demonstrate that our model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of its physically-informed design. The core implementation of our method is publicly available at: https://github.com/shawn-sypiao/GWPF.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework integrating SCADA data and NWP forecasts for wind power prediction, using scalar-vector decomposition, geometric encoding, and Fourier Neural Operator to capture spatiotemporal dependencies, outperforming baselines on three wind farms.
AI.motivation: Existing short-term wind power forecasting methods inadequately combine weather forecasting with turbine SCADA data, resulting in suboptimal predictions due to heterogeneous inputs and complex physical wind-turbine interactions.
AI.method: A multimodal framework that: (1) explicitly decomposes inputs into scalar and vector features to capture site-specific and geometric dependencies; (2) employs a geometric encoder to extract rotation-invariant features from wind vectors; (3) uses a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture performing global convolutions in the frequency domain to model long-range spatiotemporal relationships.
AI.result: The model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three real-world wind farms with weather forecasting data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the physically-informed design.
AI.conclusion: Physically-informed multimodal fusion of SCADA and NWP data, combined with geometric encoding and FNO-based spatiotemporal modeling, provides a significant advance in short-term wind power forecasting accuracy. Code is publicly available.

title: SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune
summary: Pruning long context for coding agents has been a vital technology for efficient context management. While existing context pruning methods such as SWE-Pruner realize this by attaching a separate code classifier, we find the agent itself encodes internal representations indicating the relevance of code context when reading tool output. Based on this finding, we propose SWE-Pruner Pro, which prunes tool outputs directly inside the agent. Concretely, a small head turns the agent's own internal representations into a keep-or-prune label for each line, with a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count. Across two open-weight backbones and four multi-turn benchmarks, SWE-Pruner Pro saves up to 39% of prompt and completion tokens while preserving task quality, with bounded inference overhead. Notably, on MiMo-V2-Flash SWE-Pruner Pro additionally raises the SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8% and the long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points.

AI.tldr: SWE-Pruner Pro leverages the agent's own internal representations to prune tool outputs line-by-line for long-context coding tasks, eliminating the need for a separate classifier. It uses a lightweight head with length-aware embeddings to make keep-or-prune decisions per line, achieving up to 39% token savings while preserving or even improving task quality across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing context pruning methods like SWE-Pruner rely on external code classifiers to determine relevance, adding complexity. The authors discover that the coding agent's own internal representations already encode signals about code context relevance when processing tool outputs, motivating a simpler, agent-internal pruning mechanism.
AI.method: SWE-Pruner Pro attaches a small classification head directly inside the agent that converts the agent's internal hidden representations into keep-or-prune labels for each line of tool output.
