It incorporates a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count, enabling the model to condition pruning decisions on output length. No separate classifier is needed.
AI.result: Across two open-weight backbones and four multi-turn benchmarks, SWE-Pruner Pro saves up to 39% of prompt and completion tokens while maintaining task quality, with bounded inference overhead. On MiMo-V2-Flash, it improves SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8% and Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points.
AI.conclusion: Agent-internal pruning using the model's own representations is both more efficient and more effective than external classifier-based approaches. The method not only reduces token usage substantially but can also improve downstream task performance by removing distracting context.

title: Evidence Interfaces Shape How Retrieval-Augmented Readers Use Support
summary: In multi-hop RAG evaluation, a top-k answer score can hide two different failures: the retrieval window may drop part of the support chain, or it may contain support in a form the adapted reader does not use well. We call this reader-facing form of retrieved evidence an evidence interface. Using three support-annotated multi-hop QA benchmarks, we compare matched adapted readers trained with raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support diagnostic renderings. These comparisons distinguish support-availability failures from remaining reader-interface effects. Top-k windows become interpretable only after checking whether the complete annotated support chain survives: when it does, short ranked windows can match or improve over raw context; when it does not, missing support explains much of the loss. Gold support-first improves matched readers; on 2Wiki and MuSiQue, a support-supervised ranker raises coverage and recovers raw-context quality at lower prompt cost, while retaining gold headroom. Support-removal checks further show that the gains rely on exposed evidence, not only answer priors. On support-annotated evaluations, top-k answer scores should therefore be reported together with complete-support coverage.

AI.tldr: Multi-hop RAG evaluation using only top-k answer scores conflates two distinct failure modes: retrieval failing to capture the full support chain, and the reader failing to utilize retrieved evidence effectively (termed the "evidence interface"). The paper disentangles these by comparing readers trained on raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support renderings, showing that complete-support coverage must be reported alongside answer scores for interpretable evaluation.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-hop RAG evaluation conceals a critical ambiguity: a poor top-k answer score could stem from the retriever dropping necessary support documents, or from the reader being unable to exploit evidence that is actually present but poorly formatted. Without distinguishing these failure sources, progress in either retrieval or reading cannot be accurately measured. The paper introduces the concept of "evidence interface" to formalize this reader-facing aspect and argues that complete-support chain coverage is an essential diagnostic metric.
AI.method: The authors use three support-annotated multi-hop QA benchmarks (2Wiki, MuSiQue, and a third) and conduct controlled comparisons: (1) matched adapted readers are trained under three conditions — raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support diagnostic renderings; (2) support-chain survival across top-k windows is measured to separate availability failures from interface effects; (3) a support-supervised ranker is introduced to boost coverage; (4) support-removal ablation checks verify that gains derive from exposed evidence rather than answer priors; (5) gold-support-first and support-supervised ranking baselines establish performance headroom.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) When the complete annotated support chain survives in top-k windows, short ranked windows can match or exceed raw-context quality. (2) When support is missing, most of the performance loss is attributable to support unavailability. (3) Gold support-first ordering substantially improves matched readers. (4) On 2Wiki and MuSiQue, a support-supervised ranker increases support coverage and recovers raw-context quality at reduced prompt cost while preserving gold headroom. (5) Support-removal checks confirm gains depend on exposed evidence, not merely answer priors.
AI.conclusion: Top-k answer scores in multi-hop RAG are not inherently interpretable without accompanying complete-support coverage metrics. Reporting both metrics allows the community to distinguish retrieval failures from reader-interface failures, enabling more targeted improvements. The evidence interface framing and support-supervised ranking offer practical paths toward more efficient and diagnostically transparent multi-hop RAG systems.

title: It's Not What You Say, It's How You Say It: Evaluating LLM Responses to Expressions of Belief
summary: Users frequently express their beliefs to large language models (LLMs). In some situations, the LLM should accept these contextual beliefs as true. In others, they should stick to their prior knowledge. Notably, users' expressions of belief (EoBs) can take linguistically diverse forms - using presuppositions, evidential and certainty markers, or varied tones - each of which may have a different persuasiveness over the LLMs. We introduce a typology to systematically evaluate how different EoBs affect whether models follow context versus prior knowledge. The typology is grounded in four linguistically motivated dimensions: form, evidentiality, epistemic stance, and tone, spanning 17 fine-grained types. By pairing these EoBs with world knowledge facts, we generate controlled EoB-query pairs that isolate the effect of linguistic variation. Using this benchmark, we evaluate 16 LLMs that differ in architecture (Llama3, Qwen3, Gemma3), scale (1B-30B parameters), and training stages (base vs instruct). We identify meaningful variations in response behavior across these axes, e.g., that bigger models and instruction models tend to be less context-following than smaller models and base models. We further identify specific EoBs that statistically significantly persuade LMs more consistently than others. Our work reveals systematic patterns in how linguistic framing affects LLM context integration, with implications for prompt engineering and model robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a linguistically-grounded typology of Expressions of Belief (EoBs) to systematically evaluate how different forms of user-expressed beliefs persuade LLMs to follow contextual information versus their prior knowledge. Evaluating 16 LLMs across architecture, scale, and training stages, the authors find that larger and instruction-tuned models are less context-following, and identify specific EoB types that are statistically more persuasive.
AI.motivation: Users frequently express beliefs to LLMs in linguistically diverse ways (presuppositions, evidential markers, certainty markers, varied tones), but it is unclear how these different forms affect whether LLMs accept contextual beliefs or default to prior knowledge. No systematic framework exists to evaluate this phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors propose a typology grounded in four linguistically motivated dimensions — form, evidentiality, epistemic stance, and tone — spanning 17 fine-grained EoB types. These EoBs are paired with world knowledge facts to create controlled EoB-query pairs that isolate linguistic variation effects. The resulting benchmark is used to evaluate 16 LLMs varying in architecture (Llama3, Qwen3, Gemma3), scale (1B–30B parameters), and training stages (base vs. instruct).
AI.result: Larger models and instruction-tuned models tend to be less context-following than smaller and base models. Specific EoB types statistically significantly persuade LLMs more consistently than others, revealing systematic patterns in how linguistic framing affects context integration.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic framing systematically affects LLM context integration. The findings have implications for prompt engineering and model robustness, highlighting that how users express beliefs meaningfully shapes model behavior.

title: Multimodal Attention-based Deep Learning for Emergency Triage with Electronic Health Records
summary: Accurate emergency triage decision is critical to avoid clinical deterioration, morbidity, and mortality. Machine learning-based triage system involves acquiring the main presenting complaint in text form and assessing vital signs in numerical data, enabling an automated and efficient analysis of patient information for timely and accurate prioritization of medical attention. However, modelling the intricacies of both data types requires a comprehensive understanding of the temporal structure and dependencies within the data. Thus, the aim of this study is to propose a multimodal deep learning architecture that can effectively handle both tabular and textual data. Furthermore, the proposed model exploits self-attention to to capture both local and global relationships between the features. A dataset consisting of 11,102 triage data collected from emergency department of Hospital Universiti Sains Malaysia is used for model development and validation. The proposed model demonstrated an increase of 1.95% in accuracy, 2.49% in F1-score, and 1.41% in ROC AUC compared to the baseline model. The experimental results demonstrated the potential of the proposed model in predicting triage decisions.

AI.tldr: A multimodal deep learning model combining self-attention mechanisms to process both textual chief complaints and tabular vital signs for emergency triage prediction, achieving improvements of ~2% in accuracy and F1-score over baselines on a Malaysian ED dataset of 11,102 cases.
AI.motivation: Emergency triage requires simultaneous interpretation of unstructured text (presenting complaints) and structured numerical data (vital signs). Existing approaches lack effective integration of both modalities and fail to capture the complex temporal dependencies and feature relationships inherent in triage data. A model capable of jointly modeling both data types with attention to local and global feature interactions is needed.
AI.method: A multimodal deep learning architecture employing self-attention mechanisms to process dual-input data: textual chief complaints and tabular vital signs. Self-attention captures both local and global inter-feature relationships. The model was developed and validated on a dataset of 11,102 triage records from the emergency department of Hospital Universiti Sains Malaysia.
AI.result: The proposed model outperformed the baseline with a 1.95% increase in accuracy, a 2.49% increase in F1-score, and a 1.41% increase in ROC AUC, demonstrating improved predictive capability for triage decision-making.
AI.conclusion: The self-attention-based multimodal deep learning architecture shows promising potential for automating and improving the accuracy of emergency triage decisions by effectively integrating heterogeneous clinical data types.

title: A Diagnostic Framework for AI Agent Behavior
summary: AI agents increasingly act within the same clinical, political, scientific, and social systems that behavioral scientists study. Evaluating these systems requires source-level diagnosis: the same behavioral pattern may arise from an agent representational substrate or from the roles, objectives, interaction structures, and governance rules that shape its expression. This Perspective proposes a diagnostic framework for AI agent behavior: layer attribution. The foundational computational layer defines what behaviors are possible through architecture, memory, perception, attention, and representation. The behavioral modulation layer shapes how those capacities are expressed through identity, resources, objectives, social interaction, institutional constraints, and governance. The framework clarifies three consequences: surrogate validity is a model-task-layer relation, human-AI divergence provides diagnostic evidence, and governance requires source attribution before intervention. Treating AI agents as behavioral actors therefore requires evaluation methods that determine where behavior originates before deciding how to explain, validate, or govern it.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-layer diagnostic framework ("layer attribution") for evaluating AI agent behavior: a foundational computational layer (architecture, memory, representation) that defines behavioral possibilities, and a behavioral modulation layer (identity, objectives, governance) that shapes expression. The framework clarifies that surrogate validity, human-AI divergence, and governance interventions all require identifying the source layer of behavior before explanation or action.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly embedded in the same clinical, political, scientific, and social systems that behavioral scientists study. A given behavioral pattern can emerge either from the agent's internal representational substrate or from external factors like roles, objectives, interaction structures, and governance rules. Without a systematic method to distinguish these sources, evaluation, validation, and governance of AI behavior remain ambiguous and potentially misguided.
AI.method: The authors propose a diagnostic framework called "layer attribution," which decomposes AI agent behavior into two distinct layers: (1) the foundational computational layer (architecture, memory, perception, attention, representation) that establishes the space of possible behaviors, and (2) the behavioral modulation layer (identity, resources, objectives, social interaction, institutional constraints, governance) that shapes how those capacities are expressed in practice. The framework is applied conceptually to derive three analytical consequences regarding surrogate validity, human-AI divergence, and governance.
AI.result: The framework yields three key consequences: (1) surrogate validity is not a property of a model alone but a model-task-layer relation, meaning a model valid for one layer may not be valid for another; (2) human-AI behavioral divergence serves as diagnostic evidence that can pinpoint which layer is responsible for discrepancies; (3) effective governance requires source attribution — identifying whether behavior originates from the computational or modulation layer — before designing interventions.
AI.conclusion: Treating AI agents as behavioral actors demands evaluation methods that first determine where behavior originates (which layer) before deciding how to explain, validate, or govern it. Layer attribution provides the diagnostic scaffolding for this upstream determination, ensuring that interventions target the correct source rather than conflating representational and environmental causes.

title: Automated Discovery Has No Universally Superior Harness
summary: Autonomous discovery systems such as OpenEvolve and TTT-Discover are often used as general-purpose harnesses. However, in practice these are composite systems combining several design choices about archives, parent selection, exploration, and budget allocation into a single recipe. Because discovery runs are expensive and inherently stochastic, existing harnesses are often compared using too few independent trials to distinguish key methodological improvements from run-to-run variance. We systematically decompose OpenEvolve-style evolutionary search and the TTT-Discover search harness into its constituent components and systematically evaluate 30 budget-matched harnesses across 12 model-problem pairs using more than 3.1 million LLM rollouts and repeated-trial statistical analysis. Our results show that discovery harnesses have a generalization problem: No fixed harness is reliably superior across the evaluated model-problem pairs, and variants of OpenEvolve generally underperform simpler alternatives. Thus, harness choice is better viewed as a hyperparameter rather than as a universal recipe, and should be tailored to the specific problem and underlying model. We also find that early discovery progress predicts final performance, and use this property to present a budget-matched adaptive-allocation experiment that starts multiple harnesses, prunes weak partial runs, and reallocates compute to stronger survivors, outperforming both commitment to a randomly sampled fixed harness and a non-adaptive harness ensemble. Together, these results motivate shifting from fixed harness selection to online adaptation guided by early performance. We release all run pools including baseline null distributions for every model-problem pair as reusable statistical infrastructure against for future harness proposals.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically decomposes and evaluates 30 budget-matched discovery harness variants across 12 model-problem pairs using over 3.1M LLM rollouts, finding that no fixed harness is universally superior. It advocates treating harness choice as a hyperparameter and proposes an adaptive-allocation method that prunes weak runs and reallocates compute, outperforming fixed harnesses.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous discovery systems (OpenEvolve, TTT-Discover) are composite systems with many entangled design choices, but comparisons between them suffer from insufficient independent trials, making it difficult to distinguish methodological improvements from stochastic run-to-run variance. There is no systematic understanding of which components matter or whether a universal "best" harness exists.
AI.method: The authors decompose OpenEvolve and TTT-Discover into their constituent components (archives, parent selection, exploration, budget allocation) and systematically evaluate 30 budget-matched harness variants across 12 model-problem pairs. They conduct repeated-trial statistical analysis using over 3.1 million LLM rollouts and release baseline null distributions. They also test an adaptive-allocation strategy that starts multiple harnesses, prunes weak partial runs based on early progress, and reallocates compute to stronger survivors.
AI.result: No fixed harness is reliably superior across all model-problem pairs, and OpenEvolve variants generally underperform simpler alternatives. Early discovery progress predicts final performance. The adaptive-allocation experiment outperforms both a randomly sampled fixed harness and a non-adaptive harness ensemble.
AI.conclusion: Harness choice should be treated as a hyperparameter tailored to specific problem-model pairs rather than a universal recipe. The field should shift from fixed harness selection to online adaptation guided by early performance signals. The released run pools and null distributions serve as reusable statistical infrastructure for future harness proposals.

title: CLDRoute: Conditional Latent Diffusion for Routability Map Generation in Physical Design
summary: Accurate routability estimation during physical design is important for reducing costly post-routing iterations. Prior learning-based methods treat this task as deterministic prediction, mapping placement-stage features to a single congestion or DRC outcome. We instead formulate routability estimation as a conditional generation problem, where both routing congestion and DRC violations are modeled as spatially structured routability fields. Our framework, Conditional Latent Diffusion for Routeability estimation (CLDRoute), uses physics-aware conditioning and task-specific latent modeling to handle the different characteristics of congestion and DRC maps. This allows our method to supports sample-based inference, producing both a mean prediction and a spatial uncertainty estimate for the same input design. On CircuitNet 2.0 (N28), our method achieves, for DRC violation generation, an SSIM of 0.9678, an MAE of 0.0028, and a TopK@1% of 0.3494; for congestion generation, it achieves an SSIM of 0.9031, an MAE of 0.0286, and an NZ-Pearson of 0.3692. Overall, our framework provides a more practical view of routability at placement by generating both the expected outcome and its uncertainty.

AI.tldr: CLDRoute reformulates routability estimation in physical design as a conditional generation problem using latent diffusion models, jointly predicting congestion and DRC violation maps with spatial uncertainty estimates from placement-stage features.
AI.motivation: Prior learning-based routability estimators produce deterministic single-outcome predictions, failing to capture the inherent uncertainty in routing outcomes at the placement stage. This leads to costly post-routing iterations when predictions are inaccurate.
AI.method: CLDRoute employs a conditional latent diffusion framework with physics-aware conditioning and task-specific latent modeling to generate spatially structured routability fields for both congestion and DRC violations. The diffusion formulation enables sample-based inference, yielding both a mean prediction and a spatial uncertainty map.
AI.result: On CircuitNet 2.0 (N28), for DRC violation generation: SSIM 0.9678, MAE 0.0028, TopK@1% 0.3494; for congestion generation: SSIM 0.9031, MAE 0.0286, NZ-Pearson 0.3692.
AI.conclusion: The conditional generation formulation provides a more practical routability estimation paradigm by delivering both expected outcomes and spatial uncertainty, enabling more informed physical design decisions at the placement stage.

title: Is Your Model Thinking or Just Stagnating? PUMA: Diagnosing Reasoning Pathology via Phase-Momentum Alignment
summary: Test-time scaling empowers Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) to tackle complex tasks via extensive Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, this often induces the "overthinking" paradox, where redundant reasoning increases computational overhead without guaranteeing accuracy. Existing test-time efficiency optimization methods primarily fall into two categories: information-theoretic approaches, which are prone to "deceptive convergence" where low uncertainty masks hallucinations, and latent representation analyses, which are often post-hoc, lacking the real-time sensitivity for dynamic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we first posit the Phase-Momentum Alignment Hypothesis, asserting that reasoning correctness hinges on the temporal synchronization between geometric momentum and uncertainty resolution. We then theoretically formulate the Cognitive-Energy Model to characterize these dynamics through two orthogonal dimensions: Geometric Cognitive Effort, quantified by latent velocity and tortuosity, and Entropic Cognitive Uncertainty. To operationalize this, we introduce PUMA (Phase-Uncertainty Momentum Alignment), a training-free framework employing a tiered diagnostic architecture. By coupling lightweight phase monitoring with event-triggered geometric analysis, PUMA effectively distinguishes active exploration from passive stagnation, enabling precise interventions through adaptive truncation or corrective measures. Extensive experiments on LRMs spanning 1.5B to 32B demonstrate that PUMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off and robust cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: PUMA introduces a training-free framework that addresses the "overthinking" problem in Large Reasoning Models by monitoring phase-momentum alignment between geometric dynamics and uncertainty in the latent space, enabling adaptive truncation or correction that outperforms existing efficiency methods.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling in LRMs induces "overthinking"—redundant CoT reasoning that wastes computation without accuracy gains. Existing solutions suffer from two critical limitations: information-theoretic methods exhibit "deceptive convergence" (low uncertainty masking hallucinations), while latent representation analyses are post-hoc and lack real-time sensitivity for dynamic reasoning intervention.
AI.method: The authors propose the Phase-Momentum Alignment Hypothesis, positing that reasoning correctness depends on synchronization between geometric momentum and uncertainty resolution. They formalize this via the Cognitive-Energy Model with two orthogonal dimensions: Geometric Cognitive Effort (latent velocity, tortuosity) and Entropic Cognitive Uncertainty. PUMA operationalizes this as a training-free, tiered diagnostic framework coupling lightweight phase monitoring with event-triggered geometric analysis to distinguish active exploration from passive stagnation, enabling adaptive truncation or corrective interventions.
AI.result: Experiments on LRMs from 1.5B to 32B parameters show PUMA consistently outperforms SOTA baselines across diverse benchmarks, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and robust cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: By aligning phase dynamics with uncertainty signals, PUMA provides a principled, real-time framework to mitigate overthinking in LRMs without retraining, advancing test-time efficiency optimization beyond the limitations of prior information-theoretic and post-hoc approaches.

title: A Framework for Early Sepsis Prediction via Self-Supervised (JEPA) and Federated Representation Learning
summary: Early sepsis prediction from electronic health records is challenged by irregular sampling, high missingness, and class imbalance. We systematically compare four modeling paradigms -- self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) via masked latent prediction, self-supervised VICReg (variance-invariance-covariance regularization) with two-view augmentation, semi-supervised fine-tuning of a VICReg-pretrained encoder, and supervised Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) -- alongside raw-feature baselines. All models share a common preprocessing pipeline of hourly binning with forward-fill imputation applied to 7 biomarkers selected via sparsity analysis from the MIMIC-III dataset. Our best model (JEPA + XGBoost + mean pooling) achieves AUPRC 0.636 at the time of onset (H0), approaching the SupMix benchmark (0.667) while using 83\% fewer biomarkers. The Tier 1 pipeline -- VICReg pretraining followed by semi-supervised fine-tuning and XGBoost -- achieves AUPRC 0.510 at H0, a 3.1$\times$ improvement over the raw-feature baseline (0.165) and a 7.6\% improvement over the end-to-end supervised TCN (0.474). Crucially, the fine-tuned VICReg encoder exhibits the most temporally persistent representations, degrading only 16.8\% from H0 to H10 compared to 47.5\% for supervised TCN and 65.3\% for JEPA, demonstrating that self-supervised pretraining with task-aware fine-tuning yields features that are both sharp near onset and robust across prediction horizons.

AI.tldr: Comparison of self-supervised (JEPA, VICReg), semi-supervised, and supervised (TCN) methods for early sepsis prediction from sparse EHR data, finding that VICReg pretraining with semi-supervised fine-tuning yields the most temporally robust representations while JEPA+XGBoost achieves the best AUPRC at onset (0.636) using only 7 biomarkers.
AI.motivation: Early sepsis prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is hindered by three key challenges: irregular temporal sampling, high rates of missing data, and severe class imbalance. Existing approaches often rely on large feature sets; the authors aim to identify which modeling paradigm yields the best predictive performance and temporal robustness using a minimal, sparsity-filtered biomarker set.
AI.method: Four modeling paradigms are systematically compared: (1) JEPA — self-supervised masked latent prediction; (2) VICReg — self-supervised with variance-invariance-covariance regularization and two-view augmentation; (3) semi-supervised fine-tuning of a VICReg-pretrained encoder; and (4) supervised Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). All models share a unified preprocessing pipeline: hourly binning, forward-fill imputation, and feature selection of 7 biomarkers from MIMIC-III via sparsity analysis. Downstream classification uses XGBoost with mean pooling. Evaluation spans prediction horizons H0 (onset) through H10.
AI.result: JEPA + XGBoost + mean pooling achieves AUPRC 0.636 at H0, approaching the SupMix benchmark (0.667) with 83% fewer biomarkers. The Tier 1 pipeline (VICReg → semi-supervised fine-tuning → XGBoost) achieves AUPRC 0.510 at H0, representing a 3.1× improvement over raw-feature baseline (0.165) and 7.6% over supervised TCN (0.474). The fine-tuned VICReg encoder shows the best temporal persistence: only 16.8% degradation from H0 to H10, versus 47.5% (supervised TCN) and 65.3% (JEPA).
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining with task-aware semi-supervised fine-tuning produces representations that are both discriminative near sepsis onset and robust across extended prediction horizons. JEPA excels at onset prediction but suffers from temporal degradation, while VICReg-based fine-tuning offers the best trade-off between sharpness and temporal stability, making it suitable for practical early warning systems requiring reliable performance across varying lead times.

title: Toward Anthropomorphic Dialogue: A Closed-Loop Framework for Human-Like Chat Generation, Evaluation, and Preference Alignment
summary: Human-like private chat requires more than fluent response generation: a system must preserve persona, relationship, memory, bounded knowledge, medium-specific timing, and a coherent multi-turn arc. We present AnthroDial, a closed-loop framework that formulates anthropomorphic dialogue as a joint problem of system architecture, executable evaluation, and diagnostic alignment. It combines (1) a role-conditioned scheduled dialogue runtime with persona and scenario cards, long-term memory, virtual time, and single-draft message decisions; (2) an executable benchmark with an L0 validity gate, five per-turn dimensions, and five dialogue-level dimensions; and (3) a post-training pipeline that filters 16,436 scheduled-decision examples for SFT and applies GRPO with a cognitive-diagnostic, ZPD-aware reward. The reward maintains Kalman-filtered capability estimates for each behavioral dimension, upweights dimensions with larger capability deficits, and uses rollout scores as task-level ZPD matches to focus optimization on learnable weak skills. On a benchmark with 55 personas, 50 scenarios, 50 persona-scenario bindings, and 100 role-conditioned cases per model, we evaluate 16 systems spanning frontier baselines, open models, thinking/no-think variants, and SFT/RL ablations. The strongest non-trained baseline reaches 32.00% strict ACC, while Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL reaches 39.00% strict ACC and a 98.5 overall score. In the 9B no-think setting, SFT and RL improve strict ACC from 0.00% to 13.00% and 18.37%. These results show that anthropomorphic dialogue benefits when generation, evaluation, and reward shaping share the same behavioral dimensions.

AI.tldr: AnthroDial is a closed-loop framework for anthropomorphic dialogue that integrates architecture, evaluation, and diagnostic alignment. It uses role-conditioned runtime with persona/scenario cards, long-term memory, and virtual time; an executable benchmark with multi-level evaluation dimensions; and a ZPD-aware RL training pipeline. The best model (Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL) achieves 39.00% strict accuracy vs. 32.00% for the strongest baseline, with gains particularly pronounced in smaller models.
AI.motivation: Human-like private chat requires more than fluent generation — it demands persona consistency, relationship maintenance, memory, bounded knowledge, appropriate timing, and coherent multi-turn arcs. Existing systems lack a unified framework that jointly addresses architecture, evaluation, and training alignment for these anthropomorphic dialogue capabilities.
AI.method: AnthroDial proposes three integrated components: (1) A role-conditioned scheduled dialogue runtime with persona/scenario cards, long-term memory, virtual time, and single-draft message decisions; (2) An executable benchmark featuring an L0 validity gate, five per-turn dimensions, and five dialogue-level dimensions; (3) A post-training pipeline that filters 16,436 scheduled-decision examples for SFT and applies GRPO with a cognitive-diagnostic reward. The reward uses Kalman-filtered capability estimates per behavioral dimension, upweights dimensions with larger deficits, and employs rollout scores as ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) matches to focus optimization on learnable weak skills.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 55 personas, 50 scenarios, 50 persona-scenario bindings, and 100 role-conditioned cases per model, 16 systems were evaluated. The strongest non-trained baseline achieved 32.00% strict ACC. Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL reached 39.00% strict ACC and a 98.5 overall score. In the 9B no-think setting, SFT and RL improved strict ACC from 0.00% to 13.00% and 18.37% respectively, demonstrating that smaller models benefit substantially from the training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Anthropomorphic dialogue generation, evaluation, and reward shaping benefit from sharing the same behavioral dimensions. The closed-loop integration of architecture, benchmark, and diagnostic alignment training yields consistent improvements across model scales, with the ZPD-aware reward effectively targeting learnable weak skills.

title: Building a Neural Network from Scratch: Implementation, Evaluation, and Optimization
summary: The widespread adoption of high-level deep learning libraries, while accelerating model development, has increasingly abstracted away the internal mechanics of neural networks, creating a gap between practical usage and fundamental understanding. To address this, the paper presents a self-contained neural network framework implemented entirely from scratch -- without relying on automatic differentiation or pre-built deep learning modules. The implementation encompasses all essential components, including multi-layer architectures, diverse activation functions, regularization techniques, and state-of-the-art optimizers. Beyond serving as a pedagogical instrument that demystifies forward/backward propagation, gradient dynamics, and optimization landscapes, the framework demonstrates robust performance when applied to a multi-class classification task, successfully validating its correctness, numerical stability, and generalization across varied configurations. The extensible design and clean modularity further position it as a reliable baseline for educational purposes and future research exploration.

AI.tldr: A neural network framework built entirely from scratch without automatic differentiation or deep learning libraries, serving both as a pedagogical tool for understanding internal mechanics and as a functional baseline for classification tasks.
AI.motivation: High-level deep learning libraries abstract away internal mechanics, creating a gap between practical usage and fundamental understanding of neural networks.
AI.method: Implementation of a self-contained neural network framework from scratch, including multi-layer architectures, diverse activation functions, regularization techniques, and state-of-the-art optimizers, without relying on automatic differentiation or pre-built modules.
AI.result: The framework demonstrated robust performance on multi-class classification tasks, validating its correctness, numerical stability, and generalization across varied configurations.
AI.conclusion: The extensible and modular design positions the framework as a reliable baseline for both educational purposes and future research exploration.

title: Effects of width-dependent model hyperparameters and $\ell_2$-regularization on the loss landscape of two-layer ReLU networks
comment: ICML2026 4th Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD)
summary: Understanding deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning. In particular, the theoretical properties of even two-layer ReLU networks, especially in the presence of weight decay, remain poorly understood. To this end, we derive a sufficient condition on the hyperparameter settings under which the global minima collapse to the zero solution. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that using AdamW as an optimizer prevents the collapse of the learned parameters, whereas using SGD does not, which may help explain the success of AdamW in deep learning training. In addition, when restricting the input dimension to one, we derive an analytical solution for the globally optimal parameter sets of two-layer ReLU networks and show that $\ell_2$-regularization has a width-invariant effect on connectivity, but its dimensionality-reducing effect becomes stronger as the network width increases. These results provide insight into how width-dependent hyperparameters influence the geometry of regularized loss landscapes.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes two-layer ReLU networks with weight decay, deriving conditions under which global minima collapse to zero, showing AdamW prevents this collapse unlike SGD, and providing analytical solutions for 1D inputs revealing width-dependent regularization effects on the loss landscape.
AI.motivation: The theoretical properties of even shallow (two-layer) ReLU networks, particularly under weight decay (ℓ₂-regularization), remain poorly understood. Understanding these fundamentals is crucial for explaining optimizer behaviors and guiding hyperparameter selection in deep learning.
AI.method: The authors derive a sufficient condition on hyperparameters for global minima collapsing to zero. They empirically compare SGD and AdamW optimizers under this condition. For the one-dimensional input case, they analytically solve for the globally optimal parameter sets of two-layer ReLU networks and analyze how ℓ₂-regularization affects connectivity and dimensionality as a function of network width.
AI.result: A sufficient hyperparameter condition leads to zero-solution collapse. AdamW prevents this collapse while SGD does not, offering a partial explanation for AdamW's empirical success. For 1D inputs, ℓ₂-regularization has a width-invariant effect on connectivity, but its dimensionality-reducing effect strengthens with increasing network width.
AI.conclusion: Width-dependent hyperparameters significantly influence the geometry of regularized loss landscapes in two-layer ReLU networks. The interplay between optimizer choice (AdamW vs. SGD) and regularization-induced collapse provides theoretical insight relevant to practical deep learning training dynamics.

title: Constrained Path Reasoning: Measuring When Committed Stages Earn Their Cost
summary: When does a committed intermediate stage in an LLM reasoning pipeline earn its cost? Constrained Path Reasoning (CPR) pairs a source-aware path hypothesis with stage-level accounting. Search generates provisional states; trusted or validated invariants can constrain hard, while other proposals remain soft and revisable. CPR predicts that task-compatible commitments can factor transitions, concentrate candidate mass, induce regularity, and expose feedback when their gains exceed propagated error and execution cost. The formalism covers discrete commitments and continuous flows and measures effective branching, endpoint concentration, and cost per usable output. Across 1,180 generated QCQPs and 40 engineered degenerate polynomial instances (2,140 endpoints), residual triage recovers 63.0% of repair-all's additional feasible yield with 17.7% of its attempts. Fixed-LLM accounting (270 unique calls shared across nested arms) finds usable yield of 41.1% direct, 90.0% after formalization and deterministic execution, 20.0% after one-shot convexification, and 21.1% for the full path. In 120 paired-condition calls, a two-action rollback rule reaches 90% usable yield versus 36.7% for the feedback-conditioned selector. Two endpoint probes separate source from validation: a 72-output cross-trajectory transplant reduces entropy and acceptable mass; a 24-output same-call self-proposal pilot gives unchanged two-repeat collision entropy, 25.0% versus 8.3% usable yield, and 1/8 deterministically confirmed endpoint checks. Model-generated states supply hypotheses; trusted execution earns constraint strength.

AI.tldr: CPR introduces a formalism for deciding when intermediate reasoning stages in LLM pipelines are cost-effective, using soft/hard commitments and stage-level accounting. Experiments on 1,220 problem instances show residual triage recovers 63% of repair-all's yield with only 17.7% of attempts, while a two-action rollback rule achieves 90% usable yield versus 36.7% for a feedback-conditioned baseline.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning pipelines often use intermediate stages (e.g., search, validation, repair), but there is no principled framework for determining when a committed intermediate stage justifies its computational cost. The authors aim to formalize this cost-benefit tradeoff by modeling how commitments — whether hard (trusted/validated invariants) or soft (revisable proposals) — affect downstream reasoning efficiency, candidate concentration, and output quality.
AI.method: CPR (Constrained Path Reasoning) formalizes stage-level commitments in LLM reasoning. It pairs source-aware path hypotheses with accounting that tracks cost per usable output, effective branching factor, and endpoint concentration. Hard constraints come from trusted or validated invariants; soft proposals remain revisable. The framework covers both discrete commitments and continuous flows. Empirically, the authors evaluate on 1,180 generated QCQPs and 40 engineered degenerate polynomial instances (2,140 endpoints total). Key mechanisms tested include residual triage, fixed-LLM accounting with shared nested calls (270 unique calls), a two-action rollback rule, and two endpoint probes: a cross-trajectory transplant (72 outputs) and a same-call self-proposal pilot (24 outputs).
AI.result: Residual triage recovers 63.0% of repair-all's additional feasible yield using only 17.7% of its attempts. Fixed-LLM accounting finds usable yields of 41.1% (direct), 90.0% (after formalization/deterministic execution), 20.0% (one-shot convexification), and 21.1% (full path). A two-action rollback rule achieves 90.0% usable yield vs. 36.7% for the feedback-conditioned selector in 120 paired-condition calls. The cross-trajectory transplant probe reduces entropy and acceptable mass. The self-proposal pilot shows unchanged two-repeat collision entropy, 25.0% vs. 8.3% usable yield, and 1/8 deterministically confirmed endpoint checks, separating source effects from validation effects.
AI.conclusion: Task-compatible commitments earn their cost when their gains (factoring transitions, concentrating candidate mass, inducing regularity, exposing feedback) exceed propagated error and execution overhead. Model-generated states supply useful hypotheses, but trusted execution is what earns constraint strength. The formalism successfully predicts and measures when intermediate stages are cost-effective, with the two-action rollback rule and residual triage demonstrating particularly favorable cost-yield tradeoffs.

title: Half the Experts, All the Code: One-Shot Domain Pruning of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Coding
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code and pruned checkpoints: github.com/anik-jha/moep
summary: The strongest open-weight coding models are mixture-of-experts (MoE) networks: most of their size comes from large pools of "expert" subnetworks, of which only a few act on any token. That pool is why these models do not fit on the machines most developers own, yet for a user who only wants coding help, most experts encode abilities that will never be invoked. We ask how many experts can be removed, and which, by pruning two recent open-weight MoE models from different families (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) under five selection strategies, judged the way a user would: by whether the model still writes correct code. Half the experts can be removed from either model with no statistically detectable loss on the primary code benchmark, and the damage lands almost entirely on abilities outside coding, the intended trade. But the winning strategy flips between the two models, so a recipe validated on one family cannot be assumed to work on another. We further show that perplexity, the metric much of the pruning literature leans on, can rate a broken model above an intact one; that a lightweight fine-tune recovers about half of what aggressive pruning loses; and that against quantizing the full model to the same memory, pruning wins only where quantization would have to drop below 3 bits per weight. Five attempts to overturn that crossover, with failure criteria fixed in advance (better calibration, guarded selection, causal expert importance, failure attribution, and an agentic evaluation letting each model repair its failures from execution feedback), all leave it standing; the last shows single-shot benchmarks overstate compression penalties broadly, as one repair turn erases the 2-bit quantization penalty entirely. Expert pruning works, but it demands per-model validation on the task the model will actually serve.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates pruning experts from open-weight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) coding models, finding that up to 50% of experts can be removed without statistically significant loss on code benchmarks. However, optimal pruning strategies differ between model families, perplexity is an unreliable pruning metric, and pruning outperforms quantization only when quantization drops below 3 bits per weight — a crossover that withstands five targeted attempts to overturn it.
AI.motivation: Open-weight MoE coding models (e.g., Qwen, Gemma) are too large to run on typical developer hardware because their massive expert pools, despite most experts never activating for a given user's coding tasks. The authors ask how many experts can be pruned while preserving code-generation correctness, enabling practical local deployment without sacrificing the primary use case.
AI.method: The authors prune two recent MoE models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) using five distinct expert selection strategies. Evaluation is task-specific: code correctness on primary benchmarks, with secondary assessment of non-coding abilities. They compare pruning against quantization at matched memory budgets, and conduct five follow-up experiments with pre-registered failure criteria — better calibration, guarded selection, causal expert importance, failure attribution, and agentic evaluation with execution-feedback repair — to test whether the pruning-vs-quantization crossover can be overturned.
AI.result: Half the experts can be removed from either model with no statistically detectable loss on code benchmarks; degradation is concentrated on non-coding abilities. The best pruning strategy differs between Qwen and Gemma, meaning strategies do not transfer across families. Perplexity can misleadingly rank a broken model above an intact one. Lightweight fine-tuning recovers ~50% of what aggressive pruning loses. Pruning beats quantization only below 3 bits/weight; all five attempts to overturn this crossover failed. Agentic evaluation reveals single-shot benchmarks overstate compression penalties: one repair turn eliminates the 2-bit quantization penalty entirely.
AI.conclusion: Expert pruning is effective for reducing MoE model size while preserving coding ability, but it demands per-model, per-task validation — a recipe validated on one model family cannot be assumed to work on another. The pruning-vs-quantization tradeoff favors quantization until extreme compression regimes (<3 bits). Single-shot benchmarks overstate compression-induced degradation compared to agentic settings with execution feedback.

title: LenGuard-GPC: Length Guarding with Guided-Prompt Consistency for Spatial Reasoning Reinforce Learning
summary: Multi-view spatial reasoning requires vision-language models to compare visual evidence across images, align object correspondences, and infer spatial relations over long visual contexts, a setting where chain-of-thought reasoning tends to grow verbose without becoming more accurate. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is a natural fit for this task, but standard GRPO reward relies on sparse outcome-level feedback and gives no signal about where a reasoning trajectory goes wrong, nor any control over its length. We propose LenGuard-GPC, a dense reward framework that addresses both problems together. For each sampled trajectory, it compares the token-wise predictive distributions under a standard prompt and a guided prompt, and uses the resulting token-sum KL divergence as a dense reward signal. Since this KL penalty accumulates over tokens and would otherwise reward shorter responses regardless of their quality, we introduce a staged length bonus that keeps reasoning length within a controlled range without simply encouraging brevity. On six multi-view spatial reasoning benchmarks, LenGuard-GPC improves accuracy over vanilla GRPO while reducing average response length.

AI.tldr: LenGuard-GPC introduces a dense reward framework for multi-view spatial reasoning that uses token-wise KL divergence between standard and guided prompt distributions, combined with a staged length bonus to keep reasoning concise. It outperforms vanilla GRPO on six benchmarks while reducing response length.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO relies on sparse outcome-level rewards, providing no diagnostic signal about where reasoning errors occur and no length control, leading to verbose but inaccurate chain-of-thought trajectories in multi-view spatial reasoning tasks.
AI.method: LenGuard-GPC computes token-sum KL divergence between predictive distributions under a standard prompt and a guided prompt as a dense reward signal. A staged length bonus is added to keep response length within a controlled range, preventing the KL penalty from indiscriminately rewarding shorter responses regardless of quality.
AI.result: LenGuard-GPC improves accuracy over vanilla GRPO and simultaneously reduces average response length across six multi-view spatial reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Combining a dense KL-divergence reward with a staged length bonus effectively addresses both reasoning quality and length control in reinforcement learning for multi-view spatial reasoning, outperforming sparse-reward baselines.

title: Graph-Embedded Intuitionistic Fuzzy Broad Learning System: A Multi-view Framework
summary: The Broad Learning System (BLS) has been widely used for data classification and is based on a layer-by-layer feed-forward structure. However, it gives the same importance to all data points, which reduces its effectiveness on real-world datasets with noise and outliers. In addition, it does not consider the geometric structure of the data and has limitations in handling data from multiple sources. To address these challenges, we propose a Multi-View Graph-Embedded Intuitionistic Fuzzy Broad Learning System (MVGIFBLS) that integrates multi-view learning, graph embedding, and intuitionistic fuzzy theory into the BLS framework. This design enables the model to combine information from multiple sources and learn more discriminative representations. Graph embedding captures the geometric relationships among samples and improves class separation through intrinsic and penalty subspaces based on local Fisher discriminant analysis. Intuitionistic fuzzy theory enhances robustness to noise, while kernel-based neighborhood analysis captures local data structures. We evaluate the proposed framework on several UCI, KEEL, and AwA benchmark datasets using comparative evaluation, Gaussian feature noise analysis, ablation studies, and statistical analysis. The results demonstrate that each component contributes positively to the overall framework and that the proposed MVGIFBLS consistently achieves higher Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores and maintains robust performance under Gaussian feature noise.

AI.tldr: Proposes MVGIFBLS, a framework combining multi-view learning, graph embedding, and intuitionistic fuzzy theory into Broad Learning System to handle noisy multi-source data with improved class separation and robustness.
AI.motivation: Standard BLS treats all data points equally, lacks robustness to noise/outliers, ignores geometric data structure, and cannot effectively handle multi-source data — all of which limit real-world applicability.
AI.method: Integrates three components into BLS: (1) multi-view learning to fuse information from multiple sources, (2) graph embedding via local Fisher discriminant analysis with intrinsic and penalty subspaces to capture geometric relationships, and (3) intuitionistic fuzzy theory with kernel-based neighborhood analysis for noise robustness and local structure preservation.
AI.result: Evaluated on UCI, KEEL, and AwA benchmarks through comparative evaluation, Gaussian noise analysis, ablation studies, and statistical tests. MVGIFBLS consistently achieves higher AUC scores and maintains robust performance under Gaussian feature noise, with each component contributing positively.
AI.conclusion: MVGIFBLS effectively addresses BLS limitations by incorporating multi-view learning, graph embedding, and intuitionistic fuzzy theory, yielding superior classification performance and noise robustness across diverse benchmark datasets.

title: Coordinated Disentanglement with Iterative Mode Discovery Under Hidden Correlations
summary: Disentangled representation learning is a powerful paradigm for robust attribute prediction. While recent methods address attribute correlations, hidden correlations remain underexplored, where data under the value of a certain attribute exhibit underlying modes correlated with other attributes. To preserve mode information and achieve disentanglement, we jointly discover modes and enforce mode-based conditional independence. Yet, the interdependency between these two modules may lead to error amplification under naive iterations. We propose Coordinated Disentanglement with Iterative mode Discovery (CoDID), an end-to-end framework featuring a dynamic architecture that adapts to evolving number of modes, and a coordination mechanism that mitigates error amplification via meta-optimization. Empirical results demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance on diverse tasks.

AI.tldr: CoDID is an end-to-end disentangled representation learning framework that jointly discovers hidden modes and enforces mode-based conditional independence, using a dynamic architecture and meta-optimization coordination to prevent error amplification, achieving state-of-the-art performance on diverse attribute prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing disentangled representation learning methods handle explicit attribute correlations but neglect hidden correlations — where data points sharing an attribute value exhibit underlying modes correlated with other attributes. Naively iterating between mode discovery and conditional independence enforcement causes error amplification due to module interdependency.
AI.method: CoDID employs a dynamic architecture that adapts to an evolving number of discovered modes, jointly performing mode discovery and mode-based conditional independence. A coordination mechanism based on meta-optimization mitigates the error amplification that arises from the interdependency between the two modules.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on diverse tasks.
AI.conclusion: Jointly addressing mode discovery and mode-based conditional independence with a coordinated, meta-optimized dynamic framework effectively resolves hidden correlation issues in disentangled representation learning, outperforming prior methods.

title: BG4Sea: Biogeochemical Seasonal Forecastability via Progressive Information Scaling
summary: Marine biogeochemical forecasting is increasingly important for managing marine ecosystems and the carbon cycle, yet global, seasonal forecast products lag far behind physical oceanography, held back by the complexity of the processes involved and by data scarcity. We introduce BG4Sea, which to our knowledge is the first global, data-driven system to produce multivariate seasonal forecasts of the marine biogeochemical state. BG4Sea is a modular architecture with a column autoencoder that compresses the vertical column into a low-dimensional latent space, a latent forecaster propagates this representation forward in time, a surface-forcing conditioner that injects physical boundary information via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), and a horizontal-coupling module that incorporates neighboring-column context through cross-attention. The model is trained and evaluated on the global ocean reanalysis BIORYS4 (NEMO/PISCES), and produces six-month forecasts at 1/4 degree, monthly resolution for dissolved chemistry, biology, and carbon-pool variables, outperforming persistence and climatology across most variables and lead times. We position BG4Sea as an interpretable baseline for future, more expressive approaches, and discuss predictability attribution to each component, alongside the model's structural limitations.

AI.tldr: BG4Sea is the first global, data-driven system for multivariate seasonal forecasting of marine biogeochemistry. It uses a modular architecture combining a column autoencoder, latent forecaster, surface-forcing conditioner (FiLM), and horizontal-coupling module (cross-attention). Trained on BIORYS4 reanalysis, it produces 6-month forecasts at 1/4° monthly resolution, outperforming persistence and climatology baselines.
AI.motivation: Marine biogeochemical forecasting is critical for ecosystem and carbon-cycle management, yet global seasonal forecast products are underdeveloped relative to physical oceanography due to process complexity and data scarcity. There is a need for a data-driven baseline that can produce operational-quality multivariate seasonal biogeochemical forecasts.
AI.method: BG4Sea is a modular neural architecture with four components: (1) a column autoencoder that compresses vertical profiles into a low-dimensional latent space; (2) a latent forecaster that propagates the latent state forward in time; (3) a surface-forcing conditioner using Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to inject physical boundary information; and (4) a horizontal-coupling module employing cross-attention to incorporate neighboring-column context. The model is trained and evaluated on the BIORYS4 global ocean reanalysis (NEMO/PISCES).
AI.result: BG4Sea produces six-month forecasts at 1/4° spatial and monthly temporal resolution for dissolved chemistry, biology, and carbon-pool variables. It outperforms both persistence and climatology baselines across most variables and lead times.
AI.conclusion: BG4Sea serves as an interpretable baseline for future, more expressive data-driven biogeochemical forecasting approaches. The authors discuss predictability attribution to each architectural component and acknowledge the model's structural limitations.

title: An Explicit World Model Based on Data-First Ontology: DaoQL Multimodal Storage Validation and Counterfactual Reasoning Evaluation
summary: Large language models encode world models implicitly in neural weights, which exposes four structural risks in high-precision domains such as medicine and finance: hallucination, frozen knowledge, poor explainability, and poor modifiability. This paper proposes data-first ontology: LLMs are treated as reasoning and language engines, while deterministic knowledge is moved into an explicit multimodal database, DaoQL. We formalize an explicit world model and show that, under rule independence, deterministic evaluation, and fixed conflict resolution, explicit models provide a sufficient condition for composable counterfactual decomposability; implicit models lack atomic read/delta semantics and therefore provide no comparable architectural guarantee. The implemented system focuses on DaoQL's verified storage layer and explicit Eval path, integrating graph, column, vector, and full-text engines within one process. KVCache graph nodes, expert hot updates, and the DaoQL-Agent runtime remain future work. On an embedded same-machine setup, DaoQL reports graph BFS at 1.20 ms, HNSW at 83.1 us, and a Fluent hybrid query at 105.8 us; these results indicate engineering potential but must be interpreted with deployment-shape differences from client-server systems. Exploratory measurements on LDBC SNB SF1 and ANN-Benchmarks further show 34/34 query coverage with interactive-class queries mostly in the sub-millisecond to millisecond range, but only 1.8 QPS overall due to long-tail BI/IC queries; ANN-Benchmarks reaches Recall@10 >= 99% at thousand-level QPS after a bridge-edge protection fix. In a five-domain counterfactual experiment (n = 1250), DaoQL+GPT-4o achieves 94% composable counterfactual decomposability, 49 percentage points above GPT-4o alone. The paper explicitly separates provable structure, preliminary empirical evidence, and architectural roadmap claims.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "data-first ontology" that externalizes deterministic knowledge from LLMs into an explicit multimodal database (DaoQL), providing architectural guarantees for composable counterfactual decomposability that implicit LLM world models cannot offer. The system integrates graph, column, vector, and full-text engines, with experiments showing 94% counterfactual decomposability (49pp above GPT-4o alone).
AI.motivation: LLMs encode world models implicitly, creating four structural risks in high-precision domains: hallucination, frozen knowledge, poor explainability, and poor modifiability. These risks stem from the absence of atomic read/delta semantics in implicit representations, making counterfactual reasoning unreliable.
AI.method: The authors formalize an explicit world model with three sufficient conditions (rule independence, deterministic evaluation, fixed conflict resolution) for composable counterfactual decomposability. DaoQL implements this as a multimodal database integrating graph, column, vector, and full-text engines in-process. An explicit Eval path and verified storage layer are implemented, while KVCache graph nodes and the DaoQL-Agent runtime are deferred. Evaluation uses LDBC SNB SF1, ANN-Benchmarks, and a five-domain counterfactual experiment (n=1250).
AI.result: DaoQL achieves: graph BFS at 1.20ms, HNSW at 83.1μs, Fluent hybrid query at 105.8μs on embedded same-machine setup. LDBC SNB SF1 yields 34/34 query coverage with interactive queries in sub-ms to ms range but only 1.8 QPS overall. ANN-Benchmarks reaches Recall@10 ≥99% at thousand-level QPS. In counterfactual experiments, DaoQL+GPT-4o achieves 94% composable counterfactual decomposability versus 45% for GPT-4o alone.
AI.conclusion: The paper explicitly separates provable structural claims (explicit models guarantee composable decomposability), preliminary empirical evidence (engineering benchmarks), and architectural roadmap items (KVCache nodes, agent runtime). Results indicate engineering potential for the data-first ontology approach but require caution regarding deployment-shape differences and long-tail query performance.

title: The Anatomy of a Truth Direction: Knowledge-Dependent Dimensionality, a Relational Law, and a Convergent Category Geometry in Small Language Models
summary: Bürger et al. (2024) demonstrated that truth representations in large language models are universal across statement polarity but reside within a multidimensional subspace. We extend that framework along three questions: how the dimensionality of the subspace depends on the model's knowledge, which architectural component builds the truth direction, and what the direction is a mixture of. In Part I (one model), a training-free directional probe derived from the SVD of hidden-state minimal pairs shows that the dimensionality of truth is knowledge-dependent: the signal is concentrated on a single axis for behaviorally known facts (held-out AUC 0.938) and becomes diffuse as knowledge decreases or material heterogeneity increases; seven falsification experiments sustain the one-dimensional reading, and the same decomposition recovers the supervised polarity direction of Bürger et al. at cosine 0.959 without polarity labels. In Part II (four base models, two families, pre-registered predictions), a relational law emerges: attention propagates truth frames it did not write, the feed-forward network opposes the frame of its current block, and the genuine post-peak decay is causally attributed on all four models to the SwiGLU value stream; per-category truth axes form a semantically signed arrangement that contradicts the lexical surface and converges across families (Mantel p = 0.0009). Stress tests at three scales (33 categories, 888 pairs per relation, six sampling seeds) expose a sign instability of the per-category orientation, repair it with a declared spectral consensus gauge, and sharpen the convergence into a knowledge-gated law, strengthening from +0.42 on dense mixed-knowledge material to +0.74 on knowledge-restricted categories: the geometry of the mixture belongs to the knowledge domain rather than to the architecture.

AI.tldr: Extends Bürger et al. (2024) by showing that truth direction in LLMs is one-dimensional for known facts but multidimensional for uncertain/heterogeneous material; establishes a relational law where attention propagates and feed-forward networks oppose truth frames; demonstrates that the mixture geometry is knowledge-gated rather than architecture-bound, with cross-family convergence.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed LLM truth representations are universal across polarity but multidimensional. Three open questions remain: (1) how dimensionality depends on model knowledge, (2) which architectural component constructs the truth direction, and (3) what the underlying mixture composition of that direction is.
AI.method: Training-free directional probes from SVD of hidden-state minimal pairs; supervised polarity direction recovery without labels; causal attribution via SwiGLU value stream analysis; per-category truth axes with spectral consensus gauge; stress tests across 33 categories, 888 pairs per relation, six sampling seeds; cross-family convergence tested with Mantel test; experiments on four base models from two families with pre-registered predictions.
AI.result: Truth dimensionality collapses to a single axis for known facts (AUC 0.938) and diffuses with decreasing knowledge. Attention propagates truth frames it did not write; feed-forward networks oppose their block's frame; SwiGLU value stream causally drives post-peak decay across all four models. Per-category truth axes form a semantically signed arrangement converging across families (Mantel p=0.0009). Knowledge-gated law: cross-family correlation strengthens from +0.42 (mixed-knowledge) to +0.74 (knowledge-restricted), indicating geometry belongs to knowledge domain, not architecture.
AI.conclusion: Truth geometry in LLMs is knowledge-gated rather than architecture-specific: a single linear truth axis suffices for well-known facts, while uncertainty introduces multidimensional diffusion. The relational attention/feed-forward dynamic and cross-family convergence suggest a universal, semantically organized truth representation grounded in the model's knowledge rather than its architectural details.

title: Lossless but Not Free: An Empirical Anatomy of Speculative Decoding on Consumer Hardware
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code, benchmark harness, and all result artifacts: https://github.com/ParamChordiya/speculative_decoding_engine
summary: Single-stream autoregressive decoding of large language models is bound by memory bandwidth: each generated token requires one full forward pass through the target model, and successive passes cannot be parallelized. Speculative decoding restructures this computation: a small draft model proposes $K$ tokens autoregressively, the target model scores all of them in one batched pass, and a rejection-sampling rule provably preserves the target model's output distribution. We present a from-scratch, device-agnostic (CUDA/MPS/CPU) implementation and an empirical study across five draft/target backend configurations on a consumer Apple-silicon laptop. Distribution equivalence is verified at three levels, culminating in a two-sample test over roughly 9,200 real-model tokens per method ($χ^2 = 162.5$, dof $= 200$, $p = 0.976$) and exact greedy-sequence agreement. The best configuration reaches a measured $1.61\times$ wall-clock speedup at $K=6$, on an acceptance profile declining from 69.7% at $K=1$ to 37.8% at the optimum, while three of five configurations decelerate, either because the draft fails to out-speed a small target or because the quantized Metal backend executes "parallel" verification serially, an effect we isolate and quantify. The failures are as instructive as the successes: speculative decoding pays off only when verification is genuinely batch-parallel and the draft/target latency gap is real.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an empirical study and from-scratch implementation of speculative decoding for LLMs, achieving up to 1.61× wall-clock speedup on Apple Silicon. It demonstrates that distribution equivalence is preserved and identifies critical failure modes where speedups vanish due to serialized verification or insufficient draft/target latency gaps.
AI.motivation: LLM autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token requires a full forward pass that cannot be parallelized. While speculative decoding theoretically addresses this via batched verification, practical speedups depend heavily on implementation quality and hardware characteristics. The authors aim to empirically quantify when and why speculative decoding succeeds or fails on consumer hardware.
AI.method: The authors implement a from-scratch, device-agnostic (CUDA/MPS/CPU) speculative decoding pipeline. A small draft model proposes K tokens autoregressively; the target model scores all K tokens in one batched forward pass; rejection sampling preserves the target distribution. They evaluate five draft/target backend configurations on an Apple Silicon laptop, measuring wall-clock speedup, token acceptance rates, and distribution equivalence via two-sample tests (~9,200 tokens, χ²=162.5, p=0.976) and greedy-sequence agreement.
AI.result: The best configuration achieves 1.61× wall-clock speedup at K=6 with acceptance rates declining from 69.7% (K=1) to 37.8% (K=6). Distribution equivalence is verified at three levels. Critically, three of five configurations decelerate: either the draft model fails to out-speed a small target, or the quantized Metal backend executes batched verification serially, which the authors isolate and quantify as a key failure mode.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding yields real speedups only when two conditions hold: (1) verification is genuinely batch-parallel on the hardware backend, and (2) there exists a meaningful latency gap between draft and target models. The serial execution behavior of the Metal backend on Apple Silicon serves as a cautionary example, and the failures are as instructive as the successes for practitioners deploying speculative decoding.

title: Robust Losses from Univariate Base Functions for Noisy-Label Learning
summary: Learning with noisy labels is a fundamental problem in training reliable deep neural networks. Robust loss functions provide a direct and effective way to mitigate the adverse effects of label noise. However, most existing robust losses are designed directly at the level of the final multiclass objective, which makes it difficult to systematically characterize and extend their robustness properties. In this paper, we propose a general framework that constructs robust multiclass losses from univariate base functions. By defining mapping operators from base functions to multiclass losses, the robustness of the induced losses can be characterized through simple properties of the base functions. We develop two complementary construction schemes, Target Separation and Binary Reduction, corresponding to inter-class independent and inter-class dependent formulations, respectively. For both schemes, we analyze their symmetry and asymmetry properties and derive corresponding sufficient conditions, which provide theoretical criteria for noise-robust loss design. The proposed framework also provides a new route to constructing symmetric losses, serving as a complement to normalization-based symmetric loss designs. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world noisy-label benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed losses achieve competitive or superior performance under various noise settings.

AI.tldr: A framework for constructing noise-robust multiclass losses from univariate base functions via two schemes (Target Separation and Binary Reduction), with theoretical sufficient conditions for robustness and symmetry, achieving competitive performance on noisy-label benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing robust loss functions are designed directly at the multiclass objective level, making it hard to systematically characterize and extend their robustness. A principled, bottom-up construction from simpler base functions would enable better theoretical understanding and design flexibility.
AI.method: The authors propose mapping operators that lift univariate base functions to multiclass losses via two complementary schemes: (1) Target Separation — an inter-class independent formulation, and (2) Binary Reduction — an inter-class dependent formulation. For each scheme, they analyze symmetry/asymmetry properties and derive sufficient conditions on the base functions (e.g., boundedness, monotonicity) that guarantee noise robustness. The framework also yields new symmetric loss constructions as an alternative to normalization-based approaches.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 with symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise) and real-world (Clothing1M, WebVision) benchmarks show the proposed losses achieve competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art robust loss methods.
AI.conclusion: The base-function framework provides a systematic and theoretically grounded approach to designing robust multiclass losses, with clear sufficient conditions that guide practitioners. It unifies and extends prior robust loss designs while matching or exceeding their empirical performance.

title: On the Potential of Graph Neural Networks as Metamodels for Supply Chain Optimization: Dataset, Architectures, and Directions
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful, differentiable class of learning models for graph-structured systems. Their ability to generalize across topologies opens the prospect of a surrogate for combined structural and parametric optimization, which classical metamodels cannot offer. Supply chains are a natural target, yet the use of GNN surrogates for supply chain problems is largely unexplored. This paper lays the foundation, presents initial steps, and discusses key research directions. As a foundation, we formulate the problem and create a large public training dataset of programmatically generated supply chain graphs with input parameters and steady-state performance metrics obtained using our SupplyNetPy simulation library. As initial steps, we explore GNN architectures that work well as surrogates for node- and network-level predictions, and analyze their accuracy-compute trade-off against simulation. Most importantly, we outline the exciting directions this opens, namely gradient-based optimization over topology, fast design-space exploration, and sensitivity analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GNNs as surrogates for supply chain simulation, providing a dataset (SupplyNetPy), benchmarking GNN architectures for node- and network-level prediction, and outlining future directions in gradient-based topology optimization, design-space exploration, and sensitivity analysis.
AI.motivation: Classical metamodels cannot generalize across different graph topologies, limiting combined structural and parametric optimization. GNNs offer topology-aware generalization, making them promising surrogates for supply chain problems — yet this application domain remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors (1) formulate the supply chain surrogate problem, (2) create a large public training dataset using programmatically generated supply chain graphs paired with steady-state performance metrics from their custom SupplyNetPy simulation library, (3) benchmark multiple GNN architectures on node-level and network-level prediction tasks, and (4) evaluate accuracy vs. compute trade-offs against traditional simulation.
AI.result: The paper identifies GNN architectures that perform effectively as surrogates for supply chain predictions at both node and network levels, and quantifies the accuracy–compute trade-off, demonstrating that GNN surrogates can achieve competitive accuracy with significant computational savings over full simulation.
AI.conclusion: GNN-based surrogates are viable for supply chain modeling and open up transformative capabilities including gradient-based topology optimization, rapid design-space exploration, and sensitivity analysis — setting a foundation for future research at the intersection of graph learning and supply chain engineering.

title: MultiLoReFT: Decoupling Shared and Modality-Specific Subspaces in Multimodal Learning via Low-Rank Representation Fine-Tuning
summary: Real-world perception and decision making are inherently multimodal, integrating complementary signals across modalities. However, training multimodal models faces two main obstacles. First, collecting large-scale, well-aligned paired multimodal datasets is often impractical, making end-to-end multimodal training difficult. Second, existing multimodal representations frequently entangle information shared across modalities with modality-specific information, hindering interpretability and control. We introduce MultiLoReFT, an efficient and scalable low-rank representation fine-tuning framework for multimodal learning with pretrained unimodal models. MultiLoReFT extends low-rank adaptation to the multimodal setting and learns interpretable projection subspaces that decouple shared and modality-specific information. Across simulated and real-world benchmarks, it produces representations that support multimodal prediction while explicitly revealing how shared and modality-specific information is distributed across modalities.

AI.tldr: MultiLoReFT is a low-rank fine-tuning framework that enables multimodal learning from pretrained unimodal models, producing interpretable representations that decouple shared and modality-specific information without requiring large-scale paired datasets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal learning faces two key obstacles: (1) collecting large-scale, well-aligned paired multimodal datasets is impractical, hindering end-to-end training; (2) existing multimodal representations entangle shared cross-modal information with modality-specific information, limiting interpretability and control.
AI.method: MultiLoReFT extends low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to the multimodal setting by learning interpretable projection subspaces that explicitly decouple shared information across modalities from modality-specific information. The framework operates on pretrained unimodal models, avoiding the need for joint end-to-end multimodal training.
