AI.conclusion: The optimal memory strategy depends on relative budget pressure. The utility decomposition explains the crossover pattern, and OAS provides a principled, learnable mechanism for dynamically selecting the right operator. Cross-note abstraction and merging are the preferred compression methods when consolidation is indicated.

title: Abliteration Is Not a Scalpel: Off-Target Effects of Refusal Removal on Decision Disposition Across Model Families
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Preregistered. Data and code: https://github.com/oleczek/paper-abliteration-not-a-scalpel ; dataset DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21314839
summary: Abliteration - deleting a model's refusal direction from its weights - is the standard recipe behind popular "uncensored" open-weight models. We show the surgery is not clean. As a disposition probe we use 21,600 decisions under uncertainty - weekly up/down calls on 60 Warsaw Stock Exchange equities over 18 weeks, replayed through a frozen pipeline so the decision-layer model is the only variable. The task elicits no refusals at all, so any between-arm delta is pure side effect. Holding provenance constant (official BF16 checkpoints, a single abliteration author, an identical serving stack, one byte-identical frozen prompt), we compare base and abliterated arms of two Mixture-of-Experts families, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Three effects replicate across both families (weeks-clustered bootstrap CIs excluding zero): abliterated models are systematically more optimistic (+12.2 pp Gemma, +7.4 pp Qwen; the confirmed preregistered endpoint), justify themselves at greater length, and use fewer explicit uncertainty words in forced self-critiques (both exploratory). A fourth effect reverses sign: the same operation makes Gemma-abliterated less confident and Qwen-abliterated more (family CIs non-overlapping) - one weight surgery, opposite shifts in expressed confidence. Capability covariates rule out instruction-following degradation as the driver, and no arm shows economic skill: the apparent edge of abliterated arms is regime beta, not alpha. Our provenance audit also caught two independent contamination channels - a mismatched-quantizer pilot pair and a stale community chat template that silently mangled the rendered prompt - suggesting toolchain artifacts are the rule in studies of community-modified checkpoints. Whoever deploys an "uncensored" model as an agent is deploying a measurably different decision-maker, not the base model minus refusals.

AI.tldr: Abliteration—deleting refusal directions from model weights to create "uncensored" models—produces unintended side effects on decision-making behavior. Using 21,600 stock market predictions across two MoE model families, the study finds abliterated models are systematically more optimistic, produce longer justifications, use fewer uncertainty words, and show family-dependent shifts in expressed confidence, despite the task never triggering refusals. The paper also documents contamination from toolchain artifacts in community-modified checkpoints.
AI.motivation: The widespread practice of abliteration for creating "uncensored" open-weight models lacks rigorous characterization of its side effects. The authors aim to test whether removing refusal directions is a "clean" surgery or whether it alters broader model behavior beyond the intended refusal removal, using a task that never elicits refusals to isolate pure side effects.
AI.method: A behavioral experiment using 21,600 binary decisions (weekly up/down calls on 60 Warsaw Stock Exchange equities over 18 weeks) replayed through a frozen pipeline. Two Mixture-of-Experts model families (Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507) are compared in base vs. abliterated arms, holding provenance constant (official BF16 checkpoints, single abliteration author, identical serving stack, byte-identical frozen prompts). Outcomes include a preregistered optimism endpoint and exploratory measures of response length, uncertainty language, and expressed confidence. Bootstrap CIs with week-clustered standard errors are used, along with capability covariates and an economic skill decomposition into alpha vs. beta.
AI.result: Three effects replicate across both families: (1) abliterated models are systematically more optimistic (+12.2 pp Gemma, +7.4 pp Qwen, preregistered), (2) they produce longer self-justifications, and (3) they use fewer explicit uncertainty words. A fourth effect reverses sign: abliteration reduces expressed confidence in Gemma but increases it in Qwen. No arm shows economic alpha—the apparent edge is regime beta. Two contamination channels were discovered: a mismatched-quantizer pilot pair and a stale community chat template that mangled prompts, highlighting toolchain artifact risks in community-modified checkpoint studies.
AI.conclusion: Abliteration is not a clean surgical intervention—it produces measurable, replicable side effects on decision-making behavior independent of refusal suppression. Deploying an "uncensored" model means deploying a measurably different decision-maker, not merely the base model minus refusals. The study also urges robust provenance controls in research on community-modified checkpoints.

title: When Can Safe Controllers Adapt? Information before Commitment
summary:
Safe adaptive control is online adaptation under a safety guarantee on the learning trajectory itself. The controller may use any causal, history-dependent rule and act differently across environments as data arrive. Only its safety guarantee is uniform: the same rule must satisfy it under every initially plausible model. Performance is measured against a safe oracle that knows the realized model. Many finite-time analyses assume persistent excitation of the uniformly safe closed loop, so the data distinguish every pair of models requiring different control decisions. Under that assumption, feasibility is already settled; only the rate remains. We ask instead: Do the safety constraints permit such an informative experiment at all?
  While an alternative remains plausible, the controller must preserve a safe continuation under it. We call the first action that forecloses such a continuation commitment. Chance safety allows commitment only on an event rare under the alternative, and the evidence must arrive beforehand: the observation generated by the committing action is too late. We define precommitment information as the KL divergence between learner-visible laws stopped before commitment.
  Our main result is a causal reduction. The commitment rule determines (1) the probability that safety permits commitment under the alternative, (2) the target-side cost of remaining noncommittal, (3) and the information available when the decision is made. Bounded precommitment information therefore leaves a fixed fraction of the oracle gap unavoidable. If the gap is Ω(T), every uniformly safe policy has linear regret. We establish the obstruction in a constrained linear system with quadratic regulation cost. We also prove recovery in special cases and derive semidefinite upper certificates for deterministic linear-Gaussian systems.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a fundamental information-theoretic limitation on safe adaptive control: when precommitment information is bounded, uniformly safe policies inevitably incur linear regret relative to a safe oracle. The authors characterize "commitment" — the first action that forecloses safe continuation under an alternative model — and prove a causal reduction tying regret lower bounds to the KL divergence between learner-visible laws before commitment.
AI.motivation: Existing finite-time analyses of safe adaptive control assume persistent excitation, which already guarantees feasibility and only addresses the rate of convergence. This paper asks a prior question: do the safety constraints permit such informative experimentation at all? The goal is to understand when safety itself creates an inherent obstruction to identifying the correct control policy, forcing any uniformly safe controller into linear regret.
AI.method: The authors formalize "commitment" as the first action after which safe continuation under an alternative model becomes impossible. They introduce "precommitment information" as the KL divergence between learner-visible laws stopped just before commitment. The main result is a causal reduction: the commitment rule jointly determines (1) the probability of safe commitment under the alternative, (2) the cost of remaining noncommittal, and (3) the available information at decision time. Bounded precommitment information implies a fixed fraction of the oracle gap is unavoidable. The obstruction is demonstrated in a constrained linear system with quadratic costs, with recovery results in special cases and semidefinite upper certificates for deterministic linear-Gaussian systems.
AI.result: Bounded precommitment information leaves a fixed fraction of the oracle performance gap unavoidable. If the gap is Ω(T), every uniformly safe policy suffers linear regret. The authors establish this obstruction concretely for constrained linear systems with quadratic regulation cost, prove recovery is possible in special cases, and derive semidefinite programming-based upper certificates for deterministic linear-Gaussian systems.
AI.conclusion: Safety constraints can fundamentally limit exploration to the point where uniformly safe controllers cannot avoid linear regret. The precommitment information framework provides a tight information-theoretic characterization of when and why this occurs. The problem reduces to whether the safety constraints allow sufficient information to be gathered before a committing action must be taken.

title: Why Does Feedback-Augmented Self-Distillation Fail to Improve Retrieval-Interleaved Search Agents?
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach for training large language models without relying on a separate teacher model. However, its effectiveness on complex agentic tasks remains largely unexplored. In this work, we instantiate Feedback-Augmented Self-Distillation (FA-SD), a self-distillation algorithm for agentic search that leverages successful demonstrations as privileged information. We identify that models can rely on recurring reasoning-and-search output templates, producing trajectories that appear diverse but are largely agnostic to the input question, making the KL-based self-distillation signal uninformative. We term this phenomenon decoding collapse, a failure mode that can be missed by existing evaluation metrics. To understand its underlying cause, we show that although the self-teacher achieves stronger performance, learning remains inherently unstable due to inconsistent supervision signals. We further decompose this inconsistency into model inconsistency and prompt inconsistency, and show that the latter can significantly degrade the quality of the supervision signal, limiting the effectiveness of self-teacher learning. To mitigate this inconsistency, we introduce an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher to stabilize the self-teacher and provide more consistent supervision signals. Although the EMA teacher requires a warm-up phase during which performance may temporarily regress, it ultimately improves model performance by providing more stable supervision.

AI.tldr: FA-SD is a self-distillation method for agentic search that uses successful trajectories as privileged info. The authors identify "decoding collapse" — where models produce templated, question-agnostic outputs that fool existing metrics. They trace this to inconsistent supervision from the self-teacher (decomposed into model and prompt inconsistency) and propose an EMA teacher to stabilize supervision, improving final performance despite a temporary warm-up regression.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is promising for LLM training without a separate teacher, but its effectiveness on complex agentic tasks is underexplored. The authors aim to understand failure modes when applying self-distillation to agentic search and to improve training stability.
AI.method: The authors instantiate Feedback-Augmented Self-Distillation (FA-SD) for agentic search, using successful demonstrations as privileged information. They analyze failure modes, decomposing supervision inconsistency into model inconsistency and prompt inconsistency. To mitigate these, they introduce an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that provides more consistent supervision signals, albeit with a warm-up phase where performance may temporarily regress.
AI.result: The authors identify "decoding collapse" — models produce diverse-appearing but question-agnostic templated trajectories, making KL-based self-distillation uninformative. They show self-teacher learning is inherently unstable due to inconsistent supervision signals, with prompt inconsistency significantly degrading supervision quality. The EMA teacher stabilizes supervision and improves final model performance.
AI.conclusion: Self-distillation on agentic tasks suffers from decoding collapse and supervision inconsistency. An EMA teacher effectively stabilizes the self-teacher's supervision signal, improving performance despite temporary warm-up regression. This highlights the importance of consistent supervision in self-distillation for complex agentic settings.

title: After the Euclidean Highway: Hyperbolic Expert AI as the Next Innovation
comment: 40 pages, 11 figures. Supplementary Information included as an ancillary file. Data and code: Zenodo, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21438499 (published, CC-BY-4.0)
summary: Expert domains are trees; the Euclidean transformer is not, diluting parent-child structure exponentially at depth. The hyperbolic turn left one question unasked: not how much of a network to curve, but where curvature may touch the gradient. Placement is a law, not a knob: the same geometry on a trainable adapter collapses training (seventeen training collapses, ~220 GPU-hours), yet at the loss layer alone it trains without one -- this is HySAT (Hyperbolic Structure-Aware Training), hyperbolic losses at the loss layer only. Across six expert SLMs we constructed and deployed (Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5; four adapter strategies; 18.0M-sample corpus; zero NaN over ~317K optimizer steps), a matched four-arm ablation isolates the preserved manifold invariant, and three propositions and a lemma prove why loss-only placement is stable where adapter-on-manifold is not. Four models are operationally deployed (one live, consumer-facing), two open-weight, with per-step traces and a seventeen-incident failure ledger on Zenodo (CC-BY-4.0).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HySAT (Hyperbolic Structure-Aware Training), demonstrating that hyperbolic geometry should be applied only at the loss layer — not in trainable adapters — to preserve tree-structured expert domain knowledge. Applying hyperbolic geometry to adapters caused 17 training collapses across ~220 GPU-hours, while loss-only placement remained stable over ~317K optimizer steps with zero NaN occurrences.
AI.motivation: Expert domains (e.g., legal, medical taxonomies) exhibit hierarchical tree structure. Standard Euclidean transformers dilute this parent-child structure exponentially with depth. While hyperbolic geometry can preserve tree structure, prior work treated curvature as a global architectural choice ("how much to curve"). The authors identify an overlooked question: **where** curvature should be placed — not as a tunable knob but as a placement law — to avoid gradient instability.
AI.method: The authors constructed and deployed six expert small language models (SLMs) using Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5 backbones with four adapter strategies. They compared hyperbolic geometry applied at (a) trainable adapters vs. (b) the loss layer only (HySAT). A matched four-arm ablation isolated the invariant manifold preservation. Three propositions and a lemma formally prove why loss-only placement is stable while adapter-on-manifold placement causes collapse. Experiments used an 18M-sample corpus and ~317K optimizer steps.
AI.result: Adapter-level hyperbolic geometry caused 17 documented training collapses (~220 GPU-hours lost). In contrast, HySAT (loss-layer-only hyperbolic placement) trained without a single collapse — zero NaN over ~317K steps. Four models were operationally deployed (one live, consumer-facing); two were released as open-weight. A per-step trace and 17-incident failure ledger were published on Zenodo (CC-BY-4.0).
AI.conclusion: Placement of hyperbolic curvature is a law, not a tunable hyperparameter. Confining hyperbolic geometry exclusively to the loss layer (HySAT) preserves hierarchical structure while maintaining training stability. The formal proofs establish that adapter-on-manifold placement inherently destabilizes gradients, making loss-only placement the principled choice for structure-aware training in expert domains.

title: Enhancing Personalized Bladder Cancer Treatment Through Reinforcement Learning: A Recurrent Patient State Transition Decision Support Framework
summary: Bladder cancer treatment requires personalized and adaptive decision-making, particularly for recurrent disease, where treatment effectiveness changes across successive clinical episodes. Conventional clinical decision support systems typically rely on static treatment guidelines or single-step predictive models, limiting their ability to capture disease progression over time. This paper presents a recurrent patient state-transition simulation framework for bladder cancer treatment planning that integrates predictive state-transition modeling with a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and a Deep Q-Network (DQN) reinforcement learning environment. The predictive module estimates changes in tumor characteristics following treatment, while the reinforcement learning agent sequentially optimizes treatment decisions by interacting with simulated patient trajectories. This framework enables dynamic, patient-specific treatment planning by continuously adapting recommendations to evolving clinical states. It also generates interpretable treatment trajectories and detailed simulation logs to improve transparency and support clinical decision-making. The proposed framework was evaluated against existing reinforcement learning-based treatment planning approaches. It achieved a cumulative reward of 63,918.87, an average training loss per episode of 0.0056, and a policy improvement score of 6.62%, demonstrating effective sequential learning and robust treatment optimization in a simulated recurrent treatment environment. These findings highlight the potential of recurrent patient state-transition simulation with reinforcement learning as a flexible decision-support framework for personalized bladder cancer treatment planning and AI-assisted precision oncology.

AI.tldr: A recurrent state-transition simulation framework combining predictive modeling with DQN-based reinforcement learning for personalized bladder cancer treatment planning, achieving strong sequential optimization performance in simulated environments.
AI.motivation: Conventional clinical decision support systems for bladder cancer rely on static guidelines or single-step predictive models that fail to capture disease progression and changing treatment effectiveness across recurrent episodes, creating a need for dynamic, adaptive treatment planning that accounts for evolving patient states over time.
AI.method: The framework integrates three components: (1) a predictive state-transition module that estimates post-treatment tumor characteristic changes, (2) a Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation of the treatment planning problem, and (3) a Deep Q-Network (DQN) reinforcement learning agent that sequentially optimizes treatment decisions through interaction with simulated patient trajectories. The system generates interpretable treatment trajectories and simulation logs for transparency.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieved a cumulative reward of 63,918.87, an average training loss per episode of 0.0056, and a policy improvement score of 6.62% compared to existing RL-based treatment planning approaches, demonstrating effective sequential learning and robust treatment optimization.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent patient state-transition simulation with reinforcement learning shows strong potential as a flexible, interpretable decision-support framework for personalized bladder cancer treatment planning and AI-assisted precision oncology.

title: Reinforcement Learning: From Algorithms To Foundation Models
summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for sequential decision making under explicit objectives. In its classical form, RL studies how an agent should act to maximise long-term reward in a dynamic environment. In richer settings, the problem extends beyond a single agent and fixed environment: intelligent behavior may require strategic interaction, adaptation to uncertainty, and reasoning over high-dimensional worlds. This thesis studies RL from two perspectives: algorithms in games and RL in the era of foundation models.
  The first part focuses on multi-agent RL in games. It examines how incentives, policies, and equilibrium concepts interact in competitive and general-sum environments, spanning two-player zero-sum games, large-scale video games, and multi-player settings with general structure. These works investigate learning in multi-agent systems and the behavior of RL methods in interactive environments. The second part studies RL with generative and foundation models, motivated by the idea that prior knowledge can enrich sequential decision making. Pretrained generative models and learned world models serve as representation tools and structured priors for planning, control, and policy optimization. The thesis develops diffusion-based world models, investigates RL for efficient video generation, explores generative models as policy classes, and studies interactive video world models in which actions shape future observations. It also addresses long-horizon modeling through architectures with memory. Together, these contributions present a unified view of RL as objective-driven adaptation in complex sequential domains. From strategic games to generative world models, the thesis highlights how RL connects decision making, environment modeling, and emerging foundation-model capabilities, offering a broader perspective on the principles underlying intelligent behavior.

AI.tldr: This thesis explores reinforcement learning from two angles: multi-agent RL in games (studying strategic interaction, incentives, and equilibrium) and RL with generative/foundation models (using pretrained models as structured priors for planning, control, and world modeling). It unifies these perspectives as objective-driven adaptation in complex sequential domains.
AI.motivation: Classical RL focuses on a single agent maximizing reward in a fixed environment, but intelligent behavior in richer settings demands strategic multi-agent interaction, adaptation to uncertainty, and reasoning over high-dimensional worlds. The thesis is motivated by the need to extend RL to these more complex domains, and by the opportunity to leverage foundation models as powerful priors for sequential decision making.
AI.method: The thesis is divided into two parts. Part one investigates multi-agent RL algorithms across competitive and general-sum games (zero-sum, large-scale video games, multi-player settings), analyzing how incentives, policies, and equilibria interact. Part two develops methods integrating generative and foundation models with RL: diffusion-based world models, RL for efficient video generation, generative models as policy classes, interactive video world models with action-conditioned futures, and memory-augmented architectures for long-horizon modeling.
AI.result: The contributions collectively demonstrate that RL principles apply effectively to both strategic game-theoretic settings and generative-model-driven environments. The thesis shows how pretrained generative models can serve as world simulators and policy representations, and how multi-agent RL methods reveal the dynamics of learning in interactive, competitive, and general-sum settings.
AI.conclusion: RL provides a unified framework for objective-driven adaptation across complex sequential domains. The thesis bridges strategic decision making in games with emerging foundation-model capabilities, highlighting RL's role in connecting decision making, environment modeling, and intelligent behavior more broadly.

title: Investigation of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Approaches
comment: Published in 2023 5th International Conference on Sustainable Technologies for Industry 5.0 (STI), December 2023, Dhaka, Bangladesh
summary: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) is a widespread hormone problem for women of childbearing age. Women with PCOS may not ovulate; they might have high levels of androgens and have many small cysts on the ovaries. It can cause missed or irregular menstrual periods, excess hair growth, acne, infertility, and weight gain. Machine Learning (ML) can effectively diagnose this disease at an earlier stage as tons of medical data are available now. Traditional approaches to detect PCOS encompass a combination of clinical evaluation, medical history assessment, physical examination, and laboratory tests. These approaches aim to identify the characteristic symptoms and hormonal imbalances associated with PCOS. Physical examination requires good resources and costs time and money. In recent times, data-driven techniques have substantially advanced disease prediction within the medical field. We aim to utilize ML approaches, incorporating unique feature selection algorithms, to predict PCOS. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to PCOS diagnosis, combining Feature Engineering and ML. Several feature selection approaches have been considered to select sets of features for training the ML model, including CatBoost, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), AdaBoost, Random Forest (RF). Results demonstrate that AdaBoost, with ten features selected by RF Feature Importance and Highest Correlation (HC), provides the highest test accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a data-driven PCOS diagnosis framework combining feature engineering with multiple ML classifiers. AdaBoost, using ten features selected via Random Forest Feature Importance and Highest Correlation, achieves the highest test accuracy among all evaluated combinations.
AI.motivation: Traditional PCOS diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, medical history, physical examination, and lab tests, which are resource-intensive, time-consuming, and costly. Leveraging ML with available medical data enables earlier, more efficient, and cost-effective PCOS detection.
AI.method: The authors apply feature engineering with multiple selection methods (RF Feature Importance, Highest Correlation) to reduce the feature set. Five ML classifiers are trained and evaluated: CatBoost, XGBoost, LGBM, AdaBoost, and Random Forest. The best-performing configuration is AdaBoost trained on ten features selected via RF Feature Importance combined with Highest Correlation.
AI.result: AdaBoost with ten features selected by Random Forest Feature Importance and Highest Correlation yields the highest test accuracy among all classifier-feature selection combinations tested.
AI.conclusion: A data-driven approach integrating feature engineering and ensemble ML models can effectively predict PCOS. Careful feature selection significantly improves classification performance, with AdaBoost proving particularly effective for this diagnostic task.

title: ZifaMem: Structured Memory for Persona, Preference, and Emotional Continuity in AI Companions
summary: AI companions are judged not only by single-turn fluency but by whether they sustain emotional continuity: remembering who the companion is, what the user prefers, and how the relationship has felt. We present ZifaMem, a structured memory system that organizes dialogue into session summaries, episodic memories, and a consolidated user model. Against a deployment-honest comparator that supplies the full raw dialogue history, and under a fixed LLM-as-a-judge protocol with route audits, structured memory raises pooled four-backbone emotional-intelligence scores by 11.4% (95% CI 6.3% to 17.1%), and persona grounding improves on all four backbones (Claude +42% relative). Multi-turn affect context wins a +39% net preference over a single-turn snapshot (exploratory), whereas an additional emotion state machine yields no measurable gain on any of five endpoints. Under an identical preregistered protocol, three memory systems (ZifaMem, Mem0, and filtered verbatim retrieval) each improve significantly over raw-history deployment, and ZifaMem and Mem0 are statistically equivalent within +/-5 points on the preregistered primary preference endpoint. The ZifaMem SDK, CLI, and portable Agent Skills are open-sourced at https://github.com/zifacorp/zifamem.

AI.tldr: ZifaMem is a structured memory system for AI companions that organizes dialogue into session summaries, episodic memories, and a user model. It improves emotional intelligence scores by 11.4% over raw-history baselines, with multi-turn affect context strongly preferred (+39%) over single-turn snapshots. Under preregistered testing, ZifaMem and Mem0 both significantly outperform raw-history baselines and are statistically equivalent.
AI.motivation: Current AI companion evaluation focuses on single-turn fluency but neglects emotional continuity — remembering user identity, preferences, and relationship history across conversations. This gap motivates a structured memory approach that sustains long-term relational coherence.
AI.method: ZifaMem implements a three-tier memory architecture: (1) session summaries for recent dialogue, (2) episodic memories for salient past interactions, and (3) a consolidated user model capturing preferences and persona. Evaluation uses a fixed LLM-as-a-judge protocol with route audits, comparing ZifaMem against a deployment-honest raw-history comparator. Four LLM backbones are tested. The protocol is preregistered, and comparisons include Mem0 and filtered verbatim retrieval. Exploratory experiments additionally test multi-turn affect context versus single-turn snapshots and an emotion state machine.
AI.result: Structured memory yields an 11.4% pooled improvement (95% CI 6.3%–17.1%) in emotional-intelligence scores across four backbones. Persona grounding improves on all backbones, with Claude showing a +42% relative gain. Multi-turn affect context wins +39% net preference over single-turn snapshots. The emotion state machine produces no measurable gain on any of five endpoints. Under preregistered comparison, ZifaMem, Mem0, and filtered verbatim retrieval all significantly outperform raw-history deployment; ZifaMem and Mem0 are statistically equivalent within ±5 points on the primary preference endpoint.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory systems reliably improve emotional continuity and persona grounding in AI companions. The equivalence between ZifaMem and Mem0 suggests that the memory paradigm — rather than a specific implementation — drives the gains. An emotion state machine adds no benefit, indicating that richer context representations may suffice. The system is open-sourced for reproducibility and adoption.

title: CADENCE: Closing the Reasoning Gap via Coverage-Adaptive On-Policy Distillation
summary:
On-policy knowledge distillation transfers reasoning from large teachers to compact students, but existing approaches suffer three compounding failure modes: (i) cold-start collapse, where a fresh student assigns near-zero mass to teacher-preferred tokens; (ii) state-agnostic divergence scheduling, where time-only forward/reverse-KL interpolation ignores the student's coverage state; and (iii) binary reward sparsity, where pass/fail signals discard information from partially correct traces.
  We present CADENCE, a unified framework with a targeted fix for each. Its DRIFT mechanism schedules a per-token convex mixture of forward-KL and reverse-KL surrogate objectives on student-sampled trajectories (per-token surrogates, not sequence-level KL gradient estimators). Six components extend it: (A) COVA, a coverage-adaptive $β$ schedule accelerating the forward-to-reverse transition; (B) FTB, a forking-token boost concentrating gradient at high-entropy positions via a globally-normalized entropy reference; (C) CCD, a dense reward adding numerical-proximity partial credit for incorrect-but-close traces; (D) LAP, brevity-preferential correct-rollout reinforcement; (E) EMR, an entropy-matching calibration regularizer; (F) BSD, a bootstrapped self-distillation phase.
  On GSM8K and MATH-500 (corrected 512-token protocol, 5 seeds, reported std), CADENCE distills a 0.5B student from a 1.5B teacher to 69.8 $\pm$ 0.5% GSM8K pass@1 (from 48.7% pretrained; 63.2% of the teacher gap closed) and to 72.1 $\pm$ 0.4% with a 3B teacher (76.2% closed), beating the strongest matched-compute label-using baseline (DRIFT+binary reward) by +4.4 $\pm$ 0.7 points. All experiments run on a single Apple Mac Studio (M-series, 64GB unified memory), showing principled distillation reaches strong reasoning quality without datacenter-scale hardware.

AI.tldr: CADENCE is a knowledge distillation framework that addresses three failure modes in on-policy reasoning transfer — cold-start collapse, state-agnostic divergence scheduling, and binary reward sparsity — through DRIFT (per-token KL mixture surrogates) plus six auxiliary components, achieving strong GSM8K and MATH-500 results on consumer hardware (Mac Studio).
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy knowledge distillation methods for transferring reasoning from large teachers to compact students suffer from three compounding failures: (1) cold-start collapse where new students assign near-zero probability to teacher-preferred tokens, (2) state-agnostic KL scheduling that ignores the student's actual coverage state, and (3) binary reward sparsity that discards information from partially correct reasoning traces.
AI.method: CADENCE is a unified framework centered on DRIFT, which schedules per-token convex mixtures of forward-KL and reverse-KL surrogate objectives on student-sampled trajectories. Six extensions are added: (A) COVA — coverage-adaptive β scheduling for accelerating forward-to-reverse transitions; (B) FTB — forking-token boost concentrating gradients at high-entropy positions using globally-normalized entropy; (C) CCD — continuous correctness dense reward for partial credit on incorrect-but-close traces; (D) LAP — brevity-preferential correct-rollout reinforcement; (E) EMR — entropy-matching calibration regularizer; (F) BSD — bootstrapped self-distillation phase.
AI.result: Distilling a 0.5B student from a 1.5B teacher on GSM8K yields 69.8±0.5% pass@1 (up from 48.7% pretrained), closing 63.2% of the teacher gap. With a 3B teacher, performance reaches 72.1±0.4% (76.2% gap closed). CADENCE beats the strongest matched-compute baseline (DRIFT+binary reward) by +4.4±0.7 points. All experiments run on a single Apple Mac Studio (M-series, 64GB unified memory).
AI.conclusion: Principled on-policy knowledge distillation with targeted fixes for known failure modes can achieve strong mathematical reasoning quality in compact models without requiring datacenter-scale hardware, demonstrating that careful objective design matters more than raw compute scale for distillation.

title: A Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning Framework for LLM Guardrails
summary: We propose ARBITER, a novel LLM guardrail framework that introduces two key ideas: (i) dual-hypothesis reasoning, a reasoning method for LLM guardrails that explicitly considers both safe and unsafe interpretations of a prompt before making a safety decision, and (ii) multi-component supervised fine-tuning (MC-SFT), a structured training loss for reasoning-based guardrails that decomposes LLM outputs into logical components and weights them according to their importance. Existing reasoning-based guardrails often rely on expensive procedures, such as generating reasoning traces using larger or closed-source teacher models and applying full-parameter fine-tuning. In contrast, ARBITER uses a cost-effective self-generation strategy for reasoning traces and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning while still achieving better performance than these expensive approaches. Additionally, ARBITER provides faithful evidence-phrase explanations for unsafe decisions, enabling a more transparent and interpretable guardrail method. Experiments on three safety moderation benchmarks show that ARBITER outperforms existing reasoning-based and non-reasoning guardrail baselines, with clear gains in out-of-domain evaluations.

AI.tldr: ARBITER is a cost-efficient LLM guardrail framework using dual-hypothesis reasoning and multi-component SFT that outperforms existing approaches while providing interpretable explanations.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning-based LLM guardrails rely on expensive procedures (large teacher models, full-parameter fine-tuning) and lack structured reasoning that explicitly considers both safe and unsafe prompt interpretations. ARBITER addresses these gaps with a more cost-effective, interpretable, and higher-performing alternative.
AI.method: ARBITER introduces two innovations: (1) dual-hypothesis reasoning, which forces the model to explicitly reason about both safe and unsafe interpretations of a prompt before deciding; (2) multi-component supervised fine-tuning (MC-SFT), which decomposes the LLM output into logical components (e.g., reasoning, evidence, decision) and applies a weighted loss prioritizing more critical components. Training uses self-generated reasoning traces (no large teacher models) and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.result: ARBITER outperforms both reasoning-based and non-reasoning guardrail baselines across three safety moderation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in out-of-domain evaluations.
AI.conclusion: ARBITER demonstrates that cost-effective self-generation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning can surpass expensive teacher-distillation and full-parameter tuning approaches for LLM guardrails, while also providing faithful, interpretable evidence-phrase explanations for unsafe decisions.

title: PoLoRA: A Preconditioned Orthogonalized LoRA Optimizer
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes finetuning large language models cheaper by adding to each weight matrix a trainable low-rank update parameterized as the product of two matrices. These matrices are usually trained with Adam, which treats them as a single flat vector of parameters and ignores both the matrix and product structure of LoRA. Applying a matrix-aware optimizer such as Muon to each factor does not consistently improve over Adam, and neither do the product-aware Muon variants proposed in concurrent works. To realize consistent gains, we introduce PoLoRA, a Preconditioned Orthogonalized LoRA optimizer built from three ingredients: a product-aware spectral update direction, curvature preconditioning derived from controlling the per-sample loss change, and a magnitude rule that controls the sizes of both the factor and merged updates. We evaluate PoLoRA on instruction-tuning datasets for code and math across models from 1B to 8B parameters, and find that it reaches the final held-out loss achieved by tuned Adam in 1.2-1.7 times fewer steps, while adding at most 3% per-step overhead. Compared to Adam, PoLoRA is also less sensitive to the learning rate, and its optimal learning rate is stable across ranks.

AI.tldr: PoLoRA is a new optimizer for LoRA that combines a product-aware spectral update direction, curvature preconditioning, and a magnitude rule to achieve 1.2-1.7× faster convergence than Adam with minimal overhead, while being more robust to learning rate and rank choices.
AI.motivation: Standard Adam training of LoRA treats the two factor matrices as a flat vector, ignoring their matrix and product structure. Existing matrix-aware optimizers (e.g., Muon) and product-aware variants fail to consistently beat Adam. This motivates a purpose-built optimizer that fully exploits LoRA's low-rank product structure for faster, more robust training.
AI.method: PoLoRA integrates three components: (1) a product-aware spectral update direction that accounts for the factorization structure; (2) curvature preconditioning derived by controlling per-sample loss changes; and (3) a magnitude rule that balances the sizes of factor updates and the merged weight update. The method is evaluated on instruction-tuning for code and math across 1B–8B parameter models.
AI.result: PoLoRA reaches the final held-out loss of tuned Adam in 1.2–1.7× fewer steps, with at most 3% per-step overhead. It also exhibits reduced sensitivity to learning rate choices and maintains a stable optimal learning rate across different LoRA ranks.
AI.conclusion: PoLoRA demonstrates that properly exploiting LoRA's matrix product structure yields consistent and meaningful convergence speedups over Adam, with practical benefits including faster tuning, better learning rate robustness, and rank-stable hyperparameters.

title: SurvCF(t): Counterfactual Explanations for Survival Analysis in Predictive Maintenance Multivariate Time Series Data
summary: Predictive maintenance relies on accurate Remaining Useful Life estimation, often formulated using survival analysis over multivariate time-series data. While modern deep survival models achieve strong predictive performance, their black-box nature limits their use in safety-critical settings where actionable insight is required. In this work, we introduce \textit{SurvCF(t)}, the first framework for generating counterfactual explanations for survival models operating on time-series data. \textit{SurvCF(t)} identifies minimal, plausible, and temporally consistent changes to an asset's operational history that increase its predicted life time, framing explanation as a constrained optimization problem combining validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility. We evaluate the method on multiple benchmarks, including C-MAPSS, N-CMAPSS, and a real-world case study of the Scania Component\_X dataset, demonstrating its ability to produce actionable and interpretable interventions. Our results show that \textit{SurvCF(t)} bridges the gap between survival prediction and prescriptive maintenance, enabling explainable and decision-oriented AI for maintenance strategies.

AI.tldr: SurvCF(t) is a novel framework that generates counterfactual explanations for deep survival models on time-series data, identifying minimal changes to operational history that would extend an asset's predicted lifetime, thus bridging predictive and prescriptive maintenance.
AI.motivation: Deep survival models for Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation achieve strong performance but are black-box, making them unsuitable for safety-critical maintenance settings where decision-makers need actionable, interpretable insights about what operational changes would improve asset longevity.
AI.method: SurvCF(t) frames counterfactual explanation generation as a constrained optimization problem that balances four objectives: validity (increased predicted lifetime), proximity (minimal deviation from original data), sparsity (few feature changes), and plausibility (temporally consistent, realistic interventions). It identifies minimal changes to an asset's multivariate time-series operational history.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated on C-MAPSS, N-CMAPSS, and the Scania Component_X real-world dataset, demonstrating its ability to produce actionable, interpretable counterfactual interventions that successfully increase predicted remaining useful life.
AI.conclusion: SurvCF(t) bridges the gap between survival prediction and prescriptive maintenance, enabling explainable, decision-oriented AI for maintenance strategies in safety-critical applications.

title: Mechanistic Attention Guidance for Agent Memory Refinement
summary: Existing self-evolving memory systems mainly improve agent memory based on textual outputs, such as task trajectories and reflections. However, this text-based paradigm rarely incorporates internal mechanistic signals, leaving how retrieved memory is actually utilized during task execution underexplored. This limitation can lead to unreliable error attribution and hallucinated memory modifications. In this work, we show that retrieval-head attention provides a mechanistic signal for revealing segment-level memory utilization. By aggregating attention over memory segments and decision steps, we construct a context utilization matrix that exposes recurring memory-use patterns and indicates corresponding refinement strategies. Building on this observation, we propose Attention-Guided Memory Refinement (AGMR), a framework that uses utilization patterns revealed by attention to guide targeted segment-level memory updates. AGMR corrects or enhances memory for failed executions, simplifies memory for successful executions, and verifies each update through re-execution. Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that AGMR improves both task performance and memory efficiency over text-only memory refinement baselines. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AGMR_code-3262/

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AGMR, a framework that leverages retrieval-head attention signals to reveal segment-level memory utilization patterns, enabling targeted memory refinement (correction, enhancement, simplification) with re-execution verification, outperforming text-only baselines on interactive decision-making tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving memory systems rely solely on textual outputs (trajectories, reflections) for memory updates, ignoring internal mechanistic signals about how retrieved memory is actually used during execution. This leads to unreliable error attribution and hallucinated memory modifications, since there is no feedback on whether and how retrieved memories influence decision-making.
AI.method: AGMR constructs a context utilization matrix by aggregating retrieval-head attention over memory segments and decision steps, revealing recurring memory-use patterns. Based on these patterns, AGMR performs targeted segment-level updates: correcting or enhancing memory for failed executions, simplifying memory for successful ones, and verifying each modification through re-execution to ensure the refinement is beneficial.
AI.result: Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks demonstrate that AGMR achieves superior task performance and memory efficiency compared to text-only memory refinement baselines.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-head attention provides a reliable mechanistic signal for understanding memory utilization, and attention-guided memory refinement offers a more principled approach to evolving agent memory systems, avoiding hallucinated modifications and improving both effectiveness and efficiency.

title: Mobius Learning: Cyclic Depth Folding in Transformers
summary: Transformer-based language models organize computation along an ordered depth axis, where shallow and deep blocks often develop distinct representational roles. We challenge the conventional view that these roles must remain tied to a block's position in the ordered sequence. We introduce Mobius Learning, a training architecture based on cyclic depth folding, in which different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders. The same block group is therefore applied early in the block sequence for some data streams and late for others, so it is optimized in both shallow and deep roles, a phenomenon we call depth-role superposition. Surprisingly, in four-worker experiments with a modded GPT-2 small (124M) model trained on 2.5B FineWeb tokens using Muon, Mobius Learning achieves lower validation loss than a fixed-order looped Transformer at larger numbers of Transformer block-sequence passes. This counterintuitive result shows that a block group need not remain confined to one fixed shallow or deep role within the block sequence and opens a new design space based on cyclic depth folding. Crucially, this structure makes Mobius Learning particularly well suited to memory-constrained distributed training: raw training data remain local, while each worker stores one block group rather than the complete Transformer block stack.

AI.tldr: Möbius Learning proposes cyclic depth folding for Transformers, where the same block group is applied at different depth positions for different data streams. This "depth-role superposition" surprisingly outperforms fixed-order looped Transformers on validation loss while being naturally suited for memory-constrained distributed training — each worker stores only one block group and processes local data.
AI.motivation: Challenge the conventional view that shallow and deep Transformer blocks must occupy fixed positions. Enable a training architecture where a single block group can serve both shallow and deep roles, and simultaneously address memory constraints in distributed training by having each worker store only part of the full Transformer stack.
AI.method: Introduces cyclic depth folding: during training, different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders through a shared block group (or groups). The same block group thus processes some streams early (shallow role) and others late (deep role), creating "depth-role superposition." Experiments use a modified GPT-2 small (124M) with four workers, trained on 2.5B FineWeb tokens using the Muon optimizer, comparing against a fixed-order looped Transformer baseline.
AI.result: Möbius Learning achieves lower validation loss than a fixed-order looped Transformer at larger numbers of Transformer block-sequence passes, despite the counterintuitive nature of the result. Each worker needs only one block group, making the approach memory-efficient for distributed training while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.conclusion: A block group need not remain confined to one fixed shallow or deep role. Cyclic depth folding opens a new design space for Transformer architectures and is particularly well-suited to memory-constrained distributed training settings where raw data remain local to each worker.

title: Periodic Bootstrap Thompson Sampling For Periodically Non-Stationary Bandit Problems
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, Accepted to 2025 3rd International Conference on Data Science, Advanced Algorithms, and Intelligent Computing
summary: This paper introduces Periodic Bootstrap Thompson Sampling (PBTS), an innovative extension of the classic Thompson Sampling (TS) algorithm tailored for bandit problems with periodic non-stationarity. Conventional TS accumulates all past observations, leading to biased posteriors when reward distributions cycle over time. PBTS overcomes this by synchronizing belief resets with known or inferred period intervals and embedding structured bootstrap exploration phases, effectively purging obsolete data while preserving uncertainty estimates. PBTS is tested in artificially constructed environments, which include skewed and balanced reward distributions, along with different bootstrap proportions and misaligned periodic intervals. Results indicate that PBTS generally achieves statistically significant reductions in cumulative regret against traditional TS in periodic non-stationary environments. Subsequent discussion further articulates the potential of PBTS's real-world deployment. The study mentions limitations like extreme periodic misalignment and proposes future research such as self-adjusting cycle-recognition. With memory reset and bootstrap phase, PBTS introduces a novel approach to optimizing bandit algorithms in periodic reward contexts.

AI.tldr: PBTS extends Thompson Sampling for periodic non-stationary bandits by synchronizing belief resets with period intervals and using structured bootstrap exploration, achieving significant cumulative regret reductions over standard TS.
AI.motivation: Standard Thompson Sampling accumulates all historical observations, producing biased posteriors when reward distributions cycle periodically. This renders TS suboptimal in non-stationary environments where old data becomes obsolete. The paper aims to address this gap by designing a TS variant that can adapt to periodic reward dynamics.
AI.method: PBTS introduces two key mechanisms: (1) memory resets synchronized with known or inferred period intervals to purge obsolete data, and (2) structured bootstrap exploration phases to maintain calibrated uncertainty estimates after resets. The algorithm is evaluated in artificially constructed environments with varied reward distribution skewness, bootstrap proportions, and periodic misalignment conditions.
AI.result: PBTS achieves statistically significant reductions in cumulative regret compared to traditional Thompson Sampling across periodic non-stationary environments, though performance degrades under extreme periodic misalignment.
AI.conclusion: PBTS offers a novel and effective approach for bandit problems with periodic rewards, with the memory-reset-plus-bootstrap design enabling robust adaptation. Limitations include sensitivity to severe misalignment, motivating future work on self-adjusting cycle-recognition mechanisms.

title: Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment
summary: The Credit Assignment Problem (CAP) is fundamental to developing efficient and explainable Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. Existing frameworks, whether relying on temporal contiguity or hindsight-conditioned reward reweighting, frequently fail to attribute properly between an agent's policy (skill) and environmental stochasticity (luck). A principled approach to CAP must isolate the true causal drivers of observed outcomes from spurious correlations and environmental randomness. We introduce Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, a novel framework grounded in causal theory that attributes credit and blame via the Counterfactual Shapley Value ($φ$-value). By redistributing environmental rewards, $φ$-values enhance temporal credit assignment across three critical dimensions: sparse causality, high stochasticity, and delayed rewards, all while preserving the optimal policy. We derive a consistent estimator that computes $φ$-values efficiently, enabling a new class of policy gradient methods, $φ$-PPO, combined with Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR). Empirical results demonstrate that $φ$-values align precisely to the ground truth causes of task rewards with superior sample efficiency in challenging environments where prior state-of-the-art methods fail to converge.

AI.tldr: Introduces Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, a causal framework using Counterfactual Shapley Values ($\varphi$-values) to disentangle skill from luck in RL credit assignment. Combined with $\varphi$-PPO and Prioritized Trajectory Replay, it achieves superior sample efficiency and converges where prior methods fail.
AI.motivation: Existing credit assignment methods in RL conflate the agent's policy skill with environmental stochasticity (luck), failing to isolate true causal drivers of outcomes. A principled, causality-based approach is needed to separate genuine skill from spurious correlations and randomness.
AI.method: Proposes the Counterfactual Shapley Value ($\varphi$-value), which redistributes rewards by counterfactually measuring each action's marginal contribution across all possible action subsets. A consistent, efficient estimator is derived. This is integrated into a policy gradient method ($\varphi$-PPO) with Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR) targeting three dimensions: sparse causality, high stochasticity, and delayed rewards.
AI.result: $\varphi$-values align precisely with ground-truth causes of task rewards. $\varphi$-PPO with PTR achieves superior sample efficiency in challenging environments where prior state-of-the-art methods fail to converge.
AI.conclusion: The Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment framework provides a principled causal solution to the CAP, effectively distinguishing skill from luck, preserving optimal policies, and enabling robust learning in environments with sparse, stochastic, and delayed rewards where prior methods break down.

title: FlowBlock: Wavefront-Parallel Decoding for Self-Correcting Diffusion Language Models
summary: Block-wise diffusion large language models (dLLMs) decode sequentially at the block level, enabling effective KV-cache reuse across blocks but making inter-block decoding strictly serial. Prior work has attempted to unlock inter-block parallelism through post-training methods, but achieves only modest speedups and often degrades accuracy. We observe that self-correcting dLLMs offer a training-free alternative: token-to-token (T2T) editing can repair tokens drafted with a slightly stale upstream context, so a downstream block requires only an informative draft rather than a finalized predecessor. This turns block finality from a hard dependency into a scheduling resource. We propose \textbf{\flowblock{}}, a training-free parallel decoding framework built on two mechanisms. (i) \emph{Gated Wavefront Decoding} admits blocks into a bounded wavefront only when a readiness gate is satisfied, jointly refines active blocks via T2T editing, and commits blocks in order under a windowed block-causal mask that preserves exact frozen-prefix KV caches reuse. (ii) \emph{Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing} assigns each request an independent wavefront while packing asynchronous windows into dense, shape-stable batched forwards. Across different benchmarks, \flowblock{} improves tokens per second (TPS) over LLaDA-2.1 and LLaDA-2.0, two serial block-wise dLLMs, by up to 2.95$\times$ and 4.01$\times$, while reducing latency by up to 53.6\% and 77.1\%, respectively. It also improves average accuracy by 1.3 points. Compared with D2F, a training-based inter-block-parallel baseline, \flowblock{} achieves higher accuracy and up to 16$\times$ higher batched serving throughput.

AI.tldr: FlowBlock introduces a training-free parallel decoding framework for block-wise diffusion LLMs that uses token-to-token editing to relax the serial dependency between blocks, achieving up to 2.95–4.01× throughput gains over serial baselines while improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Block-wise diffusion LLMs suffer from strictly serial inter-block decoding, which limits inference throughput. Prior post-training parallelization methods yield only modest speedups and degrade accuracy. The authors observe that self-correcting dLLMs can repair drafts produced with stale context, meaning downstream blocks don't need fully finalized predecessors — only informative drafts.
AI.method: FlowBlock uses two mechanisms: (1) Gated Wavefront Decoding, which admits blocks into a bounded wavefront only when a readiness gate is satisfied, jointly refines them via token-to-token editing, and commits in order under a windowed block-causal mask preserving frozen-prefix KV-cache reuse; (2) Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing, which assigns each request an independent wavefront and packs asynchronous windows into dense, shape-stable batched forwards.
AI.result: FlowBlock improves TPS over LLaDA-2.1 and LLaDA-2.0 by up to 2.95× and 4.01×, reduces latency by up to 53.6% and 77.1%, and improves average accuracy by 1.3 points. Compared to the training-based D2F baseline, FlowBlock achieves higher accuracy and up to 16× higher batched serving throughput.
AI.conclusion: Block finality can be treated as a scheduling resource rather than a hard dependency. FlowBlock demonstrates that training-free, T2T-editing-based parallel decoding can substantially accelerate block-wise dLLMs while preserving or even improving generation quality.

title: Scalable Causal Imitation Learning
summary: Imitation learning enables learning a policy in an unknown environment with a latent reward signal using expert demonstrations, but it struggles when the imitator's and expert's observations are mismatched and unobserved confounders are present in expert demonstrations. By identifying appropriate adjustment sets via the sequential $π$-backdoor criterion, causal imitation learning (CIL) provides a framework for approximating the expert's policy from confounded data. However, existing CIL methods, Causal Behavioral Cloning (Causal BC) and Causal Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (Causal GAIL), are designed for short-horizon, low-dimensional settings. When applied to continuous control tasks with long horizons and high-dimensional state-action spaces, these methods exhibit poor performance: Causal BC suffers from compounding errors, Causal GAIL is unstable and sample-inefficient, and sequential $π$-backdoor adjustment becomes impractical. We introduce Causal Soft Q Imitation Learning (SQIL) and Causal Inverse soft-Q Learning (IQ-Learn), two off-policy causal imitation learning algorithms that combine the causal adjustment framework with state-of-the-art inverse reinforcement learning objectives. Both algorithms operate on causally-adjusted state representations produced by an efficient approximation of the sequential $π$-backdoor criterion, exploiting the causal structure of continuous control environments to reduce the full-horizon adjustment to a fixed-size sliding window. We evaluate all methods in a suite of confounded environments and find that Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn substantially outperform prior CIL algorithms on long-horizon tasks, sometimes surpassing the expert, whereas all causally unaware imitation methods fail to learn meaningful behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn, two off-policy causal imitation learning algorithms that combine causal adjustment with inverse RL objectives. They use a sliding-window approximation of the sequential π-backdoor criterion to scale to high-dimensional continuous control tasks, substantially outperforming prior causal imitation methods on long-horizon confounded environments.
AI.motivation: Existing causal imitation learning methods (Causal BC, Causal GAIL) are limited to short-horizon, low-dimensional settings and fail on continuous control tasks with long horizons and high-dimensional state-action spaces due to compounding errors, instability, sample inefficiency, and impractical sequential π-backdoor adjustment. Meanwhile, causally unaware imitation methods cannot handle unobserved confounders in expert demonstrations.
AI.method: The authors propose two off-policy algorithms: Causal Soft Q Imitation Learning (SQIL) and Causal Inverse soft-Q Learning (IQ-Learn). Both operate on causally-adjusted state representations derived from an efficient approximation of the sequential π-backdoor criterion, which exploits the causal structure of continuous control environments to reduce full-horizon adjustment to a fixed-size sliding window. These combine the causal adjustment framework with state-of-the-art inverse reinforcement learning objectives.
AI.result: In a suite of confounded environments, Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn substantially outperform prior CIL algorithms (Causal BC, Causal GAIL) on long-horizon tasks, sometimes even surpassing the expert. All causally unaware imitation methods fail to learn meaningful behavior under confounding.
AI.conclusion: Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn effectively scale causal imitation learning to high-dimensional, long-horizon continuous control tasks by combining efficient causal adjustment with modern inverse RL, overcoming the key limitations of prior CIL methods.

title: OrientSAM: Mitigating Camera-Centric Shortcut in Multimodal Spatial Reasoning via Orientation-Aware Spatial Alignment
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with spatial reasoning that requires perspective transformation. In particular, they often rely on camera-centric cues rather than reasoning from the reference object's viewpoint, leading to systematic errors in non-camera reference settings. In this paper, we first analyze this failure mode and show that object orientation is a key factor underlying such camera-centric shortcut behavior. To address this issue, we propose OrientSAM, an orientation-aware spatial alignment framework for multimodal models. OrientSAM injects explicit orientation information into multimodal representations through orientation-aware tokens and Fourier-based angle encoding, and further adopts a curriculum learning strategy to progressively improve perspective-aware reasoning. In addition, we build a spatial data construction pipeline to generate orientation-aware spatial supervision from large-scale images. Experiments on Spatial-MM, ViewSpatial, and 3DSRBench show that OrientSAM consistently outperforms strong baselines, especially on non-camera-view, person-centric, and orientation-sensitive tasks. The results further demonstrate that explicit orientation modeling is important for mitigating camera-centric shortcut behavior and enabling more robust allocentric spatial reasoning in multimodal models.

AI.tldr: MLLMs exhibit camera-centric biases in spatial reasoning tasks. The authors propose OrientSAM, which injects explicit object orientation information via orientation-aware tokens and Fourier angle encoding, combined with curriculum learning, to enable robust allocentric (viewpoint-independent) spatial reasoning.
AI.motivation: MLLMs fail at spatial reasoning requiring perspective transformation because they default to camera-centric (egocentric) cues rather than reasoning from a reference object's viewpoint (allocentric). The authors identify object orientation as a key factor behind this systematic failure, motivating a solution that explicitly models orientation to mitigate this shortcut behavior.
AI.method: OrientSAM introduces: (1) orientation-aware tokens and Fourier-based angle encoding to inject explicit orientation information into multimodal representations; (2) a curriculum learning strategy for progressive perspective-aware reasoning; and (3) a spatial data construction pipeline that generates orientation-aware spatial supervision from large-scale images.
AI.result: OrientSAM consistently outperforms strong baselines on Spatial-MM, ViewSpatial, and 3DSRBench, with particularly strong gains on non-camera-view, person-centric, and orientation-sensitive tasks, demonstrating effective mitigation of camera-centric shortcut behavior.
AI.conclusion: Explicit orientation modeling is crucial for overcoming camera-centric shortcuts in MLLMs and enabling robust allocentric spatial reasoning. OrientSAM provides an effective framework for achieving this through orientation-aware representation learning and structured training strategies.

title: Regularize or Localize: When Training-Time KV-Cache Geometry Pays Under Quantization
summary: We study whether \sigreg -- LeJEPA's anti-collapse objective -- can reshape representations during standard autoregressive language-model pretraining, and when the resulting geometry helps \kv-cache quantization. We train 110M-parameter models on 10B FineWeb tokens and report three findings. \textbf{(1)} At $λ{=}0.01$, \sigreg reduces hidden-state pairwise-cosine anisotropy by $38\%$ across three paired seeds. Perplexity increases by less than $0.35\%$ in every pair, with no consistent zero-shot loss. \textbf{(2)} This change does not propagate from hidden states to the \kv cache. Applying \sigreg directly to K and V during continued training, however, reduces mean cache anisotropy by $94\%$ across four checkpoints. A matched continuation without the \kv term leaves cache geometry nearly unchanged, and the frozen-trunk retrofits we tested do not reproduce the effect. \textbf{(3)} Under untransformed symmetric group-free quantization, direct \kv regularization is the only training condition that prefers per-channel scaling in all three seeds, and under that same 3-bit per-channel scheme the baseline incurs $4.3$--$7.9\times$ the directly regularized model's \dnll. Under the full simulated KIVI-style configuration (mixed arrangement, zero-points, grouped scales), however, all models reach near-parity, including when storage overhead is approximately matched. In this 110M regime, the training intervention helps when quantizer scales are coarse; the advantage vanishes under the tested combination of token-local grouping, mixed \kv scaling, and zero-points. To our knowledge this is the first training-time \emph{distributional} regularization of standard \kv-cache geometry evaluated against post-hoc cache quantization.

AI.tldr: Investigates whether LeJEPA's anti-collapse objective (SigReg) reshapes representations during standard LLM pretraining and whether resulting geometry aids KV-cache quantization. SigReg on hidden states reduces anisotropy but doesn't propagate to KV cache; direct KV regularization dramatically reduces cache anisotropy. Under coarse 3-bit per-channel quantization, KV-regularized models significantly outperform baselines, but under sophisticated KIVI-style quantization all models reach near-parity.
AI.motivation: KV-cache quantization is critical for efficient LLM inference, but representation geometry affects quantizability. The authors investigate whether a training-time distributional regularization (SigReg, originally from LeJEPA for anti-collapse) can produce KV-cache geometry more amenable to post-hoc quantization, potentially offering a complementary approach to quantization algorithm design.
AI.method: Train 110M-parameter models on 10B FineWeb tokens with SigReg applied at three levels: (1) to hidden states during pretraining (λ=0.01), (2) directly to K and V during continued training, and (3) frozen-trunk retrofits. Evaluate via pairwise-cosine anisotropy, perplexity, zero-shot benchmarks, and downstream KV-cache quantization under various schemes: untransformed symmetric group-free quantization, per-channel scaling, and KIVI-style configuration (mixed arrangement, zero-points, grouped scales).
AI.result: (1) SigReg on hidden states (λ=0.01) reduces hidden-state anisotropy by 38% with <0.35% perplexity increase and no consistent zero-shot loss. (2) This anisotropy reduction does not propagate to KV cache; direct KV SigReg reduces mean cache anisotropy by 94%, while matched continuation without KV term leaves cache geometry unchanged. (3) Under coarse 3-bit per-channel quantization, KV-regularized models see 4.3–7.9× lower ΔNLL than baseline; under full KIVI-style quantization all models achieve near-parity.
AI.conclusion: Training-time distributional regularization of KV-cache geometry is effective at reducing anisotropy and improving quantizability under coarse quantization schemes, but the advantage disappears under sophisticated quantization with grouped scales, zero-points, and mixed KV scaling — at least at the 110M scale tested. This represents the first study of training-time distributional regularization of KV-cache evaluated against post-hoc cache quantization.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Understanding and Managing Transportation Behavior in Sustainable Smart Cities
summary: Urban transportation systems generate heterogeneous data, yet these data do not automatically become actionable management intelligence. This chapter adopts a behavior-centered perspective on artificial intelligence (AI), treating mobility records and passenger-generated text as behavioral evidence rather than behavioral truth. It examines four directions: bus arrival prediction for service reliability, taxi mobility pattern discovery for demand analysis and planning, abnormal behavior detection for accountable regulatory support, and passenger-perceived risk mining for service improvement. These directions are integrated through a closed-loop framework linking data input, behavior representation, AI inference, decision support, public value, and governance feedback. The chapter identifies data quality, privacy, fairness, interpretability, uncertainty, transferability, and human accountability as essential conditions for deployment. It thereby establishes a unified pathway from behavioral evidence to operational, planning, regulatory, and passenger-service decisions.

AI.tldr: This chapter proposes a behavior-centered AI framework that treats urban transportation data as behavioral evidence rather than truth, integrating four application directions (bus arrival prediction, taxi mobility pattern discovery, abnormal behavior detection, and passenger-perceived risk mining) into a closed-loop system linking data input to governance feedback, while identifying seven essential deployment conditions.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous urban transportation data do not automatically translate into actionable management intelligence. The authors argue that existing approaches treat mobility records as ground truth, whereas a behavior-centered perspective—viewing data as behavioral evidence—enables more robust and accountable AI-driven decision support for transit operations, planning, regulation, and passenger services.
AI.method: The chapter adopts a behavior-centered AI perspective and structures its analysis around four technical directions: (1) bus arrival time prediction for service reliability, (2) taxi mobility pattern discovery for demand analysis and planning, (3) abnormal behavior detection for regulatory accountability, and (4) passenger-perceived risk mining from text for service improvement. These are integrated through a closed-loop framework comprising six stages: data input → behavior representation → AI inference → decision support → public value → governance feedback.
AI.result: The framework unifies four distinct AI application areas under a single behavior-centered paradigm. The chapter identifies seven essential deployment conditions: data quality, privacy, fairness, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, transferability, and human accountability. These conditions serve as prerequisites for transitioning from behavioral evidence to operational, planning, regulatory, and passenger-service decisions.
AI.conclusion: A behavior-centered AI approach, combined with a closed-loop governance framework and strict adherence to the seven deployment conditions, establishes a unified and accountable pathway from raw behavioral evidence to multifaceted transportation management decisions, ultimately serving public value.

title: L1 Augmented Attention as an Improved Vector Similarity Metric
summary: Scaled dot product attention conflates directional alignment and vector magnitude, limiting its effectiveness as a similarity metric in Transformer models. We introduce L1 augmented attention, a simple and computationally parallelizable modification that subtracts a learned, head specific L1 distance between queries and keys from the dot product score. This hybrid similarity captures complementary geometric information. Dot product rewards directional alignment, while L1 penalizes coordinate deviations. To reduce the cost of L1 computation, we project queries and keys into low dimensional subspaces whose parameters specialize to preserve informative L1 structure. Evaluated on WikiText 2 using a compact transformer, L1 augmented attention achieves up to a 14.5% reduction in perplexity over the original transformer baseline and outperforms an RBF L2 kernel. Analysis of norm variance and learned L1 weights reveals distinct geometric roles across layers and strong head level specialization. These results demonstrate that enriching attention with L1 geometry provides a principled and effective improvement to similarity computation in modern language models, with practical benefits for both accuracy and parallel efficiency.

AI.tldr: L1 augmented attention enhances standard scaled dot-product attention by subtracting a learned, head-specific L1 distance from the dot-product score, capturing both directional alignment and coordinate-wise deviations. This yields up to 14.5% perplexity reduction on WikiText-2 over a baseline Transformer and outperforms an RBF L2 kernel, with strong head-level specialization.
AI.motivation: Scaled dot-product attention conflates directional alignment and vector magnitude, which limits its expressiveness as a similarity metric. The authors argue that a hybrid similarity incorporating both angular (dot product) and coordinate-wise (L1) geometric information provides a more principled measure.
AI.method: The proposed method augments the standard attention score by subtracting a learned, head-specific L1 distance between projected query and key vectors. To maintain computational efficiency, queries and keys are projected into low-dimensional subspaces optimized to preserve informative L1 structure. The resulting hybrid score combines dot-product alignment and L1 penalty additively before softmax normalization.
AI.result: On WikiText-2 with a compact Transformer, L1 augmented attention achieves up to 14.5% perplexity reduction over the baseline and outperforms an RBF L2 kernel baseline. Analysis of norm variance and learned L1 weights reveals distinct geometric roles across layers and strong head-level specialization.
AI.conclusion: Enriching attention with L1 geometry provides a principled, effective, and parallel-efficient improvement to similarity computation in Transformers, with practical accuracy gains and minimal computational overhead.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Air Pollution and Respiratory Health Prediction: A Socioeconomic Subgroup Analysis
summary: Air pollution and climate-related stressors are increasingly important concerns for respiratory health, especially in settings with unequal environmental exposure and healthcare capacity. This study evaluates an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting respiratory disease rates and air-quality status using structured country-level weekly data. Two supervised learning tasks were considered: regression of respiratory disease rate per 100,000 population and binary classification of air-quality status. Nine regression models and nine classification models were compared using nested cross-validation. Model interpretation was conducted using SHAP values, and subgroup analysis was performed across income levels and geographic regions. The results showed that PM2.5 concentration was the dominant predictor of respiratory disease rate, with linear and regularized linear models achieving the strongest regression performance. For air-quality classification, models achieved high balanced accuracy when PM2.5 was included, but performance decreased substantially when PM2.5 was removed, indicating strong dependence on pollutant-related information. SHAP analysis showed that, without PM2.5, socioeconomic and meteorological variables such as GDP per capita, precipitation, and healthcare access became more influential. Subgroup analysis showed similar aggregate regression error across income groups, but PM2.5 contributed more strongly to predictions in lower-middle-income countries. These results show that model accuracy alone is not sufficient for climate-health prediction. Interpretable models can help identify dominant pollution-related signals, test whether results depend on key pollutant variables, and show whether prediction patterns differ across socioeconomic groups.
