AI.tldr: This study evaluates interpretable machine learning models for predicting respiratory disease rates and air-quality status using country-level data. PM2.5 emerged as the dominant predictor; removing it exposed socioeconomic/meteorological influences. Linear models performed best for regression, while classification models heavily depended on PM2.5. Subgroup analysis revealed differential PM2.5 contributions across income levels, emphasizing that model interpretability is essential for equitable climate-health prediction.
AI.motivation: Air pollution and climate stressors increasingly threaten respiratory health, particularly in settings with unequal environmental exposure and healthcare access. There is a need for interpretable predictive frameworks that not only achieve high accuracy but also reveal which variables drive predictions and how these patterns vary across socioeconomic and geographic subgroups, ensuring models do not mask health inequities.
AI.method: The authors used structured country-level weekly data to frame two supervised learning tasks: (1) regression of respiratory disease rate per 100,000 population and (2) binary classification of air-quality status. Nine regression and nine classification models were compared using nested cross-validation. Model interpretation employed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values. Subgroup analyses were conducted across income levels (World Bank classifications) and geographic regions. A key sensitivity test involved removing PM2.5 from the feature set to assess performance degradation and shifts in feature importance.
AI.result: PM2.5 concentration was the dominant predictor for respiratory disease rate; linear and regularized linear models achieved the strongest regression performance. For air-quality classification, models achieved high balanced accuracy with PM2.5 included but performance dropped substantially without it. SHAP analysis without PM2.5 revealed GDP per capita, precipitation, and healthcare access became more influential. Aggregate regression error was similar across income groups, but PM2.5 contributed more strongly to predictions in lower-middle-income countries.
AI.conclusion: Model accuracy alone is insufficient for climate-health prediction. Interpretable models are critical for identifying dominant pollution signals, testing dependence on key pollutant variables, and revealing differential prediction patterns across socioeconomic groups. These insights can guide more equitable environmental health surveillance and intervention strategies.

title: ProEvent: An Event-centric Benchmark for Proactive Agents
summary:
Proactive agents are expected to anticipate user needs and provide autonomous assistance by perceiving environmental context without explicit instructions. A fundamental capability of such agents is to identify and track users' upcoming events, enabling continuous and event-specific assistance. For example, by recording the time and location of a planned hike, an agent can deliver weather reminders in advance or provide navigation support before departure. However, existing works on proactive agents largely overlook event-centric assistance, and the open-ended nature of proactive assistance poses challenges for reliable evaluation.
  To bridge these gaps, we introduce ProEvent, the first event-centric benchmark designed to assess an agent's ability to proactively maintain a user's timetable based on ongoing instant messaging chats. ProEvent provides synthesized yet realistic chats that consider the dynamic interaction among users, concurrent chat threads, and noise in the real world, and evaluates proactive agents on response timing, single-step response correctness, and multi-step response correctness. Experiments on eight LLMs and pipelines reveal that current agents frequently overact and struggle with event cancellation. Notably, even GPT-5.1 only reacts correctly in 26.7% of scenarios. Further qualitative analysis reveals fundamental limitations of current LLMs as proactive agents, particularly in detecting implicit events and reasoning from the user's first-person perspective.

AI.tldr: ProEvent is the first benchmark for evaluating proactive AI agents on event-centric assistance from instant messaging chats, revealing that even top models like GPT-5.1 achieve only 26.7% correct reactions, with key failure modes being overaction and poor event cancellation handling.
AI.motivation: Proactive agents should anticipate user needs by tracking upcoming events from environmental context, but existing research overlooks event-centric assistance. Furthermore, the open-ended nature of proactive assistance makes reliable evaluation challenging.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProEvent, a benchmark using synthesized yet realistic instant messaging chats that incorporate multi-user dynamics, concurrent threads, and real-world noise. It evaluates agents on three dimensions: response timing, single-step response correctness, and multi-step response correctness. Eight LLMs and pipelines are tested.
AI.result: Current agents frequently overact and struggle with event cancellation. GPT-5.1 achieves only 26.7% correct reactions. Qualitative analysis reveals fundamental limitations in detecting implicit events and reasoning from a first-person perspective.
AI.conclusion: ProEvent exposes significant gaps in current LLMs' capabilities as proactive, event-tracking agents, highlighting the need for better implicit event detection and user-centric reasoning to enable reliable autonomous assistance.

title: WorldCupArena: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Language Models and Deep-Research Agents on Football Forecasting
summary: Predicting a football match before kickoff requires more than knowing past results: a model must use changing information and make a clear prediction before the answer is available. We present WorldCupArena, a dynamic benchmark for language models and deep-research agents. The 2026 FIFA World Cup is its first evaluation, and the same process can be reused for future leagues and cups. Before each match, a model either receives a common evidence package or searches for information itself. It predicts the result and score, likely players and events, match statistics, and the outcome of the competition. After the match, these predictions are compared with the recorded result. We report result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, and a scoreline score that gives some credit when a predicted score is close but not exact, together with scores for the other prediction tasks. Across 104 matches and 13 systems, models with similar result accuracy differ more clearly on detailed predictions. Compared with betting-market and human-fan baselines, the best system shows only small gains in result and exact-score accuracy, but a clearer gain in Scoreline. New schedules can be added as they begin, allowing the benchmark to evaluate future models without using outcomes that are already known. Code, prompts, predictions, and evaluation scripts are open sourced at https://github.com/wzk1015/WorldCupArena.

AI.tldr: WorldCupArena is a dynamic benchmark that evaluates language models and deep-research agents on predicting football match outcomes (results, scores, player events, statistics) before kickoff, using the 2026 FIFA World Cup as its first evaluation cycle. Across 104 matches and 13 systems, the best model shows modest gains over betting markets and human fans in result/score accuracy but clearer gains in scoreline proximity.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for sports prediction are static and retrospective, allowing models to memorize outcomes. The authors argue that genuine predictive capability requires using changing, pre-match information to make forecasts before ground truth is known — motivating a live, forward-looking benchmark.
AI.method: WorldCupArena provides a structured evaluation pipeline: before each match, models receive either a pre-packaged evidence bundle or autonomously conduct information retrieval. They then predict match results, exact scores, likely players/events, match statistics, and tournament outcomes. Post-match, these predictions are scored against recorded results using result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, and a continuous Scoreline Score that rewards near-miss score predictions. The framework is designed to be reusable for future competitions.
AI.result: Across 104 matches and 13 systems, models with similar binary result accuracy showed greater differentiation on detailed prediction tasks. The best system marginally outperformed betting-market odds and human-fan baselines on result and exact-score accuracy, but demonstrated a more pronounced advantage on the Scoreline Score metric.
AI.conclusion: WorldCupArena offers a reusable, dynamic benchmark for evaluating predictive reasoning in LLMs under real-world uncertainty. Detailed prediction tasks (scoreline, events, statistics) discriminate model quality better than result accuracy alone, and the framework's extensible design allows continuous evaluation without data leakage.

title: ChemFusion: A Multimodal Cross-Attention Network for Reaction Yield Prediction
summary: Forecasting the outcomes of transition-metal-catalyzed reactions is notoriously complex due to the interplay of diverse physical and chemical variables. A persistent computational bottleneck has been effectively merging broad electronic descriptors with the localized, three-dimensional geometry of the reactive site. To bridge this representation gap, we present ChemFusion, a hybrid neural network that fuses conventional electronic features with explicit 3D atomic coordinates. Using a cross-attention mechanism, the model enables global electronic states to dynamically attend to specific spatial constraints within un-pooled molecular point clouds. When benchmarked against a diverse library of cross-couplings, this approach delivers exceptional predictive performance, decisively surpassing traditional single-modality frameworks. Importantly, extracting the attention matrices reveals that the architecture autonomously learns to identify and penalize restrictive steric hindrances. This provides a physically grounded interpretability, demonstrating that spatially aware networks can navigate complex reaction sterics that standard statistical models typically miss.

AI.tldr: ChemFusion is a hybrid neural network that combines electronic descriptors with explicit 3D atomic coordinates via cross-attention, enabling superior prediction of transition-metal-catalyzed reaction outcomes by autonomously learning steric effects that traditional models miss.
AI.motivation: Existing computational models struggle to merge broad electronic descriptors with localized 3D geometric information of reactive sites, creating a representation gap that limits predictive accuracy for transition-metal-catalyzed reactions where steric effects are critical.
AI.method: The authors propose ChemFusion, a hybrid neural architecture that fuses conventional electronic features with explicit 3D atomic coordinates using a cross-attention mechanism. This allows global electronic states to dynamically attend to specific spatial constraints within un-pooled molecular point clouds.
AI.result: Benchmarked against a diverse library of cross-coupling reactions, ChemFusion decisively outperforms traditional single-modality frameworks. Analysis of attention matrices reveals the model autonomously learns to identify and penalize restrictive steric hindrances, providing physically grounded interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Spatially aware neural networks like ChemFusion can effectively navigate complex reaction sterics that standard statistical models miss, demonstrating that attention-based fusion of electronic and 3D geometric representations is a promising direction for reaction outcome prediction.

title: LaT: LLM-as-Trainer for Multi-Task Vehicle Routing Solvers
summary: Multi-task neural solvers aim to handle multiple Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) variants within a unified model, avoiding separate training for each constraint combination. However, VRP variants differ in optimization difficulty, while existing methods lack stage-wise feedback on their training status, making the model biased to some specific variants. Although meta-learning can support adaptive training, it typically requires bi-level optimization and additional gradient updates, increasing computational cost. To address this limitation, we propose LLM-as-Trainer (LaT), a plug-and-play training paradigm that uses a pretrained large language model as an external trainer. LaT periodically analyzes cross-task validation metrics to generate a stage-wise guidance vector. This vector is combined with the current task's constraint vector and injected into each encoder layer, providing the neural solver with additional training information during subsequent policy optimization. Experiments on 16 VRP variants show that LaT improves the solution quality of several state-of-the-art multi-task neural solvers on both trained and unseen variants, supporting the effectiveness and generality of the proposed training paradigm.

AI.tldr: LaT proposes a plug-and-play training paradigm where a pretrained LLM periodically analyzes cross-task validation metrics to generate stage-wise guidance vectors, mitigating task bias in multi-task VRP neural solvers without costly bi-level optimization.
AI.motivation: Multi-task neural solvers for Vehicle Routing Problems (VRP) suffer from task bias due to differing optimization difficulty across variants, and existing methods lack stage-wise feedback on training status. While meta-learning offers adaptive training, it incurs high computational cost through bi-level optimization and extra gradient updates.
AI.method: LaT introduces a pretrained large language model as an external trainer that periodically examines cross-task validation metrics to produce a stage-wise guidance vector. This vector is fused with the current task's constraint vector and injected into every encoder layer, supplying supplementary training information during policy optimization. The approach is plug-and-play, requiring no architectural changes to the underlying neural solver.
AI.result: Experiments across 16 VRP variants demonstrate that LaT improves solution quality for several state-of-the-art multi-task neural solvers on both trained and unseen variants.
AI.conclusion: LaT is an effective and general training paradigm that leverages LLM-based stage-wise feedback to address task imbalance in multi-task VRP solving, outperforming existing approaches without the overhead of meta-learning.

title: Apeliotes: A Diffusion-Based Modeling Framework for km-scale Multi-Level Atmospheric Fields
summary: High-resolution atmospheric data are required to resolve mesoscale and localized meteorological structures, however such datasets remain limited in many regions of the world. Existing high-resolution weather products are typically produced through dynamical downscaling, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale across locations, variables, and forecast scenarios. These limitations motivate machine-learning-based downscaling systems that can generate multiple weather variables stochastically while producing new high-resolution fields directly. In this paper we present Apeliotes, a framework for high-resolution weather forecasting. Built on the global re-analysis atmospheric data, a pre-trained global weather foundation model, and a regionally trained generative diffusion model, Apeliotes not only provides accurate kilometer-scale weather variables, but also multi-level atmospheric fields which are not directly available in the existing global atmospheric data. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that Apeliotes achieves highly competitive performance. The model predicts vertical wind profile with less than 3\% error between truth and predicted fields, achieving correlations of 0.91 for 10-m wind speed and 0.99 for 2-m temperature, with NRMSE values of 0.42 and 0.17, respectively.

AI.tldr: Apeliotes is a machine-learning-based downscaling framework that combines a pre-trained global weather foundation model with a generative diffusion model to produce high-resolution, kilometer-scale atmospheric data and multi-level fields, achieving strong performance (e.g., 0.99 correlation for 2-m temperature, 0.91 for 10-m wind speed).
AI.motivation: High-resolution atmospheric data are scarce in many regions due to the prohibitive computational cost and poor scalability of traditional dynamical downscaling. This motivates the development of ML-based systems that can stochastically generate multiple weather variables at fine resolutions directly.
AI.method: Apeliotes integrates global reanalysis data with a pre-trained global weather foundation model and a regionally trained generative diffusion model to produce accurate, kilometer-scale weather variables and multi-level atmospheric fields not available in existing global datasets.
AI.result: Vertical wind profile error is under 3%; 10-m wind speed achieves a correlation of 0.91 (NRMSE 0.42); 2-m temperature achieves a correlation of 0.99 (NRMSE 0.17).
AI.conclusion: Apeliotes demonstrates that combining global foundation models with region-specific diffusion models enables highly accurate, computationally efficient stochastic downscaling of multiple atmospheric variables, including multi-level fields, with competitive performance relative to existing approaches.

title: Learning to Detect Cross-Modal Negation: An Analysis of Latent Representations and an Attention-Based Solution
comment: This manuscript is an accepted version of the article (published at ICNLP2026). Published in IEEE Xplore, DOI:10.1109/ICNLP69856.2026.11527861 document: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11527861
summary: Detecting high-level semantic concepts like negation across modalities remains a challenge for current multimodal systems. We analyze this as a fundamental representation learning problem, providing the first evidence that negation does not form a linearly or non-linearly separable class in the latent spaces of standard vision-language models (VLMs). We demonstrate that pretrained embeddings primarily encode modality-specific features, lacking a generalizable negation signal. To overcome this, we propose a novel cross-modal attention architecture that explicitly models inter-modal dependencies, achieving performance gains of up to +7.03% F1 over unimodal baselines. Our analysis reveals a key asymmetry: while textual negation often appears independently, visual negation is semantically dependent on linguistic context, a finding validated through our statistical analysis of 3,222 political video-text pairs automatically annotated via \textsc{Qwen2.5-VL}. By combining this analysis with self-supervised video representations (JEPA2), we advance the modeling of temporal negation. This work provides new methods and insights for learning robust, semantically-aligned representations in multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting negation across modalities, showing it is not linearly or non-linearly separable in standard VLM latent spaces. The authors propose a cross-modal attention architecture that improves F1 by up to 7.03% and reveal a textual-visual asymmetry in negation using 3,222 annotated political video-text pairs, advancing cross-modal representation learning.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal systems struggle to detect high-level semantic concepts like negation across modalities. The authors identify this as a fundamental representation learning problem, hypothesizing that pretrained VLM embeddings lack a generalizable negation signal and are primarily modality-specific, motivating the need for architectures that explicitly model cross-modal dependencies.
AI.method: The authors (1) analyze the latent spaces of standard VLMs to test linear/non-linear separability of negation; (2) propose a novel cross-modal attention architecture that explicitly models inter-modal dependencies; (3) conduct statistical analysis on 3,222 political video-text pairs automatically annotated via Qwen2.5-VL to examine textual-visual negation asymmetry; and (4) incorporate self-supervised video representations (JEPA2) to improve temporal negation modeling.
AI.result: Negation is neither linearly nor non-linearly separable in standard VLM latent spaces. The proposed cross-modal attention architecture yields up to +7.03% F1 improvement over unimodal baselines. A key asymmetry is found: textual negation often appears independently, while visual negation is semantically dependent on linguistic context. Combining the analysis with JEPA2 representations advances temporal negation modeling.
AI.conclusion: The work provides both new methods (cross-modal attention for negation) and insights (modality asymmetry in negation) for learning robust, semantically-aligned representations in multimodal systems, advancing the fundamental understanding of how negation operates across textual and visual modalities.

title: LLM-as-a-Coach: Experiential Learning for Non-Verifiable Tasks
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) on open-ended tasks compresses an LLM's rubric-based evaluation into a scalar reward, discarding rich textual feedback and conflating responses with distinct quality profiles. We propose Experiential Learning (EL), which repurposes the feedback model from an LLM-as-a-Judge into an LLM-as-a-Coach. The coach distills its assessment of each on-policy response into transferable experiential knowledge, which conditions a teacher model and is internalized by the policy through on-policy context distillation. Compared with scalar rewards, this higher-bandwidth feedback channel provides dense supervision and preserves fine-grained preferences among high-quality responses. Across two policy families, with feedback from the policy itself or a proprietary model, EL consistently outperforms rubric-based RL on held-out and unseen open-ended tasks. Notably, EL generalizes better beyond the training distribution, and mitigates reward hacking. These findings establish experiential knowledge as a richer and more generalizable learning signal for post-training on non-verifiable tasks.

AI.tldr: Experiential Learning (EL) replaces scalar rewards from LLM judges with dense, textual "experiential knowledge" from an LLM coach, improving RL for open-ended tasks. EL outperforms rubric-based RL, generalizes better, and reduces reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Standard RL on open-ended tasks compresses rich rubric-based LLM evaluation into a scalar reward, losing fine-grained textual feedback and conflating responses with distinct quality profiles. This limits learning signal density and generalizability.
AI.method: EL repurposes the feedback model from an LLM-as-a-Judge into an LLM-as-a-Coach. The coach distills its assessment of each on-policy response into transferable experiential knowledge, which conditions a teacher model. The policy then internalizes this knowledge through on-policy context distillation, providing a higher-bandwidth feedback channel than scalar rewards.
AI.result: Across two policy families, using feedback from the policy itself or a proprietary model, EL consistently outperforms rubric-based RL on held-out and unseen open-ended tasks. EL also generalizes better beyond the training distribution and mitigates reward hacking.
AI.conclusion: Experiential knowledge serves as a richer, more generalizable learning signal than scalar rewards for post-training LLMs on non-verifiable open-ended tasks.

title: Solver-Hard Is Not Model-Hard: A Hardness-Controlled Diagnostic for LLM Constraint Reasoning
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code and aggregate reproduction data: https://github.com/lucky-verma/solver-hard-is-not-model-hard
summary: LLM constraint reasoners are often evaluated near the random-SAT phase transition, confounding density and solver hardness. We test instance-level transfer while near-matching clause density. At aligned size bins, with near-matched density and matched maximum clause width, we compare proof-hard expander-Tseitin and proof-easy ladder-Tseitin formulas, pigeonhole anchors, and density-mismatched controls. Theory separates their resolution hardness; a solver-specific Glucose mean-conflict proxy differs by up to $51\times$, and five other solvers preserve the direction. Across three included models (243 instances each; a fourth is excluded for abstention), the near-matched-density accuracy gaps range from $-32$ to $+20$ points, with a pooled gap of $+1.7$ points ($p=0.74$) and a wrong-signed correctness-versus-conflict association ($r=+0.15$). A proof-preserving relabeling lowers accuracy in all five clusters for one model (mean $-93$ points) but not another, exposing model-surface sensitivity. In a preregistered extension, provider-reported completion-token spend does not consistently increase with the proxy after accounting for formula length and censoring. At 16k, the reasoning model spends more on proof-easy matched formulas and exhausts its budget on the solver-easiest UNSAT family; the 32k C1 gap is absent. These scoped dissociations concern verdict accuracy and observed token spend, not certificate solving, exact proof length, or allocation efficiency.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether LLM constraint reasoners genuinely learn proof hardness or merely exploit surface-level statistical features. Using Tseitin formulas with matched clause density but divergent resolution hardness (expander vs. ladder), the authors find near-zero accuracy gaps between hard and easy instances, a wrong-signed correlation between solver conflict counts and LLM accuracy, and dramatic accuracy drops under proof-preserving relabeling. Token-spend analyses similarly fail to track proof difficulty, revealing dissociations between LLM behavior and genuine logical hardness.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of LLM constraint reasoners confound formula hardness with clause density, particularly near the random-SAT phase transition. The authors aim to isolate whether LLMs are sensitive to genuine proof-theoretic hardness independently of surface statistical features like density and clause width.
AI.method: The authors construct paired Tseitin formula families: expander-Tseitin (proof-hard) and ladder-Tseitin (proof-easy), matched on clause density, size bins, and maximum clause width. They use a Glucose solver mean-conflict proxy to quantify hardness differences (up to 51×), validate across five other solvers, and deploy three LLMs (243 instances each) to measure instance-level transfer accuracy. A proof-preserving variable relabeling manipulation probes surface sensitivity. A preregistered extension analyzes provider-reported completion-token spend against the conflict proxy, controlling for formula length and censoring.
AI.result: Near-matched-density accuracy gaps range from −32 to +20 points with a pooled gap of +1.7 points (p=0.74); the correctness-versus-conflict association is wrong-signed (r=+0.15). Proof-preserving relabeling drops one model's accuracy by a mean of −93 points across all five clusters but leaves another unaffected. Token spend at 16k context shows the reasoning model spending more on proof-easy formulas and exhausting its budget on the solver-easiest UNSAT family; the 32k gap disappears.
AI.conclusion: LLM constraint reasoners, as evaluated, exhibit scoped dissociations from genuine proof hardness: accuracy and token spend do not reliably track solver-based hardness proxies when formula density and surface features are controlled. The findings caution against interpreting LLM reasoning performance as evidence of robust proof-theoretic competence.

title: Do Language Models Dream of Binding Molecules? Benchmarking LLMs under Spatial Constraints
summary: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) leverages the 3D structure of protein targets, often complemented by other spatial constraints, to generate candidate binding molecules. While diffusion models have dominated as a leading paradigm for high-quality 3D molecule generation, LLM-based methods are rapidly emerging in molecular design and have shown competitive performance in pocket-conditioned molecular generation. However, their ability to reason about physics and 3D spatial environments is largely underexplored. In this work, we systematically analyze whether current general-purpose LLMs are capable of navigating complex 3D constraints compared to established baselines such as specialized diffusion models. We consider 3D ligand generation conditioned on protein pockets together with ligand- and interaction-derived spatial constraints, including anchor fragments, pharmacophore points, and mandatory pocket-ligand interactions. To enable this evaluation, we introduce 3D-Fit - a token-efficient benchmarking strategy for assessing LLM performance on multi-conditioned spatial molecule generation. Our findings reveal a clear pattern in LLM spatial capabilities: while they still lag behind state-of-the-art approaches, they are promising and can handle multiple spatial constraints simultaneously, enabling scaling to heterogeneous setups.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces 3D-Fit, a benchmarking framework to evaluate how well general-purpose LLMs handle 3D spatial constraints in pocket-conditioned molecular generation, comparing them against specialized diffusion models. Findings show LLMs lag behind state-of-the-art but show promise in simultaneously handling multiple heterogeneous spatial constraints.
AI.motivation: While diffusion models dominate 3D molecule generation for SBDD, LLM-based methods are emerging with competitive performance. However, LLMs' ability to reason about physics and 3D spatial environments in this context is underexplored. The authors aim to systematically assess this capability gap.
AI.method: The authors propose 3D-Fit, a token-efficient benchmarking strategy that evaluates LLMs on multi-conditioned spatial molecule generation. The setup conditions generation on protein pockets plus diverse spatial constraints: anchor fragments, pharmacophore points, and mandatory pocket-ligand interactions. LLM performance is compared against established specialized diffusion model baselines.
AI.result: A clear performance pattern emerges: LLMs still lag behind state-of-the-art specialized diffusion models in 3D-constrained molecular generation. However, LLMs demonstrate the ability to handle multiple spatial constraints simultaneously, suggesting they are promising and capable of scaling to heterogeneous constraint setups.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not yet replacements for specialized diffusion models in 3D SBDD tasks, but their capacity to manage multiple simultaneous spatial constraints indicates significant potential. The 3D-Fit benchmark provides a foundation for tracking progress as LLM-based molecular design continues to evolve.

title: What does a Bayes-filtered transformer believe? A predictive Monte Carlo approach
summary: A Bayes-filtered transformer (BFT) is a transformer trained on sequences that are generated in two steps: first a latent task is drawn from a prior, then observations are drawn conditional on that task. Trained under autoregressive log loss, the BFT's next-token prediction, in the idealized limit, is the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution (PPD) induced by that prior and that conditional law. In practice the trained BFT is only an approximation of this ideal PPD, raising an interpretive question: what prior and posterior over the latent task has the trained BFT actually internalized? Existing work answers this question by comparing the trained BFT's predictions against the predictions of various "reference" posteriors, each standing in for a different candidate algorithm or computation the BFT might be implementing. This prediction-space comparison is fragile: different posteriors can share the same posterior-mean predictions. We use predictive Monte Carlo (PMC) as a general interpretability tool for any BFT: using only next-token generation, PMC returns an approximation to the implicit prior and posterior over the latent task, answering the interpretive question directly in latent space. We apply PMC to three stylized task families spanning 0-Markov and 1-Markov exchangeability. The phenomena previously reported in these settings remain visible in latent space. Code is available at https://github.com/afiq-aswadi/bft-pmc

AI.tldr: A Bayes-filtered transformer (BFT) approximates Bayesian posterior predictive distributions. The paper introduces Predictive Monte Carlo (PMC), a method to recover the implicit prior and posterior over latent tasks that a trained BFT has internalized, operating directly in latent space rather than relying on fragile prediction-space comparisons.
AI.motivation: Trained BFTs only approximate the ideal Bayesian posterior predictive distribution, raising the question of what prior and posterior over the latent task the BFT has actually learned. Existing methods compare BFT predictions against reference posteriors in prediction space, but this is fragile because different posteriors can yield identical posterior-mean predictions. A more direct, latent-space method is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose Predictive Monte Carlo (PMC), a general interpretability tool that uses only next-token generation from the trained BFT. PMC recovers an approximation to the implicit prior and posterior over the latent task by leveraging the BFT's own autoregressive sampling, thereby answering the interpretive question directly in latent space rather than in prediction space.
AI.result: PMC was applied to three stylized task families spanning 0-Markov and 1-Markov exchangeability. Phenomena previously reported in these settings (via prediction-space comparisons) were reproduced and remain visible in the latent space recovered by PMC, validating the method's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: PMC provides a robust, general-purpose tool for interpreting what trained BFTs have internalized about latent task structure, overcoming the fragility of prediction-space comparison methods. The approach is demonstrated across multiple exchangeability regimes, and code is publicly available.

title: Semantically Similar, Logically Distinct: Diagnosing the Semantic-Answerability Gap in Table RAG
summary: Tables are a critical knowledge source in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a retrieved table may lack sufficient evidence to answer a query, a property we call answerability. While answerability broadly concerns whether a source or collection of sources contains sufficient evidence, retrieval models optimized for semantic relevance do not guarantee it even in the single-source case, creating a fundamental mismatch. To study this, we introduce TCR-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for Table Content-level Answerability in RAG, built around sibling tables, i.e., tables with highly similar schemas but subtle content differences. On TCR-Bench, the dense retrievers we evaluate persistently exhibit a Semantic-Answerability Gap: they often retrieve the correct sibling group yet struggle to pinpoint the uniquely answerable table within it, dropping QA performance from 0.755 (oracle) to 0.330 (top-5 retrieved). Our analysis suggests this gap is associated with semantic accumulation, schema-level cue dependence, and weak row-column binding. As a diagnostic probe into the source of this gap, we test whether a lightweight two-stage pipeline, Answerability-Aware Reranking (AAR), applying direct query-table answerability judgment, can recover performance: it raises top-1 target retrieval from 18.2% to 57.4%, and this large gain is itself evidence that much of the observed failure reflects a missing answerability verification step, rather than an inherent limitation of model capacity alone.

AI.tldr: Introduces TCR-Bench, a benchmark exposing the "Semantic-Answerability Gap" in table retrieval for RAG, where dense retrievers find semantically similar tables but fail to identify which one actually answers the query. A proposed two-stage Answerability-Aware Reranking (AAR) pipeline partially recovers this gap, suggesting the failure is a missing verification step rather than a capacity limitation.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems rely on retrieved tables as knowledge sources, but retrieval models optimized for semantic relevance do not guarantee "answerability"—whether a table contains sufficient evidence to answer the query. This creates a fundamental mismatch, particularly when tables share similar schemas but differ in content. The authors aim to systematically diagnose this gap between semantic relevance and answerability.
AI.method: The authors introduce TCR-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark constructed around sibling tables (tables with highly similar schemas but subtle content differences). They evaluate dense retrievers on this benchmark to quantify the Semantic-Answerability Gap. As a diagnostic probe, they implement Answerability-Aware Reranking (AAR), a lightweight two-stage pipeline that applies direct query-table answerability judgment to rerank retrieved candidates.
AI.result: On TCR-Bench, dense retrievers exhibit a persistent Semantic-Answerability Gap: they retrieve the correct sibling group but fail to pinpoint the uniquely answerable table, causing QA performance to drop from 0.755 (oracle) to 0.330 (top-5). Analysis attributes this to semantic accumulation, schema-level cue dependence, and weak row-column binding. AAR raises top-1 target retrieval from 18.2% to 57.4%, demonstrating that much of the failure reflects a missing answerability verification step rather than an inherent model capacity limitation.
AI.conclusion: The Semantic-Answerability Gap is a distinct failure mode in table retrieval for RAG, driven by retrievers' reliance on surface-level semantic and schema cues rather than content-level answerability. A lightweight reranking stage focused on answerability judgment recovers substantial performance, indicating that the gap is addressable and that retrieval pipelines should explicitly incorporate answerability verification.

title: Logical Judgments Under Pressure: Diagnosing Syllogistic Stability with Learned Soft Prefixes
summary: To test how correct logical judgments respond to learned context, we prepend a soft prefix to an exactly labeled syllogistic reasoning benchmark while keeping the model fixed. Soft prefixes are opaque continuous vectors, so we characterize them through the behavior they induce across controlled variations in logical form and interface. By studying which prefixes succeed and how their effects generalize, we characterize how learned contextual pressure can override correct judgments and expose limits in a model's logical stability. Across Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma 4 31B, learned prefixes redirect many correct answers and remain effective across unseen forms and interface changes. In repeated tests with Qwen3.6 MoE and Gemma, they outperform paired random controls in all 16 model--direction--split comparisons by 37 to 99 percentage points. Qwen3.6 MoE flip rates remain between 72% and 90% across wording and prompt changes, while Gemma validity prefixes retain 54% to 56% flip compared with less than 1% for matched random prefixes. Diagnostic tests show that the dominant effect is a broad preference for one answer meaning rather than fixed-symbol forcing or a logical operation that transfers reliably between tasks. The form of this bias differs across models. In both Qwen models, simple score models often predict which judgments will flip but not how far their margins will move, whereas Gemma's overall response is more closely approximated by the same models. These results show that the dominant behavioral effect of successful soft prefixes is a broad answer preference, while the remaining response reveals substantial model-specific differences in logical stability.

AI.tldr: Soft prefixes prepended to LLMs can systematically override correct syllogistic reasoning, inducing broad answer-level biases rather than transferring logical operations. Effect sizes (37–99 pp) and robustness to wording/prompt changes are demonstrated across three model families, with model-specific differences in logical stability characterized via score models.
AI.motivation: To characterize how learned contextual pressure (via soft prefixes) can override correct logical judgments in LLMs and to expose limits in logical stability by studying which prefixes succeed and how their effects generalize across variations in logical form and interface.
AI.method: Soft prefixes (opaque continuous vectors) are prepended to a fixed LLM on a labeled syllogistic reasoning benchmark. The prefixes are characterized through behavioral effects across controlled variations: unseen logical forms, wording changes, and prompt changes. Diagnostic tests use simple score models to predict whether judgments flip and how much margins shift. Experiments span Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma 4 31B, with paired random controls in all 16 model–direction–split comparisons.
AI.result: Learned prefixes outperformed random controls in all 16 comparisons by 37–99 pp. Qwen3.6 MoE flip rates held at 72–90% across wording/prompt changes; Gemma validity prefixes retained 54–56% flip vs. <1% for random controls. The dominant mechanism is a broad answer-meaning preference, not fixed-symbol forcing or transferable logical operations. In Qwen models, simple score models predicted which judgments flip but not margin shifts; Gemma's overall response was more closely approximated. Logical stability patterns are model-specific.
AI.conclusion: The dominant behavioral effect of successful soft prefixes is a broad answer preference, while remaining response patterns reveal substantial model-specific differences in logical stability, exposing fundamental limits in how robustly these models maintain correct reasoning under learned contextual pressure.

title: WuYu-EnvLE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Environmental Law Enforcement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for environmental enforcement, but their ability to produce traceable enforcement decisions remains unclear. We introduce WuYu-EnvLE-Bench, a benchmark built from real enforcement cases, regulatory standards, and expert review. It contains 2,521 benchmark instances, 14 tasks, and 12 pollution-medium subdomains across pre-enforcement, in-enforcement, and post-enforcement workflows. Using Absolute Environmental Enforcement Score (AES) and Intelligent Enforcement Index (IEI), we evaluate open-source and closed-source LLMs across capability, response quality, and resource efficiency. Results show that LLMs perform well on rule-bounded tasks but remain unreliable in evidence-chain construction, contradiction detection, multi-source integration, and procedural judgment. Model scaling also shows diminishing returns: medium-sized models approach leading models in structured tasks, while larger models do not reliably overcome evidence-reasoning bottlenecks. WuYu-EnvLE-Bench highlights the need for evidence-grounded, rule-aware, and task-adaptive enforcement reasoning.

AI.tldr: WuYu-EnvLE-Bench is a benchmark of 2,521 instances across 14 tasks and 12 pollution subdomains for evaluating LLMs in environmental enforcement. LLMs perform well on rule-bounded tasks but struggle with evidence-chain construction, contradiction detection, multi-source integration, and procedural judgment. Model scaling yields diminishing returns, with larger models failing to overcome evidence-reasoning bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly considered for environmental enforcement, yet their capacity to produce traceable, legally defensible enforcement decisions is unverified. Existing benchmarks lack coverage of real-world enforcement workflows, evidence-reasoning demands, and regulatory compliance requirements specific to environmental law.
AI.method: The authors construct WuYu-EnvLE-Bench using real enforcement cases, regulatory standards, and expert review, spanning 2,521 instances across pre-enforcement, in-enforcement, and post-enforcement workflows, 14 tasks, and 12 pollution-medium subdomains. They introduce two metrics: Absolute Environmental Enforcement Score (AES) and Intelligent Enforcement Index (IEI), evaluating open- and closed-source LLMs on capability, response quality, and resource efficiency.
AI.result: LLMs demonstrate competence on rule-bounded, structured tasks but perform unreliably on evidence-chain construction, contradiction detection, multi-source integration, and procedural judgment. Model scaling shows diminishing returns: medium-sized models approach leading models on structured tasks, while larger models do not reliably resolve evidence-reasoning bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are not yet trustworthy for autonomous environmental enforcement. Progress requires advances in evidence-grounded, rule-aware, and task-adaptive reasoning rather than merely scaling model size. WuYu-EnvLE-Bench provides a rigorous framework for guiding and measuring such progress.

title: Robust Assamese Speech Recognition through Controlled Fine-Tuning of Whisper Models
summary: Developing Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) for morphologically rich, low-resource languages such as Assamese is challenging due to insufficient annotated speech data. The pretrained Whisper model performs poorly on Assamese speech recognition tasks. This paper presents a controlled, fine-tuned Whisper-based Assamese ASR system trained on the Mozilla Common Voice 24.0-Assamese corpus. A hardware-aware optimized training pipeline is implemented for resource-constrained environments, employing mixed-precision training and gradient accumulation on Tesla 4 Graphics Processing Units (T4 GPUs). The proposed fine-tuned model significantly outperformed the Zero-shot baseline, yielding Word Error Rate (WER), Character Error Rate (CER), Match Error Rate (MER), and Word Infomation Loss (WIL) of 43.17\%, 13.18\%, 43\%, and 64.81\%, respectively, achieving significant relative improvements of 78.26\%, 93.10\%, 57.0\%, and 35.19\% over the baseline. Semantic evaluation of the fine-tuned model also demonstrates notable improvement over a zero baseline, attaining Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit ORdering (METEOR) scores of 30.81 and 0.5262, respectively. Additionally, the predicted hallucination rate and Real-Time Factor (RTF) are substantially improved by 96.70\% and 32.38\%, compared to the zero-shot baseline.

AI.tldr: A fine-tuned Whisper model for Assamese ASR, trained on Common Voice 24.0 with hardware-optimized training (mixed-precision, gradient accumulation on T4 GPUs), achieves dramatic WER reduction (78.26% relative improvement) and improved semantic metrics over zero-shot baselines.
AI.motivation: Assamese is a morphologically rich, low-resource language with insufficient annotated speech data. The pretrained Whisper model performs poorly on Assamese ASR, necessitating a fine-tuned approach tailored to resource-constrained environments.
AI.method: A controlled fine-tuning pipeline for Whisper on the Mozilla Common Voice 24.0 Assamese corpus. Hardware-aware optimizations include mixed-precision training and gradient accumulation, deployed on Tesla T4 GPUs. Evaluation uses WER, CER, MER, WIL, BLEU, METEOR, hallucination rate, and RTF.
AI.result: Fine-tuned model achieves WER 43.17% (78.26% relative improvement), CER 13.18% (93.10%), MER 43% (57.0%), WIL 64.81% (35.19%). Semantic scores: BLEU 30.81, METEOR 0.5262. Hallucination rate improved by 96.70% and RTF by 32.38% over the zero-shot baseline.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning Whisper with hardware-aware training significantly boosts ASR performance for low-resource Assamese, validating the approach for morphologically rich languages under resource constraints.

title: Dynamic Defense Profiling Enables Cognitive Jailbreak of Text-to-Image Models
summary:
Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have achieved remarkable progress in synthesizing high-quality visual content, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial misuse, particularly in generating Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) images. Most existing jailbreak attacks primarily rely on heuristic prompt engineering or black-box optimization, treating model feedback as a binary signal (success or failure). This coarse-grained paradigm overlooks the rich information embedded in diverse failure modes, such as textual refusal, visual blocking, and semantic sanitization, resulting in inefficient exploration and severe semantic collapse.
  In this paper, we propose MIND, a cognitive jailbreak framework that reframes adversarial prompt generation as a belief-state inference problem over latent defense mechanisms. Instead of blindly searching for bypass prompts, MIND actively models the target system's latent defense mechanisms by interpreting multi-modal feedback as high-density signals. Specifically, the framework integrates three core components: (1) a Multi-modal Judge for fine-grained feedback decomposition, (2) a Defense Profiler for iterative belief updating, and (3) a Meta-Memory module for retrieving historically effective attack strategies. These components are unified within a reasoning-driven evolutionary optimization process, enabling adaptive and semantically consistent jailbreak generation. Extensive experiments on the I2P benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of MIND. Under six representative pre-processing and post-processing defense settings applied to the Stable Diffusion v1.5 model, MIND achieves an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 95.62%, significantly outperforming existing methods. Additionally, the effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated across four widely used commercial T2I systems, achieving the highest ASR of 91.58% on Wan-2.5.

AI.tldr: MIND is a cognitive jailbreak framework that models adversarial prompt generation as belief-state inference over latent defense mechanisms, using multi-modal feedback decomposition, defense profiling, and meta-memory to achieve an ASR of 95.62% on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and up to 91.58% on commercial T2I systems.
AI.motivation: Existing jailbreak attacks treat model feedback as a binary success/failure signal, ignoring the rich information in diverse failure modes (textual refusal, visual blocking, semantic sanitization). This leads to inefficient exploration and severe semantic collapse in adversarial prompt generation.
AI.method: MIND reframes jailbreaking as belief-state inference over latent defenses with three components: (1) a Multi-modal Judge for fine-grained feedback decomposition, (2) a Defense Profiler for iterative belief updating, and (3) a Meta-Memory module for retrieving historically effective strategies. These are unified in a reasoning-driven evolutionary optimization process.
AI.result: On the I2P benchmark with six defense settings applied to Stable Diffusion v1.5, MIND achieves a 95.62% ASR, significantly outperforming existing methods. Across four commercial T2I systems, it achieves the highest ASR of 91.58% on Wan-2.5.
AI.conclusion: Modeling jailbreaking as belief-state inference over latent defenses — rather than binary-feedback optimization — enables more efficient, semantically consistent adversarial prompt generation with state-of-the-art attack success rates.

title: Explaining and Tuning Transformer-based LLMs in Arithmetic Tasks with Human Strategies
summary: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) continue to achieve state-of-the-art performance across various natural language processing tasks. However, their subpar performance on seemingly elementary problems, such as basic arithmetic, raises concerns about model reliability, safety, and ethical deployment. In this study, we demonstrate that the performance of a vanilla Transformer model trained on integer arithmetic tasks can be improved using methods effective for human learners. We begin by decomposing the arithmetic task into well-defined subtasks and conducting loss convergence order analysis together with ablation studies for each subtask. Our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit learning patterns similar to those of human learners, with a faster learning speed for simpler subtasks compared to more complex ones. In addition, we successfully improved the accuracy of LLMs by applying problem-solving strategies and cognitive empowerment methods shown to enhance the performance of human learners. This suggests that transformer-based LLMs may share cognitive processes with human learners in arithmetic. Lastly, we provide a comprehensive demonstration of our method's effectiveness, including significant accuracy improvement experiments, visualization verification, and explanation-based analysis to illuminate the intricacies of LLMs in arithmetic learning. In general, this work explores the potential similarities between transformer-based LLMs and human learners, supported by explainable AI (XAI) verifications, ultimately fostering trust in LLMs for critical and high-stakes applications.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates parallels between how transformer-based LLMs and human learners acquire arithmetic skills. By decomposing arithmetic into subtasks and applying human-inspired learning strategies (problem-solving techniques, cognitive empowerment methods), the authors demonstrate improved model accuracy. Their analysis reveals that LLMs, like humans, learn simpler subtasks faster than complex ones, suggesting shared cognitive patterns in arithmetic learning.
AI.motivation: LLMs underperform on basic arithmetic despite state-of-the-art NLP results, raising concerns about reliability and safety. The authors aim to understand whether LLMs learn arithmetic in ways analogous to humans, and whether human-inspired pedagogical methods can improve LLM arithmetic performance.
AI.method: The arithmetic task is decomposed into well-defined subtasks. The authors conduct loss convergence order analysis and ablation studies on each subtask, then apply problem-solving strategies and cognitive empowerment methods (drawn from human pedagogy) to vanilla Transformer models trained on integer arithmetic. Results are validated through accuracy improvement experiments, visualization verification, and explanation-based (XAI) analysis.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit learning patterns similar to human learners: faster convergence on simpler subtasks, slower on complex ones. Applying human-inspired problem-solving and cognitive empowerment strategies significantly improves arithmetic accuracy. XAI-based visualization and explanation analyses further support the cognitive parallel between LLMs and human learners.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based LLMs may share cognitive processes with human learners in arithmetic learning. These findings, supported by XAI verification, can help build trust in LLMs for critical and high-stakes applications by illuminating how models learn foundational tasks.

title: Financial Audit Assistance using Misinformation Detection and Explanation
summary: Financial statements (FS) such as Balance Sheet (BS), Income Statement (IS) and Cash-flow Statement (CS) summarize the annual financial performance of a company. FS are widely used for evaluating corporate governance, credit appraisal, risk analysis, validate taxation, make investment decisions etc. Financial auditing is a complex and knowledge-intensive discipline whose one important aim is ensuring integrity, accuracy, fairness and absence of material misstatement in the published FS. Given the importance of FS, there are incentives to hide, omit or falsify information to misrepresent the true financial health of the company; e.g., reduce tax liabilities, or increase investor confidence. Given the complex, time-consuming and expertise-dependent nature of auditing, auditors would benefit from an AI-assisted system that automatically detects instances of misinformation in the given FS and identify likely sources of this misinformation in the financial data. In this paper, we present unsupervised techniques to identify misinformation in FS, and also generate explanations as to the financial variables that are likely sources of misinformation. The auditor can then explore in more detail the associated data sources and business processes to validate these suggestions. A crucial feature of our approach is the use of past corpus of FS and associated audit reports to generate insights, which help in providing assistance. We demonstrate the efficacy of these techniques on a large corpus of 11,460 FS over 5 years and associated audit reports. This paper integrates and adds more novel contributions over the previously reported research (Shinde et al., 2022)\cite{SVAP22}, (Vaishampayan et al., 2022)\cite{VSPP22}, (Pawar et al., 2023)\cite{PAPV23}, which we have used as the foundation for our AI-assisted Auditor Assistance system.

AI.tldr: Presents an AI-assisted auditing system that uses unsupervised techniques to automatically detect misinformation in financial statements and identify the likely source financial variables, leveraging a corpus of past FS and audit reports to generate explanatory insights for auditors.
AI.motivation: Financial auditing is complex, time-consuming, and expertise-dependent. Companies have incentives to misrepresent financial health (e.g., tax reduction, boosting investor confidence). Auditors would benefit from automated AI assistance that detects misinformation and explains its likely sources, reducing manual effort while maintaining audit integrity.
AI.method: Unsupervised techniques that detect misinformation in financial statements (Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Cash-flow Statement). The approach uses a historical corpus of past financial statements and associated audit reports to generate insights. Crucially, it not only flags potential misinformation but also generates explanations identifying which financial variables are likely sources of the detected anomalies, enabling auditors to conduct targeted follow-up validation.
AI.result: The techniques were demonstrated on a corpus of 11,460 financial statements spanning 5 years along with their associated audit reports. The work builds upon and integrates prior research (Shinde et al. 2022, Vaishampayan et al. 2022, Pawar et al. 2023) with novel contributions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AI-assisted Auditor Assistance system effectively detects misinformation in financial statements and provides explainable outputs that guide auditors toward likely problematic financial variables, enabling efficient and targeted validation of suspicious entries within associated data sources and business processes.

title: DADIR: Density-Aware Data-level Imbalanced Regression Framework
summary: Imbalanced learning addresses predictive modeling problems with underrepresented regions of the data distribution. Although widely studied in classification, imbalanced regression remains challenging because of continuous target variables and heterogeneous density distributions. Existing data-level methods often rely on fixed target partitioning or synthetic sample generation without jointly considering density variations and local feature-space structure. We propose DADIR, a Density-Aware Data-level Imbalanced Regression framework that exploits density information throughout the balancing process. DADIR comprises three components: (1) Density-Aware Adaptive Partitioning (DAAP), which recursively partitions the target space according to density variations; (2) a Density-Regularized Conditional Variational Autoencoder (DR-CVAE), which preserves sparse-region representations while learning latent features; and (3) latent-space data balancing, which combines feature-level clustering with oversampling to generate structurally consistent synthetic samples. Together, these components identify minority regions more effectively, preserve sparse-region information, and generate realistic synthetic data. The resulting balanced dataset can be used directly with existing regression models without modifying their architecture or learning objective. Experiments on diverse imbalanced regression datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in predictive performance, particularly in underrepresented regions, while also improving overall accuracy.

AI.tldr: DADIR is a density-aware data-level framework for imbalanced regression that uses adaptive target-space partitioning, a density-regularized CVAE for sparse-region representation learning, and latent-space clustering-based oversampling to generate structurally consistent synthetic samples, improving prediction in underrepresented regions without modifying downstream models.
AI.motivation: Imbalanced regression is challenging because continuous targets exhibit heterogeneous density distributions, and existing data-level methods fail by using fixed target partitioning or generating synthetic samples without jointly considering density variations and local feature-space structure, leading to poor representation of minority regions.
AI.method: DADIR consists of three components: (1) Density-Aware Adaptive Partitioning (DAAP), which recursively partitions the target space based on density variations; (2) Density-Regularized Conditional Variational Autoencoder (DR-CVAE), which learns latent features while preserving sparse-region representations via density-based regularization; (3) latent-space data balancing, which performs feature-level clustering and oversampling in the latent space to generate structurally consistent synthetic samples. The resulting balanced dataset is model-agnostic.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse imbalanced regression datasets show consistent improvements in predictive performance, especially in underrepresented regions, alongside gains in overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Jointly leveraging density information for adaptive partitioning, representation learning, and synthetic sampling effectively addresses imbalanced regression. DADIR provides a plug-and-play balanced dataset compatible with any existing regression model, advancing the state of data-level solutions for this problem.

title: PGN: Design and Implementation of a Vision-Language Navigation System Based on Pangu Multimodal Foundation Model
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to interpret a natural-language instruction and predict actions from temporally ordered visual observations. Adapting a multimodal large language model to VLN requires visual-language alignment, compact temporal inputs, action-space grounding, and stable training on the target hardware. This technical report presents PGN (Pangu Navigator), an offline VLN action-prediction system built on OpenPangu-7B. Training proceeds in two stages. First, PGMM aligns a frozen EVA-ViT-G/14 vision encoder with the frozen language backbone by training a Q-Former and a two-layer MLP projector. Second, PGN adapts the aligned model to expert navigation trajectories using five-observation windows, epoch-dependent temporal sampling, and a reasoning-then-action output format; this stage freezes the aligned visual pathway and updates three structural-token embeddings and LoRA adapters. The implementation combines mixed-precision computation, selective FP32 computation, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 on eight Ascend 910B NPUs. Under teacher-forced, open-loop evaluation on 500 held-out expert trajectories, V9 reports a 62.29% Normalized Action Match (NAM) and a 100.00% Non-empty Rate (NER). These metrics quantify offline expert-action alignment rather than closed-loop navigation success; evaluating error accumulation, path efficiency, and goal completion remains future work.

AI.tldr: PGN (Pangu Navigator) adapts OpenPangu-7B for Vision-Language Navigation via a two-stage training pipeline: visual-language alignment using a Q-Former/MLP projector with frozen encoders, followed by trajectory adaptation with LoRA and structural-token embeddings. On 500 held-out trajectories, it achieves 62.29% Normalized Action Match and 100% Non-empty Rate under teacher-forced open-loop evaluation.
AI.motivation: Adapting multimodal LLMs to VLN poses four key challenges: visual-language alignment, compact temporal input representation, action-space grounding, and stable training on target hardware (Ascend 910B NPUs). Existing approaches may not simultaneously address all four within a unified, hardware-efficient framework.
AI.method: A two-stage approach. Stage 1 (PGMM): Trains a Q-Former and a two-layer MLP projector to align a frozen EVA-ViT-G/14 vision encoder with the frozen OpenPangu-7B language backbone. Stage 2 (PGN): Adapts the aligned model to expert navigation trajectories using five-observation windows, epoch-dependent temporal sampling, and a reasoning-then-action output format. Only three structural-token embeddings and LoRA adapters are updated; the visual pathway remains frozen. Training uses mixed-precision, selective FP32, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 on eight Ascend 910B NPUs.
AI.result: Under teacher-forced, open-loop evaluation on 500 held-out expert trajectories (V9), PGN achieves 62.29% Normalized Action Match (NAM) and 100.00% Non-empty Rate (NER).
AI.conclusion: PGN demonstrates effective offline alignment with expert navigation actions. However, the reported metrics reflect open-loop, teacher-forced evaluation only; assessing closed-loop navigation performance — including error accumulation, path efficiency, and goal completion — remains future work.

title: DynImmune-BERT: Dynamic Immune Repertoire Modeling with Neural ODE Driven Continuous Transformers
summary: Longitudinal T cell receptor repertoires contain signals of clonal expansion, contraction, disappearance, and reappearance after immune perturbation. Static repertoire language models usually summarize a sample as a bag of sequences, so the sampling interval, sequencing depth, and clone presence pattern are only weakly represented. This paper presents DynImmune-BERT, a continuous time repertoire model for patient level immune status prediction. The method combines depth adaptive centered log ratio initialization, clone presence gated Neural ordinary differential equation dynamics, bounded neighborhood self attention, event based state restart, and a hybrid transport objective that supervises dominant and rare clone mass. A low rank meta adapter initializes reappearing clonotypes while keeping the parameter count independent of the number of observed clones. The evaluation separates literature reported baselines from internally controlled temporal comparisons, reports uncertainty for small external cohorts, adds calibration and threshold diagnostics, and visualizes latent clone trajectories and attention neighborhoods. The results indicate that event aware temporal modeling can complement strong static encoders when longitudinal repertoire structure is available, while small external cohorts and protocol differences require cautious interpretation.

AI.tldr: DynImmune-BERT is a continuous-time repertoire model that uses Neural ODEs with clone-presence gating, depth-adaptive initialization, and hybrid transport objectives to model longitudinal T cell receptor dynamics for patient-level immune status prediction, showing temporal modeling complements static encoders when longitudinal data is available.
AI.motivation: Static repertoire language models treat each sample as a bag of sequences, failing to adequately capture temporal signals — sampling intervals, sequencing depth variation, and clone presence patterns (expansion, contraction, disappearance, reappearance) — that are critical for understanding immune dynamics after perturbation.
AI.method: DynImmune-BERT integrates: (1) depth-adaptive centered log-ratio initialization for sequencing depth normalization, (2) clone-presence-gated Neural ODE dynamics for continuous-time modeling, (3) bounded-neighborhood self-attention, (4) event-based state restart mechanisms, (5) a hybrid transport objective supervising both dominant and rare clone mass, and (6) a low-rank meta-adapter that initializes reappearing clonotypes while keeping parameter count independent of clone number.
AI.result: Event-aware temporal modeling improves over strong static encoders when longitudinal repertoire structure is available. The evaluation separates literature baselines from internally controlled temporal comparisons, reports uncertainty for small external cohorts, and provides calibration/threshold diagnostics alongside visualizations of latent clone trajectories and attention neighborhoods. Small external cohorts and protocol differences demand cautious interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-time, event-aware modeling of TCR repertoires provides complementary signals to static encoders for immune status prediction, but external validation remains challenging due to cohort size and protocol heterogeneity, necessitating careful uncertainty quantification.

title: A Hardware-oriented Approach for Efficient Bayesian Inference Computation and Deployment
summary: Bayesian inference provides a principled foundation for reasoning under uncertainty, but its computational cost hinders deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. In this paper, we present a hardware-oriented methodology for accelerating discrete Bayesian inference on commercial off-the-shelf embedded GPUs. We identify that the latency of a broad class of variational message-passing algorithms is dominated by tensor contractions. Our approach restructures the memory layout of these operations using two complementary merging strategies that produce compact, regularly-shaped primitives better suited for efficient GPU execution. We then introduce optional sparse array representations and a tensor-clustering scheme to reduce the memory footprint. We instantiate the methodology and produce optimized variants of three message-passing algorithms for Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), namely variational filtering, variational message passing, and marginal message passing. Furthermore, we complement this with a machine-learning-based autotuner that automatically selects the best-performing algorithmic variant for a given generative model specification. Benchmarked on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin AGX across 770 randomly sampled realistic Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) configurations, our implementations achieve speedups of up to 5x, with typical gains of 2-2.5x, while producing numerically identical outputs to the baseline implementations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hardware-oriented methodology to accelerate discrete Bayesian inference on embedded GPUs by restructuring tensor contraction memory layouts, introducing sparse representations, and using an ML-based autotuner, achieving up to 5x speedup on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin AGX for variational message-passing algorithms.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inference is computationally expensive, limiting its deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. The authors identify that tensor contractions dominate latency in variational message-passing algorithms and aim to make these algorithms practical for embedded GPU platforms.
AI.method: The approach restructures memory layouts of tensor contractions using two merging strategies to produce compact, regularly-shaped GPU primitives. It optionally employs sparse array representations and a tensor-clustering scheme to reduce memory footprint. The methodology is instantiated on three message-passing algorithms (variational filtering, variational message passing, marginal message passing) for Hidden Markov Models. An ML-based autotuner selects the best algorithmic variant for a given model specification.
AI.result: Benchmarked on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin AGX across 770 randomly sampled POMDP configurations, the optimized implementations achieve speedups of up to 5x, with typical gains of 2–2.5x, while producing numerically identical outputs to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology successfully bridges the gap between principled Bayesian inference and resource-constrained edge deployment by leveraging memory layout optimization, sparsity, and autotuning on embedded GPUs, enabling practical real-time probabilistic reasoning on edge devices.

title: Distilled Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-training
summary: Large language model (LLM) post-training is essential for improving reasoning, adaptation, and alignment. Existing methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, RL relies on coarse-grained outcome supervision, resulting in difficult credit assignment and limited capability to acquire new knowledge. OPD, meanwhile, unconditionally matches teacher logits through KL divergence, which creates a dilemma: similar teachers provide little new knowledge, while substantially different teachers often yield ineffective guidance, largely restricting OPD to within-family distillation. We propose Distilled Reinforcement Learning (Distilled RL), which integrates teacher supervision into the RL objective to provide fine-grained guidance, selectively transfer new knowledge and avoid unconditional imitation. Distilled RL contains three components: reverse importance sampling with clipping, negative sample reset, and sequence-level geometric normalization. Through a concise and interpretable case study, we demonstrate that Distilled RL can effectively transfer previously unavailable knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. Extensive experiments across both within-family and cross-family distillation settings show that Distilled RL substantially outperforms standard RL and OPD in terms of both pass@1 and pass@k. Our code is available at https://github.com/597358816/Distilled-RL.

AI.tldr: Distilled RL integrates teacher supervision into the RL objective for LLM post-training, combining fine-grained guidance from on-policy distillation with the exploration benefits of RL, and outperforms both standard RL and OPD across within-family and cross-family settings.
AI.motivation: Standard RL for LLM post-training uses coarse-grained outcome supervision, making credit assignment difficult and limiting new knowledge acquisition. On-policy distillation (OPD) unconditionally matches teacher logits via KL divergence, creating a dilemma: similar teachers offer little new knowledge, while substantially different teachers produce ineffective guidance, restricting OPD to within-family distillation.
AI.method: Distilled RL combines teacher supervision with RL objectives through three key components: (1) reverse importance sampling with clipping to selectively transfer new knowledge, (2) negative sample reset to handle unsuccessful trajectories, and (3) sequence-level geometric normalization for stable optimization. This avoids unconditional imitation while enabling fine-grained guidance.
AI.result: A case study demonstrates effective transfer of previously unavailable knowledge from teacher to student. Extensive experiments across both within-family and cross-family distillation settings show that Distilled RL substantially outperforms standard RL and OPD on pass@1 and pass@k metrics.
AI.conclusion: Distilled RL successfully resolves the core dilemma of OPD by selectively transferring knowledge rather than unconditionally imitating, enabling effective cross-family distillation and outperforming both existing paradigms.

title: Exploratory and Assimilating Reflection: Reflective Recall Cycle for Long-term Memory
summary: LLM-based autonomous agents require external memory to overcome their statelessness and limited context window for long-term interaction and dynamic knowledge reasoning. However, existing memory retrieval methods often lack adaptability and sample efficiency, and struggle to retrieve the right mixture of memories from heterogeneous stores. We propose Exploratory-Assimilating Reflection (EAR), a framework for high initial retrieval performance and sample-efficient adaptation. EAR combines two mechanisms: Exploratory Reflection, which performs iterative search to bootstrap retrieval and collect useful experiences for each query, and Assimilating Reflection, which replays these experiences from an Experience Buffer to refine a global reranker more efficiently than methods relying only on immediate rewards. Experiments show that EAR improves retrieval by up to 17.9% over the baseline retriever on two long-term dialogue benchmarks. We also show that EAR is highly sample-efficient and robust to noisy feedback.

AI.tldr: EAR is a framework that improves memory retrieval for LLM agents via two complementary mechanisms: Exploratory Reflection (iterative search to bootstrap retrieval) and Assimilating Reflection (experience replay to efficiently refine a global reranker), achieving up to 17.9% improvement on long-term dialogue benchmarks with high sample efficiency and robustness to noisy feedback.
AI.motivation: LLM-based autonomous agents need external memory for long-term interaction and dynamic knowledge reasoning, but existing memory retrieval methods lack adaptability and sample efficiency, and struggle to retrieve the right mixture of memories from heterogeneous stores.
AI.method: EAR combines two mechanisms: (1) Exploratory Reflection — iterative search that bootstraps retrieval and collects useful experiences for each query; and (2) Assimilating Reflection — replays these experiences from an Experience Buffer to refine a global reranker, which is more efficient than relying only on immediate rewards.
AI.result: EAR improves retrieval by up to 17.9% over the baseline retriever on two long-term dialogue benchmarks, and demonstrates high sample efficiency and robustness to noisy feedback.
AI.conclusion: EAR provides an effective, sample-efficient, and noise-robust solution for adaptive memory retrieval in LLM-based autonomous agents, significantly outperforming baseline methods on long-term dialogue tasks.

title: Node4All: Learning Node Representation Beyond Datasets
summary:
Node representation learning has advanced rapidly, yet most existing methods rely on per-dataset training and hyperparameter tuning. This dataset-specific optimization comes from the difficulty of designing reusable graph models that generalize across diverse graph datasets. In this work, we introduce Node4All, a node representation learner applicable to arbitrary graph datasets without any dataset-specific optimization.
  Node4All is built on two complementary ideas. At the architectural level, we introduce the Channel Graph Transformer (CGT), which enables a single fixed parameterization to process arbitrary graph datasets. At the learning level, we propose a self-supervised learning based on a series of synthetic graphs. Together, these components enable generalization beyond individual datasets, which is infeasible with existing architectures and learning frameworks. We extensively evaluate Node4All on node classification across 25 benchmarks against 21 baselines, covering both supervised and self-supervised methods. Despite all baselines being trained and optimized for each dataset, a single Node4All, applied uniformly across the datasets, achieves a competitive ranking of 5th among 21 baselines. Moreover, Node4All supports one-shot and in-context learning with an appropriate predictor and outperforms recent graph foundation models (GFMs) in these settings.
