These results demonstrate that Node4All not only achieves reusability across arbitrary graph datasets, but also remains an effective solution in practice. Code and model checkpoints are available in https://github.com/dooho00/node4all.

AI.tldr: Node4All introduces a reusable node representation learner that works across arbitrary graph datasets without per-dataset training, using a Channel Graph Transformer architecture and synthetic graph-based self-supervised learning, achieving competitive performance across 25 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing node representation learning methods require per-dataset training and hyperparameter tuning, making them non-reusable across diverse graph datasets. There is a need for a general-purpose graph model that can generalize without dataset-specific optimization, akin to foundation models in other domains.
AI.method: Node4All combines two key innovations: (1) the Channel Graph Transformer (CGT), a fixed-parameter architecture that can process arbitrary graph datasets, and (2) a self-supervised learning framework trained on a series of synthetic graphs, enabling generalization beyond individual datasets without any dataset-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: A single Node4All model, applied uniformly across 25 node classification benchmarks, ranks 5th among 21 baselines (both supervised and self-supervised), despite all baselines being optimized per dataset. It also outperforms recent graph foundation models (GFMs) in one-shot and in-context learning settings.
AI.conclusion: Node4All demonstrates that a single, reusable graph model can achieve competitive performance across diverse datasets without dataset-specific optimization, establishing a promising direction toward general-purpose graph foundation models.

title: ST-Veto: Spatio-Temporal Token Veto for Diffusion MLLMs via Taylor Prediction and Visual Grounding
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong reasoning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting but incur high sequential-generation cost, error accumulation, and limited self-correction. Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (dMLLMs) unmask tokens in an order-agnostic process, improving efficiency and enabling iterative refinement, yet their reasoning and how to enhance it remain underexplored. We propose a training-free method, Spatio-Temporal Token Veto (ST-Veto), which leverages the ability to observe all token positions at each diffusion step. Rather than relying only on current-step confidence, ST-Veto vetoes temporally unstable tokens via second-order Taylor prediction of confidence dynamics and filters weakly grounded tokens using image-attention mass, swapping them with safer candidates. Across multiple dMLLMs and multimodal reasoning benchmarks, ST-Veto consistently outperforms standard decoding policies and prior VLM reasoning methods, improving accuracy by up to 9% with no additional training or generation cost. Analyses show that ST-Veto steers generation toward higher-confidence, better-grounded paths.

AI.tldr: ST-Veto is a training-free decoding method for diffusion multimodal LLMs that improves reasoning by vetoing unstable tokens using second-order Taylor prediction of confidence dynamics and filtering weakly grounded tokens via image-attention mass, achieving up to 9% accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: VLMs with CoT prompting suffer from high sequential-generation cost, error accumulation, and limited self-correction. Diffusion MLLMs (dMLLMs) address these via order-agnostic unmasking and iterative refinement, but their reasoning capabilities and how to enhance them remain underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by exploiting dMLLMs' unique ability to observe all token positions simultaneously at each diffusion step.
AI.method: ST-Veto is a training-free, plug-and-play decoding strategy with two components: (1) Temporal Veto — uses second-order Taylor expansion to predict confidence trajectory of each token and vetoes those with unstable dynamics (high predicted variance or downward trend); (2) Spatial Veto — uses image-attention mass (sum of attention weights from a token to image patches) to identify weakly grounded tokens and swap them with semantically safer alternatives. Both operate during the iterative denoising process without adding generation cost.
AI.result: Across multiple dMLLMs and multimodal reasoning benchmarks, ST-Veto consistently outperforms standard decoding and prior VLM reasoning methods, improving accuracy by up to 9% with no additional training or inference cost. Analyses confirm that ST-Veto steers generation toward higher-confidence, better-visually-grounded reasoning paths.
AI.conclusion: ST-Veto effectively enhances reasoning in diffusion MLLMs by leveraging their architectural trait of global token visibility at each step, applying temporal stability and spatial grounding criteria to guide token selection. It establishes a new direction for improving multimodal reasoning without training overhead.

title: AIGB-R1: Self-Evolving Generative Auto-Bidding via Hierarchical Planner-Executor Optimization
summary: Auto-bidding plays an essential role in online advertising, automatically adjusting bids for advertisers to optimize their commercial goals. The emerging AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) paradigm widely adopts generative modeling to optimize bidding strategies, yet suffers from the limited mode coverage of offline datasets and inadequate task-state understanding, hindering effective exploration of optimal strategies. Large Language Models (LLMs), with prior world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, offer a promising approach to overcome these limitations. However, directly applying LLMs to auto-bidding tasks faces inherent challenges in limited numerical precision, hallucinations, and inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose AIGB-R1, a hierarchical self-evolving auto-bidding framework aiming to enhance AI-Generated Bidding via LLMs' Reasoning capabilities, comprising a high-level Planner module for macro-level strategy planning and a low-level Executor module for fine-grained decision-making. Building upon this, we design an experience-driven self-evolving loop, enabling autonomous strategy exploration and optimization from accumulated experience. We adopt a two-stage pipeline of offline pre-training and post-training alignment, and build an interactive bidding simulation environment for strategy rollout. Furthermore, we propose Decoupled Group Relative Policy Optimization (D-GRPO) to achieve end-to-end optimization via advantage decoupling. Experimental results on a large-scale public dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of AIGB-R1.

AI.tldr: AIGB-R1 proposes a hierarchical, self-evolving auto-bidding framework that leverages LLM reasoning capabilities, combining a Planner-Executor architecture with Decoupled Group Relative Policy Optimization (D-GRPO) to overcome limitations in mode coverage, numerical precision, and inference latency in AI-Generated Bidding.
AI.motivation: Current AI-Generated Bidding (AIGB) paradigms using generative modeling suffer from limited mode coverage in offline datasets and poor task-state understanding, restricting exploration of optimal bidding strategies. While LLMs offer world knowledge and reasoning to address these gaps, they introduce challenges of numerical precision, hallucinations, and inference latency when directly applied to auto-bidding.
AI.method: The authors propose AIGB-R1, a hierarchical framework with a high-level Planner (macro strategy planning) and a low-level Executor (fine-grained decisions). It features an experience-driven self-evolving loop for autonomous strategy exploration, a two-stage offline pre-training and post-training alignment pipeline, an interactive bidding simulation environment, and Decoupled Group Relative Policy Optimization (D-GRPO) that decouples advantages for end-to-end optimization.
AI.result: Experimental results on a large-scale public dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of AIGB-R1.
AI.conclusion: AIGB-R1 effectively integrates LLM reasoning into auto-bidding through a hierarchical self-evolving framework with D-GRPO, successfully addressing key limitations of prior AIGB approaches and validating its performance empirically.

title: Stress Testing Concept Erasure with Large Language Model Agents
summary: Concept erasure aims to remove semantic concepts from a trained generative model and is increasingly important for responsible AI deployment. However, verifying whether a model has robustly removed targeted concepts remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation methods are typically pre-defined and static, failing to expose vulnerabilities under diverse natural-language probes and challenging conditions. Moreover, manually designed evaluation strategies can be biased and difficult to scale. We posit that concept erasure evaluation is best formulated as an adaptive hypothesis search, operationalised by agents that iteratively propose, critique, and verify tests to systematically expand coverage of failure modes. To this end, we propose Stress Testing Agents for Concept Erasure (STACE), a framework that autonomously stress-tests concept-erased models using multiple Large Language Model (LLM) agents, by iteratively generating and verifying stress-testing hypotheses grounded by external knowledge. We also introduce a suite of metrics for assessing the performance and efficiency of LLM-agent-powered stress-testing frameworks. Our extensive experiments show that STACE outperforms five LLM-based evaluation baselines on four concept categories. Further analysis across two T2I models, six concept erasure approaches, and various erasure strengths show that STACE is robust for different settings. We also show that STACE can be adapted beyond concept erasure evaluation to other problem domains, such as LLM jailbreaking. Our code is available anonymously.

AI.tldr: STACE is an LLM-agent framework that stress-tests concept-erased generative models by adaptively generating, critiquing, and verifying hypotheses. It outperforms five baselines across four concept categories, works robustly across multiple T2I models and erasure methods, and generalizes to domains like LLM jailbreaking.
AI.motivation: Existing concept erasure evaluation methods are pre-defined, static, biased, and non-scalable, failing to expose vulnerabilities under diverse natural-language probes. There is a need for adaptive, systematic, and automated evaluation of whether erased concepts are robustly removed.
AI.method: STACE formulates concept erasure evaluation as adaptive hypothesis search using multiple LLM agents that iteratively propose, critique, and verify stress-testing hypotheses, grounded by external knowledge. The framework also introduces metrics for assessing agent-powered stress-testing performance and efficiency.
AI.result: STACE outperforms five LLM-based evaluation baselines on four concept categories. Robustness is demonstrated across two T2I models, six concept erasure approaches, and varying erasure strengths. The framework also successfully adapts to LLM jailbreaking tasks.
AI.conclusion: STACE provides a scalable, adaptive, and effective solution for rigorously evaluating concept erasure, with strong empirical validation and promising generalizability to other safety-critical AI evaluation domains.

title: An Iterative Geometric Approach to Optimizing Separating Hyperplanes
summary: Given a binary-labeled linearly separable dataset, and the objective is to compute the maximum-margin separating hyperplane, also known as the hard-margin Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier. This paper investigates whether, if given an initial separating hyperplane, can it be exploited to reach this unique optimum more efficiently. We present a geometric approach that gradually improves the alignment of the hyperplane, starting from an initial separating hyperplane, while preserving separation and continuously increasing its margin until convergence to the global optimum. At each iteration, the method considers only local information, namely the current active set, and aims to re-align the hyperplane according to the optimal separating hyperplane of this reduced subset. Consequently, the original convex quadratic optimization problem is addressed through a sequence of smaller subproblems. The paper presents the algorithm in detail, together with a preliminary experimental evaluation and several theoretical findings. The results suggest that, when an initial separating hyperplane is available, the proposed method can be competitive on larger datasets and, in some cases, can outperform state-of-the-art approaches that solve the optimization problem directly.

AI.tldr: Presents a geometric algorithm that refines an initial separating hyperplane toward the hard-margin SVM optimum by iteratively solving smaller subproblems based on local active sets, potentially outperforming direct solvers when a warm start is available.
AI.motivation: Standard SVM solvers solve the convex quadratic optimization problem from scratch. The authors ask: if we already have *any* separating hyperplane (a warm start), can we exploit it to reach the maximum-margin solution more efficiently than solving the full problem directly?
AI.method: A geometric iterative procedure that starts from an initial separating hyperplane and repeatedly re-aligns it using only the current active set (local information). Each iteration solves a small subproblem — finding the optimal separating hyperplane for the reduced subset — to gradually increase the margin while preserving separation, until convergence to the global hard-margin SVM optimum.
AI.result: Preliminary experimental evaluation and theoretical analysis suggest the method is competitive on larger datasets and can, in some cases, outperform state-of-the-art direct optimization approaches when an initial separating hyperplane is provided.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a warm-start separating hyperplane via a sequence of local subproblems offers a viable and sometimes superior alternative to solving the full SVM optimization directly, particularly for larger datasets.

title: PEARL: Auditable Repair for Scientific Reasoning Graph Extraction
comment: Accepted at WAICA 2026 Multi-Modal Agents for Science Workshop
summary: Scientific Reasoning Graph Extraction (SRGE) aims to recover explicit links among observations, evidence, intermediate claims, and paper-level conclusions. LLMs can produce graph-like scientific explanations, but their outputs often mix malformed syntax, drifting edge labels, incorrectly oriented roots, and weak source anchors. We propose PEARL (Peircean Extraction via Abstraction and Repair Layer), a training-free framework that turns noisy LLM graph responses into auditable reasoning graphs and repairs them toward strict semantic validity. PEARL first materializes explicit graph content under a closed Peircean schema, then uses matched evidence-grounded judge feedback to repair rejected edge types, local inference steps, and terminal roots while preserving an audit trail. On five 70-paper model archives from ARCHE, a benchmark for latent reasoning-chain extraction, PEARL raises strict gate passes from 0/350 for the LLM baseline to 300/350, with average REA improving from 0.339 to 0.906. The graphs provide a reliability layer for research-agent and AI scientist workflows that need inspectable reasoning traces rather than unconstrained graph regeneration. Code and audit artifacts are available at https://github.com/BohanSu/auditable-repair-reasoning-graphs/tree/300-350_workshop .

AI.tldr: PEARL is a training-free framework that repairs noisy LLM-generated scientific reasoning graphs into semantically valid, auditable structures. It uses a Peircean schema and evidence-grounded judge feedback to fix edge types, inference steps, and root orientations, raising strict gate passes from 0/350 to 300/350 on the ARCHE benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate graph-like scientific explanations for reasoning chain extraction (SRGE), but their outputs suffer from malformed syntax, drifting edge labels, incorrectly oriented roots, and weak source anchors — rendering them unreliable for downstream use in research-agent and AI scientist workflows that require inspectable reasoning traces.
AI.method: PEARL is a training-free, two-stage framework. First, it materializes explicit graph content under a closed Peircean schema (abduction, deduction, induction). Second, it employs matched evidence-grounded judge feedback to iteratively repair rejected edge types, local inference steps, and terminal roots, while preserving an audit trail of all modifications.
AI.result: On five 70-paper model archives from the ARCHE benchmark, PEARL improved strict gate passes from 0/350 (LLM baseline) to 300/350, with average Reasoning Extraction Accuracy (REA) rising from 0.339 to 0.906.
AI.conclusion: PEARL provides a reliability layer for AI-driven scientific reasoning by producing auditable, semantically valid reasoning graphs without retraining, offering a practical bridge between noisy LLM generation and trustworthy knowledge extraction pipelines.

title: Lookahead Branching for Neural Network Verification
comment: Accepted to IJCAI 2026. Lookahead branching is part of the Marabou and $α$-$β$-CROWN verifiers
summary: In this work, we investigate the effect of lookahead branching strategies in neural network verification. We present a general recipe to integrate lookahead into any branch-and-bound verifier and demonstrate how one of the current state-of-the-art branching heuristics, FSB, can be viewed as a special instantiation of the lookahead branching strategy. We also describe how, in addition to improving the quality of branching decisions, lookahead can generate additional lemmas that accelerate verification. We instantiate the method in two representative branch-and-bound-based verifiers (Marabou and $α$-$β$-CROWN), and demonstrate that lookahead leads to consistent speedups in verification time and up to $57\%$ more solved instances. Code is available at https://github.com/ai-ar-research/lookahead-branching.

AI.tldr: Introduces a general lookahead branching strategy for neural network verification that can be integrated into any branch-and-bound verifier, showing that existing state-of-the-art heuristics like FSB are special cases. The method generates additional lemmas, achieves consistent speedups, and solves up to 57% more instances.
AI.motivation: Branch-and-bound-based neural network verifiers rely heavily on branching heuristics to split the search space efficiently. Current heuristics make branching decisions based on immediate (one-step) information, which can be shortsighted. The authors hypothesize that looking multiple steps ahead (lookahead) can yield better branching decisions and generate useful lemmas, ultimately accelerating verification.
AI.method: The paper presents a general recipe for integrating lookahead into any branch-and-bound NN verifier. The approach simulates multiple branching steps ahead to evaluate the quality of candidate branching decisions before committing. The authors show that FSB (Fast Split Branching), a state-of-the-art heuristic, is a special case of lookahead. Additionally, beyond improving branching decisions, the lookahead process generates auxiliary lemmas that prune the search space. The method is instantiated in two representative verifiers: Marabou and α,β-CROWN.
AI.result: Lookahead branching yields consistent speedups in verification time on standard benchmarks. The number of solved instances increases by up to 57% compared to baseline branching strategies. Benefits are demonstrated across both Marabou and α,β-CROWN, showing generality of the approach.
AI.conclusion: Lookahead branching is a general, effective strategy for neural network verification that subsumes prior heuristics, improves branching quality, generates useful lemmas, and delivers substantial practical gains. The approach is broadly applicable across different branch-and-bound verifiers.

title: OntoExtend: A Framework for Requirement-driven and Scalable Ontology Extension with LLMs
comment: Accepted in research track of Semantics 2026: https://2026-eu.semantics.cc/page/accepted_research
summary: Ontology extension refers to the process of enriching an existing ontology in response to emerging requirements, making it more complete. This task is a resource-intensive and error-prone process. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising performance on generating ontologies from scratch, but current approaches rarely tie ontology extension explicitly to requirements or reusable core models, and offer limited, systematic evaluation of LLM outputs. This paper introduces OntoExtend, a requirements-driven framework for ontology extension with LLMs. It uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over relevant input ontologies and requirements in the form of competency questions to propose grounded extensions. We evaluate OntoExtend on 39 CQs from two use cases: a public EU-project ontology, Onto-DESIDE, and an industrial ontology from Bosch. The generated fragments show few structural issues, satisfy all functional evaluation tests, and are rated by ontology engineers as requiring minor to moderate revision before integration. These results suggest that OntoExtend is useful as a drafting assistant for requirement-driven ontology extension in real world scenarios, while remaining sensitive to CQ specificity and modelling profile.

AI.tldr: OntoExtend is a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses LLMs to extend ontologies in response to competency questions (CQs). Evaluated on 39 CQs from two real-world use cases, it produces structurally sound fragments that pass functional tests and require only minor to moderate revision, demonstrating utility as a drafting assistant for requirement-driven ontology extension.
AI.motivation: Ontology extension is resource-intensive and error-prone. While LLMs show promise for generating ontologies from scratch, existing approaches rarely tie extension explicitly to requirements or reusable core models, and systematic evaluation of LLM outputs is limited. There is a need for a grounded, requirements-driven framework that leverages LLMs for ontology extension with rigorous evaluation.
AI.method: OntoExtend employs retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over relevant input ontologies and competency questions (CQs). The framework retrieves pertinent ontology fragments and uses CQs as structured requirements to guide LLM-based extension proposals. The approach is evaluated on 39 CQs from two use cases: the public Onto-DESIDE EU-project ontology and an industrial Bosch ontology.
AI.result: Generated ontology fragments exhibit few structural issues, satisfy all functional evaluation tests, and are rated by ontology engineers as requiring minor to moderate revision before integration. Performance remains sensitive to CQ specificity and modelling profile.
AI.conclusion: OntoExtend serves as an effective drafting assistant for requirement-driven ontology extension in real-world scenarios. The framework bridges the gap between LLM capabilities and practical ontology engineering needs, though sensitivity to CQ specificity and modelling style must be accounted for in deployment.

title: Rationalizing Boltzmann Rationality: An Axiomatic Characterization of Entropy-Regularized Policies
summary: The softmax policy $π(a \mid s) \propto \exp(βQ(s,a))$ is the default model of stochastic choice in reinforcement learning (RL). Various justifications based on robustness, exploration, and optimization have been offered in the RL literature, but none uniquely derives the softmax form from first principles. This leaves a basic tension unresolved: the entropy bonus in the soft Bellman equation violates the Independence axiom that underwrites the Markov decision process (MDP) reward structure. We dissolve this tension by distinguishing two kinds of randomness: chance and choice. By restricting von Neumann-Morgenstern (VNM) Independence to environmental lotteries over base prospects, we show that imposing independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) and monotonicity on the policy and value functions at choice nodes uniquely determines the Boltzmann policy, the entropy-regularized representation, and the soft Bellman equation. The choice between the soft and hard Bellman equations thus reduces to a design decision: whether the agent values its own ability to choose. We develop RL-specific consequences, including return monotonicity and convergence under generalized discounting, and synthesize the independent lines from economics and information theory that arrive at the same structure, offering a normative assessment of when IIA is appropriate for agent design.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the softmax policy and entropy-regularized Bellman equation from first principles by distinguishing environmental chance from agent choice, showing that imposing IIA and monotonicity at choice nodes uniquely yields the Boltzmann policy. The choice between soft and hard Bellman equations reduces to whether the agent values its own capacity to choose.
AI.motivation: The softmax policy is widely used in RL but lacks a unique first-principles derivation. A fundamental tension exists: the entropy bonus in the soft Bellman equation violates the Independence axiom foundational to MDP reward structure. The authors aim to resolve this tension by providing an axiomatic foundation for the softmax policy.
AI.method: The authors distinguish two sources of randomness — environmental chance (lotteries over base prospects) and agent choice — restricting VNM Independence only to environmental lotteries. They then impose IIA (independence of irrelevant alternatives) and monotonicity on the policy and value functions specifically at choice nodes, and prove this uniquely characterizes the Boltzmann policy, entropy-regularized value representation, and soft Bellman equation.
AI.result: The axiomatic derivation uniquely yields the softmax policy and soft Bellman equation. This reframes the hard vs. soft Bellman choice as a design decision about whether the agent values its own ability to choose. Additional RL consequences include return monotonicity and convergence under generalized discounting. The paper also synthesizes parallel developments from economics and information theory.
AI.conclusion: The softmax policy can be derived axiomatically by carefully restricting where Independence applies. IIA's appropriateness for agent design is a normative question; it is suitable when we want agents that value their own choice capacity, leading to entropy-regularized RL.

title: SAGE: Subgoal-Conditioned Action Generation for Latent World Model Planning
summary: Latent world models have emerged as a powerful planning paradigm by learning action-conditioned predictive dynamics and using them as internal simulators to imagine and evaluate candidate action sequences. However, as the planning horizon grows, performance becomes increasingly constrained by proposal quality: a fixed candidate budget must search an exponentially larger action space, making it difficult to expose the world model to high-quality candidate futures for evaluation. In this paper, we introduce a prior-conditioned planner that replaces random proposal initialization with structured guidance. At each planning stage, a goal-conditioned generator predicts the next reachable latent subgoal for a specified duration, which is then used to condition the generation of candidate action sequences. To capture semantic information across temporal scales, we use subgoals of varying durations as priors, balancing fine-grained local control with higher-level long-horizon progress. Then the frozen world model evaluates and refines these subgoal-conditioned proposals before execution. Experiments on PushT and OGBench Cube show that coupling latent subgoal decomposition with prior-conditioned action generation substantially improves long-horizon planning while preserving strong short-horizon performance. To be specific, when the target offset is $150$, it raises PushT success from $12.7\%$ to $64.7\%$ and OGBench Cube success from $26.7\%$ to $67.3\%$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a prior-conditioned planner that uses goal-conditioned subgoal generators to guide latent world model planning, replacing random action proposal initialization. By decomposing long-horizon tasks with multi-scale subgoal priors, the method dramatically improves long-horizon planning performance on PushT (12.7%→64.7%) and OGBench Cube (26.7%→67.3%) while maintaining strong short-horizon results.
AI.motivation: Latent world models suffer from poor long-horizon planning because the action space grows exponentially with horizon depth, making it increasingly difficult for random proposal initialization to expose the world model to high-quality candidate futures within a fixed budget of evaluations.
AI.method: A prior-conditioned planner that replaces random proposal initialization with structured guidance. At each planning stage, a goal-conditioned generator predicts the next reachable latent subgoal for a specified duration. These subgoals — computed at multiple temporal scales (varying durations) — serve as priors to condition the generation of candidate action sequences. A frozen world model then evaluates and refines these subgoal-conditioned proposals before execution, balancing fine-grained local control with higher-level long-horizon progress.
AI.result: On PushT with target offset of 150, success rate improved from 12.7% to 64.7%. On OGBench Cube with target offset of 150, success rate improved from 26.7% to 67.3%. The method also preserves strong short-horizon performance.
AI.conclusion: Coupling latent subgoal decomposition with prior-conditioned action generation substantially improves long-horizon planning in latent world models without sacrificing short-horizon performance. The multi-scale subgoal approach effectively bridges the gap between local control and long-range planning.

title: TAPAS: Throughput-adaptive Perception for Autonomous Systems
comment: 15 Pages, 20 Figures, Accepted at ACM/IEEE International Conference on Codesign of Embedded Systems at Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK-CODES), 2026
summary: Autonomous systems rely on a perception module to navigate through dynamic environments. In real-world scenarios, the perception module's throughput requirements vary at runtime due to changes in scene complexity. However, existing perception strategies assume a fixed FPS and static model-to-cluster mapping, resulting in either over/under provision of throughput requirements or unnecessary energy consumption across diverse scenes. Addressing this challenge requires tightly coupled \textit{scene complexity awareness} to estimate an appropriate FPS target and \textit{dynamic model-to-cluster mapping} to deliver the required throughput at minimum energy. We propose a throughput-adaptive perception strategy for mobile/edge platforms, enabling intelligent runtime resource allocation based on varying FPS targets. We use Reinforcement Learning (RL) with RRM (Reward Reasoning Model) and a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) agent to orchestrate perception tasks across heterogeneous mobile/edge platforms. We evaluate TAPAS on Jetson Orin NX across KITTI and unseen nuScenes. On the \textit{KITTI} dataset's test sequences, TAPAS achieves 93-100% throughput met rate while saving energy by 76%. On the unseen \textit{nuScenes} dataset, TAPAS maintains 97% throughput met rate with 64% lower energy compared to \textit{SOTA} approaches, proving its robustness.

AI.tldr: TAPAS is a throughput-adaptive perception system that uses RL with a GRU agent and Reward Reasoning Model to dynamically adjust FPS targets and model-to-cluster mappings based on scene complexity, achieving up to 100% throughput met rate with 76% energy savings on edge platforms.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous perception systems use fixed FPS and static model-to-cluster mappings, leading to throughput over/under-provisioning and excessive energy consumption as scene complexity varies at runtime. There is a need for scene-complexity-aware, dynamically adaptive perception that balances throughput demands with energy efficiency.
AI.method: TAPAS employs Reinforcement Learning with a novel Reward Reasoning Model (RRM) and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) agent to orchestrate perception tasks across heterogeneous mobile/edge platforms. It jointly addresses (1) scene complexity awareness to estimate appropriate FPS targets and (2) dynamic model-to-cluster mapping to meet throughput requirements at minimal energy. Evaluation conducted on Jetson Orin NX using KITTI and nuScenes datasets.
AI.result: On KITTI test sequences: 93-100% throughput met rate with 76% energy savings. On unseen nuScenes dataset: 97% throughput met rate with 64% lower energy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: TAPAS demonstrates robust, energy-efficient throughput adaptation across both seen and unseen datasets, validating the effectiveness of RL-based dynamic resource allocation for perception systems on resource-constrained edge platforms.

title: Do Maps Still Matter for Machines: Revisiting the Role of Choropleth Maps in Foundation Model Spatial Understanding
summary: Spatial understanding is crucial for foundation models (FMs), and maps have long helped humans organize and reason about geographic information. This study examines whether choropleth maps remain useful for machine spatial understanding when models can directly process structured geodata. We introduce ChoroplethMap-Bench, a controlled benchmark containing 2,400 synthetic choropleth maps, corresponding GeoJSON data, and 12,000 questions across five cognitive dimensions: Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, and Delineate. We evaluate 22 open-source and proprietary models under three input conditions: Data Only, Map Only, and Data + Map. The results show that maps substantially improve spatial reasoning, especially when combined with symbolic data and for tasks requiring higher-level understanding of spatial patterns. We further analyze the effects of map type, color hue, and spatial structure, as well as prompting strategies, language, geographic context, decoding settings, classification methods, and response stability. Overall, the Data + Map condition achieves the strongest performance, demonstrating that maps remain valuable external representations for foundation model spatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: ChoroplethMap-Bench introduces a controlled benchmark of 2,400 synthetic choropleth maps to test whether maps still benefit foundation model spatial reasoning when structured geodata is available. Evaluating 22 models across three input conditions (Data Only, Map Only, Data+Map) on five cognitive dimensions, results show that combining maps with symbolic data yields the strongest spatial reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: With foundation models increasingly capable of processing structured geodata directly (e.g., GeoJSON), it is unclear whether traditional visual representations like choropleth maps still provide unique value for machine spatial understanding, or if they have become redundant.
AI.method: The authors construct ChoroplethMap-Bench: 2,400 synthetic choropleth maps paired with corresponding GeoJSON data and 12,000 questions spanning five cognitive dimensions (Identify, Spatial Recognition, Compare, Rank, Delineate). They evaluate 22 open-source and proprietary models under three conditions (Data Only, Map Only, Data+Map) and conduct extensive ablation analyses on map type, color hue, spatial structure, prompting strategies, language, geographic context, decoding settings, classification methods, and response stability.
AI.result: Maps substantially improve spatial reasoning, particularly for higher-level tasks involving spatial pattern understanding. The Data+Map condition consistently achieves the strongest performance. Map type, color hue, and spatial structure all significantly affect model performance, with nuanced interactions across cognitive dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Choropleth maps remain valuable external representations for foundation model spatial reasoning, complementing rather than being replaced by direct structured data access. The synergistic Data+Map condition offers the best performance, affirming the continued relevance of cartographic representations in the era of multimodal foundation models.

title: Rethinking the Suitability of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms Under Practical Transfer Constraints
summary: Transfer-oriented reinforcement learning requires evaluating algorithms along dimensions that go beyond standard sample efficiency. We focus on two dimensions: practical efficiency, which asks whether conclusions about algorithm suitability change under wall-clock rather than interaction-based budgets, and robustness under dynamics mismatch, which asks how different learning paradigms respond to variability in the training distribution induced by domain randomization. We provide two insights to reinforcement-learning practitioners. First, comparing the sample efficiency of different algorithms is often an insufficient criterion in transfer-oriented settings. The wall-clock time required to train a decent policy is an important consideration for practitioners, and we find that the sample-inefficient PPO algorithm can produce a performant policy faster than relatively more sample-efficient algorithms such as SAC and TD-MPC2, validating the common understanding of massively parallel training paradigms. Second, domain randomization can help different kinds of algorithms learn robust policies. In particular, although PPO, SAC, and TD-MPC2 represent different RL paradigms - on-policy, off-policy, and model-based learning and planning, respectively - we find that domain randomization affects all three algorithms in a similar way. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first controlled comparison of the effect of domain-randomization coverage on PPO, SAC, and TD-MPC2 under the same transfer protocol. Taken together, these two insights highlight the importance of evaluating RL algorithms not only by sample efficiency, but also by practical considerations such as training time and the algorithms' ability to produce usable policies.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that in transfer-oriented RL, sample efficiency is an insufficient evaluation criterion. It demonstrates that: (1) wall-clock training time can favor allegedly sample-inefficient algorithms like PPO over SAC and TD-MPC2 due to massive parallelism, and (2) domain randomization affects PPO, SAC, and TD-MPC2 similarly despite their paradigmatic differences, based on the first controlled comparison under a shared transfer protocol.
AI.motivation: Standard RL algorithm comparisons focus heavily on sample efficiency (interaction-based budgets), but transfer-oriented settings demand broader evaluation criteria. Practitioners care about wall-clock training time and robustness to dynamics mismatch caused by domain randomization. Existing literature lacks a controlled comparison of how different RL paradigms (on-policy, off-policy, model-based) respond to varying domain-randomization coverage under a unified transfer protocol.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled empirical comparison of three representative algorithms — PPO (on-policy), SAC (off-policy), and TD-MPC2 (model-based learning and planning) — evaluated along two dimensions: (1) practical efficiency, measured by wall-clock time to reach a performant policy rather than interaction steps; (2) robustness under dynamics mismatch, assessed by varying domain-randomization coverage and measuring policy transfer performance under a consistent protocol.
AI.result: First, PPO achieves a performant policy faster in wall-clock time than the more sample-efficient SAC and TD-MPC2, confirming that massively parallel training can outweigh sample inefficiency. Second, domain randomization improves robustness for all three algorithms in a similar manner, despite their fundamental paradigmatic differences — on-policy, off-policy, and model-based.
AI.conclusion: RL algorithm evaluation in transfer-oriented settings must expand beyond sample efficiency to include practical metrics like wall-clock training time and robustness to dynamics mismatch. The findings validate the practical value of parallelizable on-policy methods and reveal that domain randomization benefits diverse algorithmic paradigms comparably, offering actionable guidance for practitioners.

title: PAMD: Structured Adaptive Distances for Bisimulation Representations in Visual Reinforcement Learning
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, plus appendix. Accepted to the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary:
Many visual reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms learn representations by matching latent distances to a behavioral distance induced by reward and transition similarity. In practice, the choice of the latent distance can strongly affect performance: using a fixed, pre-specified global norms (e.g., $\ell_p$ norms or other hand-designed metrics) may be overly restrictive to capture the behavioral distance. In contrast, unconstrained pairwise distances may admit degenerate solutions that drive the metric loss down without improving the representation. To address this gap, we introduce **PAMD: Pairwise Adaptive Mahalanobis Distance**, which parameterizes a positive-definite, pair-conditioned metric for measuring latent state similarity.
  PAMD is a simple plug-in for existing bisimulation-based methods, offering a more expressive yet structured alternative to fixed, pre-specified latent distances. We empirically validate our method on visual MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, where final performance of several recent bisimulation-based RL algorithms is substantially improved when equipped with the distance we propose.

AI.tldr: Introduces PAMD, a pair-conditioned Mahalanobis distance metric for visual RL that adaptively parameterizes latent state similarity, serving as a plug-in improvement for existing bisimulation-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing visual RL algorithms use either fixed global norms (overly restrictive) or unconstrained pairwise distances (prone to degenerate solutions) to match latent distances to behavioral distances. Neither approach adequately captures the behavioral distance induced by reward and transition similarity.
AI.method: PAMD parameterizes a positive-definite, pair-conditioned metric for measuring latent state similarity. It serves as a plug-in component for existing bisimulation-based RL methods, offering a structured yet expressive alternative to pre-specified latent distances.
AI.result: Empirical validation on visual MuJoCo continuous-control tasks shows that several recent bisimulation-based RL algorithms achieve substantially improved final performance when equipped with PAMD.
AI.conclusion: PAMD provides an effective, structured distance metric that bridges the gap between overly rigid global norms and unconstrained pairwise distances, yielding consistent performance gains across multiple bisimulation-based visual RL methods.

title: When Drift Detectors cry Wolf: False Alarm Rates in continuous ML Monitoring
summary: Drift detection is a core component of production machine learning monitoring systems, where detectors are used to compare incoming data with a reference distribution and trigger alerts when changes occur. However, these detectors are often evaluated in research settings that emphasize detection accuracy under synthetic shifts, while overlooking false alarms under continuous monitoring. In production environments, models are monitored repeatedly over time and across many features, and even small false positive rates can accumulate into frequent alerts, leading to alarm fatigue. We empirically analyze false positive behavior across five commonly used drift detectors: PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, and adversarial validation. Consistent with existing literature, PSI exhibits strong sensitivity to batch size, producing frequent false alarms at small sample sizes; however, we further observe that its behavior stabilizes and improves substantially once batch sizes exceed approximately 200 samples. In contrast, KS, MMD, and LSDD display persistent fluctuations across batch sizes, while remaining comparatively more reliable than PSI in low-data regimes. Applying a Bonferroni correction reduces false positive rates, but often at the cost of reduced true positive sensitivity, reinforcing the well-known stability - sensitivity trade-off in drift detection. This work provides a systematic comparison of false positive behavior across multiple drift detectors under continuous monitoring conditions. We identify tradeoffs across detector families and provide practical guidelines for selecting and calibrating drift detectors in production ML systems.

AI.tldr: Under continuous monitoring in production ML, even low false positive rates from drift detectors accumulate into alarm fatigue. The paper empirically evaluates five detectors (PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, adversarial validation), finding PSI stabilizes above ~200 samples per batch, while KS, MMD, and LSDD are more reliable in low-data regimes. Bonferroni correction reduces false positives but harms sensitivity, highlighting a stability-sensitivity trade-off. Practical guidelines for detector selection and calibration are provided.
AI.motivation: Drift detectors are typically evaluated on detection accuracy under synthetic shifts in research settings, ignoring false alarm behavior under continuous, repeated monitoring across many features. In production, even small false positive rates compound into frequent alerts, causing alarm fatigue. This gap motivates a systematic empirical comparison of false positive behavior across commonly used drift detectors.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze false positive behavior of five drift detectors — PSI (Population Stability Index), KS (Kolmogorov-Smirnov), MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy), LSDD (Least-Squares Density Difference), and adversarial validation — under continuous monitoring conditions. They evaluate the effect of batch size on false positive rates, and apply a Bonferroni correction to assess the stability-sensitivity trade-off.
AI.result: PSI exhibits strong sensitivity to batch size with frequent false alarms at small sample sizes, but stabilizes substantially above ~200 samples. KS, MMD, and LSDD show persistent fluctuations across batch sizes but are comparatively more reliable than PSI in low-data regimes. Bonferroni correction reduces false positive rates at the cost of reduced true positive sensitivity, confirming the stability-sensitivity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Practical guidelines are offered for selecting and calibrating drift detectors in production ML systems: PSI is viable only with sufficient batch sizes (>~200); KS, MMD, and LSDD are preferable in low-data settings; and the stability-sensitivity trade-off must be carefully managed, particularly when applying multiplicity corrections like Bonferroni.

title: Rethinking Heterogeneous LLM Merging: A Weighted Model Averaging Perspective
summary: Can large language models with substantially different parameter spaces be merged by direct weighted averaging, without training or semantic alignment? Existing heterogeneous fusion methods typically introduce distillation, adapters, learned latent spaces, routing, or feature alignment, leaving open whether a simpler recipe can work for genuinely different billion-parameter checkpoints. We revisit this counterintuitive question through training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation. In union-style merging, we expand the smaller model into the larger parameter space; in intersection-style merging, we truncate the larger model into the smaller parameter space. Across Qwen-family model pairs and benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, language understanding, commonsense reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following, deterministic expansion largely preserves the source model function, and small-ratio interpolation can improve over strong source checkpoints by transferring complementary capabilities. However, near-balanced interpolation often collapses, and task-level results reveal a seesaw effect in which gains on some capabilities coexist with regressions on others. These results show that simple parameter averaging, when paired with lightweight dimensional adaptation and carefully controlled ratios, is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging, suggesting that the limits of direct weighted fusion may also bound what more complex heterogeneous merging methods can achieve at scale.

AI.tldr: Simple weighted averaging across heterogeneous LLMs with different parameter spaces works surprisingly well when combined with training-free dimensional adaptation (expansion or truncation) and ratio-controlled interpolation, though near-balanced merging often collapses and a task-level seesaw effect emerges.
AI.motivation: Existing heterogeneous LLM fusion methods rely on complex techniques like distillation, adapters, learned latent spaces, routing, or feature alignment. The authors investigate whether a simpler, training-free recipe — direct weighted averaging — can be effective for merging billion-parameter checkpoints with substantially different architectures, without requiring semantic alignment.
AI.method: The authors propose two training-free dimensional adaptation strategies: (1) union-style merging, where the smaller model is expanded into the larger parameter space, and (2) intersection-style merging, where the larger model is truncated into the smaller parameter space. These are paired with ratio-controlled interpolation to merge the adapted checkpoints. Experiments are conducted across Qwen-family model pairs on benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, language understanding, commonsense reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following.
AI.result: Deterministic expansion largely preserves the source model's function. Small-ratio interpolation can outperform strong source checkpoints by transferring complementary capabilities. However, near-balanced interpolation frequently leads to performance collapse. A seesaw effect is observed at the task level, where gains on some capabilities coexist with regressions on others.
AI.conclusion: Simple parameter averaging with lightweight dimensional adaptation and careful ratio control is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging. The limits of direct weighted fusion may also bound what more complex heterogeneous merging methods can achieve at scale.
